10873-at-sunwich-port-part-3-contents-ch:
W. W. Jacobs's At Sunwich Port continues in this third part, covering chapters eleven through fifteen, with drawings by Will Owen. Jack Nugent's first idea on receiving his father's letter, asking him to meet at Samson Wilks's, is to send as impolite a refusal as his pen can arrange. The Kybird family talks him round, with Mr. Kybird urging him to go, lest his father plan something for him.

Mrs. Kybird warns Jack not to let his father break off his match with Amelia, while Jack insists his father may come to him instead. Jacobs's comedy of fathers, sons, and sweethearts plays out in seaside talk. Readers get the novel's middle stretch, where a letter stirs old quarrels.
15325-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
This number of The Great Round World, a weekly paper for boys and girls, announces a change of ownership. The publisher has bought the subscription list of Current Events and offers this paper in its place. Subscribers get one number for each Current Events number still due, with a special offer to run to December 31, 1897, for a dollar twenty-five.

Regular price stays at two dollars fifty a year. News, stories, and features for young readers fill the issue. The number shows a children's paper growing by absorbing a rival, a small event in publishing history, told in a friendly, direct voice.
16761-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-:
This slice of Holinshed's Chronicles covers Henry II, second son of Geoffrey Plantagenet, from his landing in England in December 1154. Born in France to Maud the Empress, daughter of Henry I, he took the crown after King Stephen died. The text, in old spelling, gives the year by world age, by Christ's birth, and by reigns of emperor, pope, and kings.

Henry first gathers his scattered force, then wins homage at Winchester and sets out to rule. The slice shows the start of the Plantagenet age in Tudor prose, with side notes naming its sources. Readers who push through the old spelling get a reign opening in full chronicle style: dates, descents, and deeds in one long march.
17316-letters-of-a-soldier-1914-1915:
Letters of a Soldier, translated by V. M. and published in London in 1917, gathers a French soldier's letters from August 1914 to April 1915. An introduction by A. Clutton-Brock and a preface by Andre Chevrillon frame the set. The first letter, to his mother on August 6, 1914, tells of depot work, want of sleep, and a clerk's life at war, far from the front.

Later letters move from calm Marne walks and strict censorship to the heat of fighting and the thoughts of a man who falls. The voice is plain, tender, and honest, without heroics. Readers of Great War letters will find a moving, intimate record of a soldier's year, from depot bench to battlefield.
17654-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
A September 1920 number of Punch, volume 159, dated September 15, opens its Charivaria with a joke on Prohibition meetings in Scotland. An official says fifty thousand people attended, and Punch doubts there are so many aliens in Scotland. At an Oldbury wedding, a brick thrown at the bridegroom draws the remark that there is no excuse for such a thing with confetti so cheap.

A third joke notes a Pacific island so small that the House of Commons could not be planted on it. Cartoons, verses, and comic pieces follow in Punch's familiar mix. Readers get a topical snapshot of Britain in the autumn of 1920. The issue works as light reading and as evidence of its moment.
18910-diary-of-a-nursing-sister-on-the-w:
An anonymous nursing sister kept this diary on the Western Front from August 1914 into 1915, published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London in 1915. It opens waiting for orders, with a voyage out to Havre, then St Nazaire, and service on the hospital ship Asturias. The epigraph speaks of a body broken but a laughing heart at peace.

Later entries follow station duty at Le Mans, trains carrying wounded from the Aisne, and the long wait for orders that marked early war nursing. The diary records work, weariness, and the sight of wounded men with restraint. Readers get a woman's firsthand account of the war's first months, immediate and unadorned, from the wards and trains behind the lines.
20306-europe-after-8-15:
Europe After 8:15, from 1914, is a bright travel book overtaken by world war. Innsbruck shows checkerboard parks and Christmas garden villas to the writer. An Austrian battalion drills in the Exerzierplatz below his view. It looks like an army of grey ants, barely visible from above.

Somewhere left, past the Hungerberg, the night train labors toward Venice. Such gay travel writing met the guns of August that same year. The title plays on trains and timetables across a continent at peace. Readers get a poignant tour of Europe on the edge of the abyss.
2115-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle opens the Second Silesian War in Book Fifteen, from August 1744 to December 1745, with Frederick choosing to strike first rather than wait. Prussia, Carlyle notes, could unsheathe its sword in three weeks, where other countries needed months. Frederick struck in August 1744, hoping speed would win before his foes could join.

French vigour, Austrian armies, and Frederick's deft hand shape a campaign that became a key episode in the general European war. The volume shows the king as a soldier who trusted speed, preparation, and nerve. Prussia's swift mobilisation, praised by soldiers, gave a small state weight beyond its size.
22300-the-menorah-journal-volume-1-1915:
Volume one of The Menorah Journal came out in 1915. The journal served the Menorah movement and its growing Menorah Societies across the country. Its opening pages say the journal must be far more than an official organ for those societies.

Inside, the volume works to carry forward the aims and hopes of the movement. That role grew more pressing as the societies multiplied in number and influence. Readers get a record of an organized Jewish cultural effort taking shape in print. It speaks to its members and to a wider public at the same time.
24281-the-creed-of-the-old-south-1865-19:
Basil L. Gildersleeve wrote this essay on the creed of the Old South, published by the Johns Hopkins Press at Baltimore in 1915, with portraits of the author in 1865 and in 1915. The piece was first prepared in 1891 at the instance of Horace Scudder, editor of the Atlantic Monthly, who planned a series by men thought lifted above vulgar passion and prejudice.

Those gentlemen were to explain what moved them to play an active part in so rude a business as war. The series halted after three numbers, and the book Scudder fancied was never published. Gildersleeve began with a light heart and ended dipping his pen in something red and briny, not ink. Readers get a scholar-soldier's elegy for his generation.
24981-trapped-in-black-russia-letters-ju:
Ruth Pierce's letters from June to November 1915, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1918, record a journey into wartime Russia that was meant to last a week. Traveling with Marie and without Peter, she crosses from Romania by a train over a river, expecting to return to Bucharest together. Instead the war closes around her, and the letters home become a record of a country under strain, written with a blind faith that her words will somehow reach her parents.

The darkest passages concern Galician Jews deported to Siberia, who reached Tomsk before a change of government sent them back over the same route. Many more died on the return journey, in jails, camps, baggage cars, and by the roadsides, and survivors found their towns pillaged. They began again, digging and planting and taking up the routine of life. Pierce's letters keep the human scale of catastrophe in view.
30643-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume fifteen of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works was printed in London in 1912. Its Roman date is MDCCCCXII, and it follows the limited pattern of the set: two thousand sixty copies printed, two thousand for sale. An illustration shows Stevenson and Mrs. Strong, posed by a strolling photographer at a fair in Sydney in 1892.

Contents gather dramatic works by Stevenson and W. E. Henley, opening with Deacon Brodie, or the Double Life, then Beau Austin, Admiral Guinea, and Macaire. The volume presents Stevenson's stage writing in collected form, with Chatto and Windus, Cassell, Heinemann, and Longmans Green as publishers. It suits readers tracing Stevenson's work beyond his famous novels.
33001-my-diary-in-serbia-april-1-1915-no:
Monica M. Stanley's My Diary in Serbia, first issued in February 1916, records seven months with the Stobart Field Hospital in Serbia, from April 1 to November 1, 1915. Stanley, attached to the hospital unit led by Mrs. St. Clair Stobart with doctors, nurses, and orderlies, writes day by day of work under wartime strain. Photographs illustrate the volume, and the book is dedicated to her aunt Elizabeth Stanley.

The diary's value lies in its closeness to events, as a woman volunteer watches a country under invasion and a hospital trying to keep pace with casualties, shortages, and retreat. Stanley does not write grand strategy; she writes wards, roads, and the people she nursed beside. For readers of First World War history and women's war work, it is a vivid, immediate account from a field hospital at the sharp end.
33006-the-home-university-library-catalo:
The Home University Library catalogue for 1914-15 presents a comprehensive series of new and specially written books. It was originally printed inside Maurice Baring's Outline of Russian Literature, and it was edited by Gilbert Murray, Herbert Fisher, J. Arthur Thomson, and William T. Brewster. Volumes cost one shilling net, or two shillings and sixpence in cloth, and ran to 256 pages each, covering history, geography, science, and letters in short, expert form.

Sample entries show the series' range: Hilaire Belloc on the French Revolution, praised for its militant color. G. H. Perris writes on war and peace, praised by James Bryce for compressing many facts and views into a small volume. As a catalogue, the book is a map of popular education before the First World War, showing what a general reader could buy for a shilling. For historians of publishing, it is a compact record of a famous series.
34152-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Alexander Leighton revised this fifteenth volume of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, published in London and Newcastle in 1885 by Walter Scott, with a glossary. Tales run from the Recollections of a Village Patriarch by John Mackay Wilson and the Old Chronicler's Tales by Leighton to the death of James the First. The Curate of Govan follows.

Gleanings of the Covenant, the story of Tom Bertram, and the Cottar's Daughter open the rest. The Surgeon's Tales, the Warning, Grizel Cochrane, Squire Ben, the Battle of Dryffe Sands, and the Clerical Murderer complete the set. The opening tale praises love of one's birthplace, from Icelander snows to Moorish heat. The volume offers Border history and fancy together.
3565-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This fifteenth volume of Bourrienne's memoirs continues the story of 1815, after the first volume on that year. Bourrienne follows the aftermath of Waterloo: the emperor's second abdication, the return of the Bourbons, and the scattering of Napoleon's friends and officials. Exile, not battle, dominates this volume, as the emperor's world shrinks to a household and a ship.

The tone here is darker than in the volumes of victory. Men who had served an empire must now save themselves, their families, and their papers. Bourrienne writes with the bitterness of a witness who has seen power change hands more than once. Readers who have followed the series to its end will find a somber close to a long career.
3595-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This fifteenth volume of Montaigne's Essays holds a single long essay from Book Three: Upon Some Verses of Virgil. Montaigne begins by noting that profitable thoughts are heavy and cumbersome, and that vice, death, poverty, and disease are grave subjects. A man should train his soul, he argues, to sustain evils and to live well, rather than merely to think well.

The essay then turns, by way of Virgil's lines, to love, aging, and the body, subjects Montaigne treats with unusual frankness. He writes about desire in old age, about marriage, and about the gap between books and lived feeling. The volume suits readers who want Montaigne at his most personal, reflecting on a life already more than half spent.
5289-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
The fifteenth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels pairs The Mandrake with The Rhemese, opening in Florence with a greater blockhead than ever appeared below. The Florentine has wed a prudent, beautiful young wife, brisk and good-humoured, whom everyone praises.

A mandrake, a plant of magic and mischief, drives the comedy that follows, as husbands, wives, and lovers scheme around it. Readers get two tales of Florentine folly and desire, told in La Fontaine's polished verse. A foolish husband proves the best foil for a clever wife in these tales.
5917-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Inn life dominates chapters forty-two through forty-six in this Don Quixote installment. Chapter forty-two treats what further took place at the inn, after the captive holds his peace and Don Fernando praises the manner of his remarkable adventure. Chapter forty-three relates the pleasant story of the muleteer, chapter forty-four continues the inn's unheard-of adventures, and chapter forty-five settles the doubtful question of Mambrino's helmet and the pack saddle.

Chapter forty-six ends the notable adventure of the officers of the Holy Brotherhood at the inn. Readers get Cervantes's inn as a small world, where captives, lovers, officers, and knights argue over truth and property. The part suits readers deep in volume one, since its helmet debate and inn quarrels distill the novel's comedy of seeing versus believing.
7102-adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chap:
This part of Huckleberry Finn opens at chapter eleven, with Huck in disguise as Sarah Williams calling on a woman in a riverside town. She bids him take a chair and quizzes him with sharp little eyes, while Huck claims to live in Hookerville seven miles below, having walked all the way tired out. His mother lies sick and out of money, he says, and he comes to tell his uncle Abner Moore at the upper end of town.

The woman, only two weeks in the place, does not know Abner, and urges Huck to stay the night and take off his bonnet. Huck, wary and quick, rests a while and presses on. Chapters eleven to fifteen close with Huck slipping away from a sharp eyed townswoman.
7601-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part fifteen travels the dreary, interminable high north road, stage after stage, while the narrator tells his companion, more plainly than before, his causes for apprehension. The Captain at first listens eagerly, then checks him on the sudden. The apprehensions turn on Vivian, whose character the narrator has come to suspect, despite the brilliant qualities that first attracted him.

The chapter asks every reader who has been young a question. Has he not formed acquaintance with someone engaging and brilliant? In that friend he still kept his dislike of defects and his quick sense of right, even while erring himself. That moral puzzle, carried along a bleak road, is the part's business. Lytton makes a coach journey into an inquiry into friendship and judgment.
9506-georgian-poetry-1913-15:
Georgian Poetry 1913-1915, the second book in its series, surveys new English verse from three years. Its preface notes that two of its youngest poets had died: Rupert Brooke, killed in war service in April 1915, and James Elroy Flecker, dead after long illness. Poets inside include Gordon Bottomley, John Drinkwater, John Masefield, and Francis Ledwidge. The book aims to show the newer generation at work.

Poems span country life, town scenes, war, love, and craft, in plain, musical forms. Some poets from the first volume drop out, while new names join the ranks. A reader gets a wartime snapshot of English verse, with Brooke and Flecker mourned in print, and a sense of a poetic age cut short by war.
987-the-scientific-monthly-october-to-de:
This volume joins Popular Science Monthly, volume 86, July to September 1915, with the first volume of The Scientific Monthly, October to December 1915. The new journal carried the older magazine's mission into a more formal setting. The Scientific Monthly, successor to Popular Science Monthly, served the AAAS.

Articles cover science, industry, and public life at the start of the First World War, in the plain style of popular science. The volume gives a snapshot of what educated readers learned about science a century ago. Its first volume, in late 1915, carried science news as America edged toward war.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-:
In chapters 11 to 15 of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Huck dresses as a girl, Sarah Williams, to go ashore for news. a sharp-eyed woman sees through him by the way he throws at a rat and threads a needle. She tells him the town blames Jim for Huck's supposed murder, and that men are coming to search Jackson's Island that very night.

Huck warns Jim in time, and the two push off on the raft into the book's great river journey. Fog separates them near Cairo, a steamboat smashes the raft, and a trick Huck plays in the fog leaves a hurt he must humble himself to mend. A wrecked steamboat, the Walter Scott, gives them a skiff and a brush with robbers.
arthashastra-shamasastry-1915:
R. Shamasastry published the first English translation of Kautilya's Arthashastra in 1915. Kautilya was chief minister to Chandragupta Maurya, founder of an Indian empire. His treatise on statecraft dates to around the fourth century BCE.

The Arthashastra is a cold-eyed manual of rule in fifteen books. Taxes, spies, diplomacy, war, and law enforcement all receive exact treatment. Kautilya advises kings on testing ministers and trapping enemies without sentiment. Shamasastry had discovered the lost Sanskrit text only years before translating it. His version first showed the work to the modern world. Readers often compare Kautilya to Machiavelli, who wrote eighteen centuries later.
arxiv-2509-00015:
Italo Epicoco leads a team with sixteen co-authors who present MedFormer in 2025, a data-driven model that forecasts the Mediterranean Sea. Sea forecasts support shipping, fishing, and coast care. Data-led models have lately beaten classic numeric tools for air forecasts, but seas move more slowly and have complex edges, which makes the shift harder.

MedFormer uses a U-Net build with 3D attention and works at fine grid scale. It trains on twenty years of daily sea records, then is fine-tuned on sharp live analyses. Nine-day forecasts roll forward step by step, fed by past sea states and air forces. The design aims to give fast, sharp sea outlooks for a busy, enclosed basin.
arxiv-2509-00115:
Manish Shukla, working alone, sets out adaptive monitoring for agentic AI systems in real-world use in 2025. Such systems join language models with tools and self-guided planning, and they are moving into high-stakes fields. A prior paper gave a five-axis frame and early gauges such as goal drift, but no working method or proof from data.

Shukla reviews eighty-four papers and finds that skill gauges dominate, while human and cost axes are rare. He then formalizes a monitoring algorithm that scales mixed gauges to one range, sets moving thresholds per axis, and flags joint anomalies. The sequel turns a frame into a testable tool for live oversight. Live checks matter as agents gain real power.
arxiv-2509-00215:
Joseph Amigo, Rooholla Khorrambakht, Elliot Chane-Sane, Nicolas Mansard, and Ludovic Righetti propose a model-based reinforcement learning method in 2025 that splits rollout from gradient computation. Gradient-based learning can beat trial-only methods, but simulator gradients are often costly or unavailable. Learned dynamics models can supply gradients, yet errors compound over training rollouts and can harm the policy.

Their method unrolls trajectories in the true simulator, then computes gradients by backpropagation through a learned differentiable model of that simulator. The split keeps rollouts exact while gradients stay cheap and consistent. First-order policy tuning thus works even when the simulator gives no gradients. The hybrid design suits robot control, where accurate sims exist but derivatives do not.
arxiv-2509-00315:
Qi Liu, Hadi Mehrabpour, and Bing-Nan Lu study how pair correlations inside oxygen nuclei shape relativistic oxygen-on-oxygen collisions in 2025. Nucleons, the protons and neutrons in a nucleus, are not placed at random: pair distances and angles carry correlations. Those patterns can imprint on the initial geometry of a high-energy collision.

Their Acceptance-Rejection Method builds nuclear ensembles with one chosen correlation at a time, while the overall radial density stays fixed. Pair-distance and pair-angle ensembles are compared with configurations from variational Monte Carlo and lattice effective theory. Radial correlations largely set the bulk scale of geometric fluctuations. Angular correlations add the extra detail needed to match eccentricity patterns.
arxiv-2509-00715:
A A Saharian and G V Mirzoyan examine vacuum currents on a curved tube. The tube has the shape of an elliptic pseudosphere. That surface has constant negative curvature throughout. They study how topology, curvature, and magnetic flux shape the vacuum current. The current is that of a charged scalar field in empty space.

The work uses two space dimensions plus one time dimension. The background geometry can be solved exactly. The pair separates the topology part in the Hadamard function. They give two equal forms for the current along the compact direction. The current repeats as magnetic flux grows, with the flux quantum as its period. Flat limits recover a known result for a conical space. Conformal links then yield currents for de Sitter space-time.
arxiv-2509-00815:
Xueqing Wan leads a team of eight authors on controlling topological magnons with electric fields. Magnons are quantized spin waves in a magnet. Topological ones carry special boundary modes. They promise lossless processing of information. But magnons carry no charge, so electric control is hard. Their high frequency adds to the challenge.

The team proposes a strategy for bilayer ferromagnetic insulators. The two layers are coupled strongly through their spins. A vertical electric field unbalances the layers' potentials. That shift modifies the exchange between spins within each layer. The modulation competes with an intrinsic interaction in the bilayer. This contest allows precise tuning of band topology. It also tunes the nonreciprocal dynamics of the magnons. Coupling with magnetic fields is strong as well.
arxiv-2509-00915:
Maximilian M Richter, with two co-authors, develops a local method to extract reconnection X-lines. Magnetic reconnection breaks and rejoins magnetic field lines. It releases magnetic energy and accelerates charged particles. Finding fast reconnection regions is key to understanding the process. In three dimensions and turbulence, that remains a challenge.

The team applies bifurcation lines from fluid visualization to magnetic fields. They show such lines can be identified with reconnection X-lines. For setups with guide fields, they introduce quasi X-lines. Using the spatial layout of X-lines, they estimate the reconnection rate locally. The rate distribution peaks near a normalized value stated in the record. A shear-based tool also highlights current sheets. The methods validate across kinetic and fluid plasma simulations.
arxiv-2509-01015:
Dragan Stankov, writing alone, approximates the number of nonunimodular zeros of a self-reciprocal polynomial, a polynomial whose coefficients read the same forward and backward. He introduces the ratio of roots not equal to one in modulus, meaning not on the unit circle, to the polynomial's degree.

For some sequences of reciprocal polynomials, Stankov shows this ratio has a limit as degree tends to infinity, each sequence defined through a two-variable polynomial. He presents several methods for approximating the limit ratio, some originally developed, building on a previous paper that calculated exact values for many cases with small Mahler measure. Comparisons using known exact values assess each method's error and duration, and the two natural sequences usually give different limit ratios.
arxiv-2509-01215:
Turning documents into clean digital text is hard when pages hold tables, formulas, and many columns. Yuan Liu, with ten co-authors, notes that hand labeling is costly, while labels from existing models can be too flawed to train strong students. Their framework, POINTS-Reader, skips distillation, the usual step of copying a teacher model's output.

First, the team generates large, varied synthetic documents, training a model to extract key elements in one unified format. Next, a self-improvement stage adapts that model to real documents. Liu and the co-authors argue this two-stage path builds higher quality data and models than teacher copying allows. The goal is document conversion that holds up across the messy layouts found in real use.
arxiv-2509-01415:
Estimating calories from a photo of food can aid diet tracking, but most vision systems were trained on Western dishes and ignore portion size. Aparup Dhar, Antu Das, Pritom Barua, and MD Tamim Hossain build a method tuned to Bangladeshi street food, which is widely eaten and culturally central. Their data set holds three thousand eight hundred eighty-five photos across six classes, from singara to peaju, plus a coin as a size reference.

Five detection and segmentation models were compared for finding and outlining the food. A Bangladeshi five taka coin in each photo set the scale, so measured sizes became real dimensions. Geometric features then fed regression models, including random forest and boosting methods, to predict calories. One detector, YOLO11n, led the comparison. The work aims at dietary tools that fit local food, not just imported menus.
arxiv-2509-01515:
Some quantum gates change a system's energy. Doing that with a finite battery has hidden costs, since the battery itself must conserve energy. Riccardo Castellano, with four co-authors, studies such gates. The gate runs through an interaction with an external battery that preserves energy. They ask what resource the battery must supply for the gate to work at a set precision.

The team proves the battery must hold entropic coherence. That is a form of quantum order, measured by a relative entropy. They derive a lower bound on how much must be present. It follows that any finite battery forces some minimal error in the gate. Under assumptions about the battery's energy levels, more bounds follow. These cover the energy and quantum Fisher information required. The bounds can beat universal limits known before.
arxiv-2509-01815:
Zhu Zhang leads four co-authors in a light based method to watch chemical reactions inside tiny holes. Cyclic voltammetry, the standard electrochemistry tool, sweeps voltage and reads current but needs bulk electrodes. Their optical version pairs a microscope with electrodes pierced by nanoholes, holes a few atoms wide in scale terms. It senses reactions in volumes as small as an attoliter, far below a drop.

The setup blends reflected light, electric layer tuning, voltage sweeps, and lock-in detection to track ions. Tests follow charging and a model reaction inside the holes. A physics model of ion flow and reaction rates matches the optical signals well. The method opens label free study of reactions in tight spaces, with uses in crystal growth.
arxiv-2509-01915:
Robert D Wilson leads five co-authors on how a narrowed aortic valve changes pulse wave shapes. Aortic valve stenosis, the narrowing, often hides without symptoms and delays care. Pulse waves are pressure ripples that travel through arteries with each heartbeat. The team builds a virtual cohort of more than sixteen thousand subjects aged fifty to seventy-five.

A full blood flow model with a four chamber heart simulates each subject. Valve narrowing is dialed by shrinking the valve opening in the model. Even mild narrowing below clinical concern leaves distinct marks on the pulse shape. Those marks hint that home devices reading peripheral pulses could flag the disease early. Early flags could speed treatment for a quiet but risky condition.
arxiv-2509-02115:
J Cepila, M Matas, and M Vaculciak use the Balitsky-Kovchegov equation to probe how nuclei are built. The equation tracks how gluon counts grow as crash energy climbs in protons and nuclei. Gluons are the bits that glue quarks in place. A fresh solve that keeps full space depth lets the team move from protons to full nuclei.

The team gives rates for deep probes and for spray of vector mesons off nuclei. A straight line form of the equation marks a strong channel to hunt for gluon crowding. A four face model of the oxygen nucleus tests drift from the smooth Woods-Saxon form. The finds also serve live meson work at the Large Hadron Collider. New colliders will test the crowding claims head on.
arxiv-2509-02615:
Mariia Drozdova and five co-authors wrote a 2025 astronomy AI paper testing whether general vision-language models can classify radio galaxy shapes without astronomy training. The MiraBest dataset, with its two fan-shaped galaxy classes, supplies the test images.

Prompt styles varied across text descriptions, schematic diagrams, and visual examples placed inside the prompt, a first for astronomy work of this kind. Prompt-only attempts already did well, suggesting useful built-in priors. But outputs swung sharply with layout, ordering, or decoding settings, even when meaning stayed fixed. Light fine-tuning of one model, with few trainable parameters, nearly matched specialist state-of-the-art accuracy. The authors warn that apparent reasoning may reflect prompt sensitivity, while still seeing promise in adapted general models.
arxiv-2509-02715:
Delin Chu and Volker Mehrmann wrote a 2025 applied mathematics paper on port-Hamiltonian descriptor systems, models that mix differential and algebraic equations while tracking energy flow. Such systems can be singular, so feedback control must first regularise them.

The authors study proportional and derivative output feedback, control laws built from measured outputs and their rates. They give necessary and sufficient conditions for feedbacks that make the closed loop regular, keep its index at most one, and preserve the port-Hamiltonian structure with chosen rank properties. All results rest on condensed forms, compact matrix shapes reachable through orthogonal transformations. Because those transformations are numerically safe, the conditions can be checked reliably in software, which matters for control design in engineering practice.
arxiv-2509-03115:
Christian Bauer and Claus Wagner showed in 2025 that a moving pattern of blowing and suction at a pipe wall can calm turbulent flow. In industry, most pumping energy is lost to turbulence hugging pipe walls. Earlier work had relaminarized, or smoothed back, such flow only at gentle turbulence levels.

Their simulations pushed the effect to much stronger turbulence. They then mapped how wave speed, strength, and length change the payoff for waves traveling with or against the flow. Waves moving against the flow could destabilize it, though slow, strong ones still saved energy. Waves moving with the flow cut drag across a wide range, but only a narrow band of settings saved energy overall. That band stayed the same across the turbulence strengths tested.
arxiv-2509-03315:
Ruth H. Keogh and 4 co-authors wrote a 2025 tutorial on the super learner for time-to-event outcomes. Clinicians often need survival probabilities tailored to a patient, yet follow-up data is censored: many people leave a study before the event happens. Nobody knows in advance which candidate model will estimate those risks best.

The super learner answers by combining many candidate models into an ensemble weighted by performance. This tutorial presents the method in accessible form for the first time. It covers the original version on a discrete time scale and two newer continuous-time versions. Properties of each are compared, and implementation in the R language is explained step by step. An open dataset illustrates the workflow, with code provided for readers to reuse.
arxiv-2509-03415:
Taekyun Kim and 3 co-authors introduced a new kind of degenerate Stirling numbers of the first kind in a 2025 combinatorics note. Stirling numbers count ways to split a set into cycles or groups, and degenerate versions add a parameter that deforms the counting. Their new sequence is of a further, new type.

Following earlier work that wrote unsigned Stirling numbers as scaled averages of specific random variables, the authors do the same for their numbers. They also express them as finite sums built from the classical unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind. As an inversion partner, they define matching degenerate numbers of the second kind. Those get finite-sum formulas in terms of ordinary second-kind Stirling numbers. Such identities tie the deformed counts back to classical ones.
arxiv-2509-04115:
Dominik Moll and five co-authors present a better way to simulate fast-ramping magnets in a 2025 engineering paper. Such magnets, used to bend particle beams, contain iron yokes whose magnetism lags behind changing currents. That lag, called hysteresis, makes field and heat-loss calculations hard. Engineers often skip the lag and add loss estimates afterward, which weakens accuracy. The authors instead join an energy-based hysteresis model with a thin-sheet model for eddy currents, the swirling currents induced in metal.

Running in step-by-step time form, the combined model handled a real bending magnet design. It calculated both fields and losses directly and precisely. Accelerator builders can use the approach when magnets must ramp quickly and predictably.
arxiv-2509-04215:
Hayeon Bang and three co-authors teach a model to link piano recordings with their scores and descriptions in a 2025 research paper. Solo piano carries rich meaning about mood and style, yet general music models blur fine differences between similar piano pieces. Piano-specific models exist, but they usually read only one format at a time. Their model, PianoBind, embeds audio, symbolic notation, and text into one shared space, so matching items sit close together.

Training strategies for small, look-alike collections are tested systematically. PianoBind beat general music models at finding the right recording from a text query, on both familiar and new piano collections. Design lessons should transfer to other narrow, homogeneous data sets beyond piano music.
arxiv-2509-04615:
Prompt-based attacks, where crafted inputs trick a large language model into unsafe or unwanted output, get a full threat model in a 2025 survey by Brennen Hill, lead author with four co-authors. The work sorts published attack methods into clear categories. It connects each method to weaknesses in model design, training, and context handling.

Inside, readers find how such attacks can lead to stolen intellectual property, false information, and loss of user trust. The survey explains the workings and effects of each exploit in plain terms. Its stated aim is to guide builders toward models that resist unwanted copying, fine-tuning, and editing.
arxiv-2509-04715:
Drones differ in sound as well as shape, and those sounds can reveal them when cameras and radar fall short. Mia Y. Wang, lead author with three co-authors, present an acoustic dataset and interactive tool in a 2025 paper. The dataset covers many categories of drones, separated by brand and model.

For each category it holds raw audio plus spectrogram and mel-frequency cepstral coefficient plots, two visual views of sound. A web application lets users pick a category, listen, and inspect the plots. The authors describe how the dataset was built and report experiments and user feedback for research and teaching.
arxiv-2509-04915:
A faint absorption feature in starlight, the diffuse interstellar band near 6196 angstroms, changes shape across the Milky Way. M. Piecka, lead author with two co-authors, survey those profile changes in a 2025 astronomy paper. They build a catalogue of profile parameters from archival spectra of hundreds of early-type stars.

Doppler-split components appear in most regions, yet they cannot explain the unusual broadening seen toward Upper Scorpius and several other regions. Broadening falls with distance from star-forming centres in two regions, pointing to a link with star formation, possibly through recent supernovae. The survey also addresses a blueshift and the quiet behaviour near the Carina Nebula.
arxiv-2509-05015:
A dying star in the Small Magellanic Cloud carries an extreme carbon-to-oxygen ratio and a rare lead signature. Meghna Menon, lead author with eight co-authors, analyse that post-asymptotic giant branch star in a 2025 astronomy paper. Such stars trace the slow neutron capture process through their surface abundances, measured here with high-resolution spectra.

The team report the first direct lead detection in a post-AGB star, from a specific lead absorption line. Comparisons with Galactic and Magellanic samples tell a plainer story. The star is short on oxygen, and that, rather than exceptional carbon enrichment, drives the high ratio. Its pattern matches third dredge-up enrichment and local chemical evolution.
arxiv-2509-05215:
Before claiming a model reasons about time series, it should at least describe one accurately. Medhasweta Sen, lead author with five co-authors, build a benchmark for that basic skill in a 2025 paper. BEDTime tests whether models can recognise, differentiate, and generate descriptions of single-variable time series, using five datasets across three modalities.

Evaluating seventeen leading models gives sobering results. Dedicated time series-language models fall short despite being built for such tasks. Vision-language models do surprisingly well, while language-only methods perform worst. Every approach proves fragile under real-world robustness tests, which the authors offer as directions for future work.
arxiv-2509-05315:
Large language models are tested as anomaly spotters for self-driving cars by Petros Loukas and three co-authors in a 2025 evaluation paper. Earlier checks mostly used synthetic scenes or hand-made driving sets, without knowing where current car systems actually fail.

Their setup pairs an open-vocabulary object detector, which can find objects named in free text, with prompt design and language model reasoning. Several leading models are run against real edge cases where today's vehicles are known to fail. The authors compare results qualitatively and discuss what the findings mean. The work gauges whether language models could serve as a backup layer beside perception and planning software.
arxiv-2509-05615:
Bias created by how medical data are collected can poison models that fuse several data types, Xiaoguang Zhu and six co-authors argue in a 2025 medical data mining paper. Patient records often miss whole modalities, such as a scan or lab panel, for cost or protocol reasons, and that missingness is rarely random.

A causal analysis separates two problems: missingness bias from the collection process and distribution bias from hidden factors affecting both features and outcomes. Their framework adds a module that mimics intervention using backdoor adjustment, plus a two-branch network splitting causal features from spurious ones. It plugs into existing prediction methods and improved results on public and hospital datasets.
arxiv-2509-05815:
Małgorzata Nowak-Kępczyk studies how simple counting rules on a grid can grow lasting large patterns, in a 2025 paper on modular Laplacian dynamics. The setup applies a discrete Laplacian, a neighbor-averaging rule, over and over while keeping values inside a fixed modulus. Pure binary versions soon fall into strict repeating cycles.

Inserting a single non-binary step changes the picture. Through wide computer exploration, the author sorts the survivors into rugs, quasi-carpets, and carpets, families whose fate depends on seed symmetry, neighborhood shape, and step sequence. Mixed sequences can hold dense carpets alive past the usual decay time. Algebraic replication laws, tied to the Lucas theorem, sit beside density tracking from simulations, linking exact conditions with observed quasi-periodic structures.
arxiv-2509-05915:
Early exiting can cut the cost of running large language models, but it can also slow them down in batches, and Sangmin Bae's 2025 dissertation resolves that tension. Letting easy tokens leave the network early saves computation per token, yet the uneven work creates bottlenecks when many requests run together. The dissertation co-designs the algorithms and the model architecture to balance adaptability with system efficiency.

First, a parallel decoding mechanism trims overheads in conventional early exiting. Next, deep parameter sharing is shown to give compact models that also ease the synchronization problems of dynamic inference. Finally, lightweight routers, pretrained for the job, assign each token its own recursion depth. The unified framework sets a new trade-off frontier between efficiency and performance in one model.
arxiv-2509-06715:
Stability of operators used in iterative image reconstruction is settled for small parameter values by Debraj Banerjee and one co-author in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Two families of operators, built from a stochastic matrix and a nonnegative matrix, arise when images are rebuilt step by step. Whether the iteration settles or blows up depends on their spectral radii staying below one.

Assuming the stochastic matrix is primitive, the authors prove a threshold exists below which both families are stable for all positive parameter values under it. The proof uses eigenvalue perturbation theory and the smooth behavior of the spectral radius. For special classes of matrices they compute the threshold explicitly. Numerical evidence supports a broader conjecture with a clean bound when the second matrix is positive semidefinite. As an application, convergence of certain iterative imaging algorithms follows.
arxiv-2509-07215:
Alejandro R. Urzúa, in a solo 2025 paper, builds the Jaynes-Cummings interaction on a finite two-dimensional oscillator. The Jaynes-Cummings model describes a two-level atom trading energy with light, a core setup in quantum optics. Here the light side is replaced by a finite oscillator, a vibrating system with only a limited set of energy states, spread over two dimensions.

Urzúa couples the paired energy states of the finite oscillator to the two levels of the atom and finds a basis in which total excitation stays fixed. He then follows how average field values evolve when the atom mediates the motion. Eigenenergy states and su(2) coherent states, a family of well-behaved quantum states, serve as worked examples. The paper closes with paths toward studying other atoms coupled to finite oscillators, a step toward smaller, controlled quantum devices.
arxiv-2509-07415:
Arslan Majal and 2 co-authors present EMORF-II in 2025, a filter that keeps tracking accurately even when sensor readings contain outliers. A filter blends a model with incoming measurements to estimate a hidden state, and stray bad readings can wreck the estimate. The setup here is general, and the measurement noise can be correlated, meaning errors at one moment relate to errors at another.

EMORF-II builds on an earlier expectation-maximization based filter, where expectation-maximization is a fitting method that alternates between guessing hidden values and updating parameters. The new version also learns the outlier pattern during use, on top of detecting outliers, which improves how it softens their impact. Numerical tests show accuracy gains over leading methods, at the cost of more computation. The cost grows no faster in order than rival practical methods, keeping the filter usable in real systems.
arxiv-2509-07515:
Adithya Ramachandran and 4 co-authors forecast short-term water demand for district metered areas in a 2025 paper. A district metered area is a bounded zone of a water network whose total inflow is measured, mixing homes, farms, and businesses. Smart meters now give hourly readings, but demand still swings with weather and other hard-to-pin-down factors, while climate change pressures supply.

Unsupervised contrastive learning first sorts end users into groups by consumption behavior, without labels. Those learned consumer representations then feed a forecasting network that uses wavelet-transformed convolutions, a way to view usage at several time scales, plus cross-attention to history. The method is evaluated on real-world district areas with diverse consumption patterns. Better short-term forecasts help utilities balance supply, spot leaks, and plan under growing water stress.
arxiv-2509-07615:
Chongqing Lei leads a 7-author team in 2025 behind FlexEmu, a framework for emulating microcontroller peripherals. Microcontrollers run countless embedded devices, and their firmware is vital to security. Dynamic analysis of that firmware is hard: real devices lack resources, and building emulators for the mass of different peripherals is costly. FlexEmu rests on a two-fold insight about how peripherals are built.

Structurally, diverse peripherals reduce to a limited set of primitives drawn from common hardware concepts. Semantically, peripherals of the same kind share similar functions, so one unified semantic model can describe them. Once such a model exists, FlexEmu automatically generates the emulation support, rather than hand-crafting each device. Flexible emulation would let security analysts run and fuzz firmware at scale, a step toward safer embedded systems everywhere.
arxiv-2509-07915:
Martin Sundermann and 12 co-authors study a rare superconductor called UTe2 in a 2025 physics paper. The key puzzle is the state of its uranium 5f electrons. Those electrons may stay close to their atoms. Or they may roam through the whole crystal. Which view is right shapes how its odd superconductivity can work.

The team runs two kinds of theory side by side. One is density functional theory. The other adds a mean-field method for strong interactions. A key input is tuned with the help of photoelectron data, which probe the electrons with light. The tuned model then matches angle-resolved measurements well. That match gives theorists a firmer base for the next round of work on this strange material.
arxiv-2509-08015:
Synthetic 3D heart and vessel anatomy with real control over shape is offered by Karim Kadry and 6 co-authors in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Generative models of cardiovascular anatomy help clinical research and device testing, but they usually force a trade: either realistic shapes that cannot be adjusted, or adjustable shapes that look artificial.

Their framework, CardioComposer, works at inference time and builds multi-class anatomical label maps from simple ellipsoidal building blocks. Those blocks encode size, shape, and position of anatomical parts in readable terms. Differentiable measurements based on geometric moments let gradients steer a diffusion model's sampling toward the requested anatomy. Programmable anatomy could supply test cases for devices and training data for rare conditions.
arxiv-2509-08315:
Long conversations eat a language model's memory, and Bohan Yu with Yekun Chai compress that memory adaptively in a 2025 machine learning paper. The key-value cache stores attention history for every layer, and existing compression uses uniform budgets or fixed eviction rules. Those heuristics ignore how each layer's patterns interact with actual task performance.

EvolKV reframes cache allocation as a multi-objective optimisation problem, balancing memory savings against quality. Evolutionary search then sets each layer's budget dynamically for the task at hand. Cache size limits how long a context a model can serve cheaply, so smarter allocation translates directly into longer documents, longer chats, and lower serving costs without surrendering accuracy.
arxiv-2509-08415:
Wei Zhang and Qi Zhou prove a rigidity result for an equation on the Heisenberg group in a 2025 maths paper. Results of this kind are called Liouville theorems. They say that a global solution must be the trivial one. The equation here is the 2-Hessian equation, built from second derivatives of the unknown function. The space mixes place with a twist, much like quantum phase space.

The proof picks a smart test function. It then integrates by parts to force the key bounds. Those bounds leave no room for exotic solutions. Such ground rules anchor work on equations in curved spaces. Before anyone perturbs or computes a solution, they need to know the base landscape holds no surprises.
arxiv-2509-08515:
Alicia Tierz and 3 co-authors build a design tool for heat flow that respects physics in a 2025 engineering paper. Good thermal design needs many trial shapes. Each trial costs a slow, costly simulation. Common generative models make that search worse. Their latent spaces are tangled and jumpy, so nearby points can give shapes that break the physics.

The team's hybrid pairs two networks. One keeps the latent space smooth and low-rank as it learns to compress shapes. The other is a deep operator network that rates heat behaviour fast. Designers could then search heatsinks and exchangers by browsing, not by waiting. A shape that looks fine but breaks heat flow is not a design. The frame is built to keep that line clear.
arxiv-2509-08715:
Sike Xiang and 2 co-authors propose BcQLM, a lightweight vision-language model, in a 2025 paper. Large multimodal models answer questions about images, but they are costly to run on limited hardware. BcQLM aims for strong visual question answering with far fewer resources.

Its core is BreezeCLIP, a compact vision-language encoder, joined with a Q-gated fusion step that mixes image and text. The full model has about one point two billion parameters. Tests on several datasets show performance close to standard size models. The modular design can extend to other multimodal tasks. Code is shared, supporting use where energy and hardware are constrained.
arxiv-2509-09015:
Rebuilding what a person saw from their brain scans usually requires training a separate model for every person. Chenqian Le and 6 co-authors present VoxelFormer, a shared alternative, in a 2025 research paper. VoxelFormer is a lightweight transformer that decodes viewed images from functional MRI data across multiple subjects at once. Subject-specific training has limited how far brain decoding can scale.

Two components keep the model small. A token merging transformer compresses the brain's voxel data efficiently. A query-driven module then produces fixed-size neural codes aligned with an image embedding space. On a large seven-tesla natural scenes dataset, retrieval performance matched heavier rivals with far fewer parameters. The authors argue token merging and query-based design are promising routes to practical neural decoding, where one model serves many brains.
arxiv-2509-09115:
Shuzhen Lv and 2 co-authors find Catalan structures in pattern avoiding Stoimenow matchings in a 2025 paper. Stoimenow matchings, also called regular linearized chord diagrams, arose from knot invariants in 1998. They connect to Fishburn numbers and several combinatorial objects.

A problem posed in 2025 asked which subsets of these matchings are counted by the Catalan numbers, a famous counting sequence. Five solutions are given in terms of pattern avoiding matchings. Four infinite families generalizing the forbidden patterns are shown to be equinumerous, meaning counted by the same numbers. Results on distributions over matchings, posets, ascent sequences, and permutations use Narayana and ballot numbers.
arxiv-2509-09315:
A drying droplet of respiratory fluid leaves a ring of protein at its edge, and that ring's story involves the evaporation itself. Javier Martínez-Puig and 3 co-authors investigate the feedback in a 2025 research paper. Classic coffee-ring models assume evaporation drives the flow without the solute talking back. In protein solutions, solute changes water activity, which changes evaporation, breaking that assumption.

The team's model droplets mixed water, salt, and mucin, a glycoprotein from mucus. Fluorescence microscopy watched a crisp protein ring form as the water left. Ring growth and shape depended strongly on the surrounding humidity. Their minimal theory couples fluid flow and solute transport through the evaporation rate. It reproduces the main experimental features. The physics may bear on how long respiratory droplets stay stable and infectious, a question with obvious public health weight.
arxiv-2509-09415:
Marcel Ausloos and 2 co-authors examined company accounts in a 2025 report on whether leading digits follow Benford's laws. They used pre-tax income and total assets for 567 firms on the FTSE All-Share index, drawn from the Refinitiv EIKON database over fourteen years. Positive and negative income cases were separated, and a ratio of the two measures was also studied.

Two statistical checks gave partly different answers, and the mean absolute deviation check rejected agreement with Benford patterns outright. The authors say the mismatch raises doubts about the reported figures and calls for more work nearby. They also treat ratios carefully, noting such derived measures can mislead digit analysis.
arxiv-2509-09515:
A cough recorded on a phone could flag respiratory disease, but labeled medical audio is scarce by nature. Yoga Disha Sendhil Kumar, Manas V Shetty, and Sudip Vhaduri test few-shot learning for that job in a 2025 research paper. Their models classify coughs as COVID-19, flu, or healthy. The method, prototypical networks over sound spectrograms, learns each class from a handful of examples.

With only fifteen examples per class, the multi-class model reached competitive accuracy. Binary models separating each pair of conditions cleared a similar bar. Flu coughs were the easiest to distinguish; healthy coughs were the hardest. Statistical tests found no significant gap between the binary and multi-class setups. That supports using one multi-class model in practice. Few-shot methods suit medical diagnostics precisely because outbreaks and rare conditions never wait for a large labeled dataset to exist.
arxiv-2509-09715:
Naveen Lamba and 2 co-authors examine in a 2025 paper why large language models invent false facts. They focus on symbolic triggers, features of a question itself, such as modifiers and named entities, that may push a model toward error. Questions from the HaluEval and TruthfulQA sets were recast into several formats so these features could be isolated and tested on Google's Gemma models.

Hallucination stayed high across the board. The smallest model averaged close to four wrong answers in five, and even the largest still failed on most test items. Larger models did better, yet modifiers and named entities kept causing errors at very high rates. The authors read this as a basic weakness in how such models handle symbolic input.
arxiv-2509-09915:
Woong Shin and 6 co-authors wrote this 2025 position paper on how AI agents may change scientific workflows. Today, researchers often spend their time coordinating facilities and resources by hand instead of doing science. The authors argue that agent-based tools could take over much of that coordination, but it is not yet clear how such tools would fit into real laboratories and computing centers.

They propose a framework that tracks workflows along two paths. One path is how smart the system is, from fixed scripts to reasoning agents. The other is how it is composed, from a single workflow to swarms of them. From those paths they sketch an architecture meant to guide the field toward largely autonomous, spread-out laboratories, with a chance of far faster discovery.
arxiv-2509-10015:
Soobin Cho and 2 co-authors argue, in a 2025 paper, that online communities need AI help with mediation, not only moderation. Moderation tools mostly remove posts or users, which keeps order but rarely settles the disagreement underneath. Mediation instead guides people toward shared understanding and agreement, which can improve decisions and repair working relationships inside a group.

The authors propose an information-focused framework for AI-supported mediation in community collaboration. Their central claim is that a mediator system must gather three kinds of information. It needs the content of the dispute, the culture of the community, and the people involved. The paper sets out that framework as a design base for tools that resolve conflict rather than merely police it.
arxiv-2509-10215:
Superconductivity in the crystal Sr2RuO4 is the puzzle behind this 2025 physics paper by Giordano Mattoni and six co-authors. Ultrasound tests hint that its superconducting state has two components, while squeezing tests suggest only one. The team settles the strain part of the dispute by applying three kinds of shear strain directly to single crystals.

After checking the strain with optical imaging, they watch the transition temperature through magnetic measurements. It shifts by less than ten thousandths of a degree per percent of strain, a sign that shear strain barely couples to the superconductivity at all. That favors a one-component picture, though the authors note other evidence, such as broken time-reversal symmetry, still needs a different explanation.
arxiv-2509-10415:
Wael Mattar and Nir Sharon build a multiscale toolkit for sequences of probability distributions in this 2025 mathematics paper. Their setting is Wasserstein space, where distance between distributions is measured by optimal transport, the cheapest way to reshape one pile into another. Distributions that evolve over time, from fluid flows to learning machines, live naturally there.

Their transform uses a refinement step built on McCann's interpolants, which respects the curved geodesic paths of the space and acts as an upsampler for both smooth and discrete measures. A new scalar, the optimality number, flags how far a sequence strays from geodesic motion at each scale, exposing irregular dynamics. They prove stability and decay properties, then demo denoising, anomaly detection, point-cloud dynamics, and the training paths of neural networks.
arxiv-2509-10615:
Mark D. Gorski and Elena Murchikova report finding an active wind from our galaxy's central black hole in this 2025 paper. Every large galaxy hosts such a black hole, and winds or jets from it shape the galaxy's growth. Sagittarius A*, the Milky Way's own, sits close enough to study in fine detail, yet its wind had escaped detection for over fifty years.

Using deep, sharp observations with the ALMA telescope array, they found a cone-shaped clearing in the cold gas around the black hole. The cleared cone runs at least a parsec long with a wide opening angle. Its shape and energy match clearing by a hot wind blowing outward from Sagittarius A* itself.
arxiv-2509-10915: Cristina Flaut, Dana Piciu, and Bianca Liana Bercea-Straton present applications of finite BL-algebras, from many-valued logic, in this 2025 paper. One is an encryption and decryption algorithm, built on properties of finite MV-algebras. The authors prove that no commutative unitary ring can have its ideal lattice equal to a finite BL-algebra that is not an MV-algebra. They give a method to generate BL-comets. A finite BL-algebra, they show, is a comet or an MV-algebra that is not a chain.
arxiv-2509-11015:
Rohan Tan Bhowmik and 4 co-authors release a huge data set for predicting California wildfires in this 2025 paper. Most AI wildfire tools detect fires after they start. Prediction needs long, rich records, which are hard to assemble. The California Wildfire Inventory gathers more than 37 million data points to fill that gap.

Daily fire records run from 2012 to 2018, with indicator data reaching 2022. Indicators come in three kinds: weather patterns that precede fires, environmental traces of earlier activity, and land features like vegetation and elevation that shape risk and spread. As a demonstration, a model trained on the set forecast most of the very large fires in a held-out year. The authors offer the data as a template for other regions.
arxiv-2509-11115:
Mengke Wu and four co-authors wrote this 2025 human-computer interaction paper on AI writing assistants, asking whether a writer's personality should shape the assistant they get. A tool-like helper suits some writers, while others may want something closer to a supportive partner.

The team ran a co-design workshop with twenty-four writers to map what personality-aligned companions could do, then built two contrasting prototypes and let eight participants react to them. Writers' profiles lined up strongly with the features they preferred, giving early evidence that one design does not fit all. The authors argue that matching an AI partner to the person matters for engagement and for how well human and machine work together.
arxiv-2509-11315:
Electrons in graphene can flow like a liquid. This 2025 review by Subhalaxmi Nayak and five co-authors gathers the evidence. Electrons collide with each other far more than with impurities. Their motion then turns hydrodynamic. Currents swirl and narrow like water in a pipe.

The review walks through the experimental signatures. Resistance dips near a current injector. Channel flow shows a rounded Poiseuille profile. The Wiedemann-Franz law breaks down strongly. That law normally ties heat and charge conduction together. Measurements of the Lorenz ratio get close attention. The theory side is summarized too. Frameworks compute the fluid's thermodynamic and transport properties. The authors include their own group's approach.
arxiv-2509-11715:
V. Pomjakushin's 2025 paper in condensed matter physics re-examines two textbook antiferromagnets. They are nickel oxide and manganese oxide. High-resolution neutron diffraction is the tool. Their magnetic structures have long been told by a single wave vector. That telling forces monoclinic symmetry. The distortions it implies are tiny. No test has ever resolved them.

Pomjakushin weighs the magnetic models that fit the data. The isotropy subgroup approach guides the weighing. Rhombohedral candidates built from the full star of wave vectors are included. One such model fits nickel oxide's data just as well. On balance, he backs the single-vector monoclinic model for both oxides. A specific magnetic space group comes with it. The paper sorts out symmetries that tests can barely separate.
arxiv-2509-11915:
Perfect detection of machine-written text is not merely hard but impossible in principle, argues Aadil Gani Ganie in a solo-authored 2025 paper. As language models grow more fluent, the line between human and artificial writing keeps blurring, and Ganie frames the problem through an analogy with quantum uncertainty.

Pushing hard to pin down a text's origin, the paper contends, disturbs the very qualities that make writing read naturally, so certainty in one place buys doubt in another. Stylometry, watermarking, and neural classifiers each run into this trade-off, and the closer generated prose gets to human prose, the tighter the bind becomes. Counterarguments get a hearing before the discussion turns to what the limit means for authorship, ethics, and policy.
arxiv-2509-12115: Servet Martinez studies Bayesian estimators of diversity indexes in a short 2025 paper. The estimators rest on exchangeable random partitions. Such a partition groups items so that the stats do not depend on the order in which members arrive. Martinez shows the estimators form martingales. In a martingale, the expected future value equals the present one. The estimators converge, almost surely and in mean, to one shared limit. Their local behavior also ties to plug-in estimators, the simpler stats that insert observed frequencies directly.
arxiv-2509-12315:
Old open clusters are natural laboratories for how binary stars age together. Ritvik Sai Narayan and three co-authors extend a long radial velocity survey of NGC 188 in 2025, a cluster more than six billion years old, adding thirty-five new spectroscopic binary orbits.

The longer baseline nearly doubles the time span of earlier work, and fresh membership checks use Gaia motions and distances. After correcting for missed systems, about a third of the cluster's stars in the sample are binaries with periods under ten thousand days. Giants seem to lack short-period partners, a clue that some transferred mass and became blue stragglers or blue lurkers.
arxiv-2509-12415:
Cities are starting to govern with language models, but a model's answers bend with the wording of its prompt, and prompts smuggle in values. In a solo 2025 paper, Rashid Mushkani proposes Prompt Commons: a shared, versioned library of prompts that a community maintains with licenses, moderation, and governance records attached.

A pilot on Montreal data compares open, curated, and veto-enabled versions of the commons. Governed prompts roughly doubled neutral outcomes on a contested policy test while staying decisive where decisiveness fit. In a simulated incident log, the veto version cut the time to fix harmful outputs from about a day to a few hours.
arxiv-2509-12515:
Blood oxygen is a vital sign that wearables struggle to measure, because cheap light sensors sample slowly and skip clinical calibration. Zequan Liang and six co-authors solve the adaptation problem in 2025 with transfer learning on a wrist band that reads the pulse optically at a low sampling rate.

A recurrent network with attention is first trained on a public clinical dataset, then fine-tuned on band data checked against an approved reference oximeter. Errors land near two and a half percentage points on the wearable data, beating plain calibration and non-transferred models. The slow sampling also cuts power use by about forty percent.
arxiv-2509-13015:
Heikki Mäntysaari and 5 co-authors investigate whether nucleon structure changes inside nuclei in a 2025 physics paper. Their setting is diffractive vector meson production studied within the color glass condensate framework, a theory of dense gluon matter. A recent global Bayesian analysis covered such production in photon-proton and photon-lead collisions.

The authors extend that analysis by allowing the effective nucleon structure parameters inside lead nuclei to differ from those of free protons. They compare fits with shared and independent parameters and assess the impact on describing photon-proton data from HERA and the LHC and photon-lead data from the LHC simultaneously. Their findings show no hint of a difference in nucleon structure beyond what the framework already contains when nucleons are embedded in a nuclear environment.
arxiv-2509-13215:
Bingxiang Zhong and Thomas Dietzen address domain adaptation for sound source tracking in a 2025 paper. Deep learning has advanced sound source localization, but training needs large labeled data sets, and real recordings are costly to annotate, especially when sources move. Synthetic data from modeled room acoustics offer an alternative, yet models trained on them suffer domain shift in real settings.

Unsupervised domain adaptation can align synthetic and real domains without labels from the real one. Current approaches focus on static localization and ignore tracking-certain challenges. Variable-length input series create mismatches in feature dimensionality across domains. The angular coverage of synthetic and real data may also be misaligned, a problem the authors call directional diversity mismatch. Their importance-weighted approach targets those challenges for moving sources.
arxiv-2509-13415:
Giulia Roccetti, Michael Sterzik and four co-authors model in 2025 a decade of Earthshine polarization spectra as an exoplanet lab. Earth seen from the Moon acts as an unresolved exoplanet at varied phases. Scenes span surfaces, clouds, and weather over ten years with VLT data.

A uniform 3D model now fits the full set in detail. Subgrid cloud variation, wavelength surface maps, and ocean glint are included. Past models missed the polarization continuum; the new fits match most spectra with high precision. Visible slopes split ocean from mixed faces in both light types. Polar light at large phases splits oceans best. Oceans, plants, and water cycle read from polar light alone.
arxiv-2509-14015:
Haldun Özgür Bayındır and Markus Land advance the classification of differential graded algebras in a 2025 algebra paper. A DGA whose homology is a polynomial ring on one generator sounds simple. Sorting all such objects resisted classification. Dwyer, Greenlees, and Iyengar left the problem open, motivated by algebraic K-theory computations.

The pair prove two structural facts. When the generator sits in even degree, infinitely many non-equivalent DGAs share that same polynomial homology. When the degree is large enough relative to the prime, every such DGA is formal as a ring spectrum. Its whole structure is then determined by its homology. Consequences include triangulated categories with infinitely many distinct enhancements. New K-theory computations for concrete rings follow, including group rings of cyclic p-groups.
arxiv-2509-14115:
Guilherme Fabris and five co-authors design a family of hybrid two-dimensional materials in a 2025 paper. Glaphene, a stack of silica glass and graphene monolayers, was made experimentally very recently. That proves such hybrids can exist. The team ask what happens when the carbon partner is instead a graphyne. A graphyne is a carbon sheet laced with triple-bonded links, in alpha, beta, or gamma forms.

They name the resulting stacks glaphynes. They study them with density functional tight-binding calculations. The structures prove energetically and structurally stable. A proximity effect between the layers can open an electronic band gap. Silicon-oxygen-carbon bonds at the interface help. A band gap makes a material switchable like a semiconductor. The effect does not appear in every variant. That selectivity itself suggests tuning knobs for device design.
arxiv-2509-14315:
Alexander Nikolaenko and Pavel A. Nosov develop theory in 2025 for wiggles in conductance in thin metal films under a magnetic field. Electrons moving along the field make conductance rise and fall in a regular pattern. Those Sondheimer oscillations were long explained with a semiclassical picture.

Strong fields and clean samples push films into a quantum regime where the old picture fails. A second pattern, the Shubnikov-de Haas effect, can then interfere with the first. Nikolaenko and Nosov build a full theory of quantum magnetoconductivity for films of finite thickness. Surface scattering, Landau quantisation in the plane and thickness effects enter together. The work tells experimentalists what pattern to expect when the two effects overlap.
arxiv-2509-14515:
Yuxuan Chen and Haoyuan Yu survey full duplex spoken language models in 2025, systems that can listen and speak at once like people do. Turn taking chat feels stilted beside natural conversation with overlap and interruption. True full duplex interaction is a stated milestone for human like AI.

The survey sorts designs into engineered synchronisation, built from modules, and learned synchronisation, trained end to end. Evaluation is unified under four headings: timing dynamics, behaviour arbitration, semantic coherence and acoustic quality. Comparative analysis of leading systems exposes shared problems. Synchronous training data are scarce, architectures diverge widely, and evaluation has gaps. A common map should help the field compare claims about natural spoken interaction.
arxiv-2509-14615: Nursultan Kuanyshov, writing alone in 2025, gives a full account of the cohomological dimension of group homomorphisms. That dimension gauges how complex a map between groups is. The main case proved is a version of the classic Stallings-Swan theorem for group epimorphisms, maps that reach every member of the target group.
arxiv-2509-14715:
Jieying Liu and three co-authors explain in 2025 the high energy emission line seen in GRB 221009A, the brightest gamma ray burst ever recorded. Its spectrum showed a series of lines sliding from high to lower energy over time. Decades of effort preceded that first firm detection, and the mechanism stayed elusive.

Their scenario starts with electron positron pair annihilation creating the line photons. Those photons then undergo down-Comptonization, repeated scattering that drains their energy, during transfer through the burst environment. The combined process reproduces the full downward evolution of the line energies in a self consistent way. A explained line turns a spectral curiosity into a probe of the burst outflow composition and density.
arxiv-2509-14915:
Shenghai Yuan and five co-authors present PERAL, a motion control framework that helps spherical robots see the ground near them, in a 2025 robotics paper. Spherical robots roll inside a ball, and their LiDAR sensors usually point sideways. A level LiDAR catches few returns from the ground nearby, weakening terrain awareness in sparse environments.

PERAL adds gentle, bounded wobbles to the robot's normal driving commands, tilting the sensor passively with no extra motors. A model of the coupling between the internal drive and sensor attitude keeps the added motion from harming navigation accuracy. Tests in a laboratory, a corridor, and tactical settings reach high map completeness and cut trajectory error. The approach trades a small amount of motion complexity for much richer vertical scanning.
arxiv-2509-15015:
Harrison Oates, Hyeonggeun Yun, and Nikhila Gurusinghe test-drive two interactive theorem provers in a 2025 formal methods paper. Theorem provers help people build machine-checked proofs, and today's systems differ widely in design philosophy. Those choices shape how usable each system feels and which problems it suits.

Both provers, Coq and Idris2, are put through the same exercise: proving the correctness of insertion sort, a standard sorting algorithm. The authors then evaluate the experience qualitatively, comparing features, workflow, and the feel of each proof development. Community size and library support get a separate comparison, since a prover is only as useful as the mathematics already formalized for it. The study aims to help newcomers choose a system and to show developers ideas worth borrowing.
arxiv-2509-15315:
Federico Coro and three co-authors compute a hard piece of particle physics by hand. When protons crash, they can throw off two jets of particles, or a photon and a jet. Rare paths for these events run through loops of heavy quarks. Getting exact formulas for those paths at two loops is a long, hard task.

The team builds on their past work on two photon events and adds new crossings of the core math pieces. They write the results with a known set of functions tied to an elliptic curve. Many hard terms cancel in the final answers. They also lay out a plan to get numbers from the formulas near tricky points. The work feeds precise tests of the Standard Model.
arxiv-2509-15615:
S. S. Agaev, K. Azizi, and H. Sundu compute the mass and decay width of a molecule like particle state. Their state pairs two excited mesons that each hold charm and bottom quarks. Such states are called hadronic molecules when their parts bind loosely. The team use a QCD sum rule method, a standard tool for such estimates.

From two point sum rules they extract the state's mass and its tie to the probing current. The mass leaves room for decays into many meson pairs, some by direct split and some after quark pairs vanish or change. Three point sum rules then give the width of each channel. The full width is assembled from those parts. The work predicts a state labs may seek.
arxiv-2509-16115:
Korea lacked a broad, public monthly data set for studying its economy in the style of rich United States data bases. Changryong Baek, Seunghyun Moon, and Seunghyeon Lee build KRED, a set of 125 monthly series reaching back to 1960. The series come from the central bank, the state stats office, and labor sources.

From a balanced set of 104 series, they extract four shared factors tied to finance, real activity, housing credit, and labor and prices. Tests then show United States rate hikes pass strongly into Korea, mostly through finance links. The open data set aids policy work and cross-country study.
arxiv-2509-16715:
Adrien Llave, Emma Granier, and Grégory Pallone build a score for spatial audio in a 2025 paper. Spatial sound places voices and effects around a listener. Judging its quality now relies on listening tests with real people. Those tests cost time and money. The team train a neural network to stand in for those listeners.

Their metric, QASTAnet, predicts how people will rate a clip. Its predictions track human scores closely. It also avoids flaws found in older metrics. Codec builders could use it to compare versions fast, without fresh listening panels each time. A shared, trusted score would help the whole field move faster.
arxiv-2509-16815:
Soh Kumabe, working alone, studies a hybrid graph deletion problem in a 2025 math paper. The task is to delete few vertices so each remaining chunk is a clique or a tree. It blends two classic deletion problems into one. Kumabe seeks a small kernel, a shrunk form of the problem that keeps the same answer.

He proves a quadratic kernel exists for this problem. He also studies the deletion count as a structural measure in its own right. Under that measure, a hard cycle problem becomes tractable in a fixed-parameter sense. Hybrid measures like this can unlock algorithms for graphs that sit between dense and sparse forms.
arxiv-2509-17115:
Nickolay Erin Titov wrote a thesis, shared on arXiv in 2025, about beating the blur limit of normal lenses. Two light sources that sit very close together merge into one blob in a standard image. His work tests a method called spatial-mode demultiplexing, which sorts light into a set of clean patterns before measuring it.

The sorting idea comes from quantum estimation theory, which says the pattern view keeps detail that a plain image throws away. Titov designed a working version of the sorter built on multi-plane light conversion, a stack of shaped plates that bends light step by step. Bench tests confirmed the device works as planned. The thesis shows a practical path toward sharper views of very close light sources.
arxiv-2509-17215:
Yassine Kebbati leads a team of four co-authors on a 2025 arXiv paper about steering driverless cars. The paper targets sideways control, the task of keeping a car on its planned path. Model predictive control is a strong fit for this job because it plans ahead and respects limits on steering and speed.
