Their version adapts as it drives, and an improved swarm search tunes its settings. A lookup table handles the online changes, swapping in stored settings as conditions shift. In simulations, the adaptive controller beat both the classic version and a pure pursuit controller on path tracking. The authors link to public code so other groups can rerun the tests. The paper adds one more tested option to the crowded field of car steering control.
arxiv-2509-17315:
Koustav Chandra and Juan Calderón Bustillo revisit how scientists read the dying ring of a merged black hole. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that a disturbed black hole rings with tones whose pitches are fixed by its mass and spin. Classic analyses treat that ringdown as a generic signal, apart from the merger that made it, which can add free parameters and clash with full-signal priors.

The authors instead model the ringdown with the post-merger part of full waveform models, an approach from earlier work by Calderón Bustillo and others. Applied to GW150914, the first detected merger, the method finds decisive support for the no-hair theorem, far stronger than classic spectroscopy gave. It also finds modest support for one overtone and none for higher modes. Fake signals confirm the method recovers the remnant well.
arxiv-2509-18015:
Advait Gosai and 6 co-authors test if chat models can point to where a chest X-ray goes wrong. Their 2025 study goes past naming a disease, to placing it on the image. That skill matters for care and for teaching, and it shows how well a model grasps body space.

Two broad chat models and one medical model were asked for map points on scans, with a grid laid over each scan. The best model placed just under half of the cases right, below a task-built net and far below a radiologist. Its misses were most often in a plausible body zone, just not the exact spot.
arxiv-2509-18415:
Software agents now act for firms as non-human identities, and their call chains need proof. Sumana Malkapuram, Sameera Gangavarapu, Kailashnath Reddy Kavalakuntla, and Ananya Gangavarapu present a lineage system for such agents in this 2025 paper. The goal is to verify where an agent came from and how it changed over time. That proof must hold across many hops, not just one link.

Their design anchors agent history in append-only Merkle trees, the same shape used by certificate transparency logs. A shared proof server gathers inclusion proofs into compact signed statements. Outside parties can check those statements without seeing the full run history. Agent cards gain built-in identity checks for both peer agents and human approvers. The authors aim the model at regulated settings with strict audit rules. It joins identity, lineage, and proof checks in one frame.
arxiv-2509-18515:
Tiny self-propelled particles wander in ways that mix drift, memory, and chance. Uma Shankari and Mamata Sahoo study one such particle that also gets reset to its start at random times. Their 2025 paper treats an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle, a standard model of a swimmer with inertia. They ask how resetting changes its spread over time.

Using a renewal approach, they compute the mean squared displacement and position spread in both low- and high-inertia regimes. With resetting, the spread grows early on, then settles to a steady value instead of growing forever. Faster resetting shrinks that steady spread toward zero. At mid-range activity times, the spread is boosted, which helps the particle find spread-out targets. In a memory-rich fluid, a plateau appears at mid times and widens with stronger memory. Slow resetting makes that plateau clearer.
arxiv-2509-18915:
When can a ring in algebra be written as a union of its proper ideals, with no ideal covering the whole ring alone? Malcolm Hoong Wai Chen and two co-authors study covers of a ring by left ideals. For a ring that admits such a cover, they define its covering number as the size of the smallest cover. They single out special rings whose covering number drops whenever a nonzero two-sided ideal is factored out.

The authors classify all of those special rings and work out their covering numbers. They also settle the same questions for covers by right ideals and by two-sided ideals. Together the results fully describe which rings admit finite ideal covers. The work extends further, to finite covers of modules by submodules, where they find all possible covering numbers.
arxiv-2509-19015:
Peng Lu and Yuanyuan Qiao study a fluid model that couples magnetism with tiny internal rotation in each fluid parcel. Such magneto-micropolar equations describe fluids like liquid crystals and some biological liquids. Their version is three-dimensional but dissipates energy only in the horizontal directions, which makes the math harder: vertical smoothing is missing, so wild behavior cannot be ruled out by standard tricks.

The authors prove the system stays well-posed worldwide in time when the starting state and its vertical changes are small enough. They also derive the best possible decay rates for the size of the solution as time grows. The proofs lean on the equations' special structure, plus inequalities tuned to the split between horizontal and vertical directions. The result adds a firm case to the theory of fluids with partial dissipation.
arxiv-2509-19115:
Following a single point through a long video, frame by frame as it streams, is the task taken up by Görkay Aydemir and two co-authors. Points change look, move fast, and hide behind other objects, yet the tracker may not peek at future frames. The team extends their earlier model into Track-On2, a transformer design built for this online setting. It keeps a memory of the past, which helps it resist drift and survive occlusions.

At each step the model first locates the point coarsely, patch by patch, then refines the spot. The authors also study how synthetic training data shapes the memory's behavior over long sequences. Across five benchmarks, synthetic and real, Track-On2 set new best results for online trackers. It even beat strong offline methods that are allowed to look ahead and behind. The model trains purely on synthetic data.
arxiv-2509-19215:
Wearable sensors that track the pulse from light on the skin produce PPG signals, rich in health clues but hard to analyze with big models on small devices. Juntong Ni and five co-authors shrink a large PPG foundation model into a small one through distillation. Their framework, PPG-Distill, transfers knowledge at three levels: final predictions, inner features, and small time patches. Two extra losses preserve the waveform's local shapes and the rhythm across patches.

On tests of heart rate tracking and atrial fibrillation spotting, the small student improved by up to about twenty percent over its undistilled version. It also ran about seven times faster and used about nineteen times less memory. Those numbers matter for watches and patches that must analyze signals on the spot. The work shows foundation-model quality can reach truly resource-limited wearables.
arxiv-2509-19415:
The KPZ fixed point is a universal limit object for random growth, much like the bell curve for sums. Pantelis Tassopoulos and Sourav Sarkar measure how closely its spatial steps mimic Brownian motion. Their bounds hold for any starting shape, with uniform strength over starting shapes in a bounded set. The comparison is quantitative: it gives rates, not just existence.

Two uses follow. One is a one-sided bound on the chance of large steps. The other shows that the centered fixed point has a density with finite entropy, a measure of spread. Earlier results often needed special starting shapes, such as flat or narrow wedge forms. Dropping that need widens the reach of KPZ theory. The work adds firm ground under a model used across physics and probability.
arxiv-2509-19515:
Companion chatbots are built to feel like friends, and some users form close bonds with them. Rose E. Guingrich and Michael S. A. Graziano ran a three-week trial to test the social effects. One hundred eighty-three adults were split by chance into two groups. One group chatted with a companion bot for ten minutes a day; the other played word games. Surveys and interviews tracked social health across the trial.

Overall, the bot group showed no clear harm or gain in social health. A closer look told a subtler story. People who longed most for social contact treated the bot as most humanlike. Those who treated it as humanlike also said it shaped their ties with family and friends the most. How human a bot feels may be the channel through which it affects real relationships.
arxiv-2509-19615:
Social feeds decide what people see by guessing taste from clicks, leaving users little direct say. Agam Goyal, Frederick Choi, and Eshwar Chandrasekharan built PILOT, a feed tool for the Bluesky network that hands control back. Actions taken inside the feed become stated preferences, and ranking follows fixed, inspectable rules. A small first study shaped a fuller version with three layers of control.

Ten users then compared the layers. Broad controls set the overall direction, in-post actions fine-tuned results, and filters cut unwanted items. Richer controls did not always feel like more work. What mattered most was whether users could check the outcome and fix mistakes. The study argues that feed control needs good repair tools as much as expressive ones.
arxiv-2509-20115:
James M. Cline wrote this short 2025 arXiv comment on a claimed new particle. Since 1991, a series of papers has argued that the Higgs particle should be heavier than the value later measured. To save the idea, it was revised to predict a second Higgs particle with a mass near six hundred ninety GeV.

Cline reviews the claims behind that prediction and the evidence offered for it. He argues that the theory side gives no solid support for a second Higgs at that mass. He also argues that experiments have not produced real evidence for such a particle. The note answers several earlier papers and a reply to his first version. It is a direct rebuttal, written for particle physicists following the dispute.
arxiv-2509-20215:
Guang Yang and five co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on chip design with language models. Engineers write hardware in Verilog, a language models handle poorly for lack of training data. Sampling many candidate programs raises the chance that one passes. But an engineer needs a single solution worth trusting, not a pile of guesses.

The authors frame the task as matching a requirement text to the best matching program. Their discriminator model, VCD-RNK, reranks sampled candidates efficiently. It was taught expert reasoning along three lines: reading code meaning, inventing test cases, and judging functional correctness. At run time it simulates that reasoning instead of executing costly tests. The approach aims to deliver one dependable Verilog answer at low cost.
arxiv-2509-20315:
Hope speech, language that encourages and lifts others, is hard for computers to spot across languages. T. O. Abiola and five co-authors compare detection methods in a 2025 arXiv study. Their framework adds active learning, which picks the most useful examples for human labeling. That matters where labeled data is scarce.

Experiments covered English, Spanish, German, and Urdu datasets, including recent shared-task benchmarks. A simple logistic regression model served as the traditional baseline. Two multilingual transformer models, mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa, clearly beat it. XLM-RoBERTa reached the highest overall accuracy. Active learning kept performance strong even with small labeled sets. The study supports pairing multilingual transformers with data-efficient training for social good applications.
arxiv-2509-20515:
An unidentified extreme gamma-ray source in our galaxy is examined by P. Bangale and X. Wang in a 2025 conference paper. The source, LHAASO J0341+5258, emits photons above hundreds of tera-electronvolts, marking it as a PeVatron, an accelerator reaching peta-electronvolt energies. It is extended on the sky and unusually bright. Most sibling sources match known objects like supernova remnants or pulsar wind nebulae, but this one's engine is unknown.

The authors present observations from the VERITAS and HAWC telescopes. Those data constrain the source's shape and its possible associations with objects at other wavelengths. Multiwavelength modeling then tests scenarios for how the ultra-high-energy emission is produced. The work narrows what kind of astrophysical system could power the source. Identifying such PeVatrons matters because they are candidate origins of the highest-energy cosmic rays in the Milky Way.
arxiv-2509-20615:
Digital twins mirror real systems in a computer. Latent twins mirror the math itself, as Matthias Chung and five co-authors propose in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their hidden stand-in for a system's equations lives in a learned latent space, run by learned operators. Fields that grew apart, like modeling, inversion, model reduction, and operator learning, fall out of this one idea as special cases.

The team proves how well such twins can match their targets, for both plain and partial differential equations. Tests span three grounds: classic dynamical systems, a shallow-water benchmark, and a real geopotential dataset with sparse, noisy reads. The twins jump across time gaps in a single shot. They also plug into pipelines for data intake, control, and uncertainty work. The pitch is a compact, theory-backed stand-in that joins data-driven learning with classic science modeling.
arxiv-2509-21015:
Diffusion processes model many things, from prices to particles, but we see them only at scattered times. Miguel Alvarez and Ajay Jasra build an estimator for that setting in a 2025 statistics paper. Their method infers the static parameters of a partly observed diffusion, with no bias from time discretization.

Most estimators carry exactly that bias. The authors use an identity tied to the gradient of the log-likelihood of diffusion bridges, the paths forced to pass through the observed points. They prove their estimator is unbiased and has finite variance. Unlike earlier methods, theirs lets the diffusion coefficient depend on the unknown parameters. It also works with more efficient Markov chain samplers, widening the reach of likelihood-based inference for such models.
arxiv-2509-21315:
Hysteresis in two dimensional material transistors is quoted everywhere as a quality sign, rarely with a method. It comes from Alexander Karl and 21 co-authors. Hysteresis is a lag in device response when voltage sweeps back and forth. It is widely reported as a sign of device quality. Yet papers often call it small with no clear method or reference. The mechanisms behind it are only partly understood.

The authors first analyse the main causes in theory. They cover charge trapping by defects, drift of mobile charges, and ferroelectricity. They then suggest experimental methods to tell those causes apart. Measurement settings also affect the observed values, and the paper addresses that sensitivity. The aim is a systematic approach for stability benchmarking and performance projection.
arxiv-2509-21615:
Open ends of acoustic waveguides have only ever been analysed in the linear regime. Freddie Jensen and 2 co-authors formulate a weakly nonlinear exit condition in a 2025 paper. Mean flow, vortex separation, and viscous effects are neglected. The result is an admittance boundary condition with a weakly nonlinear counterpart. Free space is approximated by enclosing the duct in a much larger hard walled concentric duct.

Inside the larger duct, the smaller duct exit acts as an acoustic discontinuity. The superposition principle is not needed, so the model applies in the nonlinear regime. The exit condition can be computed without solving the full problem in either duct, keeping it numerically efficient. The work extends recent weakly nonlinear modelling of curved ducts to open ends.
arxiv-2509-22015:
Sparse autoencoders unpack a vision model's inner activity into a dictionary of features, but only the features the model happens to expose. Jianrong Ding, Muxi Chen, Chenchen Zhao, and Qiang Xu present Concept-SAE in this 2025 paper, accepted at ECML PKDD 2026. Their framework adds a controllable interface, so users can probe concepts they choose, not just the ones that surface on their own.

The design splits the inner activity into two parts. Concept tokens align with user-specified ideas, trained with supervision on both whether the concept is present and where it sits in the image. Free tokens capture everything else, as in a standard autoencoder. The split keeps the concept signals faithful and cleanly separated. Tests showed sharp, well-located concept representations. The team also ran three diagnostic checks: spotting adversarial images, editing images in a controlled way, and holding up under attack perturbations.
arxiv-2509-22315:
Hieu Tran and seven co-authors present PRIME, a reasoning framework that mimics the two modes of human thought described in Thinking, Fast and Slow. Fast, intuitive thinking gives quick answers; slow, deliberate thinking checks and extends them. Their 2025 system, published at AAAI 2026, assigns those roles to agents. A quick thinking agent answers first. If its confidence looks shaky, a slower pipeline takes over.

The slow pipeline is a team of specialists: agents for planning, for generating hypotheses, for retrieving knowledge, for integrating what was found, and for making the final decision. Retrieval is built into the memory of the system, so deliberate reasoning works with grounded facts. In experiments with open LLaMA models, PRIME performed competitively with leading closed models on benchmarks needing multi-step, knowledge-grounded reasoning. The authors present the design as a scalable way to strengthen open models in knowledge-intensive domains.
arxiv-2509-22515:
Pritam Sarkar, Diptiman Sen, and Arnab Sen propose a new marker for quantum phase transitions. Fidelity susceptibility is a known probe of critical points, rooted in information geometry. The team instead tracks the metric response of quantum relative entropy. They compute it from the reduced state of a few neighboring sites in a spin chain as a Hamiltonian parameter varies. A diagonal part of that metric defines a susceptibility that diverges at critical points.

Two spin-half chains serve as tests: the solvable transverse-field Ising model and a non-integrable chain with three-spin terms. The peak grows with system size in distinct ways for each model. The measure also links to other entropy quantities and to the entanglement Hamiltonian.
arxiv-2509-22615:
Yasmine Omri and 3 co-authors replace raw pixels with smooth blobs to feed vision-language models. Sending dense images from edge devices to the cloud costs energy, and patch tokenization makes sequences long. Their alternative uses 2D Gaussian splatting: each image becomes a set of colored, stretched Gaussian blobs. A faster pipeline fits those blobs far quicker than prior code, with pruning guided by brightness.

For alignment, they adapt CLIP training to the blob form. A frozen image transformer is reused with a small new input stem, so only a tenth of parameters train. On a large DataComp set, the encoders matched pixel models on zero-shot tests while shrinking inputs many times over.
arxiv-2509-22715:
Jiho Park and 5 co-authors built a benchmark that tests language assistants on real work constraints. Existing benchmarks miss much of what makes productivity use hard. Prompts are often single-language, constraints stay explicit, and dialogues run one turn. Their benchmark, TRUEBench, spans twelve languages, mixes languages inside single tasks, and runs multi-turn dialogues where constraints pile up or the context switches.

Evaluation criteria capture both stated and implicit constraints in a request. An automated validator refined those constraints to keep scoring reliable. Even a strong frontier model passed only about seven in ten cases overall. The authors present TRUEBench as a demanding, realistic gauge of assistant quality.
arxiv-2509-22915:
Finding distant galaxies that emit Lyman-alpha light has long relied on narrow-band surveys. A Vale and 7 co-authors test whether broad-band photos plus machine learning can find the same galaxies. They trained three gradient boosting models on galaxy data from the COSMOS2020 and SC4K catalogs. The galaxies sit at redshifts from two to six.

Training sets were matched on redshift and brightness to keep scores fair. The models reached F1 scores near eighty-seven percent. All three agreed on about seven thousand new candidates, more than twice the known count in that field. Public spectra confirmed sixty of the candidates as true emitters. The team sees the method as prep work for Euclid and LSST.
arxiv-2509-23015:
María Isabel Cortez and Till Hauser study maps that are almost one-to-one between compact Hausdorff spaces. Such a map may fold a few points together but is one-to-one on most of the space. Any map between spaces also induces maps on probability measures and on closed subsets. The authors ask which traits pass to those induced maps.

They show the measure map is irreducible exactly when the base map is. They also show almost one-to-one behavior passes to both induced maps. For metric spaces, the trait of the subset map matches that of the base map. The note gives fresh proofs of some known results on semi-open maps.
arxiv-2509-23115:
Human movement mixes long-range links with daily and weekly cycles, which makes forecasting hard. Haoyu He and 3 co-authors build RHYTHM, which tokenizes time in a hierarchy. Each trajectory splits into daily segments, coded as discrete tokens. Hierarchical attention reads both daily and weekly patterns. Sequence length drops quadratically while cycle data survive.

Pre-computed prompt embeddings enrich each token before a frozen language model reasons over them. Freezing the backbone cuts training time and memory. On three real data sets, overall accuracy rose by about two point four percent. Weekend scores rose more, and training ran about a quarter faster.
arxiv-2509-23315:
Matrix-valued samples carry spatial structure that flat regression tends to lose. Khang Tran and 5 co-authors built MELCOT, a hybrid model for matrix-valued regression. One block does classical marginal estimation to preserve spatial data. A second block learns an optimal transport cost to capture global traits. Classical and deep strengths thus combine in one design.

Across diverse data sets and domains, MELCOT beat every baseline tried. It stayed highly efficient while doing so. High-dimensional settings are the main target. Storage demands stay lower than many deep rivals, the team note. The marginal block is what keeps the spatial layout intact.
arxiv-2509-23415:
Doctors query health record databases in vague words that rarely match stored values. Gyubok Lee and 7 co-authors built EHR-ChatQA, a benchmark for database agents in that setting. Agents must clarify questions, use tools to fix value mismatches, and write correct SQL. A simulated user, played by a language model, drives the chats. Two flows test distinct habits: adding constraints, and shifting goals mid-chat.

Top agents often solved tasks within five tries on the first flow. Consistent success across all five tries was far lower, with gaps up to about sixty points. Goal-shifting chats proved harder still. The team map failure modes to guide safer agent design.
arxiv-2509-23615:
A graph problem with a Roman flavor asks each site to hold troops so that bare sites have rich neighbors. Sangam Balchandar Reddy, the sole author, studies Roman {3}-domination, where labels run from zero to three. A vertex labeled zero needs neighbor labels summing to at least three, while a one needs at least two. The goal is the smallest total weight, and the problem was already known to be hard on several graph classes.

Reddy proves it stays NP-complete on split graphs and W[2]-hard when parameterized by weight. On the bright side, a polynomial-time algorithm handles block graphs. That settles an open question raised by Chaudhary and Pradhan in 2024.
arxiv-2509-23815:
A missed screw on an assembly line can mean a failed product, and one camera cannot see around corners. Ali Nazeri and 5 co-authors built a quality control module that watches assembly from three camera views at once. Advanced detection algorithms read the views, and a tailored fusion step merges their findings, resolving the ambiguities that plague single-view setups. Extra inspection stations, with their downtime and cost, become unnecessary.

The team also built a public data set of annotated images under varied lighting, occlusion, and angles. In tests the system beat single-view methods on precision and recall for spotting badly fastened small parts like screws.
arxiv-2509-24115:
Defects inside a material often set its traits, but computing their energies from first principles is slow. Evan Dramko and 6 co-authors built ADAPT, a machine-learning force field that skips the graph networks most rivals use. Graph methods can blur long-range effects, which matter a lot around defects.

ADAPT treats each atom as a token and feeds raw coordinates to a transformer that weighs all pairs of atoms. On a data set of silicon point defects, it cut force error by about a fifth and energy error by about two fifths, against a leading graph model. It did so at a fraction of the compute cost. The result points to a lighter route for screening defect behavior at scale.
arxiv-2509-24315: Zhong Yang and Xin-Nian Wang study the diffusion wake left behind by a jet in heavy-ion collisions. The wake has a unique three-dimensional structure, which shows in correlations between the jet and other particles across rapidity and azimuthal angle. A rapidity asymmetry in two-jet events offers a clean way to measure it, since that signal is essentially free of background.
arxiv-2510-00115:
Marton Beke, Olga Plamenevskaya, and Laura Starkston wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the topology of four-dimensional shapes. A surgery called rational blowdown swaps a cluster of spheres inside a shape for a simpler ball. Such clusters usually come from resolving surface singularities, which are pinched points on surfaces. Experts had conjectured that only special, highly regular singularities allow the swap.

The authors exhibit fillings for an infinite family of singularities that break that pattern. These singularities are not weighted homogeneous, yet their contact links still admit the needed disk fillings. The construction borrows from work on sandwiched singularities and uses tools called spinal open books. The result yields a new symplectic version of the blowdown operation. It overturns an expectation in the field and widens the search for exotic four-dimensional shapes.
arxiv-2510-00615:
Kang and seven co-authors from Microsoft and other labs present Acon, a 2025 arXiv framework for language model agents that work on long tasks. Such agents build up long histories of actions and observations, and that growing context raises cost and slows them down. Acon compresses both observations and past interactions into short summaries that keep the key facts.

The team improves the compression rules by comparing runs where full context succeeded but compressed context failed. A large model studies those failures and rewrites the guidelines in plain language. Tests on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and a question-answering benchmark cut peak memory use by roughly a quarter to a half while keeping task scores close to the full-context runs. A distilled small compressor kept over 95 percent of the accuracy in their trials.
arxiv-2510-00815:
Galashov and five co-authors learn the guidance weights of a diffusion model instead of fixing them by hand, in this 2025 arXiv paper on generative modelling. Classifier-free guidance sharpens conditional samples by mixing conditional and unconditional scores with one weight. A weight looks better image by image, yet it drags the sample distribution away from the conditional one. The authors let the weight vary with the conditioning, the current time, and the target time.

They train the weights by minimizing the mismatch between noised samples and samples from the guided process, using a self-consistency condition. The framework extends to reward-guided sampling, where a reward on clean data tilts the distribution. On ImageNet and CelebA the weights improved Fréchet inception distance over static guidance. For text-to-image work with a CLIP-score reward, prompt alignment improved, though a hand-tuned baseline matched it quantitatively.
arxiv-2510-01015:
Lager, Mordant, and Moscovich quantify how noise corrupts the Wasserstein distance between images in this 2025 arXiv paper on optimal transport. Practitioners score image similarity with Wasserstein metrics, treating images as mass spread over a pixel grid. Users suspected the metric shrugs off noise better than the Euclidean norm, but nobody had proved how the error scales. The authors derive non-asymptotic bounds for the signed Wasserstein distance under additive noise.

Their headline result: the error in the signed 2-Wasserstein distance grows with the square root of the noise level, while the Euclidean error grows linearly. Experiments on the DOTMark dataset confirmed the theory, and they expose an odd effect where more noise can shrink the distance. A cryo-electron microscopy case study shows the metric preserving geometric structure where the Euclidean metric fails. The bounds remain loose, which the authors flag as future work.
arxiv-2510-01215:
Kipping argues that observers like us almost certainly do not arise around the universe's most common stars. Red dwarfs host most stars and plenty of rocky planets, yet we orbit an uncommon yellow star instead. We also live absurdly early in the long era when stars will shine.

A Bayesian model weighs two escapes from the coincidence, a cutoff mass below which observers never develop, and a limited time window for observers to appear. Pure luck lost by an overwhelming factor of roughly sixteen hundred. Some truncation of the red dwarf promise proved indispensable in every surviving explanation. The result reframes where searches for complex life should concentrate. The Red Sky Paradox names the older half of the puzzle. Truncated windows would erase the longevity advantage red dwarfs advertise. Our early arrival is data, not vanity in disguise.
arxiv-2510-01315:
Gelli and co-authors simulate where neutral hydrogen hides in and around the first galaxies, so telescope spectra can be read correctly. New space telescope data show strong absorption in young galaxies, but local gas and the space between galaxies both contribute. Untangling them is essential for dating when the universe reionized.

Zoom-in simulations of about a hundred early galaxies generated mock sightlines from their star-forming hearts. Column densities vary with radius, halo mass, and cosmic time in mapped patterns. Local envelopes prove thick enough to mimic some intergalactic absorption. Interpreting the newest spectra demands this local correction first. Star-forming peaks anchor every mock sightline in the study. The serra simulation suite supplies the galaxy sample. Redshift evolution shows local gas thinning as reionization proceeds. Damped absorption features triggered the whole investigation. Circumgalactic gas deserves equal billing with the interstellar share.
arxiv-2510-01715:
Durairaju and Saruladha present PyramidStyler in this 2025 computer vision paper on neural style transfer. Style transfer redraws a photo in the manner of a painting or artwork. Older neural methods struggled with complex styles and large, high-resolution images. Transformers helped, but they still carried a heavy computing cost at fine scales.

PyramidStyler adds a pyramidal positional encoding, which records position at several scales at once. That design captures local detail and global layout while cutting the computing load. A reinforcement learning step then tunes the stylization during training, which speeds convergence. Trained on COCO photos and WikiArt images, the system cut both content loss and style loss by more than half. It produced a stylized image in well under two seconds, fast enough for practical media work.
arxiv-2510-01915:
McLatchie, Chérief-Abdellatif, Frazier, and Knoblauch rebuild the Bayesian posterior around prediction in this 2025 statistics paper. Classical Bayes quantifies uncertainty about parameters, yet modern practice often cares about prediction first. When the model is wrong, standard posteriors concentrate anyway and report false confidence. Their predictively oriented posterior instead ties uncertainty directly to predictive ability.

The new posterior beats both classic and generalized Bayes forecasts. It converges to the best model average at the best possible rate, up to log factors. Classic methods match that rate only when the model can truly recover the process behind the data. When the model is wrong, the new posterior refuses to narrow and settles at an honest level of leftover doubt. That leftover doubt reads directly as a measure of the model's error. A particle method based on Langevin dynamics makes it samplable in practice. Examples confirm the theory.
arxiv-2510-02015:
Anglés-Castillo and five co-authors review imaginary time evolution methods for finding quantum ground states in this 2025 paper. Many hard problems encode their solutions as the ground state of a Hamiltonian. Evolving a state in imaginary time filters it toward that ground state, but the evolution is not unitary and cannot run directly on quantum hardware. Two algorithms work around that obstacle.

Quantum imaginary time evolution approximates each non-unitary step with unitary operations a quantum computer can execute. Its variational sibling, varQITE, updates a parameterized circuit by natural gradient descent on the energy. The variational route is generally easier to implement on near-term devices. The paper reviews the original algorithm step by step and supplies a comprehensive computer program alongside it. It also explains how the variational form connects to the exact method. The review and code lower the entry barrier to ground-state work.
arxiv-2510-02315:
Bill, Simsar, and Hofmann use control theory to fix multi-subject image prompts. Their 2025 machine learning paper names a familiar failure. Text-to-image models handle one subject well. With several subjects, traits leak between them. Colors swap, faces blend, and subjects vanish. The authors view flow matching generation as a control problem. Steering the sampler becomes an optimizable goal. They derive two methods from that view. One steers sampling at test time with no training. The other, Adjoint Matching, fine-tunes a small control network.

Both methods ran on three major generators. Stable Diffusion and FLUX models all improved in subject fidelity. Base style and quality stayed intact during the gains. The framework also explains older attention tricks in one language. It extends to diffusion models through a known correspondence. Multi-subject prompts finally get a principled steering tool.
arxiv-2510-02615:
Bradley and co-authors detect a famous massive star and its shell in a new radio sky survey. Their astronomy paper reports results from the Evolutionary Map of the Universe. The survey runs on the ASKAP telescope array in Australia. Its radio images caught the Wolf-Rayet star WR40 clearly. A glowing shell, RCW 58, surrounds the star. The team measured the shell at a frequency near nine hundred forty megahertz. Gaia distances set the shell's true physical size. Flux measurements covered both the star and the shell.

The shell spans roughly seven by five parsecs across. The star sits about two point eight kiloparsecs away. Its radio spectrum marks the emission as thermal in nature. The shell stayed too faint for a firm spectral verdict. Earlier telescope data filled in the higher frequencies. Next generation telescopes should settle the shell's nature. Dying massive stars keep reshaping their surroundings.
arxiv-2510-02815:
Yuan and co-authors address a common gap in medical care. A full diagnosis often needs several kinds of scans. Patients rarely have every kind on hand. Scans may be missing due to cost, time, or machine access. Their system, Med-K2N, builds the missing scans from whichever ones exist. It can turn any set of inputs into any set of outputs.

Three modules judge how much each input scan should count. They weigh inputs, filter out noisy ones, and refine the mix. A fourth module keeps each output true to its target type. It uses a vision-language model to enforce that match. The design borrows the step-by-step style of a doctor's workflow. In benchmark tests, Med-K2N beat the best prior methods by clear margins. Flexible synthesis like this could fill gaps in real patient records.
arxiv-2510-03015:
Chevalier and Viseur improve a numerical method for two-body quantum problems. The Lagrange-mesh method expands a state on points of a chosen mesh. Smart quadrature then makes the needed integrals simple. The method shines in position space for many systems. Some problems, though, are better stated in momentum space. Exotic motion and momentum-based forces live there naturally. A momentum version existed, but it choked on key forces.

Coulomb and linear forces were beyond the older version. The new scheme computes the potential terms in a fresh way. It borrows a strategy from semi-relativistic work in position space. Now any kinematics and any potential can be handled. Tests checked the method against exact Coulomb results. A model of mesons gave a second, applied check. Position and momentum densities both came out with care. Hadron physics is one field that works in momentum terms.
arxiv-2510-03415:
Thimmaiah and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper that tests whether language models can run programs by following formal rules. If a model could act as an interpreter from a semantics alone, new languages could be prototyped at once. Their benchmark, PLSemanticsBench, uses a small C-like language with rules written in two formal styles. Programs come from humans, from model translation, and from a fuzzer, with difficulty tuned by size and control flow.

Models must predict final states, next rule choices, or full execution traces. Under standard rules, models scored high, even on programs with nested loops. Under mutated rules with the same surface look, scores fell sharply, which exposes memorized habits over rule reading. Giving the formal rules helped on simple programs but often hurt on complex ones. The results show promise for model based interpreters, paired with a warning that grasp of semantics is not there yet.
arxiv-2510-03515:
Huang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on speeding up reinforcement learning for small language models. Small models run on phones and laptops, and learning from their own successes can sharpen them for math or coding. Standard reinforcement learning, though, wastes time by swapping between generating text and updating weights. Their algorithm, RAPID, generates in very large batches first. It then applies many small off policy updates drawn from that stored batch.

A group advantage estimate and an importance weighted correction keep those recycled updates honest. Across three benchmarks, RAPID cut running time by between eleven and thirty four percent in the reported runs. Accuracy stayed similar or improved against leading reinforcement learning methods at the same time. The authors also study how stale samples affect quality and clip extreme weights at the generation level. Faster tuning matters most exactly where small models live: on modest hardware with tight budgets.
arxiv-2510-03615:
Polachini and Marques present a 2025 arXiv paper reporting a light bending investigation carried out by high school students in Brazil. Light rays curve when they cross a gradient in refractive index, the same effect behind mirages like the Fata Morgana. The students used a rectangular aquarium filled with sugar solutions, and with a temperature gradient in water. They photographed the distorted images and worked out when the image flips upside down.

Within their setup, the sugar concentration gradient bent light more usefully than the temperature gradient did. They derived an equation predicting a ray's path from its entry angle, the starting refractive index, and how fast the index changes with height. Using it, they reconstructed a distorted image that matched their photographs. The project needed only cheap materials and pre-calculus level ideas stretched by research. It shows how an atmospheric mystery can anchor physics learning in a classroom.
arxiv-2510-03915:
Bharadwaj and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on a shared positioning backbone for augmented reality. AR apps must know exactly where a device is, so digital content stays anchored to real places. Big firms run visual positioning services for public outdoor spaces, but private indoor spaces stay uncovered for privacy and upkeep reasons. The authors propose letting each organization run its own service for its own spaces instead.

Their system, OpenFLAME, federates many independent positioning services into one client experience. It handles finding the right local service, keeping results consistent across boundaries, and merging maps without exposing private scans. Each operator keeps access control over its indoor maps and maintains them on its own schedule. Tests with scanned university rooms showed accurate, efficient localization. Federation could widen coverage far beyond what one firm would scan, and it spreads upkeep across many owners.
arxiv-2510-04115:
Giapitzakis and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper proving that semiautomata are hard to learn from statistical queries. Semiautomata process sequences by updating internal states, and they appear in language processing, robotics, and biology. The statistical query model captures most noise-tolerant learning algorithms, including gradient methods. This paper locates hardness inside the transition structure itself.

The authors show hardness when alphabet size and input length grow polynomially in the number of states, under uniform inputs and initial states. Their proof reduces the problem to a random walk on a product of symmetric groups. Fourier analysis and representation theory yield tight spectral gap bounds for that walk. After polynomially many steps, distinct semiautomata become nearly uncorrelated, so queries cannot tell them apart. That decorrelation forces any statistical query learner to ask an infeasible number of questions. The result maps a fundamental limit for learning state machines from aggregate data.
arxiv-2510-04315:
Ouyang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on predicting spatial gene expression from ordinary stained tissue images. Spatial transcriptomics maps gene activity across tissue but costs too much for routine use, while H&E images are abundant and cheap. Earlier predictors treated each gene independently and regressed continuous values, ignoring co-expression structure and the discrete count nature of expression. Those mismatches can produce biologically implausible maps.

Their framework, GenAR, generates expression autoregressively from coarse to fine scales. Genes are clustered into hierarchical groups so cross-gene dependencies enter the generation order. Expression is modeled as discrete token generation, predicting raw counts without any learned codebook. Decoding conditions on fused histological and spatial embeddings from the image. Across four spatial transcriptomics datasets spanning tissue types, GenAR reached state-of-the-art accuracy. Cheaper molecular profiling from routine slides could widen access to spatial biology.
arxiv-2510-04415:
Kazuhito Ohmi, Hitoshi Fukuma, and Shinji Terui of KEK in Japan wrote this 2025 paper on a hazard inside particle colliders. Modern electron and positron beams carry far more energy in a tight stream than older beams did. Dust grains inside the beam pipe can heat up, charge up, and turn into a small plasma cloud.

The team simulated how a dust grain and a beam affect each other over time. The beam heats the grain until it starts to evaporate and shed electrons. The charged cloud then pushes back on the beam and makes its spread grow. In the real machine, losses strike within a few turns, with no warning wobble first. They happen most at high beam current, and they can quench nearby superconducting magnets. The simulations trace the early stages of that chain. The work helps operators judge how dust limits higher beam currents.
arxiv-2510-04515:
Emile Bouaziz wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a refinement of differential forms. The chiral de Rham complex attaches a vertex algebra to a smooth variety, blending geometry with structures from conformal field theory. Bouaziz extends the construction to a variety paired with a divisor where the forms may have log poles. The divisor has simple normal crossings.

He proves basic structural results about the new sheaf of vertex algebras. Its lowest weight part recovers the algebra of forms with log poles along the divisor. When the complement of the divisor carries a volume form, the sheaf gains a topological structure whose rank equals the dimension. When the divisor is anticanonical, that structure extends further. A character built from the pair then lands as a section of a named line bundle on an elliptic curve. The construction also admits a description through a birational change to the space of jets.
arxiv-2510-04615:
Tao and four coauthors at the Polytechnic University of Madrid wrote this 2025 paper on the design of a rehabilitation game platform. Serious games can keep patients doing therapy exercises at home, where sticking with a program is hard. Their platform, Blexer, already went through two versions in clinical work. Blexer version three is a redesign that aims to sense the user, reason, and adapt the games. The paper lays out the full design before a prototype is built.

The design splits the system into modules for data collection, state inference, and gameplay adaptation. Wearable and behavioral signals feed the state module during play. Two adaptation engines adjust difficulty on the fly and generate content as skills change. That loop aims to keep each patient in the narrow band between boredom and frustration. The authors present the framework and its data flow as the base for the next build phase.
arxiv-2510-04815:
Lorenzo Zapparoli, Blazhe Gjorgiev, and Giovanni Sansavini wrote this 2025 paper on selling backup power from pools of small energy devices. Grids with more wind and solar need reserve capacity to stay stable. Virtual power plants bundle home batteries, solar roofs, and flexible loads into one market actor. Buyers of reserve demand reliability, durations, and prices. The authors built a method to judge what a pool can promise.

First they compute the reserve the pool can deliver under forecast uncertainty. A subset simulation technique makes that uncertain calculation efficient. Then they price the offer, counting both costs and the earnings given up elsewhere. Tests used a model of a Swiss low voltage network with a device portfolio. The pool could offer reserve products reliably in their study. Opportunity costs, not hardware costs, drove the prices. Product rules, such as how long reserves last, strongly changed how much the pool could offer.
arxiv-2510-05115:
Yansen Zhang and seven co-authors fix a quiet failure mode of AI-written optimization models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language models can turn a word problem into solver code. The code often runs fine yet encodes the wrong problem. Such semantic errors slip past solver error messages completely.

Their framework, SAC-Opt, checks the generated model against the original problem's meaning. It extracts semantic anchors from the description, then reconstructs anchors from the code. Only the mismatched pieces get corrected, step by step. Across seven public datasets, average modeling accuracy rose by 7.8 percent. On the hardest dataset, ComplexLP, the gain reached 21.9 percent. No extra training or supervision was needed.
arxiv-2510-05315:
Yousef Yeganeh and five co-authors turn ordinary microscopes into slide scanners in this 2025 arXiv paper. Digitizing pathology slides usually needs costly whole-slide scanners. Cheaper microscopes drift out of focus across uneven tissue. Older auto-focus methods capture slow stacks of images at many depths.

Their model, DeepAf, predicts the needed focus shift from a single image. It fuses spatial and spectral features in a hybrid network. The system cut focusing time by 80 percent versus stack-based methods. Focus accuracy reached 0.18 micrometers on same-lab samples, matching two-image methods with half the input. On 536 brain tissue samples, the scanner's images supported cancer classification at 0.90 AUC. Cross-lab tests showed few false focus calls, aiding low-resource clinics.
arxiv-2510-05515:
Rajguru and colleagues chart how the brightest beamed quasars are spread across cosmic time. Flat-spectrum radio quasars are galaxies whose jets point nearly straight at Earth. Their gamma-ray glow makes them visible across most of the observable universe. The 2025 paper builds their luminosity function from the largest such sample yet.

The sample holds 519 quasars found by the Fermi telescope, with well-measured detection limits. Nearby, the counts follow a double power law in brightness. Looking deeper, the population grows with distance up to a peak and then fades. Brighter quasars peak earlier in cosmic history than fainter ones. Selection effects in the sample are unusually well understood. Oddly, the pattern closely matches a sister class, BL Lac objects, at mid-range brightness. That match hints at a family link between the two blazar classes, or at mixed-up samples.
arxiv-2510-06015:
Stevenson and Das audit the privacy and security practices of mobile health apps in a 2025 study. Health apps promise easy contact between patients and providers, but they also handle protected health information on phones. The authors examined 272 Android health apps listed on Google Play. Three analysis tools supplied the technical evidence for the audit.

The audit combined permission checks, static scans for known weaknesses, and mining of about 2.56 million user reviews. About 26 percent of the apps requested precise location without disclosing that fact to users. Nearly half still used the deprecated SHA-1 method for encryption, and dozens sent data without any encryption at all. More than 553,000 reviews mentioned privacy intrusions, data misuse, or unstable behavior. The authors call for enforceable permission transparency and security checks before such apps reach the market.
arxiv-2510-06115:
Gribling and three co-authors connect quantum mechanics with convex optimization in a 2025 paper. A spectral gap measures how fast a quantum system settles and governs adiabatic algorithm speed. The team studies Schrödinger operators built from self-concordant barriers, the functions steering classical interior point methods.

They prove concrete lower bounds on the gap for this operator family. The key move replaces the flat Laplacian with the Laplace–Beltrami operator, which senses barrier curvature through second-order information. With that change, the gap stops depending on the problem's condition number. Ill-conditioned problems no longer force a tiny gap and slow evolution. They turn the bound into a quantum interior point method for arbitrary self-concordant barriers, again without condition-number dependence. The construction blends semiclassical analysis, convex optimization, and quantum annealing. It widens the class of problems where quantum methods could plausibly help.
arxiv-2510-06315:
Danhaive and seventeen co-authors link galaxy sizes, motions, and star formation in the early universe with JWST in a 2025 astrophysics paper. How galaxies assembled mass in the first billion years remains a central question. Joint measurements of sizes and internal motions have been scarce.

The team studied two hundred thirteen galaxies at redshifts four to six from two JWST grism surveys. A new Bayesian tool called geko measured each galaxy's hydrogen-alpha size and kinematics. Stellar continuum sizes came from JADES imaging. Near redshift five, hydrogen-alpha spans about 1.2 kiloparsecs, wider than the roughly 0.9-kiloparsec stellar continuum. Continuum sizes showed no wavelength trend, so steady inside-out growth had not begun. Galaxies bursting above the star-forming main sequence showed expanded gas and stronger rotation, hinting at accreting gas. About half of the most elongated systems lack rotational support, suggesting a flattened, prolate population.
arxiv-2510-06915:
Zecheng Tang and colleagues at Soochow University probe a blind spot in the models that grade AI answers. Their 2025 paper studies reward models, which score responses so language models can align with human preferences. Real tasks now involve long histories, like agent trajectories. A good answer must stay consistent with that long context, yet reward models are mostly tested on short ones.

Their benchmark, Long-RewardBench, grades reward models on long-context tasks in two formats. Early tests showed even top generative reward models wobble badly as context grows. The team then trained LongRM to close that gap. Their eight-billion-parameter model beat much larger seventy-billion baselines on the new benchmark. It matched the proprietary Gemini 2.5 Pro system there. Short-context skill stayed strong on the standard RewardBench suite. Reliable grading over long histories matters as agents take on longer jobs.
arxiv-2510-07115:
Kazmierczak and co-authors study a trust problem in image software in their 2025 paper. Some models explain their choices with plain concepts, such as naming the parts they see. These models often rely on CLIP, a popular image and text system. The authors show that CLIP can claim a concept is present when it is not. Such false claims make the explanations hard to trust.

The team answers with a method called CHILI. It splits the image code into parts tied to the object, the setting, and leftover noise. It then finds the exact pixels that match a target concept. In tests, this split removed much of the misleading pull of the background. The method also yields heat maps that people can read more easily. More faithful concept maps could help doctors and lawyers check what a model truly saw.
arxiv-2510-07215:
Xu and a large team introduce SpectraNet, a neural network that reads the spectra of fleeting cosmic events. Their 2025 paper is the second from the AppleCiDEr project. Sky surveys now find vast numbers of short-lived flashes, from exploding stars to flaring objects. Color-spread spectra reveal what each event is, but older template methods miss their complexity. SpectraNet learns features directly from low-resolution spectra instead. Its filters work at several scales to catch broad and fine structure.

Trained on spectra from a dedicated survey instrument and others, the network set new marks for event classification. It also predicted cosmic distances from spectra with very low error. The pipeline around it is built for production use. Automated tools like this are vital for the coming era of giant sky surveys. They will sort millions of events far faster than human experts.
arxiv-2510-07615:
Kosec and thirteen coauthors report 2025 X-ray observations of Hercules X-1, a well-known X-ray binary. The system pairs a neutron star with a companion star and a warped, slowly precessing accretion disk. That warped disk lets astronomers view the disk wind from many heights. The team used the new XRISM observatory, supported by XMM-Newton, NuSTAR, and Chandra.

Their spectra resolve the iron lines from the wind in unusual detail. The team directly detects the binary's orbital motion in the changing outflow speed. After correction, the wind speed rises from about 250 to 600 kilometers per second with height. The wind's gas density falls with height, while its ionization changes only weakly. The data also reveal a brief second wind component that appears just after eclipse. Such winds can carry away a large share of the infalling matter.
arxiv-2510-07815:
Sun and five coauthors wrote this 2025 software engineering paper on fuzz testing MLIR, a compiler infrastructure used across many domains. Fuzzers hunt bugs by feeding programs inputs. Template and rule-based fuzzers struggle to make diverse, valid tests for MLIR's complex grammar. The authors present FLEX, a fuzzer that learns as it explores. It starts from a small seed corpus and improves its own generator over time.

FLEX generates programs with a neural network and perturbs sampling to force variety. A feedback loop retrains the model on crashing and clean test cases. In a thirty-day campaign, FLEX found eighty unknown bugs, including root causes and parser flaws. In day-long comparisons, it found fifty-three bugs, over three times the best rival, with coverage above twenty-eight percent. Ablations showed both perturbation and diversity feedback were key. Self-teaching fuzzers may harden other fast-moving compiler systems as well.
arxiv-2510-07915:
Wu and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on making video understanding far cheaper. Video floods a model with tokens, and long clips make inference cost explode. Simple token merging cuts cost but throws away information and hurts accuracy. The authors propose MARC, a retrieve-then-compress method trained with reinforcement learning. A visual memory retriever splits the video into event pieces and picks clips a question needs.

A teacher-student training scheme then distills full-video reasoning into the compressed student. Their compression variant of group relative policy optimization drives that transfer. Across six video benchmarks, MARC matched a sixty-four-frame baseline's accuracy while using one frame's worth of tokens. Visual tokens fell by ninety-five percent in that setup. GPU memory dropped by nearly three quarters, and generation latency fell by about a quarter. The authors target real-time question answering and surveillance, where budgets are tight.
arxiv-2510-08015:
Xing and Chen wrote this 2025 wireless engineering paper on building indoor radio maps without labeled calibration data. Radio maps predict signal strength across a space and guide localization. Making them usually demands costly surveys that tag channel measurements with exact positions. The authors instead recover the survey path itself from the channel data. A hidden Markov framework does the joint job of explaining the signals and the movement.

Channel behavior is modeled separately for line-of-sight and blocked conditions, across power, delay, and angle. The walking path follows a Gaussian-Markov motion model. All parameters are fitted together in alternating steps. Experiments on simulated multi-antenna networks reached average localization error well under a meter. That beat traditional baselines and nearly matched supervised methods, with better noise handling. Skipping calibration could make indoor positioning cheap enough for ordinary buildings, warehouses, and hospitals.
arxiv-2510-08415:
Leonardo Ferreira, Haroon Mumtaz, and Ana Skoblar add time-varying skewness to a macroeconomic forecasting model in a 2025 arXiv paper. Vector autoregressions track how variables like output, inflation, and spreads move together over time. Stochastic volatility lets the size of shocks change, a standard feature in such models. Skewness, the lopsidedness of shocks toward booms or crashes, is usually held fixed.

Their Bayesian model lets both volatility and skewness shift over time and feed back into the economy. Older models allowed volatility this direct effect but not skewness. They supply a Gibbs sampling algorithm to estimate the model on quarterly United States and United Kingdom data. Skewness shocks had economically significant effects, often larger than volatility shocks. In pseudo-real-time forecasts, the model beat existing alternatives in many cases. It also showed standard models tend to overstate tail uncertainty.
arxiv-2510-08515:
Georgios Karaiskos and co-authors ask how hard it is to verify a classical shadow of a quantum state, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Classical shadows are compact classical summaries built from few measurements, predicting many state properties. Verification asks whether a given shadow truly matches some quantum state's statistics. The authors initiate a complexity-theoretic study of this shadow validity problem.

For the elegant local Clifford shadow protocol, verification is QMA-complete, as hard as the canonical quantum verification class. Hardness persists for a recent high-dimensional extension of that protocol. In contrast, global Clifford protocols can be dequantized for low-rank observables, meaning randomized classical algorithms solve them under standard sampling assumptions. For exponentially many observables, the problem is complete for a quantum analogue of the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. That gives the first natural problem shown complete for such a class, they note.
arxiv-2510-08615:
Kaiqi Yang and co-authors generate harder math word problems by adding distracting conditions with language models, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Most problem sets contain only necessary information, so models never learn to ignore noise. Prior tests showed dramatic performance drops when irrelevant conditions appear. Existing distractor data sets are small, easy, and sometimes out of context, weakening their credibility.

Their iterative framework prompts models to revise problems from varied perspectives and cognitive levels. Each round adds distracting conditions plus suggestions for the next revision, building difficulty gradually. Crucially, generation is guided so distractors never change the original solution. Original and revised problems thus share answers, avoiding costly new solution writing and checking. The framework is efficient and easy to deploy, the authors say. It lowers the overhead of building credible distractor-rich benchmarks for reasoning research.
arxiv-2510-08815:
Newman and a large team release the data of a major sky survey that maps both galaxies and the gas between them, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The LATIS survey used a spectrograph on the Magellan Baade telescope in Chile to gather light from faint, distant galaxies. Many sit at cosmic noon, the era when star formation peaked across the universe. Long exposures, often around twelve hours per field, split that light into spectra.

The release holds more than seven thousand spectra and over five thousand firm distance measurements, most far beyond our cosmic neighborhood. Dimming patterns inside the spectra trace hydrogen gas between the galaxies across hundreds of thousands of sight lines. From those the team built three-dimensional maps of the gas, the largest of their kind to date. The maps and spectra are public, ready for studies of galaxy growth and the environments around galaxies.
arxiv-2510-09115:
Arslandok reports on how wobbles and correlations in particle debris reveal the inner life of quark-gluon plasma, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Colliding heavy nuclei at near light speed melts matter into this plasma, letting physicists map how it changes with temperature and density. At the highest energies the melt appears to be a smooth crossover from ordinary matter. At higher densities theory expects a critical point where the change turns sharp, and finding it is a headline goal.

Fluctuations, the event-to-event jitter in particle counts, and correlations between particles are sensitive probes of that landscape. They carry news of the system's dynamics and of which kind of transition it passed through. The report surveys recent experimental results across a broad sweep of collision energies, from programs in the United States and Europe. It weighs what the pattern of results implies for the current map of quantum chromodynamics.
arxiv-2510-09215:
Muppaneni, Yogesh, and Chockalingam blend two estimation tricks so a future wireless receiver can read fast-moving channels more accurately, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Zak-OTFS is a modulation scheme for high-mobility links, organizing signals by delay and Doppler shift. Its receiver must learn the channel's input-output relation before detecting data. A model-free method reads that relation off a pilot frame, but only inside one small region of the delay-Doppler plane.

The missing outside region hurts when the pulse shape spreads widely. The hybrid adds a model-dependent estimate, built from physical path parameters, covering that outer region, then merges both estimates. In simulations over standard vehicle and tapped-delay channels, it clearly beat the model-free method. One configuration gained about three and a half decibels. Performance approached a far heavier Bayesian method at a fraction of its cost.
arxiv-2510-09315:
Siu-Kui Au and Zi-Jun Cao study reliability sensitivity in a 2025 arXiv paper on engineering risk. Engineers want to know how the chance of failure shifts when a system parameter changes, since that guides safer design choices. The task is harder than computing the failure chance itself, which already strains under many random inputs, rare failures, and black-box responses.

The authors present a theory that expresses the sensitivity at a given response level through the average response gradient at that level. A gradient measures how fast the response changes with the parameter. Because hitting one exact level is a zero-chance event, they use kernel smoothing to estimate the average from nearby samples. One Monte Carlo run then yields sensitivity estimates for all response levels at once. They test the method on examples with very different kinds of sensitivity parameters.
arxiv-2510-09415:
Beige Jerry Jin and Leila Wehbe combine two brain imaging methods in a 2025 arXiv paper. Magnetoencephalography, or MEG, tracks brain activity with fine timing but blurry location, while functional MRI gives sharp location with slow timing. Getting both at once for natural behaviour, such as listening to stories, has remained an open problem.

The authors recorded whole-head MEG while people listened to more than seven hours of spoken stories, matching an existing open fMRI dataset with the same stories. Their transformer-based encoding model learns from both signals across several subjects at once, with a hidden layer that stands for the estimated cortical sources. The model predicted MEG better than single-signal models, and its source estimates beat classic minimum-norm solutions in simulations. The estimates also generalised to new subjects, and predicted direct brain recordings in a separate dataset better than a model trained on those recordings.
arxiv-2510-09615:
Meiyin Meng and Zaixi Zhang build a biosecurity agent for language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Models now assist across biomedical research, from reading literature to designing experiments, and that usefulness raises dual-use risks, such as help with toxic compound synthesis. The authors guard the whole model lifecycle with four coordinated modes rather than a single filter.

The first mode sanitises training data, tested on the CORD-19 coronavirus set at three strictness tiers. Removal rates rose from under half a percent to over seventy percent, exposing a safety-utility trade-off. Preference alignment then taught refusals, cutting attack success from about sixty percent to three percent. Runtime guardrails formed the third mode, with the middle tier balancing detection and false alarms best. Under continuous automated red teaming, the fourth mode, no jailbreak succeeded under the tested protocol. The authors present the system as auditable protection across a model's life.
arxiv-2510-09915:
Huang, Qianqi Yan, Shengze Wang, and Ian Lane tackle unfaithful summaries in this 2025 arXiv paper on natural language processing. Large language models write fluent summaries, but they sometimes add claims the source never made, at the level of a word, a phrase, or a whole concept. Such slips are called hallucinations.

The authors propose span-level fine-tuning, extra training aimed at the exact text spans where faithfulness breaks. Earlier fixes, such as correcting output after the fact or training against synthetic bad summaries, do not cover the full range of errors. Training on the faulty spans themselves targets each error type more directly. The goal is summaries that readers can trust to stick to the source.
arxiv-2510-10215:
Gupta, Ravi Banavar, and Anastasia Bizyaeva bound the validity of bifurcation analysis in networked systems in this 2025 arXiv paper on dynamical systems. Local bifurcation analysis predicts qualitative transitions in networks of interacting units, from neural networks to opinion dynamics. But local results hold only near the bifurcation point, and how near is usually unknown.

The authors establish explicit validity bounds for bifurcation diagrams across two classes of networked systems that evolve in continuous time. The classes mirror the Hopfield and firing rate models of neural dynamics. With explicit bounds, modelers know the range in which the classified transitions can be trusted. That turns a qualitative sketch into a tool with a stated range of safe use.
arxiv-2510-10315:
Steinacker-Olsztyn, Devashish Gosain, and Ha Dao compare robots.txt rules on news and misinformation sites in this 2025 arXiv study of the web. Language models increasingly crawl the web to stay current, and crawlers are expected to respect robots.txt files, the files that set access rules for automated visitors.

The authors ask, for the first time, whether reputable news outlets and misinformation sites configure these files differently, especially toward AI crawlers. If misinformation sites are more open to crawling, AI systems may ingest them more freely than careful journalism. That asymmetry would shape what models learn and repeat. The study treats a small technical file as a gatekeeper with outsized effects on the information ecosystem.
arxiv-2510-10415:
Bologna and co-authors present LongQAEval in this 2025 arXiv paper on evaluating clinical question answering. Long-form clinical answers are hard to judge: accurate scoring needs medical expertise, and human judges struggle to stay consistent over long texts. Evaluation is therefore resource-intensive exactly where stakes are highest.

LongQAEval is a framework plus a set of recommendations for limited-resource, high-expertise settings. It is designed to make evaluations of long clinical answers reliable without unlimited expert hours. The authors address how to sample, who should judge, and how to check agreement. Trustworthy evaluation is the gate through which clinical QA systems must pass before deployment near patients.
arxiv-2510-10815:
Meiru Zhang and three co-authors improve how language models turn informal mathematics into formal, machine checked statements, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Autoformalization is hard because models must find the prerequisite knowledge and its formal shape in a language like Lean. Existing retrieval methods query math libraries with the raw informal statement, but such statements map poorly onto library theorems. Their framework, DRIFT, first decomposes the statement into smaller sub components.

Targeted retrieval then finds premises for each piece from libraries such as Mathlib. DRIFT also retrieves illustrative theorems that show the model how to use those premises. Across the ProofNet, ConNF, and MiniF2F benchmarks, DRIFT consistently improved premise retrieval, nearly doubling the F1 score over a standard baseline on ProofNet. On the out of distribution ConNF benchmark, gains reached 42.25 percent with one model and 37.14 percent with another in their reported runs.
arxiv-2510-11015:
How long a line of waiting jobs can grow in a system with many servers is a basic question in queueing theory. Yige Hong studies the classic GI/GI/n queue, where arrivals and service times follow general distributions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A 2025 breakthrough by Li and Goldberg gave bounds with the correct scaling, but with large constant factors and a highly intricate proof.

Hong proves a new bound with the same scaling as the load approaches full use, restricted to light-tailed cases and the average queue length. Its leading constant is easier to interpret and often tighter than the earlier one. The proof uses a modified queue, a quadratic test function held stationary, and a new leave-one-out coupling technique. The method also extends to queues in which the servers have fully different service-time distributions from one another.
arxiv-2510-11215:
Globular clusters host millisecond pulsars, whose winds should glow in gamma rays from giga-electronvolt to tera-electronvolt energies, yet such detections are rare. Jiwon Shin and co-authors report the second case in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper, for the globular cluster UKS 1. They combine sixteen years of Fermi Large Area Telescope data with 1523 days of survey data from the HAWC Observatory.

The gamma-ray spectrum suggests the GeV emission comes from both pulsar magnetospheres and inverse Compton scattering by the pulsar wind. The TeV peak sits displaced from the cluster center by several tidal radii, in the trailing direction of the cluster's motion. That alignment supports a picture where particles driven by the millisecond pulsar population scatter light inside a bow-shock tail behind the moving cluster. The authors argue the offset TeV feature offers a rare probe of cosmic-ray transport in the Milky Way.
arxiv-2510-11315:
Insurance and finance losses are heavy-tailed: extreme events happen far more often than a bell curve predicts, so risk models need distributions with fat tails. Pankaj Kumar and Vivek Vijay build such a distribution in this 2025 arXiv statistics paper. Their model mixes Gaussian and Rayleigh distributions through an arctangent transformation, a construction built to produce heavier tails and fit real market data.

The authors work out statistical properties of the new model and then apply the actuarial risk instruments to it. These include value-at-risk, tail value-at-risk, and tail variance, tools estimating losses in the worst slice of cases. An application to an insurance dataset shows the proposed model fitting better than baseline distributions. The mixture was especially good at representing the extreme market behavior and tail dependencies that appear in real financial data, which is where ordinary models fail worst.
arxiv-2510-11615:
Knowledge distillation compresses a big model into a small one by training the student on the teacher's output probabilities, but standard recipes treat every token alike with one fixed temperature. Xurong Xie and co-authors make distillation adaptive in AdaKD, presented in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. A unified token difficulty metric, tracked during training, drives two modules that respond to how well the student is actually learning each token.

The first module, Loss-driven Adaptive Token Focusing, watches the student's learning stability and concentrates computation on the most valuable tokens. The second, Inverse Difficulty Temperature Scaling, does something counterintuitive: it applies low temperatures to difficult tokens, sharpening the teacher's signal for targeted error correction. It applies high temperatures to easy tokens, so the student absorbs the teacher's smooth distribution. As a plug-and-play framework, AdaKD improved distillation methods across architectures and benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-11915:
Deeksha Hareesha Kulal and four colleagues build a phishing detector for the age of AI-written bait. Old phishing emails betrayed themselves with typos and clumsy phrasing. Modern ones, drafted by large language models, read cleanly and naturally. Adversaries also perturb text deliberately to slip past filters. Their 2025 arXiv paper answers with a detection system built around tougher text preprocessing.

The pipeline corrects spelling and splits merged words before analysis, undoing common adversarial tricks. Standard language features then feed machine learning classifiers. On public datasets mixing phishing and legitimate mail, the deployed model reached about ninety-four percent accuracy with a solid F1 score. The team stress-tested robustness two ways. They attacked the detector with four methods from the TextAttack framework, and they fed it fresh phishing written by ChatGPT and Llama. The models held up well in both trials, showing resilience against AI-powered phishing.
arxiv-2510-12115:
Xin Zhao, Naoki Yoshinaga, Yuma Tsuta, and Akiko Aizawa watch a bilingual model learn medicine in two languages at once. Multilingual domain adaptation teaches language models new specialties across languages, but nobody knew exactly how facts learned in one language surface in another. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies those acquisition dynamics in English-Japanese biomedical adaptation.

Because earlier studies trained and tested on mismatched material, the team built AdaXEval, which generates multiple-choice questions from the very bilingual corpus used for training. Continual training runs with varied data recipes then reveal how domain facts are absorbed and transformed. The testbed is a thirteen-billion-parameter bilingual model. Despite a high-quality bilingual corpus, cross-lingual transfer remains stubbornly hard: knowledge planted in English blooms there far more reliably than in Japanese. The released code gives other teams a clean instrument for dissecting transfer.
arxiv-2510-12415:
Brunner and colleagues apply renormalization group ideas directly to snapshot data from quantum simulators, in a 2025 arXiv condensed matter paper. Quantum simulators now record snapshots, single measurements that fix every particle's configuration at once. Such datasets are rich but hard to interpret without shrinking them to simple correlations and losing information.

Their SnapshotRG is an exact renormalization transformation that works on the snapshot dataset itself, in real space or in the abstract space of measurement configurations. It can run on data from numerical methods such as neural quantum states or from any simulation platform. The authors show that snapshot datasets become self similar at continuous phase transitions, which explains the recently observed scale freeness of wavefunction networks. Scale invariance therefore extends beyond low order correlation functions to the full statistical structure of the state. The tool offers a general way to characterize quantum phase transitions and critical behavior.
arxiv-2510-12615:
Mason-Williams and colleagues argue that knowledge distillation, the standard trick of training a small student model on a big teacher's outputs, transfers less knowledge than assumed. It preferentially transfers the bad parts, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Distillation is usually judged by the student's accuracy, treated as compression.
