The authors instead measure its functional impact, decoupling compression from making the architecture smaller.

Using hypothesis testing, controls, and distillation from random teachers, they probe knowledge transfer across data types. They cover twelve experimental setups, nine architectures, and seven datasets. Real transfer appears in some data types and architectures, but it is less pronounced than expected, even under conditions designed to maximize sharing. Where transfer is real, negative knowledge passes to the student steadily and severely, an asymmetric payoff with safety implications. They conclude that distillation acts less like compression and more like a data dependent regularizer, a reframing with practical effects.
arxiv-2510-12715:
Cagliari, Bairagi, and Wandelt combine classical statistics with a neural network summary to sharpen the hunt for primordial non Gaussianity, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Primordial non Gaussianity, a deviation from perfect randomness in the early universe's fluctuations, would separate inflation theories. Upcoming surveys such as DESI and Euclid aim to measure its local amplitude with unmatched precision, which demands better data compression.

Their hybrid estimator combines two point and three point statistics in layers with a field level neural summary. A convolutional network called PatchNet extracts small scale information from patches of the halo density field, while the power spectrum and bispectrum retain large scale information. Theory suggests this combination is nearly optimal at separating primordial from late time effects. Evaluated on dedicated tests, adding the patch based summary always improved the constraints. The largest gains came at conservative scale cuts, and it captured information beyond the three point statistic.
arxiv-2510-13215:
Lim and colleagues plan personalized learning paths with goal-driven learner modeling in this 2025 arXiv paper. A learning path should adapt to each student's aims, but language model approaches often lack any mechanism tying the sequence of materials to the learner's actual goal, producing generic or drifting paths.

Their framework, Pxplore, structures the problem around an explicit learner state model and an automated reward function that converts abstract objectives into computable training signals. The planning policy is trained by combining supervised fine-tuning with group relative policy optimization, a reinforcement learning method comparing groups of candidate paths. The system was deployed inside a real-world learning platform. Extensive experiments validated that Pxplore produces coherent, personalized, goal-driven paths, and the authors release code and data for future research.
arxiv-2510-13515:
Gu and co-authors present UniME-V2, a universal embedding model for multimodal data with a judge built in. Their 2025 arXiv paper improves how models learn vector representations across text and images. Standard training mines hard negatives from each batch by raw similarity scores. That approach misses subtle meaning differences and lets false negatives slip through.

The team first retrieves a pool of candidate hard negatives from the whole dataset. A large multimodal model then judges each query-candidate pair and assigns soft matching scores. Those scores guide the mining of diverse, high-quality hard negatives. They also serve as soft labels, loosening the rigid one-to-one matching rule. A companion reranker, trained on the mined negatives, refines the final rankings. Experiments on the MMEB benchmark and several retrieval tasks gave top average results.
arxiv-2510-13615:
Barceló and co-authors propose an edge-based graph neural network that counts triangles as it passes messages. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles a known limit of standard graph networks, which cannot detect small motifs like triangles. Higher-order tests fix that blindness but cost far too much memory and time. The team seeks expressiveness that stays practical on real graphs.

Their test, EB-1WL, refines colours along edges rather than only at nodes. It proves far more expressive than the classic 1-WL test. The authors give a full logical characterization of what the test can distinguish. Matching results also come from counting homomorphisms, maps between graphs that preserve structure. The paired network, EB-GNN, needs only near-linear time and memory in practice. In experiments it beat plain message-passing networks and rivalled specialized designs at lower cost.
arxiv-2510-13715:
Kim, Loh, and Basu build an exact coordinate descent method for high-dimensional Huber regression with a sparsity penalty. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins robust statistics with sparse modelling. Huber loss blunts the pull of outliers while an l1 penalty keeps most coefficients at zero. Existing solvers lean on gradient steps or rough second-order approximations.

Their method updates one coordinate at a time, solving each small problem exactly. A key insight drives it: only inlier observations move a coordinate's increment. Derivatives also grow monotonically along a grid built from partial residuals, making exact search cheap. Screening rules then skip variables that cannot improve, speeding convergence further. The algorithm stays effective even when correlated, heavy-tailed predictors make the curvature ill-conditioned. The authors prove a nonasymptotic convergence rate and validate the screening rule formally. Simulations and a real dataset confirm the practical speed gains.
arxiv-2510-14015:
Sam Carey and Vishvas Pandey assess what argon-based neutrino detectors can reveal about neutrinos that refuse to behave standardly, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their tool is coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, a process where a neutrino bounces off an entire atomic nucleus at once, giving a clean handle on weak-interaction physics at low energies.

The study covers four detectors at stopped-pion sources, which produce neutrinos from decaying pions: two CENNS detectors and the Captain Mills detector in the United States, plus a proposed detector at Fermilab. Using realistic neutrino fluxes and detector designs, the authors compute event rates and sensitivities. Within the Standard Model, these detectors can pin down electroweak parameters such as the weak mixing angle well below the usual energy scale. They can also probe neutrino electromagnetic properties, including magnetic moment and charge radius, and possible non-standard interactions between neutrinos and quarks.
arxiv-2510-14115:
Philipp Bauerfeind and co-authors stage a David-versus-Goliath comparison of language models generating code for autonomous-driving scenarios, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The scenarios are written in Scenic, a language paired with the CARLA simulator. Turning descriptions into Scenic code with language models has been hampered by scarce data, poor reproducibility, and inconsistent metrics.

They release NL2Scenic, a data set of 146 description-code pairs with a thirty-case test split graded by difficulty, plus a retriever and fourteen strategies. They evaluate thirteen models: four systems, including GPT-4o and GPT-5, and nine open models. Metrics cover text and execution, validated against eleven experts. GPT-4o won, but a mid-size open model reached eighty-eight percent of its expert score while running locally. Retrieval-augmented prompting narrowed the gap for smaller models. Edit similarity tracked judgment, and scaling showed diminishing returns beyond mid-size models.
arxiv-2510-14315:
Daiqi Gao and co-authors study reinforcement learning agents that must decide not only how to act but also whether to measure the state of their environment, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Measuring is costly and can itself cause delayed harm. Their motivating example is digital health, where surveying users about their health informs interventions but burdens them and can reduce engagement.

They introduce the Actively Observable Markov Decision Process, in which a measurement action reveals the latent state but may trigger a negative delayed effect. They show the reduced uncertainty can improve sample efficiency and raise the policy's value despite those costs. Formulating the problem as a periodic partially observable process, they build an online algorithm on belief states, approximated with sequential Monte Carlo sampling that jointly tracks environment parameters and unobserved states. The algorithm is evaluated in the health application, balancing intervention delivery against assessment timing.
arxiv-2510-14515:
Andrew Adair and co-authors build a spiking neuron out of light-sensitive hardware that fires in rhythm-sensitive patterns, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The work moves photonic neuromorphic computing beyond the simple neuron model. Spiking hardware promises energy efficiency, but photonic neurons mostly mimic integrate-and-fire behavior, while real neurons also encode information in spike timing and frequency.

Their photonic-electronic resonate-and-fire neuron is built around a light-sensitive resonant tunnelling diode that produces spikes in response to nanosecond, low-power optical signals at infrared telecom wavelengths, using a hundred microwatts. The team demonstrates control of the firing dynamics through the timing between optical pulses and the bias voltage. It achieves bandpass filtering of both analog and digital inputs, meaning the neuron responds to rhythms. The device accepts optical fan-in from four laser sources combined by wavelength multiplexing, a step toward light-enabled neuromorphic processors.
arxiv-2510-14615:
Sandra and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a faster way to plan robot movements with diffusion models, the same family of models used to generate images. Classical planners struggle as the space of possible motions grows and environments get complex. Diffusion models can learn rich patterns of good trajectories. But most are trained for a single environment, and those trained for many still depend on one specific camera.

Their method, CAMPD, conditions a diffusion model on general context information rather than on one sensor's feed. An attention mechanism inside the model accepts any number of context parameters, so no retraining is needed for a new setting. They tested the method on a robot arm with seven joints, against leading approaches on real tasks. CAMPD produced high-quality, varied trajectories in unseen environments. It did so in a fraction of the time the competing methods required.
arxiv-2510-14815:
Gough studies, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how solutions of a one-dimensional wave equation can blow up in finite time. The equation's nonlinearity is quadratic in the time derivative, so regions where the solution changes ever faster can feed on themselves until the solution ceases to exist. A central question is which shapes the blow-up takes, and whether they are stable when the starting data are nudged.

Building on work for the spatial-derivative version, Gough proves that no smooth, exactly self-similar blow-up profiles exist here. Instead, he constructs an explicit family of generalized self-similar solutions branching off from the spatially uniform blow-up. These profiles are smooth inside the past light cone and blow up at a prescribed point and time, at the type-I rate. They are asymptotically stable under small perturbations in the energy topology. The uniform blow-up itself is not.
arxiv-2510-15115:
Kirill Semenov and Rico Sennrich check whether awkward wording quietly distorts a popular test of what language models know. Their 2025 arXiv paper examines MLAMA, a multilingual benchmark built by dropping entity names into translated sentence templates. Because the templates ignore grammar, many finished prompts come out ungrammatical or use the wrong word forms, especially in languages with rich word endings.

Working with four Slavic languages, the pair compared the original prompts against clean whole-sentence translations produced by Google Translate and ChatGPT. Knowledge scores rose significantly once the prompts read fluently, and checks on five more languages from other families showed the same pattern. Semenov and Sennrich urge benchmark builders to control grammatical quality, since fluency changes both the scores and what those scores can fairly claim. They released their corrected dataset and code publicly.
arxiv-2510-15715:
I Novikau and I Joseph present a fix in a 2025 paper. The fix concerns a classic math technique called Carleman embedding. It turns nonlinear equations into linear ones. The method fails where a system has several resting points. The authors split the space into local regions. Each region gets its own embedding. The method switches regions as the solution travels.

They tested three versions of the idea. One used fixed-size regions rebuilt on the fly. One also resized regions for accuracy near resting points. One used a grid computed in advance for speed. All three handled chaotic systems that defeat the standard method. These included strange attractors. The authors note the grid version may suit future quantum algorithms.
arxiv-2510-15815:
K Korshynska and colleagues test dark matter ideas in a 2025 paper. They use the motions of stars in tiny dwarf galaxies. The candidate is ultralight dark matter. Its particles are extremely light. They behave partly like waves. The team modelled seven dwarf spheroidal galaxies. Ordinary matter's effect on the star motions was included.

For repulsive self-interacting dark matter, the best fit is weak. The interaction strength is almost negligible. The fit matches non-interacting models. The particle mass is near ten to the minus twenty-two electronvolts. Attractive interactions favour different values. They point to very small masses or tiny coupling only. The viable model space narrows either way.
arxiv-2510-16015:
Qian Sun, Graham Hults, and Susu Xu design flood sensing and forecasting around the decisions they must support. Fast, reliable choices save lives in flood response, yet budgets and access limits leave awareness thin. Standard practice places ground sensors to gain the most information overall and trains forecast models to minimise average error, ignoring that equal scores can still lead to very different decisions.

Their end-to-end framework picks sensor sites and trains a spatio-temporal forecast model to cut downstream decision regret directly. A contextual scoring network, a differentiable sensor selector under a hard budget, a flood reconstruction and forecasting model, and a differentiable decision layer work as one pipeline. Implicit maximum likelihood estimation lets gradients flow through discrete sensor choices, and probabilistic decision heads approximate varied constrained response tasks in differentiable form.
arxiv-2510-16215:
Maxim V Polyakov and Illarion E Popov model how heat moves inside the body to aid a gentle kind of medical scan. Microwave radiometry reads the faint heat glow of deep tissue from the skin, with no cutting or probes. Turning that glow into a true inner temperature needs a sound model of heat flow in layered tissue.

Their computer model joins the standard bioheat equation with the physics of microwaves moving through uneven tissue. Tests vary room temperature, surface cooling, and tissue heat flow to see how the glow reading forms. A rise of eight degrees in air temperature shifted the reading by about two degrees, more than the method's usual error. The model's fields matched known solutions and lab data within a tenth of a degree, supporting tighter scan conditions.
arxiv-2510-16315:
Uktamjon Uktamov, Mohsen Fathi, and Javlon Rayimbaev chart the paths of charged particles around a black hole wrapped in a magnetic field. The hole is a Schwarzschild black hole, the simplest kind, with no spin, set in a steady external field. A charged particle feels both gravity and magnetism, so its orbits warp in ways neutral matter never shows.

By studying an effective potential, the team sorts orbits into bound loops and escape paths. They also find the settings that flip one into the other. Field strength and particle charge each reshape the orbit's size, energy, and spin. They then fit the model to the real path of the S2 star, which orbits our galaxy's central black hole. A sampling method pins down the field and charge. The work also speaks to bright hotspots seen flaring near that same hole's edge.
arxiv-2510-17315:
Robots that plan by first imagining a video often fail when a hidden property of the scene changes the outcome. Po-Chen Ko and nine co-authors tackle that weakness, for example when a door must be pulled rather than pushed, or when friction changes how an object moves. Older video planners usually start over after a failure and waste what the failure revealed.

Ko and his co-authors present RELIC, a method that refines a hidden code for the scene from past trial videos. A sampling step then rejects new plans that clash with earlier failures. Across simulated and real robot tasks, RELIC needed fewer replans and raised one shot success sharply after a single real attempt.
arxiv-2510-17515:
Pruning a neural network removes most of its connections, yet some sparse patterns train far better than others with the same number of links removed. Hoang Pham and four co-authors propose a theory for that puzzle based on graphons, mathematical objects that describe the limiting shape of very large networks. As a pruned network grows wider, its connection pattern settles toward a particular graphon, which quietly encodes the bias of the pruning method that made it.

Pham and his co-authors call that claim the Graphon Limit Hypothesis and back it with experiments. They build a graphon version of the neural tangent kernel, a tool for tracking training, and show its spectrum lines up with how fast different sparse networks actually learn. The framework explains why pruning choices that look equal on paper behave so differently in practice.
arxiv-2510-17615:
F. T. Brandt, with J. Frenkel and two co-authors, compares two ways of writing Einstein's gravity theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Einstein-Hilbert theory is the standard form of general relativity. It can be written in a first order form or a second order form. The two forms agree for classical physics, but their quantum versions needed a direct check.

The authors derive a general relation between the background effective actions of the two forms. Here an effective action is a compact summary of a theory's quantum behavior. The relation directly proves the two forms match at the quantum level. Explicit one loop calculations of the correction terms back the proof. The check was done in a general background gauge choice.
arxiv-2510-17915:
Hassan Gharoun, with four co-authors, recalibrates neural networks so their confidence better matches how often they are right. Most fixes shift all predictions the same way, yet some predictions are far more shaky than others. The method first sorts cases by how close they sit to known examples in feature space.

Likely-right cases get a standard confidence fix, while likely-wrong cases get pushed toward flat uncertainty. The aim is not just a better calibration score but better choices when a model says it is unsure. For users in high-stakes fields, the paper links confidence repair to safer day-to-day decisions.
arxiv-2510-18115:
Canyi Chen and three co-authors review a flexible way to trace how a cause flows through a middle step to an outcome. Structural equation models are the standard tool for such pathway work, but they often force normal-error guesses on messy, mixed data. Copula methods separate the dependence shape from each variable's own distribution, loosening that grip.

The review gathers the main advances in joining copulas to these pathway models. It weighs what each step changes for practice and for theory. Researchers in health and social science, where data rarely look Gaussian, get a guided tour of a more forgiving toolkit.
arxiv-2510-18415:
Amalie Davidsen and her three co-authors lay out the design for KVASIR, a neutron instrument planned for the European Spallation Source. Neutrons fired at a material and scattered back can reveal tiny energy changes inside it, which matter for the hard materials behind many advanced technologies. KVASIR uses a backscattering setup with indirect time-of-flight measurement to read those changes with very fine detail in both energy and momentum.

Detailed ray-tracing simulations, including the real shapes and flaws of the analyzer parts, guided the design choices. The instrument is built to keep its precision even under strong magnetic fields, and it leaves room for polarization analysis and harsh sample conditions. The authors argue this combination will let researchers study single crystals at a spatial and dynamic precision not seen before, especially for quantum materials under extreme conditions.
arxiv-2510-18815:
Christian Biello and his twelve co-authors update predictions for a Higgs channel. The channel makes a Higgs with a bottom quark pair. It runs at the Large Hadron Collider. Precise predictions matter for two reasons. They test the Standard Model. They also expose new physics hiding in Higgs data.

The team followed the collider working group's guidance. They computed total rates in two schemes. One treats bottom quarks as massless. One keeps their mass in full. Both were matched to parton shower simulations. Those model realistic event structure. Two state-of-the-art generators were compared in the massless scheme. The channel's role as background was studied too. It affects searches for pairs of Higgs bosons. The Higgs momentum spectrum may reveal light-quark couplings. The clean two-photon decay channel carries that test.
arxiv-2510-18915:
Chen Chen and eight co-authors present UNO-Bench. It is a benchmark for omni models, which join vision, audio, and language. The key question is simple. Does skill in one mode predict skill when modes work as one?

The test covers forty-four task types and five mode mixes. It uses hand-picked omni samples plus improved single-mode samples. Many samples fit real use in a Chinese setting. Scores for both kinds of skill sit under one system. Builders can thus track how omni models grow in a clear way.
arxiv-2510-19015:
Toni Mäkelä reviews the state of neutrino studies at the Large Hadron Collider and where the field is heading. Forward neutrinos, flying along the beam line, have moved from proposal to first measurements, and they connect collider physics with astrophysics in useful ways.

The review covers selected questions about what neutrinos are, how much they weigh, and how they interact. It also highlights projections for the current run and the later high-luminosity run. For collider physicists, the message is that this young program offers chances that other detectors cannot match.
arxiv-2510-19315:
Pascal Bergsträßer, Ryan Cotterell, and Anthony W Lin prove a sharp claim about transformers. Transformers are remarkably succinct. Succinctness measures how compactly a system can describe a language. It is a classic yardstick of expressive power. Logic and automata theory both use it.

Fixed-precision transformers can be vastly smaller than rival forms. They beat formulas in linear temporal logic by an exponential gap. They beat recurrent networks by the same gap. Against finite automata, the gap is doubly exponential. Matching upper bounds show the gaps are tight. The result explains part of the power packed into these models.
arxiv-2510-19515:
Raffaele Resta argues that the intrinsic Hall effect, linear and nonlinear alike, is best understood as a property of the many-body ground state rather than of band structure. Standard theory defines the effect's geometry in Bloch-vector space and leans on semiclassical reasoning. That foundation fails once disorder and interactions enter, since no Bloch vector exists there.

Resta presents a higher-level geometric formulation set in a more general parameter space. The expressions it yields are compact, and in the Bloch special case they reproduce the known results directly. The paper reframes a standard transport effect as fundamental quantum geometry, with the logic visible instead of buried in algebra.
arxiv-2510-19615:
Zhiping Zhou and seven co-authors present FidelityGPT, a system that repairs meaning errors in decompiled code. Decompilers turn machine code back into readable source-like text, but the output often distorts the original logic, especially for closed-source programs. Simple fixes like renaming variables do not catch semantic mistakes.

FidelityGPT pairs language models with retrieval-augmented generation: it detects distorted lines, pulls similar correct code from a database, and uses a variable-dependency analysis to keep long functions manageable. On six hundred twenty function pairs it detected distortions with high accuracy and fixed far more of them correctly than the leading earlier system. The gains matter for reverse engineering and security analysis of binaries without source code.
arxiv-2510-19915:
Yang Ni, Hongping Deng, and Xue-Ning Bai run three-dimensional radiation hydrodynamics simulations of planet-forming disks heavy enough to fragment under their own gravity. Gravitational instability is a candidate route to gas giants, especially far from the star, but earlier simulations with crude cooling produced clumps closer to brown dwarf masses. These simulations use a meshless method with proper radiation transport.

Raising the disk mass and lowering opacity strengthens cooling and promotes fragmentation, while calmer disks settle into spiral-patterned gravito-turbulence. Some bound clumps survive long term, with initial masses spanning roughly a third of Jupiter's mass to ten Jupiters, squarely gas giant territory. The results rehabilitate disk fragmentation as a plausible giant planet pathway.
arxiv-2510-20215:
Xuesong Wang reviews non-orthogonal multiple access for visible light communications and points to future directions. Visible light links complement radio systems in sixth generation networks, but current standards were adapted from cable and radio designs and do not fully use the optical character of light. Bursty, asymmetric traffic also makes time-division protocols wasteful when many users share a link.

Non-orthogonal access lets several users share the same time and frequency resources while tolerating controlled interference between them. Wang surveys progress in light communications and in this access method applied to them, sets out key optimization limits and goals, and describes usage scenarios that fit the method well. Several open research directions close the review.
arxiv-2510-20615:
Yang Han and four co-authors build MS-BART, a joint model of mass spectra and molecule forms for the task of naming a molecule from its spectrum. Few tagged spectra exist, and raw spectra are bent and mixed, which blocks the big pre-train route that helps in past fields. Their frame maps spectra and forms to one token set for cross-mode learning.

Pre-train runs on sound fingerprint-molecule sets with joint clean and swap tasks. Fine-tune then moves the model to real spectra by way of print calls from a spectra call model. A chemical check loop steers builds from fake forms to the true form. Wide tests show the joint plan works well, the team reports.
arxiv-2510-20715:
Patricio A Gallardo, Yulin Gong, Boryana Hadzhiyska. Yun-Hsin Hsu describe iskay2, a software pipeline that measures how galaxy groups move by using a subtle cooling and heating pattern in the cosmic microwave background. Moving ionized gas shifts that background light, and pairing galaxies lets the faint signal stand out.

Pairing cancels much of the noise and yields the average shared motion of halo pairs, which traces matter spread and cosmic growth. The pipeline runs the paired test on background maps plus large galaxy catalogs with good speed and care. Its outputs match earlier published results within expected scatter, clearing the way for sharp tests with new galaxy surveys and next generation background maps.
arxiv-2510-20815:
Minjie Hong and seven co-authors tackle recommendation with large language models. Recommendation systems suggest items that a user may like. Language models reason well, but they struggle in this role. Text meaning and shared user taste signals do not line up well. User feedback is also sparse and partly random.

They propose GREAM, a full framework with three main parts. One part aligns text evidence with shared taste signals. It builds neat item codes that keep meaning consistent. A second part trains reasoning step by step. It moves from user acts to guessed likes and final picks. A third part steadies later training when good results are rare. GREAM can answer fast, or show its reasoning chain first. Tests on three data sets beat strong older methods. That offers a clear path toward more checkable model recommenders.
arxiv-2510-21015:
Sebastian Horvat, working alone, draws a broad principle from a sharp fact of quantum interference, particles show wave like behavior but never third or higher order interference. Theory predicts this limit and experiments confirm it, a curious possibility and impossibility pair.

Horvat argues the pattern implies a universal rule governing statistical correlations between events at separate places, whatever objects carry them. Roughly, joint influences among mutually spacelike sources obey a fixed structural bound. If valid, the principle constrains any future theory that would replace quantum mechanics, not just its current form.
arxiv-2510-21315:
Haiyang Li and three co-authors ask why the fruit fly brain keeps two mechanisms that seem to do the same job in odor learning. Both sideways inhibition between neurons and a fading response after repeated firing are thought to sharpen the separation between odor patterns the fly must tell apart.

A computer model of the fly's smell circuit lets them test each mechanism under rising noise. Sideways inhibition helps when noise is low or moderate but can backfire when noise grows strong, while the fading response helps at every noise level. Each mechanism dominates in the setting where it works best, and together they give the strongest odor discrimination, so the seeming duplication turns out to have a clear purpose.
arxiv-2510-21615:
Orest Kupyn and five co-authors teach video generators the geometry of cameras, after finding that scale alone does not. Modern video diffusion models, trained on mountains of footage, still bend scenes, wobble motion, and spawn artifacts that break the illusion of a real three-dimensional world being filmed.

Their fix comes from classical computer vision: epipolar geometry, the rules tying together two views of the same scene. By ranking generated videos with a preference method that rewards low epipolar error, they align the model toward geometrically consistent output without needing a fully differentiable pipeline. Training uses still scenes with moving cameras, yet the skill transfers to busy dynamic scenes. Epipolar error falls by about thirty-one percent, and human judges rate consistency far higher, up from about half to nearly three quarters, with looks intact.
arxiv-2510-21815:
Kumbha Nagaswetha works on high dynamic range imaging, the effort to keep both bright and dark detail that ordinary cameras lose in a single shot. The proposed method fuses several exposures of the same scene with a neural network, learning the blend without ever being shown a true reference HDR image.

An underexposed frame protects bright areas while an overexposed frame keeps shadow detail, and the network combines those strengths into one output. Training without ground truth makes the approach usable where reference images simply do not exist. Judged by a standard structural similarity measure for fused exposures, the results looked better than earlier fusion methods, and a custom loss term was added to sharpen reconstruction quality further.
arxiv-2510-22015:
Shilin You and six co-authors, Gael Luna, Juned Shaikh, David Gostin, Yu Xiang, Justin Koeln. Tyler Summers, plan robot paths through key-and-door worlds, where a door may open only after its key is collected. The ordering rules are written in a fragment of temporal logic, and earlier general-purpose solvers handled them slowly.

The team partitions the obstacle-free space exactly into convex pieces while recording how keys, doors, and open regions connect. That map becomes an augmented graph of convex sets that encodes the precedence rules precisely. A shortest-path search on it yields an exact plan, up to how finely the path itself is parameterized. On generated key-door mazes built to be hard, their pipeline ran orders of magnitude faster than recent temporal-logic tools.
arxiv-2510-22215:
Juyeon Kim, Geon Lee, Dongwon Choi, Taeuk Kim, and Kijung Shin search documents that are meant to be looked at, contracts, papers. Reports whose meaning lives in layout as much as in words. Search systems face a fork: compress each page into one vector and go fast but coarse, or keep many vectors per page and go accurate but expensive.

Their framework, HEAVEN, takes both roads in sequence. Pages are first gathered into visually summarized bundles and retrieved cheaply with single vectors. Then the shortlist is reranked with the expensive multi-vector method, skipping query tokens that carry little linguistic weight to save computation. A new benchmark of long, multi-document, visually rich collections tests the system under realistic strain. Across four benchmarks the hybrid kept nearly all of the top-rank accuracy of the heavy method at a fraction of its cost.
arxiv-2510-22315:
Ryusuke Ikeda and Yuto Yokota calculate how a vortex lattice inside an unconventional superconductor answers an electromagnetic nudge. In a strong magnetic field, the interior is threaded by an ordered array of whirlpools. The study works in a high-field approximation. It centers on the lowest Landau level of the order parameter.

For conventional single-component pairing, the superfluid stiffness vanishes for exactly one kind of lattice. The same holds for a nonchiral triplet state with several components. The stiffness vanishes only for lattices that minimize the free energy. That is a neat consistency check between energetics and response. The d-wave case bends its lattice away from sixfold symmetry in weaker fields. Surprisingly, that anisotropy does not appear in the resulting vortex flow conductivities. The separation is worth knowing when interpreting experiments.
arxiv-2510-22415:
Zheng Wei and seven co-authors compare talk about China and United States relations on Douyin and TikTok, two sister platforms run under different rules and cultures. They study more than four thousand videos and a large body of comments with topic clustering and sentiment analysis. Themes include economic strength, technology ties, cultural views, and global challenges, with clear emotional gaps between the two sides.

Using location data that Chinese accounts must now disclose, the team links sentiment toward the United States with regional income, minority share, and internet access. The work shows how place and wealth shape online views of a rival power.
arxiv-2510-22515:
Smashing heavy atomic nuclei together creates matter that is hard and slow to simulate in detail. Jing-An Sun, Li Yan, Charles Gale, and Sangyong Jeon introduce DiffHIC in 2025, a generative diffusion model meant to stand in for traditional heavy ion collision simulations.

DiffHIC takes starting entropy patterns and transport settings, then directly produces final particle spectra in two dimensions. The authors report a speedup of about one hundred thousand times over older simulations. Its outputs still match many measured features, including flow patterns, particle correlations, and momentum changes, offering a fast tool for high precision studies of these collisions.
arxiv-2510-22715: Radu Ioan Bot, Jalal Fadili, and Dang-Khoa Nguyen prove in a 2025 paper that the iterates of Nesterov's accelerated optimization algorithm converge in the critical regimes. The steps converge, in the weak topology sense, to a global minimizer of a smooth function in a real Hilbert space. The result answers positively a conjecture posed by H Attouch and co-authors a decade earlier, and matches a recent continuous time finding.
arxiv-2510-22815:
Software projects often pin a library to one old version. Pinning keeps builds reproducible. It can also keep known security flaws. Vasudev Vikram, Yuvraj Agarwal, and Rohan Padhye study pin freshness in Maven in 2025. Maven is a Java build ecosystem.

They define stale and fresh pins by age. Over sixty percent of consumers held stale pins. Some pins were over a year old. Many pins missed security fixes. A tenth of upgrades to latest patches would cut flaws. Their Pin-Freshener tool tests upgrade safety. It borrows test signals from peer projects. That signal can encourage safer pin updates.
arxiv-2510-23515:
Yaoli Liu, Yao-Xiang Ding, and Kun Zhou present FreeFuse, a way to blend several custom image subjects into one picture without retraining anything. Image generators often use small add-on modules called LoRAs, one per subject, but mixing them causes features to leak into the wrong places. Earlier fixes retrained the modules, which is slow and limits how people can combine subjects they already own.

FreeFuse instead routes each module's effect, token by token, to the image region where its subject belongs during generation. A new attention step reads the model's own matching signals in the early denoising steps to find those regions, so no outside segmentation tool is needed. Users only supply the trigger words for each subject. In the authors' tests, the method beat rival approaches on both identity preservation and overall composition quality.
arxiv-2510-23815:
Iagoba Apellaniz and two co-authors study how to measure magnetic field gradients and background fields together with two separated groups of spins. Dicke states, fully symmetric spin states, are ideal for sensing a uniform field, but they ignore gradients. The trick explored here is to rotate the spins in just one group, partially flipping the Dicke state so it also feels the gradient.

The authors derive trade-off relations linking how precisely the gradient can be estimated in each of the three directions to the precision kept for the uniform field. Their partially flipped state hits those bounds, with matching sensitivity in two directions and reduced sensitivity in the third. Entanglement between the groups gives it roughly twice the precision of the best separable alternative. For small ensembles they name the exact measurements that saturate the quantum limit. For larger ones they propose simpler schemes based on spin correlations.
arxiv-2510-24115:
Sandeep Vissapragada and three co-authors built HistoLens, an interactive tool to help doctors check vision language models on tissue slides. For doctors to trust such a model, they need to see why it gave an answer, much like asking a trainee to explain. A black box answer is not enough in pathology, where errors carry real risk.

With HistoLens, a pathologist asks a question in plain English and gets a structured report back. The doctor can then ask why, and the tool shows a heat map over the exact cells and regions the model used. The system is also taught to ignore background and focus only on the patient's tissue, as a trained pathologist would.
arxiv-2510-24315:
Baozhe Zhang and five co-authors add obstacle avoidance to a control framework for cooperating drones and ground vehicles that works without global position estimates. The base framework, CoNi-MPC, uses only relative states between the air and ground robots, which is efficient but carries no information about obstacles. Their new algorithm, CoNi-OA, fills that gap.

CoNi-OA uses a single frame of raw LiDAR data from the drone to build a modulation matrix. That matrix directly adjusts the quadrotor's velocity to steer around obstacles in real time. The method needs no global state and no prediction of obstacle motion, suiting fast air ground cooperation in cluttered settings.
arxiv-2510-24515:
Malintha Fernando and two co-authors study team orienteering as a competitive game where self interested agents collect prizes under energy limits. The classic team orienteering problem plans routes for cooperating agents, with uses in mobility, aerial logistics, and surveillance. It does not extend to reward scarce settings where agents compete rather than cooperate.

They propose Stochastic Prize-Collecting Orienteering Games, played on a graph with stochastic transitions. A theoretical discussion on complete and star graphs establishes key properties of the game. They also address learning ordinal response policies in this rank based setting, aiming at planning methods for competing autonomous agents.
arxiv-2510-24715:
Tom Rudelius, the sole author, gives a fresh proof of a bound on how far a scalar field can move in flat space time models. The bound was proved of late by Herderschee and Wall with other tools. Rudelius uses the Friedmann rules, the core laws for such space time growth, to reach the same end.

He shows the bound can be hit just in worlds with no speed up of growth. He then argues the bound should hold in a real long run swell case, even with small quantum shifts and curved space. High order shifts could break it just at the cost of sound that moves too fast.
arxiv-2510-25015:
Chuyue Sun, Yican Sun, Daneshvar Amrollahi, Ethan Zhang, Shuvendu Lahiri, Shan Lu, David Dill, and Clark Barrett are the eight authors. They built VeriStruct, a frame that uses AI help to prove whole data modules. It works on more than lone functions. The proof tongue is Verus, used on Rust code. Chat models often slip on its mark syntax and proof sense, which has capped past work.

A plan part in the frame queues the build of short forms, type rules, specs, and proof code in set steps. Syntax help sits in each prompt, and a fix stage mends mark slips on its own. On eleven Rust modules, the frame proved near all functions in ten modules. That nears full auto proof for such code.
arxiv-2510-25115:
Drake Brown, Trevor Garrity, Daniel Perkins, Davis Hunter, and Wyatt Pochman model how dogs can herd sheep to a set point at least cost. They set state rules for both groups and a cost form for the task. A first code tool that solves edge value tasks was used to draw best paths.

That tool most oft failed to settle, due to the task's high size and bent rules. With a good first guess and tuned dials, it could be made to work. A shot based way also fell short. A loop based line and square method scaled best and took more sheep and dogs. It still shook when dogs and sheep came close, where bent rules bite.
arxiv-2510-25515:
D Calchetti led seventeen co-authors comparing solar instruments. K Albert, F J Bailen, and J Blanco Rodriguez helped. Their 2025 paper measures solar photospheric velocities in space. The Polarimetric and Helioseismic Imager flies on Solar Orbiter. It scans an iron line in the solar spectrum.

The same line is sampled by SDO/HMI instrument. They assess consistency between line-of-sight velocity measurements. Reliable flow measurements matter when Orbiter faces far side. Combining two vantage points requires consistency too. Data were taken on twenty-nine March 2023. Solar Orbiter crossed the Sun-Earth line then. Pixel-by-pixel comparison covered a four-hour time series. A clear linear relation linked both instruments. Slope was near unity and correlation high. Signals form at similar heights in atmosphere. A sunspot penumbra close-up is also presented. Both instruments agree very well after proper accounting. Instrumental effects and large-scale velocities were accounted for.
arxiv-2510-25715:
David Bate and Pietro Wald construct purely unrectifiable differentiability spaces. Their 2025 math paper studies shortcut Laakso spaces. Lipschitz functions and their differentiability are central objects. Possible Banach space targets for differentiability are investigated. Geometry of shortcut metric spaces is studied generally.

They characterize when shortcut spaces are PI rectifiable. When they are differentiability spaces for a target is characterized. A given Banach target determines that trait. Their family of spaces arises from characterizations. Laakso spaces satisfy the required hypotheses, they show. Lipschitz differentiability spaces are subtle in study. Rectifiability notions measure how Euclidean-like spaces are. Differentiability can hold despite pure unrectifiability there. Target dependence of differentiability is highlighted sharply. Metric geometry and study on metric spaces benefit.
arxiv-2510-25815:
Promila Biswas and four co-authors study how a black hole gains mass while the universe around it expands under dark energy. Dark energy is the name for whatever drives the faster expansion of space. They model the cosmic background with a modified Chaplygin gas, a fluid used to stand in for dark matter and dark energy together. They try several formulas for how dark energy changes with redshift.

Biswas and the team find that the growth of the hole is very sensitive to how dark energy evolves. Gentle formulas imply slow, steady feeding, while one sharper formula implies fast late changes. Their results treat black hole feeding as a probe of cosmic pressure over time.
arxiv-2510-26015:
Zhengtao Ma leads five co-authors in a study of what blind and low vision passengers need from fully automated vehicles. Such vehicles could greatly expand mobility for people who cannot drive, but trust and dignity shape whether the promise is real. The team ran six focus groups, on the road and in the lab, with sixteen participants who experienced real driving conditions.

Ma and the team find that participants start with high faith in the vehicles, yet need layered, value sensitive information during the ride to keep trust. Voice was the preferred channel, which prompts a rethink of touch based cues in this setting. Their dignity lens, grounded in the field data, spells out respectful design choices for automated rides.
arxiv-2510-26115:
Louis Wai-Tong Fan, Maximillian Newman, and John Wakeley introduce a population model where the family tree is fixed first and gene ancestry is studied given that tree. The model is diploid, meaning each individual carries two gene copies, allows self fertilization, and allows generations to overlap. Traditional coalescent theory averages over all possible pedigrees, an annealed view, while they study the quenched law, the distribution given one realized pedigree.

Fan and the team focus on high selfing probability as population size grows large. The conditional law converges to a random probability measure built from coalescing random walks on a fragmentation coalescence process. The result clarifies how the site frequency spectrum, a summary of genetic variation, depends on the pedigree itself.
arxiv-2510-26215:
Daniel Siebel-Cortopassi and Pei Liu analyze defect patterns in nematic liquid crystals, materials whose rod like molecules share a common direction. A defect is a point where that direction cannot be defined smoothly, and it can appear as a single core or a split core. Within the Landau de Gennes framework, a standard energy model for these materials, they study which configurations minimize the energy.

A bifurcation occurs at a critical temperature. Below it, both single and split core defects solve the governing equation, with the split core at lower energy. Above it, the split core vanishes and only the single core remains stable. The authors map how the threshold depends on domain size and measure core sizes across temperature and size.
arxiv-2510-26315:
Junlai Qiu, Yunzhu Chen, Hao Zheng, Yawen Huang, and Yuexiang Li propose a hybrid system to grade diabetic retinopathy, an eye disease that is a leading cause of vision loss. Automated grading from retinal images can speed screening and early detection. Convolutional networks excel at local features, while vision transformers capture global structure, and single backbone systems have hit a performance bottleneck in this task.

Their framework fuses features from both backbone types through the theory of evidence, a formalism for combining uncertain support from several sources. Features are transformed into supporting evidence by deep evidential networks, then combined for the final grade. The design aims to use the complementary strengths of local and global feature extraction for more reliable clinical screening support.
arxiv-2510-26615:
Yiqiao Jin, with four co-authors, builds an agent system that reads slide decks and other multi-page visual documents. Manuals, brochures, and posters carry meaning in layout, colour, icons, and links between pages. Even strong multimodal models stumble on fine detail spread across a deck.

Jin and the team present SlideAgent, which splits the work among specialist agents at three levels: the whole document, each page, and each element. At first it builds a structured summary of themes and details that does not depend on the question asked. When a question comes, it wakes only the agents it needs and merges their findings into one answer. In experiments, the system raised accuracy over leading closed models by about eight percent and over open models by about ten percent.
arxiv-2510-26915:
Zachary Ravichandran, with eight co-authors, lets mixed robot teams take missions in messy, unstructured places. Heterogeneous teams were usually designed for well-specified missions in known settings. Generative models open a different route: infer the mission's subtasks from plain language and what the robots see.

Ravichandran and the team present SPINE-HT, a three-stage framework. A language model infers subtasks from the mission text and team capabilities, the subtasks are checked for feasibility, then assigned by capability such as traversability or perception. Feedback from semantic maps and task outcomes updates the plan online. In simulation, the framework nearly doubled the success rate of prior language-based teaming. In real runs with three ground robots and a high-altitude drone, it reached eighty-seven point five percent success.
arxiv-2510-27215:
Shun-Qing Shen revisits a long-held claim about thin materials in this 2025 paper. The claim concerns Dirac fermions, particles whose energy grows in a straight cone shape. In flat sheets, such particles were said to give a half-step electric response, an effect called the parity anomaly. Shen checks the claim on a lattice, a grid that mimics a real crystal.

He finds the half-step response is not there when the grid is handled with care. A single heavy cone on a grid yields whole steps only. The half step shows up only in an unreal limit, or with a light cone plus some sideways flow. So the anomaly, he argues, belongs to light particles in metals, not heavy ones in insulators.
arxiv-2510-27615:
Liyao Lyu and Huan Lei propose a particle method in 2025 for equations where spread, flow, growth, and loss act at once and total mass is not kept fixed. Grid methods can strain when values blow up or form sharp clumps. Their method splits each step in two: a move-and-spread step run by random particle paths, and a growth step run by birth and death of particles.

The scheme needs no grid and never yields counts below zero. Tests cover two classic cases: one where phases split apart, and one where cells clump as they chase a chemical trail. Both patterns are matched well without fine grid tweaks. The method suits hard cases where mass shifts and peaks form.
arxiv-2511-00115:
Haoyuan Li, Yuanbo Tong, and Yuchen Li present ProtoMBTI, a framework for inferring MBTI personality types from text that respects the graded nature of personality judgment. Hard-label sorting hides how human judgments are prototype-like, with people matching types by degree. A balanced, quality-controlled corpus is built through language-model-guided data growth across meaning, language, and feeling dimensions.

A lightweight encoder is fine-tuned to learn vectors and unify a bank of personality prototypes, and inference fetches the closest prototypes. Computational psychology readers get an alternative aligned with cognitive theory, not blunt sorting. Prototype matching mirrors how people actually sort personalities, by resemblance to exemplars.
arxiv-2511-00215:
Code and its written notes often drift apart, and those gaps mislead programmers and cause bugs. Xiaomeng Xu, Zahin Wahab, Reid Holmes, and Caroline Lemieux built DocPrism to catch one harmful kind of gap: notes that state facts the code does not match. Plain use of a large language model flags far too many files, so the team added a filtering method.

Their method, called LCEF, uses the model's skill at finishing local text instead of long chains of reasoning. In tests across Python, TypeScript, C++, and Java, flag rates fell sharply and accuracy rose. At least eleven percent of code and note pairs held real errors.
arxiv-2511-00415:
Jotaro Yano rebuilds the theory of zero-knowledge tools on the Solana blockchain as an architecture. Zero-knowledge proofs let one party prove a fact without revealing the underlying data, and Solana projects use them for both scaling and privacy. Yano sorts those uses on two axes, purpose and placement, whether proofs live on-chain or off-chain, to give the scattered ecosystem one map.

Across that grid he defines five invariants, rules covering authenticity, replay safety, and aligned finality, as a shared vocabulary for correctness. The map spans the Solana Foundation's three pillars, compression, confidential transfers, and light clients, plus surrounding tools. From the theory he derives message formats that carry their own proofs, pointing to concrete ways to extend the pillars across chains.
arxiv-2511-01015:
Nabeel Seedat, Jiashuo Liu, and Mihaela van der Schaar argue, in a position paper, that the next frontier for artificial intelligence agents is how they handle data. Agents can now talk, use tools, and work with people, yet research focuses mostly on reasoning, while real deployments fail or succeed on data quality.

They name four abilities future agents need. Agents should gather data proactively, asking people when knowledge is missing. They should process messy, varied inputs with context in mind. Evaluation should use interactive test data made on the fly, not fixed benchmarks alone. And agents should keep adapting their data and knowledge as environments shift. The paper is a call to treat these data skills as a top design priority.
arxiv-2511-01815:
Konrad Staniszewski and Adrian Łańcucki compress the memory that makes large language models expensive to serve: the key-value cache, which stores attention data that later prompts with shared prefixes could reuse. Stale caches eat scarce graphics memory, get offloaded, or are recomputed from scratch. Their coder, KVTC, borrows the classical media compression playbook.

KVTC decorrelates cache features with principal component analysis, quantizes them adaptively, and entropy-codes the result, needing only a brief calibration and no change to the model's parameters. It reached compression of up to twentyfold while preserving reasoning and long-context accuracy, and fortyfold or more in specific uses. Tested on Llama 3, Mistral NeMo, and R1-Qwen 2.5 across benchmarks from math contests to long-document question answering, it consistently beat token eviction, plain quantization, and SVD-based baselines.
arxiv-2511-01915:
Edoardo Conti and four colleagues give a vision foundation model its first thorough examination in fetal ultrasound. DINOv3 transfers impressively across medical imaging. Fetal brain scans pose a special trap, though. Doctors must tell apart three standard planes: transthalamic, transventricular, and transcerebellar. They look almost identical. Mistaking them undermines biometric checks.

To test fairly, the team curated every public fetal ultrasound dataset into one multi-site benchmark, FetalUS-188K, with more than 188,000 annotated images from varied acquisition settings. They pretrained DINOv3 self-supervised on the ultrasound data and compared adaptation by linear probing and full fine-tuning, against initialization from natural-image weights. Models pretrained on fetal ultrasound consistently beat the natural-image starts, showing that domain pretraining matters most exactly where classes differ least.
arxiv-2511-02015:
Jace Aldrich and Odest Chadwicke Jenkins give a robot controller better dice. Model predictive path integral control steers robots by sampling many candidate action sequences. It weights the best rollouts. But it usually samples from a simple unimodal Gaussian. That starves the search when the right action distribution has several peaks. It also suffers under noisy cost gradients.

Their algorithm, SOPPI, interleaves Stein variational gradient descent updates between control steps. It reshapes the sampling distribution during rollouts. The target is the true multi-modal action distribution. It does so without excessive computation. Tests span a planar cart-pole, a seven-degree-of-freedom robot arm, a planar bipedal walker, and a Unitree G1 humanoid with 29 degrees of freedom. SOPPI inferred the underlying action distributions better than rival Stein-based methods and improved system performance with similar or better efficiency across hyperparameters.
arxiv-2511-02215:
Yiqin Zhao and Tian Guo ask whether the large pretrained foundation models reshaping computing can also rescue mobile sensing from an old trade-off. Phones and headsets cannot record and process everything their sensors see; power and computation are limited. Sparse sensing records only a subset of the data, which saves resources but injects uncertainty wherever information is missing across space and time.

Using real mobile augmented reality data, the authors evaluated foundation models on geometry-aware image warping, the technique that reuses information between camera frames. The models significantly improved warping quality and also led in three-dimensional scene reconstruction tests, and the approach scaled well. The paper closes by mapping open challenges that stand between these results and dependable sparse sensing systems on everyday devices.
arxiv-2511-02515:
Obada Kraishan, a researcher, tracks how emotions ripple through developer discussions on GitHub, using the platform's emoji reactions as the signal. The dataset covers 2,098 issues and pull requests from fifty popular repositories, holding 106,743 emoji reactions. The question is whether these tiny signals merely decorate technical talk or steer it in fact.

The landscape turned out surprisingly warm: 57.4 percent of discussions carried positive sentiment, and positive emotional cascades outnumbered negative ones by twenty-three to one. Nearly half the items, 45.6 percent, showed an instant enthusiasm pattern of instant positive reinforcement. Statistical tests confirmed strong emotional contagion, with a correlation of 0.679 between early and later reactions and a very large effect size. Kraishan concludes that first reactions shape how a discussion unfolds, challenging the picture of technical talk as purely rational.
arxiv-2511-02615:
Bao Tran Truong, Siqi Wu, Alessandro Flammini, Filippo Menczer, and Alexander Stewart stress-test the algorithm behind Community Notes, the crowdsourced fact-checking system used on social media. Notes become visible when raters who usually disagree rate them helpful, a design meant to resist bias. The authors built simulations with realistic rater and note behaviour and measured how often the algorithm publishes genuinely helpful notes versus unhelpful ones.

The results are uncomfortable. A substantial fraction of truly helpful notes never surface, and the system is highly sensitive to rater biases such as polarisation and in-group preference. Worse, a coordinated minority of bad raters, between five and twenty percent of the pool, can strategically bury targeted helpful notes, in effect censoring reliable information. The authors conclude that crowdsourced moderation's scalability comes with a fragility that platforms need stronger safeguards against.
arxiv-2511-02815:
Morgan Allen and Paul Savala test whether baseball win forecasts also capture how strongly a team will win. Earlier machine learning studies predicted the winner of Major League Baseball games. Their 2025 paper trains a broad set of such models on one shared data set, then checks the link between forecast probability and the final score gap.

The common models did show the expected link: higher win probability went with bigger wins. The pair then asked whether the forecasts could guide run-line betting, a wager on the margin. With careful strategies, the forecasts yielded positive returns. Used naively, though, the same models lost money fast. The study is a caution on turning decent predictions into bets without a plan for risk.
arxiv-2511-03115:
Christopher Dean and five colleagues test a faster way to compute radiation dose in proton therapy, where planners must know exactly where a proton beam deposits its energy. Their 2025 model treats proton motion with stochastic differential equations, building on earlier work, and uses standard approximations for interaction strengths so new materials are easy to add. They benchmark it against Geant4, the field's reference simulator, in simple phantom bodies.

Across plain, layered, and side-mixed phantoms, the model matched Geant4's depth-dose curves closely. Proton range agreed within fractions of a millimeter at two beam energies, and voxel comparisons passed strict tests over 95 percent of the time. It also ran about two and a half to three times faster than single-threaded Geant4, with room for parallel speedups.
arxiv-2511-03515:
Amir Bahador Javadi and Amin Kargarian replace a costly risk rule in power grid planning with a fast learned stand-in. Wind and solar uncertainty makes fixed planning unsafe, while joint chance rules that cap total risk are slow to solve. Their ensemble of support vector machines learns from simulated best plans.

Trained classifiers become simple flat constraints inside the planning problem through a standard big-number reformulation. The stand-in traces a faceted outline of the true risk boundary, staying readable and scalable. On a large standard test grid, costs stay near optimal while risk breaches average out negligible. Grid operators gain a way to honor joint risk caps without grinding through the full probabilistic problem.
arxiv-2511-03615:
H T Silva and co-authors compute how hydroxyl-coated carbon nanotubes grab the herbicide glyphosate across acidity levels. Glyphosate pollution drives a search for better cleanup materials, and coating nanotubes with hydroxyl groups may tune them for the job. Tubes of one zigzag type carry coatings from sparse to dense in the simulations.

Five charge states of glyphosate stand for five acidity settings. Geometry tuning, electronic analysis, and room-temperature dynamics with a fast tight-binding method map the binding in detail. Coating clearly strengthens capture, with binding growing stronger as coating density rises, and acidity shifts the balance through the molecule's charge. The results guide design of nanotube filters that could pull herbicide from water.
arxiv-2511-03715:
Peter Senchyna and colleagues lay out the case for studying massive stars in nearly pristine gas with a future flagship observatory. Black hole mergers, element origins, and the earliest galaxy snapshots all hinge on how massive stars live and die when metals are scarce. Evidence from gravitational wave events and dawn-era galaxies suggests current models miss key behavior at very low metal content.

Only a few nearby galaxies can now be resolved star by star, and none reach the extreme conditions of the early universe. A planned Habitable Worlds Observatory would push resolved stellar work into far more primitive settings. The authors frame which measurements would most sharpen formation and evolution models. Better low-metal star physics would ripple into almost every early-universe claim.
arxiv-2511-04115:
Ruksit Rojpaisarnkit, Youmei Fan, Kenichi Matsumoto, and Raula Gaikovina Kula ask whether a developer's English proficiency in a prompt changes the code a language model writes. Prompt structure has been studied heavily, but the language level itself is an overlooked factor as model tools spread through software work.

Using one hundred sixty-four HumanEval tasks, prompts were rewritten from basic to advanced English while the task stayed fixed. Models defaulted to an intermediate language level in output. Effects on code proficiency varied by model, yet higher-proficiency prompts consistently produced more correct code across all models tested. Prompt language, the authors conclude, is a real lever for reliability.
arxiv-2511-04215:
Hongwei Yao, Yun Xia, Shuo Shao, Haoran Shi, Tong Qiao, and Cong Wang present the first study of black-box attacks that reverse-engineer the guardrails wrapped around large language models. Guardrails block harmful outputs, but their visible accept-or-refuse decisions leak patterns an attacker can learn from outside.

Their reinforcement learning framework uses genetic-algorithm data augmentation, collecting input-output pairs, prioritising cases where the surrogate disagrees, and mutating examples toward the hidden policy. Against three commercial systems, rule matching exceeded ninety-two percent while costing under eighty-five dollars in interface fees, as reported. Guardrail extraction is practical today, the authors warn, exposing a real weakness in current safety design.
arxiv-2511-04815:
Richard Ehrenborg and two colleagues decode the toric g-vector of nestohedra and related polytopes. These shape invariants pack deep combinatorial data into a short vector. Nonnegativity of the entries was known for several classic families without clear meanings.

The entries of any dual simplicial polytope's toric g-vector split into gamma-vector parts with positive weights. For the associahedron, cyclohedron, and permutahedron, meanings come from pattern avoidance. Parking functions, plain functions, and new parking trees carry the counts. The parking tree model extends to all chordal nestohedra, proving nonnegativity across the whole family at once.
arxiv-2511-05415:
Srijan Bharati Das and a co-author improve how solar wind particle velocity maps are rebuilt from electrostatic analyzer data. Those maps, called velocity distribution functions, are key to telling apart modes of heating, acceleration, and turbulence in the solar wind.

In part two of their series, they extend a Slepian basis method to gyrotropic cases, where the map is symmetric about the magnetic field. The rebuild keeps kinetic detail and gives exact plasma moments. Sharp maps matter since crude ones can hide the very wave-particle acts that heat the wind.
arxiv-2511-05715:
Roee Francos and co-authors warn that a stable-looking task queue can hide endless missed deadlines. Automated assignment systems hand out jobs that arrive at random and expire quickly. A bounded backlog feels like health, yet tasks may keep failing forever while the count stays flat.

The authors define a stricter test, average cost stability, which adds missed-deadline failures to the backlog count. They prove it matches bounded expected failures under mild conditions. Then they test it on a ride-request system where fleet agents cheat, faking their locations to grab jobs they never serve. Backlogs stayed bounded while cancellations persisted, but their new measure tracked the real harm and guided better deadline-aware assignment.
arxiv-2511-06115:
Mostofa Rafid Uddin and co-authors split the description of deforming 3D objects into two separate codes: one for shape, one for deformation. Grouped objects like bodies, animals, and faces bend and stretch in patterned ways. Untangling what an object is from how it is posed helps many later tasks.

Their method jointly optimizes a generator network with the shape and deformation codes, guided by tailored regularization, all without labels. Two set-based encoders then learn to produce the codes directly for new objects. The split enables deformation transfer between objects, deformation classification, and explanation analysis. On human, animal, and facial expression data sets the approach matched or beat far more complex methods, the authors report.
arxiv-2511-06415:
Isaac Cinzori describes the tangent directions available at a point of an orbit space, the set formed when a symmetry group sweeps a manifold into orbits. Orbit spaces can be too singular for ordinary calculus, so the work uses diffeology, a flexible smooth structure for such general spaces. The group action is assumed proper, a tameness condition on how symmetries move points.

Cinzori first gives a usable description of the internal tangent space at an arbitrary point of such an orbit space. The main theorem then shows this internal tangent space matches the stratified tangent space built from the orbit-type layering. Two languages for singular geometry, diffeological and stratified, are thereby proven to agree here.
arxiv-2511-06915:
Thomas Chuna and five co-authors examine when the maximum entropy method can be trusted to extract dynamics from quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Monte Carlo gives exact results for quantum many-body systems, but turning its output into dynamic features requires analytic continuation, an ill-posed inversion with no universally accepted algorithm. The maximum entropy method is the common benchmark despite longstanding controversy over Bryan's optimization algorithm.

The authors show that stochastic sampling reduces to entropy maximization when the Bayesian prior lies near the true solution. Bryan's algorithm is appropriate when noise is near zero or the prior is near the truth, and the error scales better in the prior case. They point to data-driven priors that already exploit this advantage, supporting the analysis on a test problem.
arxiv-2511-07115:
Luiz H G Tizei, Yves Auad, Florian Castioni, and Mathieu Kociak review a family of coincidence tests inside scanning transmission electron microscopes. Electron spectroscopy in such microscopes maps chemical, electronic, vibrational, and optical features down to the atomic scale. The review covers cathodoluminescence, light injection, and electron energy-loss spectroscopy, and above all what happens when signals from different channels are recorded in coincidence, timed from nanoseconds down to femtoseconds.

Coincidence timing links photons, scattered electrons, and secondary electrons from the same event, yielding information no single spectroscopy can supply on its own. The authors focus on nano-optics uses, describe the instrument changes these tests demand, and survey where the tools are heading. The article serves as both a guide to the single methods and a look ahead for combining them.
arxiv-2511-07215:
Khoi Anh Pham and Giuseppe Strangi make a random laser point where they want. Random lasers emit through multiple scattering in disordered gain media, which normally sprays light in all directions with little control. Their device infiltrates dye-doped nematic liquid crystal into a nanostructured silica metasurface, combining disorder with an built grating.

As pump energy rises, the emission transitions from uniform angular glow to a strongly directional peak at large angles, in both the amplified spontaneous emission and random lasing regimes. The directionality comes from enhanced spatial coherence in the strong scattering regime, which lets guided random-laser modes couple out through the metasurface grating at high angles. The result is wide-angle beam steering of a random laser at submicron scale with no bulky outside optics, a route toward tunable coherent sources.
arxiv-2511-07315:
Yuxuan Zhou and four co-authors automate jailbreak attacks against vision-language models to expose their weaknesses before criminals do. Current attacks need white-box access, limiting realism, or rely on hand-crafted patterns that lack diversity and scale. Their system, JPRO, is a black-box, multi-agent system in which four specialized agents collaborate through two core modules. One is tactic-driven seed creation, and the other is an adaptive optimization loop that refines attacks against the target's responses.

Across several advanced vision-language models, including GPT-4o, JPRO achieved attack success rates above sixty percent, greatly outperforming current methods. The authors frame the work defensively: automated, diverse jailbreaking uncovers critical vulnerabilities that manual testing misses, and gives developers a realistic benchmark for evaluating and hardening multimodal model safety.
arxiv-2511-07615:
Martin Miglioli builds measures from the geometry of symmetry groups. For compact Lie groups, such measures live on adjoint orbits, the paths traced when group elements move a fixed point. Integrals over those paths give useful distributions.

Miglioli derives piecewise measures from those integrals through changes on polynomial spaces carrying an apolar inner product. For the unitary group, moments of projected orbital measures get a direct formula. Such measures support random matrix work and spectral problems. A clean proof unifies cases handled piecemeal, giving formulas that are ready to use in practice.
arxiv-2511-07815:
Karel Walter Gomez Orellana and co-authors compare controllers that keep a 5G millimeter-wave transmitter honest. At twenty four gigahertz, heat shifts amplifier gain and degrades signal quality measured by error vector magnitude. Three strategies compete for adaptive power management: classic PID, pure integral, and fuzzy-integral control.

The fuzzy design blends fuzzy logic for nonlinear behavior with steady action that erases steady error. Bench experiments show it settling faster, holding steadier, and minimizing signal error better than both classical rivals. Practical control wins matter because millimeter-wave radios must stay linear across weather, load, and aging hardware.
arxiv-2511-07915:
Kosei Fujiki, Michitaka Kohara, and Kotaro Shinmyo derive Einstein gravity from an entropy law in de Sitter space. Holographic pseudo-entropy extends entanglement entropy to wider settings. Its first law, applied through the de Sitter and conformal field theory link, is shown equal to the Einstein equation in three dimensions.

The path satisfying the law mixes a timelike curve with a complex curve. Small entropy changes obey a Klein-Gordon equation, signaling a new time direction from Euclidean data. Results like this test holography where the universe expands, the setting our own cosmos suggests.
arxiv-2511-08215:
Rizal Khoirul Anam evaluates a two part food analysis pipeline that pairs an EfficientNet-B4 vision model with the Gemini language model. Food apps need automatic nutrition estimates and cooking guidance from a photo. The system first classifies the dish visually, then asks the generative model to produce nutrition details and a recipe, so early vision errors can cascade into the text.

A new custom Chinese food data set counters cultural bias in public collections. EfficientNet-B4 gave the best balance of accuracy and efficiency among rival backbones, while Gemini led on factual quality. A formal semantic error propagation analysis shows the visual front end remains the main bottleneck.
arxiv-2511-08415:
Deshui Cao, Lina Zhang, Songbai Chen, and Qiyuan Pan investigate chaotic particle motion around a dyonic Kerr Newman black hole sitting in a Melvin swirling universe. The black hole carries electric and magnetic charge plus spin, while the surrounding universe adds its own magnetic field and swirl. Tools include Poincare sections, Lyapunov indicators, recurrence analysis, bifurcation diagrams, and basins of attraction.

Swirling and magnetic parameters make the equations nonseparable, and chaos is confirmed even after removing conical singularities and Dirac strings. Chaotic orbits grow more common as swirl and field strength rise, and fewer as charge or spin increase. The swirl parameter also reshapes the ranges where chaos appears at all.
arxiv-2511-08615:
Kosta Dakic and three co-authors release MATRIX, a dataset and tracking framework built for crowds watched by many moving drones. Eight synchronized drones film forty pedestrians in an urban scene with a large building blocking views, and the cameras keep shifting position throughout.

Static-camera methods shine on a simplified version of the scene but fall apart in the full one. The proposed framework recalibrates cameras in real time, registers the images, and fuses features into a bird's-eye view. It holds detection and tracking accuracy near ninety percent and follows about eighty percent of paths under hard conditions. Pretraining transfers well, and losing cameras one by one degrades results gracefully rather than breaking them.
arxiv-2511-09015:
Maarten Derickx and Filip Najman classify which modular curves carry sporadic points, the rare rational points that do not come in infinite families. Modular curves describe elliptic curves with extra level structure, and their sporadic points, whether tied to CM or not, mark rare arithmetic events.

The authors pin down every level N for which the curve X0(N) admits a sporadic CM point of any degree. They also pin down every N for which it admits a sporadic point at all. The result extends the famous Mazur and Kenku classification of isogenies between elliptic curves over the rationals. That classification matches sporadic points of degree one. Extending the census to any degree closes a natural gap in the arithmetic of modular curves.
arxiv-2511-09115:
Svante Janson repairs a crack in the foundations of probability theory. The Skorohod topology governs how random functions with jumps are compared and how their convergence is defined. A basic theorem by Jakubowski from 1986 extends that topology to functions taking values in any completely regular space.

Janson found a gap in Jakubowski's proof of that theorem and supplies the correction. Papers of this kind rarely announce new phenomena; their job is to make sure a load-bearing result actually holds, since later work across probability and statistics rests on it. The note is short and technical, addressed to specialists who use the Skorohod space with general state spaces and need the 1986 theorem to be fully trustworthy.
arxiv-2511-09615:
Achilleas Gitsis and Falk Hassler find an all-order formula for symmetry transformations that string theory needs for anomaly cancellation. T-duality tightly constrains how higher-derivative corrections modify supergravity, forcing Lorentz transformations to change exactly as the Green-Schwarz mechanism requires. The standard construction method becomes technically unfeasible beyond second order in the string tension parameter.

Using an alternative approach to the generalized Bergshoeff-de Roo identification, the authors obtain a very simple transformation law valid to all orders. They verify its closure by explicitly computing the resulting gauge algebra.
