A problem that stalled at low orders thus gets a closed-form answer, opening higher-derivative string corrections to systematic study at any order.
arxiv-2511-09715:
Arman Zarei and five co-authors give image editors a volume knob for every instruction in a multi-part edit prompt. Today's instruction-based editors apply each requested change at one fixed strength, so users cannot dial a single edit up or down. SliderEdit separates the instructions and exposes each as a continuous slider.

The framework learns one shared set of low-rank adaptation matrices. They generalize across edits, attributes, and composed instructions, with no per-attribute training. Sliding one control interpolates that edit's intensity while keeping spatial locality and global consistency. Applied to FLUX-Kontext and Qwen-Image-Edit, the method substantially improves controllability, visual consistency, and user steerability in the authors' tests. They claim the first such fine-grained instruction control for image editing.
arxiv-2511-09815:
Fitria Khairunnisa, Hadyan Luthfan Prihadi, M. Zhahir Djogama, Donny Dwiputra, and Freddy Permana Zen investigate traversable wormholes in a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter black brane setup. A double trace deformation couples the two boundaries of the spacetime, and the question is whether gravitational perturbations alone can open a passage. The mechanism relies on violating the averaged null energy condition, which normally keeps wormholes shut.

Working within a hydrodynamic approximation, the authors find the wormhole becomes traversable in both the shear and sound channels. They test several coupling configurations for shear, and vary sound speed and attenuation for the sound channel, which changes how long the opening lasts. A late-time power-law pattern in the energy condition is fitted and generalized across both channels.
arxiv-2511-10115:
Michał Suchorowski, Fabian Brauneis, Hans-Werner Hammer, Michał Tomza, and Artem G. Volosniev introduce a generalized Gross-Pitaevskii equation for two-dimensional bosons that attract each other. The standard mean-field equation is scale invariant in two dimensions, which hides a quantum anomaly effect. Their version makes the coupling constant depend logarithmically on density, breaking that invariance and letting the anomaly appear in direct calculations.

They first study quantum droplets, universal bound states in free space, within the new framework. Breathing modes and quench dynamics in trapped systems follow, opening a systematic route into non-equilibrium behavior of these gases. The theory also predicts universal excited states, including vortex configurations, which may be easier for experiments to reach than the ground state.
arxiv-2511-10315:
Annabel Kropf and Ivo Schulthess write a primer on strong-field quantum electrodynamics aimed at experimental physicists rather than theorists. Strong fields push quantum electrodynamics into regimes where charged particles and intense light interact non-perturbatively, and a wave of experiments is entering that territory. A formal theory review, the authors say, is not what bench scientists first need.

The document instead offers a conceptual and practical first point of contact: the core ideas, the working terminology, and the challenges most relevant to designing experiments and interpreting their results. It is meant to bridge foundational theory and hands-on laboratory work, complementing the heavier literature. Readers get the vocabulary and intuition needed before tackling full theoretical treatments of the strong-field regime.
arxiv-2511-10815:
Yuyang Huang, Dante Kalise, and Hicham Kouhkouh recast the problem of minimizing a non-convex function as a problem in optimal control. Instead of building an optimizer directly, they steer a dynamical system and ask whether its trajectories can be guaranteed to end up at the global minimizers.

Their main result says yes, with care. Quasi-optimal trajectories of a discounted control problem converge globally, and practically, to the set of global minimizers, ending within any chosen tolerance after finite time and staying there. The argument avoids solving the ergodic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, leaning instead on occupation measures that count how long trajectories linger away from the solution set. Matching results cover three formulations, the evolutive discounted, stationary discounted, and evolutive non-discounted cases.
arxiv-2511-11115:
Anne Buckner, Ana Duarte-Cabral, and their colleagues map how star clusters spread across the galaxy NGC 628 as they age, using images from the Hubble and Webb space telescopes. Their sample is the most complete yet, with cluster ages from one million years to over one hundred million. A stats tool scores how strongly clusters group together in space.

Most newborn clusters sit tightly with each other, while clusters that have emerged sit in looser groups at any age. The few huge young clusters tend to sit with smaller ones, not with each other. Tight clusters start spread widely across the disk and narrow with age, a pattern that may track dispersal or outward growth.
arxiv-2511-11315:
Jawad Ibn Ahad, Muhammad Rafsan Kabir, and their colleagues propose LAET, a tuning framework that adapts pre-trained language models for finance at lower cost. Language models have reshaped financial text work, from sentiment to credit risk, but the strongest models are costly to run and tune, which shuts out many organizations. LAET fine-tunes only the most effective layers, chosen by studying hidden states, and freezes the rest.

That selective tuning cuts compute sharply while lifting task performance. On financial benchmarks, the approach beat existing marks and large general models, even with small models of about three billion parameters. The authors frame it as a bridge from research models to scalable deployment.
arxiv-2511-11515:
Paul Jonas Jost, Frank Bergmann, and their colleagues present PEtab-GUI, a graphical tool for building parameter estimation problems in the PEtab standard format used in systems biology. Fitting model parameters to data is a cornerstone of data-driven modeling, but PEtab spreads a problem across many linked files that are edited by hand, which invites inconsistencies and daunts new users. The GUI gathers every component into one environment.

SBML models and tabular files are edited together with live error checking and customizable defaults. Interactive visualization and simulation let users inspect how a model meets its data before fitting. The open-source Python application aims to make standardized, reproducible problem setup accessible for teaching and cross-field work alike.
arxiv-2511-11815:
Hyunseok Lee and nine co-authors watch living matter reshape itself. The key force is nonreciprocity. The force one entity exerts on another is not returned in kind. Their lab system is starfish embryos at distinct growth stages. The asymmetry there can be tuned by hand.

Tests, inferred interactions, and topological analysis yield a state diagram. It spans crystalline, flocking, and fragmented phases. Weak nonreciprocity promotes order. Stronger asymmetry tears structure apart. A new tool maps how structural motifs spread across states. It reveals the transitions between them. Living and active materials may follow similar rules. The diagram may guide work from tissues to robot swarms.
arxiv-2511-11915:
Adam F. Kowalski reports high-resolution spectra of a record solar flare. It was the X9 flare of October 3, 2024. It held the brightest near-ultraviolet continuum source yet seen in such an event. The paper tests if beams of fast electrons can explain it. In the standard picture, beams slam into the lower atmosphere. They make dense chromospheric condensations that radiate the bright kernels.

One-dimensional radiative-hydrodynamic models predict extreme line broadening. They also predict bright continuum and fast iron line asymmetries. The standard high-flux beam model overshoots on all three counts. Condensations at somewhat lower densities fit better. The result narrows what powered the flare's most extreme brightening. It also refines beam physics used in flare forecasting.
arxiv-2511-12315:
Sebastian Hagedorn and three co-authors extend a classic machine learning algorithm for automata so it can handle infinite alphabets. Angluin's L-star algorithm learns a finite-state machine by asking a teacher questions, in polynomial time. In its original form it only works when the input alphabet is finite, which limits its use in software and AI settings.

The extension learns symbolic automata whose transitions are guarded by predicates over rational numbers, a dense and endless alphabet. That brings settings such as regular expressions over real values and time series within reach. The authors show their method is optimal in a precise sense: the number of teacher queries grows at most linearly with the size of the target machine.
arxiv-2511-12715:
Sushrut Thorat and four co-authors test a theory of how the brain learns to represent scenes. As eyes move, each fixation reveals a glimpse related to the last by what tends to appear together and by the geometry of eye movements. Their Glimpse Prediction Networks are recurrent models trained, without labels, to predict the embedding of the next glimpse along human-like scan paths. Such models should end up encoding objects, their co-occurrences, and their layouts.

The models did exactly that, combining information across glimpses into scene representations. More strikingly, those representations matched human brain activity in mid- and higher-level visual cortex, often as well as or better than leading artificial network models. The authors argue that next-glimpse prediction is a biologically plausible route to brain-like scene understanding. The work links a simple learning rule to the structure of visual cortex itself.
arxiv-2511-12815:
Snehinh Sen studies semirings in which every congruence is finitely generated, a class he calls Congruence Noetherian. Semirings are number systems like the natural numbers, where subtraction may not exist. Finite generation is a tameness condition: it says complicated relations can still be described with finite data. The paper builds background, gives examples, and then focuses on one test case, the canonical positive models of a real order.

Those models look like an obvious choice for the class, yet they are not finitely generated as modules over the natural numbers. Sen proves they are nevertheless Congruence Noetherian, and also flat over the natural numbers. That combination is the paper's point: module-level wildness does not block congruence-level tameness. The short article contributes a clean example to the structure theory of semirings, an area with far fewer organizing results than ring theory.
arxiv-2511-12915:
Yubo Chen, Wendong Wang, and Guoxu Yang prove that a strong enough shear flow stops bacteria from collapsing into a singularity. The Patlak-Keller-Segel equations model bacteria that drift toward chemicals they themselves release. On the plane, solutions are known to blow up in finite time once the total mass passes a threshold. The authors stir the system with a Couette flow, a simple shear, and ask how strong it must be to keep solutions smooth forever, even for large initial mass.

Their answer is quantitative, not just qualitative. They derive an explicit lower bound on the needed flow amplitude, with the sufficient constant worked out numerically, a rarity in this kind of analysis. The same conclusion extends to the harder system where the bacteria also drive the fluid through the Navier-Stokes equations. Mixing, it turns out, can be prescribed with a number attached.
arxiv-2511-13215:
Yuchen Bi and Jintian Zhu prove a link between mass and capacity on a special class of curved spaces. Their setting covers generalized spaces that look flat far away and have scalar curvature that is never negative. The result is stated for the spin case, with a sharp equality case.

When equality holds, the space can be reshaped by a harmonic conformal change into flat space with a closed bounded piece removed. That removed piece must be small in a precise sense, with Hausdorff dimension no more than a stated bound tied to the space dimension. The finding sharpens how mass and capacity control shape.
arxiv-2511-13415:
Wanqing Cui and 6 co-authors present AGREE, a training method that teaches visual document retrievers which page regions truly support a match. Screenshot-based retrievers score whole pages, but training labels never say where the answer sits. Models then lean on surface cues and miss deeper links, especially for questions whose answer is not copied text.

AGREE borrows attention maps from a multimodal language model as stand-in supervision for region-level relevance. Training joins those local signals with the global page label, so the retriever learns both whether and why a page matches. On the ViDoRe V2 benchmark it beat the global-only baseline by clear margins on top-rank accuracy.
arxiv-2511-13515:
The PandaX Collaboration searches for scalar-mediated interactions among neutrinos and dark matter particles using double beta decay data. Such a scalar could link neutrinos to each other, dark matter to itself, or the two sectors together. Their data come from xenon-136 decay watched by the PandaX-4T detector across a wide energy range.

The team performed the first direct spectral search of this kind and set the strongest limits yet on scalar neutrino self-interactions for light mediators. Those limits press on models that invoke such forces to ease the Hubble tension. If the same scalar also links dark matter particles, combined limits with cosmology follow as well.
arxiv-2511-14415:
Hung M. Bui, Richard R. Hall, and Martin Subira Jorge compute a new case of the fourth moment of the Riemann zeta-function, a central average in analytic number theory. The twisted fourth moment was found by Hughes and Young and sharpened by Bettin and co-authors. In applications the twisting polynomial usually mimics either a mollifier, which damps the zeta values, or an amplifier, which boosts selected ones.

Earlier results covered the fourth power of zeta times a squared or fourth-power mollifier, or a squared amplifier. This paper obtains the asymptotic formula with the fourth power of an amplifier instead. Applications include results about gaps between zeros of the zeta-function and lower bounds for its moments.
arxiv-2511-14915:
TaeHo Yoon, Ernest K. Ryu, and Benjamin Grimmer characterize every fixed-step algorithm that converges at the best possible rate for a broad problem class. The setting covers nonexpansive fixed-point problems, where a classic method due to Halpern, its dual, and in fact a whole family of methods all hit the same optimal speed. Until now that family had no complete description.

The authors encode each method as a lower triangular matrix of step choices and find special polynomial quantities, called H-invariants, that stay fixed across all optimal methods. Extra certificates mark exactly which matrices in that shared level set are optimal. The theory gives a fresh, complete map of optimal acceleration for first-order methods.
arxiv-2511-15215:
Arunima Arunima, Mark R. Krumholz, and three co-authors test whether stars keep the orbital fingerprints of their birth clusters inside a simulated Milky Way. Astronomers hope to trace scattered stars back to their dissolved home clusters, which assumes each star's orbital actions stay nearly constant. A real disk, with its moving spiral arms and lumps, may scramble those actions over time.

In a high-resolution simulation of a spiral disk galaxy, individual stars do drift in action within a short span. Stars born close together, though, drift in step, keeping similar actions for up to half a billion years. That coherence, steady across the disk, means cluster reconstruction should target groups rather than lone stars.
arxiv-2511-15315:
Abdelhamid Ezzerg, Ilija Bogunovic, and Jeremias Knoblauch harden Bayesian optimization against data corruption of unlimited size. Bayesian optimization steers experiments, such as tuning a material or a drug dose, by learning a response surface and probing its most promising uncertain spots. A single wild outlier can poison that surface, and older robust methods only survive a bounded total corruption budget.

The new adversary model limits how often corruption strikes, not how hard. Against it, the authors build RCGP-UCB, pairing the classic upper confidence bound rule with a robust conjugate Gaussian process, in stable and adaptive versions. Regret still grows sublinearly even when attacks can be arbitrarily large, and with no corruption the method matches the standard algorithm's guarantees.
arxiv-2511-15615:
Gábor Balázs presents an algorithm for estimating an unknown Lipschitz function from noisy data. A Lipschitz function cannot change too steeply, a common and flexible assumption in statistics. Earlier max-affine methods fit convex functions with flat pieces, but the Lipschitz setting is broader and needs new tools, including a feature expansion that builds delta-convex functions, which combine two convex parts.

That expansion can approximate any Lipschitz function while keeping its steepness limit. The estimator reaches the best possible convergence rate, up to small factors, tied to the data intrinsic dimension. Adaptive partitioning, a penalty that removes the need to know the steepness in advance, and a two-stage optimization complete the method.
arxiv-2511-16015:
Nimeshika Udayangani, Hadi M. Dolatabadi, Sarah Erfani, and Christopher Leckie improve detection of out-of-distribution inputs when training classes are long-tailed. A classifier must flag inputs unlike anything it trained on, for safe deployment, but rare tail classes are often misread and false alarms climb. Their idea is to exploit relationships between samples rather than treating each input alone.

Features from a pretrained model seed a graph over samples, after correcting differences between pretraining and training activations by Gaussianization, reshaping activations toward a standard normal form. Graph convolutional networks then refine that graph into a feature space suited to long-tailed detection. On three long-tailed benchmarks, the method outperformed leading approaches by a large margin and lifted tail-class accuracy.
arxiv-2511-16315:
Samuel Stevens presents BioBench, an ecology vision benchmark meant to move scientific machine learning beyond ImageNet as its default yardstick. ImageNet accuracy no longer predicts performance on scientific imagery, Stevens shows. Across dozens of modern vision checkpoints, it explains only about a third of variance on ecology tasks. It also mis ranks many strong models.

BioBench unifies nine public, application driven tasks across four taxonomic kingdoms. Six acquisition types range from drone images to camera trap frames, totaling millions of images. One Python interface downloads data, fits light classifiers on frozen backbones, and reports balanced scores. Vision models can be evaluated in hours on a single high end graphics card. The blueprint invites other sciences to build similar domain benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-16715:
Yuqi Li and seven co-authors present DDTime, a dataset distillation method for time-series forecasting. It squeezes a large training set into a tiny synthetic one a model can learn from almost as well. Time series resist distillation because strong autocorrelation distorts the alignment between teacher and student, and synthetic samples tend to lack diversity.

DDTime aligns value terms in the frequency domain, restoring spectral consistency and temporal fidelity. It adds an inter-sample regularizer inspired by the information bottleneck to keep synthetic trajectories diverse and information dense. The objective plugs into a range of frameworks and optimizes stably at first order. Across twenty benchmark datasets and several forecasting architectures, DDTime beat existing distillation methods with roughly thirty percent relative accuracy gains at only a few percent extra compute.
arxiv-2511-16815:
Kyla D. Jones and Alexander W. Dowling introduce BITS for GAPS, a framework for choosing experiments that teach a Gaussian process surrogate the most, while honestly carrying hyperparameter uncertainty into the choice. Standard acquisition functions fix or point-estimate hyperparameters, pretending away a real source of doubt.

Here a latent function gets a Gaussian process prior and the hyperparameters get priors of their own, encoding what the modeler knows about the physics. The sampling criterion then weighs both data scarcity and model uncertainty. The authors prove a closed-form approximation and a lower bound for the posterior differential entropy. A case study builds a surrogate for activity coefficients in a binary mixture, embeds it in an extended Raoult's law model. It shows the sampling targets high-uncertainty regions, raising information gain and accuracy for distillation design.
arxiv-2511-16915:
Mohammad Javad Habibi Vosta Kolaei studies what happens to closed planar curves evolving under a forced biharmonic flow, a fourth-order geometric motion driven by bending energy plus an external forcing term. Such flows appear in the theory of biharmonic maps and in variational problems where an outside influence cannot be ignored.

Reformulating the flow through the support function turns the geometry into a scalar partial differential equation. The author proves global existence of smooth solutions under suitable conditions on the forcing. Under specific geometric constraints the equation takes a Monge-Ampère type form that can even behave hyperbolically. Convexity is preserved along the evolution, and sufficient conditions guarantee long-time convergence to steady states, clarifying how forcing can stabilize high-order curvature flows.
arxiv-2511-17215:
Mordecai Waegell disputes a recent experiment said to challenge Bohmian mechanics, a version of quantum theory in which particles follow definite paths. The experiment claimed to watch states that should stand still in that theory, yet inferred motion from how a wave spread between two linked channels. Waegell argues the claim fails at several points, starting with what was actually observed.

In his reading, the setup recorded averaged densities of wave pulses bouncing off a step, not the still states the team claimed. The speed measure they used is also invalid for true still states, and applying it to the averaged data created a false look of success. The paper's verdict is narrow: this test, as run and read, does not settle anything about Bohmian motion.
arxiv-2511-17415:
Minshen Xu, Shiwei Lan, and Lulu Kang add variable selection to Gaussian process regression, a flexible modeling method whose cost and accuracy both suffer in high dimensions. If most input variables are irrelevant, a good model should switch them off automatically. Inspired by Bayesian bridge regression, the authors place norm constraints on key process parameters, which induce sparsity and expose the active variables.

Two versions follow: one with the familiar squared norm and conjugate Gaussian priors, and one with weaker norms that need constrained flat priors and produce non-standard posteriors. For the harder case they build a Gibbs sampler using spherical Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to explore the constrained posterior efficiently. Simulations and a real-data application show better variable selection and prediction than alternatives. The work aims at trustworthy Gaussian process models in genuinely high-dimensional problems.
arxiv-2511-17515:
Mahmoud Elkhodr and Ergun Gide report a cross-campus study of teaching systems analysis students to work with generative AI without surrendering their judgment. Their SAGE framework embeds AI into the curriculum and trains students to decide, for each AI contribution, whether to accept, modify, or reject it. Eighteen student groups across four Australian universities worked through the approach, and the authors tracked how their orchestration skills developed.

Most groups moved beyond passive acceptance and showed selective judgment, yet none spotted gaps that both they and the AI had missed, a clear competency ceiling. About half the groups struggled when the AI misclassified system boundaries or mishandled data management and exception handling. Accessibility awareness proved fragile, collapsing without prompts at every stage. The authors recommend documenting reasons for each AI decision, scaffolding accessibility continuously, and drafting specifications before consulting AI.
arxiv-2511-17815:
Robert Coulter and Steven Senger report observations on bent and planar functions. These special functions over finite fields are valued in coding and cryptography because their differences spread out as evenly as possible. Bent functions are linked, in odd characteristic, to perfect nonlinear functions.

They show that the graph of a bent function forms a Salem set in a suitable sense. They also quantify repeated values among difference operators and prove, by elementary means, that two distinct planar functions must differ in at least two places. The results add clean structural facts about a heavily studied family.
arxiv-2511-17915:
Yao Liu and three co-authors study fair task assignment in teams of different robots, where greedy matching by cost or preference can leave some tasks waiting long or poorly served. Most prior work assumes central control or ignores fairness when agents see only part of the world.

They connect a classic fair allocation equilibrium to decentralized learning under partial views. Two methods follow: a learning framework guided by the fair solution, and an online method that assigns tasks as they appear. Simulations and a warehouse test with varied robots preserve the fair and efficient balance, with one method nearly matching central control.
arxiv-2511-18115:
Wenyu Li, Sidun Liu, Peng Qiao, Yong Dou, and Tongrui Hu present Muskie, a vision backbone pre trained natively on multiple views at once for three dimensional tasks. Existing backbones process frames one by one and agree poorly across views, while three dimensional understanding needs consistency between viewpoints of the same scene.

Muskie learns by reconstructing heavily masked content in one view using geometric correspondences found in the other views, with an aggressive masking strategy. No three dimensional supervision is used, yet the model develops strong geometric understanding and beats frame wise backbones on correspondence accuracy. As a backbone it improves camera pose estimation and point map reconstruction.
arxiv-2511-18215:
Shangyuan Yuan, Preston Fairchild, Yu Mei, Xinyu Zhou, and Xiaobo Tan track the shape of a soft robot with a plain camera. Soft robots bend in smooth curves, so a controller needs the live shape to steer well. Past camera methods need marks on the robot, odd backdrops, or large training sets, which limits use in real rooms.

Their method, AFT, uses the marks the robot skin already has. A split plan first lines up small parts, then fits the whole bend. It needs just one start scan and a rough pose to begin. On a real soft arm the tip error stays near two to three percent of length. The method copes with blocked views and moved cameras.
arxiv-2511-18315:
Rajashree Bar, Daibik Barik, Adri Bhattacharya, and Partha Sarathi Mandal study how mobile agents can clean a network that keeps changing. In the cleaning task, agents must clear both nodes and links of a fault. A strict rule applies: once a part is clean, it must stay clean, with no spread back from dirty parts.

Static networks have drawn most past work, while live ones have drawn none. The team set two forms of change, based on how soon a lost link must return. For each form they prove low and high bounds on the agent count a full clean sweep needs. Edge loss and return mid task drive the hard parts. The bounds show the price of change for this strict clean rule.
arxiv-2511-18415:
Wei Yang and five co-authors fix a flaw in how vision and language models pick paths down a family tree of labels. A sound path needs each step to fit the step above, from broad class to fine type. Old tests score each level on its own, which hides breaks where a child does not match its parent.

The team add a joint test that asks for the full path in one call, plus a score that weights deep levels more. Strong models still fail it often, with invalid parent child pairs. Their fix, DuoTeach, lets one model teach itself in two roles, with no hand labels. The pupil learns from its own checked paths. Gains show steadier cross level choices.
arxiv-2511-19215:
Andrii O. Prykhodko, Ivan O. Starodub, and Yaroslav Zolotaryuk find exact solutions for a ladder of Josephson junctions, tiny superconducting devices linked in two rails. They look for fluxons, localized bundles of magnetic flux, that stay compact and still. Such states do not occur in the simpler parallel array described by the standard discrete sine-Gordon equation.

The ladder supports compact single and multi-fluxon states, some symmetric between the rails and some not. Certain symmetric states carry zero energy when their topological charge is even, while asymmetric ones always do. Depending on anisotropy, compact states may coexist with spread-out ones, and an external magnetic field rules them out.
arxiv-2511-19615:
Ulrich P. Steinwandel and Daniel J. Price clean up magnetic divergence errors in cosmological simulations of magnetized gas. Numerical fields can develop fake magnetic monopoles, measured as divergence, which corrupt the physics. The older Powell method only partly controls them by source terms while the flow carries them along.

The authors add a hyperbolic and parabolic cleaning scheme to the OpenGadget3 code, adapted to an expanding universe, so errors are actively carried away and damped. Standard tests, from a vortex to a shock tube and a collapsing pancake, confirm cleaner fields with correct physics. A full galaxy cluster run compares the schemes directly.
arxiv-2511-19715:
Theodor Hagström and Lars Herre test whether fleets of electric vehicles can profit from a fast Nordic flexibility market. The fifteen-minute mFRR market buys balancing energy on short notice, and shorter trading windows lower the entry bar for aggregators facing uncertain demand. The fleet is modeled as a virtual battery with time-varying limits.

A risk-aware stochastic plan coordinates day-ahead buying with quarter-hour bidding, using a downside-risk objective for safety. Against a day-ahead-only baseline, the joint strategy earns more expected profit with less risk on both test days. It buys less energy early, shifts purchases toward the flexibility market, and flattens the charging plan.
arxiv-2511-19815:
Fabian Barras, Andreas Aspaas, Einat Aharonov, and François Renard explain why a huge Norwegian landslide speeds up after rain. At Åknes, about fifty million cubic meters of rock creep over a rubble shear zone, with seasonal surges tied to rainfall. The standard theory blames water pressure, yet close monitoring finds that pressure stays low across the zone.

A micromechanical model separates flow effects from pressure effects in the data. The driver turns out to be seepage force, the push of channelized water flowing along the shear zone. The finding shifts how such creeping slopes are assessed for hazard work.
arxiv-2511-20115:
Kerber, Ritsch, and Ostermann stress-test a beloved shortcut for quantum many-body problems. Their 2025 paper examines the cumulants expansion approach. Quantum state spaces grow exponentially with system size. Exact treatment quickly becomes impossible numerically. The expansion replaces operator products by simpler averages.

Its lowest order is the familiar mean field approximation. Higher orders keep progressively more correlations. Two test problems probe where the method holds. A chain of interacting atoms showed textbook behavior. Accuracy improved smoothly as expansion order rose. A factoring-by-annealing problem told the opposite story. Beyond mean field, extra orders bought nothing there. Some cases produced wildly oscillating, non-physical solutions. Higher orders sometimes agreed worse than lower ones. No general rule predicts success in advance yet. The authors want rigorous criteria for safe use. Physicists get a candid map of the method's moods.
arxiv-2511-20315:
Joshi, Bhatt, and Modi trace how choices form inside language models. Their 2025 paper measures true freedom counts across model layers. Hidden states live in huge spaces on paper. Their real degrees of freedom may be far fewer. Multiple-choice questions supply the testbed.

Twenty-eight open-weight models were analyzed layer by layer. Several estimators measured that freedom count independently. Per-layer answer accuracy was tracked alongside. A steady arc appeared across the model zoo. Early layers sit on low-dimensional manifolds. Middle layers expand the working space substantially. Late layers compress it back down again. Compression settles onto choice-relevant features. Freedom peaks align with where choices crystallize. Confidence and compression evolve together measurably. Models seem to project language onto structured surfaces. Those manifolds align with the task at hand. Geometric tools may read model decisiveness directly. Model reading gains a shape-based vocabulary.
arxiv-2511-20715:
Ayrton Nascimento and Henrique Boschi-Filho compute in 2025 the mechanics of the proton using a holographic model, where a strongly interacting system is mirrored by gravity in curved five-dimensional space. Their targets are gravitational form factors, which encode how the proton's energy and momentum are distributed inside it. From those follow mechanical properties: how pressure and shear forces vary from the proton's centre to its edge.

The pair work in a deformed anti-de Sitter background, that curved space tweaked to mimic confinement. They model the proton as a Dirac field and extract the gluon contributions to two form factors. Their numbers agree well with lattice QCD results and with earlier holographic work. The pressure and shear profiles they derive satisfy the von Laue stability condition, the balance a stable particle must obey. They also obtain the energy distribution, force patterns, and the radii tied to the distributions.
arxiv-2511-20815:
Saddam Hijazi and colleagues compare in 2025 ways to shrink models of guided waves in damaged materials. Guided ultrasonic waves are a workhorse of structural health monitoring: damage betrays itself in the scattered signals, but running such waves is expensive. Model order reduction replaces it with a small surrogate that mimics it.

The authors apply four methods across three cases: the classical wave equation, a mechanical guided-wave system, and a nonlinear hyperelastic aluminium model. The methods span proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), which needs the equations, and data-driven options learning from snapshots: dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), its multiresolution variant mrDMD, and operator inference. It carries two changes, a scaling of the snapshot data and an unconstrained, structure-preserving form admitting first-order solvers. The study extends their work on that model and maps where each method earns its keep.
arxiv-2511-21315:
Jia-Yi Lu and nine coauthors chase room-pressure superconductivity in a layered nickel oxide in 2025. The bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7 superconducts near 80 kelvin, but only under crushing pressure, where its crystal takes a tetragonal shape. Guided by the Goldschmidt tolerance factor, a recipe balancing ion sizes, the team doped the material with aluminum. Annealing under moderately high oxygen pressure then locked that shape in at ordinary pressure.

Lu and his coauthors confirm the tetragonal structure by X-ray and neutron diffraction for aluminum shares between 0.3 and 0.5 of the nickel sites. The victory is partial: the doped samples behave as semiconductors with localized magnetic moments and spin-glass-like freezing at low temperatures. Worse, high-pressure resistance tests show that even a tiny aluminum share of 0.05 wipes out superconductivity almost completely, a warning about nonmagnetic impurities in nickelates.
arxiv-2511-21415:
Mingue Park, Prin Phunyaphibarn, Phillip Lee, and Minhyuk Sung fix a sameness problem in AI image generation in 2025. Visual autoregressive models, which build pictures scale by scale, rival diffusion models on quality but quietly fail on variety: ask for the same prompt twice and you get nearly the same picture. Their framework, DiverseVAR, attacks the problem at test time, with no retraining or fine-tuning of the generator.

Park and his coauthors first inject noise into the text embedding, which diversifies outputs but wrecks quality as variety climbs. Their second stage, scale-travel, rescues quality: a multi-scale autoencoder extracts coarse tokens so generation can resume from an intermediate scale, refining the noisy start back into a clean image. Across experiments, the combined method pushed the diversity-quality trade-off to a new Pareto frontier, meaning more variety at any given quality level than prior tricks achieved.
arxiv-2511-21715:
Philosopher of science Robert W. Batterman asks why deep neural networks work so well, and answers by looking at the data rather than the network, in 2025. DNNs are often called black boxes whose inner workings stay opaque. Batterman argues the explanation lies in the training datasets themselves. Real datasets, he shows, carry complex higher-order correlations, statistical patterns beyond simple averages and spreads.

The paper contends that networks succeed because they discover these higher-order correlation functions, patterns linking more than two points at once. Evidence comes from natural image statistics, including photographs taken at Hacklebarney State Park in New Jersey, whose structure repeats across scales. The conclusion urges researchers to study facts about the world baked into data. Those robust statistical features, Batterman argues, drive how network weights update during training. DNNs, on this view, implement a well-understood explanatory method long used for continuum systems.
arxiv-2511-21915:
Sorokin's doctoral thesis builds fast software for three hard computing jobs in science. The first job is quasi-Monte Carlo integration, which estimates high-dimensional integrals with well spread sample points. The second is Gaussian process regression, a method that fits data and reports its own uncertainty. The third is scientific machine learning for equations that describe physical systems. All three need answers that are quick and can be trusted.

For quasi-Monte Carlo work, he built QMCPy, an open-source Python package with vectorized error estimates. For Gaussian processes, he derived new kernels with higher smoothness and faster multitask algorithms, released as FastGPs. For machine learning, his solver recovers partial differential equations with random coefficients to machine precision. The tools are applied to failure-probability estimates, groundwater flow through the Darcy equation, and Bayesian multilevel integration. Neural surrogates for radiative transfer round out the list of test cases.
arxiv-2511-22015:
Sano, a mathematician, counts rectangulations: ways to slice a rectangle into rectangles, where two slicings count as the same if one can be deformed into the other without breaking which rectangles touch. For such strong rectangulations the total count grows with a known growth constant, and Sano asks what happens when one fixed pattern of adjacencies is forbidden everywhere inside the slicing.

Forbidding any fixed pattern strictly lowers the growth constant, by an amount the paper bounds explicitly and uniformly. The drop is at least a stated quantity depending on the pattern's size. Consequently the fraction of pattern-avoiding rectangulations among all rectangulations shrinks to zero as the number of rectangles grows. The proof converts rectangulations into quadrant walks and uses a pattern-insertion scheme to control the generating functions' radius of convergence.
arxiv-2511-22315:
Abdalla, Nabi, Eshkiki, and Caraffini, language technology researchers, create the first named entity recognition dataset for Kurdish Sorani. Sorani, written in a modified Arabic script and spoken by millions, has almost no annotated resources, so tools that find people, places, and organizations in text do not exist for it. Their corpus holds 64,563 manually annotated tokens with tagged entity spans.

Two modeling approaches are benchmarked on the new data. A conditional random field reaches an F1 score of 0.825 on the test annotations, clearly ahead of a bidirectional LSTM at 0.706 in their experiments, a reminder that well-featured classical models can beat neural ones when training data is modest. Published as an open resource, the corpus gives Sorani natural language processing its first shared benchmark and a training set for downstream tools like search and news monitoring.
arxiv-2511-22515:
Parsarad and Wagner map privacy protection's cost to recommenders in accuracy and fairness. Recommenders rank movies and other items from past ratings, but those ratings leak personal information. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise, either during training or on each user's data beforehand. They test both mechanisms on four recommender models, from classic matrix methods to neural ones, on MovieLens-1M and Yelp data.

Stronger privacy consistently reduced accuracy, but unevenly. The neural collaborative filtering model under training-time privacy lost under 10 percent accuracy at a standard level, while classic SVD and pairwise ranking models dropped more, especially for users with niche tastes. The variational autoencoder was most fragile for sparsely represented groups. On bias, training-time privacy narrowed the gap between popular and unpopular items, while local privacy preserved existing patterns. No mechanism won everywhere, so privacy should be tuned against all three goals at once.
arxiv-2511-22615:
Theofilou and colleagues fight catastrophic forgetting in medical AI by replaying examples a model is most likely to lose. When a diagnostic network is fine-tuned on a new hospital's scans, it forgets earlier hospitals' data. Stable-Drift measures latent drift: how much a sample's representation shifts after naive adaptation to the new domain. Samples with the largest shifts are at risk, so the replay memory keeps those.

Drift is aggregated per patient, storing slices with the greatest multi-layer shift, keeping the buffer diverse. On a cross-hospital COVID-19 CT task, latent-drift replay reduced forgetting versus naive fine-tuning and random replay, across convolutional and transformer backbones. Experiments also showed patient-aware selection beating global and single-slice sampling, multi-layer drift beating single-layer signals, and transformers resisting domain shift better than convolutional ones. Latent drift, they argue, is a signal for clinical continual learning.
arxiv-2512-00015:
Jack Furby, Dan Cunnington, Dave Braines, and Alun Preece study how concept explanations change human-machine teamwork. Deep networks are often black boxes, so concept models were built to predict human-defined concepts first. That intermediate step makes the final prediction easier to inspect and question.

The authors test how such explanations, and direct interventions on the concepts, affect collaboration. A user who can correct a concept may steer the model better than one who only sees scores. The work informs design of AI tools that people can genuinely supervise.
arxiv-2512-00215:
Large language models can predict what a program will print, but their reasoning on the way there is murky. Mohammad Abdollahi and co-authors study errors inside those reasoning traces in 2025, focusing on code execution simulation. They examine how intermediate states and control flow lead to final results.

Earlier studies mostly compared output accuracy and treated reasoning as a black box. Understanding a program's runtime behavior is essential for reliable code generation, debugging, and automated reasoning. By demystifying where traces go wrong, the study helps developers judge when a model's confident answer rests on broken steps. Code execution is a strict test, because one wrong intermediate value usually ruins the answer.
arxiv-2512-00315:
Dengue fever follows the mosquito, but it may also follow the street network. Marcílio Ferreira dos Santos and co-authors study dengue incidence in Recife, Brazil, across a decade, in a 2025 study. They ask whether the structural connectivity of urban roads helps explain where cases concentrate.

For each neighborhood, the team computes communicability curvature, a graph measure of how strongly a place can influence others through many network paths. A Bayesian spatial analysis then links that structure to recorded incidence from 2015 to 2024. If road structure drives spread, city planners gain a new lever for targeting mosquito control. Bayesian methods let the team state uncertainty neighborhood by neighborhood.
arxiv-2512-00515:
Sentiment analysis reads opinion from text, and doing it well in Turkish raises challenges English tools never face. A doctoral thesis summarized in 2025 develops a comprehensive framework for sentiment analysis that accounts for its many aspects, mainly for Turkish. Several approaches specific to English are also proposed.

The work reports five major and three minor contributions. Its novel feature set combines unsupervised, semi-supervised, and supervised metrics for stronger classification. Turkish is rich in suffixes and flexible in word order, so features built for English transfer poorly. A dedicated framework helps Turkish media, commerce, and research. Feature design is where the thesis stakes its main claim to novelty.
arxiv-2512-00615:
Group theory studies how the structure of a group constrains the values its commutator words can take. Martina Capasso, Liliana Lancellotti, and Pavel Shumyatsky study Chernikov-by-nilpotent groups in 2025. They focus on the lower central word and the subgroup it generates.

For each level, the authors consider the set of word values and the corresponding term of the lower central series. Chernikov groups are built from finite and quasicyclic pieces, giving the class a rich but tractable structure. Results here feed the broader program of understanding how verbal subgroups behave in restricted classes of infinite groups. Lower central series measure how far a group is from being abelian.
arxiv-2512-00915:
Junwoo Chang and five coauthors blend symmetry into robot learning in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning teaches agents by reward, and many tasks have group symmetries, motions that leave the task unchanged. Respecting those symmetries helps an agent generalize, since it can reuse lessons across symmetric states and actions.

Real settings, though, almost never keep symmetries perfectly. Dynamics, actuator limits, and reward design break them, often only in places. The team's partially equivariant method keeps symmetry where it holds and relaxes it where it breaks. That balance could make robot policies both data-efficient and honest about real-world messiness.
arxiv-2512-01115:
Tao Zhang and Yevgeniy Vorobeychik extend a privacy framework in a 2025 paper. Pufferfish privacy is a family of definitions that state exactly which secrets a data release must protect. Its Rényi version gives strong guarantees, but two practical gaps remain: calibrating noise needs high-dimensional optimal transport, and iterative learning lacks a general composition rule.

Their sliced version replaces high-dimensional comparisons with directional ones over a set of unit vectors. That makes guarantees geometry-aware and tractable to compute. They also apply it to private learning with gradient clipping. Practical accounting rules decide whether privacy methods leave the lab.
arxiv-2512-01615:
Sergiy Mankovsky and co-authors compute electric polarization driven by spin alignment. In type II multiferroics, slanted spins create electric polarization. That link lets magnetic order switch electric traits. First-principles methods can predict the effect.

Their approach parametrizes polarization with terms from a Green function method. The cell polarization is split into three-site terms. Those terms show which spin triples drive the signal. Such insight helps design materials where magnetism controls electric response for sensors and memory. Three-site terms show that pairs alone understate the effect, a lesson for model builders who truncate spin interactions too early.
arxiv-2512-02115:
Mapping the Milky Way's gravity reveals where its ordinary and dark matter sit, but star surveys see the galaxy through dust and uneven coverage. Taavet Kalda and Gregory Green present in 2025 a new variant of the Deep Potential method that infers the gravitational potential without modeling those selection effects.

The method learns from a snapshot of stellar positions and velocities, the raw material of galactic dynamics. Selection functions, the corrections for what a survey missed, normally complicate such inference and can bias it. Skipping that modeling makes the potential estimate cleaner and more direct. A trustworthy gravity map is a foundation for weighing the galaxy's dark matter halo.
arxiv-2512-02315:
Protein engineers often have only a handful of measurements for a new protein, far too few to train a predictor. Felix Teufel and co-authors introduce PRIMO in 2025, a transformer framework that predicts protein fitness from few examples by learning in context and continuing to train at test time.

In-context learning lets the model adapt to a new protein and assay from the examples in front of it, without a large task-specific dataset. Test-time training squeezes more from those few examples before predicting. Reliable few-shot fitness prediction would speed protein engineering, where every experimental measurement is slow and costly.
arxiv-2512-02515:
Lixing He and three co-authors work on clearer speech from earbuds and headsets used in noisy places. Tiny devices leave little room for microphones, yet calls and voice assistants must still hear the user well. A single all direction microphone struggles when other voices crowd the same space.

VibOmni adds bone conduction sensing, picking up voice through vibrations in the head itself. Those vibrations carry the wearer's speech while mostly ignoring outside noise. Blending both signals aims for clean voice pickup that scales across earables, a growing class of small devices people wear all day. Clear voice pickup is a must for calls made on a busy street or a loud train.
arxiv-2512-02615:
Nicolai-Leonid Bathen and nine co-authors measure the twist between two stacked sheets of tungsten diselenide. Twisted bilayers form moiré patterns, regular superlattices that reshape how electrons and light behave. The physics depends sharply on the exact twist angle, which disorder and rebuilding can shift.

Small angle errors change the energy landscape and the electron correlations researchers want to study. The team reads the angle from optical moiré phonons, vibrations tied to the pattern itself. A precise, light based ruler for twist angle helps labs build samples whose behavior they can trust and repeat. Light based checks are fast and do no harm to the flake, which keeps the best flakes in play.
arxiv-2512-02715:
Peirong Zhang and eight co-authors help AI find tiny objects in satellite images from text queries. Visual grounding links words to the image region they describe. Remote sensing makes this hard: targets can be specks in scenes kilometers wide, and queries often use relative positions.

GeoViS adds geospatially rewarded visual search to multimodal language models for this task. Rewards favor answers that respect spatial relations and context across distant objects. Better grounding speeds map making, disaster checks, and land monitoring, where analysts now hunt small features by eye for hours. Search that knows the land can cut hours of eye work for teams that map floods, fires, and crop loss.
arxiv-2512-02915:
Paweł Nosal studies very short sums of a classic number theory symbol over prime ranges. Character sums measure how evenly a sequence, here the Legendre symbol, spreads its signs. A central limit theorem describes the whole distribution of such sums, not just their average size.

Nosal proves that behavior for almost all primes, with the starting point chosen at random in a growing range. The interval length may grow slower than any power of the prime. Distributional results like this sharpen our sense of how random arithmetic sequences truly behave. Short sums are the wild west of this field. Mean based rules fail there, and full spread laws are the ones worth their ink in print.
arxiv-2512-03015:
Waves on a line of points follow rules worth knowing well. Carsten Peterson builds up the basic theory of the discrete wave equation in this 2025 work. His aim is to support study of waves on affine buildings, a newer topic in math.

Peterson works on the integers, the whole numbers in a line. From there he explains known results about waves on regular graphs, where each point has the same number of links. Clear basics help others tackle scattering and quantum chaos. The work gives a firm base for more advanced wave studies. Graph wave results then rest on a firm base built step by step from the line case.
arxiv-2512-03315:
Simulating turbulent flow needs filters that adapt to the flow. Mohammadmahdi Ranjbar, Ali Mostafavi, and Farzad Mashayek present a self-tuning filter in this 2025 work. It builds on their earlier dynamic modal filter for large-eddy simulation.

The new filter tunes its own parameters from local flow features. It also extends how modal values are found, beyond Chebyshev grids to general points and polynomial bases. Adaptive filters can cut cost while keeping accuracy in jet, wing, and engine simulations. That balance is key for practical engineering design. Local tuning avoids hand-set filters that fail when flow conditions change mid-flight.
arxiv-2512-03515:
Chaotic systems still show strong statistical patterns. David Burguet, Chiyi Luo, and Dawei Yang prove an effective form of such a pattern in this 2025 work. They study ergodic measures with large entropy for surface maps and three-dimensional flows.

They prove such measures give uniformly large weight to points with long stable and unstable manifolds. As a consequence, they establish an effective SPR property for smooth surface diffeomorphisms. Effective versions turn qualitative theory into usable bounds. That helps in dynamics, where explicit rates are often missing. Uniform bounds are the prize, since pointwise results can hide bad behavior on small sets that matter for long-term prediction.
arxiv-2512-03815:
Software teams argue endlessly about keeping code in one giant repository or splitting it into many small ones. Shayan Ghasemnezhad, Samarth KaPatel, and Sofia Nikiforova propose a middle path in a 2025 software preprint. Single repositories give consistency but strain tooling as they grow, while many small ones ease the split into parts yet complicate coordination and shared dependencies.

Their Causify Dev system is built around the runnable directory, a self-contained unit that carries its own development, testing, and deployment life cycle. A thin shared environment, common helper utilities, and container-based workflows keep setups consistent across units while the links stay isolated. Continuous integration and delivery then run efficiently per unit. The authors present the approach as a practical compromise for large, complex codebases. It aims to keep the reliability of a monorepo and the independence of separate ones at the same time.
arxiv-2512-03915:
Mixture-of-experts models save computing by sending each token to only a few specialist subnetworks, but the routing can overload some experts and idle others. X. Y. Han and Yuan Zhong supply theory for a popular fix in a 2025 optimisation preprint. The method under study is the auxiliary-loss-free load balancing procedure introduced by DeepSeek researchers, which skips the usual extra penalty term.

Han and Zhong recast the procedure as a primal-dual method solving an assignment problem, with one quick update per training step. In a simplified deterministic setting, they prove the objective improves monotonically and that tokens migrate from overloaded to underloaded experts, ending near balance. In the messier online setting of real training, they derive a logarithmic expected regret bound. Experiments on a billion-parameter DeepSeekMoE model accompany the theory. Together, the results give the heuristic a principled foundation.
arxiv-2512-04015:
To edit an image in a controlled way, say rotating only the object, a model must know which parts of its internal representation a transformation touches. Farhana Hossain Swarnali, Miaomiao Zhang, and Tonmoy Hossain automate that discovery in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Earlier latent-space methods forced researchers to split the representation into changing and fixed parts by hand.

Their framework learns group actions directly on latent image manifolds. Learnable binary masks, trained with a straight-through estimator, partition the representation into transformation-sensitive and invariant components without manual labels. Disentanglement and the transformation mappings are learned jointly in one optimisation, and the method wraps around any standard encoder-decoder. Tests on five image datasets show the system finding the right factors alone. Downstream classification confirmed the representations stay useful, and code is publicly available.
arxiv-2512-04115:
What Finnish teenagers fear about artificial intelligence depends, it turns out, on how competent they feel using it. Ville Heilala and colleagues survey upper secondary students in a 2025 preprint on computers and society. About one hundred sixty students rated their own AI competence and their concerns about AI across personal, institutional, and systemic domains, and the team mapped how answers co-occurred.

Students with lower self-rated competence dwelled on personal risks: shrinking creativity, weaker critical thinking, and misuse. Students who felt more competent looked upward instead, worrying about bias, inaccuracy, and cheating. The same technology thus reads as a threat to one's own learning or as a threat to institutions, depending on the reader. The authors argue schools should respond with AI literacy in the curriculum and guided teacher support. One-size teaching will miss risks that students actually perceive.
arxiv-2512-04215:
The Yang-Baxter equation, born in mathematical physics, has a set-theoretic shadow whose solutions are built from algebraic structures called racks and braces. Marzia Mazzotta, Paola Stefanelli, and Magdalena Wiertel open a systematic study of the 'quasi' versions of those solutions in a 2025 algebra preprint. Their motivation comes from dual weak braces, whose solutions land in these looser classes.

The authors introduce and examine quasi racks and the derived solution construction, extending the classical definitions. One family of such solutions, the quasi left non-degenerate ones, is built from quasi racks and g-twists, paralleling the well-understood non-degenerate case. They also completely characterise one class of quasi racks: those that are Plonka sums of racks. The paper sets up foundations rather than applications, giving the quasi theory the same careful scaffolding the classical theory already enjoys.
arxiv-2512-04615:
Mrinal Dev and Shraddha Sharma use a quantum algorithm to hunt a subtle kind of phase change in a chain of interacting spins. The tool is the variational quantum eigensolver, which guesses a ground state with a tunable circuit and refines the guess. The system is the long-range XXZ chain, where each spin talks to distant partners. Its phase change is of infinite order, so faint that energy curves barely bend. Their 2025 arXiv paper turns that faintness into a signal.

The team shapes their circuit so total spin stays fixed during tuning. That constraint makes the estimated ground energy sensitive to which phase the chain sits in. Reading the energy across settings then marks the transition boundary. The trick needs no direct measure of exotic order parameters. It shows how careful circuit design can make near-term quantum hardware answer questions in condensed matter that strain classical methods.
arxiv-2512-04815:
Chuanyu Fu, Guanying Chen, Yuqi Zhang, and co-authors present RobustSplat++, a method that rebuilds clean three-dimensional scenes from messy real-world photos. Gaussian splatting renders such scenes fast and true, but crowds, passing cars, and shifting light leave ghosts and smears. The team traces the flaw to densification: the process that grows new Gaussians for detail also grows them to fit passing objects and light changes. Their 2025 arXiv paper splits that growth apart from the scene's true structure.

The first fix delays Gaussian growth, letting the static scene settle before any splitting or cloning begins. Later designs separate lasting structure from passing motion and from illumination shifts. Rendered views then drop the artifacts that plagued earlier tools. Tourists' snapshots, street photos, and drone passes could all feed clean reconstructions, widening where three-dimensional capture works at all.
arxiv-2512-05315:
Lami Suleiman, Anthea Fantina, Francesca Gulminelli, and Jocelyn Read ask what telescope and gravitational-wave observations of neutron stars can really teach us about nuclear matter. The equation of state linking pressure to density is probed by pulsar timing, X-ray profiles, and merger signals. But inference depends heavily on the prior — the family of equations the analysis allows. Semi-agnostic priors, which encode knowledge at low densities while staying flexible at high ones, are the authors' testbed.

They map which nuclear parameters track the pressure at each density, then simulate observations for three candidate equations and try to recover them. Several parameters barely correlate with pressure, and at high density they compete, making them hard to pin down even with precise data. Semi-agnostic priors recover the true parameters more faithfully than assuming ordinary nuclear matter to the core — a warning and a remedy for neutron-star inference.
arxiv-2512-05715:
Maxim Krasnov, Daulet Berkimbayev, Andrea Addazi, Yermek Aldabergenov, and Maxim Khlopov study domain walls in a gravity theory with a Gauss-Bonnet term coupled to a scalar field. The field can break, and later restore, a simple twofold symmetry. Where the symmetry breaks, the field must choose between two vacuum states. The borders between regions that chose differently are domain walls.

Numerical runs follow the field. In an inflating, de Sitter universe, the coupling lets steady walls form at a fixed distance apart. In the earlier, radiation filled era, expansion melts the walls away instead. The team computes the gravitational waves such a wall network would emit, and whether collapsing walls could seed primordial black holes. Both signals fall below what near future instruments can reach. The paper thus rules out this route as a source of detectable waves or black holes.
arxiv-2512-05915:
Marius Juston, Ramavarapu Sreenivas, Dustin Nottage, and Ahmet Soylemezoglu generalize a way to build neural networks whose sensitivity is capped by design. A Lipschitz network never amplifies an input change by more than a chosen factor. That cap buys resistance to adversarial tricks and lets a network's behavior be certified, valuable from image recognition to control systems. Earlier constructions handled residual networks well.

The advance is a new decomposition, an LDLT factorization, used to certify that the matrix inequalities hold. With it, the construction escapes the residual family: any nonlinear architecture, including hierarchical ones, can be parameterized to meet a chosen Lipschitz bound. The method is a provable recipe, and it keeps the network's full expressive power. On one hundred twenty one standard datasets, accuracy rose by a few percent up to about an eighth over the leading layer design.
arxiv-2512-06115:
Mariana Sanchez and four co-authors show how the smallest stars can still raise giant planets, and what happens to any rocky worlds caught inside. Late M dwarfs weigh a tenth of the Sun. Their disks seemed too poor to build a giant's core. Their N-body simulations grow embryos on pebbles and gas.

A cold giant forms with six Earth masses of pebbles and a long lived disk. A five Earth mass core assembles within a million years. Planet collisions and efficient pebble eating do the heavy lifting. The inner rocky planet survives if it reaches the disk's inner cavity before the outer world becomes a giant. Giant formation around tiny stars does not demand rich disks.
arxiv-2512-06315:
S Sivaranjani, Vijay Gupta, Frank Allgower, and their co authors survey ways to learn a model of a moving system from data, when the model will be used for control. Fresh learning tools can fit models from noisy, rich data. Yet a model that fits data well may still lack traits a control engineer needs. Examples are keeping energy in check or respecting symmetry.

The survey sorts methods by how they bake such traits in. Some build the model so the trait holds by design. Some nudge the fit toward the trait with penalty terms. Others impose the trait as a firm rule the fit must obey. Through this lens the authors review classic, learning based, and mixed approaches side by side. Joining data fitting with physics and control needs yields clearer models that need less data and come with proofs a designer can trust.
arxiv-2512-06615:
Kaichen Shen and Wei Zhu improve the training of score based generative models, the family behind much modern image synthesis. These models learn the slope of a data distribution's density, then use it to turn noise into samples. The authors work in a latent version, where a compressed code is modeled instead of raw data. They let the forward noising process follow nonlinear dynamics rather than a plain random walk.

Rewriting a key term through a standard step for such dynamics gave their new objective. Two terms in it had zero mean but exploding variance at small time steps, which wrecked stability; they identify and remove them. On variants of the handwritten digit data set, the method sampled faster and learned structured distributions better than rival latent models, with higher quality and more varied samples.
arxiv-2512-06815:
Bowen Zhao works on holography, the idea that a space with gravity can be described by a theory living on its edge. Zhao studies scattering events where many incoming regions meet many outgoing ones inside a curved three-dimensional space. The question is when the regions that encode quantum links between the inputs form one connected whole. A known result settled the simpler case of two inputs and two outputs.

Zhao extends that result in two directions. First, a much weaker condition already forces full connection: one pair of inputs meeting a certain causal test is enough. Second, Zhao derives limits that any connected case must obey, and shows the shared bulk region faces stricter rules once more parties join. The findings sharpen what holography can and cannot say about many-party quantum links.
arxiv-2512-07915:
Frank Phillipson wrote this 2025 computing paper on judging quantum methods fairly. Quantum methods compete with classic heuristics and special hardware on hard problems. Their speed claims, though, are very hard to compare honestly.

Older benchmarking grew out of digital complexity theory's premises. Quantum and hybrid systems break those assumptions. Their workings are continuous, their results chancy, their workflows heavy with overhead. Phillipson lays out ground rules and protocols tuned to that reality. End-to-end workflows, not lone kernels, should be the unit of scoring. Tuning and write-ups must stay open for results to be trusted. Problem sets should be diverse enough to expose cherry-picking. Guesses dressed as claims deserve to be avoided in any fair protocol. Lessons from older benchmarking are extended, not thrown away. Use-driven and energy-aware measures join his scorecard. The field gains a framework for fair, repeatable judging.
arxiv-2512-08015:
Luis D Zambrano Palma, Yusef Maleki, and M Suhail Zubairy, physicists who study quantum optics, posted a theoretical study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is weak measurement, a gentle way of learning about a quantum system without fully disturbing it. They focus on null result measurements, where no photon is detected yet the state of the system still updates.

The authors build a detailed picture of how information builds up over time during such measurements. They work through qubit and qutrit cases, then extend the framework to systems with many levels. Using tools such as Shannon entropy, mutual information, fidelity, and relative entropy, they track both the amount of information gained and its rate. Their results also clarify when a weak measurement can be reversed, a question that matters for quantum control.
arxiv-2512-08315:
Ali Eghbali, Yaghoub Samadi, and Adel Rezaei Aghdam, theoretical physicists in Iran, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is Yang Baxter deformations of a Wess Zumino Witten model built on the OSP supergroup, a symmetry that mixes ordinary and fermionic directions. Such deformations are a standard way to generate new string theory backgrounds from known ones.

The team first obtains the classical r matrices of the matching Lie superalgebra, solving the graded Yang Baxter equation over the reals. Each r matrix then specifies a deformation, whose effect lands on the metric and B field of the background. All are non Abelian and non unimodular, pushing the backgrounds toward generalized supergravity equations. The undeformed background satisfies those equations with a suitable added supervector, while the deformed ones do not, which fits expectations since they do not describe a Green Schwarz superstring.
arxiv-2512-08515:
Zhen Wei Wang, Zhi Long Han, Fei Huang, Honglei Li, and Ang Liu, particle physicists in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They build a new benchmark model for dark matter that talks to ordinary matter through a heavy partner particle, a Z prime boson. In the standard version of this portal, colliders and underground detectors squeeze the allowed space hard, leaving little room for the idea to survive.

Their model, based on a gauged B minus L symmetry, gives dark matter a slightly heavier partner and a tiny mixing between them. That small mixing weakens how strongly dark matter couples to the mediator, dodging the tightest bounds, and opens fresh production routes in the early universe. Checking all limits together, the authors find the conversion mechanism is favored in both versions of the model. A squeezed theory gains breathing room.
arxiv-2512-09115:
Sander Jyhne and coauthors present SuperF, a test time optimization method for multi image super resolution. High resolution imagery is limited by sensor technology, air conditions, and cost,. Single image methods must invent detail from priors and often hallucinate structures that do not match reality.

Multi image methods instead constrain the result with several views shifted by less than a pixel. SuperF shares one neural field across all shifted low resolution frames and optimizes frame alignment together with the field itself. Alignment is parametrized directly as an affine transform, and optimization uses a super sampled grid at the output resolution. Experiments on simulated satellite bursts and ground level handheld photos show compelling results, with upscaling by large factors. A key advantage is that no high resolution training data are needed at all. The continuous representation fits the task naturally,.
arxiv-2512-10015:
Trina Basu and Richard Ruiz dissect how the polarization of the W boson affects predictions at high energy colliders. The W has more polarization states than the simple pictures used in most models, and their interference can matter. The authors work with helicity amplitudes in the polarized propagator approach. They give analytic splits of polarized propagators, valid in several gauges, that make the size of mass over energy effects plain.

Such interference can exceed the usual width corrections, limiting shortcut approximations at low energy. At the finest level, interference can outsize the squared longitudinal contributions. Yet it vanishes for bosons from unpolarized sources. When the W decays to massless fermions, non interference survives roughly even off shell. A new grouping of polarizations reduces gauge ambiguities. Case studies include W production with jets, top decay, and neutrino scattering.
arxiv-2512-10715:
Matias Cosarinsky and co-authors teach chest X-ray segmentation to say when it is unsure. Their landmark-based method outlines anatomy by placing points, using a hybrid design with a convolutional image encoder and a graph-based generative decoder. Because the decoder is variational, it carries natural uncertainty signals, and the authors turn them into two complementary measures.

One measure reads uncertainty straight from the learned latent distribution; the other samples many predictions and measures their spread. In controlled corruption tests, both rose as images degraded, and both flagged predictions that disagreed with human ground truth, as well as out-of-distribution cases. The team releases CheXmask-U, a dataset of more than six hundred and fifty thousand chest X-ray landmark segmentations, each with per-point uncertainty scores, plus an interactive demo and code. So others can weigh segmentation quality point by point.
arxiv-2512-10815:
Dario Baum, Arno Förster, and Lucas Visscher publish a mountain of high-grade quantum chemistry data. Excited-state energies for every molecule in the popular QM9 collection, more than one hundred and thirty thousand of them. Machine learning for chemistry is starved of exactly this: trustworthy numbers at scale. And the GW and Bethe-Salpeter methods give excellent accuracy for charged and neutral excitations alike, at heavy computing cost.

Their dataset, QM9GWBSE, supplies quasiparticle energies from self-consistent GW calculations. It also gives singlet-singlet and singlet-triplet excitation energies from the Bethe-Salpeter equation. Transition dipole moments and oscillator strengths come with them. Those say how brightly each excitation absorbs light. Nothing of this size existed before at this level of theory. The authors expect the collection to become a training ground for machine learning models that predict excited-state properties at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2512-10915:
Megan Gialluca and co-authors count the cost of sandblasting a space telescope's mirror, one micrometeoroid at a time. A future observatory hunting Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars needs extreme contrast and stability to photograph such faint worlds. Every micrometeoroid strike pits the primary mirror a little more, and the accumulated damage scatters stray light into the coronagraph's field of view, exactly where the planets hide.

The team modelled stray light across a range of damage scenarios and target lists, then translated it into lost science. Fewer exoEarth candidates detected, with yields falling by roughly a third to three fifths in some cases. Big uncertainties remain, chiefly the largest impactor to expect and how crater size scales with impact energy. The authors argue the effect belongs in the Habitable Worlds Observatory's design process now, shaping mitigation plans, telescope architecture, and observing priorities.
arxiv-2512-11115:
Hadrian Bezuidenhout and colleagues build a light based detector for skyrmions, swirling topological patterns that can be imprinted on beams of light. Such patterns could encode information in a huge alphabet that resists disturbance. No reliable detector for the pattern's topological number existed, partly because different patterns are not cleanly separable.

Their device is a deep diffractive optical neural network with two processing channels, each built from five patterned layers that reshape light as it passes. Training in a spatial mode basis rather than pixels cut the number of training variables a thousandfold. The detector read a large set of input topologies accurately even with strong noise. As a practical test, the team sent and received an image encoded in a fourteen level topological alphabet with no visible mixing between symbols.
arxiv-2512-11215:
Tianye Qi, Weihao Li, and Nick Barnes introduce SmokeBench, a benchmark for testing whether multimodal AI models can spot wildfire smoke in images. Smoke is transparent, shapeless, and easily confused with clouds, so catching it early is hard even for people. Early detection matters because small fires are far easier to control.

The benchmark covers four tasks: deciding whether smoke is present, locating it within tiles, locating it on a grid, and full detection. Seven leading models were tested, including commercial and open systems. Most could classify scenes when smoke covered a large area, but every model struggled to localise smoke accurately, especially at early stages. Performance tracked the amount of smoke far more than image contrast. The authors warn that current models are not ready for safety critical wildfire monitoring.
arxiv-2512-11715:
Wei Chow and a large team introduce EditMGT, a new route to photo editing with AI. Popular diffusion editors repaint the whole image step by step, so spots the user never asked to change often drift. Masked generative transformers work in a more local way, filling in hidden patches.

EditMGT leans on that local habit. It merges attention maps from many layers to pinpoint the edit zone, then holds tokens steady in low attention areas so they cannot flip by accident. The team also built CrispEdit-2M, a training set across seven edit kinds. With under 1 billion parameters the model edits six times faster than diffusion rivals. Style change scores rose 3.6 percent and style transfer 17.6 percent.
arxiv-2512-11815:
Max Kamachee and co-authors warn that the video deepfake abuse seen with image tools is repeating with video models. Since 2022, image generators have made fake intimate images cheap to produce, including abuse material. A few open models, trained on pornographic web data and released with weak safeguards, drove most of that harm.

The team finds the same pattern in 2025 video tools: a small set of open weight models now dominates fake intimate video making. They argue that developers who release such models without data care or safeguards foreseeably feed the harm. Platforms that skip moderation amplify it. Better risk handling, they say, can still cut future abuse sharply.
arxiv-2512-12015:
