Ekrem Aydıner and co-authors study black holes in Einstein-Born-Infeld gravity inside anti-de Sitter space. Born-Infeld theory caps electric field strength, smoothing the infinite fields of point charges. The team asks how that cap changes black hole heat physics and light bending.

They derive the Hawking temperature, then add quantum tweaks from the Generalized Uncertainty Principle and an exponential entropy rule, which hint at leftover remnants. Light bending is computed with the Gauss-Bonnet method in vacuum and in plasma, where the medium can hide or sharpen the nonlinear marks. As heat engines, the holes reach efficiency 0.11 to 0.21. Born-Infeld tweaks to efficiency sit near ten to the minus twelve for normal settings.
arxiv-2512-12115:
Momin N Siddiqui and co-authors built SPIRE, a spell checker that teaches instead of silently fixing. Memorizing spellings fails many learners, above all children with language based disorders. Speech language specialists teach by inquiry instead, probing a word sound, parts, meaning, and history.

SPIRE turns that teaching style into programs. Specialist moves are written in a small domain language, and the system synthesizes a custom lesson from each learner error in real time. Errors become prompts to explore word families, origins, and sound letter links, building meta linguistic reasoning beside the correction. Trials with specialists and learners show the lessons match professional practice and could slot into daily writing tools.
arxiv-2512-12315:
Roy Stegeman and Roman Zwicky study how gluons carry gravity related form factors in a 2025 physics paper. A form factor describes how a particle responds to a probe. They focus on the gluon D form factor for the pion, nucleon, rho, and delta, using lattice QCD data at two pion masses.

Their fits use a simple sigma meson pole plus a smooth background term. The sigma meson plays the role of the dilaton, a particle tied to broken scale symmetry. Fitted values match predictions from dilaton theory. New forecasts for the rho and delta follow, adding support for an infrared fixed point in QCD dynamics.
arxiv-2512-12415: Giovanni Gentili and Luigi Vezzoni revisit a key estimate for the quaternionic Calabi-Yau problem on hyperkahler manifolds. They give a simplified argument for the second order estimate. Dinew and Sroka first established that estimate. The note is short and technical, aimed at readers who know this area of complex geometry.
arxiv-2512-12615:
Yusheng Zheng and ten co-authors present gpu_ext, an eBPF based system for extensible GPU policies, in a 2025 paper. In GPU centric systems, performance hinges on policies for memory placement, scheduling, and observability, yet one fixed policy suits diverse workloads poorly. User space runtimes lack cross tenant visibility, while kernel changes add complexity and safety risks.

Gpu_ext treats the GPU driver and device as a programmable operating system layer. Safe hooks in the driver plus a device side eBPF runtime run verified policy code inside GPU kernels, giving coherent control across tenants. Across inference, training, and vector search workloads, throughput rose up to 4.8 times and tail latency fell up to 2 times, with low overhead and no app restarts.
arxiv-2512-12815:
Yihan Hong, Hengxiang Feng, Yinghan Wang, and Boxuan Li study how Bitcoin ETF approval changed Bitcoin's hedging properties in a 2025 paper. United States spot Bitcoin ETFs were approved in January 2024, a milestone for adoption by big institutions and for Bitcoin's entry into traditional finance. The authors ask how Bitcoin's links to equities, gold, and fiat currencies shifted after that date.

Using rolling correlation analysis, Chow tests, and DCC-GARCH models, they found Bitcoin's correlation with the S&P 500 rose significantly after approval, showing stronger alignment with equities. Its link with gold stabilized near zero. Its link with the United States Dollar Index stayed negative, reflecting continued independence from fiat currencies. The findings inform portfolio and market stability debates.
arxiv-2512-13115:
Xinyu Xu and co-authors build a quantum-inspired rule for finding topological materials, materials whose electron states have special protected forms. Finding them by full calculation is costly, and making them in a lab is slow. A simpler chemical rule that pre-screens options could save both kinds of effort.

Their hybrid quantum-classical network extends an older heuristic called topogivity, which scores each element's lean toward such behavior. The quantum-style form adds pairwise links between elements that classical rules miss. A matching complex valued network confirmed the links make physical sense. Screening plus first-principles checks revealed five new compounds of this kind.
arxiv-2512-13415:
Ahmed Abul Hasanaath and Hamzah Luqman present USTM, a framework for continuous sign language recognition from ordinary color video. The task needs fine reading of hand and face cues plus long-range timing across a signed sentence. Older pipelines pair image backbones with separate temporal modules and miss both kinds of detail.

USTM joins a Swin Transformer backbone with a light temporal adapter that carries positional information. It models fine spatial features and both short and long temporal context in one encoder, with no extra input streams. On three benchmarks, PHOENIX14, PHOENIX14T, and CSL-Daily, it reached state-of-the-art results against both single-stream and multi-stream rivals.
arxiv-2512-13715:
Fatemeh Lotfi and Fatemeh Afghah propose a meta hierarchical learning framework for resource management in Open Radio Access Networks. O-RAN uses intelligent controllers to allocate resources and slice networks in real time. Past AI methods often falter when conditions shift fast and without warning.

Their Meta-HRL design pairs a high-level controller, which splits resources across slices, with low-level agents that schedule inside each slice. A meta-update rule weights tasks by error variance, favoring harder scenarios and steady learning. Theory gives sublinear convergence and regret bounds. Simulations showed a 19.8% gain in management efficiency over baseline methods, up to 40% faster adaptation, and strong quality of service across broadband, low-latency, and massive-device slices.
arxiv-2512-13915:
Victor Livernoche and co-authors measure deepfakes in the 2025 Canadian federal election. Fears about AI-made political media are rising, but hard evidence on how such content circulates in a democratic election is scarce. Their study is among the first in-depth looks at that question.

They analyzed 187,778 posts from X, Bluesky, and Reddit with a detection framework trained on modern generative models. They found 5.86% of election-related images were deepfakes. Right-leaning accounts shared them more often, at 8.66% of images versus 4.42% for left-leaning accounts, often with defamatory or conspiratorial intent. Yet most deepfakes were benign or non-political, and harmful ones drew only 0.12% of views on X, so reach stayed modest.
arxiv-2512-14015:
Limin Xu, Zhen Huang, and Zhennan Zhou introduce Frozen Gaussian Sampling for simulating Markovian open quantum systems in the semiclassical regime. Such simulation is a grand challenge because highly oscillatory dynamics force grid methods to use prohibitive resolution. Their method rests on the Wigner-Fokker-Planck phase-space formulation.

The sampling error for physical observables is independent of the semiclassical parameter, breaking the scaling that blocks grid methods in that limit. Being mesh-free, the algorithm also avoids boundary-driven instabilities that limit long-time grid runs. The authors use it to explore long-time behavior of open quantum systems. They give numerical evidence for steady states in strongly non-harmonic potentials, a regime where rigorous analytical results are currently lacking.
arxiv-2512-14115:
Ramesh Gundluru, Shubham Gupta, and Sri Rama Murty K study spoken term detection and keyword spotting in a 2025 paper. Both tasks search speech for chosen words. Their method uses acoustic word embeddings, which turn short speech clips into points in a space where matching words sit close together.

Older methods trained audio and text links apart, or needed a new model for each task. The new framework trains audio to audio and audio to text links together in one shared space. It beats prior baselines on word discrimination, meaning telling similar words apart. The authors say it flexibly supports both search tasks in one model.
arxiv-2512-14215:
Gengshou Cao and seven coauthors study a fan array wind generator in a 2025 experimental paper. The device is a square grid of 10 by 10 fans, each 4 cm wide and controlled on its own, with a top speed of 17 meters per second. It aims to mimic natural turbulent flows in a lab.

The team tries two ways to raise turbulence intensity in the test region. A checkerboard pattern of fan duty cycles gives a robust, uniform field with turbulence near 0.14. Particle swarm optimization reaches higher local values near 0.28 but loses spatial uniformity. The study frames a clear trade off between local peak turbulence and an even field across the test area.
arxiv-2512-14415:
Ludwig Nützel and three colleagues ran a full molecular energy calculation on an ion-trap quantum computer. Their target was the ground state of H3+, a small charged molecule, encoded in six qubits. The state was prepared by slow adiabatic change, and its energy read out with a noise-tolerant version of quantum phase estimation.

Nothing was quietly offloaded to a classical computer, which makes the noise analysis honest. The result beat the standard classical Hartree-Fock energy. Ordinary noise did little harm, but leakage errors, where qubits slip outside their working states, blocked chemical accuracy. Simulations without leakage came close to that target.
arxiv-2512-14515:
Lin Chen and Yuya Sasaki build econometric tools for a messy real-world problem: treatments that spread through a network. When one place adopts a policy or faces a shock, neighbors feel it too, and places also choose their own exposure. Earlier methods mostly assumed away either the spillovers or the self-selection, and treated effects as uniform.

Their framework models selection as an equilibrium shaped by spillovers, then measures how effects vary with neighbors' status and hidden differences between places. Applied to import competition in American local labor markets, harm showed up as expected, but it grew stronger where treated neighbors clustered and in places that usually select into low exposure.
arxiv-2512-14815:
Björn Penning leads a large team that measured conditions inside the Bedretto tunnel in Ticino, Switzerland. Deep sites shield delicate physics tests from cosmic rays and from shaking. The team checked whether this tunnel could host rare event searches, gravitational wave detectors, and quantum sensors.

Under more than 1400 meters of rock, they measured muon, gamma ray, and neutron flows, plus radon, magnetic fields, and ground motion. The muon flow was a million times lower than at the surface. Magnetic and seismic noise were also very low, meeting the needs of the next wave detectors. The team concludes the site could be Europe's second deepest and quietest underground lab.
arxiv-2512-15515:
Zhihan Xu, Rajgopal Kannan, and Viktor Prasanna present FAME, an FPGA accelerator for matrix multiplication on encrypted data, in a 2025 paper. Homomorphic encryption lets cloud servers compute on data they cannot read, but its matrix work is very slow. Speeding that step up is key for private machine learning.

The team first models how much on chip memory a given setup needs, then designs a new datapath for the main bottleneck step that reuses data finely and cuts memory traffic. Built on an Alveo U280 chip, FAME handles many matrix shapes and parameter sets. It runs on average 221 times faster than leading CPU based versions in their tests.
arxiv-2512-15815:
Valeria Granata and co authors describe the BIG-MAP Archive, a repository for FAIR and secure scientific data sharing, in a 2025 paper. Large consortia need a common platform to exchange findings while keeping sensitive data controlled. General repositories rarely fit consortium specific rules for access and later publication.

Built on InvenioRDM, the archive serves the BATTERY 2030+ battery research consortium, with access limited to set communities or the full initiative. Fine grained permissions govern each upload, and a formal upload process keeps data ready for open release when the time comes. The design can be redeployed for other consortia, including MaterialsCommons4.eu and the RAISE resource.
arxiv-2512-15915:
Lican Huang proposes Private Virtual Tree Networks for secure multi tenant environments in a 2025 paper. Real organizations delegate authority down a hierarchy, and the VIRGO overlay network mirrors that structure for distributed systems. VIRGO, though, lacks built in security and privacy mechanisms for its membership.

The proposed networks add cryptographic enforcement on top of VIRGO. Join requests are encrypted with the manager's public key, and membership requires manager signed delegation certificates. Public keys are treated as organizational secrets, shared only inside direct manager member relationships, which makes each virtual tree private and non enumerable. The paper gives the system model, protocols, and security analysis behind those guarantees.
arxiv-2512-16515:
Pradeep Singh and three co-authors offer a sweeping view in this 38-page arXiv paper from 2025. They read the history of the universe as one chain of regimes. Each regime is a new state space, stitched to the last by a phase change. The chain runs from inflation to the cosmic web. It goes on to stars and planets, then life, brains, culture, and machine intelligence.

Gravity grows the cosmic web from tiny early ripples. Collapse in ordinary matter then builds stars and planets. Geochemical cycles settle into long-lived states far from balance. Within those states, life appears as reaction networks that maintain themselves. Evolution becomes flow across vast spaces of genes and traits. Brains act as systems poised near critical points. Human technology, including machine learning, becomes engineered learning that rewrites its own space. Shared motifs tie it all together: instability, sudden splits, and coupling across scales.
arxiv-2512-17115:
Amir Targholizadeh, Grigoriy Y. Nikulin, and Pankaj K. Jha pair a dielectric metalens with a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector, aiming for top detection marks in a smaller device. Single-element detectors face a trade-off: big areas catch more light, small areas count faster with less noise.

Their all-dielectric cryogenic metalens focuses light onto a smaller active area, lifting efficiency without the usual costs. A two-role metalens design also promises polarization-resolved detection at telecom wavelengths, shown in theory. The authors argue that merging cryogenic metasurfaces with leading detectors could add new skills while cutting size, weight, power, cost, and cooling needs.
arxiv-2512-17315:
Fanxian Pei and four co-authors study a flat crystal, Fe2SSeO, that could turn light into a flow of electron spin. Spintronics aims to carry signals with spin rather than charge, saving energy in tiny devices. The crystal is an altermagnet, a newer kind of magnet, and a Janus material, meaning its two faces differ.

Under steady polarized light, the sheet makes a strong injection current whose spin points one locked way. The computed strength reaches about 1,200 in the paper's units, a giant value for this effect. Better still, the current can be flipped by turning the magnetization or by straining the sheet. That switchable response points toward light-driven spin devices that can be tuned after they are built.
arxiv-2512-17515:
Mahsa Lavaei and coauthors, based largely at the University of Tehran, look at how to run medical image classifiers on small edge devices rather than big servers. Clinics in remote places often lack strong computers, yet fast diagnosis from scans still matters there. Their 2025 paper tests quantization, a way to shrink deep learning models.

Quantization stores numbers at lower precision, cutting memory use and computing cost. The team tuned two forms of it, one applied during training and one applied afterward, and measured the effect across medical imaging datasets. The smaller models ran in real time on edge hardware and got much faster, with large drops in size and delay. Diagnostic accuracy stayed at levels the authors judge acceptable for clinical use.
arxiv-2512-18015:
Joyful E. Mdhluli, writing for the International Astronomical Union's Office of Astronomy for Development, offers a field guide for star based aid projects. Groups around the world use astronomy to teach science and build skills, and funders want proof that the work helps. The guide shows teams how to gather that proof from the start.

It separates day to day monitoring from deeper evaluation and lays out six kinds of review, from process to cost. Teams get steps for stating how change should happen, picking clear signs of progress, and spotting risks early. The aim is projects shaped by local needs that can show real gains at home and beyond.
arxiv-2512-18315:
Isabela Belciug, Simon Ferreira, and Charles K. Assaad simplify how to adjust for background traits in summary causal graphs. Such graphs compress a whole time series into one node, which suits dynamic systems but breaks the classic rules for picking a fair comparison set. Recent work gave full conditions for when a small scale effect can be read off by adjustment, yet the rules were heavy and yielded just two valid sets.

Their restatement puts those conditions in a lighter form, and a new test certifies many more valid adjustment sets than the old rules allowed. Among the valid sets they single out the near best one, whose effect estimate wobbles least over large samples. The plainer rules also skip the slow path counting the first version needed.
arxiv-2512-18515:
Sergey Salishev revisits the Osipov-Lanchester model, a classic mathematical description of two forces wearing each other down. His version, posted to arXiv in December 2025, adds one constraint: the total population of the two forces, R plus B, stays constant over time. That single change turns the contest's ratio into a Riccati equation that can be studied completely.

He finds stable resting states exist in exactly three sign cases for the parameters alpha and beta. With both negative, a stable interior balance point appears. With one parameter zero and the other negative, one force's extinction face becomes stable. In all other cases, solutions run into the model's boundaries in finite time. He also shows that letting the parameters drift over time needs buffer dynamics that push solutions away from the axes to keep stability.
arxiv-2512-18615:
Nayana Venkatareddy, Partha Sarathi Mondal, Shradha Mishra, and Prabal K. Maiti study how mixtures of hot and cold particles separate into domains. The setting is two temperature induced phase separation, in a dilute mix of active hot particles and passive cold ones. The team combines computer simulations with a coarse grained fluid model. After a sudden quench, the cold ones gather into clusters.

Those clusters do not sit still and grow by diffusion, as in ordinary phase separation. They move ballistically, in straight lines, merging through repeated coalescence events. Domain growth follows dynamic scaling with a growth exponent near 0.7, markedly faster than diffusive coarsening. The authors name this regime ballistic agglomeration of cold clusters. It is a nonequilibrium growth mechanism in low density active systems. How active mixtures sort themselves matters for self assembling materials and living systems, where hot and cold components mix and separate.
arxiv-2512-18815:
John S. Schreck and eight co-authors convert a deterministic AI weather model into an honest ensemble. Forecasts need uncertainty ranges, and noise-injected AI ensembles can supply them cheaply, though usually with costly training and murky perturbations. Their Stochastic Decomposition Layers, posted to arXiv in December 2025, borrow StyleGAN's trick of injecting noise at several scales.

Applied to the WXFormer model by transfer learning, the layers cost under 2 percent of the original training compute. Each ensemble member comes from a compact five-megabyte latent code, so forecasts reproduce exactly and their spread can be retuned afterward. On 2022 ERA5 data, spread-skill ratios approach one and calibration rivals the operational IFS ensemble. Coarse layers steer the big weather patterns while fine layers handle local detail, an interpretable split forecasters can reason about.
arxiv-2512-18915:
Ivan Čilić and three co-authors route work across the computing continuum, where tasks spill between cloud and edge devices and every client's quality-of-service deadline still matters. Most load balancers chase global averages and let individual clients suffer. Their system, QEdgeProxy, posted to arXiv in December 2025, sits as a proxy between IoT devices and service instances and decides afresh where each request goes.

The choice is framed as a multi-player multi-armed bandit: each balancer picks instances to maximize its own clients' chance of meeting QoS, estimating success odds with kernel density estimation. Adaptive exploration lets it recover quickly when performance shifts or instances vanish. Implemented natively for Kubernetes and tested on a K3s cluster with a latency-sensitive edge-AI workload, QEdgeProxy beats proximity-based and reinforcement-learning baselines on per-client satisfaction, and rides out load surges gracefully.
arxiv-2512-19315:
Agustín Silva charts a route to quantizing gravity without ever starting from a metric. In affine gravity, the connection is the basic field, and the metric appears only as a derived object when it exists at all. The path starts from the Palatini form of general relativity, which yields an equivalent Eddington-style affine action.

For positive cosmological constant, that action is bounded below, so a statistical ensemble of connections is well defined. Silva discretizes the theory on a hypercubic lattice and builds the partition function, with and without torsion. An open C++ Monte Carlo code simulates the ensembles in any dimension, with first results in two.
arxiv-2512-19415:
Xiaoming Zhang, Chunli Li, Jiacheng Hao, and Yuan Gao grade dangerous swollen veins in the esophagus from plain CT scans. Varices strike most cirrhosis patients and bleed at a worrying rate. The standard check is an invasive endoscopy, which patients and clinics would gladly avoid when a scan can answer first.

Their network, MOON++, reads the esophagus, liver, and spleen together, since organ sizes shift jointly with liver disease. On more than sixteen hundred patients with endoscopy-confirmed grades, it beat single-organ methods clearly. Sorting severe cases reached a notably higher score in validation and held up on an independent test group.
arxiv-2512-19515:
Bruno Cavalar, Théo Borém Fabris, Partha Mukhopadhyay, and Srikanth Srinivasan show that a pinch of negation beats mountains of monotone computing. Monotone circuits ban subtraction and negation, and a classic question asks how much power that ban removes. Their answer is the strongest separation yet, in a very shallow setting.

A family of polynomials with all-positive monomials is easy for a depth-three circuit of modest size, yet any monotone circuit needs exponential size. Bootstrapping lifts the gap to constant-degree polynomials, settling an open problem from a standard survey. Boolean versions follow, and a set of linear-algebra flavored problems inherits the lower bounds.
arxiv-2512-20315:
Anne Schnattinger classifies curves that produce a special kind of three-dimensional shape. Start with a smooth hyperquadric in four-dimensional projective space and blow it up along a smooth curve. The question is exactly which curves make the result a weak Fano threefold, a shape with mild positivity that algebraic geometers catalogue.

The answer is a precise list of conditions on the curve's degree and genus. The curve must lie on a smooth cubic section. It must avoid lines meeting it four times and conics meeting it seven times, and satisfy explicit degree and genus inequalities with two small exceptional pairs. Schnattinger proves every allowed case actually occurs geometrically. That establishes weak Fano threefolds and Sarkisov links that had previously existed only as numerical possibilities.
arxiv-2512-20715:
Yash Saraswat and Abhimanyu Nag survey the race to make Ethereum confirmations final within seconds, not minutes. Ethereum's Gasper rules keep the chain safe even as validators come and go, yet a payment takes about fifteen minutes to become final. That window invites attacks that rewrite recent history, games around transaction ordering, and slow settlement. Fast finality research tries to close the gap without weakening safety.

The survey lays out the field's core ideas, among them resilience to rewrites and the generalized sleepy model, and traces the line of designs from Goldfish to RLMD-GHOST. It then studies the limits on talking and pooling votes that single-slot designs face with very many validators. A three-slot design is presented as the practical balance, trading a little speed for rules the live network can actually run.
arxiv-2512-21015:
Mingshu Cai, Yixuan Li, Osamu Yoshie, and Yuya Ieiri edit real videos with a text-to-image engine that was never built for motion. Bolting temporal attention onto Stable Diffusion works, but edits flicker between frames and the compute bill climbs. FluencyVE replaces the temporal attention layer with Mamba, a linear-time sequence module that still attends across the whole clip at frame level for a fraction of the cost.

Low-rank stand-ins for the query and key matrices lighten the remaining attention, and a weighted-averaging update during training protects the base model's generative strength. The one-shot editor changes attributes, subjects, and locations in real footage while keeping frames coherent. Video editing inherits the image model's quality without inheriting its quadratic habits.
arxiv-2512-21115:
Wenqing Zhang and Lin Zhang give asset bubbles a rigorous definition in a market unsure of its own model, one that forbids short selling. Working in discrete time and discrete states, they measure a bubble as the gap between an asset's market price and its fundamental value. That value is set by a super-hedging benchmark: the cheapest cost of a strategy that surely covers the asset's payoff. How long an asset may be held before liquidation turns out to govern the mathematics.

For bounded maturity without dividends, a supermartingale-style property of prices is equivalent to bubbles existing. With unbounded maturity, one variant stays necessary and another sufficient. A no-dominance condition excludes bubbles when liquidation is bounded. Finite-horizon claims add a split personality. Fundamental prices obey put-call bounds, and market prices obey put-call parity. American and European call values coincide in the dividend-free case.
arxiv-2512-22015:
Zwanzig's classic mean-field theory says landscape roughness cuts diffusion exponentially, by a factor set by the disorder spread. Yet simulations with uncorrelated Gaussian site energies disobey it, because rare deep three-site traps dominate. Biman Bagchi builds a unified account explaining when the prediction holds and when it breaks.

The analysis shows Zwanzig's local averaging is in effect a Gaussian expansion, destroyed by uncorrelated disorder. Gaussian spatial correlations, introduced earlier by Banerjee, Seki, and Bagchi from astrophysics models of turbulence, reshape roughness steps and remove the asymmetric multi-site traps, restoring the exponential scaling. Numerical triplet examples show how sharply correlations shorten escape times, completing the route back to the mean-field result.
arxiv-2512-23415:
Vinoth Punniyamoorthy and co-authors redesign Kubernetes autoscaling around service level objectives and cost together. The platform's built-in scalers react to load after the fact, lean on crude signals, and hide their logic, so production systems suffer objective violations and wasted spend. The authors first analyze the gaps in existing approaches, then propose a framework that is safe, explainable, and driven by multiple signals at once.

Their design couples objective-aware, cost-conscious control with lightweight demand forecasting, aiming to scale before violations happen rather than after. Experiments on microservice and event-driven workloads report shorter violation time, faster scaling responses, and lower infrastructure cost than default and tuned baselines. The headline measures improved by roughly a fifth to a third. Control behavior stayed stable and auditable throughout, which the authors argue is what makes operators willing to trust automation in production.
arxiv-2512-23615:
Julian Demeio and Damián Gvirtz-Chen work on the inverse Galois problem, which asks which finite groups occur as Galois groups of field extensions with extra regularity. Their target groups are the simple groups PSL2 over finite fields with a squared number of elements, subject to congruence conditions on the prime. The standard route uses Hilbert irreducibility on rational surfaces, but the relevant surfaces here refuse to cooperate.

The obstruction is that the Hilbert modular surfaces involved are of K3 type and not unirational, so classical arguments break. The authors establish non-unirational versions of Hilbert irreducibility for all such K3-type surfaces. Feeding those results into the machinery yields new instances of the regular inverse Galois problem for their target groups, extending the list of groups known to be realizable.
arxiv-2512-24015:
Zixiang Li and nine co-authors fix a drift problem in image editing with flow-based diffusion models. Modern editors transform a source image directly toward a target distribution without inversion. Errors in the latent velocity accumulate along the path, so edits lose the source's structure or miss the intended meaning. Their framework, Conditioned Velocity Correction, recasts editing as distribution transport driven by a known source prior.

The velocity at each step splits into two branches: one that preserves the source trajectory's structure, and one that steers semantically toward the target. Because the conditional velocity field carries a measurable absolute error against the true trajectory, the authors correct it with a posterior-consistent update grounded in empirical Bayes and Tweedie estimation. Across diverse editing tasks, the corrected flow delivered higher fidelity, better semantic alignment, and more reliable behavior than existing methods.
arxiv-2512-24115:
Julian Allagan and Benkam Bobga study a counting question in graph theory. Start with a dominating set, a set of vertices such that every other vertex sits next to one of them, and take the smallest possible size of such a set. The dominion of a graph counts how many different sets achieve that minimum.

The authors relate these two parameters, the minimum size and the number of ways to reach it, which look unrelated at first sight. They then compute dominions for concrete families: paths, some cycles, and the join of any two graphs, where every vertex of one graph is linked to every vertex of the other. Results of this kind give graph theorists exact values for structured networks and tools for thinking about how many equally good guard placements a network admits.
arxiv-2512-24215:
Canan Karahan extends the Standard Model with two additions. The first is a set of down-type vector-like quarks. They are isosinglets and share one mass. The second is a single right-handed neutrino. Three puzzles motivate the construction. Neutrino masses need a source. The electroweak vacuum needs stability. Higgs inflation needs a viable high-scale potential.

The vector-like quarks do the stabilizing work. They steer the running of couplings through loop effects. The right-handed neutrino generates light neutrino masses by a seesaw. It also smooths the Higgs coupling's running in the inflation regime. Karahan computes the running at two loops. Matching is handled at each particle's mass threshold. Allowed regions of parameter space are then mapped. Inflation predictions from those regions match current cosmic microwave background data. A version without the neutrino serves as the comparison case.
arxiv-2512-24315:
Dian-Jun Zhao and five colleagues measure how much of the proton's spin comes from gluons. The proton spin puzzle has occupied physicists for decades. Quark spins explain only part of the total. Gluon helicity is a key missing piece. The team computes it with lattice QCD, the grid-based simulation of the strong force.

Three lattice spacings test the approach to the continuum. Distillation and momentum smearing sharpen the proton states. The topological current's matrix elements are extracted in a fixed gauge. A non-perturbative renormalization scheme sets the overall scale. An error-reduction technique refines those constants. Different current components agree within uncertainties, as Lorentz symmetry demands. After continuum extrapolation, gluon helicity accounts for roughly forty-six percent of the proton spin. The result is a state-of-the-art number for this quantity.
arxiv-2512-24415:
Jingyu Zhang audits customer-service AI agents under attack. Such agents make policy-bound decisions: refunds, rebooking, billing disputes. Their helpful style can be exploited. A small share of users induce unauthorized concessions. Costs shift to honest customers, and trust erodes. The benchmark here targets profit-seeking prompt injection.

Ten service domains host a hundred realistic attack scripts. Five technique families organize the scripts. Five widely used models face them under one rubric. Uncertainty is reported with the scores. Attacks proved highly domain-dependent. Airline support was the most exploitable domain. Payload splitting was the most reliable technique. Zhang releases the data and evaluation code. The goal is reproducible auditing. Oversight and recovery workflows for agent deployments should benefit.
arxiv-2512-24515:
Jiani Wei and Xiaocheng Shang stabilize a sampling method for Bayesian machine learning. Langevin dynamics with stochastic gradients sample from posteriors using minibatches. That shortcut powers large-scale Bayesian learning. One adaptive variant beats popular alternatives. It adds a term built from the covariance of the noisy force. A moving average estimates that covariance, though.

Experiments suggest the moving average hurts stability. Integrators must shrink their steps as a result. The authors modify the method. The part with the covariance term is solved more exactly. A scaling-and-squaring step with a truncated Taylor series does the job. A symmetric splitting replaces the old discretization. Tests show large stability gains over the original. Accuracy still beats popular stochastic gradient methods. Large usable steps return without giving up precision.
arxiv-2512-24615:
Yuchen Shi and five colleagues build a framework that builds agents. Existing language-model agent frameworks share two pains. Configuration costs run high, with manual tool integration and prompt tuning. Deployed agents then stay static, adapting poorly without expensive fine-tuning. Youtu-Agent attacks both problems. Its configuration system separates environments, toolkits, and context handling.

Two generation modes cover standard and unusual needs. A workflow mode handles routine tasks. A meta-agent mode writes tool code, prompts, and settings for complex ones. Improvement continues after deployment. A practice module learns from experience in context, with no parameter updates. A reinforcement learning module trains agents at scale, end to end. Results on web and general agent benchmarks lead open-weight rivals. Automated tool synthesis succeeds most of the time.
arxiv-2512-24915:
Jinxiang Wang studies the standard Melan formula, a model of suspension bridge bending that couples the cable and the deck. For a simpler, less stiff model he gives a clear answer formula and proves it stays evenly positive. Monotone loop with lower and upper answers then tackles the original formula.

Existence, uniqueness, and approximability of answers are proven together, since the loop both proves a answer exists and works out it. Examples from actual bridges check the method's use for engineering design calculations, and open problems are offered. Applied mathematics readers get theory tied to bridge engineering practice.
arxiv-2601-00015:
Noé Stauffer, Hossein Gorji, and Ivan Lunati work on shrinking large, uncertain dynamic systems down to a smaller set of tracked variables. Such shrinking methods struggle when noise or uncertain starting points matter, and rare events are often the ones of interest. Their 2026 paper draws on the Mori-Zwanzig framework and on an older optimal prediction method, but changes how the shrinking is done over time.

Their surrogate paths follow the same flow of probabilities as the full system. A chaos-based expansion identifies the measure behind the shrinking step, so paths that start from unlikely events can still be computed well. Tests show gains over random sampling and the older prediction method, plus good estimates of averages tied to a given start.
arxiv-2601-00615:
Foo Hui-Mean and Yuan-chin Ivan Chang present a 2026 framework for hard optimization tasks. The tasks share one trait: each test of a design is slow and costly. Think of a physics run, or a long training run for a deep network. No slope hints are on hand to guide the search. Their framework, named ALMAB-DC, joins three tools to cut the cost.

One tool is a stand-in model that guesses outcomes for untested designs. A second tool picks which tests are worth their cost, in turn. A third tool spreads the tests across many machines at once, . The framework can also use graphics chips to speed the work. The authors prove bounds on how much the search can lose versus the best pick. In tests on made-up tasks, learning tasks, and science runs, it beat the best known rivals.
arxiv-2601-00815:
Mara Kalicanin Dimitrov, Marko Dimitrov, Anatoliy Malyarenko, and Ying Ni extend a fast simulation method for pricing options whose value depends on a randomly moving volatility. The Heston model is the standard setting, and its almost-exact simulation scheme was previously tested only on European options, which can be exercised just at expiry. Bermudan and American options allow earlier exercise, a harder pricing problem.

The authors derive the scheme for the double Heston model, which uses two volatility factors, and benchmark it against the standard Euler scheme under both models. Numerical experiments show accurate prices with reduced computing time. The scheme is especially effective for Bermudan options when the simulation steps line up with the allowed exercise dates.
arxiv-2601-00915:
Jacquelyn Shelton and four co-authors present, in 2026, a way to grow climate ensembles without more supercomputer time. An ensemble is a set of runs of the same model with slight twists. The team code each run of monthly surface heat into a small latent code. A plain coder, trained across ten real-world reanalysis runs, broke that code into fragments that did not line up.

Their fix pins the codes of all runs to agree at a few shared map points, called anchors. A smooth statistical fit then guesses codes at new points for a fresh run. Decoding those codes yields a full new run of the heat field. Tests show that training on a single run is unstable. Gains fade after about five runs are included. Wider map coverage trades against the quality of each rebuild. The method could stretch costly ensembles for risk and impact studies.
arxiv-2601-01115:
Gaurav Shukla, Yoshio Miura, Mayank Singh, and Shinji Isogami flip tiny magnets with electric current in a new way. Most devices use the spin Hall effect in heavy metals to push a magnet around. Their device instead uses the orbital Hall effect in vanadium nitride, a light compound, to create an orbital current that a cobalt-platinum stack turns into spin.

Measurements show a large torque strength, well above control samples with other magnetic layers. Full switching by an in-plane current is reached with the help of a small side field, and partial switching happens with no field at all. The current needed matches that of tungsten-based devices. Calculations confirm a large orbital Hall response in the nitride. The work points to lighter, cheaper materials for memory and logic that store data in magnet direction.
arxiv-2601-01615:
Brendan Reed and C J Horowitz dispute a recent claim about a small correction in electron scattering experiments. The experiments scatter electrons off atomic nuclei and measure a tiny left-right imbalance that tests the weak force. One letter claimed quantum electrodynamics corrections shift that imbalance by about five percent, which would affect three named experiments.

Reed and Horowitz argue the claim missed a needed correction at the point where the weak-force carrier couples, evaluated at the experiment's actual momentum transfer. Adding that term cancels much of the reported shift. Their two-page comment matters because the experiments aim for precision strong enough to reveal new physics.
arxiv-2601-01715:
Dwarf spheroidal galaxies, faint companions of the Milky Way, are a testing ground for theories that replace dark matter with modified gravity. Youngsub Yoon, Sanghyeon Han, and Ho Seong Hwang compare two such theories, MOND and Verlinde's emergent gravity, against the observed pull of gravity inside twenty-three of these small galaxies.

For each galaxy the authors compute the radial accelerations both theories predict and compare them with observations. Emergent gravity tracked the observed pattern inside individual galaxies more closely than MOND in twenty-one of the twenty-three cases. Combining the evidence across all samples, they conclude emergent gravity is favored over MOND at a strong statistical level, extending their earlier whole-sample result.
arxiv-2601-02015:
A fresh metaphor surprises the reader, and language models register surprise as a number: surprisal, how unpredictable a word is in context. Omar Momen, Emilie Sitter, Berenike Herrmann, and Sina Zarrieß test whether that number tracks human judgments of metaphor novelty across corpus-based and synthetic datasets, using sixteen language model variants.

A cloze-style method that conditions on the whole sentence gave significant, moderate correlations with novelty scores. Scaling behaved in opposite directions on the two data types: bigger models correlated worse on real corpus metaphors but better on synthetic ones. The authors conclude surprisal partly explains novelty annotations yet remains a limited measure of linguistic creativity. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2601-02215:
Modern cars are defined by software, and their safety and security must be designed in, not tested in afterward. Nenad Petrovic, Vahid Zolfaghari, Fengjunjie Pan, and Alois Knoll present a workflow in which large language models assist both jobs across the development of software-defined vehicles.

For code analysis, event chains give a formal basis for validating functional safety, including the semantic validity of messages on CAN buses and in the Vehicle Signal Specification. For system topology, security analysis leans on model-driven engineering with formal constraint rules. Both locally deployable and proprietary language models are evaluated on advanced driver-assistance scenarios, probing where language models genuinely help engineers meet automotive safety and security standards.
arxiv-2601-02315:
Saurabh Kaushik, Lalit Maurya, and Beth Tellman improve flood mapping from satellite data, a task where large geo foundation models have oddly lagged behind a plain U-Net baseline. The large models capture broad patterns but miss small local detail that decides whether a street or field is under water. Their encoder, called CAFE, is built to add that detail back.

CAFE runs a convolutional branch with attention modules in parallel with the pre trained Prithvi encoder, then fuses features at several scales while adapters allow fast fine tuning. On the Sen1Flood11 and FloodPlanet data sets it sets new best scores, beating the original Prithvi model and other major foundation models. The gain is largest on the held out test site, which suggests the fusion travels well to new places.
arxiv-2601-02515:
Sonia Yang, Ali Al-Bayaty, and Marek Perkowski introduce a new logic structure for building reversible quantum circuits at lower cost. Standard synthesis writes a function as a two level AND XOR expression realized with Toffoli gates, and gates with many input qubits are very expensive. Their structure uses three logical levels, with decoders in the circuit, which reduces the number of inputs each Toffoli gate needs.

The mathematics uses functions with multi valued inputs and binary outputs as a design concept, while the circuits themselves stay binary. A new form, multi valued input fixed polarity Reed Muller, organizes the expressions. Two practical algorithms find good forms, one based on product matching and one on newly developed butterfly diagrams. The best forms are then factorized and reduced toward a minimal quantum cost.
arxiv-2601-02715:
Yue Yu and six co authors build a thermal sensor on thin film lithium niobate, a material that combines low optical loss, strong piezoelectricity. High mechanical quality, and low heat conduction, all useful for optomechanics, where light reads out tiny mechanical motion with very low noise. Their integrated platform packs engineered optical, mechanical, and thermal behavior into a footprint only tens of micrometers across.

Suspended microring resonators sit over ultrathin membranes, lowering stiffness and mass while keeping optical quality very high. Mechanical quality rises sharply once the device oscillates. The design blocks heat from leaking into the silicon substrate below, which concentrates temperature changes where they can be sensed. The result is an uncooled, low noise resonator aimed at sensitive thermal measurement without cryogenics.
arxiv-2601-03315:
Dhruv Trehan and Paras Chopra report, with unusual candor, on four attempts to let language models do machine learning research end to end. Their pipeline chains six agents mapped to the stages of the scientific workflow, from idea to written paper. Three of the four attempts failed during implementation or evaluation; one completed the pipeline and was accepted at an experimental venue that required AI systems as first authors.

From the wreckage, the authors document six recurring failure modes, including drift toward training-data defaults, implementation drift under pressure, and declaring success despite obvious failures. They close with four design principles for sturdier AI-scientist systems and release all prompts, artifacts, and outputs. The case study is a concrete field report on how far autonomous research still has to go.
arxiv-2601-03615:
Binh Nguyen, Charles Fleming, and Thai Le stress-test the explanations that audio language models give when they judge whether a recording is fake. Such models promise transparent deepfake detection because they can state their reasoning, not just a verdict. But an explanation can sound plausible while rationalizing a wrong call, and attackers can target the reasoning itself.

Their diagnostic framework, SARA, grades models on acoustic perception, on whether reasoning and verdict agree, and on dissonance between them. Five open models faced both sound-based and language-based attacks. Sound attacks cut reasoning-verdict agreement sharply, by about fourteen percent on average. The findings warn forensic and media teams that an articulate explanation is not, by itself, evidence a detector can be trusted.
arxiv-2601-03715:
Weijie Shi and seven co-authors propose R3L, a reinforcement learning method for language models that reflects and retries instead of sampling blindly. Current training struggles on two fronts. Exploration rarely succeeds on hard tasks and wastes costly rollouts. Exploitation assigns credit crudely, punishing good early steps for later errors and drowning rare successes in failures.

R3L uses language feedback to diagnose errors, restart from identified failure points, and turn failed attempts into successful training trajectories. Its pivotal credit idea focuses reward on the steps where outcomes turned, and positive amplification strengthens the scarce good signals. Together these target a familiar training pathology: lots of motion, little direction. More sample-efficient reasoning training lowers the cost of teaching models genuinely hard tasks.
arxiv-2601-03915:
Julie van Logtestijn and Petru Manescu introduce HemBLIP, a vision-language model that describes leukemia cells in words a clinician can check. Judging white blood cell shape under the microscope is central to leukemia diagnosis, but most deep learning tools give verdicts without reasons, limiting trust. HemBLIP instead generates morphology-aware descriptions of peripheral blood cells.

The pair built a new dataset of fourteen thousand healthy and leukemic cells paired with expert-derived attribute captions. They adapted a general vision-language model by full fine-tuning and by a cheaper low-rank method, benchmarking against a biomedical foundation model. HemBLIP produced better captions and more accurate morphology, and the low-rank adaptation added gains at far lower computing cost. Interpretable cell descriptions could make automated blood analysis easier to audit in real laboratories.
arxiv-2601-04315:
Donald J. Liveoak and three co-authors add tidal physics to a widely used astronomy toolkit in a 2026 arXiv paper. When an orbiting body swings close on a stretched-out orbit, tides excite vibrations inside it — dynamical tides. those modes trade energy with the orbit in ways plain gravity codes miss, sometimes chaotically.

Their implementation couples the modes and the orbit together inside REBOUNDx, the add-on package for the REBOUND N-body integrator. A set of test cases drawn from exoplanet dynamics shows the coupled code matching earlier studies of tides in the slow, secular regime. Because the tool is general and fast, the authors offer it for the many high-eccentricity systems — migrating planets, tight binaries, near misses — where dynamical tides shape the outcome.
arxiv-2601-04715:
Xiao Guo, Jie Zhu, Anil Jain, and Xiaoming Liu refuse to split fake people into fake faces and fake bodies, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Generators now synthesize entire photorealistic humans, but detectors stayed fragmented — one literature for facial manipulations, another for full-body synthetic images — and each fails outside its specialty. Their framework, HuForDet, audits the whole person at once.

Two branches split the work. One hunts face forgery with heterogeneous experts across image and frequency domains, including an adaptive smoothing module tuned to catch artifacts from fine blending seams to coarse texture irregularities. The other sends the full body to a multimodal language model that judges semantic consistency, with a confidence mechanism deciding how much weight its verdict gets in the fusion. The team curated HuFor, a dataset unifying existing face corpora with new full-body synthetic humans, and reports state-of-the-art detection across manipulation types.
arxiv-2601-05615:
Lars Willas Dreyer and 6 co-authors describe ORB, a 2026 open-source radio buoy for measuring coastal waters. Ocean instruments are moving toward open designs that compete with commercial buoys on price and availability. ORB is a drifting buoy built to be reliable, cheap, modifiable, and power-efficient, using long-range LoRa radio that needs no existing infrastructure.

Validation experiments showed a telemetry range of five kilometers. Expected battery life reaches up to seven months, helped by a radio that draws very little current while transmitting. The authors discuss where ORB fits among open-source instruments and how its measurements can feed ocean modeling. Its open design invites others to copy, adapt, and deploy it locally.
arxiv-2601-05815:
Elnaz Shokati and 2 co-authors explore in 2026 whether a different acoustic resonator geometry can serve microwave-to-optical signal conversion. Such transducers link superconducting quantum hardware, which speaks microwave, to optical fibers, which carry signals far. Film bulk acoustic resonators are compact and efficient, but their sound field hides under a metal electrode, complicating the tiny optical cavities the task needs.

Lateral-field excited suspended resonators, called XBARs, sidestep that limitation. The authors outline requirements for doing this task well in this geometry. As a first step they fabricated a small phonon-trapping resonator by shaping the piezoelectric layer into a spherical lens, and report raised modal confinement with roughly fourfold better quality factor. The lens shape traps the sound in a small space, which is just what the task needs.
arxiv-2601-05915:
Matias Alvarado and Nicolas Arevalo-Hurtado analyze in 2026 the Lyapunov spectrum of the Schneider map, a dynamical system living on the p-adic integers. P-adic numbers measure closeness through divisibility by a prime, creating a non-Archimedean geometry unlike the real line. Thermodynamic formalism there connects dynamics with fractal sizes of special sets.

A geometric potential capturing how cylinder sets expand defines a Lyapunov exponent adapted to this setting. The authors show the corresponding spectrum is real analytic on its natural domain and derive a clear closed formula for it. Consequences include refined results on Hausdorff dimensions of sets defined by average continued-fraction digits. The exponent also equals the convergence rate of rational approximations from Schneider continued fractions, a p-adic analogue of standard Diophantine results. All of this takes place in a number system where size is judged by a prime, not by length on a line.
arxiv-2601-06015:
Two faint little red dots, nicknamed Red Eyes, hide inside one lensed galaxy in a 2026 report led by Hiroto Yanagisawa and 49 co-authors. Gravitational lensing by a foreground cluster magnifies the distant galaxy, which sits at redshift near 7, meaning its light comes from the early universe. The VENUS program with the James Webb Space Telescope found the pair.

The two dots sit only about 70 parsecs apart and away from the galaxy center. Without lensing, the host would look like a normal star-forming galaxy with no sign of them. The authors suggest such hidden pairs may be common. One idea is that intermediate-mass black holes form in star clusters and later merge to grow a central supermassive black hole.
arxiv-2601-07215:
Gabriel Silva wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on the spike trains sent by nerve cells. A nerve cell fires by means of an action potential, a sharp pulse of voltage. The pulse acts like a digital blip in the cell's signal line. A spike train is the set of times when one cell fires. Silva works in the field of bioengineering and brain science.

The full pulse has a shape that plays out over time. That shape is tied to the voltage across the wall of the cell. To treat spikes as bare points in time is to drop that shape. Silva argues that the two views are far apart in strict math terms. He sets out a frame that treats a spike train as a spread-out object, in the sense of functional analysis. The frame may change how teams read and weigh spike data from the brain.
arxiv-2601-07715:
Hugo Matias and Daniel Silvestre keep a moving agent safe among obstacles whose motion is uncertain. Their 2026 preprint presents a sampled-data framework for safe navigation. The obstacles follow linear dynamics with uncertainty. Collision-free motion comes from two parts working together. One part filters control commands for safety. The other estimates the obstacles' states as sets.

Safety filtering uses control barrier functions, which block commands that would breach a safety margin. State estimation uses constrained convex generators, a way to represent sets of possible obstacle states. Together they handle both control and perception uncertainty. Robots, vehicles, and drones all face moving obstacles with imperfect tracking. The paper speaks to control engineers who need guarantees, not just good average behavior. It aims for safety that survives the stated uncertainty.
arxiv-2601-07815:
Erhan Bayraktar and Jiamin Jian study how large-population control problems settle as the horizon grows. They investigate convergence and turnpike properties for linear-quadratic mean field control with common noise. The framework unifies three problems: a finite-horizon social optimization, its mean field limit, and the matching ergodic problem. Mean field control models crowds where each agent reacts to the average behavior. Common noise shakes the whole population at once.

Turnpike properties say optimal paths spend most time near a steady state, whatever the endpoints. Proving convergence links the finite and infinite versions of the problem. Such results justify using the simpler ergodic problem for long horizons. The paper serves scholars in stochastic control and mean field games. Applications range from energy systems to large fleets of devices. It supplies theory for a widely used approximation.
arxiv-2601-08015:
Abhishek Kumar presents a decoder that generates three-dimensional structures ready to print. The framework decodes latent representations into geometrically valid, printable objects. It respects manufacturing constraints such as overhang angles, wall thickness, and structural integrity. Many generative models produce shapes that look fine but cannot be built. His 2026 preprint builds manufacturability into the generation itself. The decoder is the core of the deep learning framework.

Additive manufacturing fails when designs overhang too far or walls run too thin. Checking after generation wastes most candidate designs. Generating within the constraints yields usable objects directly. That shift matters for automated design tools and rapid prototyping. The paper serves scholars in generative design and manufacturing. It argues the printer's limits belong inside the model, not in a cleanup step.
arxiv-2601-08215: Seng Pei Liew, Kenta Shinzato, and Yuyang Dong seek principled design rules for mixture-of-experts language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that modern designs rest on two factors: total parameters and active parameters. Total size sets the memory footprint, while active size sets inference cost. The authors find these two factors alone cannot describe an optimal architecture. Memory and inference limits shape real deployments, so missing factors can mislead builders. The paper aims at design rules that reflect how such models are actually run and stored.
arxiv-2601-08315: Qi Yao, Jun Zhang, Wenxian Zhang, and Chaohong Lee extend qubit coherence with a hybrid decoupling method. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses decoherence from a qubit's coupling to its environment. Dynamical decoupling and bath engineering are two parallel defenses against that coupling. The hybrid approach joins pulsed decoupling with bath spin polarization. Tests run within the central spin model, a standard testbed for this problem. Longer coherence times would let quantum processors run deeper circuits before noise erases the computation.
arxiv-2601-08415:
Brittany Davidson, Kate Muir, Florian Burnat, and Adam Joinson compare the terms of service of major language model providers. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that these models now sit inside academic research pipelines. The rules governing their use remain under-examined, though.

The team analyzes terms from Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google, OpenAI, and xAI, collected in November 2025. Gray areas in such terms can leave researchers unsure what uses are allowed. Data handling, publication rights, and liability often hide in fine print. For universities and labs, a clear comparison helps set policy before a project depends on a model whose terms may shift.
arxiv-2601-08615:
Kansei Inamura and Shuhei Ohyama build lattice models of a class of guarded states of matter. Such states hold their traits in the bulk, not just at the edge. Their models have a rare type of rule that can not be flipped like a plain switch. The team calls these states by the name cluster states, in a broad sense.

They build the models by fixing part of a plain rule group in place. They then study the traits with grid nets that stand for the states. Work covers walls where two states meet, and whole sets of states that shift by a knob. A reader in this field gets new model cases. They help map how non flip rules guard a state of matter.
arxiv-2601-08815:
Qing Ye and Jing Tan set rules for AI agents that must work with firm caps. An agent here is a program that acts on its own for a set time. Old group rules let agents pass tasks by deal, but they set no cap on cost or time. A runaway agent could burn cash or run far too long.

Their frame is called Agent Contracts. A deal states what the agent may use, how long it may run, and when it must stop. The rules are formal, so a host can check them by machine. A reader who lets agents act gets a guard rail. It lets agents work free, but only in a box that both sides agreed.
arxiv-2601-09815:
John Joseph M. Carrasco and four co-authors derive the full four-graviton effective theory from a duality. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on the Bern-Carrasco-Johansson double copy. That construction reveals a deep structural link between gauge theory and gravity.

At its heart, the double copy rests on a duality between color algebra and kinematic algebra. The authors generalize the principle beyond the Lie algebra structure of tree-level Yang-Mills theory. From it, they obtain the entire four-graviton effective field theory. The result extends a calculational trick into a statement about how gravity is built.
arxiv-2601-09915:
Andrei Kulikovsky and Tatyana Reshetenko model water inside fuel cell membranes and test the model against spectra. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins a water transport model with an impedance model for PEM fuel cells. Good water management is essential for these cells to perform at their best.

The impedance model covers liquid water moving through the membrane. It is coupled to a two-phase model for the cathode side. The full model was fitted to measured spectra at three humidity pairings, from 32 to 100 percent. Currents ranged from 100 to 1000 milliamps per square centimeter. Fits like these turn impedance spectra into a diagnostic for what limits a working cell.
arxiv-2601-10415:
R. M. F. Andersen and co authors test how cloud traits are read from burst shots of cold atoms. A Bose Einstein cloud is a gas cooled till its parts act as one. Warm clouds mix a dense core with a loose halo. A shot is taken as the cloud bursts free.

From the burst shape, labs read heat, atom count, and the dense share. The team ask how the push twixt core and halo warps that read. The core and halo shove each other as they grow. That shove can bias the halo shape. The work maps the bias so reads can be set right.
arxiv-2601-10915:
Yangshuo He, Guanding Yu, and Jingge Zhu analyze how wireless channels degrade edge inference. In edge inference, a neural network is split across nearby devices. The parts must talk over wireless links while they compute. Standard networks are trained in noiseless settings. Live channels are noisy, so a mismatch opens between training and deployment.

The authors use PAC-Bayesian analysis, a framework that bounds how much performance can drop. Their bounds tie channel noise to inference loss in a principled way. Such bounds can guide where to split a network and how much redundancy to add. The work serves designers of phone, camera, and vehicle systems that must think over the air.
arxiv-2601-11515:
Callum Donnan and six coauthors confirm a galaxy at redshift 13.53. Their 2026 preprint reports JWST spectroscopy of the source. The galaxy was a robust candidate near redshift 14. It was picked from pure-parallel NIRCam imaging data.

NIRSpec PRISM observations then gave the team a spectrum. Modeling of the Lyman-alpha break fixed the distance. The confirmed value is 13.53, with small error bars. The galaxy is large and luminous for its era. Its emission lines are weak, an odd trait so early. Such finds test how fast the first galaxies grew. Weak lines may hint at young stars and low metal content.
arxiv-2601-11715:
Nicolas Mazziotti, Michael G. Jones, Donghyeon J. Khim, David J. Sand, and Paul Bennet report a search for faint, spread out galaxies in the Fornax group. The search was done by citizen science, with the public helping to spot weak shapes in sky images. Such faint galaxies are hard for code alone to find.

Their list holds 643 diffuse galaxies in the group. They judge that about one in five has a bright core, based on counts they give in the text. They note this is the first crowd based count of this kind at the scale of a whole group. The list gives a base for later work on how such faint systems form.
arxiv-2601-12215:
Megha Thukral, Cyrus Tanade, Simon A. Lee, and a large team build foundation models for PPG signals that heed their wave structure. PPG tracks blood flow from light on skin, as in wrist wearables. Such models could learn traits that move across health tasks.

Most past training skips the spectral form of PPG, where body rhythms sit in split frequency bands. Their wavelet-driven masked method rebuilds hidden parts across scales. That should bake rhythm form into the traits. Good PPG traits aid heart and sleep tools from wearables.  Rhythm bands are the cue past models missed most.
arxiv-2601-12315:
A MAGPI survey team with Bodo Ziegler measure dark matter in star-forming disk galaxies at redshifts from about 0.1 to 0.85. They use spatially resolved kinematic data from the MAGPI survey, which uses integral field spectroscopy. Their sample holds 266 rotation-supported, main-sequence galaxies.

They analyse how dark matter content links to galaxy structure. Such links test how baryons and dark matter co-evolve. Disk galaxies at those distances show the universe at a younger age. The work gives a large, uniform sample for that test.  The sample is large for this kind of disk study.
arxiv-2601-12615:
Robert Prater and ten co authors measure the electronic band structure of a compound called CeCoGe3. They use angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy, a method that maps electron energies across a crystal. Their study covers the entire Brillouin zone, the full cell of momenta in the crystal. They work in the non magnetic regime of the compound.

The measured structure agrees in large part with first principles calculations. That agreement includes predicted topological nodal lines in the band structure. Nodal lines are features where bands cross in a protected way. Confirming them by direct measurement grounds the theory of this material. The work serves studies of topological metals and cerium based compounds.
arxiv-2601-12915:
Francesco Salerno proves a sharp lower bound for Monge Ampere torsion on convex sets. The torsion functional measures how a convex set responds to a classic equation of geometry. The deficit compares the value on a given set with the value on a matching ball. That ball shares the same quermassintegral, a mixed volume measure.

A lower bound on the deficit says how far a set must fall short of the ball. Sharp means the bound is the best possible of its kind. Results of this shape are isoperimetric in spirit: balls win, and others pay a quantifiable price. The setting covers open, bounded convex sets with smooth boundary. The work serves convex geometry and partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-13015:
Nowfel Mashnoor, Mohammad Akyash, Hadi Kamali, and Kimia Azar work on code for chips. Large language models can now draft register transfer level code, the form that tells chip tools what gates to build. The snag is that drafts for hard designs often fail on syntax or on logic.

Their fix is called MeltRTL. It blends the skill of many expert parts inside the model. It also steps in while the model writes, to steer the draft. No fresh train of the base model is needed. The authors say this lifts the share of drafts that are both well formed and right in what they do. Chip teams may find the route a cheap way to get more from models they already run.
arxiv-2601-13315:
Rakesh Kumar SivaKumar and a co-author ask why dark matter and plain matter come in near matched sums. In the Randall-Sundrum set up, space has a spare dim with two walls, called branes. Our world sits on the low energy wall, the IR brane. The team puts both dark and plain fields on that wall.

The two talk just through the graviton and the radion, the field that sets the wall gap. Dark bits are made by freeze in, a slow leak from the hot bath, not a freeze out. The team shows the count seen by the Planck craft can be met for a wide span of reheat heats. They test scalar, fermion, and heavy vector forms of the dark bit.
arxiv-2601-13515:
Huah Yong Chan and co-authors tune a Kubernetes auto scaler to both serve load and block attacks. The scaler is the HPA, which sets how many pods run an app. In their test, HTTP status codes serve as the custom mark the scaler reads. Attack floods can fool a plain scaler into waste or crash.

A random forest judge reads the codes to call if a surge is an attack. It then shifts the top pod cap the scaler may use. A true surge can still grow. An attack surge is held in check. For cloud teams, a scaler that can tell load from attack saves both cost and uptime.
arxiv-2601-13615:
Lifu Ding, Chunhui Hou, Yutong Li, and Qinmin Yang study control of small local power grids in 2026. These microgrids mix two kinds of inverters, grid-following and grid-forming units. Long-term cost plans pull one way, while split-second balance needs pull an other. Each unit also has its own hard limits, and cyber attacks add more risk.

The team sets out a layered control plan called RHPC. The plan tries to join cost aims and fast balance in one frame. It is built to stay firm when attacks or faults hit the grid. Such control could help small grids run clean power with less waste and fewer blackouts.
arxiv-2601-14015:
Jason Douglas Todd and Ismar Volić build a voting method that borrows from web search ranking in 2026. BallotRank is a ranked preference aggregation method derived from PageRank. PageRank ranks web pages by the links that point to them. BallotRank adapts that idea to ballots, without a damping factor.

The method is Condorcet-consistent, meaning it honors a candidate who beats each rival head-to-head. They tested it on nearly two thousand ranked choice elections. Over twenty thousand internet polls were also examined. At conventional damping values, BallotRank always identified the Condorcet winner.
arxiv-2601-14215:
Arianna Nigioni and co-authors build a global formation model for planets in binary systems in 2026. Roughly half of Sun-like stars have at least one stellar companion. Most known exoplanets are assumed to orbit single stars, largely from observational biases. New surveys are steadily increasing the count of confirmed exoplanets in binaries.

Astrometric surveys, direct imaging, and speckle interferometry drive that growth. Their PAIRS project models planet formation in binaries at a global scale. A global model can predict where planets form around two suns. Those predictions guide observers to the most promising pairs.
arxiv-2601-14915:
Xiao-En Huang, Shan Cheng, and De-Liang Yao study how certain charm mesons decay. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with D and Ds mesons that decay into an eta meson, a charged lepton, and a neutrino. Fresh precise data from the BESIII detector prompts the work.

The team reworks the decay form factors with QCD light-cone sum rules. They add high-twist terms and known next-order QCD fixes. Their study confirms a chiral boost that comes from twist-3 terms. It also shows that the expansion behind the method settles down fast and cleanly.
arxiv-2601-15015:
Jannis Becktepe, Aleksandra Franz, Nils Thuerey, and Sebastian Peitz build a fair test track for learning-based flow control. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with active flow control, where actuators steer a fluid flow. Reinforcement learning has shown promise in this field.

Progress is hard to judge, though. Past studies used unlike sensors, actuators, setups, and scoring rules. Existing test suites lean on outside fluid solvers and lack full 3D or multi-agent support. The authors offer a plug-and-play benchmark to fix that. One setup lets rival methods be compared head to head.
arxiv-2601-15215:
Nicolas Gilliers and David Jekel mix the five classic forms of independence into one notion. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with non-commutative probability, where random quantities need not commute. They define joint independence for several algebras at once.

The pairwise relations between the algebras are coded by a bigraph. A bigraph is a graph with two sets of edges. Depending on the edges, each pair follows one of the five types: tensor, free, monotone, anti-monotone, or Boolean. The frame thus holds all five classic types in a single unified combinatorial structure.
arxiv-2601-15715:
Zhitao He, Zongwei Lyu, and Yi R. Fung study academic rebuttal as a persuasion game in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI now helps at many stages of research. Rebuttal, the reply to reviewers, remains underexplored. It is not a plain technical debate. Authors must persuade under severe information asymmetry. They do not know exactly what each reviewer thinks or values.

The title frames their approach: strategic persuasion via theory of mind. Theory of mind means modeling the other side's beliefs. A good rebuttal guesses what worries a reviewer and answers that. The paper's title, Dancing in Chains, hints at the constraints authors feel. For researchers, rebuttal skill can decide a paper's fate. A formal account of that skill could help both humans and AI assistants.
arxiv-2601-15915:
Chen Xu proposes a first-order method for hard optimization in a 2026 arXiv paper. The problem class is nonconvex optimization. The objective averages a function over data drawn from a distribution. Such problems sit under most machine learning training. Nonconvex landscapes have many traps: local minima and saddle points. First-order methods use only gradients, so they scale well. His method is Progressive Power Homotopy, or Prog-PowerHP.

Homotopy methods solve a hard problem by morphing an easy one into it. The progressive power idea shapes that morphing. A well-built path can steer gradients past traps. Training large models is a costly search through such terrain. Any first-order method with better navigation earns attention from practitioners and theorists alike.
arxiv-2601-16515:
Tongcheng Fang and coauthors make sparse gaze fast for video spread coders. Their 2026 preprint, named SALAD, deals with video build by spread steps. Coders for video use gaze to join frames in time. Full gaze costs much and slows each build step. Sparse gaze cuts cost but can drop grade if set by hand.

The team tunes straight gaze to act as sparse gaze with skill. Tune steps keep the grade of full gaze at low cost. Fast video builds then fit more gear and more use. Gains count for long clips and high res builds. The work joins gaze tricks in one tune path.
arxiv-2601-16615:
Xiang Chen sets out a fast edge vision model named AuroraEdge-V-2B. His 2026 preprint deals with models that join pics and words. Plants now seek such models for use on the shop floor. Shop gear needs fast, strong models that run on site kit. Big cloud models oft fail that need on speed and cost.

AuroraEdge aims to be both fast and strong on edge kit. Its size sits at the two B scale in the name. Tests check grade and speed on plant like tasks. A strong edge model could spread shop AI wide. The work frames edge use as the main design goal.
arxiv-2601-16715:
Adrick Tench and Thomas Demeester help health teams find cause links in data. True cause maps make health calls clear and sound. They let teams gauge what a drug or act will do. But dozens of cause-hunt tools crowd the field. No tool wins on all data types. Their 2026 preprint blends tools with expert help.

Their blend shifts weight among tools as proof comes in. A guide tool steers which tool to trust when. The mix aims to beat any lone tool's map. Sound cause maps shape care, trials, and health spend. This blend may spare teams the trap of a poor lone pick.
arxiv-2601-16815:
Shaoqing Wang and a team of six co-authors sharpen how apps pick what to show you. Shops and feeds must pick top picks from vast pools fast. Old picks lean on item-to-item links or twin tower nets. Those tools miss fine user-item sparks. They also cut lists in blunt, same-for-all ways. Their 2026 preprint builds a pick frame tuned to each user.

Their frame weighs item links with a user's own past acts. It aims to keep the picks apt at low cost. Sharp picks lift sales and user trust in apps. The work was shared at a top web meet in Dubai.
arxiv-2601-17315:
Xiaoyang Li and Runni Zhou present ClinNet, a tool to grade knee osteoarthritis from X-ray images. Grading is hard for three reasons. Grades differ by small signs. Human labels carry real doubt. And the grades form an order, from mild to severe. Most past tools treat the task as plain class choice. That misses the order and the doubt.

ClinNet uses evidential ordinal regression to keep both. It adds a check on left-right asymmetry in the knees. It also keeps a prototype memory of past cases. The mix aims for grades a clinician can trust. Better grading guides care for a joint disease that affects many older adults.
arxiv-2601-17515:
Rudraksh Sharma studies quantum phase transitions in the transverse-field Ising model. The model is a line of spins with two rival forces. One force aligns spins with each other. The other pulls them with a cross field. Their clash drives a quantum phase change. Sharma compares three ways to study the ground state and critical dynamics.

The ways are exact diagonalisation, variational quantum eigensolver runs, and quantum hardware runs. Each has known strengths and flaws. A side-by-side test shows where cheap methods hold up. It also shows where hardware noise breaks the picture. Such benchmarks guide quantum simulation at large. They tell labs what today's machines can prove.
arxiv-2601-17615:
Rahul Bera and co-authors present Athena, a system that joins two ways to hide memory delay. Prefetching loads data before it is needed. Off-chip prediction guesses if a load will miss the cache. Both fight the same delay from unlike angles. Athena synergizes them with online reinforcement learning. The learner adapts choices as the program runs.
