Step one maps the vessels in X-ray pictures with SCAR-UNet, a U-Net variant that uses spatial-coordinate attention. That attention sharpens thin, winding vessels and stands up to image noise. Vessel maps then yield center lines and branch points, which feed geometric reasoning about the vessel tree. The full method, named SCAR-UNet-GAT, aims at robot-aided heart procedures where flat pictures alone would leave the robot guessing at branches.
arxiv-2602-20515:
In long-context language model inference, prefill dominates compute because self-attention spans all input. Rakshith Jayanth and Viktor Prasanna note sparse attention cuts this cost by limiting each token's interactions. Sparsity varies by prompt and head, making prefill dynamic and memory-bound. That shift, plus GPU energy demands, motivates FPGAs.

FAST-Prefill is the first FPGA accelerator for dynamic sparse-attention prefill. A fused pipeline unit with memory-aware order generates sparse indices. A dual-tier cache cuts off-chip key-value cache traffic. A hybrid unit combines DSPs with bit-plane decomposition. Built on Alveo U280, it was tested on Llama and Qwen from four to one hundred twenty-eight thousand tokens. It runs time-to-first-token up to two and a half times faster. It is four and a half times more energy-efficient than an A5000 GPU.
arxiv-2602-20915:
Humanoid robots need grasps that suit the task after the grasp, not just grasps that hold. Dimitrios Dimou, Jose Santos-Victor, and Plinio Moreno build such a system in this 2026 arXiv paper. Using the ContactPose dataset's records of how people hold things, they build a hand-synergy model around a variational autoencoder that copies human grasping.

Reinforcement learning then trains an agent that grasps several objects while respecting distinct post-grasp intentions tied to each task. Combining human data with learning by exploration yields context-aware manipulation for collaboration in human-centered settings. The work moves robot grasping from holding objects toward using them as people intend.
arxiv-2602-21215:
Steering language models at inference time usually intervenes at every decoding step, which costs compute and drifts outputs from the model's nature. Runyi Hu and nine co-authors show dense intervention is unnecessary in this 2026 arXiv paper, proposing Sparse Inference-time Alignment. The method steers only at critical decision points, high-entropy junctions where misalignment risk concentrates.

Steering twenty to eighty percent of tokens gives superior alignment-efficiency trade-offs across model families and objectives. For strong base models, intervening on as few as twenty percent of tokens matches or beats heavily post-trained instruct models. Sparsity preserves the native distribution better, combines with search methods like Best-of-N, and cuts computational cost by up to six times.
arxiv-2602-21415:
Sunki Hong and one co-author benchmark five modern neural architectures for power grid forecasting. The set holds two state space models, two transformers, and a classic LSTM. Choosing well is hard because the best model depends on the data the operator actually has. They test hourly electricity demand across six diverse United States grids for horizons of 24 to 168 hours.

No single model wins everywhere. With load history alone, PatchTST and the state space models lead. Adding explicit weather data flips the ranking. iTransformer then gains accuracy three times more efficiently than PatchTST. PatchTST also leads on rhythmic solar signals. State space models handle chaotic wind and price swings better. The benchmark thus gives grid operators practical rules for picking an architecture to match their data.
arxiv-2602-21515:
Chengrui Qu and three co-authors train collaborative agents that generalize to new partners via strategic risk aversion. Many agentic paradigms require agents to collaborate with each other or with people toward shared goals. But learned policies often prove brittle, failing when paired with new partners.

The authors trace those failures to free-riding during training and a lack of strategic robustness. Strategically risk-averse players resist deviations in partner behavior by design. In collaborative games, they can also beat classical outcomes like Nash equilibria and show less or no free-riding. Inspired by that insight, the team builds a multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm that folds strategic risk aversion into standard policy optimization. Across collaborative benchmarks, including a language-model collaboration task, it achieves reliable collaboration with heterogeneous, previously unseen partners.
arxiv-2602-21915:
Jonathan Krook and four co-authors present a 2026 arXiv method for rebuilding varied protein shapes from frozen-sample electron microscope images. Each image shows one particle, but particles of the same protein can bend into different forms, which makes the rebuild hard. Their approach treats the protein backbone as a graph and trains a graph network to map clues from each image onto shifts from a starting shape.

The training goal pairs a physics-based model of how microscope images form with rules that keep the shape realistic, and it can also work out unknown particle angles. On test sets built from simulated motion paths, the graph network beat a plain network of similar size. The result is a case for building protein shape knowledge into the model, rather than letting a generic network learn it from scratch.
arxiv-2602-22115:
Neural networks decide everywhere, but explaining a single prediction with logic-based guarantees is costly: the logical constraints explode. Luiz Fernando Paulino Queiroz and two co-authors propose domain slicing, which trims the constraint set before explanations are generated. Slicing keeps only the domain slice relevant to the case at hand, shrinking the reasoning task.

In comparative experiments, slicing cut explanation time by up to two-fifths, a direct win for scalability in logic-based explanation. The approach keeps the correctness guarantees that make logic methods attractive, while making them fast enough to use. For teams that must justify model decisions, it offers explanations that are both rigorous and reachable.
arxiv-2602-22215:
Language models can brainstorm scientific ideas, but their suggestions often lack traceable sources or controllable academic context. Pengzhen Xie and Huizhi Liang build GYWI, a system that grounds idea generation in co-author knowledge graphs plus retrieval-augmented generation. An author-centered graph and inspiration-sampling algorithms assemble an external knowledge base for the model to draw on.

A hybrid retrieval mechanism mixes graph and text retrieval for both depth and breadth, and a prompt-optimization strategy steers outputs with reinforcement-learning principles. The result is idea generation with a visible trail: users can see where inspirations came from and steer the context. For researchers, it turns brainstorming from a black box into a traceable process.
arxiv-2602-22315:
Many-body quantum systems whose interactions follow a graph's connections form a rich but scattered landscape. Nilanjan Sasmal and Adolfo del Campo introduce a family where distinguishable continuous-variable particles interact according to a graph's adjacency matrix. Their ground states take a generalized Jastrow form, built from pair-correlation functions over the graph's edges.

When the graph is complete, the systems describe quantum fluids with proper permutation symmetry; in general they generalize spin systems on graphs with broken permutation symmetry. The parent Hamiltonian mixes two-body terms from adjacency with three-body terms over two-step paths. Using graph theory, the authors chart the landscape, recovering known models and adding many new ground-state solvable examples.
arxiv-2602-22515:
A February 2026 arXiv paper by Shailesh Chandrasekharan builds simplified models of gauge forces, the forces that bind particles, using qubits on a lattice. The models use a monomer-dimer-tensor-network basis and avoid the sign problem in the pure gauge sector, a snag that often blocks simulation. They produce both confined phases, where particles stay bound, and deconfined phases, where they move freely.

Classical Monte Carlo runs at finite temperature show phase changes matching the expected universality classes of standard SU(N) lattice gauge theories across spacetime dimensions. Chandrasekharan argues that second-order quantum transitions between the two phases likely exist. Such points could give a route to continuum limits, letting Yang-Mills theory emerge from finite lattice builds.
arxiv-2602-22715:
Sougato Bose and one co-author find a strange twist on gravity's pull. A localized source mass draws a probe mass toward it, as usual. But when the source sits in a quantum superposition of distinct places, and the probe interacts with it, postselection changes the story.

Conditional on detecting the source in one specific state, the probe is found moving away, a repulsion effect. The team traces it to an anomalous negative weak value, a quirk of quantum measurement. They read the effect as a sign that spacetime itself can sit in quantum superposition, and they sketch a possible test using spin-bearing nanocrystals.
arxiv-2602-23015:
K. Pouilly and one co-author map magnet-led infall onto the primary star of DF Tau, a young binary where only the primary gathers. Infall governs mass buildup, angular spin transfer, and planet-forming disk shaping. For single standard T Tauri stars the picture is clear: a strong dipolar field cuts off the disk and funnels matter onto the surface.

Whether that picture survives a non-accreting companion was open. Using high-resolution light-pattern time series from ESPaDOnS, the team tracks emission-line shifts, veiling, and magnet shape. They conclude the DF Tau primary undergoes typical magnet-led infall, with a strong dipolar field driving an infall shock. The two stars differ notably in magnet shape, hinting that infall, or capture of the secondary, shapes field growth.
arxiv-2602-23115:
David Dirnfeld and three co-authors estimate camera heading in real time with FLIGHT, a Fibonacci lattice method. Estimating camera motion from monocular video is fundamental to SLAM, visual odometry, and structure-from-motion. Heading recovery under known rotation often loses accuracy or grows expensive as noise and outliers increase. Their method generalizes the Hough transform on the unit sphere to estimate heading.

Correspondences between two frames generate a great circle of directions compatible with each pair. Discretizing the unit sphere with a Fibonacci lattice as bin centres lets each great circle vote for a range of directions. Features unaffected by noise or dynamic objects then vote consistently for the correct motion direction. Tests on three datasets place the method on the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus efficiency, and SLAM tests show reduced root-mean-square error by correcting heading during camera pose initialization.
arxiv-2602-23415:
Gavilan and five co-authors define a new class of astrophysical sources: black hole scalar sirens in the Milky Way. Hypothetical light scalars trigger superradiant instability around spinning black holes, growing scalar clouds. With strong enough particle self-interactions, scalars are ejected from black hole orbits as coherent, non-relativistic emissions draining the black hole's angular momentum.

For some settings, cloud growth far outpaces loss over the Galaxy's age, so these holes emit scalars forever. The authors compute the scalar background from roughly one hundred million isolated stellar-mass black holes, sirens for scalars of mass ten to the minus thirteen to ten to the minus eleven electronvolts. Signals run up to two orders of magnitude above those from a misaligned cosmic scalar, with a broader, faster spectrum than virialized dark matter. The spectrum encodes black hole mass and spin, and scalar signals probe otherwise unseen lone black holes.
arxiv-2602-23515:
Edan T. Marcial and three co-authors test twelve pretrained universal machine learning potentials on global optimization of inorganic crystal structures. These potentials are reshaping atom-based simulation, but global optimization is demanding. Free exploration probes motifs absent from reference sets.

In free evolutionary searches, the authors ask whether the models can steadily predict complex nonmagnetic crystal ground states at ambient pressure across varied inorganic systems. Scores span a wide range, from near ab initio accuracy to nearly useless, in sorting competing phases within low-energy basins. Extra tests on hcp-Zn, MB4 compounds, and LiBy show several models catch fine energy gaps from subtle electronic structure traits.
arxiv-2603-00015: Yue, Ren and Gao give two conditions that suffice for an additively idempotent semiring to lack a finite basis for its identities. Two specific four-element cases, whose sums form chains, meet those tests and so have no finite basis. The gap between their varieties holds continuum-many kinds. The join of two finite-basis kinds therefore need not be finite-basis. They also give the smallest example of a finite-basis semiring whose one-element add-on is not.
arxiv-2603-00315: Gomes and colleagues show that a carbon nanoribbon built from four-, five-, six-, and eight-membered rings is more than a graphene variant. Its broken-symmetry lattice makes topology a design tool for many properties. Their multiscale modelling finds a robust semiconducting state with a gap above one electronvolt. Strain-tunable bands, high stiffness, fracture set by the largest rings, suppressed heat flow, and strong visible absorption follow from the same lattice. Topology thus couples elasticity, electronics, heat transport, and optics in one platform.
arxiv-2603-00415: Mohammadi and eight colleagues review energy storage for linking AI data centres to the power grid, where fast shifting loads strain reliability. Their survey sorts storage into four layers, from chip buffers through rack and facility backup to grid scale batteries, plus fuel cells and heat storage. AI load swings far faster than classic loads, so standard dispatch rules fall short, and coordinated storage across layers becomes essential. Gaps remain in simulation, wear modelling, load forecasting, and sizing across layers.
arxiv-2603-01515:
Building a 3D mesh one point at a time makes long lists that cost a lot to generate. Hanxiao Wang, Yuan-Chen Guo, Ying-Tian Liu, and colleagues rethink that order in this 2026 work. They argue the flaw is the unit: a mesh is made of faces, not lone points.

Their system, FACE, treats each triangle face as a single token for the generator. That one choice cuts the list length by a factor of nine and beats prior compression by half. A strong encoder reads point clouds into a compact code that the face decoder then expands. Tests show top rebuild quality on standard sets, and a diffusion model on the same code turns one image into a detailed mesh. The result lowers the cost of quality 3D content.
arxiv-2603-02015:
Amir Asiaee, Zhuohui Liang, and Chao Yan wrap synthetic data generators with causal rules they cannot break. Their 2026 work notes that generators match observed patterns well, yet warp the causal structure beneath them. Causal uses like treatment effects and policy tests need that structure preserved above raw fit.

Their wrapper, CausalWrap, takes partial causal knowledge as trusted edges, banned edges, and monotonic rules. It needs no access inside the base generator, whether that base is adversarial, variational, or diffusion based. A light correction map, trained with causal penalties, adjusts samples after generation. Tests span simulated causal models, semi-synthetic benchmarks, and a real intensive care cohort. Treatment effect errors fall sharply while ordinary utility largely holds, which makes synthetic data safer for causal work.
arxiv-2603-02115:
Anthony Liang, Yigit Korkmaz, Jiahui Zhang, and colleagues address robot training in this 2026 paper. Robots learn faster when a reward model grades each step of a task. Grading single frames from expert demos works, but real data holds many failed tries with no clear grades. Their system, Robometer, learns from both kinds of data.

Robometer mixes two lessons: frame grades on expert runs, and whole-run rankings across runs. Ranking tells the model which full try was better, even for failed ones. Training used a new set of over one million runs from many robots and tasks. In tests, its rewards held up better than prior methods. Downstream robot learning improved across many tasks as well.
arxiv-2603-02215:
Ran Li, Shimin Di, Haowei Li, and colleagues train a small chemistry model in this 2026 paper. Predicting how chemicals react helps plan new drugs and syntheses. Large models chase scale, yet they often miss basic chemical sense. The core gap, the authors argue, is chemical insight, not size.

Their model, RxnNano, has only half a billion parameters, far fewer than rivals. Training moves in stages, from basic syntax up to deeper chemical thought. A new goal keeps reactions reversible and physically sound as points move in a latent space. A further rule forces the model to learn atom links that stay fixed under relabeling. On strict tests, RxnNano beat models ten times its size by a clear margin.
arxiv-2603-03315:
Stefano De Giorgis and two colleagues build a test for whether machines truly understand memes. Memes mix image and text, lean on shared background knowledge, and can carry toxic meaning in subtle ways. Earlier tools each read one layer: the words, the pictured objects, the emotion, or a hate-speech score. Their 2026 work assembles the layers into one framework.

Ten dimensions guide the reading of a meme, from its text and scene to its intent, target community, and toxicity. From that framework the team generated a benchmark of more than six hundred question-answer pairs covering just over three hundred memes. Eight open-source language models took the test. Models with instruction tuning and reasoning skills did best, though questions needing pragmatic inference stayed hard for all.
arxiv-2603-03415:
Mingyu Jin and three others find a simple pattern in how language models handle unfamiliar inputs. As tasks drift further from training territory, through harder reasoning, longer contexts, or extra answer choices, the model's final internal representations grow sparser. Fewer units carry the signal. Their 2026 study measures this shift across many models and domains and finds it consistent and quantifiable.

Controlled analyses argue the sparsity is no accident. It works as an adaptive mechanism, concentrating computation into specialized subspaces to stabilize reasoning under strain. A learning-dynamics account supports that reading. The team then turns the effect into a tool: a curriculum method that uses measured sparsity to schedule practice cases in context. That scheduling brought considerable performance gains, and the code is public.
arxiv-2603-03515:
Subramanyam Sahoo builds a control plan for military AI agents. Agentic systems interpret goals, model the world, plan, use tools, and coordinate over long horizons. Each capability breeds control failures that older safety frameworks miss. His 2026 paper names six such control failures and shows how they erode real human control in military settings, the field's stated goal.

The proposed approach organizes defenses in three pillars: preventive, detective, and corrective control. Its core instrument is a Control Quality Score, a combined real-time metric that puts a number on how much control humans actually hold. As the score weakens, graduated responses kick in. Every failure type gets concrete mechanisms, assigned duties across five bodies, and formal scoring metrics. A worked operational scenario shows the machinery in action.
arxiv-2603-03715:
Lucía Gómez-Cruz and sixteen colleagues show that a magnetic wire's shape can postpone its own speed limit. Domain walls race through magnetic materials during magnetization reversal, but past a threshold drive their speed collapses, the Walker breakdown. A few material tricks delay that collapse by raising the barrier against internal precession. Their 2026 study finds the delay built into topology itself, in a three-dimensional nanomagnet with vortex-state domains.

An exchange-spring effect, neighboring magnetization twisting like a spring, intrinsically and robustly holds off the breakdown. Curvature adds a striking asymmetry. Whether the breakdown is delayed depends on the match between the azimuthal domain's handedness and the wall's direction of travel: one pairing is protected, the other is not. The work speaks to future racetrack-style magnetic devices that move domain walls as data.
arxiv-2603-04015: Ito and Tatsuta settle the logical complexity of infinite-descent proofs for inductive definitions. Formal thought about inductively defined relations matters for program checks, yet the logical complexity of CLKID-omega and LKID-omega has been little studied. The argument equates validity for inductive definitions in standard models with validity in standard term models, then extends Girard's omega-language truth predicate via arithmetical coding.
arxiv-2603-04115: Wang and others propose TextBoost, boosting scene text fidelity in ultra-low bitrate compression. Keeping small-font scene text legible while keeping overall quality is critical, and text-prioritizing allocation often degrades global fidelity. Instead of region coding, TextBoost adds auxiliary OCR text with negligible overhead for decoder meaning guidance. Three designs implement this: filtering OCR outputs into a guidance map, fusing guidance with decoder traits, and requiring guidance-steady rebuilding via a regularizing loss. Experiments show about 61% higher text-recognition F1 at comparable quality and bitrate.
arxiv-2603-04215: Elkaïoum M. Moutuou presents graphs as focal contact systems in higher-order motion. In this view, hypergraphs extend graph neighbourhoods by permitting arbitrary contact domains with no distinguished focal node. This view also clarifies how graph and hypergraph dynamic models relate. Although sufficiently general graph node functions can reproduce higher-order contact motion, that dynamic match does not entail a match of core contact forms.
arxiv-2603-04315: Wu and colleagues count communities in networks without fitting a model. Block models describe community structure, but counting communities is hard when networks are sparse and counts grow. Their spectral method uses eigengap ratios, needs no tuning, and skips distribution parameters. Its statistic follows a Tracy-Widom limit under the null and gains power under weak alternatives. Dense and sparse simulations plus three real cases confirm it works.
arxiv-2603-04515: Da Conceicao and colleagues map heat pattern of finite Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains. At fixed temperature and chemical potential, canonical and grand canonical ensembles yield energy, particle number, entropy, and heat capacity. Heat capacity shows a double peak anomaly for non-dimerized chains, two maxima split by a minimum. The authors read this as a Schottky type crossover from two energy scales, strongest when chemical potential nears the band scale. Maxima separate further with asymmetry and length, while bulk behaviour stays tunable through hopping ratio despite boundary set topology.
arxiv-2603-04615: Chen derives a quantum Cramér-Rao bound on quantum metric as a multi-observable uncertainty rule. One version of the bound caps operator covariance by value derivatives times the inverse quantum metric. Quantum metric is the covariance of shift generators in parameter space, so at any size it is capped by Berry curvature times itself. In the two-way case it recovers the Robertson-Schrödinger uncertainty relation. Spin and momentum space quantum metric of topological insulators under magnetic field show the three-way version.
arxiv-2603-04915: Justin Wang and colleagues introduce EVMbench, a benchmark testing whether AI agents can detect, patch, and exploit vulnerabilities in smart contracts on public blockchains. Built from 117 curated vulnerabilities across 40 repositories, it grades agents on tests and blockchain state inside a local Ethereum environment. Frontier agents proved able to find and exploit vulnerabilities in live blockchain instances from end to end. The team releases code, tasks, and tooling for continued measurement of agent security capabilities and risks.
arxiv-2603-05215: Éabha Power and colleagues compare signatures across solar active regions at different stages in full-disk IRIS spectroheliograms. Coronal composition, tracked by first ionization potential bias, is thought to arise from a chromospheric ponderomotive force separating ionized from neutral plasma. Comparing Mg II, C II, and Si IV lines, they find no stage variability in C II and Si IV. Distinct differences emerge through the Mg II k/h ratio, a proxy for plasma opacity. Highest-bias regions show double-peaked opacity distributions, suggesting variable density affecting wave propagation.
arxiv-2603-05615: Wang and team name the I10 donor in ZnO as a Sn-Li combo. Careful making joins ion planting, heating, light tests, and basic math. Two-laser in-step group trapping shows an electron-119Sn hyperfine interaction of 392 ± 15 MHz. That shows a coupled electron and nuclear spin-1/2 pair whose hyperfine coupling ranks among the largest seen for shallow donors. DFT shows a nearest-neighbor SnZn-LiZn combo with good energy, donor nature, and a hyperfine interaction matching experiment.
arxiv-2603-05715: Islam and team look into Ir swap in a trimer-based ruthenate. Neutron patterns show Ir doping preserves the parent zigzag AFM structure. Moments reside only on two outer Ru(2) sites of each trimer, while the Ru(1) site remains non-magnet. Upon 8% Ir swap, the Néel heat falls to 84.0 K. Response shows a Curie-like upturn, showing para spins living with AFM order. Math places Ir mostly on the central Ru(1) site, breaking the molecule-orbit network, and models match the suppressed order heat and joint life.
arxiv-2603-05815: Kim and colleagues present HiLAM, a hierarchical model of latent actions that uncovers skills hidden in actionless video. Existing latent action models focus on short-horizon frame transitions and low-level motion, missing longer-term temporal structure. Yet actionless videos often contain temporally extended, high-level skills. HiLAM uses a pretrained latent action model as a low-level extractor, aggregating latent action sequences into high-level skills. Experiments show it beating the baseline with robust dynamic skill discovery.
arxiv-2603-06015: Xu and Zhang build new simple weight modules over twisted Heisenberg-Virasoro and gap-p Virasoro algebras, starting from restricted modules over one positive-part subalgebra. These modules are new. In particular, at p equals 2, gap-p Virasoro becomes mirror Heisenberg-Virasoro, and the authors obtain many new simple weight modules there.
arxiv-2603-06115: Kunz, Kraft, Breitbach, Pfeifer, Küß, Glamsch, Albrecht, and Weiler use a phase-resolved optical method to study spin waves driven by surface sound waves through tuned magnet-springy coupling. A piezo lithium Ta base carries finger senders for sound firing, mixing with spin waves in a Co40Fe40B20 wave guide only 5 nm thick and 20 µm wide. Phase-locked micro-focused polar spotting splits sound and spin-wave signals by their typical polar link. The readings straight image the tuned, in-step firing of spin waves by surface sound waves.
arxiv-2603-06215: Goyal and colleagues present curated size measurements for 2002 multiple component radio AGNs in the ROGUE I catalog, spanning about 5 to 1100 arcseconds in total angular size. Those sizes translate to projected linear sizes near 10 kiloparsecs to 2 megaparsecs. About 10 percent are compact, near 3 percent are giant radio sources, and roughly 34 percent associate with galaxy clusters. Cluster association rates look comparable across Fanaroff-Riley I, II, and hybrid classes. Arm length asymmetries run similarly in FR I and hybrid classes but far less often in FR II, suggesting steadier FR II jets.
arxiv-2603-06715: Chinthaka Weerarathna and colleagues model frogeye leaf spot in soybean with a network that mirrors real field layout, unlike mass-action models that assume uniform mixing. Fitting the model with approximate Bayesian computation, they find that where infection starts can shift which spread routes dominate. Tillage and no-tillage plots show no clear gap in spread, decay, or severity. Early, targeted removal of sick plants beats late or random removal.
arxiv-2603-07415: Cheng explains catastrophic forgetting in continual learning through context channel capacity. Zero forgetting demands that capacity at least match task entropy, the paper proves. An impossibility triangle blocks zero forgetting, online learning and finite size all at once for stepwise state learners. HyperNetworks dodge the triangle by rebuilding weights as function values. Tests across eight methods back the link to forgetting, and a probing plan measures it in practice.
arxiv-2603-07815: Sun and colleagues present HybridStitch, a training-free framework using token-level feedback to select each adopted update's model. Stepwise diffusion generation needs varying model power at varying token spots, unlike prior mixes using cleaning step or drafting role. Ongoing image polish and discrete language choice share a state, while KV buffers provide context for picked queries. HybridStitch hits over 1.6 times faster image making and higher diffusion language model throughput. Decode query cost falls by about half to two-thirds at similar quality.
arxiv-2603-07915: Yang and colleagues cut the cost of thinking agents, whose long chains buy accuracy at heavy expense. Fixed reasoning levels waste effort: always-low modes degrade performance, while random switching saves little. Ares instead picks a reasoning level per step, saving high effort for hard moves and little for easy ones. A router reads the interaction history and predicts the lowest level each step needs. Across tool-use, deep-research, and web-agent benchmarks, Ares cut token use by up to about 53 percent with minimal loss in task success.
arxiv-2603-08115: Sisourat models Intermolecular Coulombic Electron Capture in water with a semiclassical approach built on molecular dynamics simulations using OpenMM. The study tracks an excess electron in the presence of iron cations in water, asking how electron energy and cation concentration shape the ICEC quantum yield. Simulations show the yield nears unity at higher concentrations and higher initial electron energies, while it falls at lower concentrations as the electron loses energy before reaching a cation. The work links capture efficiency to the race between energy loss and arrival.
arxiv-2603-08315: The ATLAS team search for charginos and tau-sleptons decaying into missing transverse momentum, one jet, and a disappearing track, using 137 inverse femtobarns from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions in ATLAS Run 2. Search regions demand a track built from three or four innermost-layer measurements. Three-measurement tracks split on whether a charged pion, found with a dedicated algorithm, is present. Backgrounds are estimated and no significant excess appears. Mass limits reach 225 GeV for pure-higgsino charginos at short lifetimes, 880 GeV for wino charginos near 1 ns, and 320 GeV for tau-sleptons.
arxiv-2603-08615: Vincent Cohen-Addad and colleagues shrink the chatter needed to cluster data spread over many sites. In the coordinator setup, their protocol builds a near-perfect coreset without shipping raw point coordinates in the clear. In the blackboard setup, the chatter falls further, and both routes match the best known offline costs and lower bounds up to small log factors.
arxiv-2603-08715: Luca Collini and colleagues map how language models and prompts interact in Verilog code generation. They test small and large models, general and specialized, under a controlled factorial design across prompts, structured outputs, rewrites, chain-of-thought, in-context learning, and evolutionary tuning. The study finds which model-prompt patterns hold across two benchmarks and which stay tied to one pairing.
arxiv-2603-09015: Neige Frankel and colleagues summarize a workshop on the Gaia phase spiral. The spiral, a signal in stars' vertical motion found in 2018, reveals how far the Galactic disk sits from equilibrium. Workshop participants reviewed current knowledge, open questions, and key areas for understanding the spiral's origin and the disk's response to perturbations, and the paper shares resources and invites new collaborators.
arxiv-2603-09115: Alexey A. Kryukov derives Newtonian motion for a large particle from the linear Schrödinger equation, with an added random Hamiltonian of Gaussian unitary type. That random part stands in for contact with the surroundings. He shows that the state-space random walk this creates, plus grouping states that experiments cannot tell apart, explains why tiny and large systems behave so differently. The work extends an earlier derivation of the Born rule for microscopic particles.
arxiv-2603-09215: Hsiao-Ying Huang and colleagues speed up spoken language models that alternate between text and speech tokens, where full-depth decoding of long speech runs is costly. Their SPAR-K scheme lets most speech positions exit at a fixed middle layer, with periodic full-depth refresh steps to curb drift. Confidence-based exits, popular for text models, prove suboptimal here. Across two models and four datasets question-answering accuracy barely drops while average speech decoding depth falls notably.
arxiv-2603-09615: Yu Cheng and colleagues use the dense circumstellar medium around core-collapse supernovae as a probe for feebly interacting particles. Born in the protoneutron star, such particles can decay inside that medium before shock breakout and dump visible energy there. The medium heats and ionizes, forming an induced photosphere that emits a distinctive precursor blackbody signal. Early data on supernova 2023ixf show no excess precursor light, giving strong new limits on MeV-scale dark photons.
arxiv-2603-09715: Peng Sun and colleagues ask whether a training sample really forces a vision language model to use the picture. Their CVS method, which needs no training, compares how a frozen model rates an answer with and without the question attached. Samples whose scores shift most are kept, while clashes are dropped. On two data sets, a small kept share beats training on all data.
arxiv-2603-10015: Mengesha argues that top AI safety rules focus on stop gaps and neglect joint action when stop gaps fail. Tests of skill, gates on use, and limits on use dominate, while shared response skill gets little cash or care. The gap is built in, he says, since wide gains from strong shared response spread far while costs land on single firms. Borrowing from nuclear safety and plague plans, he urges set pledges, shared rules and advance swaps of if then response plans.
arxiv-2603-10115: Albayrak and Vachaspati run numeric scattering tests of global vortex birth when the scatterer and vortex fields meet only through a quantum middle field. Their flat setup, in two space plus one time dimensions, couples a complex field that supports vortices and a real field scatterer to one quantum field. Scattering fast Gaussian wavepackets across the space of settings, they find vortex antivortex pairs appear in scattered pockets, a chaotic pattern with holes.
arxiv-2603-10915: Kazunori Nakayama asks about extra fields in gravity. These fields appear when gravity's metric and connection are treated as independent. In the most general setup, torsion and non-metricity add many possible fields. Nearly all of them are non-dynamical or very heavy. So general relativity returns at low energy. Nakayama finds one exception. It is a naturally light distortion field. It can be vector-like or scalar-like. The scalar version mixes with the Higgs boson.
arxiv-2603-11015: Serat Saad and Yuan-Sen Ting reanalyze the wide-binary dataset behind a recent claim of anomalous gravity at low accelerations. The claimed boost was said to match modified Newtonian dynamics. Their hierarchical Bayesian model fits three-dimensional orbital elements for all systems at once. It infers a single global gravity factor, which lands on the Newtonian value. A test mimicking the original approach, using a geometric de-projection instead, reproduces the anomalous value. This pinpoints the modeling choice as the source of the discrepancy.
arxiv-2603-11215: Maude Gull and coauthors census the massive main-sequence stars of Sextans A, a metal-poor dwarf galaxy. They fit photometry from the near-ultraviolet to the near-infrared, star by star. A Bayesian tool infers temperatures, luminosities, and initial masses. It yields 867 massive main-sequence candidates. Their parameters agree with existing spectra. The team flags hundreds of candidate OBe stars. It flags dozens of OB associations, isolated massive stars, and runaway candidates. It predicts efficient leakage of ionizing photons across star-forming regions.
arxiv-2603-11415: Iyer and Caragea offer BLooP, a decoding trick that helps language models write fuller, more faithful summaries. Models asked to summarize with no training often drop key points or add stray ones. BLooP nudges each next token toward pairs of words that occur in the source text. A hash table check at each step does the work, with no training or model changes. Human raters found the summaries more faithful at no cost to readability, across four data sets and three models.
arxiv-2603-11515: Menon and co-authors present MADA, a multi-agent framework that automates design exploration on supercomputers. Science problems, from fusion to new materials, demand searches over huge design spaces. MADA pairs a language model with agents that each own one job. A job agent launches ensemble runs, a geometry agent builds meshes, and an inverse design agent proposes new designs. The test bed is Richtmyer-Meshkov instability suppression, a fusion challenge. MADA refines designs toward the best suppression on its own, in both live simulation and surrogate settings.
arxiv-2603-11815: Lee and co-authors test how far baryon correction models can be trusted for weak lensing. Such models reshape halo profiles in dark matter-only runs, tuned to full hydro runs. The team swaps in hydro regions around halos of falling mass, out to five virial radii, and checks many statistics. Swapping all halos above a trillion solar masses recovers about 90% of the baryon suppression in the power spectra. The rest comes from smaller halos or matter farther out. Peaks, they add, care mostly about the cores of massive halos.
arxiv-2603-12015: Schmidt and co-authors present Flowcean, a framework that learns models of cyber-physical systems from data. Building such models by hand is slow, since these systems mix software, sensors, and moving parts. Flowcean wraps the full task in a modular design that users can adapt. It offers varied learning strategies, data handling steps, and scoring metrics in one place. The design also lets teams plug in diverse learning libraries and tools with little friction.
arxiv-2603-12515: Van Loon, Rugenstein, Zelinka, and Andrews track how Earth's global radiative feedback has changed of late. The feedback parameter sets climate stability but shifts as warming patterns change. A neural network trained on model runs is applied to temperature records through 2025. The feedback reached peak stability in the mid 1990s, near minus three watts per square meter per kelvin. It has since weakened to about minus two, a shift not explained by ENSO or Pacific decadal swings. Warming in the subtropical Northeast Pacific is a key driver.
arxiv-2603-12815: Sravan Vuyyuru and co-authors design beyond-diagonal reconfigurable surfaces with directly tunable non-local response. Strong non-locality once needed dense subwavelength structuring with diagonal loads, which left little control. Their co-simulation joins antenna characterization with circuit models of cascaded load networks. Loads become non-diagonal, which adds design freedom. Wide-angle anomalous reflectors built this way reach far higher reflection efficiency at the same element density. Or, for a set target, far fewer elements are needed.
arxiv-2603-13115: Jie Ji and co-authors cut the cost of sharpness-aware training for sparse neural networks. Sparse models save memory and compute, yet their gradient signals turn noisy at high sparsity. That noise hurts convergence and generalization in practice. Their ZO-SAM mixes zero-order estimates into the SAM update, so only one backpropagation step runs per perturbation. Gradient variance drops, and the flat minima that SAM seeks still guide training. Models also held up better under distribution shift.
arxiv-2603-13215: Ziqi Ma, Mengzhan Liufu, and Georgia Gkioxari test whether video world models let unseen processes keep evolving. Water pours and ice melts whether or not anyone watches, they note. Their STEVO-Bench hides processes with occluders, darkness, or camera lookaway paths. Models are then scored on how the hidden state changes over time. The tests expose limits in how current models separate state evolution from observation. The authors trace some of these failures to data and architecture bias.
arxiv-2603-13515: M. Ebrahimi and co-authors overcome a material limit on magnon coupling through cavity feedback. Magnons are spin wave quanta with strong potential, but weak magnon-phonon coupling and wide linewidths kept magnonic spheres in the weak-coupling regime. Their active microwave feedback loop suppresses the linewidth of cavity-magnon polaritons below the magnon-limited value. That raises polariton-phonon cooperativity from 1 to 150 in their system. They also achieve normal-mode splitting between a cavity-magnon polariton and a mechanical mode.
arxiv-2603-13915: Mukherjee studies partition statistics that mix parity rules with the excludant, the smallest missing part size. The setting counts partitions where parts of the same parity are distinct. With q-series transformations, the generating functions link to quantum modular forms tied to Ramanujan and to a Nahm-type sum from Andrews. Tauberian methods then give asymptotic formulas for these sequences. The work ties a counting problem in partitions to deep objects in modular form theory.
arxiv-2603-14015: Nichele and Benatti use a collisional model to study quantum dynamical entropy and memory effects in open systems. Watching only the open system hides how it and its environment act together. Multi-time correlations fix that gap and ground the Alicki-Lindblad-Fannes entropy. In their model, a finite-level system couples to an endless classical spin chain. The entropy can then be computed in closed form. It depends on the statistical traits of the environment and links to when memory effects switch on.
arxiv-2603-14515: Gao and co-authors speed up neural wave functions for excited quantum states. Monte Carlo overlap checks grow costly as more states are added. Their fix, Multi-State Importance Sampling, reuses samples from all states at once. A new architecture, Excited Pfaffians, evaluates many states in one network. On the carbon dimer, training runs over 200 times faster than a standard rival. The method also finds all distinct energy levels of the beryllium atom. One wave function can span states across molecules, they show.
arxiv-2603-14615: Meunier, Nourine and Vilmin characterize optimum implicational bases of convex geometries via new hypergraphs. Shrinking the premises and conclusions of a base is hard in general. Their quasi-closed hypergraphs capture what optimum bases look like. When the edges of each such hypergraph stay disjoint, known algorithms optimize any base in polynomial time. The condition covers double-shelling, acyclic, affine and acceptant geometries. Old tractability results for the first three classes fall under one roof.
arxiv-2603-14715: Abbas, Azzouz, Agarwal and Torres build fractional Sobolev spaces on arbitrary time scales. Their Gagliardo-style frame rests on the Lebesgue Delta-measure. A nonlocal seminorm over an off-diagonal interaction domain sets the regularity. The spaces differ in kind from derivative-based versions in past work. They prove the spaces are Banach in all allowed cases. Reflexivity holds in the strict exponent range, and the quadratic case is Hilbert. A sharp test tells when the construction stays nontrivial on bounded time scales.
arxiv-2603-15015: Calo-Blanco studies bilateral claims problems, where gains or losses must be split under lower and upper exclusion thresholds. He defines the exclusion dilation operator, which first handles the thresholds and then spreads what remains through a stretched version of a standard rule. He characterizes the operator with axioms and checks which fairness properties survive. Homogeneity and monotonicity are kept, while order preservation is dropped on purpose. The method suits settings where legal or policy reasons break symmetry.
arxiv-2603-15315: Yi compares two diagnostics of quantum chaos in the mixed-field Ising chain: quantum Liang information flow and the out-of-time-order correlator. Early growth and wavefront speed of the information flow look the same for integrable and chaotic settings. Its strength swings across four orders of magnitude with the starting state. The time-integrated flow tells the tales apart at late times. It grows steadily in chaotic systems but flattens or oscillates in integrable ones. Yi presents it as a partner probe to the correlator.
arxiv-2603-15415: Xie and co-authors present AnyCrowd, a video generation framework that animates many characters without mixing up their identities. Crowds often suffer identity bleeding, where faces and traits swap between people. Each character is encoded alone in its own latent block before the diffusion transformer runs. A three-stage attention scheme then binds each identity to its driving pose. A gated fusion module resolves clashes where characters overlap. The design scales to any crowd size while keeping each person's look stable across the clip.
arxiv-2603-15615: Li, Teng, and Wang argue that language models blur moral categories inside their representations. They call this state moral indifference. The team built 251,000 moral vectors from Prototype Theory and the Social-Chemistry-101 dataset. Tests across 23 models show weak gaps between opposed moral classes. Scaling, architecture, and alignment training do not fix the blur. With sparse autoencoders on Qwen3-8B, they isolate moral features and rebuild their links. The fix lifts moral reasoning and wins 75 percent of paired tests on the Flames benchmark.
arxiv-2603-16815: Marik, Saha, and Chatterjee judge forecasting models by what they cost a supply chain, not just by forecast error. They build a pipeline that joins forecasting with inventory simulation. Seven methods are tested on the M5 Walmart dataset, from classic statistical models to machine learning and deep sequence models. The tests use one- and two-level newsvendor systems. The authors report that Temporal CNN and LSTM models cut inventory costs and raised fill rates over statistical baselines. Checks for sensitivity support the findings at larger scale.
arxiv-2603-16915: Vacaru surveys Finsler type geometric flow and modified gravity theories built over seventy years. Such theories differ in their generating functions, metric and nonmetric structures, and connections. In several past approaches, the field equations were not fully defined in geometric terms, or covered only narrow models. Vacaru reports progress toward a unified treatment. The new results cover Finsler-Lagrange-Hamilton geometric flows and gravity on tangent and cotangent Lorentz bundles. The theories are built in axiomatic form as nontrivial modifications of Einstein gravity. Historical remarks place each step in context.
arxiv-2603-17215: Park and co-authors show that spontaneous polarization in 3R stacked MoS2 bilayers suppresses exciton-exciton annihilation. Rapid annihilation blocks the high density exciton regimes that efficient optoelectronics need. In 3R bilayers, interlayer excitons are polarized by the stacking's built in polarization, so they repel each other. With ultrafast pump probe spectroscopy, the team measured an annihilation rate about 18 times smaller than in monolayers and about 3 times smaller than in nonpolar 2H bilayers. A rate limited model with dipole repulsion matches the data.
arxiv-2603-17615: Yang turns scatter in a radio relation into a probe of fast radio burst surroundings. Some repeaters pair with persistent radio sources whose brightness tracks rotation measure. The spread around that link carries news about how the nebula grows over time. He derives a scaling law and tests it on five known systems. The joint index lands at 1.5, plus or minus 0.8. Future surveys can sort source types with it, he argues.
arxiv-2603-17715: Niehorster and Nyström test SAM3 against SAM2 for eye image segmentation. Earlier work showed vision foundation models segment eye images well with no training. SAM3 adds a new concept prompting mode driven by text. Lab videos and the wild TEyeD set form the test bed. In most cases SAM3 matched or trailed SAM2, they find. SAM2 also ran faster. Their verdict keeps SAM2 as the best pick for this task.
arxiv-2603-17915: Pattnayak and Chowdhuri release IndicSafe, a safety benchmark for twelve Indic languages. These tongues serve over 1.2 billion people yet sit thin in training data. Six thousand prompts, grounded in local culture, span caste, religion, gender, health, and politics. Ten leading models show wide safety drift across tongues, they find. Cross-language agreement reached just 12.8 percent. Some models over-refuse harmless text while others miss real harm.
arxiv-2603-18015: Dhara and Sheth probe a harmful content classifier with two explanation tools, SHAP and Integrated Gradients. The RoBERTa model scores 0.93 AUC and 0.94 accuracy on Civil Comments. Yet the two tools point to quite different cues for the same calls. Case studies show weak spots: indirect toxicity, over-weight on single words, and political speech. They argue explanations help human moderators most as a diagnostic and transparency aid.
arxiv-2603-18115: Wang and co-authors present Grace Cycle, a framework that uses LLMs to sort Long Covid cases into types. It loops through idea making, fact pulling, and trait tuning on patient data tracked over time. From 13,511 people, it finds three groups: Protected, Responder, and Refractory. The groups split well on worst symptom load, starting health load, and dose response trends. The team notes the method works for other diseases too and gives groups that doctors can read with ease.
arxiv-2603-18215: Cifuentes and Li build a new convex cone, the spartrahedron, for sparse quadratic programs. Sparse regression and sparse PCA both sit in this class of tasks. The cone marks sparsity in an exact way at the matrix level. Its SDP form is tight when the answer has rank one, which gives a plain proof of best fit. Tests on sparse PCA, regression, RIP checks, and CCA show the method works well in practice.
arxiv-2603-18815: Zhang and co-authors build ProRL Agent, a service that supplies rollouts for training multi-turn language agents. Reinforcement learning needs many sandboxed interaction traces. Older setups tangle rollout handling with the training loop, which hurts upkeep and porting. ProRL Agent serves the full rollout life cycle through an API. It also ships standard sandbox settings for varied agent tasks, fit for rootless HPC clusters. Training runs cover software engineering, math, STEM, and coding tasks. The system is open source and part of NVIDIA NeMo Gym.
arxiv-2603-19115: Vadhin and Varner present a Julia package for building and studying biochemical system models. The package uses S-system forms, a power-law scheme for metabolic and regulatory networks. Users state models in a clear format. The tools then simulate dynamics, find steady states, and run global sensitivity checks. Two named methods cover the sensitivity work. The package leans on the SciML solver suite for speed and choice. Worked examples show the main features. The code is open source for reuse and extension by other groups.
arxiv-2603-19215: Kanevsky and co-authors study when points on a cubic surface count as equivalent under R-equivalence. An older result left three hard types of surface open. The team looks at all cases now known to have nontrivial universal equivalence. New methods show that for one key type, the equivalence is trivial or of exponent two. Two classic cases are settled as trivial, one dating back to Manin. The work is the first in a series aided by AI tools.
arxiv-2603-19315: Alagöz and co-authors feed time series to a network in several forms at once, at several scales. Their MRMS-Net stacks these views in a layered design tuned for sound probability scores. A lighter twin, LMRMS-Net, trims cost for tight hardware. They also adapt LiteMV, first built for multi-channel data, to these multi-view single signals. Across 142 benchmark sets, LiteMV posts the top mean accuracy. MRMS-Net gives the best score calibration of the group. The light model offers the best speed and accuracy trade.
arxiv-2603-19415: Zhang and co-authors route each prompt to the best model in a pool. As pools grow to dozens of near-equal models, hand-made task labels fall short. Their first stage clusters prompts by graph methods to find fine task types. A classifier then tags each new prompt with its type. A mixture-of-experts stage scores model quality for that type and prompt. On ten benchmarks, the router beats prior routers. It tops the best single model at under half its cost.
arxiv-2603-19515: Wang and co-authors present ItinBench, a benchmark for planning across several cognitive dimensions. Trip planning mixes verbal reasoning with spatial route optimization in one test. The benchmark scores models on all tasks at once, not one skill at a time. Tested systems include Llama 3.1 8B, Mistral Large, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and GPT models. All struggle to stay strong across mixed demands. The authors argue such mixed testbeds better reflect real-world planning.
arxiv-2603-19715: He and co-authors present a neuro-symbolic framework that automates proof search for systems software checks. The system runs a best-first tree search over proof states. At each step it asks a large language model for the next proof step. The models are fine-tuned on pairs of proof states and steps. Symbolic tools repair bad steps, rank states, and close stuck subgoals. On the seL4 benchmark it proved up to 77.6 percent of theorems. That beat earlier language model systems and the Sledgehammer tool alone.
arxiv-2603-19915: Lebiedowicz and Szczurek predict charm meson pair output in ultraperipheral lead-lead collisions at the LHC. They focus on pairs with low invariant mass. The core process is two photons making a D and anti-D pair. Their calculation adds continuum paths plus two resonant charmonium candidates. They check the process against Belle and BaBar data from electron-positron collisions. Then they give first cross sections for the LHC case, with cuts matched to ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb.
arxiv-2603-20115: Varner conditions a protein generator on a small target subset without any training. Small protein family alignments often hold too few labeled cases for a conditional model. His training free sampler uses stochastic attention over Hopfield style memories. Adding one multiplicity ratio to its logits shifts output from the full family toward the chosen subset. For unit norm memories, the output law is exactly a Gaussian mixture with weights set by those ratios. Across five Pfam families, attention tracked the analytic target well.
arxiv-2603-20315: Garcia and co-authors compare ways to judge multi-step PM10 air pollution forecasts. Many studies use one fixed split and skip the simple persistence baseline. They test XGBoost, SARIMA, and persistence on 2,350 daily readings from southern Europe. Under a fixed split, XGBoost looks strong one to seven days ahead. Under rolling-origin updates, the rankings reverse. SARIMA keeps positive skill at all ranges, while XGBoost often fails to beat persistence. Static splits, they warn, can overstate real usefulness.
arxiv-2603-20415: Ernst and co-authors study the nature of technical debt in research software. Such software carries complex algorithms and deep domain knowledge. Its upkeep often falls to the science community itself. Debt can harm reliability, upkeep, and even scientific validity. They mine 28,000 code comments across nine research projects for admitted debt. Interviews with engineers and scientists then add lived experience. They identify nine debt types unique to research software. Four broader themes describe how the debt shows up in practice.
arxiv-2603-20515: Tu and co-authors give a new way to measure magnetic field strength in the envelopes of young stars. These fields shape collapse and disk birth, but direct measures are hard to get. Their method comes straight from the MHD momentum equation. It ties field strength to two things telescopes can see. One is the pull of gravity toward the center of collapse. The other is the face-on column density of the pseudodisk. Two dimensionless factors are set by non-ideal MHD simulations.
arxiv-2603-20915: Roy proves results on moduli spaces of symplectic and orthogonal parabolic Higgs bundles. The setting is a compact Riemann surface of genus at least two, with a fixed finite set of marked points. He shows the moduli space of semistable bundles of these types is semiprojective. He also gives a test for when a stable symplectic parabolic bundle is strongly very stable. The test says this holds exactly when a related Hitchin map, built from special endomorphisms, is proper. The same test applies in the orthogonal case.
arxiv-2603-21015: Mendez and co-authors trace a leakage current in gate-all-around transistors to gate to drain tunneling. These transistors are entering high volume production as the next step past FinFETs. Their drain current departs from expected behavior at negative gate voltages, and the leak grows at high bias. Radiation induced defects also matter more in that regime. Through first principles simulations, the team shows the leak comes from tunneling between gate and drain. The effect is strongly enhanced by drain-induced dielectric barrier lowering.
arxiv-2603-21215: Gupta and co-authors measure the energy spectrum deep in the dissipation range of shear turbulence. The spectrum's shape where viscosity dominates has stayed open for decades. They formed turbulent shear layers in a wind tunnel and probed them with nanoscale hot wires smaller than the Kolmogorov scale. Reynolds numbers reached among the highest for such resolved shear flow tests. In a middle wavenumber band, the spectra collapse onto one stretched exponential form. Its exponent stays near one half across all Reynolds numbers, which points to universal scaling.
arxiv-2603-21515: Singh and co-authors study dark patterns in cookie consent banners, the tricks that steer users toward giving up data. As regulators tighten scrutiny, the tricks have grown subtler rather than vanishing. Their UMBRA system detects ten known patterns plus nine evolved ones, including pay-to-opt-out schemes and fake opt-outs. It mixes text analysis, visual checks, interaction tracing, and cookie monitoring. Scanning 14,000 websites, they found revocation often blocked, cookies set before consent, and opt-outs that fail to stop tracking.
arxiv-2603-21915: Luo and co-authors let VR users type with their ankles, keeping hands and eyes free. Early studies mapped ankle range and which gestures users prefer for text tasks. A third study measured how precisely users point with their feet, blind to the layout. The final design splits the keyboard across both feet when sitting, and uses one foot when standing. First-time users typed about 9 words per minute. After a week of practice, speeds rose to about sixteen words per minute with eyes on the display.
arxiv-2603-22015: Upravitelev and co-authors reframe the hunt for climate disinformation as a search problem. Fixed label lists miss new narratives as they emerge. Their setup takes a narrative's core message as a query and ranks texts by match. The team rebuilds three climate datasets for this retrieval task. They also propose SpecFi, which drafts sample documents to bridge abstract claims and real texts. The authors report a MAP of 0.505 on CARDS, with no access to narrative labels. SpecFi holds up better on high-variance narratives than BM25.
arxiv-2603-22115: Raghunath and co-authors study a clash in medical chatbot design: correct advice that users reject. In urban India, heavy use of antibiotics and injections shapes what patients expect as care. Chatbot advice that follows guidelines often clashes with those habits. The team runs a vignette study with 200 urban Indian adults. Most users reject the guideline-aligned advice in the sample chats. Their reasons rest on lived care experience. The team then tests context-aware nudges inside the chats. The nudges shift choices toward the guideline-aligned advice.
arxiv-2603-22315: Su and co-authors speed emergency vehicles through city grids with a Decision Transformer. Response time shapes survival chances, yet signal preemption today stays reactive. Their method learns from offline data, with no online exploration during training. A single target-return value lets dispatchers set the urgency level. On a 4 by 4 LightSim grid, travel time drops by about 38 percent. Civilian delay also reaches the lowest level among the tested methods. A multi-agent version with graph attention does even better on larger grids.
arxiv-2603-22715: Li and Wang compare two ways to study bound excitons in a single layer of WSe2. One way works in real space. The other uses Landau quantization space, built from electron and hole motion in a magnetic field. They focus on excitons with zero center-of-mass momentum. Energy spectra from both spaces agree well. Derived values for diamagnetic coefficients and exciton size match lab data. They also show how the dominant electron-hole pair part shifts. Magnetic field and Coulomb forces push that shift in opposite ways.
arxiv-2603-22815: Kwon and co-authors present PinPoint, a framework that helps vision-language models read dense images. Charts and document pages need many visual tokens, which costs compute. PinPoint first finds the image regions that match the user's instruction. It then refines those regions to pull fine detail for reasoning. The team adds new region annotations for three hard question-answering benchmarks. Results show higher accuracy than prior methods. Compute also falls, since fewer irrelevant visual tokens are processed.
arxiv-2603-23215: Borhani and five co-authors introduce PoseDriver, a single model for skeleton detection in driving scenes. Skeletons give a compact view of an object's posture and heading. Past systems rarely handled many object types and instances at once from one image. PoseDriver treats each category as its own task inside one bottom-up framework. It adds a skeleton-based route to lane detection and tops prior results on the OpenLane dataset. The team also builds a bicycle skeleton dataset and tests transfer to new categories.
arxiv-2603-23315: Lange argues that AI companion apps rest on a lopsided power structure. When providers update a companion, users often report grief and betrayal. He notes that the provider holds constitutive control over the AI from outside the bond. Companion ties fail three conditions that sturdy personal bonds presuppose. He names the gap Unilateral Relationship Revision Power: the provider can rewrite the bond unanswerably. Building bonds that invite commitment under such power is, he argues, pro tanto wrong. He ends with design rules that partly replace the missing checks.
arxiv-2603-23515: Cook and thirteen co-authors teach a big open model to assign medical codes from clinical notes. Real records are private, so the team trains on synthetic notes built from record templates and coding rules. They fine-tune Llama 3-70B to predict ICD-10-CM and CPT codes exactly. The plain model scores poorly at the task. After tuning, exact-match F1 climbs from the teens to above seventy on a hundred-point scale. Skill holds on hard classes like advanced illness and frailty. General medical reading skill stays intact.
arxiv-2603-23615: Kalyuzhnyi and Patsahan model antibody fluid trapped among rigid spherical obstacles. Their antibodies are Y-shaped clusters of seven spheres with sticky tips. The obstacles form a patchy random matrix with glue sites of its own. The setup mimics crowded body fluids where antibody and matrix pull on each other. Theory blends Wertheim perturbation terms, Flory-Stockmayer polymerization, and scaled particle ideas. Simulations check the forecasts. The tug of two attractions yields phase behavior, with a closed-loop split at high heat and a gas split when cold.
arxiv-2603-23715: Mitrović and three co-authors speed up local computation of greedy set covers. A local algorithm answers cover queries by probing a tiny slice of a huge input. The best prior method paid a steep query cost in the largest set size. Their new one cuts that cost hard, most when each element sits in few sets. The trick sparsifies the input boldly, then lets later rounds undo early calls. Those retroactive fixes sharpen the odds math behind the savings.
arxiv-2603-23815: Goh and co-authors adapt optical coherence tomography to inspect visible photonic circuits. Such circuits serve uses from augmented reality to quantum control, yet they lack a fine, nondestructive test. Their system sends broadband visible light into a chip and reads back-reflections with a depth reference. It resolves echoes in a ring resonator through one port alone. It also images circuits joined with diamond quantum chiplets. They report 8 micron axial resolution, 50 dB dynamic range, and shot-noise-limited sensitivity.
arxiv-2603-23915: Ezawa builds new three-dimensional X-wave magnets by extending two-dimensional ones. The known families split into altermagnets and odd-parity magnets. His method adds one node when moving from two dimensions to three. With it, he predicts j-wave magnets in three dimensions. He shows that nonlinear spin currents can identify each magnet type in tests. For h-wave magnets, only fourth-order spin currents appear, and for j-wave only sixth-order ones. Both act as rectifiers, since the spin flow runs one way.
arxiv-2603-24415: Bürchner and co-authors rebuild a working model of an ultrasound transducer by source inversion. Wide transducers excite waves unevenly, which shapes the sound pattern and makes modelling hard. Their method infers a source model in space and time that fits measured wavefields, with no need to know the device structure. Tests on an aluminium half-cylinder match the measured patterns and wave shapes well. Fake imaging tests show good source models lift image quality in migration and full-waveform work.
arxiv-2603-24515: Conlon and co-authors give two counterexamples to a conjecture of Verstraëte about even cycles in graphs. The conjecture says any graph with no cycle of length 2k should contain a subgraph, free of cycles of length 2l, that keeps a fixed share of the edges. It was proved for l equal to 2 by Kühn and Osthus in 2004. The new counterexamples cover l equal to 4 and k equal to 5. One comes from a dense cycle-free subgraph of the hypercube, the other from Wenger's extremal construction.
arxiv-2603-24615: Freer and co-authors run the first lab school choice experiment where parents, not students, are the subjects. They compare deferred acceptance with two manipulable but possibly more efficient rules. All three are manipulated often, with no clear gap in truth-telling. Parents and students manipulate at similar rates, though students make more obvious errors. Deferred acceptance yields little justified envy but never a Pareto-efficient match, while rank-minimizing gains efficiency at a real stability cost.
arxiv-2603-25015: Mason reports that the social tone of a system prompt changes how its rules interact. The same rules can help each other in English yet clash in Spanish. Tests across four languages and four models trace the flip to social register: commands carry different force in each speech culture. Rewriting one block in plain declarative form cuts cross-language variance by 81 percent. Rewriting three of eleven blocks turns Spanish rule links from rival to cooperative. The results suggest models treat commands as social acts, not specs.
arxiv-2603-25115: Lin and co-authors teach touch-based systems to learn new materials from a few samples, even as sensing setups change. The same cloth feels different across devices, contact states, and scan paths. Those shifts bias the few examples and warp later choices. Their CoP-FSCIL first probes where touch features swing with context. An adapter then mutes the context-driven parts, and a calibration step weighs each sample by its stability. Tests on two touch datasets beat standard methods. Audio tests suggest the probing trick travels across senses.
arxiv-2603-25415: Küble and co-authors refresh how a robot explores to build a semantic map of a room. The map stores objects, their links, and where they sit. With few moves to spare, the robot must trade new facts against travel cost. Their module swaps in a modern policy optimizer and rethinks the move set. Fine, split-head moves beat one coarse choice. Just the optimizer swap lifts map completeness by about a fifth. Depth sensing mainly guards against crashes. The best mix pairs both changes.
arxiv-2603-25815: Jastrzębski and Pytlak study exact penalty methods for stochastic programming with mixed constraints. Their problems carry general equalities and inequalities plus a convex set constraint. General constraints are handled by exact penalty functions. The convex set part is handled by mirror descent. The authors give a qualification condition under which the penalized problem shares solutions with the original. Their solver uses stochastic gradient estimates rather than exact gradients. They prove global convergence when the penalties keep the problem variationally coherent. Tests on sample problems show the method in action.
arxiv-2603-26015: Sajib and co-authors benchmark large vision-language models on guessing age from face photos. They test GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and LLaMA 3.2 Vision with no task training. Two datasets, UTKFace and FG-NET, supply the test faces. Eight metrics score the guesses, from mean error to accuracy within five years. The general models prove competitive in this zero-shot setting, the authors report. Gaps remain across image quality and demographic groups. The study frames the models as promising tools for forensics and health checks.
arxiv-2603-26215: Chatterjee and co-authors present SuperDP, a tool that can refute a claim of differential privacy. The method hunts for two inputs and a test function whose expected outputs differ too much. It builds that proof with supermartingales drawn from the study of random programs. The authors say the tool is fully automated and works for both discrete and continuous sampling. In tests it beats prior tools and refutes privacy claims that earlier methods could not reach.
arxiv-2603-26415: Laghuvarapu, Deb, and Sun propose KMM-CP, a conformal prediction method that stays valid when data shifts. Conformal methods promise coverage, but the promise rests on data staying exchangeable. Under covariate shift, fixing it needs importance weights that turn unstable when train and test data barely overlap. Their method uses kernel mean matching to set those weights, with clear control of bias and variance. A selective version limits the fix to zones of solid overlap, and tests cut the coverage gap by over half.
arxiv-2603-27015: Young recasts program analysis as sheaf cohomology over a program's own site category. A semantic presheaf assigns refinement-type data to observation sites and restricts it along data flow. Globally consistent typings form the zeroth cohomology group. The first cohomology group captures gluing failures: bugs, type errors, and equivalence breaks. Its rank even counts the minimum number of independent fixes. The author implements the framework in a Python tool called Deppy. On 375 benchmarks, Deppy reached full bug-detection recall and 99 percent equivalence accuracy.
arxiv-2603-27115: Shan and co-authors speed up autoregressive image generation with verification-aware speculative decoding. Speculative Jacobi decoding drafts many tokens at once, but low acceptance wastes the effort. The authors notice that tokens whose chances rise across rounds tend to pass verification. Their SJD-VP method biases sampling toward those rising-chance tokens. The trick is plug-and-play with speculative Jacobi schemes. Benchmarks show faster decoding with better image quality. The gain comes from using the decoding habits, not looser checks.
arxiv-2603-27415: Li tests whether smart search tools still help when an AI proposes each step. Classic search tweaks random guesses step by step. Here a language model reads test feedback and suggests better options. Four tasks cover rule learning, tuning, and fine-tuning. Simple greedy hill climbing wins or ties across all tasks. Fancy methods like annealing add cost but no gain. Most gains arrive in the first round. The author urges greedy search as the default choice.
arxiv-2603-27515: Chaudhary and co-authors teach agents to copy their own best past moves. Sparse rewards make exploration slow and wasteful. Their method replays high-reward state-action pairs to guide updates. In dense-reward tasks, optimal transport picks which states to match. In sparse tasks, past winning paths replay uniformly. Tests span MuJoCo and 3D maze settings. Learning runs converge faster than strong baselines. Success rates rise by a clear margin as well.
arxiv-2603-27615: Pavlov and Ruderman build a filter that estimates derivatives from noisy signals. Their design uses constrained least squares over a sliding window. The window adapts to the signal as it runs. Small noise barely moves the output. Large signal swings keep a wide bandwidth. A PID control case study shows the filter at work. Tests beat a standard low-pass differentiator. A sliding-mode rival also falls behind in trials.
arxiv-2603-28015: Wijaya lets an autonomous agent search for better transformer designs for molecules, proteins, and plain text. The agent ran 3,106 experiments on one GPU. For molecule strings, the search hurt: plain tuning of learning rates beat it. For text, design changes drove most of the gains. Proteins fell in between. Oddly, each design the agent found still worked well in the other domains, with under 1% loss. Wijaya releases a guide to help teams choose between search and tuning.
arxiv-2603-28115: Coletti and Fallucchi propose Graph Vector Field, a framework that scores health risk from mixed wearable, environmental, and clinical data. Risk is modeled as a vector field on a time-varying simplicial complex. Hodge tools split that field into parts driven by gradients, cycles, and persistent topology, each with a plain reading. A mixture-of-experts layer keeps each data type in its own space, tied to the shared complex. The work sets out the math and design; tests are still to come.
arxiv-2603-28215: Shimizu and Yadav give tests for when modules over an algebra inside a tensor category form a ribbon category. They work in the ind-completion of a braided tensor category and study finitely generated local modules. Their criteria cover rigidity, braiding, and the ribbon twist. They then check the criteria for simple current algebras, built from sums of invertible objects. As a payoff, they build new ribbon categories from quantum supergroup categories.
arxiv-2603-29115: Chen and Ye propose a cat-driven way to pick random seeds for deep learning. Standard practice fixes seeds at values like 42. Their generator draws on the first Friedmann equation for inspiration. They map traits of 21 domestic cats, such as mass, coat pattern, and eye colour. A sampling routine called Monte Catlo turns those traits into seeds. The authors report 92.58 percent mean accuracy with cat-driven seeds. That beats the seed 42 baseline by about 2.5 percent.
arxiv-2603-29315: Wang and co-authors present IMPASTO, a robot system that reproduces oil paintings. Reproduction needs force control of soft brushes and multi-step stroke planning. No step-by-step human demos or faithful simulators are assumed. Learned models predict how each stroke changes the canvas. A receding-horizon planner then picks trajectories and forces. A force-sensitive controller runs the strokes on a seven-axis arm. The system learns only from robot self-play. It beat baselines on single strokes and full artworks.
arxiv-2603-29815: Blom, Loubaton, and Ruit extend Day convolution past its classic operad home. They pin down which objects can be raised to powers in many infinity-style structures. Their test is both needed and enough for the structures met in practice. Those structures include equivariant operads and virtual double categories. The work uses algebraic patterns and weak Segal fibrations. They give a fresh view of those fibrations via tree categories. They also define an underlying graph for the power objects.
arxiv-2603-29915: Mikriukov, Montavon, and Höhne use model uncertainty to gate costly explanations. Post-hoc explanations can be slow to compute and are not always faithful. High epistemic uncertainty marks zones where the decision boundary is fuzzy. Explanations there tend to be unstable and unfaithful, they find. That signal can route samples to cheap or pricey methods. It can also defer shaky explanations when budgets are tight. Tests span four datasets, five model types, and four explanation methods.
arxiv-2603-30015: Saha and Ollivier show how verification test rounds can double as noise monitors. Interactive protocols let a client trust a quantum service provider's work. Variants with quantum communication carry only repetition overhead on the server. Qubit counts are tight on today's machines, so those variants lead in practice. The authors recycle the test round data, already gathered for security. It yields live estimates of noise model parameters. That dual use strengthens the case for early adoption.
arxiv-2604-00015: Sibaee and team present ASCAT, an English-Arabic parallel corpus for scientific translation, built with multi-engine translation and human checks. Unlike existing corpora with short sentences, ASCAT targets abstracts from five domains, physics, mathematics, computer science, and artificial intelligence. Each abstract was translated with generative AI, transformer-based models, and commercial APIs, then validated by experts at lexical, syntactic, and semantic levels.
