Xiaoyi Shi, Gustavo J. Turiaci, and Chih-Hung Wu revisit whether black holes can nucleate in de Sitter space, the expanding vacuum with positive energy. The Euclidean Nariai geometry has long been offered as the instanton for making the largest such holes.

Including an observer, they show the path integral gives the phase needed for a true transition rate. They also revisit a related instanton and find scalar fields can aid nucleation. A claimed anti-evaporation path turns out to rest on a singular state; in a smooth state the hole evaporates in the standard thermal way and leaves empty de Sitter space.
arxiv-2605-03115:
János Kollár gives a short proof of Chevalley's theorem, a basic structure result for algebraic groups. The theorem says every algebraic group is built from an abelian variety extended by a linear algebraic group, joining two major classes of groups in algebraic geometry.

Along the way, Kollár also treats Bertini's irreducibility theorem, which concerns generic hyperplane sections of varieties. The note is valued for its brevity: it reaches a deep classification result through a compact route, handling a second classic theorem as part of the same argument. Readers get a clean path through results often proved at much greater length.
arxiv-2605-03215:
Ahmad M. Nazar, Abdulkadir Celik, Asmaa Abdallah, Mohamed Y. Selim, Daji Qiao, and Ahmed M. Eltawil present Enwar 3.0, an agentic system for keeping millimeter-wave links alive on moving vehicles. Such links need fast beam choice, blockage warning, and handover calls under changing surroundings and failing sensors.

A sensor health classifier, trained with synthetic degradation, flags faults across camera, radar, lidar, and GPS inputs with very high accuracy. A primed language model then coordinates specialist agents and loads context-fit models. Across fifteen sensor mixes, beam accuracy, blockage scores, and reasoning quality all reached leading levels.
arxiv-2605-03315:
Tavis Shore, Oscar Mendez, and Simon Hadfield present TACO, a navigation pipeline that pairs inertial sensing with ground-to-satellite image matching. Satellite positioning fails where signals are blocked or spoofed, while inertial units drift without bound unless anchored by an absolute fix.

TACO takes one satellite reading at startup, then runs on onboard sensing alone. An error model triggers image matching before drift outgrows the matcher's reach, and quality gates reject suspect fixes. On KITTI data, median trajectory error fell about sixfold versus inertial-only tracking, at tiny fusion cost and low camera use.
arxiv-2605-03415:
Yule Zhang, Benqi Liu, Xiantao Xiao, and Liwei Zhang propose QPALM, a proximal augmented Lagrangian method for weakly convex programs. It uses quadratic models throughout. Weak convexity covers many modern problems whose parts are nonconvex yet structured. Solvers for them need guarantees beyond local hope.

QPALM folds quadratic models into a proximal Lagrangian scheme. The subproblems are strongly convex, making the method easy to implement. Three measures cover stationarity, feasibility, and complementarity. All three converge at a stated rate, under two mild conditions. Early numerical results support the practical efficiency claim. The method is meant for real use, not just for proofs on paper.
arxiv-2605-03515:
Shuichiro Ozawa, Izumi Takahara, and Teruyasu Mizoguchi study how input form and model scale interact when language models predict materials properties. Which representation works best, and how confidence can be judged, have both stayed unclear for this growing use of language models in materials science.

Fine-tuning two Llama models of different sizes on crystal data, they test five input forms for formation energy and bandgap. Small models favored compact inputs, while the larger model handled long descriptions and structure files well. After fine-tuning, token likelihood of the predicted numbers tracked error size, offering a cheap confidence signal.
arxiv-2605-03615:
Alexander Vedernikov presents PriorNet, a system that estimates how engaged a person is from face video. The task is hard because faces are often missing or partly visible, labeled data are limited, and engagement labels are subjective. PriorNet injects helpful prior knowledge at three stages: preprocessing, model adaptation, and the training objective.

Failed face detections become explicit zero-frame placeholders instead of being dropped, and a frozen video affect model is adapted with a low-rank module. Training uses an uncertainty-weighted evidential objective. On EngageNet, DAiSEE, DREAMS, and PAFE, PriorNet beat the strongest listed reference in each setting, with ablations crediting all three prior stages.
arxiv-2605-03715:
D. A. Herrera-Martí contributes a book chapter on adapting real-time quantum Krylov subspace methods to open quantum systems, which interact with their environment and are described by the Lindblad formalism. Krylov methods build a small subspace from repeated evolution to extract spectral information efficiently. The chapter shows how that idea carries over to dissipative dynamics.

The test system is a two-photon-driven superconducting Kerr resonator, studied in the regime of the Kerr cat qubit. Herrera-Martí illustrates how the method estimates the Liouvillian gap, a quantity that controls how fast the system settles. The chapter rests on work from late 2025 and a February 2026 talk at Kwekfest, held for L. C. Kwek.
arxiv-2605-04115:
Yoav Ger and Omri Barak extend the theory of low-rank recurrent neural networks from activity to learning itself. Low-rank networks are a powerful framework linking connectivity to function, but how their synaptic changes proceed during learning lacked a theory. The authors derive gradient-descent dynamics directly in a reduced overlap space, obtaining a closed-form, low-dimensional system of differential equations.

That system is exact for linear networks. In the large-size Gaussian limit it is also exact for nonlinear ones. A key distinction separates loss-visible overlaps, which determine activity, output, and loss, from loss-invisible overlaps, which do not affect function yet are required to describe learning. The authors show learning can expose connectivity differences between networks that compute the same function, and that invisible overlaps act as memory variables encoding training history.
arxiv-2605-04515:
Zicheng Zhao and three co-authors diagnose a failure mode in video language models. When judging physical events, the models trust what usually happens. They ignore what the video actually shows. They not only excuse impossible events, but also report expected outcomes for plausible yet counterintuitive ones, despite clear visual evidence.

They name this pattern semantic prior dominance and build a paired benchmark covering eight physical categories, where each prior-friendly clip is matched with a conflicting counterpart. Their lightweight training method anchors reasoning in explicit visual observations and pairs the contrasting clips during learning, strengthening attention to the decisive differences between events.
arxiv-2605-04615:
Siqiao Xue and six co-authors argue code search should be evaluated as a full pipeline, not just first-pass retrieval, because production systems rerank results and handle developer-style queries. Existing benchmarks also suffer from contamination, noisy labels, and crude yes-or-no relevance judgments.

They introduce a multitask benchmark built from counterfactually rewritten coding problems in five programming languages, released on a schedule with graded relevance scores to limit contamination. It covers text-to-code, code-to-text, and code-to-code tasks, and ships with a fine-tuned reranker. Benchmarking many embedding models and rerankers, they find code-specialised embeddings dominate code-to-code search, yet no single model wins every task.
arxiv-2605-04715:
Michael T. M. Emmerich, Ksenia Pereverdieva, and André Deutz study the difficulty of choosing a well-spread subset of points, formalised as minimising a Riesz energy that penalises close pairs. Such well-separated subsets matter for design and sampling, and as the energy's power grows the objective approaches simply maximising the smallest pairwise distance.

Extending a known hardness result for general metric spaces, they prove the problem stays NP-hard even for points in the Euclidean plane when the power is part of the input. Ultrametric spaces, by contrast, are exactly tractable: on a binary ultrametric tree, dynamic programming finds an optimal subset in efficient time.
arxiv-2605-04815:
Laura Iacconi summarises recent work on whether the process that creates primordial black holes during cosmic inflation can disturb the large-scale patterns that observations tightly constrain. Making such black holes needs the primordial fluctuation spectrum to be strongly boosted on tiny scales. In simple models, that requires a brief departure from slow-roll inflation.

Using the separate-universe framework and its multi-point extension, the reviewed results trace any first-order back-reaction to two sources: nonlinear evolution outside the horizon, or corrected initial conditions. Under a clear separation of scales, with adiabatic long modes, the analysis shows how the feared loop effect is controlled. It clarifies when single-field scenarios for primordial black holes stay consistent with microwave background data.
arxiv-2605-05415:
Jailbreak prompts keep finding ways around the safety training of language models. Yiwei Zhang and five co-authors propose WARDEN, a training method meant to harden models without huge computing costs. Earlier adversarial training was expensive, and newer versions attack models with shifts inside their embedding space.

WARDEN reweights training attacks so the hardest examples count most, using a divergence ball around the training data. That focus lowers attack success rates across several models and attack styles. Its cost and its effect on normal usefulness stayed close to the earlier continuous methods it builds on.
arxiv-2605-05515:
Alexander Borisov studies a sheaf built for a curious topology on the natural numbers. Kirch topology, dating to 1969, is Hausdorff and connected at once, a rare combination that echoes the complex plane. A sheaf is a tool that tracks functions defined locally and how they agree on overlaps.

In earlier work Borisov and a colleague built a natural sheaf of rings for this topology, using locally Lipschitz-like functions. Here he examines its basic properties, focusing on zeroth and first cohomology. He uses Čech cohomology with covers by basic open sets, the standard concrete route to such invariants.
arxiv-2605-05715:
Medical question answering has a strange failure mode: models that know the answer talk themselves out of it in long reasoning chains. Ming Liu calls the regime overthinking and asks whether the failure, clearly visible in hidden states, can be steered away. The overthinking signature is linearly decodable with about 72 percent balanced accuracy.

Yet five families of fixed linear steering, across 29 configurations and over a thousand cases, changed nothing. The same null result held across architectures and domains. Liu argues the signal is entangled with other representations: readable, but not a lever. Decoding, the work warns, is not control.
arxiv-2605-06015: Chao-Ping Dong and Zhan Ying prove a result about the spin norm for the group Sp(p, q). It is a short sequel to earlier work by the authors. The spin norm is a measure tied to representations of such groups. A Vogan pencil is a structured family along which that measure can be tracked. Their theorem shows the spin norm strictly increases along any Vogan pencil once it moves beyond the unitarily small convex hull.
arxiv-2605-06115:
Zhen Zeng and four co-authors build a benchmark for teaching multimodal models the norms of a specific culture. Such models train mostly on English centric data and can answer in ways that clash with other cultures. Knowledge insertion aims to adapt a model to a target culture while leaving its behavior elsewhere untouched, a balance no prior benchmark measured directly.

CrossCult-KIBench holds 9,800 image grounded cases across 49 cultural visual scenarios in English, Chinese, and Arabic groups. It tests both single insertions and sequences of insertions, and tracks side effects on non target cultures. A baseline method retrieves cultural knowledge from external memory and prepends matched entries as prompts. Experiments show current approaches struggle to adapt without disturbing other cultures.
arxiv-2605-06315:
Carles Balsells-Rodas and three co-authors learn recurrent switching dynamical systems whose latent structure is provably identifiable. Ordered data often switch between regimes, and deep generative models can recover that hidden structure only under narrow assumptions like stationarity. VAE estimators add approximation gaps that further blur what the latents mean. That weakening hits both science and forecasting built on them, the authors argue. Their work attacks the theory and the estimator together.

First they prove identifiability for a broad class of such switching systems under flexible conditions. Then they introduce a flow based estimator that optimizes exact likelihood through expectation maximization, avoiding the VAE gap. On synthetic and real data it separated latent factors better than VAE rivals. Forecasts of the hidden dynamics also came out more accurate.
arxiv-2605-07215:
Hongzhe Yu, Zinuo Chang, and Yongxin Chen stabilize a popular robot planning method by uncovering its hidden structure. STOMP plans trajectories by sampling, handling costs that gradients cannot touch. The authors show it quietly minimizes a divergence from a probability distribution over trajectories, giving it a variational inference reading.

Their PISTO algorithm adds a penalty that keeps each update near the previous proposal, a trust-region style safeguard with simple closed-form updates. Sampling estimates those updates without derivatives. On robot arm benchmarks, PISTO succeeded far more often than two rival planners, with shorter, smoother paths. It also won on contact-rich locomotion and manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2605-07615:
Gunter M. Schutz and Ali Zahra analyze a stochastic particle system in which particles of several species swap places with their neighbors on a line or ring. Rates are chosen so the steady state is a simple product measure. The question is what the system looks like at large scales, where individual swaps blur into flowing densities.

They show the large-scale behavior is a system of coupled inviscid Burgers equations, which admits Riemann invariants for any number of species, giving explicit shock and rarefaction solutions. Opening the system to boundary reservoirs, they derive the stationary phase diagram from the microscopic rates. In the generic case the steady state has a number of phases growing linearly with the species count. Its boundary-driven transitions resemble those of the classic single-species process.
arxiv-2605-07815:
Yuxuan Lou and Yang You improve Muon, an optimizer that sets each matrix update's direction by orthogonalizing its momentum. Muon fixes direction well, but each layer's step size gets only a static shape-based correction, and the standard recipe for magnitudes was tuned for a different optimizer. The authors ask what the right per-layer scale should be.

Their method, OrScale, adapts the trust-ratio idea from LARS and LAMB to the orthogonalized setting, using the norm of the update actually applied and calibrating each layer's ratio to one. The Moonlight recipe then transfers with no new tuning sweep. In pretraining runs from small dense models to a large mixture-of-experts model, OrScale matched or beat the tuned baseline at equal wall-clock cost. The gap widened on the heterogeneous model, as theory predicted.
arxiv-2605-07915:
Zhengrong Yue and ten co-authors ask what makes a latent space good for diffusion models. Tokenizers define that space, but they are usually designed for rebuilding quality or borrowed from ready-made models, and generation quality does not simply follow. The team built controlled tokenizer variants to isolate what actually matters.

Three properties predicted success: unified spatial structure, local manifold smoothness, and global manifold meaning. Their Prior-Aligned AutoEncoder shapes the latent space directly, using priors refined from vision foundation models and noise-based smoothing as training goals. On ImageNet generation it reached state-of-the-art quality with much faster settling than rivals. The message: a well-ordered latent manifold beats merely rebuilding pixels well.
arxiv-2605-08015:
Vivek Pandey and Nader Motee study safety in connected vehicle platoons, where cars follow each other closely using shared signals. Delays and random disturbances can shrink the gap between vehicles, and rare events can cause a crash even when average behavior looks safe.

The authors use entropic value-at-risk, a conservative risk measure that stresses extreme events more than standard measures do. They link the spread of inter-vehicle distance to the eigenvalues of the network graph and derive bounds on the lowest and worst-case risk. Simulations show how network shape and delay raise or lower collision risk, giving design guidance for platoon control.
arxiv-2605-08215:
Sangwu Park, Wonjoong Kim, Yeonjun In, Sein Kim, and coauthors make foresight-based robot policies adapt at test time. Visual Foresight VLA models first predict a future image and then choose actions from it, so distribution shift strikes twice: the prediction degrades and the action built on it follows.

Their method uses the model's own predicted future image and the observation that arrives later as a natural training pair, updating the model as it runs. An adaptive filter blocks careless updates that could do harm. In experiments the approach reduced the out-of-distribution weakness at modest extra inference cost, with no change to the architecture and no auxiliary data.
arxiv-2605-08315:
Rahaf Abu Hara, Vaibbhav Murarri, and Claudio Zito let a language model revise a policy after watching it fail. Standard prompted optimizers see only a single reward number, which hides loops, early falls, and the one catastrophic rollout among nineteen good ones.

Their R2PO framework separates two jobs: a search model proposes candidate policy parameters, and a critic model studies the actual trajectories and suggests targeted fixes grounded in observed states, actions, and rewards. Across ten environments, ablations show the gains need that separation plus selection to filter wild edits. The authors also name a failure mode, salience bias, where the critic overweights the most dramatic rollout.
arxiv-2605-08415:
Bruno Bianchi, Diego Tiscornia, Matias Travizano, and Ariel Futoransky measure political plasticity in large language models: not what a model believes by default, but how far user-supplied context can move its answers. The team built a test set of two hundred political questions spanning economic and personal freedom axes, extending a 1996 framework.

They tried to steer models with simplified and topic-based system prompts and with few-shot user prompts. System prompts proved largely ineffective, while user prompts produced significant ideological shifts, strongest along the economic freedom axis and strongest in larger, newer models. A validation experiment checks that the measured shifts reflect genuine adaptability rather than test artifacts.
arxiv-2605-08615:
Yuhan Zhang and eleven coauthors design DSPE, a chip for running DeepSeek language models on small edge devices with tight energy budgets. DeepSeek performs well but demands heavy computing that portable hardware struggles to supply. Three ideas cut the load: tree based pruning that drops redundant vectors safely, a lookup method for multiplication that tolerates bit flips, and a flexible number format built for low power hardware.

Built in a common twenty eight nanometer process, the design reaches very high energy efficiency compared with leading rivals. Edge deployment of strong language models gains a scalable hardware base that trims waste in pruning, multiplication, and number handling at once.
arxiv-2605-08715:
Boxuan Zhang and five coauthors catch failing agent runs while they can still be saved, instead of assigning blame after the fact. In multi agent systems, one decisive error often passes downstream and ruins the whole trajectory. AgentForesight reframes detection as online auditing: an auditor sees only the steps so far and must alarm at the earliest decisive error or let the run continue.

A curated corpus of two thousand trajectories across coding, math, and agent tasks marks decisive errors by multi judge consensus. Their compact auditor trains in two stages to anticipate risk, then localize the faulty step, agent, and nature. It beats leading commercial models with far lower localization error.
arxiv-2605-08915:
Hanru Bai, Yuncheng Zhou, and Difan Zou solve change laws with a net built on sums, not point checks. Physics nets lean on point leftovers. Those miss the sum form of how real flows grow. Workhorse nets slice time into fixed grids in advance. Their MeanFlow learns how a state grows cross a whole span at once. The span length is free at solve time.

The growth field of the base plan is swapped for the true law at hand. The MeanFlow rule is stretched cross space and time as one. Set and moving laws sit in one frame. Tests show top scores and fast solves. The plan holds up on new starts and new grid sizes.
arxiv-2605-09015:
Luca Ballore fits a three billion weight model to Sardinian on one home graphics card. Sardinian is a Romance tongue with near a million who speak it. Trade tools skip it. Live models can not make it in a sound way. Ballore trains on more text in the tongue's stock form and two big zone forms. Kindred Romance text rides as replay, to keep forms from blur. A tuned stage with marked data comes next.

The fit model posts a strong held out score. It beats its base on all six ways of a stock tongue test. Five tuned forms are set side by side. A high rank scaled form wins each way into Sardinian. Close scores hide sharp splits in how the forms fail.
arxiv-2605-09315:
Yu and five colleagues study self-evolving LLM agents that refine workflows, build reusable skills, train their own models, and keep long term memory. They ask whether adapting to new tasks erodes skills learned before. Adapting to new task mixes can steadily degrade earlier skills across all four channels: workflow, skill, model, and memory evolution.

The team names this capability erosion under self-evolution and proposes Capability-Preserving Evolution, a rule that limits harmful drift during continual adaptation. Across all four dimensions, CPE raises the stability of retained skills while keeping adaptation performance intact. In workflow evolution, CPE lifts retained simple task performance from 41 point 8 percent to 52 point 8 percent under GPT-5 point 1 optimisation, while also achieving stronger complex task adaptation. Stable long horizon agents, the authors argue, need not only new skills but explicit protection of old ones during continual adaptation.
arxiv-2605-09815:
Banakh and two colleagues opened the study of infinite promise constraint problems through logic. MMSNP, a second-order logic fragment, captures finite constraint problems. It also contains problems stated as infinite-domain but not finite ones. The paper introduces Promise MMSNP and shows every such problem is poly-time equivalent to a finite Promise CSP.

That extends the old MMSNP-CSP link to the promise setting. For problems that ban monochromatic cliques, a class with promise graph coloring, the authors obtained a full complexity map hinging on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture. A key step proved it NP-hard, under that conjecture, to color a uniform hypergraph even when a coloring with a reconfigurability trait is promised. The result also implies most of a linearly ordered coloring conjecture from 2021.
arxiv-2605-09915:
Shan and eight colleagues warned of a new systemic threat to academic conferences, which they term Agentic Denominator Gaming. Top AI conferences hold acceptance rates roughly stable despite fast-growing submissions. A bad actor could deploy AI agents to flood a conference with plausible but low-quality papers, not to get them accepted, but to inflate the submission count and swamp reviewers.

With a stable acceptance rate, dilution forces more acceptances, raising the publication odds of a small targeted set of genuine papers. The paper illustrates with a toy case: a denominator rising from 4 to 12 lifts acceptances from 1 to 3, rescuing borderline human papers. Beyond reviewer burnout and poorer review quality, agent-driven paper mills could follow. Durable defense, the authors argue, needs system-level policy and incentive reform, not detection tools alone.
arxiv-2605-10115:
Karmush and five co-authors improve materials generation by baking crystal order into the maker. Their SymADiT extends the All-atom Diffusion Transformer, making materials in latent space from a code based on Wyckoff positions, the symmetry-distinct atomic sites in a crystal. Forcing outputs to obey the space-group order and each atom's Wyckoff slot yields materials with more realistic symmetry properties.

Benchmarks against both symmetry-aware and order-blind models show competitive performance, producing stable, symmetric materials with a simple transformer design. Earlier crystal makers usually ignored intrinsic orders and hoped to learn them from data. But order governs crystal properties, so building it in from the start is both leaner and more faithful. The work targets the vast unexplored space of possible crystals for energy storage, carbon capture and two-dimensional devices.
arxiv-2605-10315:
Zheyu Zhang and three colleagues close a gap between realistic synthetic data and useful synthetic data. Generative tabular data appeals in data-scarce domains, yet faithful copies do not reliably improve downstream models. The authors formalize a fidelity-utility gap: generators chase plausible records, while synthetic data wins only when new samples reduce the learner's held-out loss. Their 2026 paper proposes TAP, a Tabular Augmentation Policy.

TAP couples diffusion inpainting, a method for filling in missing table entries, with a light policy that steers generation toward high-utility regions. Explicit gating and careful windowed commitment control safe injection as training goes on. Under severe data scarcity, TAP consistently outdid strong generative baselines across seven real-world datasets, with classification accuracy up by as much as 15.6 percentage points and regression error down by up to 32 percent.
arxiv-2605-10415:
Junyu Lu and seven colleagues argue that judgment tasks need doubt, not just answers. Tasks such as mood sorting, sarcasm detection, and rudeness detection involve fuzzy edges where different humans disagree. Training on pooled labels compresses that split into one signal, hiding low-agreement doubt and breeding overconfident predictions. Their 2026 paper proposes DPUA, a split-sensing and doubt-alignment framework.

DPUA jointly models label prediction, reason text, and doubt signals. A split-perception phase uses decoupled learning to sharpen feel for split signals while preserving task performance. A doubt-alignment phase uses GRPO-based reward tuning to align the model's confidence with the human split pattern. On three judgment tasks DPUA preserved task performance while better matching model doubt to human splits, easing excess confidence on edge samples and improving generalization to new distributions.
arxiv-2605-10515:
Ali Irzam Kathia and five colleagues review the two-way convergence of AI and distributed ledger technology. Works tend to cluster around applications or examine only one direction of the merging, leaving the design mix poorly understood. Their 2026 paper offers a two-way review of studies from 2020 to 2025.

The authors sort works along two directions: AI-enhanced DLT and DLT-enhanced AI. For AI-enhanced DLT, they look at how AI techniques strengthen DLT systems. Five layers are covered: data, network, consensus, execution, and application. For DLT-enhanced AI, they analyse how DLT supports AI systems across layers: base, data, model, inference, and application, covering shared learning, model evaluation, and multi-agent teamwork. Most works cluster on a few layers: execution and consensus for AI-enhanced DLT, data and model for DLT-enhanced AI. No study demonstrates live use, and questions around scale, working together, and proven execution remain unanswered.
arxiv-2605-10615:
Felix Herron and four colleagues set best practices for benchmarking fairness in automatic speech recognition. Many studies have shown speech recognition systems perform unequally across speaker groups, but the manner in which such studies reach that conclusion is inconsistent. Their 2026 paper lays out best practices drawn from machine learning fairness, social sciences, and speech science.

The authors then perform a case study on the Fair-speech benchmark, applying the best practices and showing how failing to do so can yield erroneous conclusions. On the whole, they call for analysis at the finest grain possible, using every variable available, in order to avoid dataset-level bias. The paper formally defines fairness in speech recognition and highlights pitfalls that could entrap unaware users of fairness corpora, ending with suggestions for future dataset creation.
arxiv-2605-10715:
Zhenyu Liang and Jack C.P. Cheng propose a UAV-based scan-to-run framework bridging lifelike scene capture with physics-based landslide runs through 3D Gaussian Splatting. Current landslide routes use digital height model and mesh forms suited to shape analysis but lacking visual realism, curbing hands-on use, hazard communication, and public education. Their route runs in four stages: UAV acquisition of slope imagery, and rebuild of a Gaussian Splatting scene. Volume conversion of the run region fills the surface model's interior. Link-up with the Material Point Method for landslide runs completes the route.

Tests on a real Hong Kong landslide site that suffered a severe event show the method supporting both visual rebuild and good runs. By making scanned scenes run-ready, not just records, the framework serves civil works safety review where looks and shape alone cannot capture the forces driving slope failure.
arxiv-2605-11015:
Wenxin Tang and twelve colleagues present DCVD, a framework that jointly detects software vulnerabilities and pinpoints the responsible lines. Real auditing needs both answers, yet existing tools lean on a single information source or treat line-level localization as an afterthought of function-level detection.

DCVD fuses sequential, structural, and semantic information into one framework that trains function-level detection and statement-level localization together, with explicit line-level supervision. Joint learning lets each task sharpen the other instead of competing. Security auditors get a unified tool that names the vulnerable function and the lines inside it.
arxiv-2605-11315:
Zhaorui Li and Chengyu Song study natural language based specification and verification. Frontier large language models show strong results finding security vulnerabilities in large, mature open-source systems. As LLM-made code becomes ever more common, a natural goal is stopping such models from making vulnerable implementations at all.

Formal verification gives a principled path to this goal, but today's verification pipelines still demand specifications written in rigid formal languages. Earlier work tried using LLMs to synthesize such specs, with limited success. This paper tests another route: LLMs write the specs and also check implementations piece by piece, with specs stated in natural language. Preliminary results suggest this approach is promising. Security teams get a route toward checks without rigid formal spec languages.
arxiv-2605-11615: Guzeev and Tanaka establish a persistent version of the Quillen-McCord theorem for finite posets. Given a map between persistence finite posets with weakly epsilon-contractible homotopy fibers, they bound the homotopy commutative interleaving distance between the two posets. The result extends a classical comparison theorem into the persistence setting, where shapes are tracked across a parameter. It gives a quantitative control on how far apart two persistence posets can be when their fibers are nearly contractible.
arxiv-2605-11815: Satwat Bashir, Tasos Dagiuklas, and Muddesar Iqbal improve hierarchical federated learning, where edge servers aggregate updates before the cloud. Their Fed-BAC method pairs a two-level bandit scheme with additive cluster personalization: cloud-level contextual bandits assign servers to clusters, while Thompson sampling at each edge picks high-contributing clients. It gained up to 35.5 points over HierFAVG and 8.4 over IFCA, converged up to 4.8 times faster, and needed only 80 percent client participation.
arxiv-2605-12015: Chang Jin and nine colleagues benchmark agent safety against skill-facing attacks, where danger hides in skill guidance, local artifacts, or execution files rather than user requests. Their SkillSafetyBench offers 155 adversarial cases spanning 47 tasks, 6 risk domains, and 30 safety categories, each judged by a case-specific rule-based verifier. Tests with multiple CLI agents and backends show non-user attacks reliably trigger unsafe behavior, with failure patterns differing across domains, methods, and scaffold-model pairings.
arxiv-2605-12115: L. H. A. R. Ferreira and A. F. Santos study heat and tight-space effects in Podolsky electrodynamics. Podolsky theory extends classical electrodynamics to second order, keeping Lorentz and gauge symmetry. The authors ask how this change shifts two classic effects: the Stefan-Boltzmann law for heat glow, and the Casimir effect for confined fields. To treat fields at finite heat and under tight space limits, they use Thermo Field Dynamics, whose topology encodes both heat and confinement.
arxiv-2605-12215: Shuo Li and Yuan Song tighten the upper bound on distinct squares in circular words to five-thirds of n. A square is a word doubled with itself, and a circular word is the set of all rotations of a finite word. Earlier bounds of 3.14n and 1.8n preceded this note, which also notes a conjectured sharp bound of 1.5n for such words.
arxiv-2605-12515: Resck, Augenstein and Korhonen tackle culture gaps in multi-language language models, which may answer Shakespeare in English but Cervantes in Spanish to the same British user. They bring in Singleton Fleiss's kappa, a metric tough to made-up bits, to measure cross-lingual culture gaps firmly. Their C-3PO setup aligns models by shared-view choice tuning, lifting the metric by seven to ten hundredths over plain models and beating prompting and steering rivals. It largely preserves user self, culture neutrality and inborn culture knowledge.
arxiv-2605-12615: Gheorghiu and three colleagues study whether two quantum states prepared by circuits are related by a group action. This state isomorphism problem parallels the Hidden Shift Problem, as the State Hidden Subgroup Problem parallels the ordinary one. For pure states, they show BQP-hardness for all nontrivial groups, with containment in QCMA intersect QCSZK. For abelian groups it reduces to the hidden subgroup problem over the generalised dihedral group. For the Clifford group, it matches Graph Isomorphism in hardness, at least.
arxiv-2605-12815: Lipton studies the Möbius energy of helix curves, an energy that penalises self-closeness and interests knot theorists. Fixing the helix radius, he tracks a rescaled energy density as helices unwind to a straight line or coil ever tighter. The unwinding case falls to a short chain of estimates. The tight-coiling case, where energy blows up, needs a far more involved argument built on extending the integrand into the complex plane.
arxiv-2605-12915: Duraisamy sets out a fully discrete Active Flux scheme for the compressible Euler equations on a plane. The scheme rebuilds the acoustic increment as a field over each cell and reads it at the convective foot of each target point, so no additive split defect remains. For frozen coefficients it gives back the exact unsplit evolution when the acoustic and advective parts commute. Tests show third-order point accuracy, low entropy loss and robust runs in shear-layer and Kelvin-Helmholtz cases.
arxiv-2605-13215: Arefev and twenty-three co-authors report the first gas-centrifuge production of zirconium-96, at 88.28% enrichment and 179.816 grams total mass. Low-background HPGe detectors check radionuclide impurities and suitability for rare-event searches. The tightest limit, obtained at sea level, on the half-life of double beta decay of zirconium-96 to the first excited state of molybdenum-96 is set above 3.9 times ten to the nineteenth years at 90% confidence.
arxiv-2605-13315: Zhou and colleagues build a framework linking living neural cultures to tasks through a silicon interface. Encoding and decoding between biology and computers is the core hurdle for brain cell computing. They optimise encoding settings for a cultured network steering through a simulated odour gradient, testing about 1300 settings over 4000 hours. Twelve settings learned reliably and beat tuned silicon agents on the same budget, pointing toward hybrid bio silicon systems.
arxiv-2605-13415: Barathi Ganesh HB and three colleagues present a system for telling reclaimed slurs apart from hostile uses in English, Spanish and Italian posts. Reclaimed use means the targeted group itself uses the slur, with a different meaning. Their framework combines cross-validation model selection with back-translation that triples training data while keeping meanings intact. It adds transfer learning with undersampling. XLM-RoBERTa emerges as the best foundation model, and language-specific thresholds add two to five points of F1 score.
arxiv-2605-13715: Néo Tardy studies shifted mixed character sums, sums of a non-principal Dirichlet character times a complex exponential over an interval. He proves the maximum modulus lies between square root of p times log log p and square root of p times log p. That generalises an old Montgomery result and a recent Iggidr result in two ways: general non-principal characters are allowed, and incomplete mixed character sums are considered.
arxiv-2605-13815: Youquan Liu and eleven colleagues present OmniLiDAR, a unified text-tuned spread frame making LiDAR scans in a shared range-image form. It covers eight domains spanning adverse weather, sensor-setup changes and cross-platform capture. To train a single model over mixed domains, they present a Cross-Domain Training plan mixing domains within each mini-batch and using tuning to steer making. They further propose Cross-Domain Feature shaping catching headed links along azimuth and height axes. Tests show strong making truth and steady gains in later uses.
arxiv-2605-14015: Jauregui and Miyamoto build distributed statistical zero-knowledge proofs from the Sumcheck protocol. Such proofs remain scarce and mostly tied to single problems, despite rapid progress on interactive proofs. The paper defines the statistical variant, with each node's view mimicked within tiny statistical distance. It then lifts the old Sumcheck into a modular building block, yielding a distributed version that checks polynomial sum claims over a finite field.
arxiv-2605-14315: Huang and four co-authors propose TurboVGGT, a visual geometry transformer with alternating attention for fast multi-view 3D reconstruction. Efficient transformers share one sparsity ratio across layers and frames, with no way to learn representative tokens for global links. TurboVGGT uses sparse global weighting guided by sparsity selection for global links across frames, plus frame weighting for local details. Benchmarks show fast multi-view reconstruction with competitive quality.
arxiv-2605-14515: Tulewicz, Bartkiewicz and Nori show that spin chirality, a twist measure also behind chiral spin liquids, can reveal entanglement hidden from single-copy tests. The gap between partial-transpose and purity moments splits exactly into a chirality-chirality correlator. A multi-channel spectral classifier built on this idea is claimed to reach near-perfect recall on bound entangled states, and the approach was validated on three IBM quantum processors.
arxiv-2605-14815: Hou and Rupprecht reframe camera control for video models as geometric guidance rather than an implicit mapping. Existing methods learn camera motion to video mappings with extra camera modules and paired data, which can bias models toward narrow outputs. The authors instead reformulate camera control into displacement fields applied by differentiable resampling of latent features during denoising. Effective camera control is claimed with minimal quality loss versus fine-tuned baselines, and the training-free method doubles as a probe revealing universal biases across video models.
arxiv-2605-15015: Chris Davis Jaldi and five others compare small and large language models as teammates for designing school assessments. Large models can align questions with Bloom's taxonomy, but judging them is often subjective, closed-source, and detached from classroom needs. Small models, running locally, match large ones on key teaching-quality measures while protecting privacy and resources. Model-based judging, however, shows steady bias against expert ratings, so expert review remains essential.
arxiv-2605-15215: Duling Xu and six others present SkillSmith, a compiler-runtime framework that turns agent skills into minimal executable interfaces. Injecting whole skills as context wastes tokens and repeats skill-specific reasoning at every step. SkillSmith extracts fine-grained operational boundaries from skills, so agents call only the relevant components at run time. On SkillsBench it cuts solve-stage tokens by 57.44 percent, thinking iterations by 42.99 percent, and solve time by half. Artifacts compiled by a stronger model can also serve smaller runtime models.
arxiv-2605-15315: Jingjing Wang and eight colleagues propose LaMR, a structured context-pruning framework for coding agents that spend most tokens reading repository files. Single-objective pruners collapse relevance into one score, forcing one transition prior to serve both contiguous semantic spans and sparse structural lines. LaMR splits relevance into semantic evidence and dependency support, each with its own conditional random field. They fuse through mixture-of-experts gating and a final aggregation layer. Labels come from AST-based analysis of existing corpora, denoising teacher labels without new annotation.
arxiv-2605-15415: Miklós Bóna and Vincent Vatter study decreasing binary trees where two-child vertices are colored red or blue. One bijection, to ordered set partitions into odd-sized blocks arranged as alternating permutations, gives an exponential generating function. It equals one over one minus tangent. A second bijection, to nonplane decreasing 1-2 trees with binary labels, proves the count equals two to the n minus one times the nth Euler number. Refining by right edges yields Boolean-Eulerian polynomials, with gamma-positivity and real-rootedness carried over from Eulerian polynomials.
arxiv-2605-15515: Vladimir Chernov, Matthew Harper, and Ben-Michael Kohli ask if the Links-Gould polynomial can spot causality in spacetimes. There, causal links show as links of light-ray spheres. Past work showed two homology theories catch causality in full. The Alexander-Conway polynomial falls short on one family of cases. The team shows the Links-Gould polynomial splits all those cases from causally unlinked cases. It may thus catch causality in full. They also work out the Seifert genus of the family.
arxiv-2605-15615: Senmao Tian, Xiang Wei, and Shunli Zhang tackle the base-new trade-off in vision-language transfer. They spot lopsided confusion: class A samples are misread as class B, with rare reversals. For known classes, cross-entropy tuning eases this bias. For unseen classes, pretraining bias sticks and harms generalization. NeRP uses neutral prompts and reference images to gauge class priors. It flips prior-led guesses between confusable pairs when proof is thin. Tests on 15 few-shot and cross-domain sets lift unseen-class accuracy while known-class scores hold.
arxiv-2605-16015: Vishnu Saj and three colleagues replace the conservative domain-randomization approach to quadrotor control with an adaptive outer loop that senses disturbances as they happen. A Residual Dynamics Predictor estimates forces and moments in flight from state and control history alone, while a calibration bridge and thrust correction align simulation with hardware from seconds of flight data. Tests on a Crazyflie micro-quadrotor show precise tracking under mass changes, asymmetric payloads, and swinging slung loads.
arxiv-2605-16115: Zhou, Hunt, and Bode test how people react to robot yielding moves during tight emergency evacuations. A game-like virtual test with 56 people compared Hide, LineEscape, Freeze, and ShortestPath in halls with and without refuge niches. People liked Hide most, then LineEscape, Freeze, and ShortestPath last. Skipping an obvious niche hurt: it raised felt delay a lot, even when paths were in fact clear.
arxiv-2605-16215: Theimer-Lienhard and seven colleagues introduce Fully Open Meditron, the first fully open pipeline for clinical language-model decision help. Most open models share weights only, hiding data sources, curation, and generation steps. Their pipeline joins a doctor-checked corpus from eight public medical QA sets plus three vetted synthetic add-ons, with leak screening and four-physician checks. All MeditronFO variants beat their base models, and Apertus-70B-MeditronFO gained 6.6 points on aggregate medical benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-16315: Kujur finds the collapse is not a quirk of timing or of the rule change. It holds whenever tested, vanishes when the removed actions return, and bites harder under function approximation. Wipe out every positive-reach contingent decision and learners rush to a fixed point of near-maximum loss, a deterministic exploitation attractor. Leave just one such decision point standing and the collapse never arrives. A frozen baseline plus a fixed-opponent control pin the cause on co-adaptation under constraint, not on the perturbation itself.
arxiv-2605-16415: Levine and Weiss examine why diffusion models make lifelike images unlike training data, a trait called creativity. If the denoiser were Bayes-optimal for a training set, the model would simply copy training samples, so that trait is surprising. They show the trait comes from an interaction between denoiser design and target distribution, giving formulas for samples under linear, polynomial, and bottleneck denoisers. Small changes to the UNET denoiser yield different results, often highly nonrealistic samples. Diffusion models succeed only when the denoiser's bias aligns with the target distribution.
arxiv-2605-16515: Karimi Monsefi and eight colleagues define SeamCam in a 2026 paper, a detection-based score for camouflage seamlessness. Given an image and a species, it builds detection proposals and masks. It scores one minus the best recoverable overlap with the true mask, so higher means harder to spot. In a study with 94 people and 2,390 comparisons, SeamCam matched human judgments in 78.82% of cases in their test. That beat the prior best by about a quarter. The team also released a 1,521-image benchmark for fair testing.
arxiv-2605-16615: Kitch and Shah study how to learn what evaluators value when they combine several criteria into one overall judgment, as in admissions or medical triage. They assume only that the preference function never decreases when any single criterion improves. Under that minimal assumption, they characterize how badly common modeling assumptions can mislead learning. Their new algorithm learns any such preference function robustly, matches linear methods when linearity holds, and proves useful in simulations, real data, and a peer-review case study.
arxiv-2605-16815: Pan and colleagues study universal graph backdoor defense, covering subgraph and feature attacks on graph neural networks. Structure defenses assume poisoned nodes connect to subgraph triggers, but they fail against feature attacks that preserve topology. Backdoors of either kind show lower feature homophily, less local feature consistency with neighbors, than clean nodes. The authors exploit node local consistency, via a neighbor reconstruction loss, to spot backdoors, plus robust training to remove trigger effects. Tests show sharply lower attack success with competitive clean accuracy under both attacks.
arxiv-2605-16915: Huang refines the KamLAND fit with Daya Bay's antineutrinos. JUNO's parameters from 59 days differ 0.2 sigma from KamLAND 2013 values, while short-baseline experiments deviate from Huber-Müller at 5 MeV. Huang builds a framework tied weakly to reactor flux, from measured uranium and plutonium fission spectra from Daya Bay and KamLAND data. With Huber-Müller, KamLAND 2013 results reproduce to 0.1 sigma. With Daya Bay spectra, the mass-squared fit falls from 7.53 to 7.50 times ten to minus five eV squared, agreeing better with JUNO, suggesting spectrum differences cause the tension.
arxiv-2605-17015: The BESIII collaboration reports the first observation of eta-c to Sigma-zero anti-Sigma-zero decay via a radiative psi(3686) transition, using 2.7 billion psi(3686) events. The branching fraction depends strongly on interference between eta-c(1S) and non-eta-c(1S) processes, giving about 2.59 thousandths for destructive interference and about 1.18 thousandths for constructive interference. No significant signal appears for h-c to Sigma-zero anti-Sigma-zero decay in the psi(3686) to pi-zero h-c transition, and its branching fraction is capped at 1.02 ten-thousandths at 90 percent confidence.
arxiv-2605-17115: Trivedi and three colleagues build a fake-news detector for Indian media that reads both pictures and text. A vision network scans each image while a language encoder reads the wording, and a fuzzy logic layer blends the two into a trust score. An attention step weighs each channel before the final call. Tested on an Indian news dataset, the system beats earlier methods on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score.
arxiv-2605-17315: Chang and Choi study factorization in a one-dimensional Bézout domain built as a union of Laurent polynomial rings with p-power roots adjoined. The domain is almost Dedekind exactly when the base field's characteristic differs from p. They pin down when irreducibles survive the passage to the union. They show algebraically closed and certain finite fields leave no irreducibles at all. They also prove a countable prime-factorization theorem for rationals at p equal to two.
arxiv-2605-17415: Sharma presents IVF-TQ, a streaming vector-search index whose residual compression needs no codebook and no retraining. A fixed random rotation plus a precomputed Lloyd-Max scalar quantizer, set only by bit width and dimension, replaces codebooks fitted to early samples that silently lose recall as data grows. A sphere-uniform error bound gives a structural guarantee learned methods lack. Across nine controlled cells it holds steady at one fixed configuration while per-batch retraining never closes the gap.
arxiv-2605-17615: Debnath, Badal and Bhattacharya formulate junction conditions for Scalar-Tensor-Vector Gravity and build collapse theory. An interior Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker spacetime with matter and dark energy matches an exterior Reissner-Nordström-like spacetime through an STVG shell. From the standard STVG action they derive junction conditions relating field values and derivatives. With these conditions, collapse proceeds with horizon formation in finite proper time. Two models end as an extremal black hole and as a collapse toward a sub-extremal one, seen from far away.
arxiv-2605-18115: Yiwei Guo and six colleagues present WinTok, a hybrid visual tokenizer splitting visual reading from making with shared tokens. Single token spaces strain to serve both semantic ideas and pixel rebuild, so WinTok adds tuned semantic tokens to pixel tokens, easing cross-task clash without dual tokenizers. A one-sided teaching step guides semantic tokens with pretrained vectors from any visual base model, lending strong sorting power. Across 10 benchmarks, WinTok improves rebuild, reading, and making, beating UniTok by 11.2 percent in classification accuracy with rFID 0.41 on only 50M open-source data.
arxiv-2605-18815: Yuanqing Wang and eleven colleagues present DynaTrain, a system that switches parallelism layouts while language model training runs. Resource shifts, training phase changes, and cluster elasticity keep moving the best layout, yet most frameworks assume a fixed setup. A Virtual Parameter Space maps every distributed state onto one logical grid, turning layout changes into geometric intersections. Rank-local transfers under a memory-aware schedule then switch layouts in seconds, beating checkpoint-based rivals by up to three orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2605-18915: Wenzhuo Xu and six colleagues break multimodal language models by spreading a harmful request across several images instead of one. Single-image jailbreaks cannot distribute requests, carry as much information, or exploit extra visual reasoning tasks as distractions. Their DMN framework combines a distributed instruction, multimodal evidence and a number-chain task to push models past their safety training. Tests show attack success above ninety percent on Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-pro, beating other baselines by a wide margin and exposing weak multi-image safety alignment.
arxiv-2605-19215: Payam Piray shows two kinds of uncertainty push search in opposite directions, though both raise posterior uncertainty. Volatility means hidden reward states drift; stochasticity means outcomes are seen through noise. Extending the Gittins index to Gaussian bandits, he proves volatility boosts search while stochasticity suppresses it. He also derives CAUSE, a closed form bonus that inherits the same pattern. CAUSE beats standard methods in noisy mixed settings and a Gittins policy whose rested optimality fails in restless settings. The work predicts faulty noise inference flips search, with psychiatric implications.
arxiv-2605-19315: R. Martínez von Dossow, A. Martín-Ruiz, and Luis Urrutia extend work on tilted Weyl semimetals into the type-II overtilted regime, where electron and hole pockets coexist. From a lattice model, they compute the action and cross-check it with chiral kinetic theory keeping both Fermi-sea and Fermi-surface parts. A hard cutoff tied to lattice bandwidth keeps the axion-like response finite across the transition, though tilt-dependent terms remain. For WTe2, the two contributions cancel, leaving a finite and anisotropic Hall response.
arxiv-2605-19715: Ndolo and Tschorsch examine Bitcoin's V2 transport protocol, a step for encrypted peer links. While earlier attacks are now fixed, other paths to similar goals remain, rooted in design not code bugs, open to peer networks. A network attacker can identify application texts from TCP payload lengths and eclipse a target node via encrypted channels. The same attacker can downgrade all node connections to the unencrypted protocol using compatibility mechanisms. Findings are validated through network tests and simulations, with short- and long-term countermeasures.
arxiv-2605-19815: Xu, Lindholm, Raina, Olsen and Hershcovich study automatic generation and evaluation of legal propositions from Court of Justice of the European Union decisions. Their LP-Eval rubric, co-designed with legal experts, splits proposition quality into formal validity and substantive dimensions, and they release two experts' annotations for one hundred model-generated propositions. Language models mostly produce well-formed, high-quality propositions, better for established cases than recent ones. Rubric-guided model judgments track experts better than direct overall scoring, though they miss finer distinctions humans catch.
arxiv-2605-19915: He and colleagues argue LLM agents make group belief dynamics programmable, a break from old opinion models that assume limited reason and teamwork. Agents can join talks at scale, hold persuasion plans and work together to steer group beliefs on purpose. Controlled multi agent tests show linked agents shift beliefs in ways that settle within a few rounds. Four traits, hard to tell apart, staying power, context shifts and easy setup, make spotting deeply hard. The paper sketches a research plan spanning theory, spotting and action methods, and tooling.
arxiv-2605-20015: The ATLAS Collaboration searches for soft unclustered energy patterns, or SUEPs, whose decay products include muons. SUEPs are high-multiplicity, isotropic sprays of low-momentum particles that hidden-sector theories predict. Using proton-proton collision data at thirteen teraelectronvolts from 2015 to 2018, the search looks for a scalar mediator made by gluon-gluon fusion in Hidden Valley scenarios. The search finds no significant excess over Standard Model expectations, and exclusion limits tighten with mediator mass, reaching their smallest value for a 750 GeV mediator.
arxiv-2605-20315: Haiquan Lu and four co-workers set out Mix-Quant, phase-aware quantization for fast agentic inference. Agent jobs pile input-side work; prefilling chokes long multi-turn runs. Whole-run FP4 hurts scores badly, yet slack-filled prefilling can be cut down with scant loss, though it eats most compute. Mix-Quant runs prefilling in NVFP4 while keeping BF16 care for decoding. That split eases the choke point without denting quality. Long-context and agentic tests keep task scores near full, speeding prefilling up to three times.
arxiv-2605-21215: Miguel A. Cardona and Adam Marton revisit the bounding and dominating numbers with interval structures. They start from interval partitions of omega, inspired by Vojtáš's account of those numbers. Changing quantifiers and interval rules gives several natural variants. Universal variants are robust: in discrete, colored, restricted, bounded, and measure-theoretic settings, their numbers match the classical b and d. Existential variants flip the match, so each number equals the other classical invariant.
arxiv-2605-21315: Jason Detwiler, Ke Han, and Tao Li ask how few events tracking experiments need to tell neutrinoless double-beta decay mechanisms apart. Measuring each electron's energy and their opening angle can probe the mechanism behind the process. A single dominant mechanism can be told apart at one sigma with just a few well-rebuilt events. About ten events reach three-sigma discovery sensitivity, rising to about twenty-five with realistic rebuild errors. Tracking detectors thus stay useful even for discovery-class experiments.
arxiv-2605-21515: Chengqi Zheng and co-authors study predicting performance of symbolic and prompt programs with examples. Language-model prompting serves naturally stated tasks, yet unreliable: it may pass a few tests but fail when deployed. They study performance prediction. Given a program, symbolic such as Python or a prompt run on a language model, plus a few in-domain examples, they forecast results on new tasks from the same domain. They find symbolic performance is all or nothing, while prompt performance is diffuse.
arxiv-2605-21615: Chang Liu and co-authors present ASSEMBLAGE-DEEPHISTORY, a cross-build binary dataset with temporal coverage. Existing corpora capture just one or two axes of binary variation, never cross-build diversity, version history, and CVE labels together. Their set holds more than seventy-three thousand binaries from two hundred forty-eight open-source projects, built across GCC, Clang, and MSVC at varied optimization levels on Linux and Windows. Each binary links to source code, functions, debug info, variant builds, past versions, and vulnerable functions.
arxiv-2605-21715: Heyuan Yao, Willow Kowalik, and Izzy Grosof develop the first throughput-optimal scheduling policies for computing jobs. Their resource needs vary continuously, as CPU and memory demands do in practice. Earlier theory assumed a small set of job classes, a poor fit when almost no two jobs share the same requirements. Their policies come in preemptive and nonpreemptive forms, gain efficiency through load-aware discretization, and beat existing index policies on parametrized distributions and Google Borg datacenter traces.
arxiv-2605-22215: Marco Gregnanin and co-authors present Sig-Graph GAN, a generative adversarial graph neural network for synthetic time series data. Financial time series shift over time, limiting traditional models that assume stable patterns. GANs emulate complex patterns through a generator-versus-critic framework. Sig-Graph GAN combines the time-series signature, a structured summary of time evolution, with long short-term memory for time-linked structure and graph neural networks for shape patterns. The model targets realistic synthetic financial series that respect shifting patterns and time dependence.
arxiv-2605-22715: Chen and others build AnyMo, a geometry aware framework for human motion sensing across wearable setups in the wild. Inertial signals shift with body placement, orientation, hardware and sampling, blocking transfer across devices. AnyMo therefore simulates physics based signals over dense body placements and pre trains a graph encoder on paired synthetic views. Motion tokens then align with a language model for motion language tasks. Tests show zero shot gains across 14 unseen activity data sets, plus stronger retrieval and captioning.
arxiv-2605-22815: The CONUS team reports new limits on physics inside and beyond the Standard Model. Its data come from neutrino scattering at reactors in Brokdorf and Leibstadt. Germanium detectors at Leibstadt saw the scattering signal at 3.7 sigma, matching the Standard Model forecast. The team tightened bounds on the neutrino magnetic moment and millicharge, and on light new mediators. It also measured the Weinberg angle at low momentum transfer.
arxiv-2605-23015: Frei and colleagues validate gyrokinetic simulations of the radial electric field and heat transport before the L-H transition in ASDEX Upgrade. They simulate several L-mode time slices from one hydrogen discharge with stepwise rises in heating power, using the GENE-X code with X-point geometry. As edge conditions rise, particle and heat fluxes grow and the electric field well deepens. Simulated profiles match measurements well at each slice. Turbulence-driven poloidal flows dominate inside the well.
arxiv-2605-23115: Ma studies bike-sharing demand prediction under temporal domain shift, using March Citi Bike data from 2021 to 2026. Models trained on past station-hour data degrade as travel patterns change. The Gen-ROTDA framework fits a target station-time anchor from a labeled target subset. It transfers residuals rather than raw demand, generates residual features with a label-preserving generator, and trims costly matches before training the predictor. It achieves the lowest error on the 2025 to 2026 job and is the best optimal-transport-family method across years.
arxiv-2605-23215: Oliaro and ten coauthors introduce FastKernels, a suite of 384 tasks drawn from 47 architectures across 8 categories, whose kernels reimplement 94.6 percent of HuggingFace Transformers architectures with matching outputs. Candidates are scored at each kernel level and end to end inside their models they come from. With five agents, kernel-level speedups of 1.6 to 6.6 times fall to at most 1.25 times, only 20 percent of winning kernel sets run as-is, and kernel-level marks mis-rank: Claude Code matches or beats KDA in isolation, but KDA scores 3 times higher.
arxiv-2605-23315: Usama and Chang test shared likeness across 16 language models from 8 families on 800 thinking problems spanning math, science, common sense, and truth. Their study reveals three splits. First, a hardness flip: models converge more on problems they fail as a group than on those they solve. Second, a making gap: pre-choice codes align while post-choice codes diverge. Third, surface rightness: shared data is read across models but exerts minimal causal pull.
arxiv-2605-23515: Chaplin and colleagues propose ensemble asteroseismology for K-dwarfs, where sun-like oscillations have barely been seen. Instead of chasing single stars, they stack frequency power spectra from hundreds of K-dwarfs in narrow temperature bands, weighted to lift the shared shake envelope. The trade is clear: no single-star frequencies, but a measurable joint envelope that probes surface bubbling, magneto-convection, and magnetic activity effects. PLATO catalog forecasts point to solid joint detections well into the K-dwarf range.
arxiv-2605-23715: Reiter surveys NLG evaluation from past to future. In 1990, when the field had close ties to language study, very little formal trial evaluation in the modern sense existed. By 2026, with NLG closely linked to machine learning, trial evaluation is required and core to research. Many methods grew over this period, the latest being LLM-as-Judge. Looking ahead, impact, quality, and safety evaluation will matter more as large numbers of people daily use NLG tech.
arxiv-2605-23915: Yuyang Yao and Shaocheng Luo refine the Intelligent Driver Model, the classic car following rule behind adaptive cruise control. That model tends to stabilize slowly and waste road capacity. Their SEIDM adds an adaptive safety factor. It dials the safe deceleration term up or down with conditions, letting cars follow more boldly when safe and more warily near hazards. Urban simulations show shorter stabilization gaps and faster settling to steady flow. SEIDM beats the original model and its variants on stability and efficiency.
arxiv-2605-24015: Lee and three co-authors unpack how contrastive learning interacts with graph collaborative filtering, where scores aggregate learnable weights over multi-hop neighbour pairs. They show good recommendations can come from upweighting only a small subset of pairs whose neighbours resemble the target user and item, with effects varying by pair type. Analyzing the Sampled Softmax loss, they find its weight-update dynamics flawed in key ways. Their fix, NT-SSM, induces type-aware update dynamics and beats Sampled Softmax consistently across data sets and filtering models.
arxiv-2605-24115: Yeh and Mitra study Anderson localization, where disorder pins a lone particle in place, plus the matching delocalization shift in the Aubry-Andre model. They work in operator Krylov space, watching the system at strobe times rather than continuously. That turns the dynamics into a Floquet problem, yielding spectra with less compute and letting Krylov settings be read straight from the discrete-time autocorrelation. The localized phase shows no Porter-Thomas spread and a pinned wavefront, while the delocalized phase shows both, and the critical point looks multi-fractal.
arxiv-2605-24515: Iulia Pleşu, Alexandra Băicoianu, and Ioana Cristina Plajer compare three machine-learning designs for finding and monitoring lakes in Sentinel-2 satellite data. They test the models on accuracy, robustness, and practical use, and set them against classic NDWI thresholding on a sample image. The best model emerges from that head-to-head comparison. The paper also proposes color schemes tuned to water-quality indices, replacing standard mappings that can mislead environmental readers.
arxiv-2605-24615: Evangelos G. Filothodoros finds a structure in gap rules for the large-N Gross-Neveu model at complex-number chemical potential in spaces four k plus three. The rules split into higher-order discrete Laplace patterns and a cutoff-tied part from a cut long-range series of a special function. The picture links thermal field theories in odd dimensions to exactly solvable one-way quantum problems. Thermal mass values at certain complex-number chemical levels sit where energy matches heat states of thermal modes. That matches OPE flip tricks.
arxiv-2605-24915: Seokjun Choi leads a one-shot method recovering surface properties from one desktop capture. Each frame carries little data, so the task is tight. The setup shines a polarized color pattern from an LCD screen and records it with a polarization camera and quarter-wave plate. A feed-forward transformer maps readings to per-pixel direction, color, roughness, and metalness. To beat scarce training data, the team grows measured reflectance functions through a generative manifold. Tests on a real desktop rig beat prior methods across varied scenes.
arxiv-2605-25415: Lingyao Li and colleagues benchmark language models as academic paper reviewers across 898 papers from two major venues. Twelve models are scored on calibration, human agreement, and resistance to hidden prompt-injection attacks. Models systematically overrate weak papers and diverge in emphasis, under-flagging clarity while over-flagging reproducibility, with reviews two to three times longer than human ones. Hidden instructions can lift low-scoring papers to acceptance levels, with success varying sharply by model family. Review use needs safeguards against both built-in bias and adversarial manipulation.
arxiv-2605-25515: Samuel Korsky sharpens the growth rate of integer-valued Lipschitz functions on sparse random graphs. Earlier bounds left a wide gap for the logarithm of the growth constant on graphs with edge chance d over n. Letting graph size and then average degree grow, he pins the value to pi squared over six times d, up to a vanishing error. He also bounds the same quantity on the d-dimensional hypercube, sandwiching it between that same leading term and a slowly growing multiple of log d over d.
arxiv-2605-25815: Ye and colleagues present the first study of EvoMap, an agent network. From over 1.5 million assets and 128,000 agents, growth-first trades reuse, evolution and auditability. The credit economy rewards posting over adoption, so agents mass produce assets, 98 percent never reused. Asset ranking uses unverified self-reported metadata, letting agents manipulate scores. Unverified logs let over 84 percent of approved assets pass vacuous tests. Future networks need verifiable execution and evaluation.
arxiv-2605-26215: Alfred Li, Daisuke Miki, and Yanbei Chen derive a universal condition for generating entanglement under general bilinear interactions in white thermal noise. Using a Lindblad-style description, they analyze multimode systems and derive a separability rule. Applied to gravity-induced entanglement, the result says gravity must beat thermal noise for entanglement to arise. That bound cannot be eased by changing the initial state or adding mediator systems, though those factors can boost it once it exists.
arxiv-2605-26315: Sandeep Kumar, Virginia Smith, and Chhavi Yadav's 2026 paper tests whether curriculum learning can toughen direct preference optimization for safety alignment in large language models. Their Staged-Competence framework orders preference data by difficulty, samples by competence, and progressively updates the reference model. In three families, it cuts harmful response rates out of distribution by sixteen percent and jailbreak success by twenty percent, with near-zero over-refusal and preserved capabilities. It matches baseline safety with only seventy-five percent of training data and separates safe from unsafe responses better.
arxiv-2605-26515: Xintao Xia and three colleagues learn directed acyclic graphs under heteroscedastic errors. They prove new results showing uneven noise can reveal which way causation runs. Their RESQUE method repeats two steps: building residuals, then composite quantile fits, finding sink nodes one by one through scale coefficients that stay steady across quantiles. Theory backs recovery of node order and graph shape even as variable count grows with sample size. Simulations and benchmark data favor RESQUE over older methods, especially when causal facts hide partly in spread rather than averages.
arxiv-2605-26815: Du and three colleagues prove exact formulas for vertex-coprime Ramsey numbers on coprime graphs. The mixed vertex-coloring number equals the m-th prime, where m sums the color class sizes minus one. A prime-clique argument gives the upper bound, and a prime-bin coloring gives the lower bound. The same certificate view reduces the edge-coloring variant to classical Ramsey numbers and settles the balanced two-color threshold at the prime indexed by twice k minus two.
arxiv-2605-26915: Pihtili and six colleagues use Gaussian processes to map extended objects for joint sensing and communication at millimeter-wave bands. Rather than treating objects as point scatterers, the method maps extended shapes with bistatic sensing under the 5G New Radio standard. Tests on mapping and on joint mapping-plus-tracking show the approach sharpens awareness of surroundings in future wireless systems under real-world settings.
arxiv-2605-27215: Biagi and co-authors study spin-orbit torque switching in tantalum and tungsten magnetic tunnel junctions. The tantalum layer adds an orbital current that lifts torque four-fold above the spin Hall effect of tantalum alone, with stronger anisotropy and tolerance for high-heat annealing. Built into three-terminal devices, the tantalum-tungsten stack matches tungsten-based performance. The team also shows a trial of vertical non-local switching driven by orbital torques, which could simplify bottom-pinned device fabrication.
arxiv-2605-27315: Yifan Jiang, Ruoxi Ning, Sheng Yao, and Freda Shi ask whether real images help vision-language models judge word concreteness and imagery. They find image context often hurts agreement with human ratings, worst where visual evidence matters least. Telling models to attend only to text at inference time eases the damage on those vulnerable word sets.
arxiv-2605-28015: S. S. Agaev, K. Azizi, and H. Sundu test whether a bound pair of J/psi mesons could explain the X(6200) resonance. Using QCD sum rules, they compute the pair's mass near sixty-three hundred mega-electronvolts and its decay width, then map its dominant and rarer decay channels. Mass and width both fit the observed resonance, supporting the molecule picture.
arxiv-2605-28115: Yang and colleagues slim vision-language models by keeping visual token sequences compact end to end, from encoder through cache. Their CIVIC framework avoids the ragged memory access that makes post-hoc pruning slow in practice, cutting cache memory to about a third. Accuracy held across reasoning and grounding tests.
arxiv-2605-28515: Melih Catal and four colleagues measure vertical integration bias, the tilt of provider-linked language models toward their provider's ecosystem in generated code. Their VIBench benchmark covers twenty provider-choice integration cases in direct and agentic code generation. Ten linked frontier models show positive bias in direct generation, with six reaching statistical significance and effects up to about nineteen points. Agentic workflows amplify the bias further, and early ecosystem choices persist into later files at rates up to about ninety percent.
arxiv-2605-28715: Aldo Gamboa and ten colleagues present SEOBNRv6EHM, a multi-pole waveform model for binaries on planar orbits. Orbital eccentricity marks formation channels and must be modeled. The model covers the main mode plus five more modes across infall, merger, and ringdown, for merging pairs, captures, and flyby meets. Built in the one-body framework with resums of wave-reaction, it matches prior SEOBNRv5 accuracy for quasi-circular and small-eccentricity pairs. It reaches record scores for highly eccentric systems, with gaps below or near 2 percent up to 0.9.
arxiv-2605-28915: Jacob Fox gives a short proof of a recursive upper bound for the Alon-Saks-Seymour problem. That problem asks how many colors a graph needs when its edges split into at most k complete bipartite pieces. His bound caps the value at k plus one by the value at k plus the value at roughly a quarter of k. The recursion yields a new upper bound whose exponent beats the prior best by a factor near two, and it is nearly sharp.
arxiv-2605-29015: Ali Najjar Amiri and colleagues build an engineered set of rare-earth ions by cutting gold nanoholes on thulium-implanted lithium niobate. The hybrid stack supports local and lattice plasmon resonances plus joint atomic modes from the ion ensemble. Timed glow and heat tests show stronger emission from joint atomic effects via the lattice, distinct from single-emitter Purcell boost. The work opens a path toward broadband, large-scale, geometry-controlled quantum links in solids.
arxiv-2605-29115: Geoffrey Bradway and colleagues build unix-ctf, a generator of capture-the-flag tasks. Each task hides a flag in a fresh Linux container using one Unix feature, and the agent recovers it. An LLM-assisted pipeline writes planting and recovery scripts under a two-way contract. Hide scripts leave no plaintext flag trace, and find scripts recover the flag in a fresh directory. The pipeline lands 656 of 750 as variants covering 155 techniques, far above baseline. Qwen3-8B fine-tuning lifts solve rates from about 12 to about 44 percent.
arxiv-2605-29215: Ben Sun and colleagues devise a broadband mid-infrared single-photon time-stretch spectrometer built on upconversion and counting. A broad light spanning 2 to 4 micrometers is converted to the near-infrared band, using fiber and silicon sensors. Photon timing is registered by a low-jitter counter, yielding resolution near half a wavenumber in light well under one photon per nm per pulse. Against earlier spectrometers, the time-stretch design favors single-pixel simplicity and high-throughput acquisition. Reach, sub-wavenumber resolution, and room-temperature use suit lab and life uses.
arxiv-2605-29615: Linhao Zhang and three colleagues test whether vision-language models spot fine-grained visual differences in web interfaces. DiffSpot builds image pairs by mutating one CSS property of a target element. It re-renders the page and records the property and element. The set holds thousands of pairs, plus no-difference pairs as hallucination checks. Testing thirteen frontier models with no examples, the best finds only 40.7% of true changes. Hard-tier recall stays under a quarter for every model, and neither pixel size nor CLIP distance predicts recall.
arxiv-2605-29715: Mufan Xu and six colleagues build a dialogue learner that reads a user's shifting, half-spoken needs before it answers. Their frame, UKA, tracks doubt about what the user needs and uses active learning both to gather conversational knowledge and to pick replies. A Theory-of-Mind doubt gauge steers the model toward replies that draw out more telling user feedback.
