The learner thus explores user-matched knowledge while training yet stays steady at test time, beating strong rivals on reply quality and user match.
arxiv-2605-29815: Krzysztof Żurawicki and four colleagues benchmark language-model peer reviews against human reviews. The Peer Review AI Benchmark measures review specificity, style, and engagement, applied to eleven thousand machine reviews of one thousand conference papers. Generated reviews diverge from human feedback: model ratings run less variable, positively biased, and overconfident, with cross-reference patterns that depend on the model. Models also write longer, complex reviews yet miss the atomic weaknesses humans note. The benchmark diagnoses which review tasks models can support today and which need further development before deployment.
arxiv-2605-30015: Zizhen Deng and seven colleagues attack the weak real-world reach of supervised causal learning, framed as supervised prediction. Past practice gaps synthetic versus real performance, breaks under distribution shift, and fails compositional tests. Their TTT-SCL framework builds training sets on the fly for each test case, and links to score-based methods through a scoring function. Tests on synthetic, pseudo-real, and real data show it beating supervised causal learners and classic discovery methods. Test-time training can thus rescue supervised causal discovery from distribution-shift fragility.
arxiv-2605-30215: Alessandro Burzio and eleven co-authors present DéjàView, a looped transformer for multi-view reconstruction. Feed-forward transformers have grown past a billion parameters, yet layers often repeat operations. DéjàView applies one looped block recurrently to per-view features. Trained once, it matches or beats larger baselines across five benchmarks. It uses a fraction of their parameters at comparable compute, with step count as a knob. The looped design beats an identical variant with independent parameters, pointing to explicit iteration as a stronger inductive bias.
arxiv-2605-30315: Anany Kotawala frames paired LLM evaluation as a hypothesis-testing problem, inverting level and power tests, and reporting a resolution ratio. Across two LLM leaderboards, many pairwise rankings do not meet a paired-test resolution target. 11 of 40 Open LLM Leaderboard v1 comparisons and 4 of 9 MMLU adjacent pairs are unresolved at standard levels. An expansion with a second-order constant shows the unpaired Cohen shortcut deviates from the sample size by a factor of two. Three of five standard calculators inherit this deficit.
arxiv-2605-30415: Francesco De Bernardis asks how domain training reshapes talk in language models, using old cosmology. Phase 1 trains a small model on a pre-Copernican text set with sun-centered notes stripped out. Phase 2 tunes a bigger trained model on the same set. Phase 1 models give Earth-motion lines, but these stay shaky and weak. Phase 2 tuning shifts talk toward old-style frames, while stance splits stay steady inside those frames. More Earth-centered lines come from frame shifts, not from stance shifts.
arxiv-2605-30515: Panda and Pramanik study voting rules for choosing social acts, the shared outcomes a group must live with. They ask which unanimous rules, ones that follow a choice everyone ranks first, can run through obviously strategy-proof mechanisms, designs where honest reporting is plainly the best move at every step. Their answer is stark: among unanimous rules, only dictatorial ones, where a single person's ranking decides, can be implemented that way. The result draws a sharp boundary around how much honesty-friendly design can achieve in group choice.
arxiv-2605-31015: Happi-Tchakounte and colleagues present a two-patch model for disease vector-animal spread with shifts driven by landscape change. Landscape change drives spread and range of vectors and hosts, whose homes fragment through human acts. Their model mixes landscape change with vector and animal numbers, with shifts based nonlinearly on anthropization levels. Analysis shows low human acts allow them to coexist, while high human acts lead to vector die-out. For middle levels, the shift is not always steady, but may occur via splits.
arxiv-2605-31115: Zheng and colleagues propose Polyphony for dual-hand splitting, marking actions for both hands from videos. Hurdles include hand links, visual asymmetry, and meaning vagueness. Stage one swaps training between left- and right-hand batches for balance while sharing an encoder. Stage two aligns marks with action labels for similar actions. Stage three uses diffusion splitting with fusion and tuned weighting. Polyphony achieves state-of-the-art on dual-hand sets, gaining 17 points. On Breakfast, it beats a prior method using a larger backbone.
arxiv-2605-31215: Miele and colleagues make masked generative models cheaper by letting a fixed-point solver handle part of the denoising work. Standard masked models need full bidirectional transformers at every step, which costs training time and hurts quality on small sampling budgets. Their CoFRe framework adds a cross-step consistency loss and reuses prior solutions across steps, warming the solver from unchanged, still-masked and newly revealed tokens. Pretrained models convert with short fine-tuning, and OpenWebText tests cut parameters by 39 percent and training time by 12 percent.
arxiv-2606-00015:
Zhang and co-authors built a digital teaching assistant for one of the hardest courses in computer science in this 2026 arXiv paper on SortingHat. Operating systems courses challenge students with complex inner workings and varied lab setups, while usual teaching struggles to match varied backgrounds and learning speeds. SortingHat answers with a 3D digital human powered by large language models, offering personalized and context-aware guidance. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds its answers in course materials.

Beyond tutoring, the system generates exercises tailored to each student's history and performance, reinforcing weak areas while stretching stronger students. A multi-agent reinforcement learning component, where several cooperating agents learn from feedback, drives the tuning. A grading pipeline scores submissions for fairness while returning tailored, actionable feedback. The authors present the system as making the course more engaging and easier to scale, combining guidance, adaptive content, and automated grading in one assistant.
arxiv-2606-00115:
Wang and co-authors study a hard question in video learning. Can a model read true laws of motion from raw pixels alone? Their work looks at systems ruled by second-order equations that do not change over time. It asks when the hidden state can be pinned down with no doubt left.

The authors prove a slope test on level sets makes the learned space match the true state. Under that test, exact values for the physics can be read off. One short clip can be enough for systems that ring down slowly. Other cases need three runs that differ from each other. A new loss term also keeps the learned space from shrinking to nothing. Tests on made-up and real clips back the claims.
arxiv-2606-00215:
Germani and Grinstein probe the odd shape of a famed charm-linked bump, X(3872). This bump shows in decays of B mesons. Its true make-up has long sparked debate. Their frame mixes two base forms under one roof.

One form is a tight lone state. The next form is the plain part of a loose pair state in a trio. Strong force quirks that break flavor rules mix the two. The team splits the decay path into birth, spread, and clash parts. That split lets one frame serve two end states at once. Mix play can lift the charged pair path past the plain one. It can also carve sharp bends near the start of key end states.
arxiv-2606-00515:
Cao, Li, and You shield touch-rich robot work from raw sight-word-act calls. Such calls give rich sense but come at a slow rate. Force-tender tasks need fast, firm guards on touch acts. Their frame, PaCo-VLA, demotes model calls to mere bids.

A bid states task ties, stage, and a softness plan for the act. A fast guard, free of the model, vets each bid in full. Energy-tank logs and wall checks form that guard's rule book. Bad, stale, or unchecked bids can not slip past it. Tests use plug-in tasks in sims and on real gear. Marks beat raw model runs on fine place skill. No guard breach shows, even when bids turn hostile.
arxiv-2606-00615:
Vaidya and co-authors break a famed balance rule for Weyl points by loss in a light-built copy. Weyl solids must hold net twist charge at nil in full. Field use shows that rule in paired low bands of split twist. Their copy is a stacked light form of a Weyl solid.

Built gauge fields make both plain and axial fields in the stack. A plain field gives the twin low bands the rule asks for. An axial field splits the twin paths in space. One twist rides bulk bands, and its twin rides skin states. Loss at the rim damps those skin states out of sight. The seen bands thus show a twist gap in plain view. Less rim loss brings the hid path back.
arxiv-2606-00715:
Kim and Ohn study how to find the edges of objects in noisy images in this 2026 paper. The images come with no labels, so no one has marked where each object ends. There is also no set model for how the pixel values spread. The task is to rebuild the true region from raw brightness values alone.

Their method uses a smooth hinge-type loss built for this task. It can train deep neural networks with standard gradient tools. They prove the loss is Fisher consistent under a mild gap rule. They also link extra loss to the size of the error in the found region. For boundaries that are smooth in pieces, with corners and kinks, their network hits the best rate that theory allows, up to log factors. Tests show clean, stable edges across noise levels and shapes.
arxiv-2606-01115:
Guo and Guo hunt for special primes inside short intervals in this 2026 maths paper. Whether a short interval past x always holds a prime is a core number theory question. Guth and Maynard hold the best asymptotic result, and Baker, Harman, and Pintz the best lower bound. The pair turn to a sparser family: Piatetski-Shapiro primes.

Such primes come from the floor of n raised to a power c. The family echoes the famed open guess that primes of the form n squared plus one are infinite. Inside short intervals, existence is far from clear. Under set limits on the interval exponent and on c, they prove two results. An asymptotic formula counts such primes in the interval in one regime. A lower bound guarantees them in another. The work extends prime hunting in intervals to a family shaped by a power curve.
arxiv-2606-01215:
Mo and Liu merge two ways to reason about 3D scenes. Symbolic tools give clear, step-based logic for 3D tasks. But they work with a closed set of concepts. Big 3D language models take open text and new concepts. Yet their logic is a black box with no checks. APEIRIA moves symbolic patterns into a 3D language model. It uses plain language chains of thought.

Training runs in three stages of rising depth. First the model links object traits to words. Next it learns to split queries and check each step. Last it extends those skills to open concepts and nested prompts. Tests show it beats prior symbolic tools. It also matches top 3D language models on spatial tasks.
arxiv-2606-01315:
Shi, Yu, Feng, and Yuan rebuild sharp views from blurred sparse photos. Novel view synthesis makes images from new camera angles. Most tools assume clean input images. Motion blur breaks details and weakens view matching. Blur comes from camera shake, scene motion, or exposure time. Past blur-aware tools need costly per-scene optimization. DeblurNVS skips that step entirely.

DeblurNVS restores the geometry that multi-view reasoning needs. Restored structure gives back reliable correspondence cues. Those cues join target camera data to form the new view. A sharp RGB image comes out at the end. Training uses a new blurred dataset built from DL3DV-10K. Tests beat baselines on synthetic blur benchmarks. Results also hold on real blurred scenes.
arxiv-2606-01515:
Solovyev weighs how large altermagnetic splitting really is in MnF2. The compound is a widely cited candidate altermagnet. Debate persists over its band splitting size and implications. Electronic-structure calculations ground his minimal models. Those models capture the magnetic and electronic properties. Parameters for chiral magnon and spin splitting prove relatively small. The system lies in the strong-coupling regime, he finds. Most magnetic traits hinge on the ratio of hopping to repulsion.

All exchange interactions scale as one over U. A small altermagnetic hopping thus yields a proportionally small term. The anomalous Hall contribution is likewise suppressed upon doping. Optical conductivity behaves differently at high frequency, though. There the small hopping reshapes the response directly. The magneto-optical response grows dramatically as a result.
arxiv-2606-01815:
Wang and co-authors build a harder test for AI agents in service work. Real service tasks link many steps and many items. Users also act in flawed, human ways. Past tests use tidy tasks and helpful fake users. Few valid answers hide among thousands of false leads here.

Their CRAB-Bench builds tasks from a graph of constraints. A paired engine, RUSE, fakes users based on human studies. It varies persona and four traits of behavior. Tests cover four top chat models as agents. The best scores only 61 percent on first tries. Scores fall by up to 57 percent with RUSE users. Lost facts shared by users hurt most.
arxiv-2606-01915:
Díaz-Guerra and co-authors link black hole imaging to gravitational wave signals. Imaging probes the near-static geometry around a hole. Light bending in the strong field gives that view. Waves probe the dynamic response of space-time instead. Inspiral, merger, and ringdown phases carry that signal.

Both channels access the same narrow region. It lies between the horizon and the photon region. Past work tied quantities across the two channels. That link holds in the eikonal limit of optics. The team extend the correspondence to modified black holes. Such holes depart from the standard general relativity form. The work clarifies what each messenger can reveal.
arxiv-2606-02015:
Norway and Cavalié clarify what energy return ratios actually measure. Several EROI formulations coexist in the energy literature. They differ in handling self-consumption and external inputs. Those differences are not mere conventions, the pair argue. They decide what the ratio truly measures.

One reading gives the net surplus available to society. Another gives the internal efficiency of the process. Three established formulations are tested against limit cases. Only the external variant measures net surplus correctly. It excludes self-consumed energy from the investment term. Internal and standard variants converge toward efficiency instead. Multi-source systems need consistent conversion of energy flows. The paper draws lessons for energy transition assessment.
arxiv-2606-02115:
Casado-Telletxea and Rivasplata bound the error of a new drift estimator that is based on diffusion models. Estimating the drift of a stochastic differential equation is a classic problem in statistics, and it matters in many fields of science. A recent method treats drift estimation as a denoising task, using discrete samples drawn from many trajectories of the system. It leans on tools from score matching diffusion models, in a conditional form, to carry out that denoising.

Tests of that method showed promise across several classes of drift, but no proof of its accuracy had been given. This note fills that gap by drawing on results from diffusion model theory. The authors derive an explicit risk bound for the time averaged mean squared error of the estimator. The bound splits into parts that can be read and compared, so readers can see what drives the error.
arxiv-2606-02215:
Fu and co-authors let health fact-check notes learn from past corrections. Community Notes can correct health misinformation at scale. Chat model help makes those notes timely and evidence based. But each new post starts the process from scratch. Useful experience from prior cases goes unused that way.

Their EvoNote framework builds an evolving memory of past episodes. Fine-grained credit assignment is the core of the design. Feedback at the trajectory level is grounded in note quality traits. It is distilled into action level memory for later use. Steps cover claim analysis, evidence gathering, and note writing. Tests use MM-HealthCN, a benchmark of 1.2K flagged health posts. Human notes and crowd helpfulness labels come with it. Self-evolving correction is the goal of the system.
arxiv-2606-02915:
Vinaykumar, Li, Huang, and Liu address the automatic making of visual posters. Posters pack dense information into one compact page. Past evaluations of poster generators were narrow. They took paper-only inputs, covered few domains, or judged only surface looks.

The team introduces Any2Poster Bench, a benchmark spanning eight input types and five content domains. Inputs range from PDFs and slide decks to videos and notebooks. Each source comes with quiz probes that test exact fact retention and deeper understanding. Judges based on vision-language models also score layout, readability, and completeness. To test the benchmark, the team built Any2Poster Agent. It parses sources, plans a layout, renders the poster, and refines it with visual feedback. The agent averaged about 87 percent accuracy across input types and domains. On a paper-focused test it beat a prior agent by a wide margin.
arxiv-2606-03115:
Carbowitz and Kumar present SPOQ, a method for running multi-agent software work. Agent teams can write code, but they face coordination cost, weak quality checks, and thin human oversight. SPOQ joins three ideas to fix these gaps. It aims to keep speed while adding control.

First, tasks are sent out in waves computed from a dependency graph, so parallel work goes first. Second, two gates check quality: one before work starts, on the plan, and one after, on the code. Third, a human specialist joins as an agent, helps split tasks, and can be asked for help mid-run. Agents sit in three tiers by model strength. Four tests show the gains. Wave dispatch neared the best path bound and cut defects per task. Human review cut leftover defects from 0.47 to 0.03 per task. A long study across 17 code bases and more than 8,500 commits backs the lab results.
arxiv-2606-03215:
Zhang and co-authors study refund fraud in Chinese e-commerce that is powered by generative AI. Dispute systems rest on a premise: digital proof shows the physical truth. Generative AI breaks that premise. Fakes of product defects can now be made that look hyper-real, at near no cost. The team spoke with 17 merchants and 13 platform workers to map the shift.

Their account sorts the fraud into four attack paths across the deal, dispute, logistics, and chat phases. Attackers fake product flaws that look physically sound, at scale. Platforms and merchants fight back with AI screening and hard follow-up questions, such as demands for multi-angle videos. Uptake of these defenses lags. Platform structure blocks some fixes, and the tech of fakes keeps a lead. They point to privacy-safe cross-platform fraud databases. They also point to anchors built into products that can be checked later.
arxiv-2606-03615:
Hamed and Rebello test whether game or simulation should come first when teaching the photoelectric effect. Digital tools and multiple representations matter in physics teaching. Pre-service teachers in a physics course tried both tools in opposite orders. One tool is the game Photon Jump. The other is the PhET photoelectric simulation. A crossover design with 83 students measures the order effect.

Conceptual understanding was tracked across three assessments. Reflection questions capture preferences and future teaching intent. The simulation-first sequence improved scores with strong statistical significance. The game-first sequence improved far less and missed significance. Preferences for the game over the simulation depended on the assigned order. The results show the two tools complement each other. Sequence choice matters when teaching abstract physics with multiple representations. Teacher training programs can plan tool order from this evidence.
arxiv-2606-03715:
Spingarn and co-authors show that text-to-image models need far less from text encoders than assumed. Prompts are encoded into embeddings that guide image generation. Those embeddings carry rich context, like composition and attribute binding. Whether image models use that context was largely untested. The team asks which parts of the text signal are truly essential.

Two simple aspects turn out to suffice. Adjacent tokens must merge into word-level units. Word order must be marked, as positional embeddings do. A new embedding holds only word meanings plus order tags, with no context at all. It guides generation as well as full embeddings do. Visual quality and text fidelity match the standard setup. The image model itself decodes the complex language structure. Text encoder design can thus be simpler than current practice suggests.
arxiv-2606-03815:
Souza and co-authors write a hands-on tutorial for characterizing transmon qubits. Superconducting transmons lead quantum information hardware today. Reliable operation rests on careful calibration routines. Experts know those routines well. Newcomers struggle to assemble them into one working flow. The tutorial walks the full path on a commercial five-qubit processor.

Cryogenic setup and wiring come first. Parametric amplifier tuning and flux sweet-spot hunting follow. Pulse calibration and readout optimization are covered in plain steps. Qubit-qubit coupling characterization completes the pre-multiqubit checklist. The style is practical rather than theoretical. Each stage is shown on real hardware, not in the abstract. Labs bringing up transmon devices get a single reference for the whole bring-up. The guide should shorten the path from delivery to working qubits.
arxiv-2606-04215:
Naia Ormaza-Zulueta and Zia Mehrabi tackle a missed detection problem in 2026. Small informal recycling and burning sites poison poor areas. Yet they never show up in satellite images or official lists.

The pair built a detection method that does not rely on spotting the sites from above. It uses local signals: where such work tends to cluster, and how it differs from formal sites nearby. On test areas the method found sites that registries had missed. It also avoided flagging formal plants. The authors frame the work as a first step toward fairer pollution maps. Better maps could steer cleanup funds to the areas that bear the worst load.
arxiv-2606-04615:
Ignat, Nguyen, Slastikov, and Zarnescu prove sharp bounds for the Ginzburg-Landau equations, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. These equations model superconductors and related phase-transition systems. That is broader than the standard theory assumes. The system is posed on a domain in several dimensions. Its boundary data has unit length.

Their maximum principle shows every critical point stays globally bounded by one in magnitude. The bound is uniform across the domain. They then consider families of critical points. As the small parameter vanishes, these converge to a smooth sphere-valued harmonic map. For such families they prove global uniform bounds on the Laplacian. In particular, they prove global Hölder convergence of the gradients. These estimates strengthen the analytical foundation for passing from the diffuse Ginzburg-Landau model to its sharp-interface limit. The strengthening holds in this general-potential setting.
arxiv-2606-04715:
Atchadé and coauthors ask how filling in yearly life tables changes insurance surplus splits in this 2026 arXiv paper. A life table gives death rates by age, and insurers update it only once each year. Surplus is the gain or loss on policies, split here between finance causes and mortality causes.

They use a fair split method based on the Shapley value, a way to share credit among causes. Because the method needs values between yearly updates, the team tried several ways to fill those gaps. They priced a German policy portfolio with real life tables and with daily government bond prices over the study period. Two filling methods, linear and Lee-Carter, a standard mortality model, gave nearly the same split. A cruder constant filling gave a clearly different split, so the authors urge clear rules for this choice.
arxiv-2606-04815:
Mao and colleagues build language model agents that keep learning while they work, instead of freezing after training, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Lifelong learning agents for long-horizon tasks usually retrieve discrete skills or past experiences with static parameters at inference, so test-time feedback never gets internalized. Their framework, LifeSkill, is a two-stage learning system for online lifelong learning agents.

The first stage, Verifier-Guided Skill Learning, solves the lack of direct supervision for skill extraction. Candidate skills are rewarded by the average verifier success of several policy rollouts conditioned on them, so the model learns to produce skills that actually help solve tasks. The second stage, Online Skill Internalization, turns skill-conditioned trajectories into reward signals that improve the policy during test-time interaction. On LifelongAgentBench, LifeSkill improves average performance by seven absolute points over existing lifelong agent baselines.
arxiv-2606-05115:
Xiaoyang Jiang and colleagues introduce BabyCL in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that learns words and vision from a child's egocentric video in one chronological pass. Children learn word meanings from a continuous stream of first-person experience. Networks trained on recordings of that stream usually cycle through shuffled data for hundreds of epochs, nothing like how a child encounters the world.

BabyCL processes the SAYCam head-camera dataset in time order, combining streaming visual learning with an image-text contrastive objective. It adds multi-stage temporal segmentation and a dual replay buffer that manages visual and multimodal histories separately, with three contrastive losses on one shared backbone. Under a matched budget, BabyCL beat streaming baselines on the SAYCam Labeled-S benchmark and substantially narrowed the gap to offline training. The gains held across segmentation window lengths and buffer eviction rules.
arxiv-2606-05415:
Padmaja Jonnalagedda and colleagues present a system for answering questions over messy multi-source data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Real data spans tables, documents, and semi-structured files with inconsistent identifiers and semantics, and querying it requires joining evidence across sources. Existing approaches either demand manual schema work or ignore structure, and retrieval then fails on cross-source joins, multi-hop questions, and provenance.

The system discovers an executable schema from the raw data and uses it as a contract for building a knowledge graph and answering queries. Structural analysis infers identity keys, foreign keys, and source hierarchy. The schema then drives extraction, deduplication, and cross-source linking into a provenance-aware graph. In zero-shot comparisons on four question-answering benchmarks, the system beat retrieval-only and decomposition-based baselines, and ablations credited schema-conditioned routing and schema-guided construction with gains.
arxiv-2606-05515:
Muhammad Usama and colleagues introduce BRepCLIP in this 2026 arXiv paper, the first framework to pretrain CAD models in their native format. CAD models are stored as boundary representations, exact surfaces and curves stitched together by topology. Yet learning has flourished around point clouds and meshes, approximations of that precise structure. BRepCLIP instead aligns that geometry directly with language and image embeddings through contrastive pretraining.

Each CAD object becomes a sequence of face and edge tokens from separate token sets for surface and curve geometry. Descriptors tag surface types such as cylinders, tori, and freeform surfaces, and curves such as lines, arcs, and splines. A transformer encoder merges the tokens into one embedding, trained against text and image encoders. The embeddings proved far more distinctive than point-based rivals. Top-1 retrieval improved over the leading point-cloud method by roughly 40, 22, and 24 percent on three benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-05715:
Zichen Song models what happens to value as general AI replaces workers in a 2026 arXiv paper. The model separates two ceilings: what AGI could replace in principle, and what firms actually adopt given costs and friction. It tracks the span from first profitable replacement toward near-total replacement. A strict value rule anchors the math: machines transfer value but create none themselves. Only living labor counts as a source of new value.

Deeper adoption then raises the machine share of production. When adoption outruns the birth of new labor fields, total living labor shrinks. The surplus that labor feeds shrinks with it, pressing the profit rate down. At the limit of full replacement, labor, surplus, and profit all tend to zero. Song reads that limit as a boundary for value production itself, not just an efficiency leap. The paper offers the model as a lens on AGI's economic endgame.
arxiv-2606-06215:
Yijiang Yu, Hugo Perrin, Michael Graham, and Lorenzo Botto report a new instability of elastic disks in flowing fluid in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stokes flow is the slow, syrupy regime where viscosity dominates and inertia barely matters. A thin elastic disk in a shear flow, starting parallel to the flow plane, might be expected to drift sedately. The team shows it can instead start flapping.

Combining experiments with simulations, they find that past a critical flow strength the disk bends and flaps up and down in a regular rhythm. Simulations map several oscillatory solutions, including a wiggling motion that linear stability analysis predicts in advance. The flapping turns out to be a subcritical instability, one that jumps in before the naive threshold, and its key ingredient is the disk's finite extensibility, its refusal to stretch without limit. The result matters for sheet like particles such as flat polymers.
arxiv-2606-06315:
Thibaud Ardoin, Jonas Schäfer, and Gerhard Wunder show that language models can sign their own work in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self recognition means a model can tell its own output apart from other text, using signals hidden in its internal activations. As machine written text floods the internet, reliable attribution matters, and external watermarks are easy to strip. The authors ask whether the model's own representation space can carry the proof instead.

They first confirm that models reliably recognize their outputs, even when text is highly predictable. Then they steer the residual stream during generation with a random sparse vector. That nudge plants a fingerprint a detector model can later read from its activations. Attribution accuracy passed ninety eight percent across several settings, while text quality stayed intact. Sparse nudges also degraded quality less than dense noise.
arxiv-2606-06415:
João Duarte and co-authors release a software platform for designing polymers with computers in this 2026 arXiv paper on materials science. Polymers serve everywhere from electronics to medicine, but their design space is enormous, spanning monomer types, chain shapes, and mixing ratios. PolyGraphPy unifies the search in one open source Python framework. It automates quantum level simulations to build training data, then learns from it.

The simulation engine, DFTB+, generated three thousand four hundred twenty seven monomer and homopolymer cases in about twelve hours. It made eight thousand six hundred twenty seven copolymer cases in about thirty eight hours. Bayesian graph neural networks trained on that data predict properties such as static polarizability, with uncertainty estimates attached. Two generative tools propose new molecules for a target property: a transformer on text encodings of molecules, and a genetic algorithm recombining fragments. Acrylates serve as the demo family.
arxiv-2606-06715:
When readers judge a news article as liberal or conservative, does the mood toward its topic push that judgment? Chatterjee investigates in this 2026 arXiv paper, and asks whether the answer changes when software, not a person, assigns the political label. The study uses articles from AllSides, a site that rates news bias, with sentiment scores from one language model shared across all tests.

Expert human labels showed no meaningful causal effect of topic sentiment at the community level. A fine tuned GPT model told a different story: it scored best on plain accuracy, yet it was the only labeler whose output showed clear sentiment driven effects. Chatterjee reads that as shortcut learning, where tuning taught the model a fake link between sentiment and ideology that people do not use here. The warning is sharp, because accuracy scores alone cannot reveal the flaw.
arxiv-2606-06915:
Spending more computing time at answer time makes language models reason better, but the tricks are scattered. Vladislav Smirnov and a large team unify them in ThinkBooster, presented in this 2026 arXiv paper. Test time scaling includes sampling many attempts and reranking them with a scorer. Each research group evaluates its variant differently, hiding the quality cost trade off.

ThinkBooster bundles the field into one framework with three parts. A modular Python library implements the leading scaling strategies and scorer families. A benchmark grades performance and computing efficiency together. A proxy service, compatible with the OpenAI interface style, drops the methods into real applications. A visual debugger lets users inspect reasoning paths and selection choices. Experiments on math and coding tasks mapped the trade offs concretely. Uncertainty based scoring sometimes beat heavier reward models and static schemes.
arxiv-2606-07415:
He and co-authors extend their study of the fermion sign problem to finite temperature in this 2026 arXiv paper. The sign problem blocks simulations of fermionic systems, particles like electrons whose quantum states cancel against each other. Their approach uses an exchange-parity parameter and studies the zeros of the partition function, called Lee-Yang zeros. These zeros control whether results can reach the fermionic one. A one-dimensional ring model without interactions makes the analysis exact.

They track the zeros as temperature rises. The zero nearest the physical point stays close at low temperature, governing the sign factor and defeating direct extrapolation and contour-based fitting. Once temperature lifts the zeros, continuation works. From the partition function's polynomial structure they propose a low-temperature strategy: extract high-temperature fermionic properties first, then extend by fitting a temperature-dependent remainder. The model serves as a benchmark for other systems.
arxiv-2606-07515:
Luca Avena, Bet, and Busoni probe whether language models reason about chance by setting them dice and paradox problems, in this 2026 arXiv study. The team built two problem sets: standard textbook exercises and counterintuitive problems designed to trigger the heuristic shortcuts humans also fall for. Eight models were tested with and without chain-of-thought prompting, which makes models show their working. On standard problems the models averaged accuracy near 0.96, a near-ceiling performance suggesting fluent textbook competence.

Counterintuitive problems cut average accuracy to about 0.59, barely better than informed guessing on many items. Worse, disguising a problem's surface wording dropped performance by over 20 percent, evidence of token bias toward memorized forms. Embedding a misleading suggestion in the prompt cut performance by up to about a third, and no model was immune. The authors conclude current models are not yet genuine probabilistic reasoners, however strong their advanced mathematics scores appear.
arxiv-2606-07915:
Da Li and co-authors teach a neural equation-finder to fix its own mistakes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Symbolic regression hunts formulas that fit data. Neural versions generate a candidate formula in one fast pass, but errors compound: one wrong symbol early can corrupt everything after it. Earlier fixes restarted a slow global search, throwing away the speed advantage.

Their framework, EditSR, adds a second layer, a Rectifier, that edits the flawed formula step by step instead of starting over. Training data comes from an algorithm building rectification chains, edit sequences leading from wrong expressions to correct ones. Every allowed edit keeps the expression syntactically valid, so intermediate formulas always parse. Because each edit decision depends only on the current formula, early slip-ups do not poison later steps as in one-pass decoding. The design keeps inference fast while recovering much of search's accuracy.
arxiv-2606-08215:
Korbelář and Tolar analyze the Clifford groups of composite finite quantum systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Clifford group is a key group of operations on quantum systems, built from generalized Pauli matrices, and it underlies much of quantum error correction. The systems here are multipartite, meaning built from several parts whose sizes may differ, with total dimension given by the product of the part sizes. For odd total dimension the group's structure was already known to be a natural semidirect product, a tidy two-piece construction.

The even case was murkier, with partial results scattered through the literature. Using relations among generators of the associated symplectic group, the authors settle the question. Both the Clifford group and its projective version are natural semidirect products exactly when the total dimension is not divisible by four. When the dimension is a multiple of four, that tidy structure fails.
arxiv-2606-08615:
Dingyu Yao and a large team build the training data and deployment system for video models that watch endless streams, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language models are increasingly required to process unbounded video in applications such as video-call assistants, live commentary, and embodied robots. An ideal streaming system supports proactive interaction, long-horizon memory, and real-time processing. Existing models excel at offline video understanding but fall short in streaming, and dedicated infrastructure for streaming deployment is lacking.

For backbone capability, they construct a streaming training dataset of roughly a quarter million examples with a novel training objective. For deployment, their Streaming Harness is a plug-and-play system. It endows any vision-language model with three abilities: proactive interaction, long-term memory spanning hours of video, and real-time processing that keeps pace with the stream.
arxiv-2606-08715:
Yufeng Wu and Meichun Liu build a pipeline that hunts new words on the Chinese web, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neologisms, freshly coined expressions, appear constantly online. Detecting them automatically is a benchmark problem for Chinese language processing. Their method turns classic language principles into prompt-engineering skills for a language model. The pipeline has four stages: candidate generation, dictionary anchoring filtered by mutual information, a well-formedness check, and a final classification.

Applied to a corpus of over two hundred million documents, the method produced nearly a quarter million classified candidates, including several thousand labeled neologisms. For evaluation the authors develop a per-stage recall breakdown. The pipeline's overall recall factors into the product of stage-by-stage recalls. The decomposition exposes two bottlenecks: first-stage candidate coverage and the model's final judgment.
arxiv-2606-08815:
Chen and colleagues fix two failure modes in how language models are trained to reason with rewards, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The training method, called RLVR, rewards correct final answers on problems like mathematics. Its algorithm, GRPO, compares groups of solutions. Trouble arises when every attempt in a group scores the same, so the learning signal vanishes, a failure the authors name zero-advantage collapse. The model can grow confident about wrong answers late in training, which they call hallucinated certainty.

Their algorithm, ISPO, enriches the reward with signals from the model's own probabilities, no outside judge needed. One signal scores how informative the reasoning path is for the final answer. A second, token-level reward penalizes confident wrong turns at decision points. Across 3 base models and 5 mathematics benchmarks, ISPO beat strong baselines. The largest gains came on the hardest AIME-level tests, where collapsed groups are most common.
arxiv-2606-08915:
Koda and colleagues probe how hydrogen behaves inside ceria, a material used in fuel cells and car exhaust catalysts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ceria is cerium dioxide, valued for storing oxygen and conducting ions. Because hydrogen is hard to observe directly, the team implanted muons, short-lived particles acting as light stand-ins for hydrogen, into a ceria crystal. They tracked them with spin rotation measurements and density functional theory calculations.

Below about ten kelvin, the muons appeared in two states, one paramagnetic and one diamagnetic. The readings show the paramagnetic state is a polaron: the muon bonds to an oxygen while an electron settles onto a neighboring cerium atom. That electron's behavior is strongly directional, shaped by spin-orbit coupling. Warming past ten kelvin flips it, and above thirty kelvin the signal vanishes. The pattern implies rapid hopping of electrons, muons, or both at higher temperatures.
arxiv-2606-09015:
Kim and Kim complete a missing half of operator algebra, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Normal ordering recasts products of creation and annihilation operators, with all creation operators first. They are the Stirling numbers. Two twists deepen the picture: degenerate calculus, which deforms the numbers with a parameter, and the generalized Heisenberg algebra, whose commutation rules are functions of H. Second-kind operators were known in this joint setting; the first kind was not.

The first-kind family writes monomial products through degenerate factorials, undoing the second kind. The authors derive a closed product form, a recurrence relation, and a shifting rule. They prove orthogonality between the two families, showing the two maps truly invert each other. The result is a complete framework joining degenerate calculus to quantum algebras, for use where deformed oscillator systems appear.
arxiv-2606-09115:
Krieger and colleagues improve recorded robot behavior without new runs, nudging past trajectories toward better nearby ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Offline reinforcement learning learns from logged data alone, but improving beyond what the data supports can fail unpredictably. Their framework, counterfactual transport flows, starts from a low-feedback candidate trajectory. It retrieves nearby higher-feedback paths in a learned latent space, forming local preference pairs as weak supervision.

Training teaches a refinement direction specific to each source. At test time, a strength parameter controls how far the candidate is transported, trading faithfulness against improvement. The refinement is cautious by construction, since targets are real logged neighbors, not imagined optima. On D4RL benchmarks, including AntMaze and MuJoCo tasks, the method improved behavior using historical returns as feedback. It yields refinement paths practitioners can inspect, rare among offline methods.
arxiv-2606-09215:
Zheng and colleagues give a humanoid one brain for walking and manipulating, in this 2026 arXiv paper. World Action Models couple a video world model, predicting how scenes evolve, to a robot policy. They excel at tabletop tasks but denoise video latents too slowly for real-time humanoid control. The usual hierarchy worsens it: split controllers use inconsistent action spaces, reducing legs to balance-keeping.

MotionWAM conditions its policy on the world model's intermediate denoising features, skipping full video generation. It replaces the upper-lower split with a unified motion latent. Its motion tokens cover locomotion, torso motion, height, foot and hand interaction in one action space. A 3-stage framework adapts the model to egocentric dynamics and the robot's body. On 9 real-world Unitree G1 tasks it ran in real time and beat vision-language-action baselines by over 30 percent in success rate, with foot interactions split policies cannot achieve.
arxiv-2606-09315:
Jianwei Tai examines a new security risk that appears when brain signals are wired into software agents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In such systems, decoded EEG activity, the electrical signals recorded from the scalp, becomes an instruction channel for a tool-using language model. Tai calls attacks on that channel brain-prompt injection, because tampered signals or context can quietly change which action the agent takes.

Tai proposes a Route-Safety Audit Contract, a fixed logging scheme that records enough detail for dangerous rerouting to be detected afterwards. Tests used over five thousand command events drawn from sixty subjects. Adding provenance records, which state where each instruction came from, blocked the overlay attacks completely in the reported runs. A calibrated confirmation channel also drove false accepts to zero at strict settings, though it accepted fewer genuine commands.
arxiv-2606-09515:
Ichiro Jikuya and Yoichi Tamura frame mirror control for millimetre-wave telescopes as one clean control problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. Big submillimetre dishes need adaptive optics, live fixes to their shape, to keep images sharp. Heat and wind bend the surface in slow ways. Sensors read the harm as excess path length, the extra distance waves must travel.

The authors model the drive system as a plant with a first-order lag, plus a matrix that maps each actuator to what sensors see. The task becomes a disturbance suppression problem aimed at low-frequency bends. Their fix is an anti-windup proportional-integral law. A decoupling step splits the design into lone loops that can be shaped one by one. The result keeps firm stability margins. It also drives steady disturbances to zero over time, while the anti-windup part stops the integrator from overshooting when actuators saturate.
arxiv-2606-09915:
Marco Ho, Michael Hsiao, and Jeeho Ryoo fight RowHammer with a learning throttle inside the memory controller in this 2026 arXiv paper. RowHammer is a chip flaw: hammering one memory row flips bits in its neighbors. As chips shrink, the flips take fewer hits, down from one hundred thirty-nine thousand to under five thousand. Built-in guards like targeted refresh now fall to sly multi-bank patterns.

Their ARTA agent watches fine-grained access traffic within each refresh window. A small Q-table, learned by trial and reward, steers a governor that trims core speed when patterns turn hostile. In tests, ARTA wiped out all bit flips down to a harsh threshold of sixty-four. At a threshold of twenty it cut flips by up to twenty-two thousand times. It also ran up to seventy-three point six percent faster than top rival guards.
arxiv-2606-10115:
Biswas and his team add uncertainty awareness to machine-run cancer lesion segmentation in whole-body scans, in a 2026 arXiv paper on medical imaging. PET/CT scans combine metabolic and anatomical information for cancer staging, but delineating lesions is hard and radiologists face growing workloads. Using nnU-Net as the baseline, the team builds a framework around Bayesian ensembling and uncertainty maps.

On the unseen AutoPET-III test set, Bayesian ensembling improved the Dice overlap score and cut false positive volume compared with deterministic models, while uncertainty maps highlighted regions where calls were misclassified. Training with noise augmentation recovered more lesions, lowering false negative volume a lot, at the cost of more false positives. A case-adaptive routing rule that picks between models per patient achieved the best Dice score by a clear margin. The framework also carried to an out-of-sample prostate cancer dataset.
arxiv-2606-10315:
Zhang and colleagues measure how many real defects an AI judge misses in a deployed conversational agent, in a 2026 arXiv paper on language model evaluation. Their testbed is a production multi-turn food-and-beverage ordering agent, with exhaustive human transcript review as ground truth. Across three review batches, the judge surfaces well under a quarter of human-confirmed systematic problems.

In one batch the judge caught two of nine problem patterns, and its operational gate flagged zero of one hundred rounds in a batch where humans confirmed twenty-three distinct defects. Their blind-spot taxonomy shows the failure is structured: turn-local issues like a fabricated statistic are caught reliably, while cross-turn state problems, including cart hallucination and lockouts, are systematically missed. The judge's rubric exposes only three coarse scoring axes and has no category for state tracking, guardrails, or recovery, where most defects cluster.
arxiv-2606-10415:
Lu and his team adapt large language model training to a supercomputer whose design breaks the defaults of standard training software, in a 2026 arXiv paper on distributed systems. The MT-3000 platform instead has an explicit memory ladder, limited usable memory capacity, and constrained inter-cluster communication. Their runtime frames standard pipeline training as a training-state lifecycle scheduling problem.

Gradient sync, parameter updates, parameter-view fetching, and state recovery are scheduled at layer-level and stage-local level, so scarce bandwidth and memory are spent on purpose. An MT-3000-aware run backend provides fast, steady kernels for the core matrix work, attention backward pass, and explicit data movement, while a resource-aware planner selects feasible training setups. Together the pieces make dense model training practical on bandwidth-constrained mixed hardware, a setting that matters as more national supercomputing platforms, not just GPU clusters, are asked to train large models.
arxiv-2606-10515:
Colombo and de León build geometric machinery for dissipative mechanics in this 2026 arXiv paper in mathematical physics. Such systems lose energy, like a pendulum slowed by friction, and contact geometry is their natural language. The Tulczyjew formalism turns generating objects into equations of motion, even for singular systems. The authors extend it to skew algebroids, bundles whose bracket need not satisfy the Jacobi identity, and explain the extra contact term in local formulas.

Their construction adds an Euler vector field contribution on the dual bundle, giving the contact term a natural meaning. In coordinates, the matching condition yields the Euler-Lagrange-Herglotz equations, and a Legendre transform recovers contact Hamiltonian equations in the well-behaved case. A discrete counterpart follows: fixing an admissibility relation between steps produces discrete Herglotz equations by matching contact momenta, reproducing known contact integrators in the regular case.
arxiv-2606-10615:
Jordi Thijsman and colleagues present a virtual machine design for rivals who must compute together in this 2026 arXiv paper on computer security. Hospitals, manufacturers, and defence partners often need joint computation over data none may reveal, and cryptographic alternatives are too slow. The Two-Way Confidential VM pairs a hardware trusted environment, AMD SEV-SNP, with an inner WebAssembly sandbox, isolating co-resident workloads from the host and each other. A Commitment Manifest lists participants, permitted data channels, and authorised outputs, locked into the machine's attestation evidence.

Evaluation across four benchmark classes brings good news: the two isolation layers do not multiply their costs. Once code runs in the sandbox, hardware memory protection costs little extra. Overhead depends on memory access patterns, from negligible for sequential workloads to roughly twofold for pointer-chasing ones. This makes mutual-distrust collaboration practical and verifiable.
arxiv-2606-10715:
Neha Sharma and colleagues report a soft magnet in this 2026 arXiv paper on materials science. The material is a high-entropy spinel oxide, with five-plus metals in near-equal shares on its cation sites, the disorder stabilising the structure. Combining neutron diffraction, X-ray absorption, and Mössbauer spectroscopy, the team maps cations across the tetrahedral and octahedral sites. The oxide orders as a collinear ferrimagnet, its sublattices opposed but unequal, below 420 kelvin.

Its softness is the headline: coercivity of 1.8 oersted at room temperature, among the lowest known for spinel oxides, so its magnetisation flips under a whisper of field. Its resistivity is high, about 1560 ohm-centimetres, limiting eddy-current losses. Magnetic order above room temperature, tiny coercivity, and high resistivity rarely coexist; the mix suits low-loss, high-frequency devices. The study shows how site-selective disorder can be measured and tuned, not merely endured.
arxiv-2606-10815:
Van Hintum settles a twenty-year-old conjecture about averaging sets in this 2026 arXiv paper in convex geometry. Averaging a set with itself repeatedly, the iterated Minkowski average, should make it more convex. The Dyn-Farkhi conjecture quantified this: the Hausdorff distance from a set to its convex hull, squared, was claimed subadditive under addition. The claim fell in dimensions three and up, but the symmetric case stayed open. Van Hintum shows it fails there too.

For every dimension from three upward, a compact set is constructed whose distance to its convex hull does not shrink under the first n minus one averaging steps. It stays constant and positive. Averaging helps only at the nth step, and that threshold is sharp: a bound shows how far the distance must drop at step n. The counterexample closes the conjecture's last case, redrawing how convexification under Minkowski addition behaves.
arxiv-2606-11115:
Mentasti and Baghi study a subtle effect on the future LISA gravitational wave detector in a 2026 arXiv paper. LISA will hear a galactic background: the blended hum of countless unresolved Milky Way binaries, mostly white dwarf pairs. That background varies with direction, since sources crowd the galactic plane. The authors model the Galaxy's density and motion, including rotation, and compute how the spectrum changes across the sky.

Rotation matters through the Doppler effect, the frequency shift from moving sources. Each line of sight samples a different mix of velocities, so no single boost describes the sky. Using Fisher matrix forecasts, the authors show that fitting LISA data with a model ignoring rotation biases the recovered parameters. The bias lands hardest on the high-frequency cutoff, and can match or exceed LISA's expected statistical uncertainties. Galactic kinematics, they conclude, is a required ingredient, not a small correction.
arxiv-2606-11215:
Eimler and seven co-authors examine the hidden environmental cost of language models in education research in a 2026 arXiv paper. The AI in Education community now uses such models widely, in tutoring agents, writing assistants, and grading tools. The computational and carbon costs stay mostly invisible, because no standardized procedures exist for measuring or reporting them.

The team reviewed all 396 papers in the AIED 2025 proceedings, checking whether such costs were reported. Most projects used language models, but few reported the resources consumed, and almost none discussed environmental impact as an ethical concern. To close the gap, they propose an open-source method for measuring and reporting both costs. Their software estimates carbon footprints on local and cloud hardware, and a simple formula covers frontier models even when the parameter count is secret. The paper reports its own sustainability metrics, modeling the transparency it asks of the field.
arxiv-2606-11315:
Kuhn and six co-authors measure how spiral galaxy arms wind across cosmic time in a 2026 arXiv paper. From JWST's CEERS and JADES surveys, the team assembled 593 spiral galaxies with masses above ten to the tenth solar masses, out to redshift 3.5. A fine-tuned Zoobot model found the spirals; SpArcFiRe measured their pitch angles.

Across the sample, average pitch angle shows no significant redshift evolution. In the most massive systems, though, arms slightly wind up with time. Above redshift 1.25, pitch angle does not correlate with internal properties like stellar, bulge, or disk mass. Below it, pitch angle correlates weakly but significantly with those masses, and positively with specific star formation rate at low redshift. Nothing depends on tidal strength from companions. The authors read this as a transition near redshift one: earlier arms are locally driven, later ones regulated by the global potential, as density wave theory predicts.
arxiv-2606-11415:
Memar and Dehghani ask how local an electrode's signal really is, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neural signals are often read as local readings, yet a sensor's signal can also reflect activity spread across the broader network. Their Spatially Masked Regression framework reconstructs each channel's time series from the others, excluding a neighborhood of adjustable size around the target. Growing the mask turns mask size into a control knob.

Applied to intracranial EEG and to scalp EEG over sensorimotor cortex, it finds strong within-subject reconstruction in both modalities. Much predictability survives even when local neighbors are excluded. Cross-subject transfer is markedly stronger in scalp EEG than in intracranial EEG. Nearby electrodes contribute strongly but not fully, so channels reflect both local redundancy and distributed structure. Surrogates disrupting phase structure or temporal ordering degrade performance sharply, showing the method depends on structured cross-channel organization, not marginal statistics alone.
arxiv-2606-11515:
Will Asness and four co-authors present a method for risk-focused optimisation in this 2026 arXiv paper. The target is conditional value-at-risk, a measure that averages the worst losses rather than the typical outcome. Their method, called EASIeST, uses the dual form of that measure, a restatement that swaps the problem for an equivalent one about worst-case probability weights.

The algorithm alternates between ordinary and dual stages using a Bregman proximal method, a step-by-step scheme that keeps each update close to the last. Its sampling gradually concentrates on tail scenarios, the rare bad cases that drive the risk measure, while other cases are drawn less and less often. The authors prove the method converges for convex problems, where any local best answer is global. Tests on portfolio choice and support-vector machines, a standard classification method, show strong performance against other sampling approaches.
arxiv-2606-11615:
Omid Ahmadieh and Nima Karimian build a tool for fooling face recognition in this 2026 arXiv paper on security and privacy. Their system, Adv-TGD, generates realistic fake faces that a recognition system mistakes for a chosen target person. It builds on Stable Diffusion, a popular image generator, and fine-tunes small LoRA adapters, lightweight add-on weights, separately for each source and target pair, guided by short text prompts.

Blending is limited by a face-shaped mask so only identity features change. A combined objective balances fooling the recogniser against suppressing the source face and keeping the image natural. Under a strict black-box protocol, where the attacker cannot see inside the target system, the method reaches an average attack success rate near eighty-six percent across four recognition models. That beats the strongest rival by over six points, while quality scores stay high and the fakes look photorealistic.
arxiv-2606-11715:
Pengfei Tian, Fan Yang and Peng Ding order several causal effect measures in this 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. In observational studies, researchers estimate a treatment's average effect, but different weightings answer different questions. Options include the effect on the treated, on the controls, or under overlap weights, which emphasise people whose treatment status was most uncertain.

The overlap-weighted effect is popular for its robustness to extreme propensity scores, the estimated chances of receiving treatment. The authors prove a bracketing result. When the conditional average effect varies monotonically with the propensity score, the overlap-weighted effect always lies between the effects on the treated and on the controls. The result extends to local effects in the instrumental variable setting and to other weighting schemes such as matching weights. As a practical tool they recommend a CP-plot, charting the estimated conditional effect against the propensity score.
arxiv-2606-11915:
Yoon Tae Kim and three colleagues adapt classifier training to recording quality for lung sound analysis in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sorting respiratory sounds supports diagnosis of lung disease, but recordings vary wildly in quality, and disease classes are heavily imbalanced. Their framework, QLung, builds a no-reference quality score from each recording itself, using spectral entropy and signal energy.

That score adaptively scales the angular margin, the enforced gap between classes on a normalised feature sphere, so clean and noisy recordings are treated differently. A log-scaled margin stabilises training under severe imbalance, and an angular classifier applies penalties evenly. The method improves performance on the ICBHI benchmark by about two and a half percentage points over a cross-entropy baseline in fine-tuning a standard audio transformer. More importantly, it achieves the strongest out-of-distribution performance on the separate SPRSound dataset among compared methods.
arxiv-2606-12015:
Martin Law leads a seven-author team proposing a fairer yardstick for adaptive clinical trials in this 2026 arXiv paper. Adaptive designs let a trial change course midstream, for example stopping early for benefit. Guidelines often resist including them in meta-analyses, fearing their estimates are biased. The authors define precision-weighted bias: an estimator's unconditional bias weighted by the precision, the information content, of the estimate itself.

They show the bias of a common-effect meta-analysis is approximately the precision-weighted average of the studies' precision-weighted biases. Simulation studies then deliver the punchline. Adaptive designs may show clear unweighted bias, yet frequently have zero precision-weighted bias, because their biased outcomes arise exactly when precision is low. Including them therefore changes overall meta-analysis bias negligibly, while excluding them can itself distort results. The team recommends reporting precision-weighted bias alongside conventional bias measures in simulation studies.
arxiv-2606-12615:
Owen O'Neill and Costello define fairness as consistency with the data, then build a classifier that can prove it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Machine learning predictions often vary in quality across subgroups, and for small intersectional subgroups they can contradict the evidence. Regularization worsens this by collapsing small groups into big ones, hitting minorities hardest. Their two requirements: identical people get identical predictions, and no subgroup's predictions may be rejectable against its Bayesian target.

It enforces both requirements across every group and subgroup at once. Where no consistent deterministic prediction exists, it abstains rather than guess. On Adult, COMPAS, and Bank Marketing, standard tools all produce inconsistent predictions for many subgroups. It has zero consistency error by construction. It beats baseline accuracy on every dataset, where it predicts. Multicalibration competitiveness arrives as a by-product.
arxiv-2606-13715:
Styles and Miller revisit a workplace-agent benchmark two years on in this 2026 arXiv paper. WorkBench tests agents on realistic office tasks across email, calendars, and files. In March 2024 the best agent, GPT-4, completed just 43 percent of tasks. By June 2026 the best agent completes 98 percent. The authors draw out three findings. First, unintended harmful actions, such as emailing the wrong person, collapsed from about a quarter of tasks to under two percent: capability and safety rose together rather than trading off.

Second, open-weight models have lowered the cost of a given performance level, while frontier costs stayed roughly stable. Third, despite the progress, frontier models still make basic mistakes that cause irreversible harm. The authors release an updated benchmark with data and code quality, new model scores, and an analysis of progress since 2024. The report is a useful calibration point for claims about workplace automation.
arxiv-2606-13815:
Singla, Garg, and Singh argue that a single poker score hides what language models are actually good or bad at. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces Poker Arena, a no-limit Texas Hold'em tournament platform. It scores play on nine separate axes, such as bet sizing and positional awareness, and gives models a three-layer memory spanning a hand, a session, and past sessions. Seven frontier models each played fifty sessions totaling one thousand hands.

The chip ranking and the skill ranking disagreed sharply. Claude Opus 4.6 won the most chips, gaining fifteen thousand seven hundred thirty dollars with fourteen first-place finishes. Yet it ranked only fifth of seven on the mean axis score, while Grok topped that mean and finished second in chips. Lasting memory also cut both ways: it helped some models and hurt others. The authors conclude that steady performance across all axes beats brilliance on just one.
arxiv-2606-13915:
Sydora and colleagues swing an inverted pendulum upright using magnets outside the device. Electromagnetic navigation systems steer magnetic tools inside the body with coil-generated fields, aiding surgery and drug delivery. Most control for these systems assumes slow, near-equilibrium motion. Their 2026 arXiv paper demonstrates the first swing-up of a magnetically driven inverted pendulum on the Navion system, a clinically ready platform. The method targets torques and forces, so it transfers to catheters and guidewires.

The approach combines three parts. Trajectory optimization accounts for the magnet system's own dynamics. Time-varying LQR feedback, a standard stabilizing controller, corrects errors during motion. Iterative learning control then refines the feedforward command from trial to trial. LQR alone failed against the quirks of magnetic actuation. With learning added, swing-up succeeded within six iterations. Analysis showed the learned correction closely matched the torque error later found by careful field calibration.
arxiv-2606-14015:
Abe and the T2K Collaboration pin down how neutrinos interact, so oscillation results are not distorted by modeling errors. T2K fires a neutrino beam across Japan and compares near and far detector rates. Neutrino energy, which oscillations depend on, is inferred from the outgoing lepton's momentum and angle, so model bias becomes result bias. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents the near-detector analysis bounding interaction errors.

Data come from ND280, sorted into twenty-two samples across two fine-grained detectors. Neutrino-mode running alone contributed forty-nine thousand seven hundred three events in one and forty-seven thousand four hundred eighty-seven in the other. Samples separate interaction modes such as quasielastic scattering, two-particle-two-hole processes, and single-pion production. These modes bias energy estimates differently, so fitting them jointly disciplines the cross-section model. The constrained model then feeds the far-detector oscillation fit.
arxiv-2606-14115:
Sadeghi tests whether two famous holographic bounds survive when a plasma's gauge fields couple directly to curvature. In holography, a strongly coupled plasma is modeled by a black brane in anti-de Sitter space. His 2026 arXiv paper adds a nonminimal term coupling the Yang-Mills field strength to the Ricci tensor, treated perturbatively to first order in its small coupling. The fluid-gravity correspondence yields the DC color conductivity and the shear viscosity to entropy ratio.

Both bounds bend. Conductivity equals one minus a positive correction when the coupling is positive, violating the universal lower bound of one. For negative coupling it is preserved. The viscosity ratio equals the famous one over four pi value times a factor linear in the coupling. Its sign decides whether the ratio rises above or drops below the KSS bound. This is a controlled example of how curvature-coupled interactions reshape plasma transport.
arxiv-2606-14315:
Jha, Svarc, and Bagiński argue that 'AI alignment' names several rival research programs at once, with real consequences. Their 2026 arXiv position paper separates three high-level ideals hiding under the term, each answering differently what should be aligned to what, resting on different threat models and values. A realistic move can advance alignment under one ideal while being harmful under another.

They issue five recommendations for the field. Do not conflate policy distinctions with distinctions of scientific scope. Acknowledge method disagreements explicitly. Separate the ideal from the specific proxies used in tests. Use granular notions to locate harms and benefits. Acknowledge the range of notions to lay readers too. They urge finer distinctions among proxies for takeover avoidance, and among sources of harm for social judiciousness. Disagreements about alignment, they conclude, should be understood as they actually exist.
arxiv-2606-14415:
Belouadah, Kubler, and Le Traon present CSPO in a 2026 arXiv paper on safe reinforcement learning, where an agent must earn high rewards while respecting safety limits. The setting is formalized as a constrained Markov decision process. Popular primal-dual methods scale well but correct safety breaches slowly, causing oscillations and long stretches of violation near the boundary.

CSPO, short for constraint-sensitive policy optimization, folds local constraint sensitivity into each policy update. Its correction term uses the shortest signed distance to the safety boundary, guiding smarter steps back to safety and compensating for slow multiplier updates. The method preserves the original problem's optimal solutions while cutting boundary oscillations. On navigation and locomotion benchmarks, CSPO recovered safety faster and kept rewards higher than leading primal-dual and penalty-based rivals.
arxiv-2606-14815:
Upadhyay, Upadhyay, and Mandal, with Mandal as senior author, compute quantum corrections to black hole thermodynamics in exotic surroundings in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their black holes sit in anti-de Sitter space filled with a cloud of strings and a perfect-fluid dark matter background. Starting from the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, they add corrections from small thermal fluctuations.

In the perturbative sector, logarithmic entropy corrections modify the mass, both free energies, heat capacity, and pressure, and the heat capacity's sign reveals a shift from unstable to stable behavior. In the non-perturbative sector, exponential corrections matter only as the horizon shrinks toward the Planck scale, vanishing for large black holes. Searching the equation of state for a van der Waals-like critical point, they find none within the physically allowed domain in either sector.
arxiv-2606-15615:
Li and colleagues speed up diffusion transformers with mixture-of-experts layers in 2026, attacking redundant computation across denoising timesteps. Caching methods reuse features between steps, but they work at the whole-token level, while each token update inside these models splits into several routed expert branches. The team shows the redundancy is better described at the expert-branch level than at the token level.

Their framework, MoECa, caches and reuses features branch by branch across timesteps. Expert-aware adaptive control decides what to reuse, and synchronized cache updates keep the mixture-of-experts and attention paths in step, holding intermediate states stable. On multiple models of this family, MoECa reaches up to a 2.83-fold inference speedup with minimal quality loss. That is a better speed-quality trade-off than prior caching methods throughout. The lesson is to align reuse with the model's own decomposition: cache where the computation actually repeats.
arxiv-2606-15715:
Barone and Lillo test sunshine trading theory on Hyperliquid in 2026, a fully on-chain order book for cryptocurrency perpetual futures. Sunshine trading predicts that announcing a large order in advance lowers its cost, by reassuring liquidity providers the trader hides no private information. Traditional markets rarely allow the test, but Hyperliquid's native TWAP orders disclose their terms from the start and stay visible while active.

Reconstructing 4.3 million hidden metaorders from address-level data, the authors compare them with 465,000 visible TWAP executions. Hidden metaorders follow front-loaded, U-shaped schedules, while TWAPs trade almost uniformly. Visible TWAPs indeed face lower execution costs and leave a smaller permanent price footprint. Hidden orders executed alongside visible same-direction TWAP flow pay more: adverse-selection costs shift onto non-announcers. Visible programs also attract liquidity, with displayed depth rising while they run. Preannouncement, long a theoretical curiosity, measurably pays on a transparent exchange.
arxiv-2606-15815:
Liu and colleagues propose a structured definition of erasure as a harm in natural language processing in 2026, aiming to give the concept a measurable foundation. Erasure, a harm where systems render groups invisible, has attracted growing attention. Existing accounts are either so broad that almost anything qualifies, or so specific to one setting that they cannot travel.

The proposal spells out what must be present for erasure to have occurred, and asks practitioners to state and operationalise each part for their setting before measuring. Applied as a guide, it also organises prior work on erasure in NLP and points to open directions. The authors are candid about scope: their discussion centres on system outputs and behaviour, while erasure can also arise from design decisions, or land on users through system impacts. A shared structured vocabulary is the starting point for benchmarks claiming to measure this harm.
arxiv-2606-16015:
Moe and Roald present Stringalign in 2026, a Python library for comparing strings when evaluating transcription models, from handwriting and optical character recognition to speech recognition. The character and word error rates look simple but are ambiguous in practice, because tools disagree on what counts as a character or a word after normalisation and tokenisation. Stringalign makes every preprocessing choice transparent and replicable, and is Unicode-aware throughout.

Beyond the summary rates, the library provides tools to examine and visualise the types of errors a model makes, which is what informs fixes and model selection for a task. Worked examples show existing tools yielding opaque, sometimes confusing results where Stringalign gives an unambiguous answer. The design follows FAIR principles for research software: open source, few dependencies, modular, and easy to fold into existing workflows. Its authors note the focus is Latin scripts; custom tokenisation for other scripts is future work.
arxiv-2606-16415:
Das argues in 2026 that enterprise behavior simulation should predict a population's distribution, not a single plausible reply. Many business decisions hinge on the shape of responses: which customer segments accept, defect, hesitate, or drift into risk-sensitive states under a proposed action. Posterior Twins is a memory-grounded digital-twin approach that represents likely behavior as an updated spread under a specific decision context.

The paper evaluates a family of Twinning Labs operating points on a 226-example held-out benchmark, scoring modal accuracy and Wasserstein-1 distance, a measure of closeness of fit. The TL-Twin Alpha point reaches a Wasserstein-1 distance of 1.16, the lowest observed, against 2.59 for GPT-5.4, the strongest frontier model row. Two sibling points balance near the modal-accuracy frontier instead. Das frames the result as a frontier between decision-direction accuracy and fit fidelity, not a single leaderboard score.
arxiv-2606-16915:
Xu leads the MagMaR collaboration's seventh paper in a 2026 astronomy study of magnetic fields in the massive star-forming region W33 A. How magnetic fields shape the birth of heavy stars is still unclear. Polarized light from dust grains aligned by the field lets astronomers map field direction across the sky.

Using the ALMA telescope array at millimetre wavelengths, the team resolves W33 A into twenty dense cores and nine filaments. The field shows two large perpendicular patterns. One may be sculpted by a molecular outflow, while the other runs coherently along the main filaments, where turbulence is near the Alfvénic balance point. Along the main filament, gravity exceeds what turbulence can support, so magnetic backing is likely needed to stop collapse. Near one peak the field spirals along an infalling streamer, suggesting magnetically calmed accretion. Near another it pinches into an hourglass shape.
arxiv-2606-17115:
Hu and colleagues evaluate foundation models for cancer analysis in a 2026 medical AI paper. Foundation models extract rich features from medical data, but whether they survive distribution shift between hospitals is poorly tested. The study uses two real commercial cohorts, breast cancer and lung cancer, with pathology slides and gene-expression profiles.

Five foundation models are probed on eight labeling tasks. Image and omics features turn out to carry complementary signals: each sees part of what the other misses. Three fusion strategies combine the paired features. Fusion gains appear mainly when neither data type dominates the signal on its own. Trustworthiness is checked with conformal prediction, which returns a set of candidate answers with coverage guarantees. Reassuringly, when a point prediction fails, the true diagnosis usually still sits inside the prediction set. The results argue for uncertainty-aware inference, and for fusion only where data types genuinely share the work.
arxiv-2606-17215:
Li presents a 2026 arXiv paper on robustly learning halfspaces when an adversary has corrupted part of the training data.
