The reweighted-hinge method removes outliers using a sum-of-squares certificate that sees data only through low-degree moments. An adversary can hide corruption exactly where clean data already looks typical, in the blind spot no bounded-degree test can resolve, and Li shows that blind spot has an exact size.

That size is the Christoffel function of the clean data distribution, the same quantity analysts threshold to flag outliers, here read from the adversary's side. Three consequences follow for the certificate method, including a trade-off linking margin and the degree needed to certify a target error. An explicit case shows degree two stuck while degree four escapes, locating the method's low breakdown rate in the degree. An algorithm tracing the frontier across degrees is also given.
arxiv-2606-17315:
Attiya, Oshman, and Schiller present a 2026 arXiv paper on a concurrent hash table that keeps the frugal layout of linear probing, the simplest classic design. In sequential code, linear probing stores each key at its hash slot or the next free cell, giving compact storage and cache-friendly scans. Concurrent versions with strong liveness guarantees have proved hard, and earlier designs either restrict concurrency or attach heavy metadata to every entry, wasting the space advantage.

The new table is lock-free with wait-free lookups, so no operation can stall the others indefinitely. It uses only a few extra bits per entry with one primitive, or a logarithmic number with another common one. Deleted slots are reclaimed safely without rebuilding the whole table from scratch. Expected amortised step counts match the sequential design up to contention on the same key.
arxiv-2606-17515:
Molitor presents a 2026 arXiv paper on picking the best treatment policy from logged bandit data while watching the evidence arrive, without fixing the sample size in advance. Analysts often inherit data from a logging policy they do not control, and they may want to stop as soon as the winner is clear. Ordinary statistics punish that peeking, so Molitor builds an anytime-valid set that keeps the true best policy inside it uniformly over time with high probability.

Policies can be eliminated as they fall clearly behind, and stopping at data-chosen times keeps the inference honest. When one policy is uniquely best, a stopping rule and a sample bound are derived from the gap to the runner-up. Simulations show large sample savings over fixed-size designs. An online misinformation experiment shows the method tracking the best policy as evidence builds.
arxiv-2606-17615:
Bianchi and Liotta present a 2026 arXiv paper on judging human skill from multi-view video, for uses from sports coaching to surgical training. Earlier methods fit single scenarios or merge camera views in one shared way, which struggles when viewpoints and activities vary widely. Their framework, SkillMoV, instead routes view features through a mixture of experts, letting each camera angle lean on the specialists that suit it, without ever being told which camera is which.

Four stages shape the skill embedding: a soft router over a dozen small expert networks, cross-view attention aligning the cameras, anchoring to learned class prototypes, and a gated projection. On a large ego-exo benchmark across six skill domains, the joint model set the best outside-view score among compared methods. Ablations credit each stage with several points of the gain, and only a fraction of weights are trained.
arxiv-2606-18415:
Saleem and Saleem study how entanglement in a pair of interacting qubits responds when the temperature of their shared thermal state changes, in a 2026 quantum physics paper. Two-qubit thermal states are a minimal setting where both entanglement and measurement sensitivity can be written down exactly, making them a clean test bed for linking the two.

For a general two-qubit interaction, the authors derive exact formulas for thermal concurrence, the standard entanglement measure here, along with its first and second rates of change with inverse temperature. They also derive the thermal quantum Fisher information that governs thermometry precision. They prove that the speed at which entanglement changes is bounded by that Fisher information, and derive a matching bound for entanglement's curvature. Temperature uncertainty, they show, costs entanglement by an amount controlled by the same quantity that sets sensing sensitivity, tying robustness and metrological power together in one framework.
arxiv-2606-18615:
Thompson and colleagues survey the methods for converting phonograph playback equalization filters from continuous time to digital form, in a 2026 audio engineering paper. Records have been cut with a deliberate non-flat frequency curve since electrical recording began, to pack more music onto a disc and improve signal-to-noise ratio, so playback must apply the inverse curve. Before the industry standardized the RIAA curve in the nineteen fifties, each label's discs needed their own.

Digital playback makes switching among curves cheap and flexible, but every discretization method bends the response near the Nyquist frequency and differs in accuracy, computational cost, and latency. The authors explore several established transformation methods in the specific context of phonograph equalization and quantify how each performs. They intend the survey as a practical resource for anyone building digital playback systems, or facing the same continuous-to-digital conversion problem elsewhere.
arxiv-2606-18915:
Wei and colleagues report tests of a prototype module of fifteen fiber positioners built for the generation of spectroscopic telescopes, in a 2026 astronomical instrumentation paper. Stage-5 surveys such as MUST, Spec-S5, and WST need denser arrays of theta-phi robots placing fibers on a telescope focal plane, and each design's metrics must be verified against specification before production.

The module, built by the company Micro Precision Systems at a pitch of over six millimeters, was measured for datum repeatability, backlash, non-linearity, and angular tilt. Repeatability results were excellent, comfortably meeting targets. Two metrics lagged: average backlash came in above the desired five degrees on both axes, and the angular tilt slightly exceeded its target. The authors conclude the prototype is a step toward a high-density positioner solution, with accuracy, thermal, and lifetime testing to come and a larger sixty-three positioner prototype next in line.
arxiv-2606-19015:
Pandit studies a class of harmonic mappings in a 2026 mathematics paper set in the unit disk. Harmonic mappings extend analytic functions and arise in planar problems with two linked parts, one analytic and one co-analytic. For the chosen class, the author seeks a bound on the pre-Schwarzian norm, a measure of how far a function bends from simple affine behavior and a key gauge of shape control.

That norm bound is proved for the class. It then shows every function in the class is univalent, meaning it never folds the disk onto itself, and close-to-convex in shape. Growth and distortion results follow for both the analytic and co-analytic parts, bounding how large or small values can become. A coefficient bound for the analytic part closes the work.
arxiv-2606-19115:
Le Bihan and colleagues introduce finite free perpetuities in a 2026 probability paper. A classical perpetuity is a random variable defined by a fixed-point equation with random scaling and shift. The finite free version replaces the law with a monic polynomial of fixed degree that solves an affine fixed-point equation in expectation. That places the objects between classical perpetuities and free fixed-point laws.

The authors prove existence and uniqueness under weak conditions on the random pair. They also identify a broad class of admissible pairs for which the polynomial has only real, nonnegative zeros. The approach uses finite free convolutions plus a representation through the U-transform. An explicit family shows the theory at work.
arxiv-2606-19315:
Wang and colleagues present Diffusion-Proof in 2026, a framework for formal theorem proving with diffusion language models. Formal math reasoning with language models has advanced fast, but autoregressive models generate token by token. That method suffers long-range coherence problems and compounding errors over long proofs. Diffusion models generate text by iteratively denoising a multi-token block, a promising alternative barely studied for formal mathematics.

The framework trains and applies diffusion models in two roles. A prover model writes whole proofs with long-range coherent tactic use. A corrector model uses the in-filling strength of diffusion to fix local proof errors with bidirectional context, seeing both sides of a gap. Tests on formal proving benchmarks follow. Whole-proof writing plus local correction plays to what diffusion does best, global structure and local repair at once. The recipe opens a non-autoregressive path for machine-checked mathematics.
arxiv-2606-19415:
Ianina and colleagues publish a corrigendum in 2026 to their chapter on order extreme points and solid convex hulls in Banach lattices. The note has two goals. It corrects some annoying typos in the published version. More importantly, it corrects some of the proofs, where several statements in two sections omitted their convexity assumptions. A missing hypothesis can invalidate the arguments, so the fixes matter.

The corrigendum restates the affected results with the assumptions restored. A separation proposition now requires the set to be closed, positive-solid, bounded, and convex. A solid Krein-Milman theorem now states that a compact positive-solid convex set equals the closed hull of its order extreme points. A corollary gets the same repair for general solid convex sets. The note also flags that statement numbering differs between the preprint and the published version. The repairs keep these hull results reliable for later work.
arxiv-2606-19815:
Jiechao Gao and six colleagues pre-train a Tsetlin Machine with semantic clusters in 2026. Tsetlin Machines reason through readable logic clauses, unlike opaque language models. BERT-class models classify text strongly but cannot explain themselves, barring high-stakes use.

Static word embeddings were the old bridge, and they miss contextual meaning. Text samples now cluster by meaning with K-means or Top2Vec instead. Cluster-sample pairs pre-train a non-negated Tsetlin Machine with enhanced feedback. The machine learns interpretable semantic keywords during that phase. Fine-tuning on the target task follows. Across five datasets the method beats plain and embedding-based Tsetlin Machines by wide margins. Scores rival BERT while every decision stays clause-readable. Interpretability and accuracy, often traded off, here advance together.
arxiv-2606-20315:
Christos Galanopoulos, Kimon Antonios Provatas, and Ilias Georgakopoulos-Soares put genomic queries on a blockchain without exposing them. Their 2026 paper builds bioETH-Beacon, a smart-contract version of the GA4GH Beacon protocol, which lets researchers ask whether a variant appears in a cohort and get aggregate counts. Two privacy risks persist in ordinary Beacons: hosts can see plaintext queries, and repeated rare-variant queries enable membership-inference attacks.

The prototype runs the count query over encrypted data on a fully homomorphic Ethereum virtual machine. Hospitals upload encrypted marker counts; authorized researchers submit encrypted queries; the contract returns an encrypted answer released only to the named requester. A tiered grid trades confidentiality against query cost across genotype, sex, age, and phenotype queries, with bounded noise blunting probing attacks. Confidential genomic sharing, the design shows, is possible with today's homomorphic tooling.
arxiv-2606-20415:
Farhin Farhad Riya, Shahinul Hoque, Yingyuan Yang, Jinyuan Sun, and Kevin Tomsovic defend power-grid attack detectors by padding their inputs with fake features. Their 2026 paper addresses false data injection attacks, where adversaries craft inputs that evade deep neural network detectors. The defense adds an input layer that pads each sample with pseudo-feature values drawn from the input's own statistical distribution. The padding is randomized and data-aware, so its structure is unpredictable.

Because crafted perturbations do not transfer across the padded layouts, attacks become infeasible to aim. The method is lightweight and model-agnostic, needing no change to the detector's core. Tested on state estimation for IEEE 14, 30, 118, and 300-bus systems, the padding significantly improved robustness with negligible performance cost, and attacks that bypassed conventional defenses were mitigated.
arxiv-2606-20615:
Ylli Prifti proposes a protocol language for specifying where humans end and agents begin in software development. His 2026 paper notes that AI agents now act as first-class team members across the lifecycle, yet no language expresses role boundaries, approval gates, and governance constraints.

Existing approaches encode process in agent prompts, where it drifts, or target adjacent domains like workflow management. The proposed domain-specific language has formal abstract syntax, well-formedness conditions, a working semantics, and enforcement invariants. Process becomes a protocol that can be checked rather than a prompt that can wander. Teams gain a contract for human-agent collaboration that survives staff and model changes.
arxiv-2606-21015:
Vishal Srivastava and Tanmay Sah name an evaluability gap in 2026 that they argue limits AI governance in organizations. Deploying AI forces two decisions. Systems must be safe enough to operate. They must also merit continued investment. Both decisions rest on evidence. The sufficiency of that evidence cannot be assumed. Their named gap is the common lack of evidence strong enough for high-confidence decisions.

The gap, they argue, reflects a category error. Practice focuses on properties of systems. It should focus on the evidence needed to decide about them. Investment decisions are also wrongly placed outside governance. They define evaluability as a system's capability to generate, maintain, and renew such evidence. Framing governance around evidence quality could change audits: the key question becomes not only what a system does, but whether the organization can prove its claims about risk and value.
arxiv-2606-21415:
Evangelia Koskinioti, Yi Shen, Georgios Stamou, and Michael Zavlanos tackle domain shift in medical image segmentation in 2026, where a model trained at one hospital can falter on scans from another. Their architecture, ADualVUOT, adapts without target labels. A dual-encoder variational autoencoder gives flexible latent representations, and continuous normalizing flows add expressiveness to the model's picture of variation between domains.

Alignment between source and target uses unbalanced optimal transport through a Gaussian-Gromov-Wasserstein distance, which tolerates structural and topological mismatch between scans. An adversarial augmentation scheme synthesizes worst-case mixes of the domains to harden the model further. On medical imaging benchmarks, the framework gains significantly over earlier transport-based methods. The design targets high-stakes deployment, where silent failure under shifted data is the risk to remove.
arxiv-2606-21715:
Angelos Thomos and Theodore Andronikos stress-test quantum classifiers as network intrusion detectors in 2026, in today's noisy intermediate-scale quantum era. Their variational quantum classifier uses four qubits and a 24-parameter trainable circuit, with amplitude encoding packing 16 principal components of NSL-KDD traffic data into the quantum state. On held-out data it reaches a consistent 88 percent accuracy.

Two different optimizers plateau at the same place, which the authors read as an encoding expressibility limit rather than failed optimization. A tiny classical network with four nodes scores 97 percent, exposing the cost of overcompressing data into few qubits. Trained on all 22 attack categories, the quantum model collapses to 9 percent and a few classes. The authors sketch, but do not test, a 16-qubit angle-encoding design that expands rather than compresses.
arxiv-2606-22015:
Wu and colleagues propose, in 2026, using sliding ferroelectricity to control the spin Hall effect in bilayer WTe2, a layered material whose sheets can shift against each other. The spin Hall effect converts charge current into spin current and underpins fast, low-power memory concepts. A key obstacle is switching a magnet's direction by 180 degrees without an external magnetic field, which the anomalous spin Hall effect may enable.

Calculations show the monolayer already carries substantial anomalous spin Hall conductivity, and the bilayer roughly doubles those values, with one component reaching about 104 in the study's units. More importantly, sliding the layers reversibly flips both the signs and the sizes of the conventional and anomalous conductivities. The switch comes from sliding shifting how valence and conduction bands contribute spin Berry curvature. The findings show sliding ferroelectricity and spin transport are strongly coupled, a lever for field-free device designs.
arxiv-2606-22515:
Giovanna Herculano Tormena and twelve colleagues apply deep learning to forensic identification in this 2026 paper. Determining the sex of decomposed cadavers is hard, because traditional methods rely on an anthropologist's visual inspection of bones. The team ask whether image models can read sex directly from CT scans.

They analysed scans from one hundred forty-one autopsied cadavers held at a forensic institute in Goiânia, Brazil. Reconstructions of the pelvis and skull became standardized two-dimensional profile images. Seven established model families, including YOLO, ResNet, and vision transformers, were trained with transfer learning under two classification schemes. The best model was highly consistent on the pelvis and still satisfactory on the skull. Overall patient-level accuracy reached about ninety-six percent, with strong precision and recall, even in cases with trauma artifacts. The authors caution that data came from one institution and one scanner, so wider validation is still needed.
arxiv-2606-22715:
Vladimir Müller and Yuri Tomilov prove a new existence criterion in this 2026 operator-theory paper. The invariant subspace problem asks whether every bounded operator on a Hilbert space leaves some nontrivial subspace unchanged; in general it remains open. Useful criteria that apply to broad classes of operators are rare.

The authors prove that a bounded Hilbert space operator has a nontrivial invariant subspace when its spectrum contains the topological boundary of its numerical range. The numerical range collects the operator's average values on unit vectors; its boundary is a curve in the complex plane. They also give variants of the result and related statements. The criterion is then applied to hyponormal, cohyponormal, and Toeplitz operators. In those classes a weaker condition suffices: convexity of the spectrum's polynomial hull. Several examples escape well-known criteria, showing the test reaches further.
arxiv-2606-22815:
Fei Fang studies the Yamabe flow in a bounded domain in this 2026 paper. The Yamabe flow deforms a metric over time in pursuit of constant scalar curvature. Fang asks which starting data lead to solutions that last, vanish in finite time, or blow up, using a modified potential well method that sorts initial data into stable and unstable sets.

Fang first establishes local existence and regularity for weak solutions. Solutions starting in the stable set exist globally and extinguish in finite time. Those starting in the unstable set blow up, though only in infinite time. For certain high-energy data, the solution both decays toward zero over time and still blows up in finite time, a subtler combined behavior. The analysis of Palais-Smale sequences links long-time behavior to steady states. A Pohozaev identity for the equation then yields a nonexistence theorem, ruling out certain solutions entirely.
arxiv-2606-22915:
Zichuan Chen, Lucas Kock, Jeong Eun Lee, and David J. Nott make Bayesian density regression practical in this 2026 paper. Density regression lets the whole distribution of a response vary with covariates, not just its mean. Logistic Gaussian process priors suit this task and can be centered on a base model, but they require a normalizing constant for every observation, usually computed by costly numerical integration.

The authors avoid that cost with a generalized Bayesian approach built on the Hyvärinen score. That score depends only on derivatives of the log density, so no normalizing constant is ever needed. Sparse inducing point approximations and variational inference make the Gaussian process computations scalable. The method was demonstrated on one simulated and two real datasets. One was a German weather dataset with more than 150,000 observations, showing the approach handles data at a scale that blocked earlier versions of these models.
arxiv-2606-23115:
Tong Zhang and colleagues test whether conserving mass helps neural cellular automata reach a critical regime in a 2026 paper. A cellular automaton updates a grid by local rules; the neural version learns those rules. Self-organized criticality is a regime of scale-free avalanches linked to strong information processing. Reservoir computing exploits such dynamics by reading answers out of a churning system without training the system itself. The authors ask whether a mass conservation rule biases evolved automata toward critical behavior.

Zhang and colleagues evolve both conserving and standard automata over many runs. Conserving versions hit strong criticality more often, with more runs matching perfect power-law avalanche patterns. They also evolved faster. On memory, digit, and control benchmarks, the conserving reservoirs matched the standard ones. The best control score came from a perfectly critical reservoir.
arxiv-2606-23315:
Jin-Guo Liu and colleagues report a course redesign that replaces lectures with weekly closed-book tests in a 2026 education paper. The thirteen-week course covers the theory of computation at a university in Guangzhou. Students learn on their own with AI assistance, following a prepared path of learning sheets and practice checks. Weekly tests then act as a strict quality gate. AI agents help the instructor draft the path, build the course site, produce tests, and grade, all inside a version-controlled workspace with human oversight.

Liu and colleagues draw evidence from a student survey, weekly scores, and the project's version history. Students treated the frequent tests as useful accountability rather than arbitrary pressure. The AI-assisted harness made weekly test production feasible for one instructor. The authors note the limits plainly: one small, proof-heavy course and no control group.
arxiv-2606-23515:
Fairer machine learning usually starts by fixing a model. Hedman and colleagues argue in a 2026 paper that fairness should shape how data is gathered instead. Training data often already encodes social bias. A careful model can still inherit unfair patterns from such data. Their setting is Bayesian experimental design. That framework picks which measurements to collect next, based on how much each one should teach.

The proposed method, FairBED, defines fair data in a simple way. Fair data reveals little about sensitive attributes, such as demographic group. Its objectives reward experiments that teach a lot about the target quantity. At the same time, they reward teaching little about those attributes. The authors link the approach to demographic parity, a standard fairness criterion. In experiments, models trained on FairBED data trade accuracy against fairness better than models using random or conventional designs.
arxiv-2606-23615:
Senyard and colleagues release a benchmark for mapping hedgerows from satellite imagery across France, in a 2026 paper on remote sensing. Hedgerows, lines of shrubs and trees along field edges, support wildlife, store carbon, and protect soil. They have declined sharply, yet their extent is poorly mapped because field surveys are costly. Satellite images could fill the gap, but models must work in new regions and climates too.

The benchmark, called Hedgementation, merges harmonized Sentinel 2 imagery, learned image embeddings, and ground truth labels from a French national hedgerow inventory. Its splits test generalization across distance and across climatic zones, a harder challenge than random splits. Three baseline models are evaluated, covering supervised deep networks and a self supervised embedding approach. The best reaches above forty percent segmentation accuracy, stronger in farming areas and temperate zones.
arxiv-2606-23815:
Bolchini and colleagues turn measurements of a young disk's glowing surface into a weighing scale for its smallest dust grains, in a 2026 paper on planet formation. Telescopes with extreme adaptive optics photograph protoplanetary disks in scattered starlight. What they see is the scattering surface, where starlight last bounces off tiny grains. Its height depends on how much small dust the disk holds, and small grains steer the disk's heating and growth toward planets.

The authors build a semi analytic model linking surface height to disk mass, temperature, and opacity, and validate it against a full radiative transfer code. The surface sits where the optical depth along the starlight path reaches about one. Temperature strongly shifts the height; settling matters little. For ten disks, small dust is roughly a thousandth of the mass.
arxiv-2606-24215:
Carroll and colleagues crash Kerr-Sen black holes together on a computer, to see whether the exotic fields around them survive. Kerr-Sen holes arise in Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton-axion theory. It extends general relativity with extra dilaton and axion fields alongside electromagnetism. Using numerical relativity with approximate initial data for head-on binaries, the team evolves mergers across part of the theory's parameter space.

For holes with nontrivial electric charge, a dilaton field persists straight through the merger. When spin is present, the remnant also keeps an axion field. That is evidence the holes are nonlinearly stable in this theory. The team further asks whether initially bare holes grow hair in a scalar background. Immersed holes retain scalar hair throughout. Even Kerr-Newman black holes, which start unscalarised, spontaneously scalarise in the background and stay that way. Carroll's 2026 simulations suggest these alternative-gravity holes are robust objects.
arxiv-2606-24315:
Yusupova, Izmailov, and Karimov compute how gas disks glow around an acoustic black hole. It is a lab-style analogue: sound in a moving fluid cannot escape it, mimicking a gravitational horizon. Their Schwarzschild-like acoustic hole carries a background fluid flowing inward, at a speed set by a tuning parameter. The team applies the Novikov-Thorne thin-disk framework, comparing disk observables against an ordinary Schwarzschild black hole.

Two regimes appear, divided by a threshold value of the tuning parameter. Below it, the disk strengthens. Flux, temperature, and luminosity all exceed the Schwarzschild case. Above it, the disk weakens, falling below the standard profiles. The sharpest change traces to the marginally stable orbit, the innermost safe circular path for orbiting gas. Its radius switches branch near the threshold, dragging every radiative profile with it. The 2026 analysis maps where analogue holes outshine or underperform their gravitational twins.
arxiv-2606-24415:
Ebert, Lindeberg, and Hellmuth define new puzzle pieces for rebuilding evolutionary networks from local clues. Rooted phylogenetic networks represent histories where lineages merge as well as split. They must be inferred from fragmentary evidence. Sequence data often suggests only that two species sit closer to each other than either does to a third, classically encoded as a rooted triple. In networks, ancestral relationships misbehave compared with trees.

An ancestor-based reading is adopted. A triple is displayed when the least common ancestor of the close pair sits strictly below the shared least common ancestor each forms with the third species. Anchored triples then relax this, keeping only the asymmetric comparison between two of the pairwise ancestors. The 2026 paper studies several such variant problems for network construction. It asks which collections of local statements determine a network, and how hard reconstruction becomes.
arxiv-2606-24515:
Sumyk and Kosovan teach desktop software agents with a judge, instead of a reward engineer. Computer use agents pursue user goals inside graphical interfaces. Reinforcement learning needs success signals, though. Open ended desktop tasks rarely provide machine readable ones. Handcrafted reward functions and manual labels do not scale. Their 2026 framework uses autonomous vision language evaluation. Given the final screenshot alongside the original instruction, a vision language model judges completion and returns terminal feedback.

Imperfect judges make noisy rewards. The team therefore models evaluator feedback as a noisy binary channel. A noise corrected reward estimator is derived for proximal policy optimisation, a standard reinforcement learning algorithm. Across macOSWorld, Windows Agent Arena, and OSWorld benchmarks, corrected evaluator rewards beat both zero shot baselines and raw, uncorrected evaluator rewards. If the grader is biased but measurably so, learning can still proceed honestly on its verdicts.
arxiv-2606-24615:
Sabrina Burgardt leads an eleven author team asking whether active matter can exist at the scale of single atoms. Active matter means particles that pull energy from their surroundings and turn it into motion. Scientists know this behaviour from bird flocks, bacterial swarms, and tiny synthetic swimmers. At the size of one atom, though, quantum effects take over, making real activity there an open challenge.

The team held single cesium atoms in an optical trap. The atoms sat in an ultracold bath of rubidium atoms. Burgardt and colleagues show the cesium atoms draw energy from the bath through quantum spin interactions. They then convert that energy into active motion. A model of the motion, built from kinetic theory with no fitted parameters, matches the measured dynamics well. Computer collision simulations support the same picture. The authors identify spin exchange as the engine that turns spin energy into movement.
arxiv-2606-24715:
Giorgio Corani and three colleagues ask how to pick the best forecasting model across many time series. Each model earns an average proper score on one series. Combining scores across a dataset is the hard part. Workers either scale and average them, or use ranks and win rates. These choices can point to different winners. The authors trace the conflict to skewness in the scores, worst when test sets are short.

Corani and colleagues show that rank, median, and win rate rules can pick a misspecified model. The plain mean scaled score does not suffer from this flaw. As test sets grow, all the rules converge on the same decision anyway. Experiments on intermittent demand data, including the M5 competition, stress the need for large test sets. The mean scaled score also stayed consistent across scaling factors. The advice, reflected in the title, is to prefer that mean.
arxiv-2606-24815:
Pablo Valle, Shaukat Ali, Aitor Arrieta, and Lionel Briand automate the testing of robots controlled by vision language action models. Such models merge perception, language, and action in one system. Testing them needs oracles: rules that judge whether a task succeeded. Hand built symbolic oracles cost expert effort, tie tightly to one task, and only grade the final state. MANGO, their framework, generates fine grained oracles from plain language task descriptions instead.

Three agents, a Generator, an Assessor, and a Judge, refine the outputs through structured feedback. MANGO first builds a reusable library of atomic tasks. It then grounds an oracle definition for each atomic task in the simulator. Complex instructions are split into ordered atomic steps, each with its own oracle. On the LIBERO and RoboCasa humanoid benchmarks, the generated oracles catch a similar number of failures as symbolic ones. They also localise faults and give richer diagnostic detail.
arxiv-2606-25015:
A team including Jingyuan Wang studies how gravity could have made dark matter during multifield inflation. Particles can be created by the changing spacetime, with no coupling to the inflaton fields. Two fields move through a field space that may be flat or curved. Benchmarks run from the flat limit to a sidetracked attractor on hyperbolic field space. The team computes the production spectrum of a spectator for couplings to curvature, minimal and conformal.

Negative curvature amplifies how the Ricci scalar swings after inflation. Production rises up to ten times the flat yield, for minimal coupling. On the sidetracked attractor the gain competes with a lower inflation scale, so the relic abundance depends on parameters. The team maps the region in spectator mass and reheating temperature. The conformal case, whose mode equation mirrors a fermion's, is less constrained by isocurvature limits and gives a minimal case for gravitational dark matter.
arxiv-2606-25715:
Splitting a data table into two nonnegative factors is a data analysis workhorse. The exact version asks for factors whose product reproduces the table perfectly. Mithil Ramteke studies the gap regime in 2026, where the nonnegative rank exceeds the ordinary rank. He sorts every recoverable factorisation into three regimes, by the rank of one factor. A footnote notes AI help with the drafts. The author takes full responsibility for the content. A two sided gauge built from the singular value decomposition drives the main pipeline.

In the full rank regime the pipeline recovered all one hundred random test matrices at two gap sizes. That beats the companion paper's saturation rates. A structured block family breaks the method completely. Yet a column subset branch restores perfect recovery in milliseconds. A third, intermediate regime appears through the regular octagon's slack matrix. There an exact factorisation exists, reachable but delicate.
arxiv-2606-25815:
Schrödinger cat states, superpositions of two macroscopically distinct states, are precious and fragile resources for quantum technology. Volker Karle, Florian Kluibenschedl, Mikhail Lemeshko, and Vasil Rokaj propose making them from spinning molecules in 2026. An ensemble of polar molecules sits inside a microwave cavity. The cavity talks to the molecules' rotations collectively, with a coupling strengthened by the square root of their number. In the dispersive limit, virtual transitions through the rotational ladder bend the cavity's response into an effective Kerr nonlinearity, the ingredient that sculpts cats.

The predicted states are hybrids, part rotation, part photon, with cat structure locked by parity in the cavity sectors. Wigner tomography and a Schrieffer Wolff analysis confirm the mechanism in theory. Molecules bring their own built in anharmonicity, so no fabricated nonlinear element is needed. Collective rotation becomes a new route to light matter cat states.
arxiv-2606-25915:
Pengwei Wang and colleagues address a practical problem in eye screening: judging the quality of colour fundus photographs, images of the back of the eye used to spot retinal disease. Existing quality labels judge the whole image at once, yet damage like blur or poor lighting often ruins only part of a photo. Wang's team argues that quality should be scored pixel by pixel, based on whether anatomical structures stay visible.

FunPiQ, the benchmark they introduce, is the first fundus dataset with pixel-level quality annotations. Their companion method, EFIQA-CP, trains a neural network on quality pseudo-labels derived from anatomical visibility, using a learning scheme built for partly labelled data. Across their evaluations, explainable-by-design methods beat ordinary classifiers with after-the-fact explanations and anomaly detectors, with EFIQA-CP performing best overall.
arxiv-2606-26415:
Anthony Ruffa and Bourama Toni find a new route to the Bickley-Naylor functions, special functions used in radiative heat transfer and neutron transport that cannot be evaluated in closed form. Their derivation runs through a small system of equations rather than the classical integral definitions.

Solving a three-by-three system yields explicit expressions for the second, third, and fourth functions, and a recurrence extends them to any order. The whole infinite family spans just a four-dimensional space of modified Bessel and Struve functions over polynomials. That finite description gives researchers a fresh computational and modeling tool for these functions.
arxiv-2606-26515:
Rajat Modi, Sebastian Noel, Xin Liang, and Yogesh S. Rawat adapt video models while they run. Test-time training updates a model's weights on the incoming video itself, using a self-teaching task that needs no labels. For long videos, older methods update on a sliding window of past frames. The computing cost grows with the window and becomes unworkable for videos hours long.

Their Frame Forgetting Network uses only three frames at a time. It keeps the frame leaving the window, the current frame, and the next one. Temporal context survives despite the tiny window. A surprise measure, defined mathematically, gauges how much new information each frame carries. That measure drives an adaptive window that spends effort only when the scene changes. The team also built EpicTours, a data set of walking tours up to three hours long. Earlier sets held only minutes of video.
arxiv-2606-26915:
Chang Liu and Kun Xu decompose gas flows into a wave part and a particle part to simulate every flow regime in one framework. Kinetic equations describe gases from free flight to near-fluid behaviour. The split is set by a local timescale and its horizon, the distance over which particles travel freely. Beyond the horizon, motion is purely kinetic; inside it, effects accumulate into a wave.

The wave part obeys its own equation whose averages reproduce the classic Euler and Navier-Stokes fluid fluxes. Its coefficients depend on the horizon, adapting to local conditions. The particle part carries the remaining non-equilibrium transport. A conservative macro-micro scheme computes both together. Deterministic or Monte Carlo particle solvers plug in. The unified system spans the whole spectrum from thin gas to continuum flow.
arxiv-2606-27015:
T. Torres and five colleagues demonstrate wave trapping in an optical fibre driven by a single travelling pulse. A moving change in refractive index can act like a mirror in time, reflecting light waves. Here a high-order soliton, a self-sustaining light pulse, evolves as it travels and reshapes the boundary it creates. Other waves meeting it can be reflected, transmitted, or caught between behaviours.

Experiments ran in a five-kilometre nonlinear fibre. Measurements confirmed all three components coexisting, matching theory closely. The trapped component rides with the pulse, guided in time rather than space. A single pulse thus forms a versatile temporal waveguide. The authors see routes to all-optical control of ultrafast signals, where light steers light with no electronics.
arxiv-2606-27115:
Zhou measures how strongly distant quasars cluster together in space using the second data release from the DESI survey. Their clustering strength, called bias, reveals the mass of the dark halos hosting them. The sample holds roughly seven hundred fifteen thousand quasars seen when the universe was young. Redshift, a stretch measure of cosmic distance, splits the sample into four slices for the 2026 analysis.

Bias climbs strongly with redshift and follows a neat fitted curve across the slices. That pattern matches a typical host halo mass near a trillion solar masses, steady across cosmic time. Only about one halo in a hundred hosts an active quasar at any moment, a share called the duty cycle. Splitting by brightness gives the first firm sign that brighter quasars cluster slightly more strongly at these distances. That pattern tests black hole growth models.
arxiv-2606-27315:
Lee and colleagues prove that gradient equilibrium, a recent solution concept for online learning, is exactly Blackwell approachability in disguise. Approachability asks whether a player can steer average payoffs toward a target set against any opponent. Gradient equilibrium was introduced separately, through regret-style conditions on vector-valued losses. Black-box reductions run in both directions with no loss in long-run guarantees. During 2026, equivalence with regret minimisation and calibration follows, in a learning theory paper accepted at COLT.

Necessary and sufficient conditions for gradient equilibrium round out the picture. Algorithms transfer freely between the frameworks, so results proved once apply everywhere. Calibration, long treated as its own topic, lands inside the same circle of ideas. The merger simplifies a crowded landscape of online-learning concepts. Future work can pick whichever formulation fits the problem at hand. A cleaner map of the territory is the deliverable.
arxiv-2606-27515:
Ramadhan, Hosseini, and Lake test how faithfully the artificial boundaries of a truncated simulation domain must be treated when modelling geological carbon storage. Ten boundary treatments are compared against full-domain reference runs in two reservoir types. In 2026, pressure errors and plume overlap scores grade each treatment.

Conserving corner pore volume proves the single most important requirement. Uniform treatments that neglect corner storage produce large pressure errors and misplace roughly a sixth to a fifth of the plume area in the reported comparisons. Corner-adjusted treatments cut errors sharply and lift plume overlap above zero point nine four in the same metrics. The gradual modifier with transmissibility correction performs most consistently, keeping pressure error below three point seven percent and plume overlap above zero point nine seven across both reservoir types. Transmissibility correction alone helps uniform rock but backfires in variable rock.
arxiv-2606-27715:
Alec Dewulf examines a failure mode of the Muon optimiser in 2026. Muon is a spectral training method for neural networks. For tall matrix parameters, such as MLP projection matrices, its updates can have wildly uneven row norms. Some neurons then receive persistently tiny updates. A feedback loop can leave them contributing almost nothing to network outputs. Row normalisation fixes this, but existing fixes distort Muon's geometry.

Dewulf proposes Aurora, a leverage-aware spectral optimiser. Aurora enforces row-uniform updates across matrix parameters. It respects the polar factor geometry of the momentum matrix at the same time. In pretraining experiments, Aurora outperformed Muon. Combined with existing methods, it reached state-of-the-art results among spectral optimizers on the modded-nanoGPT speedrun optimizer track. Its gains over Muon grow with the MLP expansion factor. That scaling hints Aurora may suit very wide MLP layers, the author suggests.
arxiv-2606-27815:
Dynamic time warping classifies time series by aligning them flexibly. Its Euclidean distances miss links between channels in multivariate data. Diego Alvarez-Estevez and two colleagues replace that distance in 2026 with quantum geometry. Their hybrid design measures distance inside a parameterised quantum Hilbert space. Tests reach up to eight spatial channels.

A new circuit layout, the Unified Pre-Embedding Adjoint Ansatz, is the key piece. It keeps trainable entanglement apart from the classical data. Older designs suffer phase scrambling and information bottlenecks at measurement; this one avoids both. Even untrained quantum kernels act as strong baselines. Training then untangles deeply overlapping data further. A strict trade-off appears as well. Extra temporal depth helps narrow one-channel circuits. On wide multi-qubit registers, the same depth triggers frequency explosions and collapse of the representation. By steering around those hazards, the quantum design beats classical baselines.
arxiv-2606-27915:
The Ryu–Takayanagi relation ties entanglement entropy to geometry in holography. Entanglement entropy itself diverges in the ultraviolet, though. Albert Much and three colleagues rebuild the relation in 2026 around relative entropy instead, which stays finite. The setting is the AdS3/CFT2 correspondence. A diamond region on the boundary carries the states being compared, the vacuum and a coherent state.

Hollands' exact result for chiral relative entropy is adapted to that diamond. The boundary relative entropy becomes a Schwarzian functional. The holographic dictionary reads it as data of a Bañados geometry, and the rigidity of three-dimensional gravity promotes the identification into the bulk. To first order in the metric perturbation, a clean formula results. The relative entropy equals the change in the Ryu–Takayanagi geodesic length, divided by four times Newton's constant. The construction rests only on a classic modular theory theorem and the dictionary.
arxiv-2606-28115:
Fast X-ray transients linked to supernovae puzzle astronomers. Several are tied to broad-lined Type Ic supernovae. Yu-Fei Li and four colleagues propose a unified model in 2026 for their emission. A rapidly spinning magnetar sits at the centre. It drives a collimated jet dominated by Poynting flux, plus an isotropic wind. The jet bores through the stellar envelope and inflates a hot cocoon. The wind interacts with the ejecta to form a pulsar wind nebula.

Early thermal emission comes from the cocoon. The nebula supplies the mid-term non-thermal emission, once the cocoon turns transparent. Late emission is the supernova itself, powered by nickel decay and the magnetar. X-ray afterglows come from the structured jet. Three events anchor the case studies, two Einstein Probe transients and the low-luminosity burst GRB 171205A. A shared origin with some gamma-ray burst supernovae is revealed.
arxiv-2606-28215:
Jiaxin Li and thirteen colleagues, with Yong-Lu Li as senior author, want three-dimensional reconstructions of several objects interacting over time, built from a single ordinary video. Recovering such 4D scenes would cheaply supply training data for embodied artificial intelligence, but existing methods handle lone objects and break under heavy occlusion.

Li's team built HAT-4D, which pairs vision-language models with a person who gives feedback at several stages. Human guidance resolves depth ambiguities and untangles objects hiding each other during generation and tracking. The system produced a new open benchmark of multi-object interaction scenes, with scoring that stresses physical plausibility and steadiness over time. It reached state-of-the-art results on most measures, and its data improved other models when used for fine-tuning.
arxiv-2606-28415:
Thomas Fernique, writing alone, describes an art project built on a football icon. The Telstar, the black-and-white ball of the 1970 World Cup, joins thirty-two leather pieces. Its hexagons and pentagons are arranged like a truncated icosahedron, a shape that spreads the surface's curvature evenly over sixty vertices.

Fernique's project fabricates every ball that random assembly of those thirty-two pieces can produce, more than three and a half thousand distinct balls in all. Most are strange, lopsided cousins of the familiar design, since the classic pattern is only one arrangement among thousands. Along the way the text explains why flat leather needs many pieces to fake a sphere at all. It invokes Gauss's theorem that curvature cannot change without stretching the material, and the Gauss-Bonnet accounting that fixes the total.
arxiv-2606-28515:
Floor S. Broekgaarden, writing alone, pushes back on claims of a crisis in black hole astrophysics. Several studies had argued that simulations of isolated binary evolution predict far more local black hole mergers, as a rule, than gravitational-wave observatories see. They were said to force drastic rewrites of stellar evolution theory.

Broekgaarden compiles nearly fifteen hundred simulated merger rates from fifty-seven published studies and compares them with the latest LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA constraints. About eighty percent of submodels do overshoot, but a large subset matches or undershoots the observed rate, and the literature spans orders of magnitude. Thousands of controlled pairwise changes show many single choices, not just strong natal kicks or suppressed metal-poor star formation, can lower rates into agreement. Rates also cluster by simulation code, so apparent consensus within one framework may be a silo, not a verdict.
arxiv-2606-28715:
My Chiffon Nguyen, Aulia Adila, Saksorn Ruangtanusak, Kittiphat Leesombatwathana, Vissuta Gunawan Lim, Patomporn Payoungkhamdee, and Samuel Cahyawijaya test artificial intelligence agents in the languages of Southeast Asia. Agents that book, buy, and troubleshoot in English are being readied for a region of many tongues, yet their skill in those languages was barely measured, a gap with real sovereignty weight.

SEATauBench adapts a known tool-agent-user benchmark into Mandarin, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, and Filipino, then localizes step by step: first the conversation language, then tool specs, then whole task domains. Across three recent models, skills carried over fairly well when only the chat language changed. Quality and toughness then fell sharply with deeper localization, worst under full domain adaptation. English-only testing, the authors conclude, badly overstates what agents can do for Southeast Asian users.
arxiv-2606-28815:
Bercic and Stanojevikj describe Mathswitch, an open-source project gathering records of mathematical concepts from sources such as Wikidata, Wikipedia, MathWorld and several specialist encyclopedias. Records that name the same concept are linked, but each source keeps its own structure and wording. Because Wikidata is edited collaboratively and queried broadly, the imported set is noisy, with some items not mathematical at all and others ambiguous.

To clean the set, the pair test a voting ensemble of language model judges, meaning several models vote on whether each item truly belongs. They check the voters against items known to have MathWorld entries, and rerun the test with database identifiers hidden to see if labels sway the vote. Where judges disagreed with MathWorld, the cases fell into three groups, including thin descriptions and scope mismatches, each pointing to a different fix.
arxiv-2606-28915:
Ohshiro and nine colleagues use a new X-ray instrument to weigh the white dwarf in EX Hydrae, a binary where the dwarf pulls gas from a companion star. White dwarf masses shape how such systems evolve, and high-resolution X-ray spectra can track the dwarf's orbital motion via Doppler shifts in emission lines that form near its surface. The XRISM satellite's Resolve instrument observed the system for 83 thousand seconds.

Iron emission lines in the spectrum shifted back and forth coherently with the orbit. The measured velocity amplitude was about 58 kilometres per second, with an uncertainty under nine. This is the first detection of orbital motion in individual iron K-shell lines from such a dwarf. Resolve's sharpness and frequent calibration enabled it. The X-ray value agrees with optical and ultraviolet measurements. Combined with known orbital parameters, it gives a dwarf mass of about 0.79 solar masses.
arxiv-2606-29015:
Garg models Herman Kahn's nuclear escalation ladder as a mathematical game. Kahn's ladder lists rungs of rising conflict, from calm to nuclear use. Garg reindexes each rung by how far it sits from the nuclear threshold, turning the ladder into a subtraction game, a tractable class in combinatorial game theory. The doctrine that neither side wishes to fire first selects the misere convention, where the last mover loses.

He proves that one ladder's stability is governed by a congruence, an arithmetic pattern. He also derives a design rule: the burden of first escalation depends on ladder length and step size. For several theatres at once, under normal play, joint stability equals the Nim-sum of the theatre-wise distances. That rule is neither additive nor set by the most dangerous theatre. Under misere play it fails. Garg replaces it with the misere quotient, computing it fully for two-step escalation.
arxiv-2606-29215:
Jin and ten colleagues speed up diffusion language models by decoding several text blocks at once. Block diffusion models generate text block by block, with caching and flexible lengths. Decoding a running set of blocks in parallel promises more speed, but models are trained seeing only one noisy block after a clean prefix, so training and parallel decoding mismatch.

Their fix is Multi-block Teacher Forcing: post-training on bounded groups of noisy blocks after clean prefixes, with randomised noise schedules that mimic real decoding states. A Block Buffer decoding algorithm then keeps prefix-cache reuse and static input shapes, turning the extra parallelism into wall-clock speed. On their test model, tokens per forward pass rose from about three and a half to over six, and accuracy improved slightly. A combined variant reached over nine tokens per pass with a small accuracy cost.
arxiv-2606-29615:
de la Cerda characterizes cumulants, classical quantities built from the moments of a random variable. Moments are expected values of powers of the variable. Cumulants are polynomial functions of those moments, set apart by additivity: the cumulant of a sum of independent variables is the sum of their cumulants.

She proves the converse. Any statistic that depends smoothly on finitely many moments, and is additive for independent sums, must be expressible as a linear combination of cumulants. Her proof recasts the problem through the Hurwitz product and a change of coordinates. A more general theorem by Mattner already implies the result, as de la Cerda notes openly. Her contribution is a basic, self-contained route showing why cumulants are forced.
arxiv-2606-29815:
Li and eleven colleagues study data leakage in code large language models, where a model's test scores are inflated because it saw the benchmark data during training. Their paper presents SrDetection, a self-referential framework that detects this leakage without access to the training data or hand-set thresholds.

SrDetection creates rewritten versions of each test sample that mean the same thing, then compares how the model behaves on the original and the variants. If the original is far easier for the model, leakage is flagged. On a controlled testbed the method raises the F1 score, a balance of precision and recall, by 21.52 points with access to model scores and 14.46 points with outputs only. A study of 15 code models on four benchmarks then shows leakage patterns that differ by benchmark.
arxiv-2606-29915:
Peh, Roy, and Fernando propose H-GRPO, a training framework that makes vision-language models show their visual evidence instead of answering as black boxes. Such models can score well while hallucinating or leaning on shortcuts.

The framework applies decompositional evidence grounding. The model must split a question into a chain of atomic sub-questions, and for each one give a sub-answer plus a bounding box marking the image region that supports it. An example is locating a container before judging its contents. The final answer then follows from verified visual facts in sequence rather than a statistical guess. The reinforcement learning in the title is permutation-invariant, meaning the training does not depend on the order in which the sub-questions are listed.
arxiv-2606-30015:
Xuan Zhao, Haonan He, and seven colleagues improve how language model agents use skills. Skills are written recipes capturing proven ways to solve tasks. Agents often fail to follow long instructions in crowded contexts. Their framework, ParametricSkills, converts a written skill into model parameters. The agent then uses it without rereading the text.

The authors first build a large, high quality skill library. They generate practice trajectories around those skills with a coding tool. Both single turn and multi turn trajectories are included. They then train a hypernetwork to convert each skill. A hypernetwork produces the weights of another network. Here it outputs a small LoRA adapter for the skill. On six software engineering subtasks, this beats in-context learning clearly. Judge scores rise by more than six points. Because parametric skills accumulate, test-time continual learning looks plausible.
arxiv-2606-30115:
Filippo Balli and eight colleagues probe how easily an AI observer for CT imaging can be fooled. The model observer detects and localizes low-contrast objects in phantom scans. Such tools help optimize CT protocols before clinical use. Adversarial examples, tiny crafted changes to inputs, test its robustness. Both gradient-based and optimization-based white-box attacks are used.

Fast gradient attacks cause high misclassification, up to three quarters of cases. The perturbations remain invisible to the human eye. Localization proves hardier, failing less often under the same attacks. Optimization-based attacks succeed about half the time on both tasks. Dynamic adversarial training then hardens the model substantially. Attack success falls to single digits for classification tasks. Radiomic texture analysis explains part of the vulnerability. Successful attacks consistently shift specific local texture features.
arxiv-2606-30715:
Urvi Thakurdesai and sixteen colleagues hunt for supermassive black holes that wander off-centre in young galaxies. Theory predicts that frequent minor mergers and lopsided gas inflows can knock a growing black hole away from its galaxy's centre in the early universe. A displaced, active black hole should light up gas away from the stellar centre, leaving an offset glow of highly ionised gas.

Using spectroscopy from the James Webb telescope's CEERS survey, the team analysed ninety galaxies seen as they were when the universe was young. They mapped the ratio of doubly ionised oxygen to hydrogen emission across each galaxy's image. Twenty-six galaxies, about thirty percent, showed strong local peaks in that ratio. In twelve of them, the peak sat clearly offset from the stellar centre, and six showed the largest offsets. The authors present these offsets as a promising route to probing early black-hole growth.
arxiv-2606-30915:
Neerja Aggarwal and fourteen colleagues introduce the Spectral DiffuserScope, a compact microscope that captures a full spectrum at every point of an image in a single snapshot. It serves biology and medicine, but conventional systems are bulky or must scan, which limits speed and throughput. Their device uses compressed sensing, recovering a rich data cube from fewer measurements, and reaches higher spatial and spectral resolution than earlier snapshot designs. The whole unit measures about 15 by 6 by 6 centimetres and clips onto standard microscopes.

Simulations benchmarked it against existing snapshot methods. In the lab, the team imaged fluorescent beads, labelled cells and lanthanide hydrogel beads, which carry spectral codes for assays. The results show a practical, high-throughput route to this imaging for biological and clinical work.
arxiv-2606-31215:
Qian and three colleagues study when the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on a two-sphere has well-behaved local solutions. The equation tracks a wave whose own size feeds back on its motion, with a gauge-invariant power-type nonlinearity. Well-posedness asks whether small changes in starting data stay small, and the threshold regularity marks where that control breaks.

The team prove a new lower bound for that threshold and show norm inflation below it, meaning tiny inputs can blow up at once. For stronger nonlinearities their bound matches the known well-posedness result, fixing the exact threshold at the scaling-critical value. For weaker powers they show the solution map fails to be uniformly continuous, again proving ill-posedness by a direct route.
arxiv-2606-31515:
Nikopoulos and six colleagues measure the metal content of the galaxies hosting little red dots. These compact, distant sources found by the James Webb Space Telescope look like accreting supermassive black holes in dense gas. Whether their gas is pristine, metal-poor, or richer was untested until now.

The team gather 24 little red dots at redshifts near 2.3 to 7 with medium and high resolution spectra. Oxygen abundances come from the direct electron-temperature method on narrow line components, cross-checked with strong-line calibrations. The average metallicity lands near eight percent of the Sun's value, firmly metal-poor for high-redshift star-forming galaxies yet far from pristine. The hosts were already enriched when their black holes lit up, a fact formation models must now absorb.
arxiv-2606-31815:
Busolini and Valencia-Pabon study independent set reconfiguration under the token sliding rule. Tokens sit on an independent set of vertices, with no two adjacent. A move slides one token along an edge, keeping the set independent at every step. Deciding whether one set can be transformed into another is PSPACE-hard even on quite restricted graph classes.

Polynomial-time algorithms already existed for trees, interval graphs, claw-free graphs and cographs, among others. Busolini and Valencia-Pabon extend the tractable territory to two broader families. Their algorithm handles P4-tidy graphs and (q, q-4)-graphs, both of which generalize cographs. The result sharpens the boundary between easy and hard cases for this reconfiguration problem.
arxiv-2606-32015:
Jain and two colleagues solve an online filling game exactly, to first order. An array of length n starts empty, and uniform random samples from the unit interval arrive one at a time. Each sample must be discarded or placed irrevocably into an empty slot, keeping the occupied entries non-decreasing from left to right. The question is the fastest expected time any strategy needs to fill the array.

A natural coupon-collector strategy, reserving one slot per equal interval, takes about n log n steps in expectation. The authors prove no strategy, even randomized and adaptive, can beat roughly half that leading constant, and they give an explicit deterministic strategy matching the bound. A with-replacement variant, where placed entries may be overwritten, separates provably from the original game.
arxiv-2608-00015:
Roy and Singirikonda test retrieval help for optimization and constraint modeling. Both tasks need deep domain skill and formal modeling fluency. Language models often give inconsistent or incomplete formulations. The flaw bites hardest in combinatorial settings. Their pipeline adds retrieval over a curated synthetic data set.

Five hundred problems were built from Text2Zinc seed descriptions. Each came in JSON with a checked Python solver script. Similar past problems were pulled from a Chroma store at query time. A LangChain agent used them as context for Qwen 3 30B Instruct. Accuracy on NL4OPT rose from 40 to 72 percent. MAMO scores rose from 40 and 32 to 56 percent. Retrieval beat the need for fine-tuning in their tests.
arxiv-2608-00115:
Ai, Gutin, Lei, and Shi settle the complexity of two spanning subdigraph problems. A trail is antidirected when its arcs alternate in direction. A digraph is antistrong when such trails join every ordered vertex pair. Bang-Jensen and co-authors posed the two problems in 2017. Each asks for paired spanning subdigraphs with set connectivity traits.

Both decision problems prove NP-complete, they show. The first stays hard even with small in- and out-degree caps. The second stays hard for strong, antistrong oriented digraphs with tight degree bounds. Its underlying graphs can be 3-vertex-connected in the hard cases. The result does not rely on digons, they note. Polynomial-time hopes for both problems are thus closed.
arxiv-2608-00215:
Jin and co-authors personalize LLM agents with a small policy model called FABLE. Agents can fetch memory, call tools, and vary style. Adapting those execution choices to one user stays hard. Fine-tuning a separate model is costly or barred for closed systems. Prompts expose user facts but do not teach execution choices from feedback.

FABLE sits outside the frozen host agent as a light policy layer. It factorizes memory, information, and response decisions for shared learning. An external feasible set filters actions before exploration. Bayesian contextual Thompson sampling learns each user's residual tastes. A calibrated variant carries an expected-regret bound. Tests show gains on preference-sensitive behaviours, they report. End-to-end task performance stayed competitive.
arxiv-2608-00315:
Tabbara, Yang, and Sibai test language-conditioned safety filters for robot policies. Vision-language-action models let one policy run many tasks from natural language. Safe deployment must adapt to safety demands as well as tasks. Those demands vary by user, setting, and application. Existing filters are tied to set constraints and must be rebuilt when demands change.

Their filter conditions a Hamilton-Jacobi safety actor and critic on language-stated constraints. Tests span pick-and-place, table-wiping, and block-stacking tasks. All run in a vision-based setting. The filters cut constraint violations in their experiments. Partial transfer to unseen constraint cases within known families also appeared. General language-conditioned safety is the direction they probe.
arxiv-2608-00415:
Shao and co-authors boost generalizable depth estimation in endoscopy with a self-supervised framework. Depth reading is key for 3D perception in endoscopic surgery. Illumination interference and scene diversity still block general depth models. Their framework, EndoMINI, attacks both issues. A mixture of low-rank experts fine-tunes the model with few parameters.

Those experts also lift adaptation to scenes with distinct traits. An intrinsic image alignment term joins the training loss. It eases the influence of light reflectance through a decomposition network. Tests cover supervised depth on SCARED data. Zero-shot tests run on Hamlyn and SERV-CT sets. The model shows outstanding performance against state-of-the-art works, they report. Ablations credit both main contributions.
at-sunwich-port-part-3-contents-chapters:
Part 3 of W. W. Jacobs's seaport novel holds chapters eleven through fifteen, with drawings by Will Owen. Jack Nugent receives a letter from his estranged father asking a meeting at Samson Wilks's house. His first impulse is a rude refusal, but the Kybird family, who lodge him, argue that the old man may mean to do something for him.

Mrs. Kybird hopes for help starting Jack in business, provided the meeting does not break his match with 'Melia. Elsewhere an invalid steward recovers under Mrs. Silk's care, devouring arrowroot, beef-tea, and milk while she promises him on his feet in a fortnight. Jacobs balances the feud's diplomacy with sickroom comedy in his usual deadpan portside voice.
austen-emma-1815:
Jane Austen published Emma in 1815, a comedy of self-deception in a small town. Emma Woodhouse is handsome, clever, and rich, with too much free time on her hands. Austen feared only she would like a heroine so sure she is always right.

Emma takes up matchmaking and vows she will never marry herself at all. Her schemes for Harriet Smith misfire and cause pain she did not foresee. Mr. Knightley, her old friend, corrects her with patience and growing love for her. A picnic, a riddle, and a harsh word at Box Hill force her to grow. Few novels mix charm and moral schooling with such a light hand.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-15:
Volume fifteen of Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud, in its 1902 printing, opens Tract Sanhedrin, the law of the high court. Sanhedrin is the Talmud's most solemn tractate. It governs the courts that could judge life and death.

Part one sets how judges are chosen and how a capital trial must run: witnesses warned, votes counted from the junior judges up, and every doubt stretched toward mercy. The rabbis make a death sentence hard to reach on purpose. The tractate also asks who has a share in the world to come. Rodkinson's volume is the Talmud's courtroom at its gravest.
bel-inconnu-williams-1915:
Renaut de Beaujeu wrote Le Bel Inconnu, the Fair Unknown, in Old French in the early 1200s. Hugh Williams's 1915 edition prints the full poem of 6,266 verses for the modern reader. A young man with no name comes to Arthur's court and begs a quest.

Sent out unproved, the Fair Unknown wins his name, Guinglain, through rescues, fights, and a serpent kiss that frees a lady from a spell. The poem blends love, magic, and courtly grace in equal parts. Critics prize it as a jewel of its age. Williams's edition gives the French text clean and whole.
bonaventure-life-of-st-francis-1915:
Bonaventure, minister general of the Franciscans, wrote the Legenda Maior, the official life of Saint Francis of Assisi, around 1260. The order then ordered older lives destroyed, and his became the one true tale. Miss Lockhart translated the Latin into English in 1915. Bonaventure is the Seraphic Doctor, and his Francis is a mystic's portrait.

The life moves from Francis's wild youth to his conversion, the founding of the order, and the stigmata on La Verna. Miracles crowd the later chapters, told as signs of a soul made like Christ. Bonaventure writes theology in story form: Francis as the pattern of the gospel life. The book shaped how the West pictures its most loved saint.
booth-battle-of-waterloo-1815:
John Booth, a London publisher, made this set of the records of Waterloo in 1815, the year of the fight. Its full title says it holds the accounts writ by public order, British and from abroad. The set came out while the news of the great day was still fresh in all minds.

Dispatches, lists, and the tales of the chief men fill the book, as 1815 read them. It is the record the Rothschild news tale claims the house beat to London by sly means. As a plain source of its own time, the book lets readers test that tale for themselves.
bracton-de-legibus-woodbine-vol1-1915:
George Woodbine, a Yale legal scholar, opened a new critical edition of Bracton with a first volume in 1915. Bracton's De legibus is the great thirteenth-century treatise on the laws and customs of England. Woodbine went back to the manuscripts to improve on Twiss's Victorian text, which had served scholars since the 1880s.

The opening volume gives a fresh Latin text of the treatise's first part, with the manuscript evidence set out in detail. Woodbine studied how the work was copied and altered over time, which changed how later volumes were read. His edition aimed at accuracy where Twiss had sometimes guessed. The project set the modern standard for Bracton study, and scholars still cite Woodbine's text when the wording of the treatise matters.
campis-sendbrieff-1615:
Julianus de Campis wrote his Sendbrieff, a German open letter, in 1615. Its long title offers a report to all who had heard of the new brotherhood of the Rose Cross. The Rosicrucian Fama, a short manifesto, had just stirred print debate across German lands.

Campis writes as one of the first printed voices to answer that manifesto in public. His letter shows how fast the news of a hidden brotherhood could spread and excite hope. The pamphlet is a first-hand record of the furor of 1614 to 1616. Historians of the Rose Cross still start with texts like this one.
cannon-bodily-changes-1915:
Walter Cannon was a Harvard physiologist who used early X-ray methods to watch digestion at work. His 1915 book Bodily Changes in Pain, Hunger, Fear and Rage reports what strong feeling does inside the body. It grew from lab studies of animals under stress.

Cannon shows that pain and fear release adrenaline, speed the heart, and free sugar for quick action. He named this whole pattern the fight-or-flight response, and his later work named the body's steady balance homeostasis. Doctors still use his frame to explain stress and the roots of psychosomatic illness.
cantor-transfinite-numbers-jourdain-1915:
Georg Cantor created set theory and the mathematics of infinity in papers gathered here in English. Philip E. B. Jourdain translated Contributions to the Founding of the Theory of Transfinite Numbers in 1915. Jourdain also supplied an introduction and notes for new readers. Cantor's transfinite numbers measure sizes of sets that never end.

He proved that some infinities are larger than others, a result that shocked his peers. The counting numbers form one level, the points on a line a greater one. Cantor builds his cardinals and ordinals with great care. Many leading mathematicians at first resisted the work. It now anchors the foundations of mathematics. Jourdain's edition made it open to English readers.
cather-song-of-the-lark-1915:
Willa Cather published The Song of the Lark in 1915, her third novel. Its heroine is Thea Kronborg, the daughter of a Swedish pastor in a small Colorado railroad town. Thea has a fine singing voice, and the novel follows her long climb toward a career in opera.

Thea studies in Chicago, works in church choirs, and slowly learns what art demands. Time in the cliff dwellings of Arizona helps her grasp the depth of her calling. At last she reaches the stage as a leading singer in New York. Cather shaped the novel as a study of talent, discipline, and the cost of becoming an artist.
christopher-columbus-and-the-new-world-o:
Volume 8 of Filson Young's Columbus life closes the story with the Admiral's last defense of himself. The text prints Columbus's own letter pleading his services to the Sovereigns: he has served, he writes, as diligently as if to gain Paradise. The Porras brothers, left in posts beyond their capacity in the Indies, stand among the charges he answers one by one. An old man dictates his record to an ungrateful court, forgiving much and forgetting nothing.

Young ends his eight volumes where the documents end, with the Admiral's heritage of hatred and his death in Spain in 1506. The final judgment is left to the reader, as Young promised: hero, fanatic, and failure in one frame. Readers finishing the set get the most readable English life of its generation. It is built from Spanish and Italian archives, by a sailor who knew what the voyages cost.
cia-0000012315:
Someone was left alone for a few minutes in Buzinov's office, and a CIA document from January 1962 thought the moment worth recording. Buzinov was a Soviet official in the trade and science world the Penkovsky case moved through. In espionage, a few unguarded minutes in the right office can be worth months of patient work, and officers wrote such moments down.

The document preserves the vignette without the dressing of a finished report. Its brevity is its intrigue: who, what room, what seen, all compressed. For readers, it is a small human gap in the tradecraft, the kind great cases turn on.
cia-0000012415:
Meeting number thirty-five falls on September 27, 1961, near the Paris phase's peak. The sessions' intensity never flagged that month. By the thirty-fifth sitting, the count itself had become a measure of the operation's enormity. No source in memory had been worked this long, this often, or this deeply by two allied services acting as one team.

The record preserves the session's place in September's run. Handlers' notebooks filled while their source stayed willing and precise. For readers, the page shows momentum sustained across a season, in a city far from the danger waiting at home.
cia-0000013215:
Twelve years after the war ended, a Vietnamese official's comments on the POW and MIA issue were recorded in June 1987. The official spoke for the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, Hanoi's state. His words also touched on relations between Vietnam and the United States, the larger question into which the missing men had become permanently woven by then.

The record preserves Hanoi's late Cold War position in its own phrasing. The accounting was still unfinished, and both sides knew the issue blocked every other dealing. For readers, the page shows the war's longest aftermath still alive in diplomatic language.
cia-0000013615:
Peru's political prospects are weighed in a CIA paper from April 1963, in a season of generals and ballots. The military had seized power the year before to block an election result it disliked. New voting was promised, and the Andean republic's future hung on whether the soldiers would allow it. Parties, officers, and campesino movements all pressed their claims on the state at once.

The paper notes the generals' ambitions alongside the civilians' hopes. It treats the Andes' politics as the hemisphere's most volatile mixture. For readers, it shows Peru at one of its recurring crossroads, with Washington reading the signs.
cia-0000014715: Poland's government offered sanctuary to Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, in a CIA file dated May 1, 1952. The offer would have given the condemned couple a home abroad. Offers like it formed part of the worldwide campaign around their case. The file shows how even exile plans for two prisoners in New York became Cold War news.
cia-0000015315: A letter to Lloyd Berkner from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1958. It concerns Leon Davidson's possible move, per the clipped title. Berkner got the same word sent to Page, Goudsmit, and Alvarez that day. The spread shows one amateur's claims treated as a matter for the top of science.
cia-0000021515: Capture of an American pilot in Xieng Khouang Province in mid 1970 leads a CIA record dated in 1971. The title's second item begins with an observation, then breaks off in the catalog. Xieng Khouang held the Plain of Jars, a much fought over part of Laos. One capture there joined hundreds of cases tracked by the prisoner offices.
cia-0000039115:
First Lieutenant Gerald Francis Kinsman is the subject of a CIA record dated February 2, 1971. The title notes that a first document in the file also mentions the execution of two men. Kinsman's own case stands at the head of the record.

Inside, the file concerns the lieutenant and the grave matter mentioned beside his name. Records that join a named officer to an execution report are among the hardest in the set. The file preserves what was known and reported at the time. Later readers must weigh a case that mixes one man's fate with a report of killings in the same pages.
cia-0000044015:
Possible FMLN links to the priests' murder were suggested, in a CIA record dated January 2, 1990. The title ties the suggestion to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The suggestion ran against the charge most voices laid on the army.
