Tangle load tracks memory loss more closely than other signs. Yet tangles do not seem to kill cells directly. The team read gene patterns in tangle bearing nerve cells from human brains.

Those patterns matched senescence, a stress state where cells stop dividing and change their work. Four mouse models showed the same link for tangles, but not for amyloid plaques. A marker gene rose in step with tangle load and brain shrinkage. Human tissue from another tau disease showed the pattern too. Drugs that clear senescent cells cut tangle counts in mice. Neuron loss and brain swelling also eased. The work names a new target class for tau diseases.
europmc-pmc6300015:
Stoeckius and co-authors introduce Cell Hashing, a way to pool samples in single cell studies. The method appeared in Genome Biology. Single cell sequencing faces batch effects, hidden doublets, and high costs. Hashing labels cells from each sample before pooling. Barcoded antibodies against common surface proteins carry the sample tags.

The tags are read alongside each cell's gene activity. Each cell can then be traced back to its source sample. Cross-sample doublets stand out and can be removed. Pooling also lets labs load more cells per run. That cuts the cost per cell. The team validated hashing against a genetic approach. They show it fits many sample types and study designs.
europmc-pmc6362415:
McAuley and co-authors review influenza neuraminidase in Frontiers in Microbiology. Neuraminidase is a protein on the surface of the flu virus. It was long studied mainly for its role in freeing new viruses from infected cells.

Work now shows the protein does much more. Its shape helps the virus attach, enter cells, and leave again. It must also stay in balance with hemagglutinin, the other main surface protein. Changes in neuraminidase can shift how severe an infection is. The authors argue this drug target needs deeper study as new flu strains keep emerging.
europmc-pmc6368215:
Winter and co-authors present a research article in Chemical Science on learning molecular descriptors with neural networks. A molecule can be written in several text notations, such as SMILES and InChI. The team trained a model to translate between equivalent notations, forcing it to compress chemical meaning into a fixed-size numeric vector.

The model was pretrained on about 72 million compounds, with no labels needed. The resulting descriptors matched or beat standard circular fingerprints on prediction tasks for activity and physical properties. On two virtual screening benchmarks they significantly outperformed rival descriptors. The continuous space also lets users decode small moves into new chemical structures.
europmc-pmc6406315:
Williams and Cooper argue for action on racial gaps in health, in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Proof on what drives these gaps is already strong, they say. Waiting for perfect proof only delays change.

They call for communities of opportunity that cut the harms of systemic racism. Such places back early childhood, cut child poverty, and give safe housing. Health care must also change, with equal access to good care for all. They ask for more staff who reflect the patients served. New research should test what works on the ground.
europmc-pmc6478715:
Wang and co-authors show that the RNA methylation writer Mettl3 switches dendritic cells on. These antigen-presenting cells need co-stimulatory molecules and cytokines to wake T cells. Deleting Mettl3 only in dendritic cells blunted all of it: CD40, CD80, and interleukin-12 fell, and T cell stimulation weakened in dishes and in animals.

The mechanism is translational. Mettl3 lays m6A marks on the messenger RNAs for CD40, CD80, and Tirap, an adaptor in TLR4 signaling, and marked transcripts get translated more efficiently. More adaptor means stronger NF-κB signaling and more cytokine output. The study gives epitranscriptomics a concrete immune job: licensing the cell that starts adaptive responses.
europmc-pmc6480215:
Komori maps the career of Runx2, the transcription factor without which no bone forms at all: mice lacking it have neither osteoblasts nor mineralized skeleton, and cartilage maturation stalls. Its own expression follows the job, faint in uncommitted mesenchymal cells, peaking in immature osteoblasts, then falling as they mature.

Runx2 pushes progenitor proliferation by directly switching on the Fgf receptors Fgfr2 and Fgfr3, and in skull sutures it recruits hedgehog, Wnt, and parathyroid hormone-related signaling plus the factors Dlx5 and Sp7. Half dosage is not enough there, which is why heterozygous mutation leaves fontanelles open. In vitro, Runx2 drives the major bone matrix genes; its in vivo role in finished osteoblasts remains an open question.
europmc-pmc6541315:
Kariisa and co-authors report CDC data on US overdose deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants, writing in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. The analysis spans 2003 to 2017, with a close look at the final two years. Stimulant deaths climbed sharply late in that window, inside a wider overdose crisis.

In 2017, of 70,237 overdose deaths, 13,942 involved cocaine and 10,333 involved psychostimulants such as methamphetamine. Rates rose across sexes, ages, regions and states. Opioids appeared in nearly three quarters of the cocaine deaths, and synthetic opioids drove the cocaine rise since 2012. The psychostimulant rise, by contrast, grew mostly apart from opioids. The authors call this a polysubstance problem and urge stronger surveillance, prevention and linkage to care.
europmc-pmc6562915:
Akwii, Sajib, Zahra and Mikelis review angiopoietin-2, a growth factor that loosens blood vessels, writing in Cells. Ang2 works through the Tie2 receptor on vessel-lining cells, the same receptor its sibling Ang1 uses to stabilize vessels. Long cast as Ang1's blocker, Ang2 turns out to play both sides depending on context.

The review follows Ang2 through vessel growth and regression, then through disease: inflammation, pneumonia, sepsis, cancer, heart disease and diabetic eye damage. It explains the signaling in detail, including routes that bypass Tie2 through integrins. Because tumors and inflamed tissue pour out Ang2, blocking it has become a therapeutic idea, and the closing section weighs the strategies now being tested.
europmc-pmc6653815:
Larson and co-authors guide readers on measuring patient experience and satisfaction with care. Their article appears in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. Person-centred care is now central to quality debates. It matters for dignity in its own right. It also tracks with better use and outcomes. Yet measures of it are often misused. The authors separate two broad measure types. Patient experience covers interactions with the health system. Patient satisfaction judges care against expectations.

Three design questions anchor their guidance. How will results be used? How is patient subjectivity handled? Has the measure been validated or tested? Examples come from maternal and child health. The piece targets policy-makers, researchers, and implementers.
europmc-pmc6670015:
Bleijs and co-authors compare patient-derived xenografts and tumour organoids as cancer models. Their review appears in The EMBO Journal. Both systems preserve features of the parent tumour. Genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity survive in each. Organoids grow straight from primary patient material. They establish and expand with high efficiency. Xenografts need host animals instead. In return they keep tumour-stroma interactions intact. Those interactions feed tumorigenesis in patients.

The review traces recent advances in both systems. Applications span drug testing and resistance studies. Promises and challenges are weighed side by side. Neither model wins on every front. The authors guide readers on matching model to question.
europmc-pmc6718415:
Yang and co-authors mapped the variety of human natural killer cells at single-cell level. Natural killer cells attack virus-infected and cancerous cells. How they develop and differ in people was still unclear. The team sequenced RNA from single cells taken from bone marrow and blood.

They found distinct NK groups, including one showing signs of steady activation. Fully mature cells carried high levels of CX3CR1, TIM-3, and ZEB2. A middle group linked the bright and dim forms of NK cells. In a donor with a GATA2 mutation, bright NK cells were scarce and died more often. The work charts how human NK cells grow and diversify.
europmc-pmc6785715:
Forster and co-authors built a human gut bacterial genome and culture collection. Learning what gut microbes do requires living bacteria for tests and reference genomes for data analysis. Their culture collection holds 737 sequenced isolates from the human gut. These cover 273 species, 105 of them novel, from 31 families of gut bacteria in total.

The collection raised the count of genomes from the human gut by 37 percent overall. Merged into a global genome set, it classifies 83 percent of genera by abundance across 13,490 samples. Classification improved by 61 percent over the older Human Microbiome Project set. Nearly half of sequences can now be classified down to subspecies. The resource makes shotgun studies cheaper and more accurate.
europmc-pmc6889315:
Li and co-authors report a study in Cell Death and Differentiation on gut injury after blood flow returns. Cutting blood supply to the intestine, then restoring it, paradoxically wounds the tissue. Ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death stoked by damaged fats, was a suspect. Most studies watch the reperfusion phase. This team watched the starved phase before it.

Signs of ferroptosis rose right after ischemia, peaking near 30 minutes of reperfusion. The guard protein GPx4 fell while damage markers climbed. An enzyme called ACSL4, switched on by ischemia, prepares the fats that ferroptosis burns. Blocking that axis eased the injury in their tests. The authors argue the death decision starts before flow returns.
europmc-pmc6917215:
Rifaioglu and co-authors survey machine learning for computer-based drug discovery. Their review appeared in Briefings in Bioinformatics. Finding which compounds bind which targets is central to making new drugs. Lab screening alone is slow, costly, and hard to scale. Virtual screening uses computer models to predict likely interactions first.

The authors explain how compounds and proteins get turned into numbers a model can use. They list key toolkits, bioactivity databases, and benchmark data sets. Recent studies get close attention, above all those using deep learning. Work in vision and language helped spark that shift. The review closes with open problems and likely next steps for the field.
europmc-pmc6929615:
Zhao and co-authors show how immune cells help broken bones heal. Their study appeared in Theranostics. About 10 percent of fractures fail to heal well, with heavy costs for patients and health systems. Macrophages, a type of immune cell, guide stem cells in bone marrow toward forming bone.

Mice lacking a macrophage receptor called MSR1 healed a tibia defect more slowly than normal mice. In mixed cell cultures, MSR1 switched on a signalling chain, PI3K/AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin. That chain pushed stem cells to become bone-forming cells. It also steered macrophages toward a healing, M2-like state by boosting their energy production. A gene called PGC1α linked the two effects. Targeting MSR1, the authors suggest, could aid fracture repair.
europmc-pmc6953215:
Freisling and co-authors link lifestyle habits to the risk of stacking up several major diseases. Their study appeared in BMC Medicine. People increasingly live with combinations of cancer, heart and metabolic disease, and diabetes. How habits shape that combined risk was scarcely studied.

The cohort held 291,778 adults from seven European countries, mostly aged 43 to 58. All began free of cancer, cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes. Over a median 11 years, 3244 developed multimorbidity, meaning two of those diseases in sequence. A healthy lifestyle score combined weight, smoking, alcohol, activity, and Mediterranean diet. Higher scores cut the risk strongly after any first disease. After diabetes, ten-year risks ran far higher for people with unhealthy habits than for those with healthy ones.
europmc-pmc6962315:
Garcia-Rubio and co-authors review the fungal cell wall, the shield that also betrays fungi to our immune system. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. The wall sits outside the cell membrane. It gives shape and stiffness, and shields the cell from stresses such as sudden water shifts.

Walls are built mainly from glucans, chitin, and glycoproteins. Some parts stick out as anchors and sensors for the outside world. Others provoke strong immune responses, which can help or harm the host. Because humans lack these components, the wall is a prime drug target. The review covers wall makeup and construction in Candida, Cryptococcus, and Aspergillus species. It ends with the wall's role in infection and hopes for next-generation antifungal drugs.
europmc-pmc7006215:
Zhang and co-authors forecast physician shortages across the United States to 2030. Their study appeared in Human Resources for Health. Demand for care is surging as the population ages and grows, and as more people hold insurance after the Affordable Care Act. The authors built supply and demand models for all 50 states.

States were graded by their projected shortage per 100,000 people. States earning a D or F rise from 4 in 2017 to 23 by 2030, with a national deficit of 139,160 physician jobs. The West faces the worst ratio, 69 missing physicians per 100,000 people. The Northeast instead runs a surplus of 50. Retirement looms large: nearly a third of active doctors are 60 or older, and new graduates cannot replace them fast enough. The authors offer the state-by-state picture as a base for policy debate.
europmc-pmc7049515:
Tan reviews drugs aimed at a major growth pathway in lung cancer for Thoracic Cancer, writing as sole author. Lung cancer classification has shifted from simple cell types toward the molecular faults that drive each tumour. One fault stands out: overactivation of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling pathway, which feeds many hallmarks of cancer. In non-small cell lung cancer the pathway is implicated in both tumour formation and progression.

Inhibitors of PI3K, Akt, and mTOR are in preclinical work and early trials. Results so far disappoint, Tan notes, partly because trials mostly enrolled patients without selecting for pathway faults. Future trials that enrich for patients with predictive biomarkers stand a better chance. Understanding the pathway's molecular biology, including epigenetic changes, should also guide drug combinations. The review maps where this crowded drug class stands and what smarter trial design might rescue it.
europmc-pmc7088015:
Wu reviews five nutrients found richly in beef and their roles in human health, in Amino Acids. The five are taurine, creatine, carnosine, anserine, and 4-hydroxyproline. All five were first discovered through work on cattle. Several are absent from plants, so diet choices decide how much a person gets.

These compounds act against oxidation and inflammation and support the nerves, muscles, eyes, immune system, and heart. Eating 30 grams of dry beef can cover a healthy adult's daily need for taurine and carnosine. Wu argues the nutrients help guard against obesity, heart trouble, and ageing-related disorders, and may strengthen defence against infections.
europmc-pmc7100515:
Ou and co-authors characterised the spike glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 and its cross-reaction with the earlier SARS virus, in Nature Communications. Using a pseudovirus system built on the spike protein, they tested how the new virus enters cells. Little was known about the virus's biology at the time.

Human ACE2 was confirmed as the entry receptor, and the virus entered mainly by endocytosis, the cell's swallowing route. Three cell factors proved critical for entry, and the new spike was less stable than the SARS one. Antibodies against SARS spike blocked SARS but not the new virus. Blood from recovered patients showed limited cross-neutralisation, so one infection might not protect against the other.
europmc-pmc7228715:
de Lusignan and co-authors hunt for risk factors behind positive SARS-CoV-2 tests in English primary care. Their study appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. They used records from a long-running GP surveillance network. Patients tested between January 28 and April 4, 2020 were included. The data were pseudonymised routine records.

Men tested positive more often than women, at 18.4 versus 13.3 percent. Chronic kidney disease stood out among medical conditions. Obesity was also linked to a positive test in adjusted analyses. Common conditions such as hypertension were frequent in those tested. The study gave early community-level evidence, outside hospitals, on who caught the virus. Such sentinel networks can spot risk patterns fast in future outbreaks too.
europmc-pmc7303615:
Huo and co-authors show that an antibody called CR3022 can neutralize SARS-CoV-2 by wrecking its spike before the spike can work. Their study appeared in Cell Host and Microbe. The spike's receptor binding domain grabs ACE2 on host cells, then reshapes itself to drive membrane fusion. The team solved the crystal structure of CR3022 bound to that domain at 2.4 angstrom resolution.

CR3022's target site is highly conserved and normally hidden inside the closed prefusion spike. To reach it, the spike must open, and binding pushes it toward the spent post-fusion state, destroying the prefusion structure, as cryo-electron microscopy confirmed. Exposing that hidden site in a vaccine based on the binding domain might focus immune responses usefully, and blockers at the same site could become treatments.
europmc-pmc7338915:
Endo and co-authors estimate how unevenly COVID-19 spreads, in Wellcome Open Research. Some infected people infect many others, while many infect nobody, a pattern called overdispersion. The team fitted a branching model to outbreak sizes reported outside China in World Health Organization situation reports.

Their model points to strong individual variation. The spread parameter came out near 0.1, which implies that roughly 10 percent of infectious people may cause about 80 percent of onward infections. Such superspreading means outbreaks can die out by chance, yet also flare from a single event. Readers get a compact estimate that shaped thinking about targeting controls at high-risk settings rather than spreading effort evenly.
europmc-pmc7352415:
Banks and co-authors study how extracellular vesicles cross the blood-brain barrier in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Vesicles are tiny parcels that cells use to ship cargo, and they can pass the barrier that guards the brain. Almost nothing was known about the details, so the team timed the passage of 10 vesicle types.

All 10 crossed, but rates differed more than tenfold. An immune activator, LPS, sped uptake for six types without breaking the barrier, and slowed one. A plant protein changed transport for five types, pointing to a ferry mechanism across barrier cells. Neither species of origin nor cancer status predicted behavior. The findings matter for using vesicles as drug couriers to the brain.
europmc-pmc7383515:
Bryan and co-authors evaluate a commercial COVID-19 antibody test in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology. Slow diagnostic rollout in the United States left many early infections untested, so blood tests had to reconstruct who had been infected. The team checked the Abbott Architect IgG assay in three patient groups, and measured past infection around Boise, Idaho.

On blood drawn before the pandemic, the test wrongly flagged only 1 of 1,020 samples, a specificity of 99.90 percent. On samples from confirmed patients, sensitivity reached 100 percent when blood was taken at least 17 days after symptoms began, at the right cutoff. Earlier samples read less reliably. The study gives labs hard performance numbers for a widely used test.
europmc-pmc7425015:
Yu and co-authors test whether tiny cell parcels called exosomes can speed the healing of diabetic wounds. The exosomes came from bone marrow stem cells. Some stem cells were first treated with atorvastatin, a common statin drug.

In diabetic rats, shots of exosomes from treated cells closed skin wounds faster than plain exosomes. New blood vessels grew more strongly in the treated wounds. Tests on vein cells showed more growth, movement, and tube formation. The effect ran through the AKT/eNOS pathway and a small RNA called miR-221-3p. Blocking either one weakened the benefit. The authors propose treated-cell exosomes as a therapy for hard-to-heal diabetic skin wounds.
europmc-pmc7429815:
Harmon and co-authors train deep learning tools to spot COVID-19 pneumonia on chest CT scans. CT can help doctors manage COVID-19 lung disease. The tools learned from scans gathered in many countries.

The system first outlines the lung, then classifies the scan for COVID-19 pneumonia. On an independent test set it reached up to 90.8% accuracy. Sensitivity was 84% and specificity 93%. Among patients with other confirmed pneumonias, the false positive rate was 10%. The authors report that the tools separate COVID-19 pneumonia from other lung disease well. That skill held across varied patient groups, which supports use in busy clinics.
europmc-pmc7468815:
Żółkiewicz and co-authors review postbiotics as a step beyond prebiotics and probiotics. A skewed gut microbiome can feed diseases such as type 1 diabetes and cancer. Postbiotics are substances that microbes release or make through their activity.

These substances help the host, directly or through other paths. Since they hold no live microbes, their risks are lower than those of probiotics. The review details how postbiotics act in the body. Their effects span immune tuning, anti-inflammatory action, antioxidant action, and anti-cancer effects. Clinical traits and possible treatments get a full survey. The authors call the approach attractive for reshaping the microbiome. They also ask for more proof of benefit and safety before wide use.
europmc-pmc7532215:
Bengtsson, Andersson and Ansari measure actual long-term survival in pancreatic cancer using registry data. Most reports use estimates rather than counted survivors over time. Their study draws on the United States SEER program records.

They studied 84,275 patients diagnosed from 1975 to 2011, all with at least five years of follow-up time. Actual five-year survival rose from zero point nine percent in the first year to four point two percent in the last. Among patients who had surgery, it rose from one point five percent to seventeen point four percent. It stayed flat for patients who had no surgery at all. Age, grade and stage predicted survival in both patient groups.
europmc-pmc7579415:
Abu-Raya, Michalski, Sadarangani and Lavoie review immune adaptation in normal pregnancy. Pregnancy raises risk and severity for some infections. The mother must also tolerate the genetically different fetus.

The review describes immune changes across a normal pregnancy. Both antibody and cell-based responses shift over time. There is little proof of broad immune suppression. Changes appear targeted and change with gestation stage. Hormone and body changes also shape infection risk. Lung capacity and blood flow shifts play a part. Knowing these changes can guide vaccine timing. The aim is to protect mother, fetus and newborn. Strategies for maternal vaccination are discussed in that light.
europmc-pmc7583715:
Biasizzo and Kopitar-Jerala review interplay between the NLRP3 inflammasome and autophagy. The inflammasome is a protein complex that drives inflammation. It also triggers a fiery form of cell death.

Activation leads to caspase-1 switching on in cells. Inflammatory cytokines are then cut and released outside. Excess activation can drive disease and cancer growth. Autophagy recycles damaged proteins and organelles in cells. It can remove inflammasome triggers and parts. That removal lowers inflammasome activity and inflammation. Signals from the inflammasome can also steer autophagy. The review covers diseases where this balance matters, from gout to sepsis.
europmc-pmc7687015:
Ren and co-authors test curcumin, a spice compound, against heart damage in diabetes. Diabetic cardiomyopathy weakens the heart muscle and drives heart cells to die. The team used diabetic rats plus heart cells grown in high sugar and fat. Curcumin was given by mouth or direct to cells.

Diabetic rats showed high stress markers and more heart cell death. Curcumin eased heart dysfunction and cut both stress and cell death. It acted on two signal paths, Sirt1-Foxo1 and PI3K-Akt. Cell tests matched the animal results. The authors say curcumin shields the diabetic heart by tuning these two paths.
europmc-pmc7695715:
Alexandersen and co-authors test whether a virus RNA signal in swabs means live infection. Labs can detect subgenomic RNAs of SARS-CoV-2, short copies made when the virus multiplies. Some had proposed these as proof of active replication. The team tracked such RNAs in diagnostic samples over time.

They found subgenomic RNAs up to 17 days after the first positive test. Tests showed these RNAs resist enzymes that chew up bare RNA. They seem shielded by cell membranes in the sample. The authors conclude that finding them does not prove the virus is still active. This matters for how labs judge if a patient can spread infection.
europmc-pmc7725515:
McMichael and co-authors investigate a COVID-19 outbreak in a Washington nursing home. A resident case was found on February 28, 2020, in King County. The probe covered February 27 to March 9. The facility housed about 130 residents with chronic health problems, cared for by some 170 staff.

The probe linked 129 cases to the facility: 81 residents, 34 staff, and 14 visitors. Of these, 23 people died. Staff who worked at several facilities helped spread the virus between sites. Weak infection control added to the spread. The authors urge care homes to bar sick staff and visitors early and to act fast on first signs.
europmc-pmc7729615:
Ichimiya and co-authors review autophagy and the diseases tied to its failure. Autophagy is the cell's system for breaking down and recycling its own parts. It answers starvation, clears faulty goods, and shapes early development. Its products feed the cell anew.

Faults in this system now link to nerve diseases and to tumor growth. Some diseases trace to mutations in autophagy genes. Other work ties active autophagy to longer life and slower aging. The review covers selective forms, such as disposal of mitochondria. It maps where each disease enters the story and what remains unknown.
europmc-pmc7770915:
Liu and co-authors review a technology that coats nanoparticles with real cell membranes. Bare nanoparticles are often spotted by the immune system and cleared fast. A cloak of cell membrane gives them the surface marks of a body cell. This helps them travel longer and reach their targets.

The review covers use in drug delivery, cancer care, vessel disease, immune tuning, and toxin removal. Membrane-coated particles can soak up poisons like a decoy cell. The authors also collect patent filings from the past 10 years. They close with the hurdles to clinical use, from scale-up to safety checks.
europmc-pmc7795815:
Khan and co-authors review COVID-19 as the third coronavirus pandemic of this century. SARS and MERS came before it. All three viruses cause severe respiratory infection. SARS-CoV-2 likely began in bats, like its relatives.

The disease first appeared in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. By the time of writing it had infected 48,539,872 people. It had caused 1,232,791 deaths across 215 countries. No approved treatment or vaccine existed yet. Many vaccine and drug candidates were in trials. The authors sum up the history of these respiratory diseases. They track COVID-19 spread and the state of the response so far.
europmc-pmc7815315:
Maldonado and co-authors solve the atomic shapes of plant respiratory complexes. Complex III and complex IV drive cell breathing in mitochondria. They can join into a larger supercomplex. Plant versions of these structures were unknown. The source plant was Vigna radiata, the mung bean.

Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy yielded the models. The plant complex III shows a distinct processing domain. The subunit makeup of complex IV is now defined. Motion analysis found coordinated movement across complex III. Its iron-sulfur head domain swings as part of that motion. The plant complex IV seems to skip one classic proton route. The supercomplex contact face differs from yeast and bacteria. These findings reset old assumptions about plant respiration.
europmc-pmc7844215:
Prati and Mancini review the mental health effects of COVID-19 lockdowns. Lockdowns changed daily life across the world. Most earlier reviews leaned on one-time surveys. Such surveys cannot prove that lockdowns caused the harm. This team limited itself to stronger designs.

Only studies that followed people over time were kept. Natural experiments counted as well. The team pooled their results in a meta-analysis. Symptoms such as anxiety, low mood, and stress were tracked. Effects turned out smaller and more mixed than snap polls suggest. Most people coped without lasting harm. A clear minority did suffer, though. The authors call for care aimed at that group.
europmc-pmc7845215:
Pickerill argues against common views on immunity to dental caries. The piece is a journal article in The Dental Register. It was read before a Liverpool dental society in December 1917. Caries kept rising despite wide use of alkaline tooth pastes. The author takes that fact as his starting point.

He holds that several popular stances on caries immunity cannot stand. Many cases strike people who never use any paste at all. Claims built on paste use alone thus miss the mark. The article works through the weak points of rival views. It presses for a sounder account of why teeth decay. The piece shows early dental science arguing over cause and prevention.
europmc-pmc7857415:
Wang and co-authors show that paired IgA antibodies neutralize SARS-CoV-2 with extra force. IgA guards the wet surfaces of the body. It often travels as a two-part dimer. The team drew antibodies from COVID-19 patients.

Dimeric forms beat single forms of the same antibody. They blocked the virus at far lower doses. The gain fits IgA's job at entry surfaces. Two binding heads can cross-link spikes on one virus. Potency rose beyond simple doubling. The authors say dimeric IgA deserves a place in therapy design. Sprays for the nose and airways are a natural fit.
europmc-pmc7884415:
Liu and co-authors present a review of mitochondrial transfer between cells. Mitochondria make the energy that keeps cells and tissue alive. Cells usually keep their own, but they can also pass mitochondria to neighbours. The review surveys when and why that sharing happens.

Transfer shows up in normal tissue upkeep, in repair after damage, in tumour growth, and in immune control. The authors summarise what triggers it and the routes mitochondria take between cells. They also flag what is still unknown about the traffic. The review then turns to therapy. Moving healthy mitochondria into damaged tissue may aid recovery. Blocking transfer may slow tumours that use it to grow. Readers get a full map of a fast-moving field.
europmc-pmc8017015:
Christidi and Brunham review the regulated cell death pathways behind doxorubicin's damage to the heart. Doxorubicin treats many cancers, but up to a quarter of patients develop cardiotoxicity. The harm can cut the heart's pumping power and end in failure. How exactly the drug kills heart muscle cells stayed elusive for years. New work has named several distinct death programs.

The review covers apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis in turn. Autophagy gets its own treatment, since its role remains unclear. It may shield heart cells, or it may harm them. Sirtuins appear as protectors across several pathways. The authors ask which pathway matters most, and whether one drug could block several at once. Answers would sharpen safety testing for new cancer drugs.
europmc-pmc8092915:
Painter and co-authors report the first human trial of molnupiravir, an oral antiviral aimed at SARS-CoV-2. The drug is a prodrug of a ribonucleoside analog. Inside the body it turns into a faulty building block for viral RNA. The viral polymerase inserts it and errors pile up past survival. That error catastrophe kills the virus's fitness.

Healthy volunteers took single and repeated doses in the phase 1 study. The trial was randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled. It also tested how food changed the drug's blood profile. The authors report the drug was well tolerated at doses from 50 to 800 mg given twice daily. No subject in the study had a serious adverse event. Reported side effects stayed mild in kind. Blood levels supported the dosing plan for later trials. The work cleared the path for patient studies.
europmc-pmc8373615:
Collier and co-authors examine how age shapes the immune response to the BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccine. Two doses give strong protection, but little was known about variants in people over eighty. The team compared older adults with younger health care workers.

After the first dose, older people had lower antibody levels and weaker virus blocking. People over eighty showed the steepest drop. Their blood was also weaker against the Alpha, Beta, and Gamma variants. After the second dose, blocking of variants could be found at all ages. Memory B cell counts set responders apart from non-responders. T cell output of key signals was lower in older people.
europmc-pmc8380115:
Dessie and Zewotir pool the evidence on what raises the risk of death from COVID-19. Their systematic review and meta-analysis draws on studies found in many databases up to 31 August 2020. Earlier reviews on this question used small samples.

Forty-two studies with 423,117 patients met the rules for inclusion. The pooled death rate among hospitalized patients was 17.62 percent. The authors report that older age, male sex, and smoking raised risk. So did obesity, high D-dimer levels, and other diseases present before infection. Acute kidney injury also marked higher risk. The results help doctors spot patients who need closer care.
europmc-pmc8456215:
Demir and co-authors hunt for fresh drug targets in type 2 diabetes and its complications. Many drugs control blood sugar, yet all carry side effects. Once diabetes sets in, it is rarely reversed. Damage to kidney, eye, heart, nerves, and liver also lacks cures.

The review centers on new targets that may drive how the disease starts. It traces how insulin resistance and high blood sugar grow into organ injury. Each target is weighed for its role in that chain. The authors argue that deeper mechanism work can open new therapies. Some may even prevent the disease or its complications outright. The piece maps where drug hunters should look next.
europmc-pmc8465115:
Lam and co-authors set out a shared protocol for measuring cell parts in electron microscope images. This imaging shows fine detail inside cells and tissues. Two cell parts draw special interest in work on metabolic disease. Those are mitochondria and the ER network. A clear shared method for measuring them was lacking.

The protocol uses ImageJ, free software from the National Institutes of Health. It shows how to get the length, width, area, and roundness of mitochondria. Steps also cover their inner folds, called cristae. Ways to measure contact points between the two cell parts are included. The authors aim for results that are accurate, repeatable, and easy to share.
europmc-pmc8469615:
Kirillova and co-authors review the role of mitochondria in egg cell maturation. Mitochondria carry their own small genome, unlike most cell parts. As an egg matures, copies of that genome rise sharply. The spread of mitochondria inside the cell shifts as well.

Maturation burns much energy, so enough working mitochondria are crucial. Egg quality tracks with both genome copy number and energy output. Poor lab maturation can warp mitochondria and their gene activity. Weak mitochondria also fail to check reactive oxygen, which raises oxidative stress. The review weighs antioxidant tests in animals and human eggs. New mitochondria-targeted additives raise hopes for better lab systems.
europmc-pmc8471715:
Dutta and co-authors explain how oxidative stress and testicular inflammation harm male reproduction. Inflammation is a core cause of male infertility, a serious world problem. Many men with fertility trouble show silent inflammation of the urinary and genital tract.

During inflammation, pro-inflammatory signals rise in the male tract. Oxidative stress runs alongside it, and each feeds the other. Excess oxidants damage sperm cells and their inner parts. The review traces the pathways that link root causes to these two processes. It shows how oxidant-sensitive cascades then impair fertility. The authors aim to fill gaps in a complex causal chain.
europmc-pmc8516415:
Vallat and Walker present an open-source tool for automatic sleep staging. Sleep measurement has grown fast in clinics and society. Yet scoring still rests on human eyes in most labs. Hand scoring is slow, dull work and can bend with the scorer.

Their algorithm trained and tested on over 30,000 hours of sleep recordings. The records came from mixed populations around the world. The tool matched human scoring accuracy and agreement between scorers. It does so across population types. The software is free, open source, and light to run. The authors hope it becomes a shared standard for the field. Ease of use was a design goal throughout.
europmc-pmc8591115:
Huang and co-authors review KRAS, a gene long seen as too hard to drug in cancer. KRAS is the most often mutated cancer gene. For four decades, drug work on it failed again and again. New drugs that hit the G12C form have changed that view.

The review covers the basic biology of KRAS and how its mutations help tumors hide from the immune system. It then tracks new drugs such as sotorasib and adagrasib and their trial results. Sotorasib was the first drug for KRAS G12C cleared for clinical use. The authors also cover drug resistance and drug pairs that may beat it. The goal is care matched to each patient.
europmc-pmc8681215:
Couch and co-authors give a brief history of extracellular vesicles, the small cargo carriers cells release. The field has grown fast over two decades. Vesicles were once seen as a cell waste system. They are now known to pass working cargo between cells and shape many body processes.

The review returns to the first experiments, near their 75th anniversary. It sums up the key finds that drove the field's rise. It also traces how an organized research community formed. Disease links give the topic added weight. The authors close with the field's current state and its main open problems.
europmc-pmc8728215:
Parks and co-authors update the Genome Taxonomy Database, a genome-based family tree for bacteria and archaea. The database draws genomes from a public assembly archive. Its taxonomy stays consistent with evolutionary relationships and evens out rank levels. The newest release spans 254,090 bacterial and 4,316 archaeal genomes.

These genomes group into 45,555 bacterial and 2,339 archaeal species clusters. Counts have grown fast since the database began. Genomes built from environmental samples drive much of that growth. The website now tracks name changes and flags genome quality. The authors also explain how species clusters get updated.
europmc-pmc8755715:
Hao, Leven, and Head-Gordon ask if electric fields at the surface of water microdroplets can drive their fast chemistry. Reactions in tiny droplets can run one to six orders of magnitude faster than in bulk water. The reason for that speedup was poorly understood. The team used a coarse-grained electron model to probe the droplet surface.

Fields along free O-H bonds at the surface ran about 16 megavolts per centimeter stronger than inside. Local fields could spike far higher still. Such fields may weaken or break chemical bonds at the surface. That could explain much of the surface reactivity. The model avoids the cost of full quantum methods.
europmc-pmc8780115:
Jang, Kwon, and Lee review the pathogenic roles of diverse immune cells in rheumatoid arthritis. This chronic autoimmune disease inflames joint lining tissue. It destroys cartilage and brings problems beyond the joints. Much has been learned about the cells and signals that drive it, though gaps remain.

Self-reactive CD4 T cells sit near the center of the process. B cells, macrophages, and autoantibodies each add their own harm. Inflammatory cytokines and chemokines spread the attack. The review updates the disease model cell by cell. Each part is weighed as a source of new drug targets. The authors aim to unveil routes that current care misses.
europmc-pmc8843115:
Fernandes and co-authors review how new SARS-CoV-2 variants strain the tools against COVID-19. Each fresh variant can change symptoms and spread. Tests built for earlier forms may miss or misread it. Vaccines aimed at older spike proteins may protect less well. The review takes stock of all three fronts. Detection, treatment, and prevention each get a full pass.

The authors survey nucleic acid, antigen, and antibody test methods. They judge speed, sensitivity, and robustness for each. They then cover antiviral and immune-modulating drugs. Vaccine platforms are compared by design and response. The immune impact of each platform is weighed. Post-vaccination infections are also discussed. The piece gives clinicians a variant-era briefing. It stresses tools that can adapt as the virus changes.
europmc-pmc8971115:
Qu and co-authors build vaccines from circular RNA against SARS-CoV-2 and its variants. Variants keep eroding standard vaccine protection. Circular RNA offers a sturdier template than linear RNA. Their vaccine expresses the spike's receptor-binding domain in trimer form. It raised strong neutralizing antibodies in animals. T cell responses came with them. Mice and rhesus macaques both gained robust protection. Antigen production ran higher and lasted longer than a modified mRNA rival.

The immune profile also differed. Neutralizing antibodies formed a larger share of the response. T helper responses skewed to the Th1 type. A version tuned to Omicron neutralized Omicron well. It failed against Delta, though. A Delta-tuned version covered both variants. It also worked as a booster after other vaccines. The authors favor that broader candidate. Circular RNA is their bet for variant-proofing.
europmc-pmc9030615:
Khalid and co-authors review how advanced glycation end products drive type 2 diabetes and its complications. Long-term high blood sugar makes these products form on proteins, lipids, and DNA. When they engage their main receptor, RAGE, they switch on pathways that raise oxidative stress and inflammation. The result is weaker insulin signaling and direct harm to the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas.

The review covers where these products come from and how the signaling chain unfolds. It ends with prospects for drugs that block the pathway. Slowing this axis, the authors argue, could slow diabetes itself.
europmc-pmc9040015:
Yin and co-authors present rMVP, an R software package for genome-wide association studies. As sample sizes and marker counts grow, older tools strain under the computation load. rMVP uses little memory, runs tests in parallel, and adds rich plotting. It checks population structure and estimates variance parts through three built-in algorithms.

For the association tests themselves, it offers general and mixed linear models plus the FarmCPU method. In benchmarks it ran much faster than PLINK, GEMMA, and the earlier FarmCPU package. The authors release it freely for studies of human disease and farm traits.
europmc-pmc9078015:
Tao and co-authors review the triglyceride-glucose index, known as the TyG index, as a sign of heart and vessel disease. The index is built from blood fat and blood sugar tests. It serves as a simple stand-in for insulin resistance. Many studies now link a high index to worse heart outcomes.

The review traces how the index came into use and where it helps most. It covers its links to many forms of cardiovascular disease and the ways it might signal risk. The authors also set out clear limits. They note gaps in proof and cases where the index may mislead. Readers get a balanced guide to when this cheap test adds real value.
europmc-pmc9163715:
Iso-Markku and co-authors pool cohort and case-control studies on physical activity and dementia risk. Activity is linked to lower dementia rates, but many studies follow people for too short a time. Short follow-ups can flip cause and effect, since early disease cuts activity. The team tested whether study length changes the link.

They included 58 studies in the meta-analysis. Activity was tied to lower risk of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia. The link held even in follow-ups of 20 years or more. Dose-response patterns also appeared for all-cause dementia. Study quality and age at start did not change the result much. The authors support activity as a modifiable shield against dementia.
europmc-pmc9332215:
Chatenet and co-authors review water electrolysis from textbook basics to the newest lab and factory work. Splitting water with green electricity would yield hydrogen with a tiny carbon footprint. Hydrogen is cast as the most promising clean energy carrier. Progress still hinges on cheap, durable catalyst materials and better efficiency.

The review covers the core electrochemistry of water splitting first. It then surveys the latest findings from universities and research institutes. Current industrial systems and large pilot plants get detailed treatment. New design methods lean on first-principles math and machine learning. A cost analysis weighs how far mass rollout could cut emissions. The authors aim to link chemists, materials scientists, and engineers. Better junctions between those fields, they argue, speed deployment.
europmc-pmc9376115:
Peng and co-authors review regulated cell death pathways in cancer and the drugs that target them. Unlike accidental death, these programs run under gene control. Cancer growth leans on their failure. Each program, from apoptosis to ferroptosis, offers a distinct attack route.

The review details apoptosis and autophagy-linked death first. It then covers necroptosis, pyroptosis, parthanatos, entosis, and other subroutines. Small-molecule drugs aimed at each path are cataloged. Single-target, dual-target, and combo strategies all appear. China faces a high and rising cancer load, which frames the urgency. The authors argue that hitting death programs can expose hidden cancer weaknesses. Cross-talk between pathways, though, complicates dosing and timing.
europmc-pmc9465115:
Skowronek and co-authors set out a faster, deeper way to run dia-PASEF proteomics. Data-independent acquisition gives wide coverage in mass spectrometry work. The dia-PASEF variant adds ion mobility sorting to the scan. Its window placement is more complex than plain DIA schemes.

Their fix places variable windows where precursor density demands. The design is automated in a free Python package, py_diAID. Deep project libraries and a fast liquid flow system complete the setup. The team found over 7700 proteins in a human cancer cell line in 44 minutes. At 100 samples per day, they still measured more than 6000 proteins per lysate. For phospho work, they counted more than 35,000 phosphosites in 21 minute runs. Such depth suits large systems biology studies.
europmc-pmc9580915:
Pudjihartono and co-authors review feature selection methods for machine learning disease risk models. Such models can spot patterns in huge, messy data sets. Genetic risk prediction is a prime use in precision medicine. Gene data holds far more features than samples, though.

That imbalance is the curse of dimensionality for model builders. Feature selection trims the set to the most telling items. It drops noise, repeats, and dead weight from the data. Better picks make models travel better to new patients. The review sorts methods by family and use case. Pluses and minuses are weighed for each approach. Worked focus falls on single letter variants linked to disease. Hybrid methods that blend approaches get a chapter. Searches for variant pair effects close the survey.
europmc-pmc9588915:
Li and co-authors track the global burden of Alzheimer's disease and other dementias from 1990 to 2019. The count draws on the Global Burden of Disease 2019 database. Ageing populations make dementia a fast growing health concern. Sound trend data can steer health plans and budgets.

Case counts rose steeply across the three decades. Incidence climbed by 147.95% and prevalence by 160.84% in that span. Age-standardized rates also rose for both sexes. Rates in women stayed higher than in men throughout. Yet the rises ran faster in men than in women. Burden tracked the sociodemographic index of each country. Richer, older regions carried the heaviest loads. Smoking was the top risk factor in men. Obesity was the top risk factor in women.
europmc-pmc9881015:
Bertsch and co-authors give a critical review of self-healing injectable hydrogels for tissue regeneration. These soft materials flow under stress in a syringe, then regain their structure after placement. That trait allows local, low-invasive delivery without open surgery. Their moldable form also suits patient-specific treatment.

Injected hydrogels can support tissue, deliver cells or drugs on a set schedule, and recruit host cells. The review surveys current designs and uses across tissue types. It flags three barriers: stability versus injectability, weak shared test standards, and limits in real formulations. The authors call for shared rheology benchmarks. The work maps what must improve before wide clinical use.
europmc-pmc9898515:
Julkunen and co-authors present an atlas of plasma NMR biomarkers from 118,461 UK Biobank participants. Blood lipids and metabolites mark current health and future disease risk. The dataset covers 249 measures, from lipoprotein lipids and fatty acids to amino acids and ketones. The team linked these measures to over 700 common diseases.

The atlas maps links to disease prevalence, new cases, and mortality. It finds ties to infection risk, cancers, joint disorders, and mental health outcomes. Those links extend well past heart and metabolic disease. Clustering showed similar biomarker patterns across unlike diseases. The authors argue this points to shared systemic roots of risk. The atlas is shared online for public health research.
europmc-pmc9971315:
Chowdhury and co-authors estimate global and regional prevalence of multimorbidity in adults. Multimorbidity means living with several long-term conditions at once. High rates signal higher death risk and heavier health care use. The review supports a global goal to cut early death from non-communicable diseases.

The team searched PubMed, ScienceDirect, Embase, and Google Scholar. They kept community surveys published from 2000 to 2021. A random-effects model pooled prevalence across studies. The final set held 126 studies with nearly 15.4 million people. Subgroup checks varied by continent, age, sex, and definition used. The authors aimed to show how common multimorbidity is across WHO regions. Their pooled picture guides health system planning.
ford-good-soldier-1915:
Ford Madox Ford called his 1915 novel the saddest story, and its first line says so outright. The Good Soldier tells of two rich couples, English and American, whose orderly lives of spas and seasons hide adultery, lies, and quiet ruin.

John Dowell, the American husband, narrates years later, still unsure what he knew and when he knew it. His unreliability is the novel's engine: every calm scene returns darker on a second reading. Ford's impressionist method here taught modern fiction how to lie beautifully. The book is now widely held to be his masterpiece and one of the great English novels.
frus-1861-d115:
Chevalier Hülsemann received an answer from William H. Seward on 22 August 1861. The letter is document 115 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's reply to the Austrian envoy came two weeks after the note it answered. The pace was normal for formal exchanges of the day. In it, the Secretary states the Union's terms to a court whose weight in Europe was still great. Austria's cool stance denied the South any hope of a friend in Vienna's court. A cool Vienna was worth much to a Union that could not court all Europe at once.
frus-1861-d15:
From Washington on 26 July 1861, William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Norman Judd in Berlin. It is document 15 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Orders from Washington reached Berlin about two weeks after they were sent. Judd had to act on them in a court that had its own fresh news. Seward's July letter shows the Secretary steering his man in Prussia through the first shock of defeat at Bull Run. Orders sent after a defeat had to steady the envoy as much as guide his talks. Steadying an envoy mattered, since his face in court was the Union's face.
frus-1861-d215:
From his post abroad, Mr. Marsh wrote to William H. Seward on 27 June 1861. It stands as Document 215 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d115:
On 31 July 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 115 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d15:
On 7 February 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 15 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d215:
On 12 June 1862 Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward, and the note appears as Document 215 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It resumes the Seward-Lyons file after a spring gap in the printed papers.

June found Union forces stalled before Richmond and foreign opinion unsure which side would tire first. Lyons, writing from Washington, kept his government informed while pressing its cases with Seward. A note from mid-June belongs to the season when British and French leaders began to talk. Still loosely, about whether the war could be stopped from outside. The channel stayed open through the whole war, which was itself a kind of success.
frus-1862-d315:
Document 315 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 24 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed the whole set to Paris.

When one mail carries four letters, the subjects divide cleanly among them by clerical design. Each sheet could be copied, filed, and answered on its own track. For historians, the 24 September set is a compact exhibit of the Department's method in the week the war's meaning changed in European eyes. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d415:
On 8 March 1862 Horace J. Perry wrote from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is Document 415 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's record for the year.

Perry's Madrid reports tracked a court that ruled Cuba, held Puerto Rico, and had joined the allied expedition to Mexico. Each dispatch told Washington how Spain weighed the Union's chances and what Confederate agents were seeking in Spanish ports. Read in sequence, his 1862 letters trace the slow work of keeping Spain neutral. The task mattered because Spanish harbors ringed the Gulf where the war's blockade was enforced.
frus-1862-d515:
On 27 August 1862 James Shepherd Pike reported from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 515 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Pike wrote two days before the second battle of Bull Run, in the last calm before another Union disaster filled the European papers. His subject was the Netherlands in late summer: its ministry's caution, its press's judgment, and the standing questions of ports and trade. Reports like this reached Washington in October and were read against news Pike had not yet heard. That layered quality, each letter answering an older world, runs through the whole volume and gives the Hague file its documentary charm.
frus-1862-d615:
Bradford R. Wood at Copenhagen received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 February 1862. It is Document 615 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

A fortnight after his last Danish order, Seward wrote again, in a month when the Department's European mail ran heavy with good war news. The standing business with Denmark was maritime and commercial, conducted in a friendly key. Wood at Copenhagen also served as a listening post for the Baltic, where Russia's friendship to the Union gave the region its tilt. The letter continues a correspondence that never made headlines and never needed to, which in wartime diplomacy is a kind of success.
frus-1862-d715:
On 29 September 1862, Luis Molina wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Molina served as Costa Rica's envoy in Washington. The letter is document 715 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, part of a tight fall exchange between the two men.

Envoys in the capital pressed their lands' claims and questions in person and by letter. Molina, an old hand in Washington, kept Costa Rica's business before the State Department week by week. This letter is one of those steady pushes. Read in line with Seward's replies, it shows how a small republic held its place in a great power's day book during wartime.
frus-1863p1-d115:
Three letters to London on 11 March 1863 close with this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 115 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The third sheet of a set often carried the day's last word: a small order, a tone to hold, a fact just in. Seward's close of 11 March is in that place. The run of his March letters shows a secretary driving the London brief hard as spring came on. Twelve came in a day, then three more. This letter is the tail of that drive.
frus-1863p1-d15:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 15 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By mid-December the talk in London had cooled on stepping into the war, and Adams's mail charted that shift. He wrote of the cabinet, the papers, and the men who spoke for the South in Britain. Each report helped Seward judge how much risk lay across the sea. This dispatch is a mid-run piece of that watch, plain in tone and rich in use when read with the rest.
frus-1863p1-d215: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 18 June 1863. It is document 215 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d315:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 3 November 1862. The note is document 315 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Britain had taken a neutral stand in 1861, and its legation in Washington guarded that stand case by case. A note like this one is neutrality being practiced, not just proclaimed. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d415:
Frederick W. Seward, Assistant Secretary of State, addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 14 March 1863. It is document 415 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

The younger Seward often signed for the department when his father, the Secretary, was absent. Notes to Lyons still carried the full weight of the American position on neutral rights and British complaints. Lyons reported the exchange to London, so each reply spoke to two audiences. The channel stayed busy because small disputes, left alone, could grow into a breach between the two countries.
frus-1863p1-d515:
Under the date 15 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d615:
From F. W. Seward, the assistant secretary to Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart: a letter dated 18 August 1863. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1915:
The 1915 volume works in the war's shadow without a war file. Its circulars abrogate treaty clauses that clash with the Seamen's Act. Bolivia and Britain accept the change. The Panama Canal's opening is postponed in another notice. Pan-American conferences fill the ceremonial pages. A financial conference and high commission lead them. Enlistment of Americans in foreign armies draws a ruling.

Italy supplies a mid-volume case. A Boston firm sends its agent's family to Italy. The son will study architecture there. Washington presses Rome for an answer sent in June. Such small files fill the country sections. Presidents' messages from South America print in translation. The volume's diplomacy is hemispheric and legal. Europe's war enters only by its edges.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d115: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on November 11, 1943, Armistice Day in the old calendar, as the president readied to sail. The message is Document 115 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The coincidence of dates is the record's own; no topic is given for the note. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the final letters exchanged before the two parties converged on Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d15: For the third day running, Churchill put a message to Roosevelt on paper on June 29, 1943. It is Document 15 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. That pace, three notes in three days counting the president's replies, shows how much of the alliance ran through this one channel. The record names no subject. The letter's own text in the Foreign Relations volume is where its business must be found.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d215:
Ambassador Averell Harriman telegraphed Secretary of State Cordell Hull from Moscow at noon on 12 November 1943, in message 1925, marked secret and personal. It closes out the paperwork over the Allied agreement meant to draw Turkey into the war.

Acting under the department's telegram 1180 of 9 November, Harriman reports one step taken. He has had his letter of 10 November to Molotov attached as an annex to the Moscow protocol. The letter carried the President's agreement on Turkey. The protocol itself was the Soviet-British one signed by Molotov and Eden on 1 November. Since Molotov preferred that arrangement, Harriman did not press to fold the papers into the conference's secret military record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d315: Marshal Stalin sent President Roosevelt a personal, strictly secret telegram from Moscow on 25 November 1943, marked urgent. Sent by Navy channels through Harriman at Cairo, it answers Roosevelt's message of 22 November proposing their first meeting at Tehran. Stalin's whole reply is one sentence: he will be at Roosevelt's service in Tehran on the evening of 28 November. The brief note fixed the opening day of the first meeting of the three Allied leaders.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d415: Ambassador Averell Harriman sent the Secretary of State an urgent telegram, number 2113, from Moscow on 4 December 1943. It reports that the Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill conference at Tehran is covered in that day's Moscow newspapers in a Tass dispatch dated at Tehran on 3 December. The dispatch text is not repeated here. The editors note that it follows, in a slightly different translation, the version quoted in Hull's telegram to Harriman of the same day. That telegram is printed earlier in the volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d515:
Louis G. Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, reported to Secretary of State Hull on December 9, 1943, a week after the Tehran Conference ended in his host capital. Iran was under Allied occupation, and its government had just received the Big Three's pledge to respect its independence. The State Department printed the report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Dreyfus watched Tehran pick up the pieces after hosting Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin: the politics, the security, and the mood of an occupied country. His reports told Washington how the summit looked from the ground it had occupied. That local view is exactly what makes legation reporting valuable to historians.
frus-1944-quebec-d115:
British chiefs of staff representatives circulated this top-secret paper on August 29, 1944, replying to the American proposal in C.C.S. 618/1. Attached is the British chiefs' own memorandum on coordinating the war effort with the Soviet Union. The idea had come from Marshal Stalin, who raised it with Ambassador Harriman in Moscow in June.

London flatly opposed a standing United Chiefs of Staff committee, fearing it could claim authority over the Combined Chiefs of Staff. Instead the British backed a purely advisory combined committee in Moscow, limited to operations and intelligence. The existing mission chiefs would sit on it. Generals Burrows and Deane were to put the plan to the Soviets.
frus-1944-quebec-d15:
A second message from Prime Minister Churchill reached President Roosevelt on July 16, 1944. Paired same-day letters were Churchill's way of keeping subjects separate and pressure steady. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

July 1944 was thick with questions that would reach the Quebec table: the campaign in Italy, the landing in southern France, and aid to Russia and China. Two letters in one day show the Prime Minister sorting that load on paper. For readers, the message completes a single day's diplomacy between the two busiest correspondents of the war.
frus-1944-quebec-d215:
Hull's telegram of September 13, 1944, brought Roosevelt a milestone from London. Ambassador Winant reported, in telegram 7511 sent at midnight on September 12, that the European Advisory Commission had that day approved and signed the protocol on zones of occupation in Germany. The protocol also covered the administration of Greater Berlin, and went forward for submission to the three governments.

One gap remained in the signed text, as Hull's own parenthetical note flags: the British and American zones were left blank. The Soviet zone and Berlin's joint occupation were settled, but which of the two western zones each ally would take awaited Roosevelt and Churchill. Quebec settled it two days later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d115:
Vandenberg wrote to Hoover again on 19 July 1946, sixteen days after his first letter. Two letters in a month from the new director mark the Latin American question heating up. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The FBI's wartime Special Intelligence Service had covered Latin America, and Hoover meant to keep it. Vandenberg meant the CIG to take the field over, as foreign intelligence was its charter. Their letters are the duel's public moves. Readers can follow the exchange into August, where it peaks in appeals to the attorney general and the National Intelligence Authority. Few paper fights in the volume show institutional rivalry so purely, or mattered more to the map that resulted.
frus-1945-50-intel-d15:
President Truman wrote to Secretary of State Byrnes on 20 September 1945, the same day he signed the order dissolving the OSS. The letter is the order's companion paper. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A president's letter to his secretary of state on such a day explains and directs. It said what the State Department was to take from the wreck of the OSS, and what the president expected of it. The State Department gained the analysts of the research branch and, with them, a claim to lead peacetime intelligence. Readers can pair this letter with the order itself. Decision and reasoning sit side by side, a rare completeness in the record of a famous act.
frus-1945-50-intel-d215: "Memorandum for the Record" bears the date 26 May 1947. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 215, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group. The form is a note to the file: no request and no order.
frus-1945-50-intel-d315:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to Secretary of Defense Johnson on 18 October 1949. It is document 315 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Two years into the CIA's life, the question in these papers is less how to build it than how to fix it.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d415:
W. Park Armstrong, who led intelligence work at the State Department, wrote to Under Secretary James Webb on 16 February 1950. The memo is document 415 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Armstrong's bureau wrote the reports the Secretary of State relied on most. Webb ran the department day to day and heard its senior aides in turn. A memo from the intelligence chief to the Under Secretary shows the bureau making its case near the very top of the house. Armstrong's run of memos to Webb forms one of the clearest threads in the whole volume.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d115:
Secretary Morgenthau's report from Quebec fills this 20 September 1944 memorandum by H. Freeman Matthews. Matthews, deputy director of the Office of European Affairs, records a meeting in the Secretary of State's office. The paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

At a Quebec dinner on 13 September, Morgenthau says, Churchill fought the harsh plan for Germany's economy with real anger. “England would be chained to a dead body,” the prime minister protested. Morgenthau told Stimson that Churchill was even angrier than he had been. The talks broke up with a plan to argue the case to Lord Cherwell, Churchill's adviser. Cherwell was won over, and then carried it back to his chief.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d15: Writing to Stalin on 24 October 1944, Roosevelt kept the direct presidential channel to Moscow active that autumn. The message is document 15 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Set among the Churchill letters around it, it shows the president balancing both allies at once as plans for the next Big Three meeting took shape.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d215:
“Rearming of French Forces” is a briefing book paper that traces the plan to a British initiative of the previous August. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The British embassy had raised the matter with the State Department in the summer of 1944.

The idea was to equip certain Western European allies to guard their own countries and share in occupying Germany. Since French ground units already carried American arms, the United States would furnish the French. Britain would arm the Belgians, Dutch, and Norwegians, and in time the Danes, and would supply the French air equipment. The American Joint Chiefs found the scheme sound in military terms, but ruled it a matter for governments, not staffs.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d315:
Equipping friendly forces in freed Europe took up much of this Combined Chiefs of Staff session at Malta on February 2, 1945. Sir Alan Brooke reported talks between Generals Somervell and Riddell-Webster on the supply bill. The need for rear-area and labor units could be cut from 460,000 men to 400,000. Those units would be fitted out on British scales rather than American ones.

Brooke judged that Britain could take on that load. The minutes show the alliance counting rifles, trucks, and rations as closely as battle plans. Feeding and arming freed peoples was a military problem long before it was a political one.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d415:
London asked Moscow to press Tito on two points in this British memorandum of February 9, 1945. Dr. Subasic, the royal Yugoslav premier, was returning to Belgrade with his government. He meant to raise both points with Tito at once. Britain hoped Stalin would advise Tito to give good assurances on each.

First, the AVNOJ assembly should be widened to include members of the last Yugoslav parliament who had not compromised themselves. Together they would form a temporary parliament. Second, laws passed by AVNOJ should face ratification by a constituent assembly. The memo shows Britain using Soviet influence as a lever inside Yugoslavia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d115:
William Rigdon, an aide in the President's naval office, compiled the official list of Truman's party for the Berlin trip. The undated memorandum is document 115 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, and it names everyone who traveled with the President for the whole journey or parts of it.

At the top stand Secretary of State James Byrnes, Admiral Leahy, press secretary Charles Ross, and Judge Samuel Rosenman. Below them come aides, doctors, Map Room officers, State Department men such as Charles Bohlen and Benjamin Cohen, Secret Service agents, a Navy photographer, and the President's valet and mess staff. The roster is a plain record of the small traveling White House that served Truman on his first trip abroad as president.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d15:
Grew urged the President to raise de Gaulle himself in this memorandum of May 19, 1945. Bidault, in his May 18 conversation, had not directly raised the General's attendance at a proposed Big Three meeting. He was extremely likely to do so at their next meeting. Even if he did not, Grew suggested Truman seriously consider raising the question.

America had in the past been held largely responsible for de Gaulle's absence from the Big Three meetings. The French government and people held it so, and large sections of the American people did too. No single step, Grew argued, would be more appreciated by the French nation. The plea failed in the event, but the memo shows its strength inside the Department.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d215:
A Soviet aide acknowledged the reparations plan in a note dated July 13, 1945. The note from V. N. Pavlov of the Soviet Foreign Commissariat, printed in translation, is document 215 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is addressed to Edward Page at the American embassy in Moscow.

Pavlov writes, at Molotov's instruction, that Molotov has received Harriman's letter of July 12 about considering the reparations problem at the coming meeting of the heads of the three governments. Page is asked to pass the word to the ambassador. The formal little note matters as a receipt: Moscow had now acknowledged in writing that reparations would be on the Potsdam table, closing the exchange that Pauley had pushed for a week.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d315:
Melbourne cabled from Bucharest at midnight on July 13, 1945, that Soviet armistice demands on Rumania had not eased.
