Responsible sources, he said, contradicted hopeful statements by War Minister Rascanu and Premier Groza. No time extension had been granted for the deliveries due under Article XII.

Fresh Soviet requests under Article X, covering the third quarter of 1945, topped the second quarter's in value. Business circles, already pressed by the Communists, feared a heavy capital levy dressed up as fair sharing of the armistice burden. Melbourne's report reached Washington while the Potsdam conference was about to open on Rumania's fate.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d415:
Additional requirements on Germany form the fourth topic of the European Advisory Commission's summary report, in an extract dated July 12, 1945. From the first talks on the German surrender instrument, the extract explains, the allies saw they needed joint action far beyond military terms. Political and economic questions demanded agreement too.

After first discussions in late 1944 and early 1945, the Commission spent May and June 1945 drafting an agreement on additional requirements to be imposed on Germany. It covered a wide range of common concern, including joint control of German production, trade, and finance. The draft stood ready for the four governments, save for approval of one passage.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d515:
Zhukov's bombshell on Silesia appears in extracts of Murphy's cable from Hoechst of July 7, 1945, reporting the Berlin Kommandatura meeting of that day. Discussion of the fuel supply drew illuminating comments from the Marshal. As the Silesian coal deposits were now in another jurisdiction, he said, that is, Poland, they were not available.

Murphy expressed surprise, stating that his understanding was that Silesia formed part of the Soviet zone of occupation of Germany. Zhukov corrected him. Germany did not exist, he said, and everyone knew the Crimea Conference established the Polish frontier along the Oder and Neisse rivers. Murphy began a reply that this was not the American understanding. The extract catches the frontier quarrel at its first open flash.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d615:
British staff representatives presented a memo on Britain's part in the final phase of the Japan war on July 6, 1945. It is document 615 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The memo was drawn up for debate at the next Allied conference.

The attached British text restates the agreed aim: Japan's unconditional surrender. That aim would be won by blockade, heavy bombing, and the ruin of Japan's sea and air strength. It would be sealed by invading Japan's industrial heart. The British call that invasion the supreme operation of the war. With Singapore's recapture in view for November 1945 and the Malacca Straits reopened, Britain offers more than its Pacific Fleet. Very long range air forces are part of the offer as well. Views from Australia and New Zealand were still awaited.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1015:
A special committee of admirals reported on disposal of the German navy and merchant marine on August 1, 1945. Kuznetsov for the USSR, Cooke for the United States, and McCarthy for Britain signed it. The committee met on July 31. Its two enclosures draft the conference decisions on both fleets, marking points where the three sides still differ.

The report warns against early publicity. If German crews learn their ships will be divided, they may scuttle them before transfer. The committee urges a short joint statement only: agreement in principle, with experts to work out detailed plans. A fuller statement would follow in due course.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1115:
H. Freeman Matthews, Director of European Affairs, wrote to his special aide Samuel Reber on 27 July 1945. The note came a week after Reber had written to him. By then the Potsdam Conference was deep in its second week, and the office's work was near its peak.

Guidance, choices, and fresh questions flowed between a director and his aide as the talks ground on. Read as a pair, the two men's notes show staff debate moving in both directions inside the American team. This is the craft of foreign policy at the working level. It took place far from the cameras, in memos like this one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1215:
Russell, special aide to the Secretary of State, wrote to his chief on 20 July 1945. A special aide's notes carried the errands and judgments closest to the secretary's own work. This one dates from the summit's first week.

Staff at that level saw the whole board: papers, people, and the chief's mind. Their notes often fixed what a meeting meant or what should happen next. This message is that inner-office traffic at Potsdam. It shows the secretary's own circle handling business while the great talks ran around them. The form was plain: a note between aide and chief.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1315:
The White House issued this press release on 6 August 1945, four days after the summit closed. The date is the key. That day, the first atomic bomb fell on Hiroshima, and the White House spoke to the world about the new weapon.

A press release is the public face of a secret kept for years. The Manhattan Project, the test, and the Potsdam counsels all stood behind this text. Its words told the public what the summit's insiders had known in whispers. This entry closes the volume's atomic thread in daylight. It is the moment the secret became history.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1415:
James Bonbright, assistant chief of the Division of Western European Affairs, wrote a memorandum on 4 September 1945. Bonbright's desk handled the department's work on the lands of Western Europe, France among them. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

A desk officer's memorandum is where raw reports become department thinking. Bonbright wrote a month after Potsdam, as the French questions raised there were being worked into policy. Readers get the view from the engine room. Not the ambassador's cable or the secretary's reply, but the staff paper that helps turn both into a line. It is a quiet, fitting close to the volume's French papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-115: Standing unnumbered after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume, this editorial note carries the editors' guidance to the reader. The Foreign Relations series prints such notes where a document needs a frame. They state sources, supply missing links, and warn where the record is thin. This note plays that part amid the heavy traffic of late July 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-15:
While Truman lunched with Churchill on July 18, 1945, Secretary of State Byrnes was a guest at Eden's quarters. A brief editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers records that second lunch. It is an unnumbered item among the conference records.

No record of the substance of the two men's conversation has been found. The editors rest the bare fact of the meeting on a single press source. They cite the London Times of July 19, 1945, page 4, for Byrnes's presence at Eden's table. The note is one of several in this stretch of the volume with the same admission. Side talks among the foreign secretaries plainly shaped the conference, yet the archive holds nothing of what was said at them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d715:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to Ambassador Patrick Hurley in China on July 27, 1945. Document 715 opens a run of Byrnes-Hurley letters in the second Potsdam volume. Hurley led the American mission in wartime China, an ally still fighting Japan. Byrnes wrote from the conference, where the Pacific war stood high on the agenda.

Letters to a distant ambassador show strategy being shared across the world. China policy could not be set at Potsdam without the man on the spot. Readers see the Secretary keeping his envoy in the picture. The exchange widens the volume's lens from Europe to Asia at a key hour.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d815:
Schuyler sent a further report to the War Department on July 25, 1945, in document 815. The head of the American military team in Rumania wrote as the conference entered its second week. His reports run beside the diplomats' letters in the second Potsdam volume. Together they cover Bucharest from two angles.

A second Schuyler report in two days signals business that would not wait. Military members of the commissions faced daily tests of the armistice. Readers see those tests recorded while the summit debated the same lands. The document tightens the link between Potsdam's table and Rumania's streets. What was argued in Germany was lived in Bucharest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d915:
American delegates drafted this memorandum on reparations at Potsdam on July 23, 1945. It starts from the Crimea Conference pledge. Defeated Germany would make reparation and restitution to the Allied nations that suffered and fought most. The paper then argues that war itself has changed the sums.

Bombing and fighting destroyed much of what could be taken. Armies also seized goods as booty or for their own support, and those goods cannot be taken twice. The paper says splitting war trophies from reparations is therefore pointless. Zone commanders should handle all removals together. The zones, it notes, roughly match the agreed division of reparations among the big powers.
frus-1955-57v15:
The Arab-Israeli dispute fills Volume XV of the 1955–1957 set for the first half of 1956. Aswan Dam funding and the Anderson mission lead, through March 12. Secrecy wraps the mission's trips and terms in these files.

The choice to drop the dam offer follows, and with it the road to crisis. Egypt's seizure of the Suez Canal Company on July 26 closes the volume. Memos weigh how far to stand with Britain, whose acts in Jordan and Buraimi drew sharp words. The record ends at the edge of war. Anderson's secret trips are logged with care in the early files.
frus-1958-60v15:
South and Southeast Asia share Volume XV of the 1958–1960 set. A package plan for India-Pakistan peace leads, with Kashmir and the Indus waters treaty in the same block. Afghanistan follows, its border dispute with Pakistan in the files.

India takes a long run, crowned by the President's visit. Pakistan follows, also with a visit. The Philippines and Thailand close the volume, on bases and firm alignment. Aid was the common thread. Each capital's file shows the price of friendship counted in loans, arms, and visits. Ceylon and Nepal take shorter runs in the middle.
frus-1961-63v15:
The Berlin crisis of 1962–1963 fills Volume XV of the 1961–1963 set, the sequel to Volume XIV. The talks opened with Gromyko run on, with the city's status still the core dispute. Air and road access scares fill the middle files.

The missile crisis offstage changes the tone late in 1962. Probes for a settlement follow, without a signed result. The record shows a crisis cooling by inches. Each side kept its rights and its garrison. The volume closes with Berlin held, divided, and watched, as the Kennedy years end. Probes continue in the closing files without a signed settlement.
frus-1964-68v15:
Germany and Berlin are the subject of Volume XV in the 1964-1968 series. Its 301 documents run as one sequence. They cover ties with the Bonn government, the status of Berlin, and talks with the Soviet Union on both. Money questions run through the records. German payments to offset the cost of U.S. troops form one long thread.

The papers include memos of talks with German leaders and cables from Bonn and Berlin. They show Washington pressing Bonn on troop cost offsets and nuclear plans. They also track East-West talks on access to Berlin. The volume is the main record of U.S.-German ties in the Johnson years.
frus-1969-76v15:
The Soviet story in the 1969-1976 series continues in Volume XV, from June 1972 to August 1974. Early chapters deal with the wake of the Moscow summit and Kissinger's return trip that fall. Trade and Soviet Jewish emigration take up the next chapters. The Jackson-Vanik amendment links the two in Congress. The June 1973 Washington summit follows.

Later chapters cover the October 1973 Arab-Israeli war and fresh summit work in 1974. The volume ends with the Moscow summit and the Cyprus crisis of that summer. Talks on a ban on the use of nuclear weapons appear in the middle chapters. Trade, arms, and emigration tangle throughout.
frus-1977-80v15:
Volume XV of the 1977-1980 series is devoted to Central America. Short opening chapters cover Belize and Guatemala, Costa Rica, and Honduras. Nicaragua takes the bulk of the volume, with documents 59 through 329. El Salvador follows. A regional chapter closes the set. The Nicaragua papers follow the fall of Somoza and the Sandinista victory of 1979. They weigh aid to the new regime and fears of a second Cuba.

One cable discusses building a new National Guard leadership free of the old regime's taint. The El Salvador chapters trace the slide toward civil war. The volume shows a policy overtaken by events in 1979.
gao-gaoreports-b-296915:
Cherry Road Technologies and Electronic Data Systems protested an Army portal award in GAO decision B-296915, dated October 24, 2005. The winner was Lockheed Martin. The system was Army Knowledge Online. It is the Army web gate for staff. The firms hit the winner's use of leased state space. They also hit all marks and the pick.

GAO denied the protests. The call did not bar leased state space. It said space would not be free state goods. Leases at fair rent gave no unfair edge. A lease rule in the books did not bind these leases. Marks were backed by clear notes. Broad dissent did not undo a sound review.
gao-gaoreports-b-297115:
Johnson Machine Works protested the rejection of its low bid in GAO decision B-297115, dated October 20, 2005. The buyer was the Army Corps of Engineers. The work was gates for the Emsworth Locks and Dams. That site is on the Ohio River. The bond form for the bid was flawed.

GAO denied the protest. The bond form did not name the signer as a true agent for the bond firm. It was thus not clear the bond firm was bound. Proof of the signer's power must come with the bid, before bids open. A gap there makes the bid not fit. Low price cannot cure a bond gap. The rejection thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297215:
Systems Plus protested a Labor Department deal for tech work in GAO decision B-297215, dated December 16, 2005. The winner was Aquilent. The work was software growth work. The buy was set aside for small firms. It used schedule firms. The winner was higher rated and higher priced. The firm said that pick broke the scheme.

GAO denied the protest. Marks and the pick fit the call scheme. They were also sound on the record. The call warned that low price need not win. A higher rated quote can win when the scheme lets tech count. That was the case here. The deal thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297915:
CIGNA Government Services protested a Health award for Medicare claims work in GAO decision B-297915, dated May 4, 2006. The winner was Noridian Administrative Services. The claims were for durable medical goods. Sellers and users of such goods file the claims. The firm hit the cost check on the winner's price. Past cost data was key.

GAO denied the protest. The cost check was sound and deep. It weighed each cost part of the bid price. It matched those parts to past costs of the winner and of peer firms on like work. That match gave a true base to judge the price. A cost check that tracks past real costs is the gold norm here.
gao-gaoreports-b-298715:
Relm Wireless Corporation protested an Army plan to buy land mobile radio gear. The Communications-Electronics Command sought the gear through a task order. The radios serve tactical, intra-squad voice links. GAO ruled in B-298715 on December 4, 2006.

Relm said the tactical radio fell outside the base contracts' scope. Those contracts grew from a 2001 buy for base radio systems. GAO read the scope terms with care. It found the new gear fit well within them. The base deals spoke in broad terms of radio systems. A buy inside the stated scope needs no fresh contest. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-304715:
Mack Mechanical, Inc. protested a Forest Service contract award in GAO decision B-304715, dated April 27, 2005. The Forest Service sought work on the Open Pond Rehabilitation Project. The project sits in the Conecuh National Forest. The work covered campsite sites under request for proposals SAZ-01-04-25. The award went to Lewis & Associates Construction Co., Inc.

The protester argued that the review of offers was flawed. It also argued that the source choice was flawed. GAO read the full record of the buy. It found the review fair and in line with the stated factors. It found the source choice sound as well. GAO denied the protest. Contract staff can use the ruling to see how GAO tests claims of a flawed review.
gao-gaoreports-b-308715:
Loan backstops for new energy tech drew two rulings in this GAO opinion, B-308715, dated April 20, 2007. Title XVII of the 2005 energy law lets the Energy Department back loans for fresh tech. House appropriators asked if that power stands on its own. They also asked if early setup work for the plan was lawful.

GAO split its answer. The clause at issue does give the department power to back loans on its own. That power holds despite the Federal Credit Reform Act. But the setup work broke the law. A bar at 42 U.S.C. section 7278 blocked such work at the time. The work also broke the purpose law and the Antideficiency Act.
gao-gaoreports-b-309715:
Crash cover bought for staff trips is ruled unlawful in this GAO decision, B-309715, dated September 25, 2007. The National Transportation Safety Board bought accident cover for staff on work trips. The cover paid out for death or grave harm. The board asked if its funds could bear that cost. It also asked what flows from a wrong spend.

GAO held the funds could not bear it. No fund of the board is open for such cover. The cost fails the test of a needed work expense. Each payment thus broke the Antideficiency Act. The board must report the breaches to the President and Congress. A copy must also go to the Comptroller General.
gao-gaoreports-b-400215:
G. Koprowski, dated August 12, 2008, is the file for a protest over medical research work at Naval Medical Center San Diego. GAO handled it as B-400215. The request for quotes No. N0025908T0135 sought eye research help for the Navy Refractive Surgery Center. It required the work to be done on site.

The protester argued the on-site rule broke a law that bars agencies from pushing firms to curb staff telework. GAO found the Navy had good grounds for on-site work. Staff would need rare on-site gear and close contact with test subjects and Navy staff. The protest was denied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-215:
Performance Budgeting, GAO-05-215 of February 28, 2005, draws lessons for Washington from five states that tie budgets to results. The states are Arizona, Maryland, Texas, Virginia, and Washington. Each has a long past of such work. Each took a unlike path to it. Hard budget years in each state put the craft to a true test.

GAO tells how lawmakers in each state use result data when they set budgets. It tells how that data shaped cuts in lean years. It names the drags that still slow the work. The sum aims to guide federal chiefs who face the same long-term cash strain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-415:
Mutual Fund Industry, GAO-05-415 of August 17, 2005, grades a new test plan at the fund watch after a fraud wave shook faith. Near half of U.S. homes hold funds, worth around $8 trillion in 2005. The Securities and Exchange Commission stands first guard. Fraud in the trade bared how thin its tests had run. A new test plan was its reply.

GAO lists the shifts made and planned in that plan. It grades the checks that keep each test true. It asks if the watch on the trade's own guard arms is firm enough to shield holders from sales fraud. Gains may come; hard tests stay.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-615:
The Armed Forces Institute of Pathology's business plan is tested in GAO report GAO-05-615, dated June 30, 2005. The plan promised $17.5 million a year in gains from better billing, more military work, fewer staff, and merged sites. GAO found some billing controls in place but no system to price the institute's own work. The gains look overstated: real savings may run $5 million to $12.5 million below the claim.

As military work grew, civilian consults and research shrank, worrying outside pathologists. GAO told defense health leaders to redo the benefit math. The department agreed. Weeks earlier it had proposed closing the institute in the base closure round.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1015:
Nuclear emergency response capability is examined in GAO-06-1015, dated September 21, 2006. The Energy Department keeps teams ready to answer nuclear and radiological threats inside the United States. Their role grew after the 2001 attacks. GAO described the teams and tools the department holds. It checked security at its two key response facilities. And it weighed the value of aerial radiation surveys.

Headings give the findings. The department holds unique teams and methods to prevent an attack and to limit harm after one. Security at the two key facilities may not suffice, GAO found. They are guarded at the lowest level guidance allows, on the theory that assets are dispersed. The assets are not fully dispersed, so loss of a site would badly hamper response. Aerial surveys aid detection, but neither Energy nor Homeland Security owns the duty to fund them. Only one major city has been surveyed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-115:
Bribery in visa decisions is the risk examined in GAO-06-115, a report GAO issued on October 6, 2005. Selling a U.S. visa for money is a crime that can admit people who mean the country harm. The State Department keeps internal controls to stop such abuse. GAO tested whether posts abroad follow those controls. It also studied malfeasance cases from 2001 through 2004 and the barriers to catching and trying offenders.

State's controls match accepted standards, but posts did not apply them fully or evenly. At 6 of 11 posts visited, required oversight steps were skipped. Staff failed to inventory visa materials, review decisions, or follow referral rules. Investigators confirmed 28 cases involving U.S. employees in the period. Justice lawyers won convictions against 10 employees. Poor records hid case trends, and investigators could not get search warrants for offices overseas. GAO urged stronger use of the safeguards State already has.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-15:
How federal agencies can work well together is the theme of GAO-06-15, issued on October 21, 2005. Many national problems cut across agency lines, so no single agency can solve them alone. Yet agencies face real barriers when they try to join forces. GAO named key practices that help joint work last. It drew on cases such as Healthy People, wildland fire management, and shared health work between the veterans and defense departments.

GAO lists eight practices. Partners should set a common outcome and joint strategies. They should pool resources, agree on roles, and align their rules. They should track results, report them, and hold both agencies and staff to account. Laws on planning give Congress and the budget office a frame for such work. GAO urged the budget office to flag more programs that need joint action. It also urged wider use of the eight practices it describes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-215:
A Navy support computer system faces a value test in GAO-06-215, a report dated December 5, 2005. The Naval Tactical Command Support System began in 1995. It helps sailors manage support work for ships, submarines, and aircraft. About $1 billion has been spent to place it at roughly half its planned sites. GAO checked whether the program follows defense buying rules and sound practice for tech projects.

Weak data on cost, benefit, risk, and status cloud the program's case. GAO urged the Secretary of Defense to have the Navy retest the planned investment. A sound economic analysis should come first, built with cost experts. It should weigh all real options, including the Navy's newer resource planning system. Cost estimates must follow best practice, GAO said. The report asks whether a decade-old system still earns the funds left to finish it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-315:
Two giant health systems learning to share is the story of GAO-06-315, dated March 20, 2006. A 2003 defense law told the veterans and defense departments to share care more deeply. It created a joint incentive fund and a set of demonstration sites. Congress ordered GAO to track both programs. GAO also reviewed steps the departments took on their own to share staff, space, and services. It judged whether their progress measures truly show movement toward the sharing goals.

Chances to share more still remain, GAO found. Joint sites can cut duplicate clinics and labs where bases and veterans' hospitals sit near each other. Incentive money helps seed projects that neither side would fund alone. Useful measures matter: without them, sharing stays anecdote. The report presses both departments to prove gains in access and cost. Every shared scanner or ward is capacity bought once instead of twice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-415:
Nine years of audits still ended without an opinion on the government's books. GAO's April 21, 2006 financial audit, GAO-06-415, details control flaws in preparing the consolidated financial statements. Material weaknesses blocked GAO from giving an opinion. The government lacked sound systems, controls, and steps to prepare the statements. GAO issued a disclaimer of opinion on the fiscal year 2005 statements in December 2005.

This report gives detail on further weaknesses at the Treasury. It recommends improvements. It also reports the status of action on GAO's earlier 154 recommendations. Readers see the depth of the problem. They also see how much repair work remained.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-515:
Nursing homes and other care homes carry mortgages insured by the federal government. In GAO-06-515 (May 24, 2006), GAO reviews the Section 232 mortgage insurance program. The Federal Housing Administration insures about $12.5 billion in such mortgages. A 2005 appropriations report and a congressional request prompted the study. GAO examined how the housing department manages the program. That includes loan underwriting and monitoring.

GAO checked how federal oversight meshes with state oversight of care quality. It weighed risks the program poses to its insurance fund. It also reviewed how yearly credit subsidy costs are estimated. Chances exist to improve program and risk management, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-815:
Testing English learners under the school law is examined in GAO-06-815 of July 26, 2006. The No Child Left Behind Act of 2001 required states to track the progress of students with limited English proficiency. These students must gain English skills and meet academic goals at the same time. GAO measured their progress in 2004 and studied how states test them. GAO also reviewed the new English proficiency tests most states had adopted.

GAO found that these students fell below progress goals in two-thirds of states in 2004. States GAO studied were working to lift their performance. States did weigh language issues when building academic tests, but concerns over validity and reliability remained. New proficiency tests brought their own challenges. GAO said help from the Education Department could improve measurement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-115:
Ship guns that guard landing troops are hard to build, GAO reports in GAO-07-115, dated November 30, 2006. Since the mid-1990s the Navy and Marine Corps have sought better naval fire support for forces ashore. Two paths lead the work: a long-range shell for current ships, and the future Zumwalt class destroyer.

GAO asked if fire support needs have been set in firm terms. It tracked headway on the shell, the destroyer, and later systems. It tested those systems against the stated needs, and looked for gaps left. The work rests on key program papers, and talks with Navy, Marine, and other staff. Hurdles remain, the title states.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-15:
Amtrak loses money year after year and needs about $1 billion a year in federal aid. GAO weighed the future of passenger rail in GAO-07-15, dated November 13, 2006. The report reviews the U.S. system and its possible public benefits. It studies rail reforms in Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom. It then lays out options for the federal role.

The current system targets federal funds poorly, GAO found. Long-distance routes cause about 80 percent of Amtrak's losses. Yet they carry only 15 percent of its riders. Corridor routes carry most riders and lose far less. They also compete better with cars and planes on time and cost. Foreign reforms shared common steps, such as clear national goals. GAO said the system would keep underperforming without structural change. It urged a national policy to aim funds where rail helps most.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-315:
California's heavy crude sells at a discount to the national benchmark, and that gap swung wide in 2004. GAO explained the moves in GAO-07-315, a report dated January 19, 2007. The gap matters because royalty payments track crude prices. GAO studied 20 years of price data. It compared California grades with the West Texas benchmark. It also weighed gaps for foreign heavy crudes.

The discount for one California grade jumped from about $6 to about $15 a barrel, GAO found. The spike began in mid-2004 and ran into 2005. Gaps for other California and foreign heavy crudes widened too. More heavy supply from the Middle East pressed heavy prices down. Light fuels rose faster than heavy ones, lifting the benchmark. Hurricane Ivan also tightened Gulf supply in September 2004. The gaps have since narrowed but stay high by past standards.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-415:
Fighter fleets old and new compete for the same dollars in GAO-07-415, a GAO report released April 2, 2007. The Defense Department planned to spend $109 billion on tactical air forces between 2007 and 2013. New stealth jets cost far more per plane than the ones they replace. Delays in new programs force costly life extensions for old jets.

GAO charted the state of each new program and the strain on legacy fleets. It found that cost growth in new jets threw off upgrade and retirement plans across the services. The Joint Strike Fighter sat at the center of the risk. GAO's charge was blunt: the department lacked a joint, joined-up plan for the whole fleet. Without one, buying power shrinks and gaps in the force grow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-515:
Regional federal boards could do more in a crisis, and GAO-07-515, issued May 4, 2007, tells the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) how. Federal executive boards link agency leaders in big metro areas outside Washington. There are 28 of them. Since the September 11 attacks, OPM has cast the boards as emergency helpers. Pandemic flu planning is one new task.

GAO reviewed 14 boards chosen for their size or recent crisis work. The boards can convene local federal leaders fast, a rare asset. But their emergency role appears in no national plan. Standards to judge their crisis work are not fully built. Funds and staff support rest on year-to-year goodwill from host agencies. GAO urged OPM to define the role, set measures, and steady the support. The value is clear; the footing is not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-815:
Basic training for federal law officers is surveyed in GAO-07-815, dated August 10, 2007. Officers must finish basic training before they can make arrests or carry firearms. GAO built this report on a survey of 105 federal civilian law components. Each body reported the training its officers must take. GAO sorted the programs by job series. It also sorted them by who teaches and where. The report makes no recommendations.

The survey maps a wide spread of programs across the government. Some officers train at central federal centers. Others train at sites run by their own agencies. Course demands vary with the duties of each job series. Investigators, inspectors, and uniformed officers face distinct tracks. GAO's tables let Congress compare the paths side by side. The report builds on a December 2006 survey of what these bodies do. Together they give a full picture of federal law work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-915:
Human trafficking enforcement is reviewed in GAO-07-915, dated July 26, 2007. A 2000 law punishes traffickers and protects victims. Justice and Homeland Security lead federal cases. Since 2000, their work has led to 139 prosecutions. Agencies train staff and run hotlines and conferences. Special units focus on trafficking full time. State and local task forces get federal support. GAO asked how well the pieces work together. It also checked aid given to the task forces.

Coordination lacks a shared strategic frame, GAO found. Agencies run their own goals and plans side by side. Joint investigations could be stronger with common direction. Task forces need better-targeted technical help as well. GAO urged the two departments to build a joint framework. It also urged a plan to focus task force aid. Both departments broadly agreed on closer collaboration. Justice listed steps it will take for the task forces. The report lands as the 2000 law faces renewal.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-15:
Teen steroid abuse and federal efforts against it are surveyed in GAO report GAO-08-15 (October 31, 2007). Steroids are lab-made forms of testosterone. A 2006 survey found that fewer than 3 percent of 12th graders had abused them. Yet about 40 percent of seniors called them easy to get. Abuse can harm teen health and behavior.

GAO sorted federal efforts into two groups. Some target steroids alone, such as two school sports programs. Others fight drug abuse in general. GAO also reviewed the research base on teen use. Officials and experts named gaps in that research. The report shows where knowledge runs thin.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-315:
GAO report GAO-08-315, dated March 5, 2008, reviews two supply-related choices from the 2005 base closure round. The Base Closure and Realignment Commission had estimated the two moves would save the Department of Defense about $4.8 billion over 20 years. Both moves shift supply work to the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA).

GAO's analysis of DLA data showed net savings over the 2006-2011 period cut by more than $1.8 billion, leaving a net cost of about $222 million. Projected savings over 20 years fell to $1.4 billion. GAO said DLA counted almost $243 million in savings that were not a direct result of BRAC. GAO recommended steps to track costs and savings more accurately. DOD agreed with two recommendations and disagreed with a third.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-415:
Paying food stamp users to buy healthy foods is weighed in GAO report GAO-08-415, dated July 30, 2008. In fiscal year 2007, the Food Stamp Program gave about $30.4 billion in benefits to 26.5 million people, paid through electronic benefit transfer cards. GAO convened 17 experts and reviewed studies on diet incentives.

Studies show that cash incentives and nutrition lessons can lift purchases of targeted foods, at least in the short term. Far less is known about steps that improve access to such foods. Design choices include which foods to favor, how large the incentive should be, how to tell users about it, and how to police and judge the program. GAO sets out electronic and paper options the Food and Nutrition Service could use. The service generally agreed with the findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-615:
Troops heading to war zones now get health checks meant to catch mental health problems and brain injury early. GAO-08-615, dated May 30, 2008, reviews how the Department of Defense runs those checks. Reviewers focused on the Army, the Marine Corps, and the Army National Guard, and visited three bases.

The department set clear mental health standards for deployment and built screening into the health check before troops leave. But its own rules clash on one point: whether the doctor must review each troop's medical records first. That gap means some checks may miss key facts. GAO asked the department to fix the rule so record review is required.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-715:
A small foundation that honors young volunteers had its books checked by GAO. GAO-08-715, dated May 15, 2008, gives the audit verdict on the Congressional Award Foundation's statements for fiscal years 2007 and 2006, which ended September 30 of each year.

Auditors found the books fairly stated under standard accounting rules. Controls over money and rule-following were sound, and tests found no breaches worth reporting. An older worry, whether the foundation could stay afloat, has been resolved. One past mismatch between its tax form and its books is also covered. Readers get a clean bill of health, with the audit scope spelled out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-915:
Help for small exporters is graded in GAO-08-915, a July 2008 report on the Export-Import Bank. The bank backs U.S. exports with loans, guarantees, and insurance. In 2006 Congress ordered it to set performance standards for its small business help. The law gave special weight to firms owned by disadvantaged individuals and by women. Congress also ordered GAO to review those standards.

The bank built 28 standards, covering most functions the law named, but none directly covers outreach to firms with fewer than 100 employees. Its measures look sound in design, yet 11 of 27 lack targets and deadlines, and some standards have no measure at all, including one on financing for disadvantaged and women-owned firms. GAO recommends closing those gaps, and the bank agreed.
georgian-poetry-1913-15:
Marsh's second survey of new English verse covers the years 1913 to 1915, and war shadows it. The book is set in memory of two dead poets, marked only by their initials. Edward Marsh names them in his note: Rupert Brooke, who died on service the past April, and James Elroy Flecker, who died in January after a long illness. Both had seemed among the most gifted of the young.

Some poets from the first volume drop out, for lack of new work or by the plan of the book. Others take their place. The poems move between peace-time scenes and the first grief of war. Marsh hoped readers of the first book would want this mate to it. Read together, the two volumes show a bright school of verse meeting a dark time.
gilman-herland-1915:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman published Herland in 1915, in her own magazine, The Forerunner. The novel imagines a country cut off from the world for two thousand years, where no men live. Gilman was a leading feminist thinker, and fiction let her test her ideas in story form.

Three male explorers, a rich playboy, a doctor, and a sociologist narrator, stumble into the hidden land. They find a peaceful, prosperous society of women who reproduce without men and raise children as a shared duty. The visitors' assumptions about women collapse one by one. Herland founded feminist speculative fiction and still reads as a bold thought experiment about gender and power.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-12-1915:
Volume 12 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1915. James George Frazer's twelve-volume study of magic and religion ends not with a new theory but with its tools: a full bibliography and a general index. After eleven volumes of evidence, the twelfth lets readers find and check it.

The bibliography lists the travelers, missionaries, and scholars whose reports Frazer used, a map of his sources in itself. The index sorts gods, rites, peoples, and customs across the whole set. Students of religion still use such apparatus to trace a custom through the work. The volume completes the landmark edition of a founding work of comparative religion.
govdocs-archive_org-ufo2_20240815: UFO made public docs 2: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers and readers.
haslmayr-sendtschreiben-1615:
Adam Haslmayr answers the Rosicrucian manifestos in his Sendtschreiben, printed in German in 1615. The Tyrolean physician writes back to the unknown Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross with open joy. His letter, the first printed reply to the mysterious Fama, set all learned Europe buzzing with hope, doubt, and wild surmise.

Haslmayr begs the brethren to reveal themselves to a waiting world. He had already suffered prison for his alchemical faith and hopes. Enthusiasm, not irony, marks every line of his simple address. The pamphlet launched the strangest learned craze of the seventeenth century, the Rosicrucian furor, whose echoes ran for a hundred years.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle devotes volume fifteen, book fifteen, to the Second Silesian War, from August 1744 to December 1745. Friedrich struck first, fearing Austria would retake Silesia once free of France. Carlyle stresses Prussia's speed: an army ready in three weeks while other states needed months. France, meanwhile, shifted its main effort to the Netherlands under Marshal de Saxe.

Campaigns in Bohemia and Saxony follow, with Friedrich left carrying most of the German war alone. Carlyle mixes marches, diplomacy, and portraits of ministers and mistresses at the French court. The book ends with peace signed at Dresden on Christmas Day 1745, Silesia confirmed as Prussian, and a harder war still to come.
hoffmann-devils-elixir-vol1-1815:
E. T. A. Hoffmann published The Devil's Elixir in German in 1815, and R. P. Gillies translated it into English in 1824. Volume one follows Brother Medardus, a Capuchin monk tempted by a relic said to be an elixir of the Devil. One taste breaks his vows and starts his ruin.

Medardus flees the monastery into crime, disguise, and a haunting double who shares his face. Love, murder, and madness crowd the road as his past hunts him down. Hoffmann mixes Gothic horror with sharp irony about faith and desire. The novel became a founding study of the double in modern fiction. Its wild plot still grips readers who like their tales dark.
hoffmann-devils-elixir-vol2-1815:
Volume two of The Devil's Elixir brings Hoffmann's monk novel to its close, in R. P. Gillies's translation of 1824. Medardus, worn by crime and pursuit, faces the full truth of his family's curse. The double who has dogged him steps out of rumor into plain sight.

Confession, trial, and penance take the place of flight and disguise. Hoffmann untangles the knot of births, sins, and mistaken selves that drove the tale. The ending weighs guilt against grace in a haunted, Catholic frame. Read with volume one, the novel stands complete: a Gothic landmark on the divided self. Its fevered method later fed Poe, Stevenson, and many more.
holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-slice-:
Raphael Holinshed's chronicle covers Henry the Second's whole reign in this long slice. Henry, second son of Geoffrey Plantagenet and the Empress Maud, began on the twenty-fifth of October 1154. He landed in December after storm scattered his companies. The sidenotes cite Trivet, Matthew Paris, and Hoveden.

Rebellion by his own sons darkens the later annals. Young Henry's men take Nottingham at dawn, burn the town, and divide the goods. Fear drives the country round to submit to him. Holinshed tracks councils, wars in France, and the church strife between. At 423 thousand characters this is the fattest slice of the volume.
homer-iliad-pope-1715:
Homer's Iliad came to Georgian England in Alexander Pope's version of 1715 to 1720. Pope's was the great Augustan Iliad, and the most famous English Homer of its age. He worked in heroic couplets and grew rich from the book's subscription sales alone.

Achilles' wrath drives the war tale, from quarrel to Hector's fall at Troy's walls. Gods scheme above while men bleed below, in Pope's polished and balanced verse lines throughout. His notes and essays frame Homer as the supreme poet of nature and fire. Purists charged Pope with making Homer a London wit, but readers loved the sheen. The version ruled English taste until the next century's plainer fashions arrived at last.
homer-odyssey-chapman-1615:
Homer's Odyssey came to England in full in George Chapman's version of 1615. Chapman's was the first complete English Odyssey, companion to his famed Iliad of that era. He used a broad, rolling ten-syllable couplet full of sea wind and strange compounds throughout.

Odysseus, after Troy's fall, wanders ten years toward home and his wife Penelope in Ithaca. Cyclops, Circe, sirens, and the dead test his craft on the long road home. At Ithaca he finds suitors eating his wealth and slays them in his own hall. Chapman's verse is rougher than Pope's but wilder, and many still prize its force. Keats linked both Chapman Homers in the sonnet that made his early name.
indrajalavidyasangraha-1915-1915:
Indrajalavidyasangraha, printed at Calcutta in 1915, gathers Sanskrit works on magic and ritual in one volume. The title page lists the Indrajala Shastra, the Kamaratna, and the Dattatreya Tantra among its parts. A work on six ritual acts and a Kakshaputa linked to Nagarjuna are also named. Editors from the family of Jivananda Vidyasagara prepared the edition.

Verses in the middle teach worship of Rudra with due rites and offerings. Meditations picture the god with trident in hand, fierce and bright as the full moon. Mantras and ritual steps fill the pages. The volume preserves tantric practice in Sanskrit.
jack-sheppard-a-romance-pg16215:
William Harrison Ainsworth's Jack Sheppard appears here in the same Berlin 1922 English Library printing. Underscores mark italics from the original, the transcribers note. Epochs divide the romance into 1703, 1715, and the prison-breaker years. Jonathan Wild and Thames Darrell head the first two epochs.

Winifred Wood, tall and graceful with deep blue eyes, is introduced at her father's table. Mrs. Wood greets a handsome young guest with warm civility. Winifred's welcome is kind but more distant, the scene notes. Love for Winifred softens the thief's tale amid Wild's hunting and Jack's escapes.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-15:
Volume 15, from 1898, follows the Hurons through 1638 and 1639. A strange pattern fills the reports that Thwaites prints here. Converts grow in number even while the plague years still cast a shadow.

The fathers' hope stays stubborn in the face of grim facts. Their letters home ring with trust that the mission will thrive. Modern readers know that hope is doomed, which sharpens each page. Baptisms, feasts, and new chapels mark a brief, bright season. The great chronicle keeps a steady beat as the storm builds offshore. Hope and dread share every report in this book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-asher: Aaron ben Asher of Karlin, called Rabbi Aaron the Second of Karlin, is treated in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. Born in 1802, he died on June 23, 1872. He was one of the most famous Hasidic rabbis in northwestern Russia, the entry says. Thousands of followers visited him yearly about the Jewish New Year. Despite a severe manner, he was highly esteemed by his adherents. He reigned in Karlin, near Pinsk, after his father and grandfather, then moved to Stolin after a quarrel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abednego-aramai: Abednego is the Aramaic name given to Azariah, one of Daniel's three companions at the court of Nebuchadnezzar. The name looks like a bent form of Abed Nebo, servant of Nebo, the Babylonian god. That true form is found in an inscription of the seventh century B.C. and in early Syriac writings. The swap of Nego for Nebo was likely made on purpose. It spoiled the name of the heathen god, the entry argues. Barnabas is read the same way, as a soft form of Barnebo, son of Nebo.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abin-b-kahana-3: Abin ben Kahana was a Palestinian amora, and one of the teachers of R. Abun ben Ḥiyya. He was also the junior peer of R. Hoshaya II, the entry notes. One further thread ties his name into the record. R. Jonah, of the fourth amoraic generation, passes on a discussion of law in Abin's name. That discussion is cited from the Jerusalem Talmud, on Horayot. No saying, work, birthplace, or date for Abin ben Kahana is given beyond these three links to other men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrahams-abraha:
Abraham Abrahams wrote on shehitah, the laws of ritual slaughter of animals. Born at Siedlce in Poland in December 1801, he died at Jerusalem on January 23, 1880. Folk knew him simply as Rabbi Abraham.

Russian persecution drove him from Poland to England in 1837. He became shohet at Leeds, then chief shohet of London two years later, serving near half a century in all. His Hebrew works on slaughter and other Talmud topics won a wide name, above all in Poland. His best known are Bet Abraham and Yizkor le-Abraham, his life story. A year before his death he settled in Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-felix-815:
Felix Adler founded the Society for Ethical Culture. He was an educator and author. He was born at Alzey, Germany, on August 13, 1851. He was the second son of Rabbi Samuel Adler. In 1857 the family moved to New York. His father had been called to Temple Emanu-El there. Felix finished at Columbia College in 1870. He went to Germany to train for the rabbinate.

His studies changed his mind on Jewish faith. He found he could not serve as a rabbi. Cornell gave him a chair in Hebrew and Oriental letters from 1874 to 1876. In 1876 he went back to New York and set up his new society. Its rule was right living, free of creed or sect. He also helped start district nursing in 1878 and a free kindergarten in 1880. His books take in "Creed and Deed" of 1877.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agrippa-simonid: Agrippa Simonides was the youngest son of Flavius Josephus, the historian. His mother was Josephus's second wife. She was a Jewess of a high family from the island of Crete. Agrippa was born about the year 82. The hosted text gives only those facts. It names his father, his mother and her home and rank, and his rough birth year. It cites Josephus's Life, section 76, for them. It tells no act, no post, and no death date for this son of the famed writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ain-kades-1015: Ain Kades is a well near the Arabah. Rowlands first saw it in 1842. He identified it with the Kadesh Barnea of the Bible. No European saw it again until 1881. In that year Trumbull visited the site. He showed, in the entry's word, conclusively that Ain Kades and Kadesh Barnea are one and the same.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aleppo-arabic-h:
Aleppo is an ancient town of Syria, capital of a Turkish vilayet. It lies between the Orontes and the Euphrates, on a desert stream. It stands seventy miles east of Alexandretta, its port. Its wealth once came from the road to Bagdad and southern Persia. It is said to have held 200,000 souls, and it shelters one of the oldest Jewish communities of all.

Its synagogue keeps four prized Biblical manuscripts in a damp shrine. The greatest is a codex ascribed to Aaron ben Asher. The entry judges it hard to date before the twelfth century, and not the original of 922. About 10,000 Jews lived in Aleppo when the entry was written, each paying a poll-tax. The Alliance kept a boys' school there from 1869, with 250 pupils. Benjamin of Tudela had found 1,500 Jews there in 1173. Tamerlane's men pillaged the Jewish quarter in 1401.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algazi-moses-be: Moses ben Abraham Algazi wrote as a rabbi in Smyrna in the seventeenth century. He was a brother of Solomon Algazi the elder. He added notes to two works by his grandfather. That grandfather was Moses Benveniste the elder. One of those works deals with the roots of Hebrew words. The entry gives rival dates for its printing. One source says 1799. Another source gives 1722-23 and 1807.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alsari-jacob-13: Jacob Alsari taught Hebrew and wrote on Hebrew grammar. For eighteen years he gave talks in Zerkowo. That town sits in Prussian Poland near the Russian line. His son Joseph was born there in 1805. The son took the German name Julius Fürst and won fame. Jacob wrote a work on angels and accents. He also wrote a sacred poem. Notes on the Targumim came from his pen as well. None of his works was ever printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amnon-steadfast:
Amnon was the first-born son of King David. His mother was Ahinoam of Jezreel. As heir to the throne he drew envy and hate. His half-brother Absalom bore him a deep grudge. Amnon shamed Tamar, the full sister of Absalom. That act fed the grudge with fresh cause. Two years later Absalom struck back.

At a sheep-shearing feast Amnon was killed. All the king's sons had been called to that feast. Sages of the Mishnah weigh the case at length. They say his love was lust, not true love. It turned to sharp hate once he had his way. A rule on men and women alone grew from the tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-angel-ben-hayyi: Angel ben Hayyim was a Turkish commentator on the Bible who lived at Salonica in the last half of the eighteenth century. His work Ez Hayyim, or Tree of Life, contains studies on Genesis. It was printed at Salonica in 1772, bound together with works by M. Algazi and H. J. Varshano. The entry is very short and rests on Zedner's catalog of Hebrew books in the British Museum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antonia-1615:
Antonia was the younger daughter of the triumvir Mark Antony and sister-in-law of the emperor Tiberius. She was friendly with Berenice, daughter of Salome, and with Berenice's son, the future King Agrippa I. Her freedman Petrus had lent Agrippa money when he was broke.

Agrippa owed the Roman treasury 300,000 silverlings and fled to Alexandria, where Antonia's property guardian supplied him. He then borrowed the full sum from Antonia herself and paid the treasury, later paying her back as well. Her son, the emperor Claudius, grew up alongside Agrippa, and their boyhood friendship lasted for life, the entry notes from Josephus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arauxo-daniel-1: Daniel Arauxo was a physician who lived in Amsterdam in the seventeenth century. The whole of this very short entry adds one dated act to that bare outline. In the year 1655 he composed an elegy on the martyr Isaac de Almeyda Bernal. It gives no birth or death dates, no training, and no other works. Readers are left with a name, a city, a profession, and a single poem of mourning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aronstein-phili:
Philipp Aronstein, who wrote under the name Arnstein, was a German schoolteacher and author born on December 4, 1862, at Halver in Westphalia. He studied at the gymnasium in Soest, at Berlin and Bonn, and at the Academy of Munster, where he took a doctorate in philosophy. After teaching in England and Germany, he held a senior post at the Progymnasium at Myslowitz in Silesia by 1902.

English subjects fill most of his writing. He published studies of Ben Jonson's theory of comedy and of Dickens in 1890s journals, plus work on John Marston and on local government in England. His chief books treat the life and poetic works of Benjamin Disraeli, in 1895, and the growth of English boys' schools, in 1897. He also turned Bishop Creighton's Age of Queen Elizabeth into German in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-artapanus-12415:
Artapanus, a historian living in Alexandria in the second century B.C., wrote a history of the Jews. Parts of it survive in Eusebius and in Clement of Alexandria, and later writers used it too. The verdict here is harsh. Artapanus belonged, the entry says, to a narrow circle of Greek-speaking Jews. Eager to glorify Judaism before Greek readers, they invented fables about the Jews. They missed, in this view, what was truly great in their faith.

His Moses shows the method. Moses becomes Musaeus, not the pupil of Orpheus but his teacher. He invents navigation, building, war craft, and philosophy. Strangest of all, he founds the worship of Egypt and is called Hermes by the Egyptians for expounding the priests' sacred writings. The Exodus story follows, padded with legend, and the entry traces how such claims grew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashenheim-louis:
Louis Ashenheim, a Scottish physician and surgeon, was born at Edinburgh in 1817. He took honors at the university there and became a licentiate of the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh. Travel to Paris, Berlin, and other European cities added to his training. He practiced for a time in London, lectured often, and wrote for the Anglo-Jewish press.

In 1843 he emigrated to Jamaica and settled at Kingston. He practiced there until 1850, then moved to Falmouth, a port on the island's north coast. Through the press he urged sanitary reform and compulsory vaccination, which he ably defended. During a cholera outbreak at Falmouth he gave valuable service. He died in Jamaica on November 26, 1858.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-askenazy-simon-:
Simon Askenazy, a Polish historian, was born in 1867 at Zawichwost, in the government of Radom in Russian Poland. He studied at the universities of Warsaw and Gottingen and took his doctorate in philosophy at Gottingen. In 1897 he became a lecturer, and in 1902 professor extraordinary of general history at the University of Lemberg.

His books treat the last Polish royal election and studies in history and criticism, the second in a second edition of 1897. Two works of 1897 and 1898 take up the minister Lubecki and the ministry of Wielhorski. Many of his essays ran in the Biblioteka Warszawska and the Kwartalnik Historyczny. They deal chiefly with Polish history of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyons-jacques-j:
Jacques Judah Lyons, an American minister, receives a biographical entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Surinam, Dutch Guiana, on August 25, 1814, he served its Spanish and Portuguese congregation for five years. In 1837 he left for Richmond, Virginia, where he ministered for two years. He died in New York in 1877.

The article follows his thirty-eight years at Shearith Israel in New York. There he resisted every move to change the congregation's form of worship. Beyond his pulpit he helped found the Jews' Hospital, now Mount Sinai. He also backed the Jewish Board of Delegates and the Hebrew Free Schools. He ran the Polonies Talmud Torah School and built a fine library, now held by the Jewish Theological Seminary. With Abraham De Sola he published a fifty-year Hebrew calendar in 1857. The entry portrays a traditional minister who built lasting institutions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makower-hermann:
Hermann Makower, a German jurist, is profiled at length in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Santomischel, Posen, on March 8, 1830, he was sent to Berlin at nine, nearly penniless. There he sang as a synagogue chorister and found schooling. He died at Berlin on April 1, 1898.

The article follows a rise built on commercial law. Makower reached a judgeship at the Berlin city court, a post no Jew had held before. He left the bench for a richer practice. His commentary on the German commercial code, written with Siegmund Meyer, reached an eleventh edition by 1893. Famous clients followed, including the historian Mommsen, whom he defended against a slander charge by Bismarck. Mommsen was acquitted in 1883. Makower also backed Berlin's Jewish seminary and lectured for its benefit. The entry joins legal fame to communal loyalty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mariamne-10415:
Mariamne, Herod's Hasmonean queen, is portrayed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The hosted text opens on her unhappy marriage. Herod loved her passionately, the article says. She could not forget that he had murdered her family and taken their throne. Her pride toward the upstart king stung his mother and his sister Salome.

The article follows the court's deadly intrigues. Mariamne's mother pressed Herod to make her young brother Aristobulus high priest. He yielded in 35, meaning to kill the youth when he could. Before facing Antony over that killing, Herod left orders that Mariamne die if he did not return. His brother-in-law Joseph, set to guard her, told her the secret as proof of Herod's love. Salome then accused the two of adultery. Herod executed Joseph at once and jailed Mariamne's mother. The entry shows a queen destroyed by one king's love and suspicion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayer-henry-105:
Cyrus Adler and Edgar Mels profile Henry Mayer, an American caricaturist, in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Worms on July 18, 1868, the son of a Jewish merchant of London, and was educated in his birthplace. He went to Mexico in 1885, then on to Texas. There, the entry says, he discovered that he could draw, and he taught himself the craft with no master. Cincinnati and then Chicago gave him his start as a caricaturist and illustrator.

His picture books came quickly. “The Autobiography of a Monkey” came in 1898. “In Laughland” and “Fantasies in Ha! Ha!” came in 1899, and toyland and doll adventures came after those. His drawings appeared in comic papers in Munich, London, New York, and Paris. His cartoons on the Dreyfus affair, printed in English periodicals, drew wide attention on both sides of the Atlantic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-memorial-servic:
Memorial Service, the prayer for the dead, is treated by Cyrus Adler and Kaufmann Kohler in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Prayer for the dead appears already in the Second Book of Maccabees. Reading the Torah chapter on death on the Day of Atonement seems to have suggested a special remembrance that day. Later the custom spread to other festivals.

Its real subject is the Reform remaking of the rite. Reform Judaism rebuilt the old liturgy. It rested on the immortality of the soul and on comfort for mourners. In time it became a most solemn feature of the Day of Atonement. The entry sets out the common order. First come verses on life's brevity and the twenty-third Psalm. Then come medieval poems by Ibn Gabirol, Judah ha-Levi, and Bahya, in translation. Next comes the prayer naming the martyrs. Many congregations also read the year's death-roll.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-j:
Meshullam ben Jonah is the subject of a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach. He was a physician and translator who lived in southern France in the thirteenth century. The entry presents him as a scholar of medicine rather than a working doctor.

According to the article, Meshullam studied medicine but seems never to have practised it. At the request of a friend named Ḥafeẓ, or Shalem, he translated Zahrawi's medical work Kitab al-Taẓrif into Hebrew, opening his version with a Hebrew poem in his friend's honor. A brief bibliography points readers to Steinschneider and to Neubauer's catalogue of Hebrew manuscripts at the Bodleian Library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miedzyboz-medzh:
Miedzyboz, a town in Russian Podolia, held 3,400 Jews among its 5,100 people when Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. More than a thousand of its Jews were artisans, and its charities aided some 300 families with fuel and Passover help in 1898. A Jewish community there reaches back to the sixteenth century.

That community was destroyed in the Chmielnicki uprising, rebuilt to a few tax-favored houses by 1661, and struck again by the sword in 1664. The town's lasting fame came about 1740, when Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem-Tov, settled at Miedzyboz. From there he began spreading the teachings that became Hasidism, making the small town a place of pilgrimage in Jewish memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moghilef-mohile:
Moghilef, or Mohilev, on the Dnieper, gets a documentary town history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its authors are Herman Rosenthal, J. G. Lipman, and S. Janovsky. The surviving narrative turns on friction with the Christian merchants. Their complaints about Jewish competition reached the king. Their pressure produced a royal edict that redrew where Jews could live.

On July 23, 1626, Sigismund III ordered every Jew owning a house on the market-place to move. They were to go to the street of the prayer-house, with equivalent ground assigned there. Ladislaus IV confirmed the order in 1633. He also banned Jewish baths and breweries inside the city. The article then tells of a 1639 scare. A Christian servant's death was laid at a Jewish household's door. Inquiry showed she had drunk herself senseless at the monastery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morgenstern-kar:
Karl Morgenstern was a German landscape-painter born at Frankfurt-on-the-Main on October 25, 1812. He receives a brief Jewish Encyclopedia notice in 1906. He trained at the Munich Academy of Arts. In 1834 he made the young painter's classic trip through the Bavarian highlands and into Italy. Italy stayed his subject for good.

The entry names three canvases. They are a view of Naples, the Bay of Baiae, and the gulf of Villefranche near Nice. The last was painted in 1843. By then it was hanging in the Städel Museum at Frankfurt. He died in his native city in 1893. Singer's artists' lexicon is the sole source. He is a painter preserved by his Italian views and one museum wall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-kiev-1:
Moses of Kiev was a Russian Talmudist of the first half of the twelfth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Louis Ginzberg wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He seems to have reached western Europe after the Jews were expelled from Kiev in 1124. He may have been a pupil of Jacob Tam, the great French tosafist.

From Russia, Moses corresponded with Samuel ben Ali, head of the Babylonian academy. Through Moses, western scholars learned of an important legal decision of the Geonim that Samuel had sent him. Another responsum from Samuel to Moses survives in a manuscript. Whether he is also the Rabbi Moses the Russian of the Sefer ha-Shoham, the entry leaves doubtful.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munden-11215:
Münden, a town in the Prussian province of Hanover, first mentions Jews in the sixteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. When Duke Heinrich drove the Jews from Brunswick in 1557, those of Münden were allowed to stay. The Thirty Years' War then swelled their numbers.

The article is a string of grievances and odd dues. Citizens petitioned General Tilly in 1626 to restrain the Jews, and the town charged burial fees by age. Jews also had to give a silver spoon each year as the marksmen's prize, a duty kept into the eighteen hundreds. The synagogue of 1834 burned and was rebuilt, and by 1903 the community counted one hundred ten souls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-hirsch: Naphtali Hirsch ben Menahem was president of the Lemberg community in the sixteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives him a very short notice by its editorial committee and S. Mannheimer. He wrote Perush ha-Millot, explanations of difficult words in the Midrash Rabbah. The book was printed at Cracow in 1569.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-negeb-dry-land-:
The Negeb is the dry tract of southern Judah. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word often means simply the south. The Authorized Version renders it that way throughout. Yet the Negeb is also one named region. It forms a plateau of moderate height.

Water was scarce there, but pasture was rich. Moses' spies found Amalekites living in the Negeb. Joshua gave its twenty-nine cities to Judah. Part later passed to the tribe of Simeon. Five districts bore the names of their peoples. Judah, Jerahmeelites, Kenites, Cherethites, and Caleb each held one. Its grape cluster needed two men and a pole. Prophets later promised its ruined cities a return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nezhin-nyezhin-:
Nezhin was a Russian town in the tobacco trade. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It lay in the government of Chernigov. In 1648 Cossacks took it and slew its Jews. Poles of the town died at their side.

In July 1881 an anti-Jewish riot raged three days. Most Jewish houses in Nezhin were destroyed then. Troops fired twice on the mob, killing ten rioters. New tobacco duties then crushed the small Jewish workshops. Great manufacturers absorbed the trade instead of them. The census of 1897 counted 32,108 people there. About one third of them were Jews. Jewish artisans alone numbered 980 in that count. Schools and a loan association served the community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novy-israel-116:
Novy Israel, or New Israel, was a short-lived sect. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It arose at Odessa at the end of 1881. Jacob Prelooker, a schoolteacher, founded the movement. It leaned from Judaism toward Christianity in tone.

His stated aim was a reformed synagogue for Jews. He preached softening the split with Christians too. Brotherhood in religion was his public watchword. In secret he hoped to join Russian dissenters. Molokans and Stundists were the allies he sought. Learning and depth, the entry judges, he lacked. Few adherents ever rallied to his flag. Press and government favored it briefly, then saw through it. All trace vanished before he left for England.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-opatow-samuel-b: Samuel ben Eleazar Opatow was a rabbi in Moravia. The board and Alexander Kisch wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Bohemia, part of the Czech lands. He served as rabbi at Prossnitz in the fifteen hundreds. He wrote a book of new notes and replies on the law. Its theme was the marriage laws of the Talmud, in the tracts Ketubot and Kiddushin. The book came out at Prossnitz in 1602 or 1618.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolenghi-emil:
Emilio Ottolenghi was an Italian giver of aid from Acqui. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Acqui on November 5, 1830. Since 1848 he had lived at Alessandria, in Piedmont. King Humbert the First made him Count of Vallepiana.

That high title came to Emilio on February 22, 1883. In 1882 he was first named to the town board. He was named to that board for years in a row. He sat on the board of the home for beggars. He founded homes and asylums for the poor and sick. He was a chief of the Bank of Italy there. He led the aid group for his whole province. The crown gave him rank three times in his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parnas-colloqui:
A parnas is the chief or trustee of a Jewish flock. Cyrus Adler and Gotthard Deutsch wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word is a new Hebrew word for that post. It is found in the Targum for words that mean steward. It is met with oft in the books of the Talmud.

Men have sought the source of the word in Greek. One source may be a Greek word for one who provides. In some tongues of today it stands as a term of law. In Bavaria it came as barnos in a decree of 1813. In Dutch law it stands as parnassijns, in set form. In the Middle Ages the title was not in wide use. The piece goes on to trace the post through those ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pera-12015:
Peræa was the part of Palestine east of the Jordan. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Josephus set its bounds from Macherus to Pella. In fact the region stretched much farther north and south.

The land is a rough plateau above the river. It drops steeply west and slopes gently east. Its rivers include the Jabbok and the Arnon. The region mattered little until the Maccabees came. Judas first brought it under firm Jewish rule. Rome's general Vespasian took it back in 67.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-samuel:
Samuel Phillips was an English journalist and critic in London. He was born there in 1815 and died at Brighton in 1854. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At fifteen he acted at Covent Garden.

Phillips then studied at Cambridge and at Göttingen. In 1841 he turned to letters and the press. His novel Caleb Stukeley won notice in Blackwood's. As the Times critic he struck at Dickens and Carlyle. His bold reviews became the talk of the town. He later directed letters for the Crystal Palace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plungian-plungi:
Mordecai Plungian was a Russian Hebraist caught between two camps. Herman Rosenthal and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Plungian in 1814. He died at Wilna in 1883, poor and embattled.

Young Plungian won fame as a Talmudist early. An unhappy marriage drove him from his town. At Troki his freer ideas angered the strict. At Wilna he lectured and taught for bread. The seminary made him instructor in Talmud in 1867. When it closed, he corrected proofs at Romm's press. Orthodox called him heretic; liberals called him backward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-potchi-moses-12: Moses Potchi was a Karaite scholar who lived at Constantinople. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the second half of the sixteenth century. He belonged to the Maruli family. His son Joseph took the family name as his own. One work is ascribed to Potchi but stayed in handwriting. It treats the making of the world and the being of God. A poem of his praises a book printed in 1581.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinowitz-hirs:
Hirsch Zebi Rabinowitz was a Russian man of science and public writer. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Linkovo near Poneviezh in 1832. He died at St. Petersburg in 1889. His father, the town rabbi, was his chief teacher. Talmud and kindred lore filled his first years of study.

Yet the boy leaned toward science from a young age. He was glad when his father let a friend teach him. That friend taught him the first steps of mathematics. At twenty his life took its new turn in full. The entry follows his path from study house to science. It lists the works that made his public name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-recanati-12615:
Recanati is an Italian family named for the city of Recanati. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The city lay in the former Papal States. The article opens with a family tree.

The entry then profiles the family's leading members. Amadeo translated Maimonides into Italian in 1583. Elijah wrote a confession in rimed prose about 1660. Emanuele practiced medicine at Verona and wrote Hebrew grammars. He also made Hebrew dictionaries in both directions. Jacob Hayyim served as rabbi in many Italian towns. He wrote on Jewish law, arithmetic, and doctrine. The entry traces one family across three centuries of learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revere-giuseppe:
Giuseppe Revere was an Italian dramatist and humorist born at Triest in 1812. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died on November 22, 1889. His parents meant him for a career in commerce.

The article says he left commerce for study at Milan. He pursued literature, philosophy, German, Greek, and Hebrew. His plays treat Italian historical figures and places. Lorenzino de' Medici appeared in 1839. In 1848 he joined a Mazzini plot at Venice. Banishment followed, and he later defended Rome. He was banished again on suspicion of republican plotting. His many poems fill the entry's later list. He also edited an official bulletin at Rome. The entry joins stage work with patriotic action.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romberg-moritz-:
Moritz Heinrich Romberg was a German physician born on November 11, 1795. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Meiningen in Saxony. He died in Berlin on June 16, 1873.

The article says he graduated from Berlin University in 1817. He settled in the capital after a stay in Vienna. He served as physician to the poor from 1820. During cholera epidemics he ran a Berlin hospital. He rose to a full professorship in 1845. He retired in 1867 after his doctor's jubilee. His specialty was neuropathy, or nervous disease. His textbook gave the first systematic review of nervous maladies. It appeared from 1840 to 1846. He also translated Bell and others into German.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roussillon-1291:
Roussillon is a province of ancient France, now the department of Pyrénées-Orientales. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews settled there early in the thirteenth century, forming many congregations.

Congregations stood at Perpignan, Collioure, Céret, Elne, and a dozen smaller towns. At Villefranche was born Levi ben Abraham, a figure in the fight over philosophy study. In 1228 King James I barred Jews from public office there. He also capped the interest Jews could charge on loans. Later kings eased some rules, such as the badge while traveling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salamanca-13015:
Salamanca is a Spanish city, capital of its province and famed for its university. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its Jews served King Ferdinand II of Leon well in war in 1169.

In return the king granted them equal rights with Christians in 1170. The town council must protect and even defend them, for a yearly tax. They were not spared, though, in the persecutions of 1391. In 1412 Vicente Ferrer preached there to convert the Jews by sermon. The great synagogue then became a church named Vera Cruz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jose:
Samuel ben Joseph Joske was a Polish Talmudist of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, born at Lublin. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was the first known rabbi of Jung-Bunzlau in Bohemia.

Joske's Lehem Rab, printed at Prague in 1609, supplements the Shulhan Aruk. It follows the Orah Hayyim section and keeps that code's own order throughout. Judah Löw ben Bezaleel, the famed Maharal of Prague, approved the work himself. A supplement so endorsed helped rabbis apply the code in practice. The entry is short, but it fixes Joske's place in that chain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sason-joseph-be:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Joseph ben Jacob Sason, an editor and perhaps an author. He lived in the sixteenth century. Sason edited the Maḥazor Sefardi, the Sephardic prayer book. It was printed at Venice in 1584. He also paid for a Jewish calendar covering 1585 to 1639.

The author of Shemen Sason may be this same Joseph Sason. That work treats the Masorah, the notes guarding the Bible's exact text. It quotes the ancient works on that subject. Later scholars cite it in their own books on the Masorah. Lonsano quotes it in Or Torah. Norzi quotes it in Minḥat Shai. The entry leaves his authorship open, as the evidence does.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schreiner-abrah:
Abraham Schreiner, an Austrian who discovered petroleum, is profiled by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Schreiner was born in Galicia early in the nineteenth century. He died sometime after 1870. He traded at Boryslaw, where he owned land. A greasy, tarry ooze seeped from a hollow on that land.
