Local farmers had long used the stuff as a cure-all. Schreiner rolled it into a ball, stuck in a wick, and lit it. It burned with a red flame. His first try at distilling ended with an exploding pot. He bought proper gear from an apothecary. In 1853 he produced petroleum and sold it to druggists. The Austrian Northern Railway tested his refined oil for lamps in 1854. Fire twice gutted his works. After the 1866 blaze he was ruined. American oil then flooded the market.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semitic-languag:
Semitic languages are the tongues spoken by the Semitic peoples of the ancient Near East. Crawford Howell Toy and George A. Barton wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. The group includes Babylonian, Assyrian, Aramaic, Hebrew, Canaanite, and Phoenician speech. Arabic and Abyssinian tongues belong to the family as well.

The entry compares this family with the Aryan, or Indo-European, languages. Both build words by bending stems, yet their deep differences suggest separate roots. The authors then turn to the traits that mark Semitic speech itself. For readers, the piece maps a language family that shaped scripture, trade, and empire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheba-queen-of-:
Sheba's queen was a south Arabian monarch who visited King Solomon at Jerusalem. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on her. She had heard of Solomon's wisdom and wealth from afar. She came with a brilliant retinue to test that fame.

At Jerusalem she found the truth greater than the reports. The two rulers exchanged costly presents before she went home. Josephus instead made her queen of Egypt and Ethiopia. He credited her with bringing balsam plants to the Holy Land. Scholars place her realm at Saba in southern Arabia. Yet no Sabean inscription found yet names any such queen, and one rabbi read the word as a kingdom, not a queen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-samu:
Simeon ben Samuel of Joinville was a French tosafist and Bible commentator of the thirteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He is once wrongly called Samson ben Samuel by copyists. Elsewhere he appears under the name Shemaiah in error.

Simeon learned from Isaac ben Samuel the Elder in France. He in turn taught Eliezer ben Joel ha-Levi. As a tosafist he is quoted as Simeon of Joinville. Sometimes the sources cite him simply as Simeon alone. As a Bible commentator, Isaac ben Judah quotes him. That citation comes in Isaac's work Pa'neah Raza. The entry untangles a scholar hidden behind three similar names in the old books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-song-of-moses-1:
The Song of Moses is a poem found in Deuteronomy chapter thirty-two. Emil G Hirsch and George A Barton wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Moses is said to have spoken its words to all Israel. The poem shows a scale of prophetic thought found nowhere else. Its form is praised as striking and original throughout.

Heaven and earth are called to hear the opening words. The theme is God's faithfulness toward a faithless people. Next comes God's care in the wilderness and gift of land. Then Israel's lapse into idolatry is described in full. God threatens disaster, then resolves to save and vindicate them. Critics hold that Mosaic authorship is impossible on its terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinhardt-mend:
Mendel Steinhardt was a German rabbi who held the rabbinate of Minden. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He lived across the late 1700s and early 1800s. In 1807 the Westphalia consistory chose him as a counselor. He became known as a defender of early Reform Judaism.

Steinhardt defended Israel Jacobson's push for reform among Westphalian Jews. His 1804 book holds ninety responsa on rabbinical subjects. An index arranges them by Talmudic tractate for easy use. A second work, printed in 1812, defended the Cassel consistory reforms. It argued the changes fit Talmudic principles. The entry shows a rabbi making the legal case for reform.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-triesch-friedri:
Friedrich Gustav Triesch was an Austrian dramatist born at Vienna in 1845. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied sculpture briefly at the Vienna academy. Lack of money pushed him into business for a time. His farce Lachende Erben succeeded in 1867.

That success let him write plays full time. The Hofburgtheater honored his comedy Im XIX. Jahrhundert in 1868. Two more plays won similar honors in 1877. His comedy Neue Verträge took Munich's first prize in 1879. His drama Ottilie beat 383 rivals for first prize in 1892. He wrote under three pen names as well. Poems and short stories round out his output.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vital-david-b-s:
David ben Solomon Vital, called ha Rofe, was a Spanish scholar. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He left Spain early in the fifteen hundreds. He settled at Patras, in Greece. When that city fell in 1532, he lost almost his whole library. He spent his last years at Arta.

His main work is Keter Torah, printed at Constantinople in 1536. It lists the 613 commandments in verse form. It also covers rules for Hanukkah and the Sabbath. Another book gives rules for examining slaughtered oxen. His Mikhtam le Dawid versifies Maimonides' thirteen articles of faith. He wrote many liturgical poems as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiga-judah-1491:
Judah Wiga was a Polish preacher of Lublin. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the late fifteen and early sixteen hundreds. Sources disagree even on his name. Sternberg calls him Wiga, from Polish records. Basnage calls him Judah Vega instead.

Basnage says Vega published sermons under King Sigismund. Wolf links him to a book called Derashot. He may be the Judah ben Moses of another record. That man wrote Malke Yehudah at Lublin in 1616. It holds fifteen sermons in one collection. The entry lays out the tangled evidence honestly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ze-enah-u-re-en:
Ze'enah u-Re'enah is a Yiddish gloss on the Hebrew Bible tales. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jacob ben Isaac of Janow made the work in his day. He lived in the 1500s and the 1600s in Poland.

The work treats the Pentateuch, the Haftorah, and the Five Scrolls. It is rich in tales drawn from the Midrash books. It draws from gloss books of tales in like measure. Each week part oft starts with a verse from Proverbs. That verse is then fleshed out with tale and gloss. The book was meant most of all for the use of women. Its name comes from a motto on its first title page. That motto is a verse from the Song of Songs.
jordanes-getica-mierow-1915:
Jordanes, a sixth-century writer, told the Goths' story in his Getica, here in Charles Mierow's 1915 English version. Origins, migrations, and kings fill his brisk Latin history. Attila's Huns, the Visigoths, and Rome's fall all pass through its pages.

Nearly all we know of early Gothic history flows through this one book. Jordanes drew on lost works, above all Cassiodorus's great history. His tale mixes legend, pride, and hard fact in equal parts. Mierow's version opened the text to English readers in clear form. It remains the most important barbarian history to survive from the age of migrations.
journal-of-discourses-vol-15:
Panic on Wall Street shapes Volume Fifteen of the Journal, from 1873. Young answers hard times with the United Order, his boldest scheme. Saints are called to pool property and labor for the common good.

Cooperation rises, in his preaching, to the rank of God's own law. Towns across Utah try shared farms, shops, and herds under the plan. Sermons praise the order as Zion's shield against greed and want. A godly economy takes shape, for a time, in the desert. The volume shows faith turned into a full plan for daily life and work for all.
kafka-die-verwandlung-1915:
Die Verwandlung, published in 1915, is Kafka's novella in the original German: The Metamorphosis. Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes one morning to find himself changed into a huge insect, and his family's horror becomes the story.

Told in calm, exact prose, the tale follows Gregor's shrinking place in the flat, his sister's turn from care to disgust, and his quiet death. Kafka never explains the change, which is the point: the absurd is treated as fact. This Kurt Wolff era text is the founding work of the literature of alienation, read here in the language Kafka wrote.
kathavatthu-points-of-controversy-1915:
Shwe Zan Aung and C. A. F. Rhys Davids translated the Kathavatthu in 1915. Their English version bears the title Points of Controversy. The Kathavatthu is the fifth book of the Abhidhamma Pitaka.

Tradition says a council in the third century BCE composed the work. It knocks down more than two hundred disputed doctrines, point by point. Questions about the soul, the Buddhas, and time receive disciplined refutation. The method proceeds by questions that corner each opponent logically. Shwe Zan Aung, a Burmese scholar, worked from deep commentarial knowledge. The translation opens ancient Buddhism's great debate book. Philosophy as careful argument fills these pages, two thousand years old.
lawrence-rainbow-1915:
D. H. Lawrence published The Rainbow in 1915, his most ambitious novel of three Brangwen generations in the Midlands. The tale follows the Brangwens seeking fulfillment across the industrial Midlands as canals, mines, and railways remake England. Police suppressed the book for obscenity within weeks, and copies were burned by court order in 1915.

Tom Brangwen weds a Polish widow, Lydia, and their marriage of strangers opens the family saga in Marsh Farm. Anna, her daughter, weds Will Brangwen, and their struggle of wills fills the stormy, fertile middle of the book. Ursula, the granddaughter, becomes a teacher, loves and leaves Skrebensky, and seeks a self beyond marriage and chapel. A rainbow over the colliery at the close promises renewal for a world Lawrence found mechanized and spiritually starved. The novel's biblical cadence and frank desire made it a landmark of modernism.
legge-forerunners-and-rivals-vol-1-1915:
Francis Legge published the first volume of Forerunners and Rivals of Christianity in 1915. His subject is the crowded religious world around the early church, from 330 B.C. to A.D. 330. He asked what faiths came before Christianity, which ones competed with it, and how they shaped the ground it grew in.

Legge starts with the conquests of Alexander and the gods of Alexandria, where Greek and Egyptian beliefs mixed. He then traces the roots of Gnosticism and the Gnostic teachers who taught before Christ. The volume gives readers the pagan and mystery faiths that later Gnostic systems, covered in volume two, built upon.
legge-forerunners-and-rivals-vol-2-1915:
Religions competed with early Christianity across the Roman world, and Francis Legge spent two volumes mapping the rivals. Forerunners and Rivals of Christianity, Volume Two, published in 1915, takes up the story from the year 330 backward and forward through the great systems. The Gnostic schools receive the deepest treatment here.

Valentinians, Basilideans, and Marcionites appear as serious religious thinkers rather than cartoon villains. Legge's sympathy for these so-called heretics set his history apart in its day. He traces how their ideas about creation, evil, and salvation challenged the young Church. Readers gain a fair hearing for voices mostly known through their enemies. The volume remains a humane guide to a tangled religious landscape.
letters-of-a-soldier-1914-1915:
Eugène Emmanuel Lemercier's Letters of a Soldier cover August 1914 to April 1915. Constable published this authorized translation in London in 1917. André Chevrillon wrote the preface, and A. Clutton-Brock the introduction.

Lemercier writes most often to his very dear mother. His first letter calls these his first days of life at war. One line became the book's motto: you do not know the things taught by him who falls. He adds simply, I do know. The letters carry a French soldier's faith, fear, and tenderness home. Lemercier was an artist as well as a soldier. His eye for light and place sharpens even trench scenes.
lidzbarski-johannesbuch-1915:
Mark Lidzbarski, a German scholar of Semitic languages, published Das Johannesbuch der Mandaer in 1915. The book gives his German translation of the Mandaean Book of John, a scripture of the small baptist community of southern Iraq and Iran. It was the first Western rendering of the text.

The Mandaeans revere John the Baptist and practice repeated baptism in running water as their central rite. Their book tells of John's life, of light-world beings, and of the soul's ascent after death. Lidzbarski's edition, with the Mandaic text and notes, opened a living Gnostic tradition to European scholarship.
machen-bowmen-1915:
A short tale of Machen's made the most famed legend of the Great War in 1915. The Bowmen, in The Angels of Mons collection, tells of saintly archers who cover a British retreat. Readers took the fiction for fact and would not let it go.

Machen said plainly that he had made the tale up, and the legend grew all the same. The other pieces in the book are legends of the war in the same vein. The volume shows a story walking out of its author's hands into history. It is a case study in how myths are born.
magna-carta-1215:
Magna Carta, the Great Charter, was sealed by King John of England at Runnymede in June 1215. England's barons had rebelled against his taxes and abuses, and forced the charter on him at sword point. The English text here comes from Yale Law School's Avalon Project.

Most of its 63 clauses deal with feudal dues, inheritance, and the church's freedom. Two clauses outlived the rest: no free man may be punished without lawful judgment, and justice may not be sold or delayed. Later ages read those lines as the seed of liberty under law. The charter became a symbol far beyond its feudal start.
masters-spoon-river-1915:
Edgar Lee Masters published Spoon River Anthology in 1915, his groundbreaking portrait of small-town America in free verse. The dead of Spoon River speak their own epitaphs in this corrosive book of linked monologues from the hill. Masters, an Illinois lawyer, drew his town from Lewistown and Petersburg and their courthouse gossip.

Some two hundred and forty speakers confess adultery, murder, greed, faith, and thwarted love from beyond the grave. Judges, teachers, drunkards, and saints correct the town's official pieties with what they hid in life from neighbors. The Trainor the druggist, Lucinda Matlock, and Fiddler Jones stand out in a chorus of plain American voices. Masters's method, the graveyard chorus, reshaped American poetry and theatre for the century that followed his book in 1915. Its bite and pity still sting readers who think small towns simple.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-15: Volume fifteen is etext 3565 in Gutenberg's Napoleon series. Its head note, like its neighbours, pairs the title with 1815. Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne is the author named in that head. What follows in the sample is boilerplate alone: rights, gifts, and posting dates. No page of the secretary's memoir is preserved in the held portion. Only the facts in this note can be verified from that sample.
meyrink-der-golem-1915:
Gustav Meyrink dreams a clay giant to life in Der Golem, his famed novel of 1915, in German. In the old Jewish ward of Prague, a gem cutter takes up a strange scroll and lives the life of a man from years past. The Golem, the clay shape said to prowl the ward in times of dread, stalks his dreams and steps at last in flesh through the fog bound lanes.

The prose is dense, weird, and full of occult lore. Meyrink was a sage of such lore in his own life. The book is the chief tale of the Golem.

Public Law 114-109, the Federal Improper Payments Coordination Act of 2015, opens a federal anti-fraud tool to more users. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015. Its heading says it gives federal agencies access to and use of information in order to reduce improper payments, the payments the government makes in error or to the wrong party.

The act amends a 2012 law on the same subject. States, their contractors and agents, and the judicial and legislative branches gain access to the Do Not Pay Initiative. That system checks whether a payee is fit to be paid before money goes out. A state group gains access when the Director of the Office of Management and Budget finds the system is set up in the right way for that state. A like finding is needed for each branch.
plaw-114-11-2015:
Public Law 114-11, the Energy Efficiency Improvement Act of 2015, promotes saving energy in buildings and gear. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015. Its heading is short: to promote energy efficiency.

Title I is the Better Buildings Act of 2015. Its sections cover energy saving in federal and other buildings, separate leased spaces fitted with high-performance saving measures, and a Tenant Star program that rates tenants on energy use. Title II turns to grid-enabled water heaters, heaters that can shift their load to help the power grid. Title III covers energy information for commercial buildings, so owners and buyers can see how a building performs.
plaw-114-110-2015:
Public Law 114-110, the Surface Transportation Board Reauthorization Act of 2015, makes the rail regulator its own agency. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015. The Surface Transportation Board is the federal body that watches railroads, and the act sets it up as an independent establishment, apart from the Department of Transportation.

The contents show the sweep. Early sections cover board membership, closed-door joint talks among members, reports, funding, and a District of Columbia agent. Later sections set the steps for rate cases, when shippers fight what a railroad charges, and give the board probe power. Arbitration of set rail rate and practice disputes is covered, as are the effects of rate proposals that span many origins and destinations.
plaw-114-111-2015: Public Law 114-111, the Emergency Information Improvement Act of 2015, adds two words that open disaster aid to broadcasters. Passed by the 114th Congress, it amends the Robert T Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act. Broadcasting facilities join the list of private nonprofit facilities that can gain aid. The term critical services now reads communications, including broadcast and telecommunications, in the clause on repair aid.
plaw-114-112-2015: Public Law 114-112 stretches a pause on enforcement by one year. Passed by the 114th Congress in 2015, it extends the enforcement instruction on supervision requirements for outpatient therapeutic services in critical access hospitals and small rural hospitals through 2015. The act amends Public Law 113-198, adding and 2015 to its heading and swapping calendar years 2014 and 2015 for calendar year 2014 in its text.
plaw-114-113-2015:
Public Law 114-113, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016, is the main funding law for fiscal year 2016. The 114th Congress passed it in December 2015. Its heading names military construction, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and related agencies, but the act as a whole funds the federal government for the year ending September 30, 2016.

The front sections set shared rules on references, the explanatory statement, fund use, and corrections. The act then runs as a stack of divisions, each a funding law for its own area. Division A covers agriculture, rural growth, the Food and Drug Administration, and related agencies, with titles for farm programs, conservation, rural growth, and food programs. Division B covers commerce, justice, science, and related agencies.
plaw-114-114-2015:
Tiny plastic beads in face wash and toothpaste are banned by Public Law 114-114, the Microbead-Free Waters Act of 2015. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015, amending the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The beads wash down drains and end up in lakes and rivers, which is the harm the name points to.

The act adds a new barred act to section 301: making, or bringing into interstate commerce, a rinse-off cosmetic with plastic microbeads added on purpose. A plastic microbead is a solid plastic bit less than five millimeters wide, meant to scrub or clean the body, and rinse-off cosmetic includes toothpaste. Making must stop by July 1, 2017, and sales across state lines by July 1, 2018, with a year more for nonprescription drugs.
plaw-114-115-2015:
Public Law 114-115, the Patient Access and Medicare Protection Act, adjusts how Medicare pays for set care. The 114th Congress passed it in late 2015, amending titles XVIII and XIX of the Social Security Act. Its heading names better payments for complex rehabilitation technology and set radiation therapy services. It also names a softer hardship exception for the 2015 electronic health record reporting period.

The first operative section is a hold. Before January 1, 2017, the Secretary of Health and Human Services may not use prices from competitive bidding programs to cut Medicare pay for set wheelchair gear. The gear is wheelchair add-ons and seat and back cushions fitted to Group 3 complex power wheelchairs. The act then orders a study and report by the Comptroller General on those same add-ons and cushions.
plaw-114-12-2015:
Public Law 114-12, the Rafael Ramos and Wenjian Liu National Blue Alert Act of 2015, builds a fast alert net for threats to police. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015. Its aim is to back, strengthen, and join Blue Alert plans across the United States. Word should spread fast when an officer is badly hurt or killed on duty, goes missing on duty, or faces a real and near threat.

The act defines its terms at the start. A Blue Alert is word sent through the network about an officer's grave injury or death on duty, a missing officer, or a credible threat to do an officer grave harm. A Blue Alert plan belongs to a state, a local government, or a federal agency in the network, and it sets how that word is spread. The Attorney General runs the network, with a Blue Alert Coordinator in the Department of Justice.
plaw-114-13-2015: Public Law 114-13 clears up a start date and nothing more. Passed by the 114th Congress in 2015, it amends the Border Patrol Agent Pay Reform Act of 2014. The main pay clauses take effect on the first day of the first pay period that starts on or after January 1, 2016. Two parts may run sooner, as the Director of the Office of Personnel Management decides: rules for elections and advance duty assignments, and any regulations needed. The fix counts as if passed with the 2014 act.
plaw-114-14-2015:
Public Law 114-14, the Don't Tax Our Fallen Public Safety Heroes Act, keeps death benefits for fallen officers out of taxable income. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015, amending section 104 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. That section lists sums that do not count as gross income.

A new paragraph covers two streams of money. The first is sums paid under section 1201 of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968, the federal benefit for public safety officers killed on duty. The second is sums paid under a state program that gives money to the dependents left behind when an officer dies as the direct result of an injury borne on duty. Pay that would have come due for a death from any other cause stays outside the shield.
plaw-114-15-2015: Providence, Rhode Island gains a renamed post office under Public Law 114-15 of 2015. Its site at 820 Elmwood Avenue takes the name Sister Ann Keefe Post Office. That name is the one federal records must use for the site. Nothing else changes: the act pairs the naming with a short rule on references.
plaw-114-16-2015: For the port of entry on First Street and Pan American Avenue in Douglas, Arizona, Public Law 114-16 sets a new name: the Raul Hector Castro Port of Entry. The act is a 2015 law of the 114th Congress. The name holds in all federal maps, rules, and papers that touch the place.
plaw-114-17-2015:
Public Law 114-17, the Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act of 2015, gives Congress a say over any nuclear deal with Iran. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015. It adds a new section 135 to the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, on congressional review and oversight of agreements with Iran.

Within five days of reaching a deal on Iran's nuclear program, the President must send Congress the full deal, with all side papers and annexes. A verification report from the Secretary of State must go with it. The President must also certify two things about the deal. It states its terms, length, and the sanctions to be lifted or eased by the United States, other nations, and the United Nations. And he finds the deal meets United States goals on blocking the spread of nuclear arms.
plaw-114-18-2015:
Public Law 114-18, the WIOA Technical Amendments Act, makes fix-up changes to the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, the main federal job training law. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015. Its heading says the aim is to improve that act, and the changes are small and pointed.

One clause lets a Governor clear a rural concentrated employment program area as a local area for workforce work. Another swaps a date phrase in the rules for local workforce boards, tying it to the Workforce Investment Act of 1998 in place of the newer act. The performance system gets cross-reference fixes. The state allotment clauses gain the words less than in two spots, and matching fixes renumber the clauses they point to.
plaw-114-19-2015:
Public Law 114-19, the Construction Authorization and Choice Improvement Act, funds a new veterans hospital in Denver and tweaks the veterans Choice program. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015. It extends the grant of power to replace the Department of Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Denver, Colorado, and makes set improvements in the Veterans Access, Choice, and Accountability Act of 2014.

The Secretary of Veterans Affairs may carry out the Denver replacement in fiscal year 2015, in an amount not over 900,000,000 dollars. A hard cap bars spending that would push the total for the project past the sum set in law. A later section clears up the distance rule for care outside the VA. The 40-mile test is counted by distance traveled. A new clause speaks to veterans who face an unusual or heavy burden in travel to a VA site.
plaw-114-2-2015:
Public Law 114-2, the Clay Hunt Suicide Prevention for American Veterans Act, is called the Clay Hunt SAV Act for short. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015, the second law of that Congress. It aims at the mental health care and suicide prevention work of the Department of Veterans Affairs.

The act orders yearly reviews of those programs. Each review must use measures common in the field and name the most effective mental health and suicide prevention programs the Secretary runs. It must weigh how cost-effective each one is, and gauge how pleased patients are. The heading also names a pilot program of loan repayment for psychiatrists who agree to serve in the Veterans Health Administration.
plaw-114-20-2015: In Pennsylvania, the courthouse at 700 Grant Street in Pittsburgh takes a new name under Public Law 114-20. It becomes the Joseph F Weis Jr United States Courthouse. The 114th Congress passed the naming act in 2015. Federal laws, maps, rules, and records must use that name for the place from then on.
plaw-114-21-2015:
Public Law 114-21, the Highway and Transportation Funding Act of 2015, is a stopgap that keeps road and transit money flowing. The 114th Congress passed it in 2015. It extends the federal-aid highway, highway safety, motor carrier safety, and transit programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund.

The Secretary of Transportation must trim the sums handed out under the act. The trim equals the sums already given for fiscal year 2015 under the 2014 act of the same family, for the span from October 1, 2014 to May 31, 2015. Title I is the surface transportation program extension. Its subtitles cover federal-aid highways and their office costs, highway safety programs of the traffic safety and motor carrier safety agencies, and public transportation programs.
plaw-114-22-2015:
Public Law 114-22, the Justice for Victims of Trafficking Act of 2015, was passed by the 114th Congress. The act deals with human trafficking. Its stated aim is to give justice to the victims of trafficking.

The table of contents shows a broad plan. One part sets up a fund for victims in the United States. Other parts add grants to deter child trafficking, raise pay and court awards for victims, ease probes, boost reports, and cut demand for sex trafficking. Later parts cover task forces, child predators, victims' rights, and missing children.
plaw-114-23-2015:
Public Law 114-23, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress, is called the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015. Its full title is the Uniting and Strengthening America by Fulfilling Rights and Ensuring Effective Discipline Over Monitoring Act of 2015. The act reforms how the government seeks business records, wiretaps, and pen register data for spying, terror, and crime work.

The first title shown reforms business records under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act. It adds new rules for call detail records and for urgent cases. It bars bulk collection of tangible things, and adds court review, shield from suit for those who help, and pay for that help. Later parts cover pen registers and reports by watchdogs.
plaw-114-24-2015:
Girls Count Act of 2015 is the short title of Public Law 114-24, passed in 2015. The 114th Congress lets the Secretary of State and the head of the United States aid agency give help to back the rights of women and girls in poor nations. Birth records are the core concern in the findings shown.

Congress finds that close to 900 million people in the world are girls or young women aged 10 through 24. It finds that four in ten babies born in 2012 were not logged at birth. It also finds that about 230 million children under age five lack a birth record. Without proof of birth, the text says, girls face more risk of trafficking, child marriage, and loss of health care and schooling.
plaw-114-25-2015:
In 2015, Public Law 114-25 was passed by the 114th Congress. It Funds the swap of an old health site in Colorado. The site is the medical center of the Department of Veterans Affairs in Denver. The act stretches the time to build its replacement and lets the agency move funds to pay for the work.

One clause raises the project cap. It strikes the old cap figure in the prior law and puts in a higher cap figure. A second clause gives a one-time right to move set sums from named agency accounts into the main build account. The sample lists sums from health, support, sites, cemetery, and general accounts before the list is cut off.
plaw-114-26-2015: Passed in 2015, Public Law 114-26 is the Defending Public Safety Employees' Retirement Act. The act changes the tax code on early draws from retirement plans. It lets named federal staff take funds from a government plan with no penalty after age 50. The groups named are federal law officers, customs and border officers, federal firefighters, and air traffic controllers. The act also extends the rule to savings-style plans and guards set yearly payment plans from being treated as changed by such a draw.
plaw-114-27-2015:
Trade Preferences Extension Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-27, passed by the 114th Congress. The act extends three trade break programs. They are the African Growth and Opportunity Act, the Generalized System of Preferences, and the duty break program for Haiti.

The contents show the first two titles. Title I extends the Africa program. It also tweaks origin rules for duty-free goods from poor African lands, adds checks on who still counts for the breaks, and backs a larger role for women in African growth. It calls for two-year plans on use of the program and for deeper trade and farm aid ties. Title II then extends the broad trade break system.
plaw-114-28-2015: Passed in 2015, Public Law 114-28 ends a charter for an Indian tribe in Oklahoma. At the plea of the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma, the act takes back the tribe's charter of incorporation. That charter was given to the tribe and backed by its members on June 1, 1940, under the Oklahoma Welfare Act of 1936. The act states that the tribe's plea to give up the charter is taken, and the charter is revoked.
plaw-114-29-2015: Public Law 114-29 of 2015 bears two names: the Department of Homeland Security Interoperable Communications Act and the DHS Interoperable Communications Act. The phrase in the title means gear that lets separate units talk to each other. The act makes one senior manager own that goal. The Under Secretary for Management must act so the parts of the department gain and keep such shared talk systems, through clear rules and orders for all units.
plaw-114-3-2015: The 114th Congress passed Public Law 114-3 in 2015, and it holds a single section headed Further Continuing Appropriations. The enacted text does not match the health topic in the catalog title; the text itself is the guide. The act amends the Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2015. It strikes the date named in section 106(3) of that resolution and puts in March 6, 2015. The change keeps stopgap federal funds in place to that new date.
plaw-114-30-2015:
Boys Town Centennial Commemorative Coin Act is Public Law 114-30, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act tells the Secretary of the Treasury to mint coins for the 100th year of Boys Town. Boys Town is a charity group that saves children and heals families, based in Boys Town, Nebraska.

Findings trace the group to Father Edward Flanagan, who set up his home for boys on December 12, 1917. The home served children of all races and faiths. A 1938 film spread word of the work around the world. Findings say the group now works in 11 regions, runs a phone line that counsels more than 150,000 callers a year, and touches more than two million children and families each year.
plaw-114-31-2015:
Veterans Identification Card Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-31, passed by the 114th Congress. The act amends title 38 law. It tells the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to issue a veteran card, on request, to named veterans who ask for one.

Findings explain the gap the card fills. Before the act, cards went only to veterans who had met the set time for retirement or who left service for health reasons. A veteran who served the least required time, but met neither test, had no proof of veteran status save the DD-214 discharge papers. Findings call it hard to carry those papers at all times, though shops and groups often ask for proof of service to give goods, services, or deals.
plaw-114-32-2015: Cedar Hill, Missouri, holds the postal site named by Public Law 114-32, passed in 2015. The site is at 7050 Highway BB in Cedar Hill. The 114th Congress called it the Sergeant First Class William B. Woods, Jr. Post Office. A reference to the Highway BB site in a law, map, rule, or other record of the United States is a reference to the Woods post office.
plaw-114-33-2015: Public Law 114-33, passed in 2015, names a postal building in Floresville, Texas. The building stands at 141 Paloma Drive in Floresville. The 114th Congress designated it the Floresville Veterans Post Office Building. The name honors veterans as a group. Mentions of the Paloma Drive site in federal laws, maps, or records are mentions of the Floresville Veterans Post Office Building.
plaw-114-34-2015: Mulberry, Florida, holds the postal site named by Public Law 114-34, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The site is at 2000 Mulford Road in Mulberry. Congress called it the Sergeant First Class Daniel M. Ferguson Post Office. If a law, map, rule, or other United States record cites the Mulford Road site, it cites the Ferguson post office.
plaw-114-35-2015: Public Law 114-35, passed in 2015, assigns a name to a postal building in Bronx, New York. The building is at 442 East 167th Street in the Bronx. Under the act of the 114th Congress, it is the Herman Badillo Post Office Building. Federal records that speak of the East 167th Street site speak of the Badillo building.
plaw-114-36-2015: Public Law 114-36 of 2015 amends the United States Cotton Futures Act. A futures contract is a deal to buy or sell a good at a set price on a set date. The act leaves some cotton futures deals out of the act's reach. A deal that lets a seller hand over cotton grown outside the United States is left out, to the extent that such cotton is in fact handed over under the deal. The change covers deals made on or after the act.
plaw-114-37-2015: Chisholm, Minnesota, holds the postal building named by Public Law 114-37, passed in 2015. Find it at 14 3rd Avenue, NW, in Chisholm. The 114th Congress designated it the James L. Oberstar Memorial Post Office Building. A reference to that site in a law, map, rule, or other record of the United States is a reference to the Oberstar building.
plaw-114-38-2015: Veterans Entrepreneurship Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-38, passed by the 114th Congress. The act amends the Small Business Act to widen access to funds for veteran founders, and to help create jobs. Its first part shown makes a fee break last. The agency head may not charge a guarantee fee on an Express loan to a veteran or a veteran's spouse, for loans on or after October 1, 2015. The break pauses for a year if the President's budget shows a cost above zero for the program.
plaw-114-39-2015: Public Law 114-39 of 2015 bears a long name: the Medicare Independence at Home Medical Practice Demonstration Improvement Act of 2015. The whole act makes one change. In the Social Security Act, it strikes the words 3-year and puts in 5-year. The change sets how long a deal may run under a Medicare test program. That program tests care given at home by a medical practice.
plaw-114-4-2015:
Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2015 is Public Law 114-4, passed by the 114th Congress. The act grants funds to the Department of Homeland Security for the fiscal year that ends September 30, 2015. Funds come from cash in the Treasury not set aside for other ends.

Title I covers department lead and work. It grants a named sum for the Office of the Secretary and top managers, with a small cap on costs for formal events. It also orders a full plan, due in 30 days, for the fingerprint entry and exit data system set by a 2004 law. The plan, sent to named groups in Congress, must give the guessed costs to build the system.
plaw-114-40-2015:
Steve Gleason Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-40, passed by the 114th Congress. The act amends title XVIII of the Social Security Act, the Medicare title. It widens what Medicare pays for when a person needs a device that speaks for them.

One part adds eye tracking and gaze tools for speech devices to the paid list. A person must show a medical need for them, and the part covers devices given on or after January 1, 2016. A second part lifts the rental cap on long-use medical gear for speech devices. That lift covers devices given from October 1, 2015, to before October 1, 2018, where the sample ends.
plaw-114-41-2015:
Surface Transportation and Veterans Health Care Choice Improvement Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-41. Passed by the 114th Congress, the act extends road, safety, transit, and like programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund. It also gives the Department of Veterans Affairs more freedom to move health funds.

The act first settles the books. The Secretary of Transportation must cut sums under the act by sums already given for the span from October 1, 2014, to July 31, 2015, under two prior road laws. Title I then extends the road programs. Its parts extend federal-aid highways, highway safety work, and truck safety work, as the contents list shows.
plaw-114-42-2015:
Notice of Observation Treatment and Implication for Care Eligibility Act, or NOTICE Act, is Public Law 114-42. Passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress, the act amends title XVIII of the Social Security Act. It deals with patients a hospital keeps under observation status rather than taking in as inpatients.

The act orders hospitals to tell such patients their status. Starting 12 months after the act, a hospital or critical access hospital must give notice to a person who gets observation care as an outpatient for more than 24 hours. Notice is due no later than 36 hours after care starts, or at release if that comes first. It pairs a spoken account with a written notice set by the Secretary.
plaw-114-43-2015: DHS IT Duplication Reduction Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-43, passed by the 114th Congress. IT means data tech systems. Within 90 days, the Chief Information Officer of the Department of Homeland Security must send a report to two named groups in Congress. The report must count the department's tech systems, judge how many copy or split each other's work, and give a plan to cut such copies, with guessed savings. It must also state how to pick which system to end. No new funds are granted.
plaw-114-44-2015: Need-Based Educational Aid Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-44, passed by the 114th Congress. The act renews rules on how antitrust laws apply to need-based aid for students. Antitrust laws bar firms from fixing terms together; schools had a named break for joint aid work. The act strikes one paragraph of the old break and trims two more. It also moves the end year in the old text from 2015 to 2022, so the break runs seven more years.
plaw-114-45-2015:
Drinking Water Protection Act is Public Law 114-45, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act amends the Safe Drinking Water Act. It deals with algal toxins, poisons from algae, in drinking water from public water systems.

Within 90 days, the agency head must build and send Congress a full plan to judge and handle the risk. The plan must state steps and dates to weigh the harm to human health from such water. It must set, print, and update a full list of algal toxins that may harm health at likely levels in water. It must also sum up the known harms of each toxin on the list, and what makes the toxin-making blooms grow and give off toxins.
plaw-114-46-2015:
Sawtooth National Recreation Area and Jerry Peak Wilderness Additions Act is Public Law 114-46, passed in 2015. The 114th Congress used the act to set up named wild areas in central Idaho. It also grants land swaps that involve Forest Service land and Bureau of Land Management land in that part of the state.

The contents list two titles. Title I adds land to the National Wilderness Preservation System in Idaho. Its parts cover how the land is run, water rights, army flights over the land, care of land next to it, Native American cultural and faith uses, and buys of land. Title II grants land for public ends in Blaine County, Custer County, and the towns of Challis, Clayton, and Stanley.
plaw-114-47-2015:
Land Management Workforce Flexibility Act is Public Law 114-47, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act amends title 5 law to open a path for short-term seasonal staff. Such staff in federal land agencies may vie for open lasting posts through inside merit rounds.

The act names six land agencies. They are the Forest Service, the Bureau of Land Management, the National Park Service, the Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, and the Bureau of Reclamation. It then adds a new chapter on staff freedom for those agencies. The chapter sets terms and covers time-limited posts in the competitive service, where the sample ends.
plaw-114-48-2015: Passed in 2015, Public Law 114-48 names a federal site in Charleston, South Carolina. The site, at 83 Meeting Street in Charleston, serves as a federal building and United States courthouse. The designation clause calls it the J. Waties Waring Judicial Center. Any mention of that site in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of it under that name. The section heading in the text uses a longer form of the name.
plaw-114-49-2015: In 2015, the 114th Congress passed Public Law 114-49, which names a stretch of highway in Texas. The stretch is Interstate Route 10 from milepost 535 to milepost 545 at Kendall County, Texas. Under the act, that stretch is known as the PFC Milton A. Lee Medal of Honor Memorial Highway. Any mention of that stretch in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of it under that name.
plaw-114-5-2015:
The 114th Congress passed Public Law 114-5 in 2015, and it awards a Congressional Gold Medal as a group. The medal goes to the Foot Soldiers who took part in Bloody Sunday, Turnaround Tuesday, or the last Selma to Montgomery Voting Rights March in March of 1965. Those marches helped bring about the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

Findings mark the date. March 7, 2015, is 50 years since the Foot Soldiers first tried to march from Selma to Montgomery on Bloody Sunday. They marched to protest the denial of their vote, and were hit with force by Alabama state troopers. Findings say more than 500 marchers, led by John Lewis and Rev. Hosea Williams, met a wall of troopers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge and were beaten as they crossed.
plaw-114-50-2015:
Gerardo Hernandez Airport Security Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-50, passed by the 114th Congress. The act aims to improve joint planning and talk between levels of government when a safety event hits a home airport. Such events are the core of the act.

The Assistant Secretary for Transportation Security must reach out to all airports where the agency runs or watches safety checks. That officer must give tech help as needed, and check that each airport has its own working plan to meet safety events inside the airport grounds. Events named are active shooters, acts of terror, and events aimed at the screening points for guests. Plans may cover how to move people out and care for them, with thought for people with disabilities, and how to set one joint command.
plaw-114-51-2015:
E-Warranty Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-51, passed by the 114th Congress. The act lets makers of consumer goods meet warranty and label rules in a new way. They may post the terms of a warranty on a web site rather than only on paper.

Findings say many makers and buyers favor the choice to give or get warranty facts online. They say the rules must be brought up to date so the United States can keep pace in world trade in goods linked to the web. They also say a web choice widens buyer access to facts, cuts paper use, and gives makers more freedom. The act then lets warranty terms be shown in a clear digital form on the maker's site. A note on the goods, pack, or book tells buyers where to read them.
plaw-114-52-2015: National Windstorm Impact Reduction Act Reauthorization of 2015 is Public Law 114-52, passed by the 114th Congress. The act renews the National Windstorm Impact Reduction Program, a program to cut harm from strong wind storms. It first fixes three terms in the 2004 act. The program head is now the standards institute chief, not the science policy chief. A new term, lifelines, covers public works and key systems such as roads, power, and water. The word northeaster is added to the list of storm kinds in the windstorm term.
plaw-114-53-2015:
TSA Office of Inspection Accountability Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-53, passed by the 114th Congress. TSA is the Transportation Security Administration. The act makes the agency match federal law and rules on who counts as a criminal investigator, a post that draws extra pay.

Findings state the test. To earn that extra pay, officers must in general spend at least half their time probing, catching, or holding people thought to have broken United States crime laws. The homeland watchdog found the agency did not check that its Office of Inspection sleuths met that test. Findings say those staff mainly watch probes by other agencies, probe staff misconduct claims, and run checks and secret tests, work the watchdog says cheaper staff could do. The sample ends mid-finding, as it turns to the cost to taxpayers.
plaw-114-54-2015:
Agriculture Reauthorizations Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-54, passed by the 114th Congress. The act amends the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946. It extends the rules that force reports of livestock prices, and renews two other farm and land programs.

The contents list three titles. Title I extends livestock price reports, with parts on swine reports, lamb reports, and a study of the report system. Title II renews the National Forest Foundation Act. Title III renews the United States Grain Standards Act, with reports on breaks in federal checks of grain sent abroad and on policy blocks for grain growers. One clause shown moves the livestock report end date from September 30, 2015, to September 30, 2020.
plaw-114-55-2015:
Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-55, passed by the 114th Congress. The act amends title 49 law to extend the airport improvement program. It also amends the tax code to extend the funding and spending power of the Airport and Airway Trust Fund.

The contents list two titles. Title I extends airport and airway programs. Its parts extend expiring powers, agency work, air travel sites and gear, and study and build work. It also covers funds for flight programs and the essential air service, which keeps flights to small towns. Title II holds the money parts: spending power from the trust fund, and an extension of the taxes that fill that fund.
plaw-114-56-2015: In 2015, Public Law 114-56 was passed by the 114th Congress. It Gives land to a health group in Alaska. Within 180 days, the health chief must hand all United States right and title in the named land to the Yukon Kuskokwim Health Corporation in Bethel, Alaska. The land, 22.98 acres in a named survey lot, is for use with health and social service programs. The gift is made by warranty deed, with no price, no duties laid on the group, and no United States right to take the land back.
plaw-114-57-2015:
New Mexico Navajo Water Settlement Technical Corrections Act is Public Law 114-57, passed in 2015. The 114th Congress made small fixes to the Navajo water rights settlement in New Mexico, set in a 2009 land law. One fix corrects a name, striking Arrellano and putting in Arellano, with one letter changed in the text. A second fix changes a number in a term from 75-185 to 75-184.

Other fixes make a cited article plural in two places, and add the word Project before water in a contract part. They widen funds to cover planning and design, and swap two percent caps, one from two to four and one from four to two.
plaw-114-58-2015:
Department of Veterans Affairs Expiring Authorities Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-58, passed by the 114th Congress. The act amends title 38 law to extend some parts of law set to end. Those parts are run by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs.

Title I extends health care powers. The list shown covers fees for hospital and nursing home care, nursing home care for some veterans with harm from service, and funds for help to caregivers. It also covers cost claims from third parties for care of veterans with health plans, a child care help pilot, and grants to move rural veterans. Two joint funds with the defense agency are extended as well, plus a retreat program for women veterans new to civilian life.
plaw-114-59-2015:
STEM Education Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-59, passed by the 114th Congress. STEM stands for science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. The act defines STEM education to include computer science, and backs STEM programs at the National Science Foundation.

The definition holds for six named agencies, among them the energy, space, oceans, standards, and environment agencies. A next part keeps a grant program for learning outside school. The science agency head must keep giving grants, won by contest and judged on merit, for study and growth of new out-of-school STEM learning and new STEM learning sites. The grants also back study that moves the field of casual STEM learning ahead.
plaw-114-6-2015: Office of Compliance Administrative and Technical Corrections Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-6, passed by the 114th Congress. The act makes office and wording fixes to the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995, the law on work rights for Congress staff. One fix changes how mediators are picked for disputes. They must now come from a master list kept by the Executive Director, drawn from people skilled in such cases, such as state bar members and retired judges. Names may be put forth by two named federal bodies.
plaw-114-60-2015: Protecting Affordable Coverage for Employees Act is Public Law 114-60, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act revises what small employer means in health law. In both the Affordable Care Act and the Public Health Service Act, it cuts the top size from 100 staff to 50 staff. It does so by changing the numbers 101 to 51 and 100 to 50. A state may still choose the wider mark, and count a firm with an average of 1 to 100 staff as a small employer.
plaw-114-61-2015: Public Law 114-61 of 2015 cuts a planned rise in the minimum wage for American Samoa. The act amends the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2007. The wage for each trade and class stays at the rate in force on September 29, 2015. It then rises by a set small sum per hour on September 30, 2015, and on September 30 of every third year, till it meets the main federal wage. The act also moves dates for wage reports by the Government Accountability Office.
plaw-114-62-2015: Gold Star Fathers Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-62, passed by the 114th Congress. The act amends title 5 law on hiring preference in the civil service. Mothers of some dead or fully disabled veterans held that status before. The new text speaks of a parent, so fathers are treated the same as mothers. The status holds if the parent's spouse is fully disabled, or if the parent is single or lawfully apart from a spouse at claim time. The change starts 90 days after the act.
plaw-114-63-2015: Ensuring Access to Clinical Trials Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-63, passed by the 114th Congress. A clinical trial tests a new treatment on people. The act strikes one subsection from the Improving Access to Clinical Trials Act of 2009. That struck part held an end date. With it gone, a break in the Supplemental Security Income program and the Medicaid program lasts for good. The break lets pay given to people who join trials for rare diseases or conditions not count against their benefits.
plaw-114-64-2015: Passed in 2015, Public Law 114-64 names a courthouse in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. The building stands at 200 NW 4th Street in Oklahoma City. Under the act, it is known as the William J. Holloway, Jr. United States Courthouse. Any mention of that courthouse in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of it under that name.
plaw-114-65-2015:
Federal Vehicle Repair Cost Savings Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-65, passed by the 114th Congress. The act aims to cut the cost to run and fix the federal fleet of cars and trucks. It does so by backing the use of rebuilt parts in place of new parts.

Findings cite a 2013 report. The civilian federal fleet holds about 588,000 vehicles, and agencies spent about 975 million dollars to fix and keep that fleet in 2011. Rebuilt parts, such as engines, starters, and steering racks, tend to cost less than new parts of like kind. The act defines a rebuilt part as one brought back to as-new or better state by a set factory process, with a full warranty. A duty to use such parts follows, where the sample ends.
plaw-114-66-2015: Waldwick, New Jersey, holds the postal building named by Public Law 114-66, passed in 2015. The building is at 1 Walter Hammond Place in Waldwick. The 114th Congress designated it the Staff Sergeant Joseph D'Augustine Post Office Building. Federal records that cite the Walter Hammond Place site cite the D'Augustine building. The act makes no other change to the site.
plaw-114-67-2015: Public Law 114-67, passed in 2015, names a federal building in Helena, Arkansas. The building stands at 617 Walnut Street in Helena. It houses a post office and a court as well. Under the act of the 114th Congress, its name is the Jacob Trieber Federal Building, United States Post Office, and United States Court House, with Court House as two words. A law, map, or record that names the Walnut Street building names the Trieber building.
plaw-114-68-2015:
Border Jobs for Veterans Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-68, passed by the 114th Congress. The act seeks to draw troops who are leaving military service into jobs as Customs and Border Protection officers. Those officers screen guests, returning citizens, and cargo at ports of entry.

Findings say ports must be staffed in time, and cite a funded goal of 23,775 officers for fiscal year 2015. Each year, about 250,000 to 300,000 troops leave service. The act tells the Secretary of Homeland Security to weigh fast hiring of fit leavers who can do the core work and who count for a veterans hiring path. It also boosts current hiring drives aimed at such leavers.
plaw-114-69-2015:
Albuquerque Indian School Land Transfer Act is Public Law 114-69, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act tells the Secretary of the Interior to take four parcels of federal land into trust. The land is for the gain of named Indian Pueblos in New Mexico.

The act defines its terms first. The 19 Pueblos are 19 named New Mexico Pueblos, among them Acoma, Cochiti, Isleta, Jemez, Laguna, Taos, and Zuni. A map from August 12, 2011, with a long survey title, marks the land in Bernalillo County. The Secretary in the act means the Secretary of the Interior, where the sample ends.
plaw-114-7-2015: Slain Officer Family Support Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-7, passed by the 114th Congress. The act speeds tax gains for cash gifts that aid the families of two slain New York detectives, Wenjian Liu and Rafael Ramos. A gift made from January 1 to April 15, 2015, may be treated as if made on December 31, 2014. A phone bill showing the charity name, date, and sum counts as proof. A gift does not lose its status just because it aids those families alone.
plaw-114-70-2015: Adoptive Family Relief Act is Public Law 114-70, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act amends the Immigration and Nationality Act to give relief on visa fees to adoptive families in some cases. The sample shows the validity rules first. An immigrant visa lasts as set by rule, up to six months. A visa for a child adopted by a citizen who serves or works abroad lasts till that parent comes home, up to three years. The sample ends inside the next rule, on visas for guests.
plaw-114-71-2015: United States Commission on International Religious Freedom Reauthorization Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-71. Passed by the 114th Congress, the act renews the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom. Congress states that the group was made to judge, on its own, threats to freedom of faith around the world, and to tell of them in plain terms. The act strikes the end date of September 30, 2015, in the 1998 law and puts in September 30, 2019. It then calls for a plan of work from the group.
plaw-114-72-2015:
Quarterly Financial Report Reauthorization Act is Public Law 114-72, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act extends the power of the Secretary of Commerce to run the quarterly financial report program. It strikes the year 2015 in a 1983 law and puts in 2030, a 15-year stretch.

A second part turns to data safety at the Bureau of the Census. The Secretary must review how the bureau guards its data, with steps taken since the 2015 breaches of the personnel office systems were made known. A report is due in 90 days to two named groups in Congress. It must name all bureau systems that hold private facts, and tell what steps were taken to guard those facts.
plaw-114-73-2015:
Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-73, passed by the 114th Congress. Like its sister act of the same year, it extends road, safety, truck, transit, and like programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund. The two acts cover back-to-back spans of time.

The act first settles the books for fiscal year 2016. The Secretary of Transportation must cut sums under the act by sums already given under the prior act for October 1 to October 29, 2015. Title I then extends the programs. Its parts extend federal-aid highways and highway safety programs run by the road safety and truck safety agencies, as the contents list shows.
plaw-114-74-2015:
Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-74, passed by the 114th Congress. The opening line of the sample speaks of a tax appeal right for some groups, which does not match the budget contents that follow. The contents list is the guide to what the act holds.

Title I enforces the budget, with changes to the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985 and a path for a 2017 budget vote in the Senate. Title II covers farm policy through a standard crop cover deal. Title III covers trade through gains in debt claims. Title IV covers the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, with test sales, a note rule, and a fix to a term. It also covers work to ready the reserve, and a new fund for energy safety and build work.
plaw-114-75-2015: Wounded Warriors Federal Leave Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-75, passed by the 114th Congress. The act gives leave to a new federal worker who is a veteran with a harm from service rated at 30 percent or more. In the first 12 months, that worker may take paid leave to get care for that harm. The leave is capped at 104 hours, and unused leave is lost. The worker must give a signed note that the leave was used for that care.
plaw-114-76-2015: Chesterfield, Missouri, holds the postal site named by Public Law 114-76, passed in 2015. The site is at 16105 Swingley Ridge Road in Chesterfield. The 114th Congress called it the Sgt. Zachary M. Fisher Post Office. A reference to the Swingley Ridge Road site in a law, map, or other United States record is a reference to the Fisher post office.
plaw-114-77-2015: Public Law 114-77, passed in 2015, names a postal site in St. Louis, Missouri. The site stands at 55 Grasso Plaza in St. Louis. Under the act of the 114th Congress, it is the Sgt. Amanda N. Pinson Post Office. When a federal law, map, rule, or file speaks of the Grasso Plaza site, it speaks of the Pinson post office.
plaw-114-78-2015: St. Louis gains a second named postal site in this set, under Public Law 114-78, passed in 2015. That site is at 11662 Gravois Road in St. Louis, Missouri. Congress designated it the Lt. Daniel P. Riordan Post Office. References to the Gravois Road site in laws, maps, rules, or other records of the United States are deemed references to the Riordan post office.
plaw-114-79-2015: In 2015, the 114th Congress passed Public Law 114-79, which names a postal building in Springboro, Ohio. The building is at 55 South Pioneer Boulevard in Springboro. Its name under the act is the Richard Dick Chenault Post Office Building, with Dick in quotes in the text. A law, map, or record that cites the Pioneer Boulevard site cites the Chenault building.
plaw-114-8-2015: Public Law 114-8, passed in 2015, assigns a name to a federal building in Miramar, Florida. The building stands at 2030 Southwest 145th Avenue in Miramar. The 114th Congress designated it the Benjamin P. Grogan and Jerry L. Dove Federal Building, a name that joins two men. Any mention of that building in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of it under that joint name.
plaw-114-80-2015:
DHS Social Media Improvement Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-80, passed by the 114th Congress. The act amends the Homeland Security Act of 2002. It lets the Department of Homeland Security set up a social media working group inside the department.

The group has a clear charge. It must find, and share with the readiness and response world, guides and best practice on the use of social media tools. The tools are for use before, during, and after a natural disaster, an act of terror, or a like man-made disaster. The charge also covers better spread of facts between the department and its partners, and better use of the tools to aid readiness, response, and repair. Members come from across federal, state, local, tribal, and charity work.
plaw-114-81-2015:
Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated Fishing Enforcement Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-81, passed by the 114th Congress. The act strengthens the tools used to stop fishing that is illegal, not reported, or not controlled by rules. It also amends the Tuna Conventions Act of 1950 to put the Antigua Convention in force.

Title I amends a long list of older fishery laws. The list shown covers high seas driftnet laws, North Pacific salmon laws, Pacific salmon treaty law, and Antarctic sea life law. It also covers Atlantic tuna law, dolphin label law, halibut law, and the main Magnuson-Stevens fishery law. Title II then puts the Antigua Convention into United States law, where the sample ends.
plaw-114-82-2015: Kingston, New York, holds the postal building named by Public Law 114-82, passed in 2015. The building is at 90 Cornell Street in Kingston. The 114th Congress designated it the Staff Sergeant Robert H. Dietz Post Office Building. A citation of the Cornell Street site in a law, map, or other United States record is a citation of the Dietz building.
plaw-114-83-2015: Public Law 114-83, passed in 2015, names a postal building in East Rochester, New York. The building stands at 206 West Commercial Street in East Rochester. Under the act of the 114th Congress, it is the Officer Daryl R. Pierson Memorial Post Office Building. Federal records that speak of the West Commercial Street site speak of the Pierson building.
plaw-114-84-2015: Del City, Oklahoma, is the home of the postal building named by Public Law 114-84, passed in 2015. Find it at 4500 SE 28th Street, Del City. Congress called it the James Robert Kalsu Post Office Building. The catalog title gives the name without quotes, as the text does. Laws, maps, or records that mention the SE 28th Street site mention the Kalsu building.
plaw-114-85-2015: The 114th Congress passed Public Law 114-85 in 2015, and it makes one citation change to title XI of the Social Security Act. PACE programs give all-inclusive care for the elderly. The act clears up waiver power for such programs. It strikes one cited clause in section 1115A and puts in a wider set of cites, adding section 1934 with two named parts left out. That single swap is the whole act.
plaw-114-86-2015: Librarian of Congress Succession Modernization Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-86, passed by the 114th Congress. The act sets a 10-year term for the Librarian of Congress, the head of the national library. The President picks the Librarian, with the advice and consent of the Senate. A Librarian may be picked again for a new term in the same way. The term rule covers picks made on or after the act. A like phrase is struck from an 1897 funds law to match.
plaw-114-87-2015:
Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2015, Part II is Public Law 114-87, passed by the 114th Congress. It is the third road extension act in this set for the same span. It extends road, safety, truck, transit, and like programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund.

The books are settled for fiscal year 2016 first. Sums under the act are cut by sums already given under the prior extension act for October 1 to November 20, 2015. Title I then extends the programs. Parts shown extend federal-aid highways and agency costs, highway safety and truck safety programs, and formula grants for rural transit, a part the prior acts did not list in the sample.
plaw-114-88-2015:
Recovery Improvements for Small Entities After Disaster Act of 2015, or RISE After Disaster Act of 2015, is Public Law 114-88. Passed by the 114th Congress, the act aims to improve the disaster aid programs of the Small Business Administration.

The contents list two divisions. Division A covers Superstorm Sandy relief and disaster loan gains. Its title on disaster aid lists a revised disaster deadline, and use of damage loans to build safe rooms. It also lists less delay in loan closing and payout, guards for taxpayer funds, and clearer loan grants. Division B covers gains for small parties after disaster, starting with more awards to small business growth centers, where the sample ends.
plaw-114-89-2015: Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act is Public Law 114-89, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act amends the Controlled Substances Act on drug timing advice and on sign-up for makers who run trials. For a new drug the health chief plans to judge and urge controls on, grant of the drug request does not take effect till a first controlling rule is issued. The grant date is the later of the grant date or the rule date.
plaw-114-9-2015: In 2015, Public Law 114-9 was passed by the 114th Congress. It Is a joint resolution, not a bill. It fills a seat on the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. The seat, in the class other than Members of Congress, fell open when the term of David M. Rubenstein of Maryland ran out on May 7, 2015. The resolution puts Rubenstein back in the seat for a term of 6 years. The term starts on May 8, 2015, or on the date of the resolution, whichever is later.
plaw-114-90-2015:
U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act is Public Law 114-90, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act aims to aid growth in the young commercial space trade. It backs private funds and seeks more stable, clear rules for firms in that trade.

Title I bears a second name on spurring private space work and firm starts. Its parts shown cover world launch contests, pay cover for space flight guests, and more freedom in launch permits. Other parts cover permit reports, federal court power, cross waivers, space powers, and traffic control in orbit. Later parts cover space watch data, shared safety norms, government space flyers, and the running and use of the space station. Title II, on remote sensing from space, begins where the sample ends.
plaw-114-91-2015:
Protecting Our Infants Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-91, passed by the 114th Congress. The act deals with harms tied to opioid use before birth. Opioids are strong pain drugs that can hook a user. Babies born to users may face a withdrawal illness named in the act.

The health chief must review how the health agency plans and joins its work on such use. The chief must then build a plan to close gaps in study and in federal programs, and to cut overlap and copies of work. Study gaps named are the best care for pregnant women with opioid disorders, the best care for infants with the withdrawal illness, and the long-term effects on children. A report is due one year after the act, where the sample ends.
plaw-114-92-2015:
National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2016 is Public Law 114-92, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act grants funds for fiscal year 2016 for armed work of the Department of Defense. It also grants funds for army building and for defense work of the Department of Energy, and sets troop strength for the year.

The act is split into four divisions. Division A grants Department of Defense powers. Division B grants army building powers. Division C grants Department of Energy national safety powers and other powers. Division D holds the funding tables. Unlike the 2017 act in this set, the 2016 act has no fifth division in the list shown.
plaw-114-93-2015: Equity in Government Compensation Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-93, passed by the 114th Congress. The act halts the pay packages for the chiefs of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the two mortgage bodies the act calls enterprises. The housing finance chief must set each chief's pay and gains at the level in force on January 1, 2015, and that level may not be raised after. The halt holds only while a body is in conservatorship or receivership, the two forms of federal control named in the act.
plaw-114-94-2015:
Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act, or FAST Act, is Public Law 114-94, passed in 2015. The 114th Congress granted funds for federal-aid highways, highway safety programs, and transit programs in this long-term road law. It is the full act that the short extension acts in this set had kept alive.

Division A covers surface travel. Title I covers federal-aid highways. Its parts shown set grant sums and a spending cap, sort out shares for states, and back large freight and highway projects of national weight. Other parts cover the national highway results program, aid for federal roads hit by disasters, rail and road crossings, a block grant program for surface travel, and joint bridge projects.
plaw-114-95-2015:
Every Student Succeeds Act is Public Law 114-95, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act renews the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965. Its stated aim is to make sure that every child achieves.

Title I covers basic programs run by state and local school agencies. Its parts shown set the aim and grant sums, and cover school gains, direct services for students, and state and local plans. Other parts cover which school zones count, schoolwide programs, schools that get aimed aid, and parent and family roles. The title also covers children in private schools, a rule that funds add to and do not swap out other funds, and grants for outlying areas.
plaw-114-96-2015: Further Continuing Appropriations Act, 2016 is Public Law 114-96, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act holds a single change. It amends the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2016, which sits inside Public Law 114-53. It strikes the date named in section 106(3) of that act and puts in December 16, 2015. The change keeps stopgap federal funds in place to that new date.
plaw-114-97-2015: Improving Access to Emergency Psychiatric Care Act is Public Law 114-97, passed in 2015 by the 114th Congress. The act extends and widens a Medicaid test project on urgent mental health care. The project runs for 3 straight years. A state picked on or before March 13, 2012, may ask to stay in the project through September 30, 2016. Two tests guard that stay: the Secretary must project no rise in net program spending, and the chief actuary for Medicare and Medicaid must back that view in writing.
plaw-114-98-2015:
Grassroots Rural and Small Community Water Systems Assistance Act is Public Law 114-98, passed in 2015. The 114th Congress amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to renew tech help for small public water systems. Such help aids small and rural towns as they meet federal water rules.

Findings state why small systems need the help. More than 90 percent of town water systems serve fewer than 10,000 people. Small and rural towns have the most trouble giving safe, low-cost water and waste services, due to small scale and a lack of skilled staff. Findings say tech help and training keep federal rules from swamping small town funds. They also say such help is the main source of urgent aid in small and rural towns.
plaw-114-99-2015: Breast Cancer Research Stamp Reauthorization Act of 2015 is Public Law 114-99, passed by the 114th Congress. A semipostal is a stamp sold above its mail price to raise funds for a cause. The act extends the Postal Service power to issue such a stamp for breast cancer research. It strikes the year 2015 in title 39 law and puts in 2019. It also adds a clear rule: an agency that gets funds from the stamp sales must use those funds for breast cancer research.
plos-pbio-0020015:
Jun R. Huh, Stephanie Y. Vernooy, Hong Yu, and co-workers studied sperm formation in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. Caspases are enzymes best known for driving cell death. Yet in fly testes, they help shape sperm in a process that splits a shared mass into single sperm cells.

The surprise is that death enzymes do careful building work here without killing the cell. The team found that more than one caspase chain is needed for sperm to separate properly. That means the system has backup and fine control, not a single switch. The study broadens what caspases are for. It hints that other tissues may also borrow death tools for safe, local tasks.
plos-pone-0000015:
Masato Nagaoka and co-authors published a cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. The paper asks how embryonic stem cells can be grown without forming tight colonies. The team coated culture plates with a fusion protein made from E-cadherin, a molecule that helps cells stick to each other.

Mouse stem cells on the coated plates did not touch each other or form colonies. They still kept all stem cell features, including the power to form all three germ layers after long culture. The cells also grew faster, needed less of a growth factor called LIF, and took up new DNA more readily.
plos-pone-0000115:
Ashraf Yusuf Rangrez, Kannayakanahalli Maheshwarappa Dayananda, Santosh Atanur, and colleagues report this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2006. They searched the bacterium Aeromonas culicicola for a type four secretion system. This is a molecular machine bacteria use during conjugation, the process of passing DNA to a neighbor cell.

Finding such machinery matters because conjugation spreads genes, including ones for drug resistance, between bacteria. The authors report detecting the parts of this system in this species. The result adds a data point to the map of which bacteria carry the tools for gene swapping, and how those tools are built.
plos-pone-0000215:
Marie-dominique Franco, Jonathan Bohbot, Kenny Fernandez, and colleagues published this insect neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the moth Manduca sexta, the olfactory epithelium lines the antennae and holds the smell-sensing cells. The authors study how sensory cells proliferate, keep being born, within that tissue as the moth develops into an adult.

A moth's sense of smell guides it to food and mates, and its sensors are renewed over life. Tracking where new sensory cells come from explains how the system stays sharp. The work adds to the study of adult neurogenesis, the birth of new nerve cells in mature animals.
plos-pone-0000315:
Chen Chen, Jiaqi Tang, Wei Dong, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Streptococcus suis is a pig bacterium that can infect people and, rarely, cause streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. The authors compare the genomes of two Chinese isolates of S. suis 2 to get a glimpse of what makes such strains dangerous.

China had seen human outbreaks of this syndrome, so the isolates mattered beyond pig farming. Comparing their genomes with milder strains highlights candidate virulence genes. The study is an early example of using comparative genomics to investigate an emerging zoonotic threat.
plos-pone-0000415:
Frank Powilleit, Tanja Breinig, and Manfred J. Schmitt turned a yeast virus's shell into a building platform, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The L-A virus of yeast wraps itself in a protein capsid. The team used that capsid inside living yeast to assemble chimeric virus-like particles, shells that mix the original protein with foreign pieces.
