Lev Prasov, Nadean Brown, and Tom Glaser scrutinized a retinal gene's message processing in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, called Math5 or Atoh7, switches on briefly as retinal cells leave division, and it is essential for making ganglion cells, the eye's output neurons to the brain. Its message is made from a single exon, a simple design, and mice without the gene grow retinas almost entirely missing those output cells.

Their critical analysis checks claims about how that message is spliced in the developing mouse retina. In a field where one gene decides an entire cell type's existence, the exact form of its message matters. Settling the record prevents other labs from building on a splicing pattern that may not be real.
plos-pone-0012415:
Maria Motta, Carolina Catta-Preta, Sergio Schenkman and colleagues filmed a bacterium that lives inside another cell dividing in step, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The host, Crithidia deanei, is a single-celled parasite relative that carries a bacterial tenant it cannot live without. In such hosts, division must copy the nucleus, the DNA granule, and the tenant in the right order.

The team showed that the tenant bacterium divides in tight coordination with the host nucleus. That sync keeps each daughter cell supplied with its tenant. Studying this partnership helps explain how lasting cell tenants evolve, the same road that long ago produced mitochondria, the energy parts of our own cells.
plos-pone-0012515:
Ofra Benny, Kei Nakai, Takeru Yoshimura and colleagues tested a broad vessel-blocking treatment for eye diseases, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Wet age-related macular degeneration blinds older adults when abnormal vessels grow and leak under the retina. Current drugs target one growth factor, VEGF, and need repeated eye injections, so broader blockers are sought.

Their treatment hit neovascularization across models, aiming wider than single-factor drugs. A broad antiangiogenic agent could help patients who respond poorly to VEGF blockers alone. Eye disease is a proving ground for vessel drugs, since success can be photographed directly in the living retina.
plos-pone-0012615:
Liao, Gock, Michie and co-authors asked whether a tiny worm can smell the chemicals given off by explosives. Finding hidden explosives from a distance is a hard safety problem. The roundworm C elegans carries a huge family of smell receptor genes, far more than its simple body suggests.

Their 2010 tests gave both behaviour and genetic evidence that the worm detects those vapours. A living sensor of that kind could one day be built into cheap detection tools. The study also shows how much sensing power sits in a worm with only a small set of nerve cells.
plos-pone-0012715:
Mayorek, Naftali-Shani and Grunewald tested an old pain drug against pancreatic cancer in mice. Diclofenac has been in pharmacy use for decades as an anti-inflammatory. Besides its known targets, it blocks other enzymes tied to inflammation and growth signals.

Their 2010 mouse study found the drug slowed tumour growth, partly by changing VEGF levels and arginase activity in the tumour setting. Pancreatic cancer has few working treatments, so any cheap, known drug with an effect earns attention. The work supports trials of drug reuse in this disease.  The authors link both shifts to the slower growth they measured in treated mice.
plos-pone-0012815:
Halton, Cook, Paterson and co-authors priced a bundle of care steps meant to stop infections from central vein lines. A central venous catheter feeds drugs and fluids into a large vein, but the line can also carry germs into the blood. Hospitals were being urged to use a fixed bundle of hygiene steps every time.

Their 2010 analysis weighed the bundle's costs, including its consumables, against the infections it prevents. Bundle steps are cheap beside the cost of one blood infection, yet hospitals still need proof before adopting them widely. Their figures make the economic case concrete.
plos-pone-0330015:
Maxwell Ateni Assibi and his team set out a plan for a study in Ghana. The site is the University for Development Studies. There, health trainees learn by work in the towns they will serve. Such town-based work is a fine place to teach mixed crews to act as one team. Yet few have asked how the trainees and staff feel about it.

The plan calls for one-on-one talks with last-year trainees and staff of two town schemes. The team will sort the talks by theme and check the themes back with those who spoke. They hope to learn what helps, what blocks, and how team drills could be built in with more care.
plos-pone-0343915:
Karambu Kiende Gatimbu and Paul Njiru Nthakanio study Kenya's housing drive. Can the national programme last? Their work covers Meru and Embu counties. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Two hundred and fifteen people rated the programme. They were residents, academics, and builders. They scored its economic, social, and green performance. The drive was launched to close a severe housing shortage. That shortage hits low- and middle-income families hardest.

Respondents praised better affordability and social safety. But green design lagged behind. So did use of local materials and real public input. Older respondents prized safety and sound basic services. Postgraduates prized green features. The authors urge stronger public involvement. They also want green building standards. Both should come before the programme grows further.
plos-pone-0344615:
Anna M Knochel, Mark V Erdmann, and co-authors attached satellite tags to reef manta rays in Papua New Guinea's Samarai Islands, the first tracking of this population. Reef mantas roam tropical Indo-Pacific waters, yet their local habits decide whether tourism and protection plans can work. Their 2026 study followed ten adults for up to six months across two monsoon seasons, recording horizontal travel and dive depth.

The rays proved homebodies: three quarters of their positions fell within ten kilometers of the tagging site, and none wandered beyond about eighty-seven kilometers. Shallow water rich in plankton pigment drew them most. They adjusted their diving to the ocean's mixed surface layer, going deeper when that layer thinned. The authors say such loyalty to place supports site-based tourism and local management.
plos-pone-0344915:
Tayyaba Shehzad and colleagues built the first paired sentence collection for simplifying Punjabi written in the Shahmukhi script. Shahmukhi is one of the two main scripts for Punjabi, yet computer tools have largely ignored it. Each hard sentence in the new collection sits beside a plainer version that keeps the meaning with clearer words and form.

An automatic system trained and tested on the pairs rewrote hard sentences with strong scores on a standard quality measure for simplification. Human aims stayed central: keep the sense, drop needless difficulty, and help readers who struggle with formal text. The collection opens a path for reading aids, school tools, and wider access to written Punjabi in daily life.
plos-pone-0346515:
Roshan Puri, Lucia R Levers, and Amit K Pradhananga valued the control of invasive species in fresh water, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Invaders choke lakes and rivers, harming native life and recreation, and removing them costs real money. The team used a survey method that asks people what such management is worth to them.

Puri's contingent valuation turns those answers into estimates of economic benefit. Policymakers can set those benefits beside program costs when arguing budgets. Invasive species work is often funded after damage is obvious and control is dear. A hard cost-benefit case for acting early helps agencies move sooner, when prevention is still cheap and ecosystems can still recover.
plos-pone-0347415:
Zhongqun Guo and co-workers use helpful bacteria to harden and clean up waste piles left by rare earth mining. The tailings are weak as soil and laced with heavy metals that can wash away. Their 2026 study treats samples with a microbe that forms a chalky mineral, varying the feeding solution and metal load to see what works best.

Strength rose with the amount of mineral formed, reaching its peak at the strongest feeding mix. Leaching of heavy metals dropped sharply after treatment. Under the microscope, lumps of mineral had trapped metals inside, locking them in place. The method could turn loose, polluted waste into firmer, safer ground, though scaling it up needs more work.
plos-pone-0348015:
Juliet Furaha Karisa and co-workers take stock of coral reef repair efforts across the Western Indian Ocean. Reefs there are badly degraded, and local repair projects remain small and scattered. Their 2026 review draws on published studies, online sources, a survey of practitioners, and a regional workshop to gather lessons and judge current practice.

Twenty-two active projects ran across eight countries, most involving local communities closely. Nearly all grew coral by fragments, a cheap method, while breeding from eggs stayed rare. Watching results varied a lot, and few projects tracked social or economic gains. The review fed into a new regional network meant to help projects share methods and grow.
plos-pone-0348115:
Sheila Timp, Nicky van Foreest, and Willem van Rhenen asked whether the professional guiding a sick employee back to work changes how long the absence lasts. They analysed more than thirty thousand mental health related absence cases in the Netherlands, where occupational health professionals coach workers through recovery and return. A multilevel statistical model separated the professional's influence from that of the worker, the employer, and the sector.

The professional mattered a lot. Under the most effective professionals, typical absences lasted eighteen weeks or less; under the least effective, twenty-eight weeks or more. Employers mattered too. The authors urge professionals and organisations to coordinate, and call for research into which habits make the difference.
plos-pone-0348215:
Jeyalakshmi Kandhavelu, Clement Penny, and co-authors tested two old drugs, used together, against colon cancer cells grown in the lab. One drug, valproic acid, loosens how DNA is packed, and the other, zebularine, blocks a process that silences genes. Their 2026 study treated an early-stage and a late-stage colon cancer cell line and tracked two genes that help control cell growth.

Together the drugs slowed cancer cell growth more than either drug alone. They raised levels of a protective gene, strongly in the late-stage cells, while lowering a growth-driving gene in a dose-linked way. Treated cells also showed signs of orderly self-destruction. The authors say the pairing deserves further study as a possible low-cost way to fight colon cancer, though all tests so far are in dishes, not patients.
plos-pone-0348315:
Zhaohua Chai and Na Yang asked how art founders dare to try bold new work with so little cash. Most studies of this kind look at big tech firms. Their survey reached two hundred three art founders in China. It used tools that hunt for mixes of traits, not lone causes.

No one trait proved a must. Three mixes led to bold work. One lined up skills inside the firm. One seized a chance from outside. One sensed a tech shift and moved fast. The team says there is more than one road to the same peak, which should cheer small art firms.
plos-pone-0348515:
Hao Tang and his team hunted for genes that weak bone and bad kidneys share. The two ills often strike the same people. The team mined large gene data sets with smart tools. Four hub genes rose to the top of the list. They then checked these genes in mice bred with each ill.

All four genes split sick from well with high marks. One gene did best of all. In the mouse checks, all four genes dimmed in weak bone. In bad kidneys, three of the four rose. The genes also tied to immune cells in the blood. The team sees drug targets and test marks here.
plos-pone-0348615:
Shinhaeng Cho and colleagues compared two ways of checking radiotherapy plans on a modern ring-shaped treatment machine. One method uses the machine's own built-in imaging panel to verify each beam separately; the other uses an external phantom device to verify the combined dose. Both were run on prostate, throat, and breast cases, then stressed by deliberately shifting the treatment centre to see which check caught the error.

Both methods agreed excellently under standard scoring rules. The phantom check reacted more sharply to shifts, while the panel check scored consistently higher and steadier, so steady that its natural pass rates sat far above the conventional alarm thresholds. The authors conclude the panel method is a dependable clinical alternative, provided departments set their own tighter limits for it.
plos-pone-0348715:
Ryan SangBaek Kim studies how people writing about relationships online balance story detail against raw feeling. The 2026 study draws on more than three hundred fifty thousand English posts from support communities. Each story is scored for how built out it is. Each is also scored for how intense its expressed emotion sounds. The gap between the two scores is the focus.

Most posts kept story and feeling fairly matched, but three smaller patterns appeared often enough to count as real styles. Some writers poured out feeling with little story, some built detailed stories with muted feeling, and some showed feeling with almost no story support. A chatbot tested the same way covered a narrower range and hugged the matched middle. Human telling, it seems, keeps room to pull back or lean in.
plos-pone-0349015:
Isac Davidson Santiago Fernandes Pimenta and Grasiela Piuvezam set out a plan to audit safety gauges in intensive care. Such gauges track harm to patients. Yet many were never built or checked in a sound way. Bad gauges make fair contrast between hospitals moot. This 2026 paper is a protocol. It fixes the method in print before the work starts.

The team will search seven databases plus grey sources. They seek studies that build or test care safety gauges. Two staff will screen each study on their own. Set tools will judge study and gauge quality. Gauges will be sorted by type and by unit, from newborn to heart care. The aim is a sound, shared set for the field.
plos-pone-0349115:
Ingunn Fride Tvete and Marianne Klemp followed more than thirty-six thousand Norwegian women with breast cancer to show how the meaning of a risk factor changes with time since diagnosis. Standard survival models assume each factor's effect stays constant, which may mislead over long horizons. Their 2026 registry study compared cancer deaths against other deaths across tumor subtypes, body weight, and treatments, letting effects vary over time.

The most aggressive subtypes carried over triple the cancer death hazard of the reference group in the first three years, but that excess largely faded or shrank in later years. Radiation's protective effect likewise peaked early and then dwindled. Body weight groups showed no difference in cancer mortality. The authors warn that fixed-effect models can badly misstate long-term prognosis.
plos-pone-0349215:
Anna Tubek-Krokosz, Jarek Baran, and co-authors tracked the daily movement of one hundred forty-one healthy young women to see how moderate activity relates to immune cells that patrol for cancer. Natural killer cells and killer T cells are central to that surveillance, and exercise is thought to tune them. Activity was recorded with wrist trackers across two menstrual cycles while blood samples measured the cell populations.

Women who walked more and spent more minutes active carried higher shares of certain bright natural killer cell subtypes. More very active minutes went with stronger natural killing power in lab tests, though the cells then responded less to a stimulating signal. Total killer cell counts and T cell measures showed no clear links. The authors say moderate daily activity may quietly sharpen parts of immune surveillance.
plos-pone-0349315:
Wenxin Zhu and Huanxing Zhu developed a single lab test that detects two major causes of deadly calf diarrhoea at once: a cattle virus and a toxin-making strain of E. coli. Young calves die quickly from scours, and testing for each germ separately wastes time farmers do not have. Their combined test uses fluorescent probes that light up only when the matching germ's DNA is present.

The test proved extremely sensitive, picking up tiny amounts of either target, and it stayed silent for other cattle germs, avoiding false alarms. Repeated runs gave steady results, and trials on real clinical samples confirmed it works outside the development bench. The authors present the assay as a faster way for vets to pin down outbreaks and limit losses on cattle farms.
plos-pone-0349415:
Anna Savio and colleagues updated a systematic review of surgery's carbon footprint, gathering studies from 2023 to 2025. Operating rooms burn far more energy than any other hospital department, three to six times as much by some counts, and lean heavily on single-use materials and anesthetic gases. Twenty-six studies met the review's criteria, and each was checked for scope, boundaries, and quality.

Reported footprints varied enormously, from under five kilograms of carbon equivalent for minor procedures to over four hundred for a complex operation, and around a thousand for a whole multi-stage patient pathway. The spread reflects both real differences and inconsistent accounting. Standardizing how surgical emissions are counted is the review's central plea, because hospitals cannot cut what each study measures differently.
plos-pone-0349515:
Yolanda María de la Fuente-Robles and colleagues surveyed two hundred and nine women aged sixty and over living at home in eastern Andalusia, Spain, about abuse suffered in the past year. Using a standard mistreatment scale, they counted overall abuse and its forms, from psychological harm to neglect, and looked for the circumstances that raise the risk.

Nearly half the women reported some form of abuse. Psychological abuse was most common, reported by more than a third, followed by physical harm, financial abuse, sexual abuse, and neglect. Age, marital status, poor self-rated health, and loneliness all tracked with higher risk. The authors urge health and social services, especially frontline social workers, to get better at spotting quiet forms of abuse inside the home.
plos-pone-0349615:
Mohammadreza Eslami and colleagues looked back at ninety-four stem cell transplant patients in western Iran to see how donor and recipient blood traits jointly affected survival. Transplant doctors still struggle to predict who will do poorly years later. The team focused on two simple measures: the donor's hemoglobin level and whether the recipient had very low infection-fighting white cells before transplant.

Higher donor hemoglobin alone showed only a weak trend toward worse survival. The striking result was the interaction: the effect of donor hemoglobin depended on the recipient's white cell state before transplant. Because the study is small and exploratory, the authors treat it as a lead for larger studies, not a rule for choosing donors today.
plos-pone-0349715:
Nickson Severian Kahigi and three colleagues audit the environmental cost of a plant based building material across its whole early life, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their product pairs sisal yarn, grown and spun in Tanzania, with a corn derived plastic, and is pressed into plates in Denmark. Marketed as a green alternative, it first has to survive an honest accounting that includes shipping fiber between continents.

The audit found air freight responsible for nearly two thirds of the product's warming impact. Switching to ocean shipping, wind power, and a higher fiber share cut the footprint by about forty-four percent. Judged per unit of stiffness, the improved version then beat common plastic and aluminium window frame materials on warming. But some harms, notably certain toxic effects on people, grew worse, a burden shifting trade off the authors say designers must face openly.
plos-pone-0349815:
Tamer Abdelrehim and colleagues validated a high frequency ultrasound method for measuring jaw bone loss around teeth, with detail finer than a millimetre. Tracking tiny bone changes helps judge gum disease treatment. In lab bone models, controlled bone cuts were measured by hand and by automated ultrasound, against photo based truth.

System error stayed near a tenth of a millimetre, and the smallest reliably seen change was about one hundred and forty micrometres. Detection hit rates ranged from about eighty to one hundred percent by method and step size. Automated reads tracked change with tiny bias and excellent consistency. Radiation free ultrasound could let dentists follow bone healing visit by visit.
plos-pone-0350015:
Xitong Yang and colleagues hunted for genes tied to the immune system in pulmonary arterial hypertension, a disease where lung arteries narrow and strain the heart. They merged three public gene datasets from patient lungs and layered several analysis methods, including network mapping and machine learning, to find genes that sit at the center of the disease's activity.

Eight hub genes survived the screening and held up in separate datasets, with one gene, BCLAF1, best at telling patients from healthy tissue. Immune cell patterns in the lungs also shifted with the disease. A mouse model was used to confirm key genes in living tissue. The shortlist offers starting points for diagnostic tests and immune-focused treatments.
plos-pone-0350115:
Javier Urban-Olivares and colleagues mapped the small second genome found in copepods, tiny crustaceans that fill seas and lakes. Despite huge diversity, copepod genetic tools stay thin. The team compared nineteen full copies from public records with five fresh ones from a Mexican genus, checking size, gene order, and stretches that do not code for proteins.

New copies were the largest yet seen in copepods, swollen by long non coding stretches full of repeats and odd structures. Gene order shifts a lot, even breaking blocks that stay fixed in most animals. Some groups kept near ancestral layouts while others expanded greatly. Most genes also bear marks of active change, hinting at fast, ongoing evolution.
plos-pone-0350515:
Hongmin Wang, Zhiyong Lei, and Xing Liu proposed a joint method in 2026 for passive radar, which listens to broadcast signals instead of sending its own. Quiet radar suits covert watching, but weak signals and slow targets make both naming and locating targets unreliable.

Their framework couples a learning encoder, which judges whether a target moves, with a physics based position solver, each feeding corrections to the other in a loop. Broadcast television signals supplied the test case. Enforcing the true signal geometry at every step kept the two answers consistent. The loop design aims to stop the common failure where class and position contradict each other.
plos-pone-0350615:
Lena Jelinek and co-authors followed German patients one year after a very short, intense treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder. The Bergen four-day treatment packs standard exposure therapy into four days instead of many weeks. Earlier outcome reports came mostly from Norway, so the team tested whether the gains hold in a German day clinic.

Fifty-eight adults were checked a year after treatment. Symptom scores stayed far below where they began, and about seven in ten people still met the standard for a good response, with about half in remission. Mood, daily functioning, and quality of life also stayed better. The findings support the brief format as a real option where long therapy waits block care.
plos-pone-0350815:
Qinhui Lu, Yanli Yang, and Biao Ruan investigated why cell power units falter in allergic rhinitis, the long term nose inflammation behind endless sneezing and blockage. Gene data pointed to two linked genes that were raised in diseased nose cells. Dish tests used human nose lining cells stirred into an allergy like state with a signal protein.

Raised genes went with lower levels of two proteins that start cleanup of worn out power units, plus more cell stress and weaker power unit charge. Quieting the first gene lowered the second, restored cleanup proteins, and eased stress. Blocking that gene pair, the team proposes, might restore healthy cell cleanup in allergic noses.
plos-pone-0350915:
Jason Johnson-Peretz led a team of eight authors on this 2026 interview study of home-based blood pressure care in rural Kenya and Uganda. Inside a pilot trial, community health workers visited adults with serious hypertension and linked them by telehealth to clinicians, instead of relying on clinic trips. Forty patients and fifteen providers described the experience.

Both groups welcomed the model, praising saved travel and steady contact, and suggested adding services like medicines delivery. Johnson-Peretz presents worker-led telehealth as a patient-centered route to better hypertension control where clinics are far.
plos-pone-0351115:
Lili Sun, Chenwen Wei, and Heliang Huang ran an online experiment on how shoppers come to feel a natural food will taste good before any bite exists. Three hundred twenty volunteers saw food pages that varied by platform style, by whether the photo showed a lifestyle scene or raw nature, and by whether the text stressed eating or producing. The team modeled the chain from seeing naturalness to trusting the seller to imagining taste to thinking hard about the product.

Perceived naturalness fed engagement through several routes: directly, through credibility, through taste imagination, and through a chain where trust unlocks taste imagination, which keeps people thinking. Platform type changed which routes carried the effect. Sellers of natural foods online are really selling a simulation, and this study maps the wiring between a rustic photo and a shopper's willingness to linger, compare, and believe.
plos-pone-0351215:
Tamar Klaiman and seven colleagues explore how underrepresented Americans view taking part in clinical research. Their 2026 study covers Black, Hispanic or Latinx, women, and rural participants. These groups join studies at low rates, which weakens the science and deepens health gaps. The team worked across the Philadelphia, Atlanta, and Washington, DC areas.

Instead of standard survey questions, they used freelisting. Participants simply listed words that came to mind about research participation. Shared word patterns reveal what each group values, fears, or expects. Comparing lists across groups shows where concerns overlap and where they differ. Recruiters can then design outreach that answers each community's real concerns, rather than relying on one generic message for everyone.
plos-pone-0351315:
Gerald Agyapong-Opoku and colleagues set out a plan for mapping non-drug approaches to anxiety and depression in young people aged ten to twenty-four. Talk therapies, school programs, digital tools, and exercise schemes have multiplied, but they vary so widely that nobody can see the whole field at once. This protocol describes a scoping review that will chart what exists rather than judge what works best.

Searches across six databases will gather studies of any design, screened by two reviewers working independently and reported against a standard checklist. As a protocol, the paper reports no findings. Its contribution is the map's design: by sorting interventions by format, setting, and who they target, the finished review should show busy areas, blank spots, and the questions trialists should tackle next.
plos-pone-0352015:
Marijane Luistro Jonsson and four colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for a wide-ranging review linking symptoms people report to proteins measured in their blood. Earlier reviews usually stayed inside one disease. This team wants a diagnosis-free map, hoping shared biology behind common symptoms will show up across conditions.

The protocol describes searching four large databases and screening the huge yield with an artificial intelligence tool, after a pilot run showed it saved real time. Five reviewers will extract each reported symptom-and-protein pairing and chart the patterns. The finished map is meant to guide clinicians and point symptom research toward the most promising leads.
plos-pone-0352115:
Yujie Yan, Yanling Wang, and Na An published this 2026 simulation study of acid treatment in carbonate oil reservoirs. Pumping acid into the rock dissolves winding channels called wormholes, which let oil flow more freely. Using a coupled flow-and-etching model, they tested how uneven rock, directional layering, and natural cracks shape those channels.

More uneven porosity produced bushier wormholes and slower acid breakthrough. Strong directional layering instead grew one main channel across the grain, and cracks steered growth strongly. Yan's results give field engineers a clearer picture of where injected acid will actually travel underground.
plos-pone-0352315:
Gloria Anderson and seven colleagues publish the protocol for a Rome trial, in 2026. The trial tests whether women can learn to push more effectively in labor by watching ultrasound images of their own bodies. Pushing works best when abdominal effort pairs with relaxation of the pelvic floor, yet a sizable minority of first-time mothers do the opposite, narrowing the passage and prolonging labor. The trial will enroll just under two hundred seventy women having their first baby, before labor begins.

Half receive standard midwife-led pushing training, and half add a session using real-time perineal ultrasound as biofeedback. The main measure is how long the active pushing stage lasts, with secondary measures covering muscle co-activation, type of birth, perineal injury, bleeding, continence months later, and the birth experience. The authors frame the study as a test of whether seeing changes doing in one of childbirth's hardest skills.
plos-pone-0352515:
Shrawan Patel and four colleagues redesign a basic microwave component for modern antenna arrays. Their 2026 paper presents a Wilkinson power divider that splits one signal into any number of equal outputs. Conventional designs need awkward crossovers or impossible wiring for odd counts. Their topology stacks simple one-to-two and one-to-three units, mixing equal and unequal stages. Tapered transmission lines keep every impedance inside factory-friendly limits. A two-stage triple divider was built and measured as the proof.

The prototype performed broadly and evenly. It worked across most of its target band around a common wireless frequency. Output balance stayed tight in both loudness and timing. The layout shrank by well over half against conventional equivalents. Beamforming networks, which steer 5G and radar signals, need dozens of exactly such splitters. A compact, scalable, crossover-free design removes a quiet bottleneck in building them.
plos-pone-0352815:
Zhang and Yu examined an underground ring road in a future technology district of Hangzhou in a 2026 study. The loop was built to move cars below ground and free the surface, but few drivers use it. The team gathered traffic counts on site and asked drivers about their experience with the loop.

Only about one in ten cars used the loop for arriving or leaving the district. Drivers cited low awareness, weak guidance signs, uneven access rules at each plot, and little flexibility in how the loop runs. Gains in cutting carbon also fell short of hopes. Drawing on similar projects in other Chinese districts, the authors propose clearer guidance, shared access rules, and smarter traffic control.
plos-pone-0353115:
Shelly Loewenstein and eight colleagues show that the cells lining the belly cavity send out tiny parcels that encourage new blood vessels to grow, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. That lining, the mesothelium, sits where gut and ovarian cancers spread, and the vessels they grow help tumours settle. The team harvested the parcels — extracellular vesicles — from mesothelial cell cultures and tested them on vessel-lining cells in dishes and in living tissue.

The parcels made vessel cells multiply, migrate, and form tubes, in dishes and in implanted plugs alike. A cargo protein that drives vessel growth proved to be the key messenger. Blocking that pathway, the authors propose, might starve peritoneal metastases of their blood supply.
plos-pone-0353215:
Donough, Mthimunye, and Daniels explored how exams are designed at a South African nursing school in a 2026 study. Written tests should match what students were taught and mix easy and hard thinking fairly. Interviews with nine nurse educators and reviews of moderator reports supplied the evidence.

The authors recommend training in test design, tighter matching of questions to learning goals, and stronger moderation routines. Weak tests misjudge students and can pass nurses who are not ready for clinical reasoning. Nursing programs under resource pressure still need valid exams, since patient safety later depends on the judgment those exams certify.
plos-pone-0353615:
Charlotte Lee and three colleagues test whether remembering a good or bad doctor's visit changes what patients later remember, in this 2026 PLOS ONE experiment. Two hundred and forty-five adults living with chronic pain recalled either a consultation where they felt believed and respected, or one where they felt dismissed. Afterwards everyone listened to twenty health messages and was tested on recall.

Those who had recalled feeling validated remembered more of the messages — roughly a fifth better odds for each one — than the dismissed-memory group. The boost was not explained by changes in fear of pain. The authors suggest that feeling taken seriously may free up mental room for medical advice to stick.
plos-pone-0354015:
Marloes Oomen, Lyke Esselink, and Floris Roelofsen published this 2026 experiment on yes-no questions in Dutch Sign Language. Signers acted out conversations while the researchers varied what the asker likely expected and what evidence sat in view. The team catalogued the question forms produced and what extra elements contribute.

Contrary to earlier claims, raised eyebrows were not the steady marker of a yes-no question; lowered brows appeared often too. A forward lean of head or body looked like the real signal. Oomen suggests eyebrows instead carry a range of side meanings in nonstandard questions.
plos-pone-0354115:
This 2026 notice from the PLOS One editors is a formal correction to an earlier cancer study, and it should be read before anyone relies on that study's figures. The original article claimed that a small RNA molecule slows triple-negative breast cancer by targeting a gene called KLF5. After publication, readers flagged problems in a key figure and in the statistics described in the methods.

One panel in the figure duplicated another, and a protein signal appeared in a cell line known to lack that protein entirely — raising contamination worries. The corresponding author supplied a corrected figure and conceded the signal should not be read as genuine protein. The correction leaves the paper's conclusions in a clouded state.
plos-pone-0354515:
Sugjit Singh Padda and Bradley Cardinale carried a famous farming debate into streams: share land with nature, or spare it by farming intensively elsewhere. The sharing-versus-sparing question had barely been tested in fresh water. Their 2026 study paired Pennsylvania streams flowing through shared and spared farm landscapes, matched for habitat and water quality.

Water invertebrate communities looked much the same in both stream types. Richness, evenness, total numbers, and overall composition showed no meaningful differences. Only a small shift appeared in one feeding group, which the authors judge biologically minor. Padda and Cardinale caution that land strategy lessons from forests and fields may not transfer to streams.
plos-pone-0354715:
Alice Vinet and Denis Guilbeau published this 2026 archaeology study of obsidian arrowheads deliberately cut with marks in Neolithic central Anatolia. Eleven newly identified pieces from a Cappadocian settlement joined a known set of only a few dozen, all dating to roughly nine thousand years ago. The team examined the stone sources, making sequence, wear, and the cuts themselves.

The marks varied widely and matched nothing about material, shape, or use, and they were cut at different stages of manufacture. Earlier guesses called them hunters' identity marks. Vinet urges caution, while noting the odd custom persisted through cultural change.
plos-pone-0354915:
Monica Emendi and co-authors model a lung support machine in 2026. The machine takes over when lungs fail badly. It drains blood, adds oxygen, and returns the blood. The study asks what a second drainage tube changes. Computer fluid models were built in an average heart chamber. Layouts, tube types, and tube positions were compared.

One standard layout wasted the most flow in a short loop. It also gave the lowest blood oxygen level. A dual layout did far better on both counts. It used a multi hole tube placed in the neck. Pressures and wall stress differed sharply by layout. Stagnant blood volume also varied a lot. The best choice should fit each patient, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355315:
Ameerah Ibrahim and co-authors interview in 2026 community pharmacists in Amman, Jordan, about offering services that promote health and prevent disease. Such services could ease pressure from long term diseases, and pharmacists are easy for the public to reach. Themes from the talks were mapped onto a framework covering capability, opportunity, and motivation.

Pharmacists described wide and growing roles, but heavy workload, weak patient engagement, no pay for the extra work, and little owner support held them back. Training, better undergraduate teaching, and closer work with doctors were seen as needs. Fixing those blocks could let pharmacists prevent more illness, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355415:
Matthew J Hardy and a team of wildlife and poultry researchers track wintering geese with GPS collars on the Delmarva Peninsula, a hotspot for both wild waterfowl and chicken farming. Bird flu carried by wild geese threatens flocks, and response teams cannot guard every farm equally. Across four winters, the team followed several dozen snow geese and Canada geese and scored thousands of poultry sites by goose traffic nearby.

The scoring separated risk well: farms that later saw outbreaks sat high in the ranking, one among the very top of thousands. A third of all farms had collared geese nearby at some point. Timing mattered, with each goose species peaking in a different part of winter. Hardy and colleagues offer the ranking to aim scarce biosecurity effort where birds actually gather.
plos-pone-0355515:
Correction notice. Asuka Tanno and co-authors correct three figures in their published study of a four-celled green alga and its response to light. The original paper reported weak swimming behaviour toward light and strong protection against light damage. This 2026 notice replaces faulty panels and data traces.

In one figure, the control panels had duplicated the treated panels at three time points; corrected panels from the original experiments now replace them. A supplementary legend carried a wrong sample number for swimming speed. A third figure's model traces came from an earlier paper by the same group and should not have been included. The authors supply the underlying images so readers can verify the corrected record.
plos-pone-0355715:
Violeta Carrillo and colleagues describe in 2026 how they tagged two fungi that attack pyrethrum, a crop grown for natural insecticide. Using a bacterium based method, they inserted glowing markers into each fungus. One strain glowed green and the other red, letting infection be watched under a microscope.

Genome checks showed mostly single insertions, and tagged strains grew and infected leaves much like wild ones. In one fungus, spores sprouted within a day and hyphae entered leaf skin by three days. These tools give the first clear view of early infection for that species and support later work on how the disease spreads.
plos-pone-0356815:
Jianxing Liu and colleagues studied how freezing changes the grip of a railway track bed, the crushed stone that keeps rails from sliding sideways. Their 2026 study combined full-scale track bed tests, compression tests on stone and ice mixtures, and computer simulations of individual stones, varying ice content, temperature, and freezing depth in a systematic design.

Ice content and freezing depth dominated: both pushed sideways resistance upward as they grew, while temperature mattered only weakly and indirectly. The simulations showed the microscopic reason, ice bonding stones into a stiffer mass. Their predictive model helps engineers in cold regions judge how track strength swings through freeze and thaw, information that feeds into winter safety margins and maintenance planning.
plos-pone-0356915:
Md Golam Kibria and colleagues surveyed 660 tobacco-using patients with chronic diseases at government hospitals in Bangladesh. They asked what the patients knew about services that help people quit. They also asked whether the patients would use them. Their 2026 cross-sectional study is, the authors note, among the first to measure this. In Bangladesh, tobacco use remains heavy and quit support is thin.

Knowledge was strikingly low: only about one patient in ten knew the services moderately well. Yet two thirds said they would use them. Schooling drove knowledge. Knowledge in turn tripled the odds of willingness, alongside frequent hospital contact. The practical conclusion writes itself. Tell patients the help exists, every visit, and most are already willing.
plos-pone-0357015:
Si Yang leads a team of five examining how sex shapes the gut and metabolism story of aging, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their subjects were mice: young and older animals of both sexes, with and without a gene called Nrf2 that defends cells against oxidative stress. The team ran glucose tolerance tests, measured fats and sex hormones, examined liver and fat tissue, and sequenced gut bacteria from droppings.

Aging male mice lacking the gene showed clearly impaired glucose handling, a combination that spared the other groups. Fat piled up in liver and body fat stores with age across genotypes and sexes. Blood fat patterns diverged by group rather than marching together. One striking gut result: older females without the gene carried notably less diverse gut bacteria than both their male counterparts and normal females. The study argues that aging research ignoring sex will keep averaging away real effects.
plos-pone-0357115:
Moritz Unnerstall led a team of six authors improving a lab separation method, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Porphyrins are pigments in blood whose levels signal certain diseases, but separating them cleanly from serum is hard. The team analyzed serum porphyrins and tested a special column type for liquid chromatography.

Unnerstall's group showed that inert biphenyl columns give cleaner, sharper separations. Better separation means more reliable readings for labs that test these pigments. Small method gains like this rarely get attention, yet diagnosis depends on them: a muddy separation can hide or fake a result. Labs adopting the column advice can cut fuss and repeat tests in porphyrin work.
plos-pone-0357215:
Jasmine S Turner and colleagues build, together with refugee communities in Uganda, a program to keep refugee children attending school consistently. Attendance falters for reasons that outsiders often misread. In settlements across Uganda, caregivers and teachers joined workshops to map what drives attendance. The maps were checked in validation meetings. The resulting program, called SchoolLinks, was then tried in one school. Its pupils were young children and catch-up learners.

The maps showed caregiver attitudes and encouragement at the center, shaped by how well caregivers and teachers communicate across language barriers. The program therefore works on that relationship as much as on the child. Turner and colleagues collected feedback from staff, families, and children during the trial run to refine the design before any wider rollout.
plos-pone-0357315:
Nabasmita Malakar, Ravikanth Gudasalamani, and Ganesan Rengaian published a 2026 taxonomy study in PLOS ONE untangling two Asian trees in the laurel family that botanists have confused for two centuries. The two names have been mixed in herbaria and books, blurring where each species actually grows. The team combined twenty-eight physical traits, family trees from two nuclear gene markers, and ecological niche modeling.

Every line of evidence agreed: the two are distinct species with separate homelands. One is confined to the Indo-Burma biodiversity hotspot, the other to India's Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats–Sri Lanka hotspot. Physical trait clustering matched the genetic split, and their modeled ranges barely overlap. Sorting out such confusion matters: conservation plans protect species, and a species wrongly merged with another can quietly vanish. The laurel family in India, they say, needs more of this integrative attention.
plos-pone-0357815:
Yael Rozman and Miri Tal-Saban compared inner strengths in teenagers with attention and movement disorders, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Adolescents with ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, or both face daily friction at school and in sport. Yet some thrive. The team measured resilience, feelings of hope, and a sense of coherence across these groups and typically developing peers.

Rozman and Tal-Saban's comparisons reveal which inner resources differ, and which protect struggling teens most. That matters because support often focuses only on deficits. Building on strengths that a group already has can be more effective than generic help. The study gives therapists, teachers, and parents a map of where each group's reserves lie, and where they run thin.
plos-pone-0357915:
Jun Lin published a 2026 engineering study in PLOS ONE on tightening bolts evenly in curvic couplings, the toothed metal joints used in aircraft engines. If the ten bolts in such a coupling end up with uneven grip, the joint loses precision and loads spread unevenly. Using computer simulations plus an elastic-interaction model, Lin compared ways of tightening the bolts in stages and in different orders, with a flat disk joint as a reference.

The toothed surface made grip differences between bolts much larger than in the flat reference, and the outcome became more sensitive to the tightening path. Tightening one bolt after another in sequence performed worst, while a crisscross pattern across two axes gave the most even result. A three-stage version of that pattern, rising gradually to full tightness, worked best overall. The findings warn engineers not to carry flat-joint rules over to toothed couplings.
plos-pone-0359015:
Xiangcai Luo and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on lithium-ion batteries. It estimates state of health, how much capacity a battery has left, using data-driven methods with feature sifting, selecting the most telling signals. The model joins KPCA with a transformer-LSTM hybrid whose tuning is optimized by an algorithm called NRBO.

Accurate health estimates decide when electric vehicle and storage batteries are safe, tired, or ready for a second life. Hybrid models that both compress signals and read their sequence aim for accuracy without huge computing cost. Battery engineers and energy storage researchers are the readers for this estimation recipe.
plos-pone-0359215:
Carver and co-authors reported in 2026 on genomic surveillance of ticks collected from farm animals living in communities in Eastern Ontario, Canada. The work follows the One Health idea, that human, animal, and environmental health are one connected system. Ticks picked off animals such as horses, cattle, and goats can carry the microbes that cause tick borne illness in people.

By reading the DNA in those ticks, the team identified which microbes are circulating in the area before they show up as human cases. Surveillance of this kind gives public health officials an early map of risk by place and season. It also shows how much can be learned from animals that share fields and trails with their owners.
plos-pone-0359415:
Dong Hun Lee and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on breast surgery. It addresses red breast syndrome, a complication that can follow reconstruction using ADM, a processed tissue material that supports the rebuilt breast. The authors build an exploratory scoring model to predict which patients face this problem.

The model uses routine hematologic markers, ordinary blood test values already collected before surgery. A score built from cheap, standard tests could flag high-risk patients early without extra procedures. Reconstructive surgeons are the audience, since forewarning lets them watch or treat the patients most likely to develop the syndrome.
plos-pone-0359515:
Daniel Wright published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies survey scales, the multi-question measures used across social research. The question is whether adding follow-up probes to selected responses, extra questions attached to some answers, changes how people respond to those very items.

Probes are meant to clarify answers, but any change to a question can shift the answers it collects. If probing some responses alters later ones, surveys using the technique may not match surveys without it. Survey methodologists, who design questionnaires for governments and researchers, are the readers for this cautionary test.
pmc-10320115:
Blin and co-authors describe version seven of antiSMASH, a software tool for finding useful chemistry in microbes. Small living things make special compounds as part of their normal growth. Many of these compounds can kill germs or fungi, fight viruses, or attack cancer cells, so they matter for drugs and farming.

Version seven improves how the tool spots the gene groups that make these compounds. It also improves guesses about how those groups are switched on, what the compounds look like, and how results are shown. Better maps of hidden chemistry help teams choose which microbes deserve costly lab work.
pmc-11683415:
Kumar, Stecher, Suleski, and co-authors introduce MEGA12, the twelfth version of a widely used program for studying evolution from DNA. MEGA stands for Molecular Evolutionary Genetic Analysis. Researchers use it to build family trees and test how species changed over time.

The new version cuts the computing time for key steps, such as picking the best model of change and running repeat tests of tree support. It also aims at leaner, greener computing that uses less energy. Faster analysis lets teams handle larger datasets on ordinary computers, widening who can do this work.
pmc-13122015:
Mackenzie Hagood and Brandon Lucke-Wold review long-term brain effects of high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy in a 2026 systematic review. Preeclampsia and eclampsia, the severe forms, can cause seizures, swelling, bleeding, and stroke around birth. Their lasting effects on the brain were less charted.

Searching studies from two thousand and five to two thousand and twenty-five, the authors included forty-nine that assessed outcomes at least three months after birth. A history of these disorders linked to higher long-term stroke risk, greatest for bleeding strokes and after eclampsia. Brain scans showed white matter lesions, shrinkage, and barrier leakage. Self-reported thinking problems appeared, though objective tests differed. Tailored follow-up care is suggested.
pmc-13193715:
Dana M S Cheung leads a 2026 study of how bacterial signals rewire B cell metabolism. B cells are immune cells that mature into antibody makers. A bacterial wall component called LPS can wake resting B cells into dividing. Using quantitative proteomics, a method that measures thousands of proteins, the team tracked the change in mouse B cells.

Activation raised amino acid transporters and cholesterol-making enzymes. One transporter proved essential, since deleting its gene impaired B cell growth. Blocking cholesterol production also stopped growth, through two downstream needs. The same rewiring appeared with other activation routes, not just LPS. Metabolic change, the authors conclude, is an essential feature of B cell activation.
pmc-13196915: Marie-Josée Angue Zogo and colleagues issued a 2026 correction to a study of Pahon Cave in Gabon. The original study covered Later Stone Age life in the African rainforest. One figure was uploaded in error, and the captions for Figures 4 to 9 were rotated out of place. The notice gives the correct first figure and the right captions, covering cave pottery, stone tools, and a polished axe piece. The images themselves were in the right order.
pmc-13198515:
Akhil Reddy Pashapu and colleagues studied winter stress in timothy grass across seed generations in a 2026 paper. Timothy is the top forage grass in northern Norway, where winters grow less predictable. The team compared two northern cultivars, Engmo and Noreng, for gene activity and gene variant shifts under freezing and ice cover.

Over generations, freezing tolerance fell while ice tolerance rose. Under freezing, one cultivar shifted activity in several stress genes, including hormone-linked switches. Some DNA spots with large variant shifts sat near those genes. Genetic diversity ebbed in both cultivars over time. Hormone-driven gene control may aid winter adaptation. Watching seed lots for drift could keep cultivars stable.
pmc-13201215:
Ruxin Ji and colleagues compared JAK inhibitor drugs in acute versus long-standing alopecia areata in a 2026 cohort study. Alopecia areata is patchy hair loss caused by immune attack on hair roots. JAK inhibitors, drugs that block immune signal switches, help regrow hair, but whether timing matters was unclear.

The study covered 158 patients treated at one center from 2021 to 2025 with one of two JAK drugs. Acute cases, forty-one patients, fared far better: sixty-five percent reached full regrowth scores by week twenty-four, versus about forty percent of long-standing cases. One drug and milder starting severity predicted top response. Early treatment seems key, though the single-center size limits certainty.
pmc-13207915:
Falling birth rates leave obstetric nurses fearing for their jobs, and a 2026 survey headed by Dengmei Chen measures that insecurity in Chongqing, China. Four hundred six obstetric nurses answered a job insecurity scale in spring 2025, and a mixed-effects model separated personal factors from hospital-level influences on their scores.

Insecurity ran high overall, with most nurses scoring above the scale's midpoint in the survey. Contract nurses felt less secure than permanently staffed colleagues, as did nurses in secondary hospitals compared with tertiary ones. Lower pay and mid-range experience added to the worry, while team leaders felt somewhat safer, and the authors propose targeted fixes for managers.
pmc-13208915:
Tiny scandium particles strengthen aluminum for aircraft, and a 2026 simulation study led by Hao Xiong models how those particles grow during heat treatment. The research article builds a high-resolution population dynamics model of Al3Sc precipitation, improving on the classic Kampmann-Wagner approach that smears out sharp size distributions.

The team simulated aging of two aluminum-scandium alloys at a fixed temperature and tracked nucleation, growth, and coarsening stages. Predicted particle sizes and size distributions matched experimental data closely, including a plateau in average radius mid-process. Raising scandium content sped the whole sequence markedly, and the authors offer the model for optimizing aging recipes in other dilute alloys.
pmc-13210315: A retraction notice published by the PLOS One editors in 2026 withdraws an article on a stability test method for artificial hip socket shells. After publication, concerns arose that the article overlapped substantially with an earlier Japanese-language paper by the same authors, spanning its introduction, methods, discussion, several figures, and quantitative results. The corresponding author acknowledged the overlap and apologized for not declaring the related work, and all authors agreed to the retraction. The article was removed from the journal website, and only this notice survives here.
pmc-13212415:
Mugurel Constantin Rusu, Diana Alexandra Bănică, and Răzvan Costin Tudose review in 2026 the small valves inside head and neck veins. Textbooks long taught that these veins lack valves and let blood flow either way, a claim newer dissection and imaging work now challenges.

Searching two databases, the reviewers found valves documented in facial, lingual, jugular, and several other veins, usually two-leafed and clustered near junctions. The internal jugular valve appears in most specimens, though it often fails when central pressure stays high or after catheter damage. By contrast, brain veins and dural sinuses remain truly valveless. The findings matter for surgery, cannulation, and understanding reflux toward the brain.
pmc-13212715:
Brent James Raiteri leads co-authors Ricardo De Lorenzo, Malte Kraul, and Daniel Hahn in a 2026 study of what happens to muscle steadiness after a strong contraction is quickly eased off. Earlier work after muscle lengthening hinted that later force control might suffer.

In two experiments, volunteers held shin muscle contractions while researchers varied how fast or how far effort dropped before a steady hold. Faster or larger drops stretched the muscle fibres more, as ultrasound-based measures showed. Electrical activity during the steady hold stayed unchanged, yet larger fibre lengthening made the held force noticeably less steady. Why steadiness falls remains unclear, a gap the authors flag for work with relevance to movement control and fatigue.
pmc-13213015:
Roberto R. Gonzalez Alvarez describes in 2026 a single striking case of a blistering skin reaction driven by sunlight plus a sequence of three medicines. A 44-year-old commercial driver first took an antifungal for ringworm, then two antibiotics as his rash was mistaken for skin infection.

Each new drug made the rash worse, and it stayed confined to sun-exposed arms, legs, and neck, with fluid-filled blisters and peeling but no mouth involvement. Tests ruled out infection and autoimmune disease. Stopping all three drugs, plus steroids and supportive care, cleared the redness within three hospital days. The case warns clinicians to suspect light-driven drug reactions before adding more medicines.
pmc-13213715:
Hua Wang and co-authors test in 2026 whether fermenting buckwheat bee pollen with a friendly bacterium makes it a stronger shield against sudden inflammation. Pollen's tough outer shell limits how much of its goodness the body can reach.

Fermentation cracked that shell and raised the levels of phenolics, flavonoids, and free amino acids substantially. Test-tube assays showed stronger antioxidant power on several measures. In mice given a bacterial toxin that triggers acute inflammation, a high dose of the fermented product cut key inflammatory signals sharply, eased liver strain, and strengthened the liver's antioxidant defences. The work supports fermented pollen as a candidate functional food ingredient.
pmc-13213915:
André Castanheira and colleagues report in 2026 a benign but bone-eating cyst found by chance in a small shoulder-blade projection called the coracoid process. Such cysts favour long bones and the spine, and this location is so rare that diagnosis easily goes astray.

Their 37-year-old patient arrived with shoulder pain first blamed on tendon calcification, while advanced imaging revealed the silent cyst. Surgeons scraped out the lesion and packed the cavity with a two-phase synthetic bone substitute. Tissue tests confirmed the diagnosis, and one year later the man had full function, no recurrence on scans, and no more tendon pain. The substitute performed as a safe stand-in for harvested graft bone.
pmc-13217415:
Seo Yeon Ahn and co-authors present a 2026 study testing whether exendin-4, a diabetes drug that mimics the hormone GLP-1, can protect the blood-brain barrier when ammonia builds up in liver failure. Excess ammonia loosens this barrier and fuels the brain disorder called hepatic encephalopathy.

In a mouse model made by tying off the bile duct, liver enzymes soared and brain tissue showed lost barrier proteins with more oxidative stress and cell death signals. In dishes, ammonia made brain endothelial cells leakier and stripped their sealing protein claudin-5, while astrocytes poured out inflammatory signals. Exendin-4 reversed these changes in both systems, preserving barrier tightness and calming cytokine release. Gene sequencing mapped further shifts the authors link to protection.
pmc-13217715:
Sasirin Chitwattananont and co-authors present a 2026 cell study of a berry pigment, cyanidin-3-O-glucoside, protecting insulin-producing cells from fat toxicity. Palmitic acid, the saturated fat that floods the blood in type 2 diabetes, kills pancreatic beta cells through oxidative and organelle stress.

Mouse beta cells bathed in palmitic acid lost viability sharply, with live cells dropping from about 79 to 41 percent and apoptosis climbing. Adding the pigment at high concentration continuously restored viability by about 41 percent and cut cell death in one assay from about 31 to 5 percent. It trimmed reactive oxygen species by roughly a quarter and suppressed the stress protein CHOP and the executioner caspase-3. The authors position the compound as a candidate for preserving beta cells.
pmc-13217915:
Johanna I. Keigler, Juliana Maria Leite Nobrega de Moura Bell, and Maria L. Marco wrote a 2026 narrative review on fungal foods and the gut microbiome. These myco-foods include mold mycelium eaten as extracts or biomass, plus foods fermented by molds such as Aspergillus and Rhizopus. The review asks what eating them does to intestinal microbes.

Four human trials covered in the review each found a measurable shift in the gut microbiome, and animal and laboratory studies pointed the same way. Feeding studies often raised the shares of Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium, and lactobacilli, along with bacteria known for breaking down fiber. Levels of short-chain fatty acids in feces also rose in many studies. The authors note that effects depend on the fungal species and food format, and they identify beta-glucans and chitin as likely drivers worth further study.
pmc-13221315:
Jude Zziwa Byansi and colleagues asked stakeholders what keeps school toilets working in Kampala, Uganda, in a 2026 decision-analysis study. Thirty-five people, including head teachers, officials, researchers, and civil society workers, joined a facilitated workshop. They weighted domains and indicators for operating and maintaining school sanitation facilities using two structured methods.

Service planning ranked as the top domain, followed by resource handling and facility design standards. Governance, service delivery, and monitoring scored lower. The top individual priorities were having an upkeep plan, a dedicated budget line, clear roles, sound budget use, and reliable water. The rankings give schools and city officials a shared order for sustaining facilities.
pmc-13221415:
Erika Hitre, István Láng, and Dénes Páll report a 2026 crossover trial testing whether food changes how an oral paclitaxel drug behaves in the body. Twenty-five patients with advanced solid tumors took DHP107, a lipid-based oral form of paclitaxel, in fed and fasted sequences across two cycles. Blood levels were the main outcome.

Average drug exposure was nearly identical after a high-fat meal and after fasting, meeting the preset criteria for no food effect. Diarrhea, vomiting, and low white cell counts were the common side effects. Some patients had tumor shrinkage or stable disease. The result means patients can take the drug with or without food.
pmc-13221515:
Faouzi Addad and co-authors summarize a 2025 summit on cardiometabolic disorders in the Maghreb, published in 2026. One hundred ten clinicians from Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia met in Saclay, France, to share regional data on diabetes, hypertension, and related disease. These conditions are common in the region yet often undertreated.

Sessions covered regional research, Ramadan fasting with diabetes, and whole-person strategies for patients with several conditions. Poor adherence and clinician inertia both blocked good care, with inertia possibly the larger culprit. Recommendations included single-pill combinations for blood pressure and affordable drug pairings for blood sugar that also protect heart and kidneys. Prevention through modifiable risk factors ran throughout.
pmc-13221715:
Lukas Svendsen and co-authors set out a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of how skeletal muscle mass changes during systemic cancer treatment. Muscle at diagnosis already predicts survival, toxicity, and quality of life across cancers. Change during therapy may carry even stronger signals, yet studies differ in cancer types, regimens, and measurement timing.

Following standard review methods, two reviewers screened abstracts and full texts independently, settled disagreements by discussion, and extracted data on a shared form. The introduction frames why a single baseline scan misses the trajectory that matters. Pooling change over time should help clinicians judge which patients lose ground fastest and may need support during treatment.
pmc-13222015:
Khadija Muhamed Ahmed follows dental students with bad breath through two weeks of a probiotic mouthrinse, in a 2026 prospective single-arm study. Thirty-four students with confirmed halitosis used a rinse containing two Lactobacillus strains three to four times daily. Breath scores, tongue coating measures, and saliva bacteria were checked at the start, one week, and two weeks.

Breath odor scores and all tongue coating measures fell significantly across the period. Gene-based testing showed fewer of two tracked bacteria, with a modest drop in a third. Better breath tracked with the bacterial shifts, and tongue coating stayed tightly linked to odor scores. The rinse offers a gentler option than standard antimicrobial washes.
pmc-13222315:
Arthur K. Chan, Michael J. Scanlon, and Gladys F. A. Melo-de-Pinna trace how leaf sheaths fuse in a dayflower relative, Commelina erecta, in a 2026 plant anatomy study. Sheaths in this family close around the stem, unlike the mostly open sheaths of grasses. The team sectioned shoot tips and young leaves for microscopy and tested for activity of a KN1-related gene.

Anatomy showed the sheath margins first form apart, then fuse after contact, a pattern called postgenital fusion. No KN1 signal appeared at the fusing margins. Grasses build sheaths with KN1 involvement, so this family seems to use a different molecular route. The contrast sharpens how plant organs can reach similar forms by separate means.
pmc-13222615:
Nesrin Alharthy and colleagues test whether procalcitonin levels predict proven infection in young infants suspected of sepsis, in a 2026 retrospective study at one tertiary center. Records covered 352 babies aged twenty-eight to ninety days seen from 2020 to 2021. Blood tests were drawn alongside blood, urine, and spinal fluid cultures plus viral swabs.

Procalcitonin showed no significant link with positive blood cultures, and none with respiratory viral infection either. Higher levels did associate significantly with positive urine cultures. The authors conclude the marker cannot stand in for blood or spinal fluid results in this age group, though it may help flag urinary infection. Single-center size limits the reach of the finding.
pmc-13223615:
Floriane Michaloud and co-authors lay out a protocol for mapping world research on undergraduate medical students' mental health, in a 2026 scoping review protocol. Student distress emerges early in training under heavy academic and organizational pressure. Existing literature is fragmented across themes, regions, and methods, with equity gaps rarely charted.

Four databases will be searched without date or language limits for quantitative studies. Two reviewers will screen and extract data independently onto a standard form. Domains range from symptoms and distress to social support and lifestyle, with equity variables tracked by how studies actually use them. Tables and visualizations will synthesize the map, following established scoping guidance.
pmc-13224415:
Yihong Chen and colleagues test a 2026 eye-measuring device, the AL550, designed to size up eyes before lens surgery. Accurate sizing of eye length and corneal shape decides which lens a patient gets. The new machine combines two optical techniques in one automated unit, and the team tested it against a widely used standard device.

Healthy volunteers numbered 112, each measured many times by two operators. Repeat readings agreed closely, with scores above 0.939 on every test. pmc-13285515:

pmc-13285715:

pmc-13285815:

pmc-13285915:

pmc-13286415:

pmc-13286915:

pmc-13287415:
