In 2026, Victor Ferrer and co-authors test whether bark left over from Chilean eucalyptus plantations can protect wood. Alkali extraction pulled nearly twice as much material from the bark as water alone, rich in phenolic compounds with antioxidant strength.

Pine samples soaked with the extract resisted stain fungi and brown rot, and held up better under ultraviolet ageing with less colour change. Washing tests showed the alkali extract stayed in the wood better than water-based versions. Heat tests also favoured the alkaline product. The authors propose the waste bark extract as a greener wood preservative.
pmc-13296315:
Yu Wang and colleagues study, in 2026, three switch genes in pepper plants that turn on strongly during attack by Phytophthora capsici, the mould behind a devastating blight. Such NAC genes guide growth and stress responses, but their role in pepper defence was largely unknown.

Turning the genes up or down showed all three act as brakes on resistance: plants with more of them fared worse, and plants with less resisted better. The proteins sit in the cell nucleus, as expected for gene switches. The authors flag the trio as targets for breeding tougher pepper varieties.
pmc-13296415:
Emily Wilfurth and colleagues study, in 2026, what controls the stress protein GDF15 in human fat tissue. Fat samples from ninety-six obese patients and two fat cell lines were tested against hormones, immune triggers and low-oxygen signals, with protein levels tracked in blood.

Fat tissue levels matched blood levels in the same patients. Most immune triggers did little, but one receptor pathway and low-oxygen signals raised production, while another signal lowered it. Insulin and a bile acid also raised output in mouse cells. The authors link GDF15 control to fat inflammation and whole-body metabolic strain.
pmc-13296615:
John W. Figg and colleagues review, in 2026, suppressor cells that blunt immune attack in glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumour. These immature myeloid cells gather in the tumour and shield it, one reason immunotherapy struggles there.

The review gathers clinical and large-scale molecular evidence placing the cells at the centre of suppression, then details the chemical signals and receptors that draw them in and keep them alive. Treatments that remove, block or reprogramme the cells, now in trials, get close attention. The authors aim to guide neuro-oncology teams targeting this shield.
pmc-13296715:
Raju Panta and colleagues survey artificial intelligence use in osteopathic medical education in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Students and faculty at one college, across two campuses, answered an anonymous online questionnaire. Questions covered knowledge, training, classroom use of tools such as ChatGPT, and attitudes toward policy.

Fifty-eight complete responses were analysed. Formal training in artificial intelligence was rare in both groups, though faculty reported more of it. Students used the tools far more for studying, drafting exam questions, and writing patient notes. Both groups showed interest in wider adoption. The authors call for structured literacy teaching, faculty development, and clear institutional rules for responsible use.
pmc-13296815:
Rio Oshima and co-authors report, in 2026, a man in his seventies leaking over a litre of lymph fluid daily after bladder removal surgery with pelvic node clearance. Rest and drainage failed, and scans showed leaks spreading through the belly, ruling out local sealing injections.

Imaging through groin lymph nodes pinpointed the leaking ducts near the pelvis. Sealing them from upstream with a glue-and-oil mix through several groin nodes quickly dried the drainage. Drains came out by day four and he went home by day ten without lasting swelling. The authors offer the approach as a low-burden fix.
pmc-13297315:
Dominika Przywara and co-authors ask, in 2026, whether the acidity of cord blood at birth sets the quality of stem cells drawn from the cord for regenerative medicine. Cells from three acidity groups were gene-profiled, then key growth factors checked in fifty samples.

Acidic blood flipped the cells from a growth programme toward a structural, migrating one with heavy matrix remodelling. Stress at birth, including excess carbon dioxide and threatened suffocation, cut output of several nourishing and nerve-protecting factors. The authors say screening cord blood chemistry could standardise cell selection for therapy.
pmc-13297415:
Camille Schunder, Agnès Gras-Vincendon, and François Brezin describe transgender adolescents followed at Strasbourg University Hospital in a 2026 review of past cases. The centre serves a region of nearly two million people, yet only 115 adolescents began follow-up there before age eighteen across seven years. Most were transmasculine, and rates of added psychiatric conditions ran very high.

Just over a third received hormone therapy before eighteen, after a median of fifteen months in follow-up. Paths through care differed by the type of schooling a young person attended, a pattern not reported before. Return to the birth-assigned sex was rare under any definition used, and no one who started hormones expressed regret. The authors urge structured, kind support and a shared definition of retransition.
pmc-13297615:
Alka Ashok Singh, Fazlurrahman Khan, and Minseok Song review whether toxins from microbes help drive diseases that waste the brain, in a 2026 article. The diseases covered include Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and multiple sclerosis, all marked by failing nerve cells. Toxins from fungi and bacteria, once tied only to infections, now show links to core features of these diseases.

Gut microbes make toxins that may cross into the brain and stir inflammation there. The review traces routes through oxidative stress, protein misfolding, and failing cell powerhouses, plus signals between gut and brain. Mapping these pathways could open new treatment ideas, the authors argue, for diseases that still lack cures.
pmc-13297815:
Joud AlBashtawi and a large team ask whether high uric acid in the blood can flag circadian syndrome, in a 2026 study. The syndrome ties metabolism, sleep, and mood to a broken body clock. The team mined a national health survey covering 27,410 adults across fifteen years. The syndrome required at least five of eight traits, from blood fats and pressure to short sleep, depression, and fatty liver.

About one adult in thirteen met the syndrome bar. High uric acid proved the strongest single predictor, tripling the odds, ahead of kidney disease, female sex, and smoking. The link ran strongest to the metabolic traits rather than to sleep or mood. A cheap, routine blood test may thus serve early risk spotting.
pmc-13297915:
András Telcs sets out a 2026 method for applying a nonnegative partial information decomposition, called MAR-PID, to continuous variables. Quantile binarization turns each variable into a balanced binary tree at a chosen depth, so binary target pieces can be analysed and then brought back. The pipeline covers channel estimation, bit-level computation, projection, and aggregation.

Worked cases involving XOR and mixed redundancy and synergy show how the approach separates information patterns that signed interaction measures can blur together. Telcs stresses that the values are estimates drawn from data at finite resolution. Related summary measures are named as future work rather than developed here, which keeps the scope clearly bounded for readers.
pmc-13298115:
Kyeong Min Han and colleagues ask whether psoriasis raises colorectal cancer risk, in a 2026 nationwide Korean cohort study. Insurance data from 2002 to 2019 supplied more than sixteen thousand patients with psoriasis and four matched controls for each. Weighting balanced other health and social factors between the groups.

Colorectal cancer appeared at comparable rates in both groups, and the adjusted estimate showed no increased risk from psoriasis. Subgroup checks by age, sex, income, region, and comorbidity burden gave the same null pattern. The authors conclude psoriasis alone does not justify extra colorectal screening beyond standard recommendations, even where cancer burden is high.
pmc-13298515:
Stefania H. Caceres and co-authors measure how common endo-periodontal lesions are at a Buenos Aires teaching hospital, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Such lesions connect the tooth's inner tissues with its supporting gum tissues through a pathological pathway. Consecutive new periodontics patients received clinical and X-ray examinations during a three-month window.

About one participant in seven had at least one affected tooth. Most affected patients also carried advanced, generalised gum disease of faster-progressing grades. Statistical analysis flagged advanced periodontitis stage as a potential risk indicator for these lesions. The authors note evidence on causes, diagnosis, and treatment for the condition remains limited overall.
pmc-13299215:
Printed patches loaded with plant extracts could dress burn wounds while feeding them healing compounds, report Roxana Colette Sandulovici and a large team in a 2026 formulation study. They extruded alginate emulgels containing calendula, chamomile, plantain, sea buckthorn, and St John's wort extracts into flexible patches set with calcium.

The patches came out uniform, bendable, and able to swell and pass water vapor at 1270 g per square metre daily, a rate suited to moist wound care. Polyphenols seeped out steadily, reaching 64.42% release over twenty-four hours, and antioxidant activity beat the unprinted gel. Skin cells tolerated lower doses well, with viability above 90%, supporting preclinical follow-up.
pmc-13299315:
Qiankun Liu, Mengyuan Zhu, Dongchao Ji, and Libo Jiang propose a triclustering model for gene expression data measured across genes, time, and conditions, in a 2026 methods paper. Standard module-finding tools often ignore how temporal, spatial, and environmental dimensions interact. Their approach uses a multivariate Gaussian mixture with polynomials describing change over time.

A model selection criterion chooses the number of clusters, and heavy injected noise in simulations failed to shift that choice or spawn false modules. The method recovered planted structure in simulated data and found distinct expression modules in a real plant dataset. The authors offer the framework for hunting coordinated regulatory programmes.
pmc-13299715:
Hao-Rui Gao and colleagues test how chilli's active compound affects black soldier fly larvae raised on high-fat feed, in a 2026 insect study. These larvae convert food waste into protein and fat-rich biomass, and Chinese food waste often arrives both fatty and spicy. Capsaicin doses ranged from very low to moderate across the feeding trials.

Low doses barely changed growth, development, or conversion efficiency. Higher doses weakened the growth boost that fatty feed normally gives. Strong doses also trimmed major amino acid shares in parts of the body and shifted fatty acid ratios noticeably. The results guide substrate tuning when farms process spicy, fatty waste streams.
pmc-13299815:
Circular RNA molecules, once written off as splicing accidents, act as control hubs in heart disease, review Camilo Rebolledo and Luis A Salazar in a 2026 article. These closed RNA loops resist breakdown, concentrate in specific tissues, and influence genes by sponging microRNAs, scaffolding proteins, and occasionally encoding small peptides.

Across heart failure, heart attack, scarring, rhythm disorders, and drug-induced heart damage, particular circular RNAs track with harmful growth, inflammation, cell death, and matrix buildup, and others with repair. Their stability in body fluids makes them attractive blood biomarkers and drug targets. The authors list the field's obstacles: spotty functional proof, inconsistent methods, and messy naming.
pmc-13300115:
M Ziacchi and others test a new absorbable antibiotic envelope for implanted heart devices in animals, in a 2026 animal study. Beyond fighting infection, the envelope should support healthy pocket healing and device stability. Sheep implants were examined over thirteen weeks for capsule growth, inflammation, breakdown, and device movement, joined by lab germ challenges.

Capsules matured normally, inflammation stayed mild, and both new and standard envelopes vanished fully by the final check. The new envelope fitted curved surfaces far better and erased every tested bacterial strain. Drug release lasted at least a week with low body-wide exposure, unlike the standard's quick burst. Procedural benefits are suggested.
pmc-13301015:
A Menezes Junior and co-authors review sudden death risk in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a 2026 paper. Current prediction models miss the tissue level story. So the authors searched four databases for studies tying death or serious rhythm events to scar burden on magnetic resonance imaging. They sought studies on blood flow reserve on perfusion scans, or on immune and gene expression signatures. Twenty-five studies made the cut from 289 records.

Deaths were uncommon overall but clustered in patients carrying adverse tissue features. Heavier scar alone predicted sudden death and appropriate defibrillator therapy beyond standard variables. Flow reserve ran impaired where events and scar concentrated. Tissue studies showed more killer T cells, inflammatory macrophage dominance, and switched on cell death pathways beside disarrayed, scarred muscle. Widening the narrowed outflow tract eased gradients without erasing risk when scar or microvascular trouble persisted. The authors propose a substrate framework for registries.
pmc-13301515:
V La Fazia and co-authors count heart tracing spikes during pulsed field ablation in a 2026 two center study. Across 411 procedures with two catheter types, nineteen episodes of ST segment elevation appeared, the signature of a coronary artery clamping shut in spasm, a feared quirk near vessels. Most events struck while ablating in the coronary sinus or along the mitral isthmus and cavotricuspid isthmus, all near coronary arteries. Protocol demanded phenylephrine then intravenous nitroglycerin.

Speed decided outcomes. Seventeen episodes were treated within about a minute and closed without complication. The two recognized late, at eight and eleven minutes, caused a ventricular fibrillation needing a shock and a complete heart block needing temporary pacing. Every elevation melted within two minutes of the nitrate dose, and follow-up found no lingering damage. The authors' lesson is vigilance: the event is uncommon, visible, and reversible if the team reacts at once.
pmc-13301815:
Maqsudur Rahman and a large team offer, in a 2026 review, a map of the computer systems needed to run learning that mixes quantum and classical machines. Such hybrid pipelines split work between standard chips and quantum hardware, which creates hard problems in timing, memory, and moving data. Medical imaging serves as the main test field for judging readiness.

The team screened 364 records and kept 40 studies from 2020 to 2025, sorting each by system layer and how far testing had gone. Only eight studies used medical data directly; the rest aimed at medicine or were general systems work. Support looked strongest for running hybrid jobs, sharing quantum machine time, and wrapping work so others can repeat it. Evidence stayed thin for real clinical running, remote quantum access, and safe sharing between users.
pmc-13302015:
An oral targeted drug keeps working in older sarcoma patients, Mehmet Mutlu Kidi and colleagues report from four Turkish cancer centers in a 2026 real-world study. They reviewed 109 people aged sixty-five and up with advanced soft tissue sarcoma who took pazopanib between 2010 and 2022. Response, survival, and side effects were the measures that mattered.

Tumors shrank measurably in 11.0 percent and disease control reached 45.9 percent of patients. Median progression-free survival was 4.11 months and overall survival 7.85 months across the group. Survival slid steeply with age band, yet fitness for daily activity, not birthdays, best predicted who lived longest. Severe side effects touched 27.5 percent, led by hypertension, with no drug deaths.
pmc-13302315:
M Van Der Graaf and a large registry team compare two commercial pulsed field ablation systems head to head in a 2026 one-year study. Both systems isolate the lung veins to treat atrial fibrillation, but long-term comparisons between brands were missing. Patients received either the FARAPULSE or the PulseSelect system at multiple centres.

The registry included 428 first-time ablation patients treated during 2024, split fairly evenly between the systems. Total procedure times ran longer with one system, although analysis tied that gap to mapping use and centre habits rather than the device itself. Serious early complications were rare in both groups. Rhythm recurrence struck about a third of patients in each group over a year, with no meaningful difference between systems.
pmc-13304215:
Islam Elmitwalli, John A. Ruth, and Gabriela Moraru present a 2026 case of Kawasaki disease in a young infant with unusual signs. The illness inflames blood vessels in children and usually shows a blotchy rash, but ring-shaped rashes and seizures are rare.

A five-month-old girl arrived after five days of high fever with a target-like rash and convulsions that mimicked brain infection and other rash syndromes. Young infants often lack the full classic feature set, which delays recognition. The case urges doctors to keep Kawasaki disease in mind when fever, odd rashes, and seizures appear together in early infancy.
pmc-13306015:
Candice D Fike, Frederick E Barr, and Judy L Aschner review in 2026 whether the amino acid L-citrulline can protect children at risk of blood vessel disease. Such disease follows blood, heart, and lung disorders in infants, and death rates remain high despite better care. Citrulline feeds production of nitric oxide, a molecule that keeps vessels relaxed and healthy.

Evidence is reviewed for three groups: children having heart bypass surgery, premature infants facing lung-related pulmonary hypertension, and children with sickle cell crises. The review also considers understudied settings such as kidney disease. Citrulline raises the supply of arginine, the direct raw material for nitric oxide. The authors set out where trials stand and which questions about dosing, timing, and patient selection remain open.
pmc-13306215:
Robert Vučina reviewed lab studies on olive and pomegranate compounds blocking enzymes in a 2026 systematic review. Both plants carry polyphenols long tied to health effects, and the review asks how widely their enzyme actions reach.

Compounds such as oleuropein, hydroxytyrosol, punicalagin and ellagic acid slowed inflammation enzymes tied to pain pathways in the gathered studies. Brain-related enzymes, sugar-handling enzymes and the drug-processing cytochrome P450 family were also slowed. Benefits for nerve protection and diabetes care look possible, yet the P450 effects warn that food extracts could interact with common medicines.
pmc-13306915:
Yeeli Mui and co-authors argue in 2026 that powerful GLP-1 weight-loss drugs need a systems view if obesity care is to last. The medicines produce large weight loss and are reshaping clinics, markets, and policy quickly. Their paper applies systems thinking habits to promises, pitfalls, and hidden feedback loops.

Heavy reliance on drug treatment alone risks a costly, reactive model that leaves root causes untouched and widens health gaps. The authors map mental models and missing connections that steer current obesity management. Dietitians appear as a critical but underused workforce, blocked by structural barriers. Suggested changes include systems training, links to local food resources, and payment reform. Elevating dietitians as community advocates also features in their plan for fairer, more durable care.
pmc-13307615:
Daniel Petek and co-authors ask in 2026 whether burning around the kneecap during total knee replacement truly removes nerve tissue at the outer edge of the cap. In a randomised trial with 19 patients, tissue was cut either before or after the burning step, and a blinded expert checked the samples.

Nerve fibres turned up in soft tissue in every sample, no matter which order the steps took in theatre. Burned samples showed focal heat harm, yet clear nerve fibres still stayed in place after the burn. Counts did not differ in a firm way between groups. Standard burning may thus fail to cut pain signals as surgeons often assume it does.
pmc-13307715:
Enrico Gugliandolo and co-authors pilot in 2026 a plasma-derived joint treatment for sport horses with chronic degenerative joint disease. Ten client-owned horses received one injection of an alpha-2-macroglobulin enriched preparation into the affected joint. Lameness, flexion response, swelling, and function were followed for up to six months in field conditions.

Several clinical measures improved over time in the treated horses. Joint fluid sampled a month after treatment showed within-horse drops in markers of inflammation, tissue breakdown, and pain. Comparison horses did not receive the same fluid analysis, and allocation was not randomised. The authors therefore label the findings exploratory and hypothesis-generating, not proof of a treatment effect. Larger randomised trials in more uniform horse groups come next. The preparation targets the enzyme cascades that digest joint tissue, beyond simple symptom control.
pmc-13307915:
Binjie Wu and colleagues review neutralising antibodies against Rift Valley fever virus in 2026, a mosquito-borne virus with no approved human vaccine or targeted drug. Antibodies drawn from immunised animals and healed patients were set side by side for target, strength, and shielding. The virus wrecks livestock breeding and can blind or kill people.

Most strong antibodies aim at the two coat proteins that mediate cell entry. They work by blocking dock binding, freezing the entry gear, or stopping membrane fusion outright. Two lead candidates blocked virus at tiny doses and shielded rodents against lethal, aerosol, and mother-to-offspring challenge. Two-headed antibodies and pairings raised potency and the barrier to viral escape. Left problems include virus escape, antibody heat staying power, and testing in better animal models. The authors map a route from lab antibodies toward clinical leads.
pmc-13308515:
Eve Namisango and co-authors test in 2026 a phone based palliative care tool, mPallCare, for people with advanced cancer in the Bidibidi refugee settlement in Uganda. Over six weeks, 32 patients gave symptom and outcome reports through village health workers, and clinic teams saw the data on a shared dashboard.

Patients finished 84.9 percent of symptom reports asked of them, and total reports reached about two thirds of the plan. Headache, muscle pain, and dizziness topped the symptom list for this small group of patients. Staff and patients both liked the tool for better talk and steadier care. Weak signal, rough translation, and sync faults need fixes before wider rollout.
pmc-13308615:
Gro-Hilde Severinsen and co-authors assess in 2026 the rollout of a shop bought artificial intelligence tool that spots bone fractures, in a large Norwegian health trust. They tracked buying, set up, and launch from 2020 to 2024 with 65 talks, site watches, and file checks, all framed by a known rollout model.

Clinician trust, fit with daily workflow, clear task splits, and digital readiness all helped the launch take hold in clinics. Thin proof files for approved tools, fear of skill loss, and skewed payment drives held it back in places. The frame caught social and tech knots well, yet it missed how workflows and views shift over time, so tweaks are needed.
pmc-13309415:
Mustafa Öz and colleagues review feed-based ways to protect farmed fish from pollutants in a 2026 article. Farmed fish now meet farm chemicals, industrial waste, and tiny plastic particles in their water. Drugs alone cannot handle such mixed exposure, so diet-based defense has drawn interest.

Plant compounds, select amino acids, and trace elements can switch on the fish body systems that break down poisons and repair cell damage. Gut microbes and immune health also shape how well these defenses work. Results differ by fish species, so one recipe will not fit all farms. The authors present tailored feeding plans as a way to cut drug use and keep fish resilient.
pmc-13310915:
Ke Zhou and co-authors review how gut germs drive cancer drug resistance in a 2026 paper. Cancer care often fails when tumors stop responding to chemo, immune, or targeted drugs. Gut germs can change that outcome by breaking down drugs, tuning immunity, altering host drug handling, and reshaping the tumor setting.

Some germ types switch off chemo drugs directly, while germ products rewire survival paths in tumor cells. Diet change, helpful germs, stool transplant, and smart drug carriers are under study as counters. Joining germ data with tumor data may let doctors predict resistance and tailor care. Human proof remains early.
pmc-13311115:
Yvonne A. B. Buunk-Werkhoven and colleagues sort diet patterns in young children and their link to oral health habits in a 2026 study. Diet and tooth health shape each other in growth, yet care often treats them apart. Parent reports from Kaunas, Lithuania, were used to find food groups and test ties to family traits.

Reports covered 420 children aged 5 to 12 years, scored on 17 food items. Three patterns emerged: healthy core foods, poor drinks and snacks, and dairy foods. Parent schooling type linked to healthier patterns, while older child age linked to weaker patterns. Good oral habits tracked healthy foods and clashed with poor snacks.
pmc-13311215:
De-Jing Yuan and co-authors report their 2026 trial testing whether writing down good daily events helps older heart patients who feel anxious. Poor mood can slow recovery after heart disease care.

A total of 309 older patients with coronary heart disease and anxiety were split into two groups, with 154 asked to record positive events. Mood, confidence, and how well patients followed treatment were checked at three and six months after discharge. The recording group felt less anxious and scored higher on confidence and treatment-following scales. The low-cost habit may support both mood and heart recovery in older patients.
pmc-13311615:
Nitsuh Kassahun, Atsedemariam Andualem, and Melsew Dagne Abate report a 2026 study of thinking problems in adults with asthma in northwest Ethiopia. Night symptoms can wreck sleep, and poor sleep can dull the mind.

The team surveyed 635 adult asthma patients at several hospitals from June to August 2024, using interviews and chart review. About a third, 32.9 percent, showed impaired thinking in this group. Poor sleep quality carried over fourfold higher odds of impairment after adjustment, and male sex raised odds by about half. The authors urge routine sleep and thinking checks in asthma clinics.
pmc-13311815:
Giovanni Ragozzino and Edi Mattera write a 2026 letter arguing that fatty liver disease belongs in the staging of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome. The staging now in use leaves the liver out.

Fatty liver, they note, is a primary metabolic organ disease that worsens insulin resistance, skews blood fats, feeds low-grade inflammation, and harms vessel lining. Its scarring stages predict heart and overall death about as strongly as classic risk factors. Because it is common in obesity and diabetes, leaving it out can park high-risk patients in early stages. Adding liver status could sharpen the staging's honesty.
pmc-13312915:
Niklas Bogovic and colleagues describe, in a 2026 study, a 3D human liver model built to expose the role of Kupffer cells in fatty liver disease. Animal and flat cell models miss the cell-to-cell interactions that drive metabolic liver disease toward its inflamed, scarring stage. The team grew spheroids combining liver cells, stellate cells, vessel-lining cells, and Kupffer cells, the liver's immune cells. They pushed them toward healthy, fatty, and inflamed states.

The spheroids organized themselves in patterns resembling real liver tissue. Fat loading was strongest under fatty conditions. The inflamed state brought the heaviest inflammatory and scarring signals. One messenger, TNF-alpha, rose most clearly in step with Kupffer cells. Cell injury markers, by contrast, tracked severity rather than Kupffer cells alone. Scar-related proteins, including fibronectin, increased as disease deepened. The platform gives researchers a controlled system for dissecting who does what in this disease.
pmc-13314415:
Daniel O. Omokpariola reviews how climate swings shape the food and health of herding peoples in dry Africa in a paper from 2026. Livestock anchor food security and diet quality in arid and semi-arid lands, yet the paths from herds to human nutrition under climate stress were scattered across studies.

The review followed PRISMA rules and searched five databases for work from 2006 to 2026, keeping 60 studies for close reading. Outcomes spanned household diet variety and food security marks, plus milk intake, micronutrient gaps, and child growth faults such as wasting and stunting. The evidence shows herds feed families through linked paths, both by giving milk and meat and by giving income for other foods. The synthesis gives policy makers a clearer map of where climate shocks cut nutrition first.
pmc-13314515:
Hailin Zhu and colleagues review how immune and tumor cells talk through surface pairs to rewire cancer metabolism, in a 2026 journal article. Drug resistance in cancer cannot be blamed on tumor genes alone; the living setting around the tumor teaches it to adapt.

Signals passed by ligand and receptor pairs link inflammation, checkpoints, and chemical messengers to fresh tumor traits. These axes can reshape how tumors burn sugar, fats, and amino acids and handle redox stress, backing growth, survival under therapy, and escape from immune attack. Lactate-based signals, macrophage-made messengers, and checkpoint paths such as PD-L1 stand out in the review. The authors argue that cutting these talk lines may break resistance where tumor-only drugs fail.
pmc-13314615:
José Tomás Garrido Santos, Daniel Tornero, and Marie Karam review the gut-brain axis in stroke in a 2026 journal article. Gut microbes steer immune, metabolic, and brain inflammation work, and a skewed gut mix seems both to precede stroke and to be caused by it, forming a loop.

Microbe products such as short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan offshoots set the firing state of microglia and of border macrophages that guard brain vessels. Those border cells, above all the ones hugging vessels, keep the blood-brain barrier tight and watch for threats, yet they have drawn less study than microglia. Diet strongly shapes the gut mix and thus brain immune tone. The review frames gut care, from food to microbe therapy, as a live route to soften stroke harm.
pmc-13315615:
Chen-Kang Chang and Ching-Lin Wu present Taiwan's 2025 report card in 2026 on physical activity for children and youth aged 6 to 18 years. Grades were given for ten core global indicators plus one extra, using national surveys and government data from 2022 to 2025 and shared grading rules.

Overall activity earned an F and sedentary behavior a D minus, while school support scored A plus and government strategy A minus. Several areas, such as active play and active transport, lacked enough data for a grade. The contrast between strong institutional support and weak daily behavior is the central finding for policy.
pmc-13316215:
Carl-Fredrik Flach and colleagues compare in 2026 two ways to use sewage for tracking antibiotic resistance, against clinical rates. Lab testing of patients anchors resistance management but is missing in much of the world for lack of resources, and sewage checks could fill the gap cheaply.

Sewage from ten European countries was tested both by growing E. coli isolates for drug sensitivity and by metagenomic sequencing of resistance genes. Results were set against clinical resistance rates for four drug classes, including aminopenicillins and fluoroquinolones. Combining both sewage views may mirror clinic rates best.
pmc-13318015:
Johan Ljunggren and a Swedish team scan, in a 2026 population study, how kidney function relates to 791 small molecules in blood. Waste buildup may be the bridge from weak kidneys to heart disease. Three community cohorts gave 3,444 people for a discovery and validation design.

Ninety-six molecules tied to filtration rate in the same direction across both classic statistics and a genetics-based causal check, nearly all rising as kidney function fell. Beyond creatinine itself, a few modified amino compounds topped the list, and five pathways lit up, two in amino acid handling. The hormone ratio of cortisol to cortisone also shifted. Several flagged molecules may help explain the heart risk that shadows kidney decline.
pmc-13318915:
Ying Dong leads a large team reporting a 2026 decade-long field study of legume planting on reclaimed coal mine land. The Shanxi site compared natural restoration with alfalfa and villose vetch planting. Soil structure, nutrients, microbe diversity, and plant growth were tracked. Such green manures are common in low-resource farming.

Legume planting, especially alfalfa, clearly raised plant biomass. In the top soil layer, organic carbon rose by 23.84 percent and total phosphorus by 47.17 percent under alfalfa in the reported values. Large soil aggregates grew by 36.56 percent in wet sieving tests. Alfalfa also boosted bacterial diversity and lignin breakdown capacity. Soil properties and microbes together drove plant growth differences. The authors back legumes as a natural reclamation tool.
pmc-13320015:
Lisa J Asbroek and co-authors lay out a study plan in a 2026 protocol on late harms after childhood stem cell transplant for blood cancers. Survivors face high risks of sugar and fat illness, vessel harm, and faster aging, yet past counts swing widely and harms were rarely checked together in one group. Modifiable risks such as habits and body swelling also stay unclear.

Two Dutch survivor groups will be joined, one of 102 people treated before 2002 and one of about 120 treated in the two decades after, all seen at a late effects clinic. Checks will count how often each harm shows, how often they overlap, and which treatment, habit, and swelling factors track with them. Clear counts could sharpen lifelong follow up care.
pmc-13320215:
Yuan Chai and co-authors report a light based slicing method for clear solids in a 2026 study that turns a flaw into a tool. Scattered light has long been seen as a foe in laser cutting, since it blurs the cut. Guided scattering, seeded on purpose and read against the main beam, was used here to place cuts with far finer depth control.

The method cut slots as thin as a few billionths of a meter scale features in the tests described, far finer than past depth limits for clear solids. Waste from slicing solid blocks into wafers fell from near a third of the mass to under one percent in the reported runs. Gains could reshape how laser crystals, solar cells, and chips are cut.
pmc-13320315:
Danni Wu and co-authors gather best proof on getting patients fit before stem cell transplant in a 2026 evidence summary. Transplant care strains the body hard, and a three part build up of exercise, food tuning, and mind support may raise reserves before the strain hits. Past proof sat scattered across guides and trials, so a wide sweep joined it into one practice set.

Eleven sources, from one full guideline and two expert accords to trials and reviews, were drawn from sources spanning 2015 to 2025 and read for best steps. Proof was sorted into five fields, from team setup and exercise dose to food, mind care, and safety notes, yielding 34 clear practice points. The set gives wards a ready base for personal build up plans.
pmc-13320415:
Frédéric Frappart and colleagues present, in 2026, a public dataset of satellite time series for more than fourteen hundred farm fields in southwest France. Monitoring crops from space supports food security, yet large Earth observation datasets need heavy preprocessing that shuts out many potential users. Ready-made field-level series lower that barrier.

The data combine radar images from Sentinel-1 with optical images from Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 at ten to thirty metre resolution, revisited every few days. Vegetation indices and biophysical variables were averaged for each field over several years. Field boundaries and crop types came from the French land parcel register, and processing was done by a specialist firm. The set is deposited in a national open repository for agronomists, environmental researchers and policy users.
pmc-13320515:
Sophie Franziska L’habitant leads a 2026 simulation study on team size during cardiac arrest care outside hospital. Crews must act fast on five invasive steps, from shock delivery and airway fitting to vein access and drug preparation. The study asked whether larger crews finish those steps sooner.

At three training centres in Germany, 210 paramedic students formed 59 teams of two to five members for a standard arrest drill. Mean total time fell step by step, from over six minutes for pairs to just over two minutes for five-person crews. Earlier vein access and drug work drove most of the gain. Every team finished all tasks, and four or five member crews worked fastest.
pmc-13321015:
Louise P.M. da Cunha and co-authors compare two growth charts for preterm babies in a 2026 study. The Fenton and INTERGROWTH charts both judge birth weight for gestational age, but they can place the same baby in different classes. Records for 2529 preterm infants admitted from 2018 to 2021 were scored on both charts.

Overall agreement was fair, with a mean bias of minus 0.08 in Z-scores and slight overestimation by the INTERGROWTH charts. Gaps widened in the smallest babies; among extremely preterm infants classed as small, half fell outside the agreement limits. Fenton tended to give higher scores there, softening how severe low weight looked. Agreement was strong for average and large babies, above all in more mature preterm groups.
pmc-13322215:
Maksim V. Zakhartsev and colleagues automate cell counting in an industrial methane eating culture in a 2026 study. Makers of single cell protein from natural gas must watch the mix of cell shapes in Methylococcus capsulatus KN2 cultures, a slow and subjective job by microscope. A vision network was trained for the task instead.

The network learned from 250 microscope images holding 50,410 labelled objects across nine cell shapes. On held back images it reached a precision of 0.87 and recall of 0.85 in weighted scores. pmc-13322615:
Elsa Carolina Landeros Gálvez and co-authors report a mite skin disease case in a dog from Coahuila, Mexico, in a 2026 veterinary report. Canine demodicosis follows overgrowth of Demodex mites that normally live in hair follicles. The adult mixed breed female dog had two bare patches near the nose and mouth, with no sign of secondary infection.

Deep skin scrapings under the microscope showed two mite species together, Demodex canis and Demodex cornei, told apart by body shape and spine and throat features. The authors call it the first confirmed record of both species in domestic dogs in Coahuila state. The case adds a point to the map of mite diversity in Mexico.
pmc-13322915:
Alexander Schwärzler and co-authors compare milled guides with freehand placement of orthodontic anchor screws, in a 2026 preclinical study using micro-CT. Sixty temporary anchorage devices were placed in 30 dental models, either with computer-designed milled guides or by freehand work from an orthodontist and an oral surgeon.

Guided placement proved more accurate on almost every linear and angular measure of drift from the plan, in the team's statistical models. For freehand work, the oral surgeon placed devices more accurately than the orthodontist. Agreement between observers was excellent. The authors argue that milled guides could bring real clinical gains for single-session guided work, whatever the operator's background.
pmc-13323015:
Zhaoting Gong and Yuyan Xiong review the fat layer around the heart as a treatment target, in a 2026 article on epicardial adipose tissue. This depot sits between heart muscle and the inner pericardium, close to the heart, with a secretion profile unlike other visceral fat.

The review covers its anatomy and normal roles, imaging methods for measuring it, and its links with cardiovascular disease. Because this fat can both protect and harm the heart, its amount and activity may serve as a biomarker for risk. The authors discuss ways to shrink or calm this tissue, while noting that proof of benefit from targeting it directly is still building.
pmc-13323115:
Johannes Lachmann and his team report, in 2026, how paediatric practices in Germany were recruited into a study aiming to raise HPV vaccination rates. Recruiting medical practices is a known weak point in intervention research, with little published evidence on what works. Their study, called InveSt HPV, targeted practices in Bremen and chosen Bavarian districts.

Practices were contacted by post and through the professional association for child and youth doctors, with payments up to two hundred euros per person. Fourteen of thirty-nine Bremen practices and a quarter of one hundred Bavarian practices joined, giving an overall rate just over a quarter. Staff take-up inside joined practices exceeded ninety percent. Practices most often credited association outreach, and motives included raising vaccination rates and wanting the training. Phone follow-up added few recruits despite high effort.
pmc-13324215:
Gheorghe-Andrei Dan writes on the state of research and medical care in countries hit by war, in a 2026 article opening with a Sartre quotation on who dies in war. Health as a human right rests on access, equity, community voice, joined-up care, affordability, cross-sector action and state duty, the author notes.

Heart disease, once cast as a rich-country problem, now kills mostly in low and middle income countries, a shift the article ties to poverty from conflict and disaster. Poor diet, high stress, weak care and heart-damaging infections drive younger deaths there. Many such countries face infection and chronic disease burdens at once, while war hollows out the clinics and studies meant to answer them.
pmc-13324315:
Hong-Mi Choi and co-authors test an AI electrocardiogram tool for cutting needless heart testing before non-heart surgery, in a 2026 cost and use study at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. Records covered 41,218 patients and 46,135 ECG-surgery pairs from 2020 to 2021.

The algorithm scored eight heart conditions and labelled 92.3 percent of cases low risk in the cohort data. Cases were sorted by whether advanced imaging followed and what it found, against a thirty-day outcome joining death and unplanned artery intervention. The authors ask whether AI-flagged low-risk patients can safely skip echocardiography, CT angiography and similar tests, trimming cost and delay without raising post-surgery harm.
pmc-13325115:
Guiyang He and a large team test sheep placenta vesicles as a skin treatment in a 2026 study. Tiny extracellular vesicles can carry healing signals without cells, but human sources raise ethical, cost, and scale problems.

Sheep placenta vesicles measured about 150 nm across and carried typical vesicle markers. Their RNA and protein loads leaned toward regrowth and anti-inflammatory pathways. In cell tests the vesicles sped skin cell growth, movement, and vessel formation. Mouse models of psoriasis-like damage, ultraviolet burns, and diabetic wounds all improved under treatment. The authors pitch sheep placenta as a plentiful, ethical supply for future skin therapies, pending human trials.
pmc-13326715:
Leslie K. Arrazolo and colleagues measure copper loss from catalysts during nitrate reduction in a 2026 study. Copper catalysts clean nitrate from water well, but quiet shedding could shorten their working life.

Single-atom copper and copper nanoparticles were compared with timed leaching checks and live X-ray spectroscopy. Both forms lost copper, mostly at the very start of electrolysis during fast reshaping. Nanoparticles consistently shed more than the single-atom form. Nitrate itself made reshaping and loss worse, which flags the liquid recipe as a durability lever. Single atoms largely recovered their spread-out form after voltage release, while particle surfaces stayed changed.
pmc-13326915:
Kondwani Kaitume Kaunda and team weighed how partners are told about syphilis while expecting in Blantyre, Malawi. Their 2026 mixed-methods study, run at four main health centers, asked women with syphilis on file at birth, and dug into their stories. Telling a partner means flagging a risk and the need for a test, which can stop repeat infection and spread to the child.

Among 131 women, 89.3% said they told their partners, but just 58.0% of partners got tested and about the same share got treated. Full partner care was done in only 30.5% of cases. Care was likelier for wed or cohabiting women. Age, HIV status, schooling, and birth results made no clear gap. Fear of backlash, shame, false beliefs, and fear of care held women back. Community talks and staff support helped. The team calls for shared yardsticks and combined programs to close this gap.
pmc-13327615:
Yuange Duan and colleagues challenge the idea that eukaryotic RNA editing originated as a defense against mobile genetic elements. Their 2026 commentary responds to a review by Bendich and Rogers, answering the claim that RNA editing serves mobile element defense with evidence against that theory. The piece acknowledges departing slightly from the original article's broader scope to focus on the editing-origin question.

The commentary weighs two fungal A-to-I editing systems: the OLD-ZAO system, partly associated with defense in some contexts, and the Tad2/3 system, which appears unrelated to mobile element defense. It also notes the dual role of RNA virus editing, which can both fight viruses and, by generating mutations, accelerate viral escape or drug resistance. The authors argue against treating antiviral and virus-promoting roles as separate, presenting them instead as stages of one process, and urge a revised account of editing's origin.
pmc-13327915:
Khali Mohammed and co-authors review how computing is reshaping parasite research in a 2026 article. Computer methods now offer fast, cheap, and scalable ways to study parasite biology, host contact, drug resistance, diagnostic markers, vaccines, and treatment targets. Toolkits span genomics, family-wide genome comparisons, family trees, and protein and molecule modeling.

Growing parasite databases sharpen genome annotation, blocker searches, and immune target forecasts, helping teams pick shared antigens and weak points across the main disease groups. Yet many pipelines rest on patchy, poorly labeled data and simple assumptions that miss life cycle and host effects. The authors insist computer findings must merge with lab data before guiding drugs or vaccines.
pmc-13329015:
Pei Liu and colleagues scan global safety reports in 2026 for drugs linked to bone metabolism disorders. Such disorders include weak or soft bones, and drug-caused cases are a growing worry. The team drew on United States reports from 2004 to 2024 and on the VigiAccess system, checking signals with four different methods.

In total, 55,783 reports were included, and 33 drugs showed steady positive signals in both sources. Named groups include bone drugs such as alendronic acid, antiviral drugs such as tenofovir, stomach acid drugs, and hormone-related cancer drugs. Signals clustered in anti-infective, cancer and immune, and muscle and bone drug classes. A Bradford Hill check was used to judge how plausible each link was.
pmc-13332115:
Ayden Watt and a large team tested simple mineral films against wet gangrene in a 2026 animal study. When blood-starved wounds get infected, tissue can liquefy and spread, and care today often ends in surgical removal or amputation.

The films release hydroxide ions, and one version also gives off oxygen and hydrogen peroxide from calcium peroxide in an alginate gel. In blood-starved rat skin wounds, both the peroxide film and a matched calcium hydroxide film restored closing to normal levels and cut bacterial load. In rabbit ear wounds, treated sites reached 75 to 80 percent closure in two and a half weeks against about 50 percent in controls, and cartilage and skin death fell sharply. Since plain hydroxide worked as well, the authors credit the alkaline attack on the wound environment rather than the extra oxygen.
pmc-13332815:
Syeda Abeerah Tanveer and Robia Ghafoor compared two nickel-titanium file systems for shaping curved root canals in a 2026 laboratory study using cone-beam CT. Files that wander from the canal's natural path can cause treatment errors, and opinion was split on which system stays truer.

Sixty single-rooted teeth with moderate curves of 10 to 30 degrees were split between the WaveOne Gold and ProTaper Next systems and scanned before and after preparation. WaveOne Gold shifted the canal less in the side-to-side direction at the 6 mm level and stayed better centered at the 9 mm level. Both systems mostly drifted toward the distal and tongue sides. Every shift measured stayed under the accepted safety limit of 0.15 mm. The authors judge both systems clinically acceptable and note the small statistical gaps may not matter in practice.
pmc-13333315:
Xander Verbeke and co-authors compared the scan signatures of lung inflammation after different lung cancer treatments in a 2026 retrospective study. Chemoradiation and immune checkpoint drugs can each inflame the lungs, and telling radiation injury from drug injury on a scan is notoriously hard.

The single-center study covered 71 patients who developed pneumonitis: 36 after chemoradiation alone, 17 after chemoradiation plus durvalumab, and 18 after pembrolizumab alone for stage IV disease. Lung inflammation struck 47.2 percent of the combined group against 22.1 and 15.5 percent in the single-treatment groups. Severe cases came earlier, were always two-sided, and linked to pre-existing lung scarring and lower breathing capacity. Computer measures of scan texture showed the combined group suffered worse damage in high-dose zones, hinting the two treatments amplify each other.
pmc-13333515:
Shuai Shi and colleagues compare two keyhole routes for extended thymus removal in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Coming up under the breastbone instead of between the ribs changes the view, the reach, and the soreness afterwards, and surgeons lack a clear verdict on which trade-off thymoma patients should take.

Between January 2020 and May 2024, 168 thymectomy patients were split almost evenly, 85 subxiphoid and 83 lateral intercostal, with similar tumors and baselines. The rib route ran the leaner operation: less blood loss, shorter drainage and hospital stay, and lower bills. The under-breastbone route won on comfort, with pain scores lower on days 1, 3, and 7. Complications ran close, at 8.24 versus 6.02 percent, myasthenia outcomes matched, and recurrence struck two patients in each group. The authors conclude both approaches are safe, with the intercostal route favouring efficiency and the subxiphoid route favouring a gentler first week.
pmc-13333615:
Cristina Jiménez-Moreno and colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional study of mobile phone habits and unfinished nursing care in Spain. Their focus is nomophobia, the uneasy fear of being without a phone, and whether it distracts nurses from care tasks.

The team surveyed 161 primary care and hospital nurses in Almería using the Nomophobia Questionnaire and the Unfinished Nursing Care Survey. Nurses showed moderate nomophobia and moderately high levels of unfinished care. Hospital nurses scored higher on nomophobia than primary care nurses, as did nurses who wanted to change units. Statistical modeling identified nomophobia as a predictor of unfinished care, which raises a practical patient safety concern for managers and educators.
pmc-13333715:
Ziyan Wu and co-authors characterized five wheat recurrent selection populations built to widen the crop's genetic base in a 2026 study. The populations descend from common wheat, spelt, French wheat, Tibetan semi-wild wheat, and spike-branched wheat donors, improved over 20 selection cycles.

The team measured farm traits and genotyped 94 materials, including selection lines and donors, plus 120 common wheat cultivars, using a 90K SNP array. Genetic distance and trait variation were mapped within and between populations. Twenty-three elite lines then served as parents in cross designs that compared matings within and across populations for hybrid vigor. Plant height and grain weight showed signs of convergent selection, while other traits kept wide variation. The work guides breeders pairing lines for stronger hybrids.
pmc-13334415:
Dhruva Govil and colleagues report a 2026 case of probable late-onset FMF presenting as recurrent sac inflammation. Late-onset cases are rare and often missed because symptoms resemble other germs or inflammatory diseases. Despite several hospitalizations, tests for germs and cancers ruled out other causes, including chest taps, a sac window, a pleural biopsy, and bone marrow analysis. Tissue study showed fibrous sac inflammation and chronic pleura inflammation with scarring, without signs of cancer. Colchicine treatment brought quick gains. Considering presentation and response to colchicine, clinically probable familial Mediterranean fever was diagnosed.
pmc-13334815:
Frances B Schulenberg and co-authors piloted a patient-led discussion model called ZIP in VA primary care in a 2026 trial-run study. Regular visits last about fifteen minutes, leaving little room for careful shared choices.

ZIP, short for Zeroing in on Individualized, Patient-Centered Decisions, was tried for lung cancer screening talks and blood pressure drug decisions. The single-center study enrolled 23 patients and 10 primary care physicians, taping visits and gathering survey and feedback. The team timed ZIP talks, checked whether all parts were completed, and scored choice quality with a standard questionnaire. Feedback themes judged acceptability from both sides of the conversation. The early-stage work tests whether guided, tailored discussion can fit inside real appointment slots.
pmc-13336415:
Kailong Lu and co-authors steered an electric methane conversion reaction by tuning nickel's oxidation state in a 2026 electrocatalysis study. Methane is both a fuel resource and a potent greenhouse gas, and turning it directly into two-carbon products at mild conditions is a prized goal.

The team reasoned that a nickel-oxygen dual site with moderate orbital mixing would split methane's first C-H bond and then couple carbons. Raising nickel's valence shifted its d band down; nickel oxyhydroxide hit the sweet spot, oxygenating methane capably without shedding its own oxygen as the dioxide would. The catalyst produced acetic acid at a Faradaic efficiency of 53.5 percent and a rate of 401.6 micromoles per gram per hour in the reported tests, running over 50 hours without structural decay.
pmc-13336815:
Xi Luo and co-authors sharpen CRISPR base editing in a 2026 study aimed at precise single-letter DNA changes. The team paired a flexible Cas9 variant, SpRY, with shortened cytidine deaminases.

That pairing could reach almost any cytosine but worked weakly at first. The editors performed well in both yeast and rice. More precise, flexible editors widen options for therapy, breeding, and basic research.
pmc-13336915:
Rui Peng and co-authors propose sliding layers to switch spin states in a 2026 theory study. Altermagnets split electron spins by direction without overall magnetization, a prized mix for fast, field-proof devices. The team used first-principles calculations on stacked copper fluoride layers.

Sliding one layer over another flips a built-in electric polarization. That flip directly reverses the d-wave spin splitting, and the splitting stays locked to its layer. Four stacked layers offer four polarization states, hinting at multi-state logic. Because sliding is nonvolatile, the state persists without power. Voltage-controlled sliding could give spintronic memory that is quick, dense, and frugal with energy.
pmc-13337015:
Tingting Chen and co-authors build a clear solid electrolyte that bends without leaking in a 2026 study. Their copolymer weaves hydrogen bonds and ion-dipole links among acrylamide, succinonitrile, a lithium salt, and methyl methacrylate.

Strong, clear solids suit safer batteries and smart windows.
pmc-13337315:

These inherited defects in telomere upkeep cause multi-system disease, and adult lung scarring is well known, but childhood lung involvement was poorly mapped. The European chILD-EU database supplied cases with confirmed or suspected gene variants.

Ten children carried variants across six telomere genes, including TERT and DKC1. In 6 of the 8 tested patients, telomere length fell below the 1st percentile for age in the cohort checks. Scans and tissue patterns varied widely, from ground-glass haze to cysts and emphysema-like change. The course was often severe: 7 of the 10 children needed long-term oxygen, 3 received stem cell transplants, and 4 died during follow-up.
pmc-13337715:
Bohan Li and colleagues mine United States safety reports for severe skin reactions tied to seizure drugs in 2026. Reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are rare but can be life threatening. Seizure drugs are often blamed, yet comparisons across drugs and timing patterns were thin.

Reports from early 2004 to mid-2024 were screened for drugs coded as suspect. Signal methods using odds ratios and a Bayesian network flagged drug and reaction pairs. A total of 6,212 cases passed cleaning and met both signal rules reported by the authors. Timing analysis then compared how soon reactions began across reaction types and individual drugs.
pmc-13337815:
Tao Liu, WenJing Zhang, and Rong Fu study mindfulness and distress among Chinese undergraduates in a 2026 survey. Mindfulness training often helps well-being, yet its workings under strong study pressure and family expectations were unclear. Culture is treated here as part of the mechanism, not background.

Stratified sampling drew 432 students from four universities. Scales measured mindfulness, distress, resilience, emotion control, support, pressure, and family expectations. Mindfulness linked to lower distress overall in the reported models. That link weakened under high study pressure and strengthened under high family expectations. Resilience and rethinking worries together carried much of the effect, with differences by gender and subject area.
pmc-13338215:
Yahya Khan leads a 2026 computer search for new blockers of PI3K alpha, a growth signal often faulty in lung cancer. Non-small cell lung cancer makes up about 85 percent of lung cancers as cited. Existing blockers face toxicity, resistance, and weak body handling.

Screening of 650,000 compounds by docking picked five leads with the strongest binding scores. Motion simulations over 100 nanoseconds and energy calculations suggested stable binding for all five in the reported modeling. Electronic and drug-likeness checks followed. The pipeline narrows a huge library to a handful of candidates ready for lab testing, rather than claiming proven drugs.
pmc-13339115:
Chiara Meneghini and colleagues reviewed molecular brain imaging in 2026 in genetic forms of Parkinson disease. Around 15 to 20 percent of Parkinson cases link to gene variants, which offer clues to disease mechanisms. The review searched PubMed and Scopus for imaging studies in carriers of SNCA, PRKN, PINK1, PARK7, LRRK2, and GBA1 variants, symptomatic and presymptomatic alike.

The goal was markers that separate genetic from sporadic disease and early signs of conversion to symptoms. Such markers could improve diagnosis, trial selection, and timing of future disease modifying treatments. The review maps what imaging can already show and where evidence remains thin.
pmc-13339515:
Marc B. Gros-La-Faige, Emmanuelle Génin, and Anthony F. Herzig benchmark free tools that call drug-gene variants in a 2026 study. Correct star alleles predict how a person handles medicines, and many callers claim that task. Four open tools were compared across genes and data types.

PyPGx and Aldy led overall in the reported tests, except for CYP2D6 where ursaPGx with its dedicated caller won. Against a commercial tool, the free leaders also scored better except again for CYP2D6. Filling missing data by imputation lifted chip and low-depth results to sequencing level. Ancestry effects were checked, guiding labs to the right caller per gene.
pmc-13339815:

Distinct responses mean metal antimicrobials could be tuned per metal rather than treated as interchangeable.
pmc-13340115:

Genome study of the mutant begins to explain the trade-off, supporting combination therapy design.
pmc-13341415:
How strongly young athletes see themselves as athletes relates to fear of reinjury, in a 2026 study by Antonia L. Dinulescu's team. Surveys went to 220 lately injured players with a mean age of 14.6 years, most playing soccer or basketball, using standard identity and kinesiophobia scales.

Athletic identity came to 54.70, a fairly strong score, while fear of reinjury stayed slight at 19.27 on average. No sex gaps showed. Fear scores rose weakly with age and with the identity facets of exclusivity and negative affectivity. Knowing that tightly bound athletic identity can accompany reinjury fear may help doctors pace return-to-play support.
pmc-13341615:
Eye socket cancers in Norway are charted over 22 years by Bendik Alvheim Sundfjord's team in a 2026 series. Medical records at Haukeland University Hospital from the years 1999 to 2020 yielded 76 patients in total, a yearly incidence of 0.30 per 100,000 people in Western Norway.

Median age at diagnosis was 64 years. Invading secondary tumors led at 46%, then lymphoproliferative disease at 24%, metastases at 16%, and primary orbital tumors at 14%. Surgery removed tumors in 55% of patients, radiotherapy reached 72%, and relapse or spread hit 42%. Five-year disease-specific survival was 59% overall for all patients but 82% for the lymphoproliferative group alone.
pmc-13341915:

Antibiotics improved symptoms but not the collapse, so bronchoscopy found and removed obstructive casts of plastic bronchitis. Lavage fluid identified Bordetella pertussis and Rhinovirus A with high confidence. Targeted therapy plus cast removal fully re-expanded the lung, with no recurrence over 6 months. Vaccination, the case shows, does not erase pertussis from the differential.
pmc-13342715:
Philippe Voruz and colleagues tracked thinking before and after COVID-19 in 2026 using the Swiss Lc65+ ageing study. The study spanned three waves from 2016 to 2024. Pandemic lockdowns worsened health gaps and posed fresh challenges to ageing minds. Analyses took in 1,940 people with full data.

Groups were 412 from Cohort 1 born 1934 to 1938 and 702 from Cohort 2 born 1939 to 1943. Cohort 3 born 1944 to 1948 added 826 people. Women made up 58 to 63 percent of each group. Thinking was read by the Mini Mental State Examination, with equations testing shifts and linked factors. Long term data split pandemic effects from normal ageing trends. The findings guide care for older adults whose thinking slipped during lockdowns.
pmc-13342815:
Yuan Liu and co-authors systematically review, in 2026, machine learning models that forecast recovery after spinal cord injury. Studies vary widely in outcomes, inputs, and checking methods, so the reviewers graded reporting quality and bias risk with tools built for prediction models.

Nineteen cohort studies met the bar, drawn from eight databases through May 2025. Reporting completeness ranged widely, and every study carried high bias risk, mostly from weak analysis choices. Only one study tested its model on outside data, sample sizes were never justified, and calibration was rarely shown. The reviewers see promise in the approach but urge bigger, stricter studies before clinics rely on these models.
pmc-13342915:
Xianzhi Liu and co-authors study ready-to-eat kiwifruit in 2026, asking why the fruit's eating window closes so fast. Gene readings for starch, ethylene, and energy steps matched the fruit behavior, marking routes handlers can target.
pmc-13343415:
Shixiong Zhou and colleagues talked in 2026 about low sky flight, from delivery drones to electric air taxis, below 1,000 metres and up to 3,000 metres. In 2025, registered drones in China passed 3.28 million, with flight hours hitting 45.3 million, up nearly 70 percent in a year. The low sky web links drones, satellite links and navigation, ground sites, and city airspace.

Safe growth needs smooth coordination across that web. China first named the low sky economy in its April 2024 work report, a policy milestone. The talk frames how rules, ground sites, and tech must line up for low sky flight to grow safely.
pmc-13344215:
Niclas Carlberg and colleagues assessed brain blood flow control in 2026 in women with preeclampsia and normal blood pressure pregnancies during pregnancy and one year postpartum. Brain harms of preeclampsia threaten pregnant women worldwide. Impaired brain blood flow control may add to adverse outcomes plus long term brain vessel disease. The multicentre, prospective, observational cohort drew women from the UPMOST and GoPROVE studies.

Women with preeclampsia were checked at diagnosis, with transcranial Doppler tests at inclusion and one year postpartum. Groups covered normal blood pressure pregnancy and preeclampsia with or without maternal harms, with blood flow control scored by an index. During pregnancy, mean index was higher in normal blood pressure pregnancies at about 7 versus about 6 in preeclampsia. The gap was under one. Postpartum patterns were weighed for persistence or recovery.
pmc-13346115:
Martin Selin and colleagues describe SmartTrap in a 2026 methods report, an optical tweezers system built to run precise experiments on its own. Optical tweezers can hold and move tiny particles and single molecules, yet they normally need constant handling by a trained operator.

SmartTrap links live three-dimensional tracking, custom electronics, and fluid handling so trials can continue for long periods with little help. Tests covered tasks such as DNA stretching, red blood cell bending, sizing particles, and measuring forces between colloids. Because the design is open source, other labs can copy it for larger studies with less operator bias.
pmc-13347615:
Edward Cunningham-Oakes and a large team bring gene sequencing into routine hospital care. Their implementation study was published in 2026. It covers bacteria reads in NHS hospitals. Older Sanger and mass methods checked the results. Antibiotic changes were tracked for months.

Results often backed current therapy. At times they left therapy unchanged. Still, they guided narrower prescribing. Gain was highest for patients with weak immunity.
pmc-13348215:
Iñigo Caballero Quiroga and colleagues present the complete genome of bacteriophage Shea, a virus that infects Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in an announcement published in 2026. Mud puddle water from Flushing, New York City, gathered in November 2017, yielded the phage after filtering, growth with its host. Repeated plaque cleaning, and cloudy plaques hinted at a dormant lifestyle.

The genome spans 43,333 base pairs in the reported assembly. The phage likely lives as a pseudolysogen, resting inside host cells for generations without joining the host genome before waking or being lost. pmc-13348415:

pmc-13350315:
Shunlin Lin and co-authors reported in 2026 a womb fibroid that turned fully into a fluid-filled cyst and fooled scans into suggesting an empty pregnancy sac. Their patient, a 42-year-old mother of two, had two months of irregular bleeding and new lower belly pain.

pmc-13350515:
Kerry A. Mullan and co-authors examined the immune fingerprints of a milder skin reaction to the seizure drug carbamazepine in a 2026 laboratory study. Reactions to this drug span a harmless-looking rash to life-threatening skin loss, and the severe form's immune basis is far better understood.

pmc-13351915:
Katie Lee and co-authors track recovery after front versus back neck fusion surgery in a 2026 cohort study. pmc-13352515:
Bereket Woldegbreal Taklu and co-authors design a protective skin for lithium metal battery anodes in 2026. Lithium metal promises top energy density, but spiky dendrite growth threatens safety. pmc-13352615:
Saeed Babaei and co-authors model how gas uptake warps kerogen, the organic matter in shale rock, in 2026. Storing gas forecasts go wrong if soaking gas reshapes the pores that hold it. pmc-13352715:
M M L Fochi and others tested an ultra-brief two-question screen for delirium in hospitalised older adults, in 2026. Delirium is common in older inpatients and linked to worse results, yet ward teams often miss it. A fast, standard check could catch cases that busy medical routines overlook.

pmc-13354015:
Debajyoti Banerjee led a 2026 study of vitamin D deficiency in children with TB in a high-burden setting. TB remains a major cause of childhood illness and death in countries such as India, and food shapes susceptibility through immune defences. Vitamin D supports white cell action and anti-germ defences beyond its familiar role in calcium balance.

The study checked deficiency rates in affected children and tested links with demographic and medical traits. Adult studies had already suggested an link, but childhood data were thinner. Child teams gain a clearer picture of how often deficiency goes with childhood TB and which children are most affected.
pmc-13354415:
Naveed Ahmad and others discussed the role of PET/CT imaging in myocarditis linked to antiphospholipid syndrome, in a 2026 letter. This rare heart swelling arises in an autoimmune clotting illness driven by defenders against vessel-lining cells, damaging heart muscle through complement pathways without necessarily forming clots.
