The letter sets out the medical and imaging clues that point toward this finding. Cardiologists gain a sharper approach to a rare illness where the wrong label can lead to the wrong care.
pmc-13354815:
Andres Meraz-Brenez and co-authors surveyed cancer doctors in Mexico in 2026 about using low doses of immune checkpoint drugs. These drugs have changed cancer care but cost so much that many patients in poorer countries cannot get them. Some proof hints that lower doses may still work, which could widen access.

Eighty-one doctors replied, and all named at least one block to using these drugs, most often cost or lack of coverage. Near half had given low doses, mainly to cut costs for patients. Yet many worried about safety and felt the proof and dosing guides were weak, so the authors call for firm trials and clear policy on low-dose use.
pmc-13355815:
Chang Liu and co-authors studied in 2026 a heat shock protein called Hspa1b that guards heart cells when blood flow returns after a blockage. That return, while vital, also injures the heart through two death paths: apoptosis and ferroptosis, an iron-driven path. The team tested mouse hearts and heart cells in dishes under low-oxygen stress.

Injury raised both Hspa1b and p53, a master death switch. Silencing Hspa1b made cell injury worse and boosted both death paths, while silencing p53 at the same time partly rescued the cells. The authors identify Hspa1b as a brake on p53-driven death and a possible drug target for heart protection.
pmc-13355915:
Poleth G Medrano-Madrid and co-authors report a 2026 case of Todd's paralysis, a temporary weakness after seizures that can look just like a stroke. Their patient, a 32-year-old woman with epilepsy, had lasting loss of speech and right-side weakness after several seizures, scoring six on a standard stroke scale. A head scan showed no bleeding or early stroke signs.

A brain MRI found no stroke or other damage, while a brain wave test showed seizure activity that had spread. After her anti-seizure drugs were adjusted with added valproate, seizures stopped and all weakness cleared. The authors stress this diagnosis in epilepsy patients, above all where advanced scans are lacking.
pmc-13358515:
Gabriella R. Rasmussen and co-authors present a 2026 study on lung cancer in people who have already had cancer once. As more people survive a first cancer, more face a second one in the lungs. The team used a huge national database to see how this group differs in how their lung cancer looks, is treated, and turns out.

They studied over 1.3 million patients with non-small cell lung cancer from 2010 to 2021. About one in five had an earlier cancer. That group tended to be older and to have smaller tumors found at an earlier stage. The findings can help doctors plan screening and care for cancer survivors.
pmc-13358615:
Li Xie and co-authors describe a refined breast rebuilding method in a 2026 paper. After mastectomy, surgeons can rebuild the breast with the patient's own belly tissue, a flap that keeps its blood supply through small vessels. For large, drooping breasts, one set of vessels may not feed the whole flap well. The team used two sets instead.

They reviewed 92 rebuilds done from 2022 to 2023: 21 with the double supply and 71 with a single one. All double-supply flaps survived, and patients in that group reported higher satisfaction. The paper sets out the technical points so other surgeons can judge when the extra work is worth it.
pmc-13359015:
Kenji Itao finds hidden order in how populations change in a 2026 study. Across the modern world, birth rates and death rates fall as countries develop, a shift called demographic transition. Most accounts were built on Western history. Itao used data from 237 countries and territories spanning 1800 to 2020 to test whether the pattern is truly global.

He finds two universal pathways that nearly all countries follow or switch between. One ruled until the mid-twentieth century, with high child deaths. The other, tied to schooling and rising income, has ruled since 1950. A simple model of the trade-off between children and education explains the switch between them.
pmc-13360815:
Hao Wang and co-authors hunt for gene markers of alcohol-caused liver cirrhosis in a 2026 study. This scarring of the liver lacks markers that tie it clearly to alcohol as the cause. The team first used a national health survey of 17,007 adults from 2017 to 2023 to weigh the alcohol link. Heavy drinking came with a far higher cirrhosis risk, roughly five times that of others.

They then mined four public gene datasets from liver tissue, using network analysis and three machine learning methods to pick marker genes. Picks were checked in a fresh set of 93 samples. The team also searched drug databases for compounds that match the markers and tested the fit on a computer. Such markers could sharpen diagnosis and point to new drugs for this disease.
pmc-13362015:
Mohanad Almaimani and Sadin Ayman Alamri review a kidney drug's wider promise in a 2026 paper. Finerenone blocks a hormone receptor whose overactivity drives inflammation and scarring across heart and kidney disease. Large trials already prove it protects kidneys and hearts in people with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes. The authors gather newer signs that its reach may extend further.

Signals include heart failure outcomes, reshaping of the heart's upper chambers, lung vessel biology, the tiny vessels of the eye, and metabolic problems. The authors grade this extra evidence with care. Much of it is early, from animal work, subgroups, or after-the-fact analyses of trials. The review separates solid ground from hopeful leads for doctors watching this drug class.
pmc-13362715:
Waraporn Chanakul, Nissaya Chuathong, and Kanyarak Prasertboonyai describe a 2026 food testing study built around a northern Thai green chili dip. They needed a clean way to measure benzoate, a preservative, in the dip. Their method shakes the sample in plain water with ultrasound, then reads the benzoate with ion chromatography, a lab separation tool. A structured trial design tuned the time, heat, and amounts.

The tuned method proved sharp and steady, with good recovery from spiked samples across repeat runs. A greenness score beat the standard solvent-based method, since water replaces organic solvents and no such waste is made. Stores and food labs could use it for routine checks of this and similar condiments.
pmc-13363715:
Dariusz Szukiewicz and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on how inflammation-driving diets may open the door to brain diseases. They use the dietary inflammatory index, a score for how strongly a diet fans or calms body swelling. Western-style eating scores high. The review follows the chain from such diets through a disturbed gut microbe mix to leaky gut and blood-brain barriers, and on to signaling along the gut-brain axis.

Once those barriers weaken, inflammatory signals can reach brain tissue and feed the slow damage behind diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. The authors gather the current proof for each link in the chain and mark where it is firm or thin. Their frame argues that diet scoring belongs in brain-risk research.
pmc-13364315:
Shuang Li and co-workers present CoDepth in 2026, a tool that judges depth from a single camera view inside the body during keyhole surgery. Two kinds of depth tools err in unlike ways. One draws sharp edges but fails on flat, bright zones. The other keeps fine texture but can bend the shape.

CoDepth blends the two by trust, giving more weight to the output it trusts most at each spot. Tests on a surgery data set beat single tools, and the blend held up on three more sets with no new training. It also stood up well to dark or noisy test views.
pmc-13364415:
Sofia Otavio and co-workers test a 2026 add in for printed dental plastics: a changed form of chitosan, a shell based sugar chain, dosed with phosphate groups. They blend it at two low doses into short and long use print resins. Then they check surface, strength, color, and germ kill.

The mix cut mouth germ counts by a clear gap, though it worked on touch, not at a range. It raised surface rough traits and wet ease. The low dose lost some strength, while the high dose held strength near plain resin. The add in suits short term dental prints.
pmc-13365515:
Zaid S Alajlan and others numerically tested failure load and contact stress beneath concrete footings on cohesionless soil, in 2026. Footing-soil link governs settlement, load room, and stress spread, yet classical solutions often overestimate edge stresses and ignore soil nonlinearity, growing cracking, and stiffness loss. Tests show non-uniform, saddle-shaped stress patterns, but design ways still assume uniform contact.

Numerical models captured changing footing stiffness and soil conduct, forecasting failure loads and contact stress distributions more realistically than uniform assumptions. The testing shows how stress redistributes as footings crack and soil yields. Built builders gain a refined basis for footing design on sandy soils.
pmc-13366215:
Chandrashekhar T. Sreeramareddy and others documented selling of oral nicotine pouches on Malaysian social media and e-commerce sites, in 2026. Oral nicotine pouches are marketed in high-income countries, but Malaysia now does not control them, leaving online ads largely unchecked. Grasp that selling is a first step toward policy.

Content study of e-stores, searched via Google Malaysia, Facebook, Reddit, TikTok, and Instagram in March and April 2024, coded brands, prices, discounts, and flavours. It also coded nicotine strength and selling claims, with three independent coders. The study reveals how pouches are promoted to Malaysian consumers. Policymakers gain evidence for regulating a product category that now escapes oversight.
pmc-13366415:
Havagiray Chitme and co-workers open in 2026 a work set on drug care and well life for folks with sugar ill. The ill and its harms test health sys world wide. Old herb care holds a deep store of plant goods that may help, and new lab tools can test them fast.

The set joins herb and old care proof with new routes like code drug design and net drug maps. Works span how plant goods act, how safe they are, and what they do in real cases. The aim is team care that blends old and new for better sugar paths.
pmc-13369915:
Helmi Ben Saad and co-workers warn in 2026 that war in the Middle East turns nuke plant risk from a thought case to a near threat, with water at its core. Gulf lands draw most fresh water from sea salt plants. A plant on the Gulf shore sits near many Gulf state caps.

pmc-13371015:
Zhiyi Liu and colleagues untangle how two regulators, SIAH1 and SIAH2, act on liver cancer through the protein PEG10 in a 2026 study. Both regulators bind PEG10, but whether PEG10 carries their effects was unknown. Cell tests, animal tumours, and patient samples were combined with protein binding and mutation experiments.

The work points to PEG10 tagging as a possible lever for future liver cancer treatments, tuned to block the harmful regulator while keeping the protective one.
pmc-13371515:
Kridipaka Sindhvananda and colleagues test AI simulated patients for teaching headache history taking in Thailand in a 2026 study. Scores for history taking and clinical reasoning, plus usability ratings, were compared before and after. Focus groups explored how students experienced the tool. The study gauges whether AI patients can safely expand practice for a skill that usually needs real patients.
pmc-13376115:
Chunmiao Luo and others review KIF23, a motor protein with roles in cancer and rare disease, in a 2026 paper. KIF23 drives cell splitting, cell part transport, and signals. In contrast, loss changes cause congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia type III and primary microcephaly through splitting failure. Regulation spans gene reading, epigenetics, and competing RNAs. Preclinical work supports KIF23 as a diagnostic and treatment target.
pmc-13377415:

Virus kills ruled the tale, not gene rides in viruses. Proof germs in the pit were rare in virus loads and mute when there. In their place, the war drove proof germs to stock strong shields. pmc-13380015:

She had taken the blood pressure drug lercanidipine for a long time. The drug is known to widen vessels and cause flushing and ankle swelling. The case raises the possibility that it can also trigger this skin pattern.
pmc-13380715:
M Vanmeenen and colleagues report a 2026 study of germs found on mobile nursing workstations in hospitals. These wheeled stations are used daily on wards, handled by many staff in many places, so they could carry germs between patients. The study measured how contaminated they actually are.

In total 327 micro-organisms were found, and a small share were classed as potential pathogens. None resisted antibiotics. pmc-13383215:

pmc-13384415:

pmc-13386615:

pmc-13387815:
Aoi Suenaga and Shoji Oura report a breast imaging sign that misled toward invasive cancer in a 2026 case report. pmc-13388415:

pmc-13390015:

pmc-13390115:

pmc-13390215:

A coat or additive that fights germs is of little use if the aligner cracks or softens in the mouth. The design lets readers judge protection and strength side by side. Each mix faced the same set of tests, so the ranks rest on a fair base.
pmc-13391715:

pmc-13392115:

Female trial participation matched or exceeded disease share in about two thirds of cases. pmc-13392415:
Abdul Hadi Hassan Mallick and colleagues report a 31-year-old man who lost sight in his left eye after cosmetic surgery on both eyelids. Testing showed strong vision in the right eye and no light perception on the left, with scans revealing thinning of the inner retina that fits a settled arterial blockage. The authors urge surgical teams to watch vision closely after eyelid work so any loss is caught at once.
pmc-13392915:
Anne-Laure Turpin and the Medit-Ageing Research Group tested whether eighteen months of learning a foreign language could protect memory in healthy older adults. On delayed word recall, the language group held steady while the comparison group slipped, a divergence that reached statistical significance. Within the language group, gains in that recall score tracked gains in blood flow through the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub. The authors read the pattern as language study helping preserve long-term memory in ageing, possibly by keeping hippocampal circulation strong.
pmc-13393415:
Claire Lallement, Thomas Jové, Cécile Pasternak, Sandra Da Re, and Marie-Cécile Ploy investigated how the jumping genes of the ISCR family switch on the enzyme that moves them. Several antibiotics trigger that SOS alarm, so treatment itself may loosen these elements to move. The authors frame the result as a starting point for understanding how resistance spreads under drug pressure.
pmc-13393915:
Soomar and co-authors present a 2026 prospective study of poisoning in children and adolescents treated at the largest poison control centre, based at Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Center in Karachi, Pakistan. The median age was 17 years, with boys and girls represented equally in the cohort. Most incidents happened at home, which the authors link to unsafe storage and unregulated access to toxic products. They identify factors tied to longer hospital stays and call for safer household storage, tighter regulation of poisons, and public awareness campaigns aimed at families.
pmc-13394815:

Blocking PARP or boosting SIRT1 restored vessel calm in the tests. Swelling markers and sticky vessel walls also eased. The authors suggest these levers could guard patients during cancer care.
pmc-13395315:
Jordan E. Rumford and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether immune cells named microglia are needed for eye repair in zebrafish. Rebuilding of cones went ahead much the same without microglia. Division of the support-cell pool dipped only modestly at some stages. A spare set of immune cells still showed up in mutant eyes after harm, though in smaller counts. Those stand-ins blur firm claims about microglia. The authors say backup responses may mask what microglia truly do.
pmc-13396115:
Yijun Quan and co-authors tackle a practical problem for British steelmaking, which is shifting toward melting scrap in electric furnaces: nobody knows exactly what is in each load of shredded scrap. Their 2026 study uses copper as the test case, since stray copper weakens finished steel.

Lab chemistry on every load is too slow and costly, so the team trained image-based methods on photos of fragmentized scrap, first cutting the images into pieces with segmentation software. The goal is a quick estimate of tramp elements, the unwanted metals mixed into scrap, from appearance alone. A reliable version could let mills sort loads before melting rather than reject steel after.
pmc-13396515:
Francesco Cesa and others offer stock-state quantum RAM for fast, fixable lookups in a 2026 paper. Quantum math needs swift file loads, but quantum RAM asks for huge kit, worse once error fixes join in.

The team shrinks the whole RAM job to a stock-state prep job, since the stock state cares not what file it holds and can be prepped off-line. A flagged RAM factory lifts match rates with high take rates, keeps noise grit, and joins with error fixes, with a neutral-atom build sketched. The notion opens fresh craft paths for quantum file loads.
pmc-13396815:

pmc-13397315:

pmc-13397515:

pmc-13398715:

pmc-13399115:

pmc-13399815:

pmc-13400015:

pmc-13400115:

pmc-13400515:

pmc-13400715:

pmc-13401315:

pmc-13401415:

pmc-13401815:

pmc-13402215:

pmc-13402615:

pmc-13402815:

pmc-13403015:

pmc-13403615:

pmc-13405415:

pmc-13406715:

pmc-13406915:

pmc-13407015:

pmc-13407815:

pmc-13408415:

pmc-13408815:

pmc-13409615:

pmc-13411615:

pmc-13411715:

pmc-13418515:

pmc-13418715:

pmc-13419015:

pmc-13419215:

pmc-13419415:

pmc-13419915:

pmc-13420315:

pmc-13421115:

With repair enzymes suppressed, tumour cells could not recover from the damage.
pmc-13421315:

pmc-13421715:

pmc-13422115:

Readers can now recheck every affected number against the corrected tables.
pmc-13422315:

The scheme still needs prospective validation, they note.
pmc-13424015:

pmc-13424115:

Tongue coating held the fewest kinds per sample yet the longest tail of rare genera, 340 in total. Each site kept signature species, underlining that one swab cannot speak for the whole mouth.
pmc-13424315:
Qisheng Liu and co-workers built a better tuning method in 2026 for planning mini-grids that pair cells with H2 storage. Green on-off swings plus hybrid storage makes planning highly twisty. pmc-13425215:

Randomized trials and multicentre real-world studies supply much of the material they highlight.

The review positions China as an active shaper of future rheumatology rather than only a validator of work begun elsewhere. Two years is a short span, yet the pace of change was swift.
pmc-13425715:
Kecheng Tang and coauthors tested ganoderic acid A. This compound comes from the fungus Ganoderma lucidum, for osteoporotic fracture healing in a 2026 study. pmc-13425815:
Yibo Zhou and colleagues mapped a microRNA pathway in laryngeal cancer in a 2026 laboratory study. pmc-13425915:
Zinnia Chung and colleagues measure spin, or slanted reporting, in small pilot and feasibility trials for hip and knee replacement. Such early trials should test whether a larger trial can run, but rosy framing can mislead readers about what was shown.

Searching PubMed, the team drew 147 trials from 2017 to 2023 by stratified random sampling. The main aim was how often spin appears, with a second aim of finding factors tied to heavier spin. Trial readers and editors get a check on a quiet bias in orthopaedic research, where popular operations drive fast publication.
pmc-13426915:
Hirpa and colleagues studied in 2026 how Ethiopia's ban on tobacco advertising, promotion, and sponsorship works in practice at shop level, interviewing forty-one officials and stakeholders across ten cities. Ethiopia passed a strong tobacco law in 2019 that bans all such marketing, including at points of sale. Whether the ban is enforced on the ground had not been examined.

Against that stood missing regional offices of the food and drug authority, no locally adapted laws, and unclear enforcement duties. Shops and many non-health officials barely knew the rules, illicit tobacco was openly advertised, and industry interference was reported, alongside social habits that normalize smoking. The authors call for clearer regional rules, more staff and funding, and campaigns exposing industry tactics.
pmc-13427215:
Espírito Santo and Boing assessed in 2026 how complete and how fast Brazil's records were for severe COVID-19 cases logged in the national SIVEP-Gripe surveillance system. Good records steer the response to an epidemic, and gaps can hide who is being hit hardest. Most fields scored very poorly for completeness across the whole period, with only slight gains by 2023, and quality varied sharply by state. Speed fared better: average time from symptoms to notification fell from about two weeks to one week, and most records were typed into the system on time. Still, the target for timely notification was missed, and the authors urge better entry habits, steady training, and routine monitoring.
pmc-13427315:
Elise Nauwynck and colleagues describe variable resistance to thyroid hormone alpha within one family in a 2026 case report. The rare disorder, caused by variants in the THRA receptor gene, produces tissue-level hypothyroidism despite near-normal blood hormone levels. pmc-13427515:
Maria Carmen De Santis and colleagues re-examined radiation after mastectomy in HER2-positive breast cancer using the ALTTO trial in a 2026 retrospective exploratory analysis. Results can refine which HER2-positive patients still need chest wall radiation after mastectomy. The trial ran at scale across lands, so its stored data hold a breadth no lone site could match when a sub group this size is in view.
pmc-13427715:
Tianyi Chen, Xiangyi Hu, and Jiafen Wang introduce, in a 2026 study, a detector for tiny infrared targets seen through laser glare. Defense sensors must spot small hot objects even when an enemy laser floods the image with glare and speckle. Standard networks miss wide context, while transformer models cost too much computing for small field devices. Rival detectors, including recent YOLO and transformer versions, trailed on accuracy or toughness against jamming. Real-time defense imaging on modest hardware is the intended payoff.
pmc-13428415:
Gaber and colleagues surveyed drug-resistant hospital bacteria in 2026 among critically ill patients at Fayoum University Hospitals in Egypt. Enterococcus faecium was commonest, and over three quarters of those strains resisted vancomycin, a last-line drug. The gene qnrB appeared in nearly seventy-nine percent of resistant strains tested, and most carried more than one such gene. The authors warn that resistance is spreading on mobile DNA in intensive care.
pmc-13428615:

The case studies show research mattering most when evidence speaks to other sectors' priorities, reveals synergies policymakers can support, and comes from real-world evaluations of measures already tried. Constructive engagement between nutrition and economic policymakers recurs as a success factor throughout the cases. Thow closes with three research priorities: policy innovation, knowledge equity, and gender.
pmc-13429015:
Esra Özgöçmen Tula and colleagues adapt, in a 2026 study, a smile-judging questionnaire for Turkish schoolchildren. How children read smiles shapes social life and self-image, yet few tested tools exist for this age group. The team translated a questionnaire for 8 to 10 year olds using forward and backward translation plus expert review. Statistical checks supported the scale's structure, and consistency scores landed in the good range. Children who retook the test later answered much the same way, showing stability over time. Most fit measures cleared their benchmarks, with one index right at its threshold. Dental researchers in Turkey now hold a checked tool for studying how children perceive teeth and smiles.
pmc-13429115:
Sherman and colleagues compared in 2026 two small-device glaucoma operations for lowering eye pressure. Glaucoma means raised pressure inside the eye that can damage sight. The stent group showed only small changes that were not statistically reliable. Untreated control eyes stayed flat on both measures over the same period. They conclude the blade gave stronger measured effects in this series, while the stent result needs larger studies.
pmc-13431015:

Twelve adults, aged 25 to 70, were interviewed on both sides of their transplant. The team sums up adaptation as striving for a life in social belonging, through grasping, accepting, adapting, coping, and balancing. Before surgery, patients worked to keep daily life going despite disruption, doubt, and hope. A year later, they rebuilt a steady new normal while living with weakness and an unsure future.
pmc-13431815:
Viresh Krishnan Sukumar and colleagues reprogram tumour-associated macrophages with pulsed magnetic fields to attack breast cancer cells. Flipping these immune cells from a tumour-helping M2 state to a tumour-fighting M1 state is attractive, but drug approaches carry body-wide toxicity.

pmc-13432615:
José Antonio Baz and colleagues report one-year results for a new delivery system for the ALLEGRA transcatheter aortic valve. The EMPIRE I study first tested early safety at thirty days for patients with severe native aortic narrowing or a worn surgical valve.

This prospective, single-arm, pre-market study ran at eleven centres in three European countries, with independent safety and events committees plus an independent echo core lab. It recruited 121 patients with severe native narrowing and 16 with degenerated surgical valves, judging outcomes by VARC-3 definitions. Heart teams get a fuller durability picture for a fully repositionable delivery system.
pmc-13432915:

Variant cases also returned for care more often within a year, so the authors urge whole-household treatment and follow-up.
pmc-13434015:
Céline Philippe and co-authors traced in 2026 how one stress arm in the cell's fold shop rewires which gene drafts get spliced, by way of a two-step relay. The set marks stressed tissue in health and cancer alike, the authors say.
pmc-13434515:
Ji Eun Kim discusses a paradox of bowel disease therapy in 2026: drugs that block a key swelling signal can spark fresh immune illness. A Korean study using national health records links the drugs to new cases of psoriasis and lung tissue disease. Risk rose soon after exposure began, then leveled off.

Skin change in the form of psoriasis is the most often reported twist. The piece links the effect to a shift in immune balance toward other pathways. Early onset hints that some patients carry the risk from the start. Clinicians are urged to watch skin and lungs closely in the first months of therapy.
pmc-13434715:

Restoring the active gene mark alone did not fix the mess. Models and rescue tests show droplets and marks work as a pair. Space itself becomes a sorting tool in division.
pmc-13435415:

The fusion joins chlorotoxin, which ferries cargo across the blood-brain barrier to tumor cells, with CNF1, a bacterial protein that stirs anti-tumor immunity. pmc-13435915:
Madeline Chardon and coauthors follow Swiss medical students across two survey years in 2026, asking whether hardship at home tracks mental strain. Long surveys in late 2022 and late 2023 drew 631 students who answered both rounds. A hardship index scores money, social, and health lacks together.

Depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and burnout form the outcome set. Models adjust for shields such as support and coping resources. Schools may need aid that targets hardship itself.
pmc-13438615:

pmc-13439015:

Thirty-six parents received the program, against 32 in the control group. The program is cheap and simple to run, the authors note. Mood gains add a fresh reason to offer shared reading early. Health visitors could fold the program into routine baby checks cheaply.
pmc-13439315:
Jorio Mascheroni and co-authors test whether simulator training for heart device implants carries into real operations, reporting in 2026. Earlier trials showed far fewer errors in simulation with that method, but real-world transfer was unproven.

The team followed 21 early-career implanters from a prior trial into their first two routine cases after training. Each case was scored against expert-agreed technique with a standard form. Benchmark-trained implanters strayed from ideal technique far less often than peers with standard simulator training. Case difficulty matched between groups. The authors back benchmark-based simulation as a safer on-ramp to live implant work.
pmc-13440115:

Participants were split into four age bands, with Cox and competing-risk models for all-cause, cardiovascular, and other deaths.

Diabetes clinicians get an age-tailored message: tight targets matter most in younger patients, while older patients need individualized, less aggressive goals.
pmc-13441515:
Pei and colleagues study ikigai, a Japanese notion of a life worth living, and ask whether it grows from social contact or drives it. pmc-13442815:

A wide know-do gap stood out, since 90.1 percent named an ambulance call as right, while only 56.2 percent said they would call for chest pain past five minutes. pmc-13443315:

Gene reads showed more matrix build and less matrix chew in the mix. A signal good, TGFB2, proved to be the stem cells' key gift: blocking it erased gains in wall cell growth and motion. The authors pitch the mix as a living patch path.
pmc-13444315:

Non-heat jobs held a 17 percent share, with 3,023 procedures. Non-heat patients skewed older, at a median age of 61 years against 58 years for heat patients. A large slice, 39 percent of patients, fell out for missing method data, a gap the authors flag for registry care.
pmc-13445515:

The growths appeared seven and nine years after treatment, with bleeding, fatty deposits, and swelling. Both patients got injections that block vessel growth signals. The case near the center of sight ran a fiercer course and also needed laser treatment and steroid shots. Care followed both vessel activity and other radiation harm in the eye, a balance the authors stress for late cases.
pmc-13445815:
Rasaq A. Ojasanya and colleagues hunt for what drives drug resistance in urinary Escherichia coli from dogs across the United States, in a 2026 study of lab records from 2018 to 2024. The odds of resistance climbed in a straight line with each past positive culture in the prior six months, the strongest patient-level signal. pmc-13447315:

Distinct gut communities may help each species persist in the desert grassland, the authors suggest.
pmc-13447415:

Past surgery type and reason for surgery also mattered, supporting prevention and better operative planning.
pmc-13448215:

Simulations and experiments confirmed 96.13 percent efficiency, low harmonic distortion, and reliable operation under varied loads and frequencies. The compact design suits photovoltaic and other renewable systems.
pmc-13449015:

Time below range was just 1 percent after lactose or galactose, against 8 percent after placebo in the crossover comparisons. The authors back galactose and lactose as steadier pre-exercise strategies.
pmc-13449315:

pmc-13449415:

The authors present the pair as a scalable platform for making this enzyme family for research and therapy.
pmc-13449515:

Strain EP61.1T, a rod-shaped, motile, oxygen-using bacterium, was tested by a full taxonomic approach combining shape, chemistry, and genome data. Genome similarity scores fell well below the cutoffs for existing species, confirming it as new. Its genome spans 4.82 million base pairs with high guanine-cytosine content. The species, named Sphingomonas incarnata, adds a candidate source of bioactive compounds from inside a medicinal leaf.
pmc-13449915:
Chen and co-authors map glaucoma treatment choices by ethnicity in a huge United States records network. Their 2026 retrospective study uses the TriNetX database. It compares patients with primary open-angle glaucoma, Asian Americans against non-Asian Americans. The groups were balanced statistically on demographics, other diseases, family history, and smoking. They were then split by disease severity.

In mild-to-moderate disease, covering over twelve thousand matched patients, Asian Americans were slightly more likely to receive topical medication. The direction flipped in severe disease. Asian Americans were less likely to receive topical therapy. They were notably less likely to receive laser procedures, with odds about a quarter lower for laser. No significant differences appeared for traditional surgery or microinvasive surgery in either severity band. The authors conclude the disparity concentrates in adjunctive medical and laser care for severe disease, and call it a target for equity work.
pmc-13450415:
Sarah Commaroto and colleagues unravel in 2026 a leg plaque in a man whose immune system has been compromised since childhood. Their patient, a 65-year-old diagnosed at twelve with chronic granulomatous disease, carries a defective microbe-killing enzyme that leaves him prone to bacterial and fungal infections despite preventive antibiotics and antifungals. A red-purple plaque on his lower leg had enlarged for three years before biopsy suggested infectious granulomatous inflammation.

The workup wandered. Special stains came back negative, and recommended cultures and molecular tests went unfinished at the first clinic. A second biopsy was read instead as the skin reaction of his underlying disease. The differential stayed wide, spanning fungal infections, other granulomatous conditions, and skin cancer. The authors frame the case as disseminated blastomycosis with skin involvement, a rare invader in this disease. They use the delay to argue for pressing tissue diagnosis to completion.
pmc-13450615:
Josina Straub and a large team weigh in 2026 how much extra scanning helps older adults who hit their heads. Neck spine breaks are more common in this group, and a second break lower down can hide behind the first. The study covered 2,748 patients aged 65 and over at a top-level trauma center.

Neck breaks showed in six percent of patients, split evenly between upper and lower neck zones. Most were treated without surgery. Risk rose with age, with a stiff spine disease, and with chest injury. The team worked out how many scans it takes to find one extra hidden break and argues that wide scans, plus chosen MRI use, are worth the cost for safety.
pmc-13451815:
Hongwei Shao and a large team build in 2026 a heat-set gel meant to break the loop where sore joints wear down their own padding. Joint wear, called osteoarthritis, feeds on lining swelling and cartilage loss at once, and most care hits only one side. Their gel carries a drug that steadies low-oxygen signals, set at a tuned dose.

The gel pushed immune cells toward a calm state, eased joint rubbing, drew in stem cells, and shielded cartilage cells from swelling-driven loss. In mice with surgery-made joint wear, treated joints kept their cartilage and calmer linings at ten weeks. Wiping out the immune cells erased most of the gain, which the team reads as proof the immune shift does the work.
pmc-13451915:
Herman Setiadi and co-authors share in 2026 a pipeline that turns land maps and sharp satellite photos into training sets for rice field spotting. Official field border maps for five Indonesian regions were lined up with very sharp space images. The flow cuts both into paired picture and mask tiles, each about a thousand pixels square, with overlap.

Tiles with almost no rice were dropped, brightness was leveled band by band, and shape measures were logged for each field patch. The run yielded over 3,000 pairs. A small check with two vision models showed standard tools can eat the pairs at once, though the authors say the check is a smoke test, not a scoreboard. Source files sit in public stores.
pmc-13452215:
Zakaria El Kouzi and a very large team gather in 2026 cases where a gel spacer placed before prostate radiation strayed into the rectal wall, and how teams reversed it. The gel is shot into the fat plane between prostate and rectum to shield the rectum from dose, guided by ultrasound in an outpatient visit. Trials show it cuts mild rectal harm, and use has soared.

Rarely, the gel slips from its plane and can wound the rectal wall, with ulcer or tear among the feared harms. The series walks through how such slips were spotted on scans and what steps undid them. The authors aim to give radiation teams a playbook for a rare but serious slip.
pmc-13453615:
Joon Young Kim and Joon Bum Kim told of a valve-sparing fix for a bad mitral valve infection in 2026, sparing the patient's own aortic valve. Germs that hit the wall between mitral and aortic valves most often force both valves to be swapped, with a rebuild of that wall. When the aortic valve flaps stay clean, a sparing fix may work.

The plan cut the top vena cava and split a valve join lengthwise, to clear all germ-struck tissue while keeping the aortic valve in place. The hard redo case shows the fix in use, with a rebuild of the wall once the germs were gone. Heart surgeons gain a choice that spares a sound aortic valve in picked infected cases.
pmc-13454115:
Jingxin Zhang and seven co-authors test whether a Chinese herbal formula can ease statin linked muscle trouble in diabetic mice with heart disease. Statins guard the heart yet can burden muscle, a sore point for patients with type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 study breeds the disease pair in ApoE knockout mice and treats them for 90 days, comparing drug mixes with and without the formula, called QiShenYiQi dropping pills.

The formula group showed better sugar and fat profiles than the rival mixes. It also protected liver and skeletal muscle function best of all the arms. Gene, microbe, and metabolite scans tied the gains to steadier gut microbes and calmer swelling and cell death genes. The authors present the pills as a companion strategy that may soften statin side effects, pending human proof.
pmc-13454215:
Jenkins and colleagues ask why breast cancer peaks twice, near ages 45 and 65, and whether the way the breast ages helps explain it. Their 2026 study uses two mouse models of mammary gland aging, the tissue that becomes the breast. One model ages in a steady, step by step way. The other ages in waves, and the team compares gene and protein activity plus cancer cell growth across the animals' lives.

In the wave model, cancer linked genes and proteins rose at 11 and 19 months but not at 3 or 14 months of mouse age. Glands at those peak ages also let cancer cells grow more readily, while the steady model grew more permissive only after 14 months. A gene signature from the wave pattern, built from single cell data, was enriched in women diagnosed at ages 45 to 65, matching the mouse ages.
pmc-13454615:
Liu and co-authors paired the androgen blocker enzalutamide with dalpiciclib, a CDK4/6 cell-cycle blocker, against castration-resistant prostate cancer. That is the lethal form that escapes hormone therapy. Across cell lines, a patient-cell xenograft, and a lymphatic metastasis model, they tested the pair with sequencing and gene screens.

The pairing showed potent antitumor activity in every preclinical model tested, beating either drug alone in the reported comparisons. Together the drugs stalled the cell cycle, curbed migration, blocked DNA replication, and drove cancer cell death in culture. Enzalutamide stopped the androgen receptor from switching on MCM4, a core part of the DNA unwinding helicase. That deepened the replication block set by cell-cycle inhibition. The authors call the pairing powerful and argue it deserves trials in men with castration-resistant prostate cancer.
pmc-13455215:
Yin-Che Lu and seven colleagues test, in a 2026 lab study, a plant compound against mouth cancers tied to betel nut chewing. In Taiwan, the chewing habit drives aggressive oral cancers that shrug off standard chemo and radiation. The compound, evodiamine, comes from a traditional medicinal fruit and has shown anti-tumor effects elsewhere.

Cell tests split the story by cancer type. The compound cut growth and survival strongly in betel-linked cancer cells, in step with dose, while sparing the non-betel type comparatively. Treated cells died through the classic caspase cascade, with the executioner enzymes switched on and cut. Their energy hubs faltered as death signals rose, pointing to the internal suicide route. The authors argue the selective hit makes evodiamine worth developing for this hard-to-treat cancer group.
pmc-13455415:
Emile Whaibeh and colleagues test whether Lebanese primary care clinics are ready for video and phone care in a 2026 pilot study. Lebanon's crises have left care costly, distant and scarce, above all for rural and vulnerable patients, while telehealth could bridge some gaps. Five primary care centres run by the Order of Malta across five governorates were assessed in August and September 2022, surveying patients and interviewing staff, providers and patients.

Telehealth promised lower costs, easier access and shorter waits, and patients and staff welcomed it, above all for mental health care at a distance. Power cuts, patchy internet, low digital skills and thin infrastructure stood in the way. The authors present telehealth as a workable scale-up for low-resource primary care, provided upgrades to power and internet, digital training and supportive policy arrive with it.
pmc-13455515:
Berk Bas and six colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, two electrical settings used to seal blood vessels during stomach tumor removal by endoscope. The procedure, endoscopic submucosal dissection, cures early stomach growths, yet bleeding during the work is common. One center reviewed 194 patients treated from 2021 to 2025, split between spray and swift coagulation modes.

Spray mode finished faster, averaging about 38 minutes against 44 for swift. Bleeding during the procedure struck about 44 percent of spray cases against 75 percent of swift cases, and rescue forceps were needed less often. Severe bleeding stayed rare and similar in both arms. Later bleeding, perforation, recurrence, and narrowing also matched between groups. Success rates sat near 94 percent in both. The authors favor spray mode for speed and calmer procedures at their center.
pmc-13457015:
Anping Wang and eight colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a candidate vaccine from empty virus shells against goose astrovirus 2, the main cause of gosling gout in China. The disease costs farms heavily, and no commercial vaccine exists. The team grew the virus's shell protein in insect cells using a baculovirus carrier, then watched how the protein matured inside and outside cells.

Inside cells, the shell was trimmed into mature core and spike pieces. Outside, more half-built precursors remained. Under the electron microscope, the protein self-assembled into tidy particles about thirty nanometers wide. Both the inside and outside particle batches raised strong antibodies and neutralizing power in birds, matching a killed whole-virus vaccine. Challenged birds shed far less virus, with protection equal to that vaccine. The authors offer the particles as a clean subunit platform for gosling protection.
pmc-13457515:
Madhur Verma and colleagues re-measure obesity among older Indians using a new clinical framework that splits excess weight into pre-clinical and clinical stages. Body mass index alone cannot tell harmless extra weight from weight already damaging organs. Drawing on the first wave of the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, their 2026 analysis covers 59,854 adults aged 45 and over.

A high BMI registered in 27.1 percent of the group. The framework sorted the same share, 27.0 percent, into pre-clinical obesity and 15.1 percent into the clinical stage. Geography split the picture: clinical obesity ran at 24.33 percent in the South against 7.77 percent in Central India, peaking in Chandigarh at 37.88 percent and bottoming in Meghalaya at 4.52 percent. Women, city dwellers, and the better educated and wealthier carried higher odds of both stages; poor self-rated health clustered in the clinical group. The authors say the distinction can guide triage where resources run thin.
pmc-13458615:
Gengmu Qin and colleagues improve helmet detection for underground miners in a 2026 study. Dim light, occlusion and cluttered mine backgrounds defeat standard detectors, yet helmet compliance is a core safety check. The team enhanced YOLOv5 with a lightweight attention module, SENet-tn, combining multi-scale average pooling with Swish activation, plus a new INWDLoss blending normalised Wasserstein distance and IoU losses for small, overlapping targets.

On a self-built mine helmet dataset, the improved YOLOv5s-tn model raised mean average precision by 2.91 percent over baseline YOLOv5s. Mine operators gain a more reliable automated safety monitor for dark, crowded tunnels, though performance on an in-house dataset needs independent testing across mines, cameras and lighting before deployment.
pmc-13458815:
Arta Grosmane-Bataraga and colleagues build Latvia's first myasthenia gravis patient list in a 2026 single-centre study. The disease, a rare immune disease of muscle weakness and fatigue, lacked long-term real-world data in Latvia. Adults with confirmed disease were recruited from January 2022 to May 2025 at Pauls Stradiņš Clinical University Hospital. They were assessed with standard severity, daily life, quality of life and fatigue scales, and stored in a secure digital list.

The list enrolled 112 patients across 523 visits, with median disease span 4.5 years and antibody profiles mostly AChR positive at 76 percent. Remission rose from 25 to 34 percent over a median 1.3 years, severe classes fell from 19 to 2 percent, and total, daily life and quality scores improved clearly, while fatigue eased only modestly and still affected half of patients. The list proves structured follow-up feasible and flags fatigue as the persistent burden.
pmc-13458915:
Hongling Su leads a large author group reporting in 2026 on fibrosing mediastinitis, a rare condition where excess fibrous tissue in the chest squeezes the pulmonary veins, pulmonary arteries, and airways. Their multicenter study drew 369 patients from 16 referral centers across 10 provinces in China, diagnosed between 2010 and 2021. Diagnosis rested mainly on contrast-enhanced chest scans read by experienced clinicians and radiologists.

The team tracked symptoms, blood tests, imaging, heart function, and survival, using all-cause death as the main endpoint. Follow-up ran into 2022, and statistical models searched for factors tied to a worse outlook. Readers get a rare long-term picture of a disease where evidence on survival and prognosis has stayed thin.
pmc-13459215:
Imane Badran and co-authors describe a trial testing whether community pharmacists should routinely see patients' kidney function results when dispensing blood-thinning drugs. These medicines, direct oral anticoagulants, prevent clots but raise bleeding risk, and failing kidneys clear them slowly, so the right dose depends on kidney function that pharmacists often cannot see. Their 2026 protocol paper outlines a cluster randomized trial across 96 community pharmacies in France, mainly the Grand-Est region.

Half the pharmacies will systematically retrieve each patient's latest kidney result before dispensing, while the other half give usual care. The trial will enroll 1,920 patients over twenty-four months and follow them for six months after enrollment. The main outcome is clinically relevant bleeding within three months of dispensing, with secondary outcomes covering later bleeding, clots, and what interventions pharmacists actually make. The authors hope the results will shape best practice for ambulatory pharmacy care.
pmc-13460015:
TTDuong Doan and colleagues measure spread in clinical practice across Vietnam hospitals in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Care spread harms outcomes and wastes resources, yet skill checks in Vietnam had been limited. The study used the EQIS fake e-patient platform with 216 birth and 71 cardiac staff across seven private hospitals, each completing three field cases scored for correct decisions.

Mean scores reached 73.5 for birth cases and 80.0 for cardiac cases, with test scores lowest and most spread, below 70 percent. Scores varied by staff type, education, department, patient volume, hospital, age and experience. Staff ordered 2.4 to 2.9 needless tests per case, costing about 330 to 495 million VND a month. Hospital leaders gain a fake tool for checking quality and curbing wasteful testing.
pmc-13461015: Muhammad Farooq and co-authors issued this 2026 correction to their article on growing conditions for a fungus used in biological pest control. The notice is a correction only. It fixes author affiliations, removing one wrongly assigned to three authors and adding a Korean crop research institute affiliation that had been omitted, with later affiliations renumbered. It also replaces the acknowledgements, correcting a project number and adding a second funding project from Yancheng. The original article has been updated accordingly.
pmc-13461315:
Xingyu Duan and co-authors built in 2026 a deep learning system that outlines spinal tuberculosis lesions on MRI scans and, crucially, reports how unsure it is about each outline. Fuzzy lesion borders make hand tracing subjective, and black-box models leave doctors guessing where to distrust them. Scans from 210 patients across three centers trained and tested the system, which added a boundary-focused loss and repeated sampling to estimate uncertainty.

On the outside test set the model beat three established rivals on overlap accuracy, and its uncertainty tracked actual pixel errors closely. A threshold flagged unreliable regions with good sensitivity. Nine physicians reviewing cases with uncertainty overlays trusted the output more and finished faster, with trainees gaining most, and obvious failures were caught in most instances.
pmc-13461415:
Shi and colleagues re-sequenced in 2026 the genomes of 110 Leiwuqi yaks, an indigenous breed from eastern Tibet, to map its genetic makeup and local adaptation. Yak are vital high-altitude livestock, but this breed's traits were poorly charted. The team merged their data with public genomes from other domestic and wild yak groups, applying one strict pipeline to all samples.

Shi found nearly twenty million high-quality variants across the samples, mostly in non-coding regions. The breed kept rich genetic diversity, though stretches of uniform DNA hinted at isolation or recent inbreeding. Chinese domestic yaks shared a broad background with wild yak, while Indian yak stood clearly apart. The breed did not form its own genome-wide cluster. Yet selected regions held 466 protein-coding genes tied to development signals, immune and stress response, and light sensing. Together they sketch how local adaptation may have formed.
pmc-13461515:
Yining Fu and colleagues compared in 2026 surgery against medicine alone for Takayasu arteritis patients whose descending aorta had narrowed severely. This inflammatory artery disease lacks agreed long-term management for that pattern. Their Peking Union cohort covered seventy-eight patients treated between 2011 and 2022, sixty-two undergoing surgery and sixteen managed with medicine. Mortality was the main outcome, with quality of life plus event-free survival tracked over long follow-up.

Surgery cut all-cause mortality sharply and improved quality of life on both physical and mental measures. Blood pressure and the number of pressure medicines needed both fell after surgery compared with medical care. Open operations brought more complications in the first month yet resisted re-narrowing better over time than endovascular approaches, a trade-off the authors lay out for decisions fitted to each patient.
pmc-13461715:
Zheng Zhang and colleagues pull together, in a 2026 review, trial evidence on exercise and mind-body movement for mood in people with inflammatory bowel disease. Bowel inflammation there is long-lasting, and depressive symptoms are common, harming life quality and care routines. Movement programs are low-cost and available, yet their mood benefit in this group had not been summed up. The team searched four databases through May 2026.

Seven articles with nine comparisons from randomized trials met their rules. At the start, mood scores were alike across groups. After the programs, symptoms fell more in the movement groups, with a steady effect and no clash across studies. Gains appeared across delivery styles, movement types, lengths, and disease types, though no single kind proved best. The authors welcome the signal while stressing the trial count is small and methods vary. Larger, stronger trials are needed to settle type, dose, and format.
pmc-13462115:
Seyedeh-Tarlan Mirzohreh and colleagues test gap-aware machine learning for heart attack outcomes in a 2026 study. Machine learning could improve outlook after ST-elevation heart-muscle attack, yet records carry heavy missing data that can degrade models. The look-back study covered 659 patients in a row undergoing primary through-skin heart-vessel treatment. It analysed 80 factors with up to 40 percent gaps, comparing native CatBoost handling against fill-in and a pretrained tabular model.

Major bad heart events hit 42.8 percent of patients. CatBoost trained directly on gappy data performed best with 8 to 10 clues, reaching an area under the curve of 0.73, while other fill-in added nothing. Impaired pre-treatment flow, reduced pumping fraction, high heart marker, ST shift, swelling and kidney trouble drove predictions. Doctors gain a handy model approach for gappy real-life records.
pmc-13462415:
Shenggang Li and colleagues design, in a 2026 study, a drug carrier that rides immune cells into the injured brain after stroke. When blood flow returns to a brain area starved by stroke, the return causes fresh harm, called reperfusion injury. The blood-brain barrier blocks most drugs from reaching it. Their nanoparticles carry minocycline and wear a peptide tag that locks onto neutrophils, a first-responder immune cell.

Tagged particles bind a receptor on activated neutrophils, which ferry them across the barrier into the stroke zone. Once inside, the particles calm the burst of oxygen species, block an iron-driven cell death, ferroptosis, and nudge the brain's immune cells from attack toward protection. The study sits at the design and proof stage. The authors offer neutrophil hitchhiking as a general route for delivering drugs past the barrier in stroke care.
pmc-13462815:
Mengqi Zhao leads a 2026 literature analysis of twenty years of research on heterotaxy syndrome with congenital heart defects. The syndrome scrambles the body's left-right patterning before birth, producing complex heart malformations. No one had mapped the field's global shape. The team pulled publications from 2006 to 2025 from a citation database and charted them with two mapping tools.

493 publications from 184 journals, written by over two and a half thousand authors, were included. Output climbed over time and peaked in 2022. The United States contributed most, and Harvard Medical School with Boston Children's Hospital led institutions. One author, Anderson RH, published most in the field, and a specialty journal carried the most papers. Keyword shifts show focus moving from anatomy labels and staged repair toward gene mechanisms, outlook prediction, and long-term results. The authors offer the map as a first reference for planning work in this rare condition.
pmc-13463415:
Shi and colleagues worked in 2026 to find genes that steer macrophage polarization and change esophageal cancer risk. Polarization is how macrophages, a type of immune cell, switch between attack and repair modes. The team combined three kinds of genetic data: chemical marks on DNA, gene activity, and protein levels. They tested those data against cancer records from the UK Biobank. They then checked the findings in the Finnish FinnGen cohort.

The analysis flagged 54 methylation sites, seven genes, and one protein tied to cancer risk. Five genes stood out once the evidence was ranked into tiers. A gene called LEP sat in the top tier. Stronger chemical marking at one LEP site tracked with higher risk, while greater LEP activity tracked with lower risk. That pattern suggests the mark turns the gene down. INPP5D and PGF formed the second tier, while SPP1 and USP18 rounded out the list.
pmc-13463615:
Aneri Shethji and five co-authors map cell talk in skin from children with juvenile systemic sclerosis, a rare disease that hardens tissue. Why fibrosis starts in these children has stayed unclear. The team read gene activity cell by cell in skin from nine young patients and nine healthy children.

Eleven fibroblast groups appeared, and several grew larger in sick skin. One group made heavy amounts of collagen and growth signals, matching a harmful type seen in adult disease. Macrophages, immune cells that eat debris, clustered near these fibroblasts in dense patches. The paired pattern points to drug targets where the two cell types push each other toward scarring.
pmc-13463815:
Erik Svensson and four co-authors test an upgraded molecular assay for tuberculosis, the FluoroType MTBDR. The older version read one gene target and missed cases that rival tests caught. The update adds IS6110, a stretch that appears many times in the germ genome, to lift detection.

In a head-to-head trial on 1,483 patient specimens, the new version caught eighty-seven percent of true cases against seventy percent for the old one. Gains ran largest in specimens where germs were too few to see under the microscope. False alarms stayed rare and equal for both versions. Drug resistance calls, based on unchanged targets, gained little from the update.
pmc-13463915:
Hui-Lan Li leads a team that built a one-tube PCR test for Helicobacter pylori that also reads its drug resistance. Standard gene tests can miss resistant strains when silent letter changes block their probes. The new test folds those silent variants into its probe design from the start.

Probe plans drew on mutation records from 453 isolates and covered nearly all known natural variants. The test sensed the germ at very low copy counts and stayed steady across repeat runs. On 316 stomach tissue checks it matched a store kit closely and matched full gene reading almost fully for both target drugs. Clinics gain a faster way to pick the right cure the first time.
pmc-13464015:
Jennie Vu and a large team test a hardy apelin mimic against pulmonary arterial hypertension in rats. The disease scars lung arteries, drives pressures up, and overloads the right side of the heart. Apelin is a natural signal that guards vessels, yet the body chews it up fast, so the team built a version that lasts.

Rats raised under a drug-plus-low-oxygen regime grew severe disease, then received the mimic. Lung vessel lesions largely reversed, and artery pressures came close to normal. The strained right heart shrank back toward normal size and strength, and early kidney strain eased too. Cell-level gene reads showed the mimic restored a protective growth pathway that the disease had tipped off balance.
pmc-13464815:
Yaqi Zhang and seven co-authors fold a simple blood ratio into machine learning models that forecast lymph node spread in colorectal cancer. Early tumors can be cut out through a scope, yet hidden node spread in about a tenth of cases makes that risky. The ratio divides neutrophils by lymphocytes, two white cell counts from routine blood work.

Data from 533 patients fed several learning models, and high ratio values tied to node spread on their own strength. The best tuned model sorted patients into high and low risk groups with the strongest accuracy of the set. Such sorting could spare low-risk patients big surgery they do not need. The team frames the tool as decision support for tailoring operations to each patient's risk.
pmc-13464915:
Mustafa Yurdakul and four co-authors build BloodContourNet, a vision system that finds blood cells in dense microscope smears. Touching red cells, tiny platelets, and uneven staining trip up standard box-drawing detectors. Their system layers three add-ons over a YOLO base model to sharpen crowded fields.

One module tunes features with local and windowed attention, and a second reweights the training loss toward hard, sparse cases. A third draws smooth Bézier outlines to untangle overlapping cells in the densest zones. On a set of 1,260 smear images with over eighteen thousand marked cells, the system topped twenty-five YOLO variants and ten rival detectors. Outside validation on fresh patients must still come, the authors note.
pmc-13465015:
Jinmei Zhao and three co-authors isolate a polysaccharide from sea buckthorn pomace, the pulp left after oil and juice pressing, and test it on gut lining cells. Oxidative stress tears at the gut barrier, letting unwanted material leak through. Their fraction, named SPP-0.2b, was cleaned through two column steps and profiled sugar by sugar.

Hydrogen peroxide weakened the cell sheets, dropping electrical resistance and opening leaks. Adding the polysaccharide restored much of the resistance and cut the leak of a tracer dye sharply. Two sealing proteins at cell joints rose back up under treatment. Harmful oxygen forms and damage markers fell, while the cells' own antioxidant enzymes worked harder, which supports food-ingredient trials.
pmc-13465315:
Krysińska and co-authors announced in 2026 a new subfamily of jumping genes in the Glomeromycota, fungi that partner with plant roots. The elements belong to the CryptonA lineage of transposons, DNA segments that move using a tyrosine recombinase enzyme. The team named them Glomhoppers. Each carries a domain called DUF3504 with the working parts of an active enzyme. Structural modeling suggested a groove for gripping DNA.

Across 72 fungal genomes, about 1,800 Glomhopper copies turned up. Most were truncated or interrupted by introns. About a quarter lacked introns and kept their enzyme motifs intact, consistent with possible mobility. The elements cluster in repeat-rich genome regions alongside other transposon families. In Gigaspora species, the intronless versions responded to stress with several-fold higher activity than intron-bearing forms. Direct proof of jumping is still lacking, but a subset looks transcriptionally alive.
pmc-13465515:
Lingdan Lu and four co-authors build a discharge-day risk model for unplanned readmission after womb cancer staging surgery. Complications often strike after patients leave, so a score usable at the discharge desk fills a real gap. Their data came from a national readmissions file spanning 2016 to 2022, with 89,627 stays.

The model uses only facts known at discharge, from age and insurance to the hospital course itself. Internal checks showed fair sorting power with clean calibration. Discharge to home health or a care facility, emergency entry, and a heavier illness burden each raised readmission risk. Later-year test sets held the same performance, and benefit curves favored using the score to target follow-up care.
pmc-13466315:
Mia Omerašević and colleagues lock radioactive cesium into a stable mineral form for long-term storage, in a 2026 materials study. Cesium's long half-life makes stray contamination a lasting hazard. Their route first pulled cesium ions from water into a zeolite crystal by ion swapping, then set that loaded zeolite inside a geopolymer made with kaolin clay.

Heating the composite to very high temperature grew two stable cesium-bearing crystal phases, splitting the cesium between zeolite-born and matrix-born minerals. Samples carrying half loaded zeolite by weight showed the best crystal content, density, and crushing strength. The work supports a practical chain from cleaning contaminated water to sealing its hazard in rock-like form.
pmc-13466915:
Rasha S. El-Tawil and colleagues review nano-scale cathode materials, the positive poles that largely set how well a lithium-ion battery works. Cars and gadgets need cathodes that hold much charge, stay stable and safe, and cost little, all at once.

The review covers the three main cathode families, layered, spinel, and olivine, weighing what each does well and where each falls short. Two fixes recur: doping, swapping in extra elements, and coating particle surfaces to shield them while the battery cycles. Cheap, scalable making routes are set out beside the lab tools that read structure and behaviour at nano scale. El-Tawil stresses that nano sizing lifts conductivity and ion speed, the keys to faster, longer-lived batteries.
pmc-13467015:
Saleh and colleagues refine how to predict thyroid danger for babies of mothers with Graves disease. Their 2026 prospective study, run across 44 Dutch centres from 2010 to 2023, measured maternal TSH-receptor antibodies, which cross the placenta and can overstimulate the fetal thyroid. It covered 500 women with past Graves disease and 178 with active disease, and guidelines currently apply one antibody threshold regardless of timing or test type.

Trimester-specific thresholds predicted fetal and newborn thyroid problems with high accuracy. In women with past disease, cut-offs set per trimester missed no cases, giving a negative predictive value of 100 percent across pregnancy. In active disease, the cut-offs caught roughly five of six cases or better. The authors note newborns sometimes developed overactive thyroids despite low maternal levels when mothers took antithyroid drugs, so thresholds must be read alongside treatment.
pmc-13467515:
Roberto Perulli and co-authors review in 2026 hip replacement strategies that preserve bone in young, active patients. Younger patients face a lifetime revision risk as high as 35 percent, and each revision is harder when the first implant has wasted the bone around it. Standard long stems protect the hip well in older patients but starve the upper thigh bone of load over time, shrinking future options.

Two femoral approaches try to keep that bone: resurfacing, which caps the natural ball of the joint, and short-stem total replacement. Each suits different patients and carries its own complication and revision profile. The review also covers the socket side, which has been studied less. The authors weigh patient selection and surgical technique so the first operation leaves the most bone for any later one.
pmc-13467915:
Zhu and Wang propose a computer system for scoring stroke rehabilitation exercises, in this 2026 study. A key challenge is telling genuine recovery from compensatory movement. In compensation, patients cheat a task using the wrong muscles. Their system, called CTCG-Net, combines camera-based skeleton tracking with wearable motion sensors worn on the body.

The network uses the wearable sensor stream to adjust how much it trusts the skeleton data, and it scores two things separately: the main movement outcome and a control factor capturing compensation. On a public rehabilitation benchmark dataset, the system posted the lowest average errors among the methods tested, with a mean absolute deviation of 0.4001 against therapist scores in the comparison. Follow-up analyses confirmed that the compensation-aware design and the sensor gating each added useful information. The authors position the tool as support for clinician-supervised monitoring, not diagnosis.
pmc-13468315:

The authors suggest pressure reshapes blood vessel behavior and macrophage mood through force-sensing pathways, and they pitch compression as a drug-free tool for surgical recovery and soft tissue injury.
pmc-13493815:
Maaod and colleagues built an artificial intelligence system to grade diabetic retinopathy, eye damage caused by diabetes that can blind people who miss regular screening. Their 2026 framework blends several model families: networks that read local image detail, vision transformers that weigh the whole picture, and transfer learning from pre-trained models. They screened 23 ready-made models on the APTOS 2019 dataset of retina photographs, then combined the strongest performers.

The winning design stacked the best hybrid models in sequence and merged their judgements by soft voting, where each model's confidence counts rather than a simple majority. That ensemble graded test images with accuracy in the low nineties and separated disease grades almost perfectly on the ranking measure reported. Combining different model types proved more stable than any single network. The authors pitch the system as a step toward dependable automated screening for clinics with few specialists.
pmc-13493915:
Dharmaprakash and colleagues built a diabetes-relevant material by making copper oxide nanoparticles with an extract of red seaweed instead of harsh chemicals. The tiny particles can slow the enzymes which release sugar from food. In the 2026 work, the particles were spun into nanofibre scaffolds, fine webs of starch and a synthetic polymer. The team verified the particles formed correctly and spread evenly.

Tested against the two enzymes that finish digesting carbohydrates, the scaffolds blocked just over four fifths of amylase activity and a similar share of glucosidase activity at the top dose used. Half-blocking doses also favoured the composite, suggesting the fibre format keeps the particles available and active longer. The authors frame the scaffold as a candidate for managing blood sugar spikes after meals, while stressing that all tests so far are in glassware, not bodies.
pmc-13494015:
Takaya Nakashima leads an eight-author team testing in 2026 whether disagreement between two kidney function estimates warns of trouble ahead for Japanese patients. Kidneys are usually graded from creatinine, a muscle byproduct, but a second marker, cystatin C, gives an independent estimate, and a wide negative gap between them has predicted decline in Western cohorts. A national chronic kidney disease database supplied the test population.

Patients in the most negative quarter of the gap faced about double the risk of severe progression compared with the near-zero group. Severe progression meant kidney failure stage or a forty percent function drop within five years. Curved risk analysis showed danger climbing steeply as the gap deepened, then flattening for positive gaps. The cheap two-test comparison earns a place as a prognostic flag.
pmc-13494115:
Subhashini Sellers and colleagues report an analysis, published in 2026. It covers lung cancer screening among people with HIV. The patients received care at a large Southeastern United States centre. The period ran from 2018 to 2023. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in this group. Yearly low-dose scans can cut mortality. The team measured who was eligible and who was actually screened among 2,798 patients.

Smoking history was common. Expanded 2021 guidelines raised the eligible share of patients. It rose from about six percent to about fifteen percent. Yet fewer than a third of eligible patients had ever been screened. The authors call this a critical missed opportunity. Targeted work on barriers is needed.
pmc-13494215:
Paola Mogna-Peláez and Marta Guasch-Ferré argue, in a 2026 perspective, that the swift spread of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs has left nutrition care behind. These drugs curb appetite and food intake sharply, which brings large weight loss and broad metabolic gains. The same curb can leave patients short on protein, key vitamins and minerals, and fiber, and can strip lean mass along with fat.

The authors note that diet checks are rare in daily practice even though obesity societies urge them. They make the case for dietitians and behavioral health staff as core members of the care team, able to keep nutrient intake sound and ease stomach side effects. Research needs include sound screening tools, clear nutrient targets, and profiles of patients at highest risk. With prescriptions now in the millions, they call the fix urgent rather than optional.
pmc-13495315:
Xiaoli Xiang, Xiaoyu Zhu, Zijia Ji, and Min Lu test, in a 2026 study, a virtual simulation platform for teaching cataract surgery to undergraduate medical students in China. Eye surgery teaching tools are still young, and the team asked whether a simulator could build grasp of the operation's steps and risks. Fourth-year students worked through eighteen modules covering the whole care path, with scores and surveys taken before and after.

Best scores ran well above first tries. Students rated the platform warmly, above all its clinical reasoning gains, and most would recommend it. Instant correction of wrong moves and step prompts were the favorite aids. Learners drilled the lens-opening and lens-breaking steps most, and named the corneal cut and handling of a torn back capsule as most memorable. The authors call the tool workable and welcome, while warning that with no comparison group, cause cannot be claimed.
pmc-13495515:
Yukyung Park leads a large team testing, in a 2026 randomized trial, a transitional care program for patients leaving hospital with COPD, the chronic lung disease. The weeks after discharge are fragile, with breathlessness and readmissions common. Across three South Korean university hospitals, 465 patients were assigned by lot to the program or usual care, and followed for three months.

The program gave each patient a personal plan: full assessment, training, phone check-ins, links to community services, home visits, and team case talks. Readmissions ran a little lower with the program, though not clearly enough to count as proven. Breathing symptom scores improved clearly on two scales, and inhaler adherence improved at one month before fading by three. COPD-specific readmissions were few in the program group, but counts were too small to lean on.
pmc-13498515:
Esther Wainwright and co-authors set out in 2026 to define normal testosterone levels for adult women across age, rather than with a single fixed range. Testosterone matters for mood, bone, muscle, and sexual health in women, and clinicians need a reliable yardstick to spot excess hormone conditions. Prior ranges often ignored how levels shift steadily through adult life.

Using private health service blood samples, the team analysed 5,323 women aged 19 to 59 who had regular cycles, a healthy weight range, and no reproductive conditions. Average levels fell with age while spread widened, a pattern captured by their best statistical model. Women reporting excess hair growth showed clearly higher levels than the reference group, supporting the range as a tool for separating normal variation from disease.
pmc-13498915:
W. Murray Thomson and others launch a staging and grading plan for oral health in older adults. In 2026, the international initiative addresses gerodontology's lack of a unified language for case complexity, where current systems miss frailty, function, and social context. Companion papers detail the full rules.

Staging covers three domains: the person, oral function both medical and subjective, and oral disease including caries, gum disease, and mucosal states. Grading adds risk at oral, systemic, and social levels, from prosthetic maintenance and dry mouth to many ills, care dependency, feeding, socioeconomic position, and support. The plan reached strong international consensus for care, research, education, and policy.
pmc-13499515:
Takahiro Hirayama and co-authors describe in 2026 a live imaging view of lymph flow inside the swollen skin areas seen in lymphedema, a condition where lymph fluid drains poorly and tissue swells. Fluid backing up into small skin vessels, called dermal backflow, guides diagnosis and treatment, yet it had mostly been pictured as a one-way reflux in still observations. Their team used ultrasound with a microbubble contrast agent after a dye-based lymph scan had mapped the affected areas.

Watching the first spots where backflow emerged, they traced a network running from a collecting vessel into finer skin channels. Microbubbles inside those channels moved in both directions, forward and backward in sequence, with multidirectional motion over time and space. The finding revises the simple reflux picture, suggesting backflow also involves rhythmic to-and-fro flow that may matter for treatment planning.
pmc-13499615:
Markéta Supa and others reflect in talks on how children live, imagine, and make meaning of time. In 2026, the group article gathers an opening and nine thoughtful pieces built through long talks among teams in Canada, Czechia, Finland, and the United States. The pieces span reading, ecology, place-shaping, and media across home, school, public, digital, and natural settings.

Time emerges as non-straight, many-sided, set by setting, and tied to others, opening out through motion, pauses, and looking back, in tension with forward-looking hopes and nature time spans. Slow and stretched time supports creative, thoughtful, and playful practice. The set backs quick, kind research rooted in care and deep hearing.
pmc-13499815:
Tomoya Kobayashi and others compare postmortem CT with forensic autopsy in eight deaths from falling trees or large branches. In 2026, the look-back study covers consecutive cases from 2012 to 2025 where trunk or branch impact was the primary event and both examinations were performed. Four lethal mechanisms emerged, each in two cases: fatal head or brainstem injury, bleeding shock, traumatic shock with heart or aortic rupture, and asphyxia.

Postmortem CT excellently mapped fractures, bleeding, and gas collections and suggested aortic injury once, but brainstem lesions, exact rupture sites, and low-contrast organ injuries appeared only at autopsy. The authors conclude that CT delineates global injury patterns while full autopsy remains vital for the exact mechanism of death.
pmc-13500715:
Lei Zhu leads a nine-author team with a 2026 materials study on cellulose insulating paper, the paper used with oil inside high-voltage electrical equipment. The paper conducts heat poorly, lets water in, and has electrical properties that mismatch the oil. The team treated the paper with a low-temperature plasma at atmospheric pressure. Their precursor mixes boron nitride powder into a silicone compound called OMCTS, so a cross-linked network forms on the surface and inside the paper's pores.

Microscopy and spectroscopy checks confirmed the new network. Heat conduction rose by about 15.9 percent, while the dielectric constant fell by about 27.3 percent, bringing the paper closer to the oil. Flashover voltage and breakdown strength also improved. Water absorption dropped by roughly a third as the surface turned water-repellent.
pmc-13500815:
Ivan Buryk leads an eight-author team with a 2026 study of nanocrystalline tungsten thin films, coatings built from extremely small crystal grains. Such films interest nanoelectronics makers because tungsten is hard, heat-resistant, and conductive. The team measured electrical resistivity, the temperature coefficient of resistance, and the strain coefficient while the films were heated and stretched, linking this behaviour to changes in the grain structure.
