Conduction was governed mainly by electrons scattering at grain boundaries and film surfaces. An electron's typical run before scattering was about 8.0 nanometres, limited by those edges, and the boundary reflection coefficient was near 0.49 (plus or minus 0.02 on that value). Under small elastic strains of 1 to 2 percent the strain factor reached about 4.7. That coefficient stayed near 1.3 thousandths per kelvin between 300 and 800 kelvin.
pmc-13501315:
Al Noman and Sashittal built FateSens, a computational framework that stress-tests the cell fate trajectories inferred from single-cell RNA sequencing, in a 2026 methods paper. Such sequencing gives snapshots of cells partway through changing fate, and tools reconstruct the flow paths cells take through gene-expression space. Nobody checked how stable those paths are, which genes steer them most, or where rival fates split.

Al Noman adapted sensitivity analysis from systems theory to handle the size and sparseness of the data. It measures how small perturbations bend each trajectory and flags the regulatory genes and split zones that decide outcomes. Applied to how mouse blood forms, the branch where cells choose between neutrophil and monocyte fates, the tool recovered regulators matching known biology. This dataset unusually carries lineage-tracing barcodes that record true family relationships, and the predicted fate splits agreed with that ground truth.
pmc-13501615:
Fahad Zeed Alanezi leads a four-author team with a 2026 cross-sectional study of how AI literacy relates to fear of being judged for using AI in academia. Students and researchers at public and private universities in Saudi Arabia answered surveys between August and October 2025. Two established scales measured AI literacy and fear of negative evaluation, and the team analysed 154 responses with group comparisons and multiple regression.

Respondents showed moderate AI literacy and low fear overall, agreeing most strongly about weighing AI's pros and cons. Researchers, though, expressed far stronger worry than students on several items about being judged for AI use. Age and AI self-efficacy both positively predicted fear: older and more confident users reported slightly more concern, an odd pairing. The authors recommend structured AI teaching, explicit campus guidelines, and supportive settings so that being answerable for ethics supports, rather than chills, careful use.
pmc-13501715:
Zelal Kharaba leads a fourteen-author team with a 2026 survey of community pharmacists in the United Arab Emirates about caring for children with autism spectrum disorder. Pharmacists are highly accessible yet rarely studied in this role. The cross-sectional survey reached 322 licensed community pharmacists and tested their familiarity, knowledge, and attitudes, with regression hunting for predictors of stronger knowledge. The average knowledge score was 8.7 out of 15, a moderate result overall for the group.

Most pharmacists correctly named autism as a developmental disorder, 96.2 percent, and as having genetic origins, 96.8 percent, though misconceptions persisted elsewhere. Some 63.7 percent felt comfortable dispensing autism medicines, but only 49.9 percent felt confident counselling parents. Higher knowledge tracked with holding a PharmD degree, with six to ten years of experience, and most strongly with prior autism coursework, which carried an odds ratio of 3.9. The authors press for autism content in pharmacy training.
pmc-13501815:
Mathilde Hyvärinen leads a six-author team with a 2026 mixed-methods study of why pregnant women in western Switzerland struggle to get sound advice on physical activity. Two maternity hospitals took part. Ninety-five women completed a survey about how different jobs communicated activity guidance, sixteen of them sat for interviews, and nineteen hospital midwives were interviewed about their own habits. Analysis used the Theoretical Domains Framework and the COM-B behaviour model, then merged the strands.

Most women were in their third trimester and highly schooled, yet 37 percent had received no activity information at all and 59 percent wanted more. Getting answers depended on women's own pushing. Midwives admitted forgetting or dodging the topic when untrained, pressed, or doubtful of interest. Patchy advice bred wrong ideas and anxiety. The team built a COM-B framework to grow midwives' capability, opportunity, and drive for on-the-spot, tailored counselling.
pmc-13502215:
Niemann and Watzl published a 2026 protocol for measuring serial degranulation, the ability of natural killer cells to kill target after target. Natural killer cells are innate immune cells that destroy infected or cancerous cells by releasing toxic granules, and only a minority perform most of the killing through repeated attacks. Bulk tests report only population averages, hiding those star performers.

Niemann exploits the fact that each granule release exposes a granule membrane protein, CD107a, on the cell surface. The protein is stained in successive rounds while killer cells mix with targets. Reading the cells by flow cytometry then lets researchers count when and how often each cell fired. The protocol trades away the contact and movement details that live microscopy gives, but gains speed, throughput, and combination with cell-surface phenotyping. The authors note degranulation signals activation rather than proving a target died, a caveat for interpretation.
pmc-13503915:
Shelly Ginzburg and four colleagues probe how nitric oxide signaling rewires protein switches in a mouse model of autism, in a 2026 study. The model lacks part of the Shank3 gene, a high-risk gene for autism. Past work showed excess nitric oxide in these mice, and blocking its making eased their traits.

The team read the full protein set and its phosphate tags in brain cortex tissue. Mutant mice showed shifted tags on proteins tied to synapses, growth, and RNA handling. A drug that blocks the nitric oxide enzyme flipped many of those shifts back. Several high-risk autism genes were among the proteins restored. The work ties nitric oxide to the kinase web that sets those tags, and hints at new drug targets.
pmc-13504815:
Alamri and Alamri, in a 2026 qualitative study, interviewed 35 Saudi adults, twenty women and fifteen men, about how smoking is judged differently depending on who holds the cigarette. Health disapproval turned out to be the smaller part of the story. Women's smoking was read as a breach of femininity, modesty, and family honour, and participants tied it to bad upbringing, emotional instability, and failing as future mothers or caregivers.

Men's smoking, by contrast, was treated as an ordinary if unhealthy habit, at times even a marker of masculinity, despite identical medical risks. Read through theories of gender roles and social control, the authors argue the stigma works as behaviour policing: it disciplines women far beyond the individual smoker, staining her family's reputation too. They recommend tobacco programmes that are gender-sensitive and non-moralising, and frame smoking purely as a health issue.
pmc-13505015:
Marta Gómez-Iglesias leads a team adapting a well-known illness uncertainty scale into Spanish for cancer patients, in a 2026 study. Uncertainty shadows every stage of cancer, shaping stress and coping. Spain lacked a checked version of Mishel's scale, the standard tool for this trait.

The team tested the scale on 174 patients in chemotherapy or immunotherapy care. Analysis kept the original scale's four dimensions, and the full 33-item form held up well. A trimmed 26-item form kept the structure, lifted the share of variance explained, and stayed reliable. Mean uncertainty sat in the mid range. Patients with stronger family and social support felt less uncertainty. More hospital admissions for the disease also went with lower uncertainty. Nurses can use the scale for screening.
pmc-13505115:
Tuba Yalçın, Seda Çiftçi, and Elif Esra Ozturk untangle the links between brooding thought, stress, and emotional eating in Turkish adults, in a 2026 study. Rumination, the loop of replaying negative feelings, can stretch stress and push eating off course. The three are usually studied apart.

The survey covered 626 adults in Izmir, classed as brooding or not by a standard scale. About half were brooders and a third were emotional eaters. Both felt stress and emotional eating tracked with brooding at first pass. After full adjustment, emotional eating stayed the strongest tie, at more than triple the odds, while felt stress faded out. Older age lowered brooding odds. Eating in happy settings raised them slightly. The authors note the snapshot design cannot set the order of cause.
pmc-13505615:
Campbell explains a puzzle in plant immunity: how a guardian protein knows a pathogen has struck when the attack leaves its partner cut in two. Pseudomonas injects a scissor enzyme, AvrRpt2, that snips RIN4, a brake on plant defense anchored at the membrane. The guard protein RPS2 fires only when that cutting happens, and only with NDR1, a second membrane protein, present. Her 2026 commentary walks through experiments by Afzal and colleagues that untangle the tripwire.

Freeing RIN4 from its membrane anchor, rather than destroying it, proved to be the trigger. Loose RIN4 copies set off RPS2 driven cell death on their own. Without NDR1, neither the cut nor the loose copies could activate the guard, placing NDR1 at the scene as a partner. The freed fragment emerges as an alarm signal. For crop science, knowing which fragment trips the guard sharpens efforts to breed or engineer disease resistance.
pmc-13506115:
Charan Makkina, Tony Varghese Panicker, and Baylis Vivek Joseph describe a surgical strategy for lesions that partly destroy the second neck vertebra, the C2 body. Tumours and infections at this level sit close to major arteries and the spinal cord, leaving narrow and risky operating corridors. Their review covers six patients whose damage spared the odontoid peg at the top of C2.

The operation removed the diseased centre of the vertebral body from the front while keeping healthy bone. The gap was rebuilt with the patient's own bone taken from the hip or lower leg, using the intact peg as an anchor instead of front hardware. Screws and rods added from behind completed the support. The authors judge the combined approach viable, safe, and effective across varied causes of C2 damage, and present it as a repeatable framework for a notoriously awkward region.
pmc-13507215:
Brodie J Thomson and others develop a one-pot sulfur(IV) fluoride-driven route to tagged oxetane rings and azetidines. In 2026, the lab paper uses XtalFluor-E to prepare 3,3-aryl-amino oxetane rings and azetidines in modest to high yields of thirty to ninety-seven percent through mild, single-step oxygen removal. Four-sided mixed rings are hopeful stand-ins, yet screening sets remain limited by scarce man-made methods.

Test screening merged with many-factor straight fit spells out factors ruling reaction scope, while tests paired with density working theory math light up nucleus-loving swap at the sulfur(IV) center. The ease and short reaction times speed set making of these amide and amidine stand-ins for drug and crop picks.
pmc-13508215:
Weimin Liu and seven co-authors examine what drives fear that cancer will return among breast cancer survivors, in a 2026 multicenter study. Such fear is common and can shadow daily life long after treatment ends. The study ran from late 2024 into early 2025 and screened 387 potential participants. Survivors rated their fear on a standard short scale, along with symptoms and social support. Statistical models sorted which factors carried real weight.

Fear ran higher in survivors under forty, in those with heavy medical costs, and in those with stage III disease. A diagnosis six to twelve months earlier and having chemotherapy also raised scores. Worry and nervous feelings were strong mental drivers. Feeling unlike oneself and lacking energy added to fear on the physical side. Social support alone did not explain the pattern. The findings point to targeted help for younger and harder-hit survivors.
pmc-13508315:
Noelia Rodríguez-Blanco leads a seven-author survey of working conditions among midwives in Spain, in work published in 2026. Midwives face expanding roles, pay concerns, and widespread temporary contracts that fuel discontent. The national web survey carried 23 questions across five areas, covering job traits, training, and rights. Responses came from 2,499 midwives, and 2,310 met the study rules, a large share of the country's practicing midwives. Most worked in public hospitals. Analyses compared views by contract type, adjusting for age and experience.

Only about four in ten respondents held permanent contracts, though that share rose with age and experience. Temporary contracts clustered in the private sector. They came with lower pay, weaker pay satisfaction, and more unfavorable conditions. The findings sharpen a policy debate about stabilizing the midwife workforce. The authors argue that contract reform matters for keeping skilled birth care staffed and satisfied across Spain.
pmc-13508515:
Chiamaka Obasi leads a twelve-author team hunting genome regions that control grain yield and protein in mungbean, a protein-rich legume, in 2026 work. Breeding progress has lagged because the genetics of these traits were poorly mapped. The team grew 120 mungbean types at two Nigerian sites across wet and dry seasons. Yield swung widely with place and season, while protein stayed in a narrow band near twenty-three percent. A rapid genotyping method produced thousands of markers spread over all eleven chromosomes.

Multi-method genome scans then found fifteen marker links for protein content, landing near genes for amino acid handling and other core jobs. Yield links were hunted in the same framework, against a backdrop of strong season effects. Such markers let breeders select seedlings by DNA instead of waiting for harvest. The study gives mungbean programs in the tropics a firmer genetic footing.
pmc-13510715:
Lage and colleagues ran a trial in 2026 on short-term ginger intake in CrossFit athletes, who train with intense mixed workouts. Thirty-two athletes were split by chance into ginger and placebo groups. The ginger group took 2 grams a day for nine days. Performance was scored by a ten-minute test counting as many repetitions as possible, with effort ratings and jumping tests before and after exercise.

Lage found the ginger group completed clearly more repetitions than the placebo group. They also reported markedly lower feelings of effort. After exercise, their jump peak force fell less, which shows the supplement blunted one sign of muscle fatigue. Peak power and jump height change did not differ between groups. The authors call ginger a possible natural aid for high-intensity training, while asking for larger trials to confirm the effects.
pmc-13511515:
Inoue and co-authors describe a 2026 case in which MRI scanning guided spinal anesthesia for a pregnant woman with spina bifida occulta. That is a hidden spinal defect where the backbone does not fully close. Such defects can hide a low-lying spinal cord or tethered cord, raising the risk of nerve injury from a spinal needle. Their patient was a thirty-one-year-old at thirty-seven weeks of pregnancy, scheduled for cesarean delivery because of marginal placenta previa.

A preoperative MRI confirmed that her spinal cord ended normally at the first lumbar level and showed no tethered cord or abnormality at the planned puncture site. Before the procedure, lumbar ultrasound located the L3/4 space and estimated needle depth. Spinal anesthesia succeeded with a fine pencil-point needle, and the cesarean finished without neurological problems. The authors say imaging-based planning made anesthesia safer in this single patient.
pmc-13512015:
Fabricio González-Andrade, Fausto Coello, and Henry Vásconez study children in Ecuador born with a small or malformed outer ear, a condition called microtia that often pairs with hearing loss, in 2026 work. The study joined clinical severity, type of hearing disability, family history, and social position in a tertiary referral group. Hearing rehabilitation was the central concern, since early sound access shapes language, schooling, and social growth.

Hearing devices were used rarely despite frequent hearing impairment, a gap the authors call preventable. In this referral group, microtia acted as a marker of unmet needs across diagnosis, rehabilitation, and specialist face and skull care. Clinical vulnerability and social barriers appeared to stack on the same families. The authors urge stronger early hearing screening, faster referral, paid protection for devices, and joined multi-specialty care for these children.
pmc-13514415:
Lukas S. Fiedler and colleagues checked whether obesity and diabetes raise early wound infection risk after surgical tracheostomy in intensive care patients. A tracheostomy is a surgically made breathing opening in the neck for patients needing long ventilation.

The team reviewed 92 patients who had bedside tracheostomy at one centre during 2022 and 2023. Wound infection around the opening appeared in 18 patients, about 19.6 percent, within the first two weeks of follow-up. Infection struck about 35.7 percent of patients with obesity versus 12.5 percent without, and 38.7 percent with diabetes versus 9.8 percent without. Fiedler calls the analysis exploratory, since follow-up records were incomplete and the links were not adjusted for other risks.
pmc-13514615:
Thawatphong Boonma and six co-authors describe a new ginger-family plant from northeastern Thailand in a 2026 taxonomic study. Field surveys in Loei Province found a Boesenbergia population tucked into shaded limestone pockets, a habitat type known for narrow local endemics. The team compared its form against herbarium material and published accounts, then ran a numerical analysis over twenty-five chosen traits to test whether the population truly stood apart.

The analysis separated the plant cleanly from every comparison species, and the authors name it Boesenbergia lamudiae. It sits closest to a recently described relative, differing in leaf shape and surface, maroon bracts, a longer hairy calyx, and a lip petal marked by a sharp maroon band. So far it is known only from one district, Nong Hin, and the team provisionally rates it critically endangered under a small-population criterion.
pmc-13515115:
Yan and colleagues produced in 2026 a bacteria-killing enzyme from a virus that attacks Klebsiella pneumoniae, a germ behind cow mastitis. The team expressed the phage enzyme, named Lysin K, in bacteria and purified it. They then tested its strength, stability, and effect in a mouse mastitis model.

Lysin K kept strong antibacterial activity across wide temperature and acidity ranges. Its minimum inhibitory concentration, the lowest dose that stops growth, was very low, and it stayed active in milk. It lysed three types of drug-resistant hypervirulent Klebsiella strains in the lab. In infected mice, treatment cut bacterial load sharply, eased inflammation, and restored normal mammary gland structure. The authors present Lysin K as a candidate for preventing and treating resistant mastitis without antibiotics.
pmc-13516015:
Mohamed Hussein H Awaad leads a nine-author team testing a probiotic feed additive for broiler chickens in a 2026 trial. The product, TechnoCare200, blends two spore-forming Bacillus strains meant to stabilise gut flora. Five hundred day-old chicks were split evenly between a plain diet and the same diet carrying the additive throughout. The team tracked growth, deaths, litter state, foot sores, carcass yields, immune responses, and gut structure.

Supplemented birds died at a rate about a fifth lower than controls and finished heavier, with better feed conversion and a higher production score. Litter stayed drier and footpad sores grew rarer. Carcass, breast, and front yields all rose. Blood and skin tests showed stronger immune responses, and gut sections showed taller villi relative to crypts with lively lymphoid tissue. Awaad's team presents the additive as an effective stabiliser that lifts both productivity and welfare under farm conditions.
pmc-13517215:
Ashleigh Flowers leads a ten-author evaluation of a train-the-trainer programme preparing Indian doctors to push the HPV vaccine in a 2026 study. India bears a fifth of world cervical cancer deaths, yet vaccine coverage sits low ahead of a national campaign. Two medical societies cascaded training outward: master trainers taught doctors, who taught peers. Over eighteen thousand physicians were trained; surveys before and after, monthly engagement checks, fidelity reviews, and twenty interviews judged the effort.

Doctors answering after training scored higher on vaccine knowledge and reported stronger confidence, better beliefs, and firmer intent to recommend. Delivery stayed consistent, with role-play sessions varying most. Interviews described doctors sharing knowledge with peers and engaging their communities. Both societies adopted the programme and plan to continue. Flowers's team calls society-led cascades a workable way to ready doctors at national scale before rollout.
pmc-13517615:
Volkhin and colleagues published a 2026 study on whether two bat flu viruses deserve their own species. H17N10 and H18N11 flu viruses, found only in bats, sit awkwardly in current taxonomy. No hard numeric rule existed for drawing the species line here. The team compared 3,328 flu genomes from the full family.

Seven of eight genome segments split the bat pair cleanly from other flu types. Genetic gaps between groups ran far above the spread within groups. One segment broke the pattern, likely due to an ancient swap event. The bat viruses also cannot swap parts with standard flu viruses. Together, the numbers back a separate species for the pair. Selection-pressure ratios told the same split story as raw distances did.
pmc-13518815:
Zhenge Huo and five colleagues introduce DAIGNN in 2026, a recommendation system that borrows facts from a knowledge graph to suggest items. Such systems ease sparse data and cold starts for new users, though many underuse the user-item interaction record and blend side information poorly.

DAIGNN first fills gaps by building an imputation graph from guessed ratings based on similarity, which thickens the sparse interaction network. Extra information about users and items then enriches the graph. A dual-adaptive fusion step learns how much weight each source deserves. Tests on four real datasets beat leading rivals, averaging 3.1 percent higher AUC and 2.0 percent higher F1 score.
pmc-13518915:
Helgi Hilmarsson leads a seven-author team presenting Gnomix in 2026, software that labels the ancestry of each DNA segment in people and animals with mixed heritage. Local ancestry inference powers studies of population history and ancestry-linked traits, yet older methods scale badly to biobank-sized data, deep time, and many source populations.

Gnomix bundles several inference methods that beat existing tools on both accuracy and speed, with shareable trained models that expose no private training genomes. A companion tool, Gnofix, corrects phasing errors quickly. Tests on worldwide human and dog genomes dated ancient New World segments in the Xoloitzcuintli dog breed back over 100 generations, showing the fine resolution achieved.
pmc-13519015:
Bogdan Postolnyi and a large team tune copper levels in 2026 in a five-metal high-entropy alloy, copper-chromium-iron-manganese-nickel, seeking one coating that is hard, corrosion-proof, and germ-killing at once. Such triple duty suits marine and energy hardware, where microbes themselves drive corrosion in salty water.

Electron-beam coatings came out dense and nanocrystalline, with hardness near 9.4 gigapascals and a favorable strain-to-failure ratio for wear resistance. Copper content steered the surface oxide chemistry, which balanced rust protection against bacterial killing. Pseudomonas aeruginosa counts fell by up to 71 percent at the best settings. Postolnyi and colleagues map how phase structure and surface chemistry jointly set performance.
pmc-13520215:
Gang Deng leads a team in 2026 testing an injectable gel that slowly releases healing vesicles into heart attack-damaged rat hearts. Exosomes from human umbilical cord stem cells show repair promise, yet the body clears them too fast to help. The gel blends silk fibroin with a tea-compound-grafted hyaluronic acid and hardens with light after injection.

In cell tests under low oxygen, the vesicles improved survival, movement, and tube formation. A single injection into injured hearts lifted pumping efficiency from about 31 percent in untreated animals to about 71 percent, cut scarring, and reduced cell death. New vessel growth rose, immune cells shifted toward a repair-friendly type, and the electrical coupling protein connexin 43 increased.
pmc-13520315:
Yara Neaimeh and colleagues report in 2026 a young child with sickle cell disease who developed bone infection at several sites from an unusual gut bacterium. Bone pain in sickle cell disease is often blamed on a pain crisis, so infection can be missed at first.

The patient was a 6-year-old boy who arrived with fever, headache and irritability, then developed back and neck pain. Blood tests grew Bacteroides caccae, with infection in the femur and near the lower spine. Surgeons drained one abscess and sampled bone, while prolonged metronidazole treatment brought improvement. The authors present the case as the first of its kind in this setting.
pmc-13520415:
Kirstin P West and colleagues survey in 2026 knowledge, attitudes and livestock safety habits around animal-to-human diseases in Ada East District, Ghana, where families live closely with farm animals. Surveys plus a group discussion covered adults recruited through five health facilities.

Among 252 respondents, about two thirds showed good overall knowledge, yet only about one in ten knew Ebola symptoms well. Positive attitudes appeared in under half, while reported handling practices scored high. Schooling beyond primary level doubled the odds of good knowledge. Discussion themes covered transmission beliefs and outbreak readiness, pointing to education as the clearest lever for safer practice.
pmc-13520915:
Frédéric Dumont, Charlotte Bourgin and Timothée Vignaud argue in 2026 that surgery needs many proof methods, not one ladder with trials on top. Surgery leans on operator skill. Technique also shifts fast, and learning curves are steep. Drug-style trial logic fits this world poorly.

The essay traces the roots of evidence-based care. It then surveys staged innovation models, registries and Bayesian tools. Large-data work and mixed methods earn a place as well. Each method answers a distinct slice of surgical truth. Slices range from body plausibility to patient felt experience. Cancer surgery shows the joined path at work.
pmc-13522315:
Ruiqi Xie and colleagues present in 2026 a 46-year-old man with a rare prostate cancer. The type is adenoid cystic basal cell carcinoma. Normal prostate blood tests can hide this cancer. Vague urinary signs add to the delay.

Blood in urine grew over time, and urine flow blocked. Scans showed a prostate mass with small nearby nodes. PSA was not clearly raised. Biopsy showed solid nests and sieve-like patterns. Nuclei looked dark and uniform, with edge lining. Stain tests backed basal cell roots. Growth index sat near 40 percent. Standard screening logic fails here, so tissue proof rules.
pmc-13522515:
Akiyama and co-authors probe an electron acceptor built like a cube. Their 2026 paper studies perfluorocubane, a carbon cage ringed with fluorine whose empty orbital is made entirely of sigma-star orbitals rather than the pi-star systems of conventional acceptors. An accepted electron sits confined in the compact cage, almost like a point charge, promising electron-transfer behaviour outside established models.

The team built a molecule pairing perfluorocubane with an electron-donating fluorene unit and fired light pulses to trigger internal electron transfer. Picosecond spectroscopy in polar solvents directly showed charge separation and recombination. Fitting the kinetics to the standard semiclassical Marcus framework produced an unusual pairing: very large electronic coupling together with substantial reorganisation energy, a combination rarely seen in conjugated donor-acceptor systems. The authors credit the sigma-star orbital and cubic shape, and offer the molecule as a platform for unexplored electron-transfer regimes.
pmc-13522615:
Tomas Kozubek leads a team studying a nonlinear water wave equation in a 2026 study. The equation, from the AKNS family, models how waves travel and interact in fluids, plasmas, and optical media. Exact solutions were derived with a modified method, producing stationary and traveling wave profiles that show how nonlinearity and dispersion shape coherent patterns.

The team then reduced the model to a simpler system and mapped its behavior with phase portraits, time series, and chaos measures. Depending on parameter choices, the system moved through periodic, quasi-periodic, and fully chaotic motion. Strong sensitivity to starting conditions and parameters was confirmed. The analysis gives scientists a fuller picture of when orderly wave trains give way to hard-to-predict dynamics.
pmc-13523215:
Yasuaki Yanagawa and colleagues investigate why a gut parasite can persist without symptoms in a 2026 multi-omics study. Silent carriage of Entamoeba histolytica spreads the parasite, yet the gut conditions that support it were unclear. Stool DNA profiling in a small screened clinic cohort was paired with laboratory assays exposing the parasite to a bile acid modified by gut microbes.

Overall gut communities did not separate clearly by carriage state, although cyst carriers held richer communities and several candidate bacterial genera emerged. The bile acid helped the parasite survive under nutrient-poor conditions and reduced its sensitivity to the standard drug after pretreatment. Gene activity shifted toward transport, lipid handling, and stress responses. The authors propose a microbe, bile acid, and parasite axis that may sustain silent carriage.
pmc-13523315:
Xiaoyan Feng, Hongjun Zhu, Liyun Shang, and Yuanyuan Tao review how staff weigh the ethics of physically restraining older patients in a 2026 scoping review with ethical synthesis. Literature in English and Chinese from 2015 to 2025 was searched across five sources, with special attention to Confucian-influenced, family-centered care. Eight studies survived screening from an initial pool of several hundred records.

Four linked themes emerged. Setting-level factors shape restraint decisions. Other themes covered balancing autonomy against safety, the ethical strain felt by nurses, and family choices guided by filial duty and cultural expectations. Primary studies were weighted more heavily than reviews in the synthesis. The authors map how relational autonomy and family duty complicate restraint choices in these care contexts and offer the themes as a guide for practice and policy.
pmc-13523515:
Taner Yılmaz and colleagues examine, in a 2026 survey study, how perceived stress relates to psychological well-being among combat athletes, and whether awareness of mental fatigue carries part of that link. Combat sports impose heavy mental demands. Understanding a pathway from stress to well-being could point to practical support.

A total of 303 combat athletes completed scales for perceived stress, mental fatigue awareness, and psychological well-being. Higher stress was tied to greater fatigue awareness and to lower well-being directly. Fatigue awareness itself was also tied to lower well-being. Statistical mediation analysis showed fatigue awareness partly carried the stress effect, accounting for a modest indirect path. The authors suggest stress management and fatigue regulation as useful components of athlete support programs, while noting the design cannot prove cause.
pmc-13524315:
Wang wrote a 2026 commentary on new regulators of salt gland development in Limonium bicolor, a sea lavender that sheds excess salt through leaf glands. Salty soil already claims a large share of farm land and is spreading with climate change, while only about one percent of flowering plants, the halophytes, thrive in it. This species has become the model for studying multicellular salt glands, backed by a full genome and an efficient mutant library.

The study under discussion adds two regulators, LbWOX5 and LbCUL1, to the known network guiding gland formation and salt tolerance. Wang places the finds in a decade of work that has slowly mapped how these glands arise and secrete. Understanding the circuit in a salt-loving plant, the commentary argues, offers design clues for breeding or engineering crops that can hold yield on salty ground.
pmc-13524415:
Sherwin and co-authors reported a 2026 case report of stubborn low blood sugar in a woman in her sixties with liver cirrhosis. She arrived after a fall, had never actually used the insulin prescribed two weeks earlier, and yet her glucose kept crashing. Scans also found a large pelvic mass over sixteen centimetres wide.

Across a thirty-six day hospital stay, Sherwin treated repeated glucose values near the bottom of the measurable range with sugar infusions and boluses. She became drowsy enough to need a breathing tube and intensive care. No biopsy or full hormone sample was obtained, so a tumour driven cause stayed unproven. The team judges the cause mixed, with poor intake, critical illness, and a failing liver that could not release stored sugar.
pmc-13524815:
Zoë L. Semersky and colleagues announce, in a 2026 study, a new family of nickel-dependent enzymes found through a bioinformatic search pipeline. Nickel enzymes catalyze demanding reactions in nature, from methane formation to hydrogen handling, yet only about a dozen were known. The pipeline hunted for enzymes using a nickel pincer nucleotide cofactor.

One family member, named NphT, was characterized in detail. It moves a hydride, a hydrogen atom with its electrons, between separate molecules, shown through its scrambling of sugars. A very high-resolution crystal structure captured the enzyme with its cofactor, and mutation studies probed the mechanism. The family sits inside the large aldo-keto reductase superfamily and acts on varied substrates including sugars and drugs. The authors offer the pipeline as a route to more nickel enzymes.
pmc-13525915:
Simmi Arora and colleagues report a randomised clinical trial, published in 2026. It compares two orthodontic appliances for tongue thrust. Tongue thrust is the habit of pushing the tongue against the teeth. Forty patients aged 14 to 30 took part. One group received a tongue crib. This is a fixed barrier device. The other received tongue tamers. These are small attachments meant to retrain tongue position.

The team used three-dimensional cone beam scans. They measured tongue position and tooth angles. Measurements came before and after treatment. Both devices improved tongue posture and bite measures. The crib produced greater tongue retraction. Overbite correction was also greater with the crib. Tamers were more comfortable, though. Patients accepted them better. They did loosen from the teeth more often.
pmc-13526215:
Kandhan and colleagues present a case where a prostate cancer changed identity under treatment. Their 2026 report follows a man in his early sixties first treated with prostate resection and testicle removal for high-grade metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma, then stable for two years. Scans later showed avid pelvic lymph nodes and bone spread, and he suffered repeated urinary blockage and bleeding.

A repeat resection through the urethra revealed the transformation: the cancer had become neuroendocrine prostate cancer, a rare, fast-moving variant that emerges after long hormone suppression. The team used the salvage resection as both diagnosis and therapy, clearing the channel, then added systemic chemotherapy and repeated scope procedures with tissue burning. Voiding improved, bleeding resolved, and the systemic disease stabilised. The authors argue repeat resection is a useful bridge in this setting, offering real symptom relief despite the variant's poor prognosis.
pmc-13526315:
Abureesh and colleagues present a 2026 analysis of the global burden of Crohn's disease from 1990 to 2023, using modeled estimates from the Global Burden of Disease 2023 study. Crohn's disease is a long-term gut inflammation, and the team tracked disability and early death across 21 world regions.

Total disability-adjusted life years rose from about 271,700 to about 414,300 over the period, an increase driven mainly by population growth rather than higher individual risk. The age-standardized rate in fact fell slightly. Australasia had the highest rate, while East Asia had the lowest, with more than a twenty-fold gap between them. Disability also made up a growing share of the burden, rising from about half to over 55 percent of the total.
pmc-13528015:
Kyung E. Rhee and eleven colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a trial that refines food security screening in children's clinics. The program, called I-FRESH, screens families for food insecurity. It then checks needs and readiness, helps with referrals to community food programs, and follows up. Four pediatric clinics will roll it out step by step.

The design tests rollout strategies as much as the program itself. Two frameworks guide adaptation and the scoring of reach, uptake, and durability. The trial will enroll 240 participants. It will also track family food security and child health markers such as weight, blood pressure, and blood sugar. Findings will shape a larger hybrid trial. The goal is a screening routine clinics can actually sustain.
pmc-13529715:
Xun Wang and eight colleagues build a prediction model for radiation response in advanced lung cancer in a 2026 study. The cancer could not be removed by surgery. Data covered 222 patients across several centers. Three groups split the work: training, internal check, and outside check. The model fused image texture, dose-map texture, and clinical facts.

Clinical-only models leaned on tumor volume and lymphocyte counts. The fused model beat them clearly on response calls. Its accuracy score reached about 0.90 in training and 0.87 in outside patients. Survival forecasts also improved, with tighter error scores across groups. Decision analysis showed more net benefit from the fused version. The authors say such models could time treatment changes better. They also suit future trial design, by flagging likely non-responders early.
pmc-13530215:
Shibili Said and Imad Barhumi compare in 2026 three ways of using diffusion models to rebuild images in photoacoustic tomography. The technique turns light pulses into sound waves that reveal tissue structure, yet scanners that see from few angles leave severe gaps. Learned image priors from diffusion models may fill those gaps.

Tests used synthetic and anatomical data under full and limited viewing. One model excelled with full views yet faded under limited views without a physics-based cleanup step. A faster variant matched quality with fewer steps. Score-based models held up best across settings, at the cost of longer sampling time.
pmc-13530815:
Dove and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 241, a comparison of surgery against non-operative care for midshaft collarbone fractures in teenagers. It is a common sports injury with no settled best treatment. Surgery can speed return to sport but brings reoperations to remove hardware.

The retrospective cohort included 84 patients aged ten to eighteen, nearly nine in ten of them competitive athletes, followed for at least two years after treatment. The surgery group had arrived with worse fractures by every imaging measure and included more athletes. After accounting for follow-up length, shoulder scores did not differ between the groups, though one athlete-focused score trended toward the surgery group. Return to the preinjury sport was equally common, and of 51 operated athletes who tried, 50 succeeded.
pmc-13531915:
Yuting Yang and colleagues test in 2026 a combined score for forecasting survival after liver cancer surgery across two Chinese hospitals. Records covered 1,174 patients operated between 2014 and 2024. A fibrosis index from routine blood work, a tumor marker called AFP, and their blend were compared head to head.

The fibrosis index alone failed as an independent predictor. The tumor marker predicted both recurrence-free and overall survival on its own. The blend beat both, predicting outcomes in every cancer stage subgroup where each single measure failed somewhere. Chart accuracy also favored the blend, though absolute discrimination stayed modest.
pmc-13532915:
O Krug, A Thomas, and M Thevis study in 2026 how the body breaks down and clears tesofensine, a weight-loss compound sold online as a supplement. The drug is banned in competition as a stimulant, so labs need to know how long it and its breakdown products stay in urine. Six volunteers took a single small dose as a supplement.

Urine was gathered for up to 600 hours and tested with a sensitive method. Four main breakdown products were named, peak levels varied a lot by person, and traces lasted up to 500 hours. Normal supplement doses may stay below reporting limits now in force.
pmc-13534415:
Chuntao Song and Zian Cheng develop in 2026 a machine learning framework to predict risk in malignant intestinal obstruction, a severe blockage tied to advanced cancer. Static scores miss how the disease shifts over time, which limits their value at the bedside. The team built the model from 320 patients split into training and check groups.

Features were screened by two methods, and a paired model produced risk scores with solid accuracy in internal checks and steady results outside. Clinical use in the study cut ventilator time and lowered drug resistance rates. Readers see a dynamic aid for timely, tailored decisions.
pmc-13534715:
Ekaterina Chirikova and colleagues review in 2026 breast cancer risk in women exposed to ionising radiation across population studies. High-dose risk is known, yet low-dose effects and factors that change risk stayed uncertain. From 3,522 screened papers, 106 met the criteria and 40 gave dose-based risk estimates.

Overall, radiation exposure linked to higher breast cancer risk per unit dose. Higher summary risks appeared for fast dose delivery, moderate doses, childhood exposure, and older attained age. Variation between studies fell sharply in low dose-rate groups, helping readers judge where evidence is firmest.
pmc-13536715:
Allyson L. Dir, Brielle L. Batch, and Matthew C. Aalsma study how child welfare staff and substance use treatment providers work together in a 2026 interview study from Indiana. Parental substance use appears in many welfare cases, so referral and joint care matter for family outcomes. The team interviewed 31 welfare staff and 28 treatment providers between late 2023 and mid 2024 about strategies, helpers, and obstacles.

Joint work centered on referrals, first connections to care, and ongoing coordination, plus informal efforts by frontline staff. Respect for each role and belief in teamwork helped collaboration. High turnover, heavy caseloads, and differing priorities around child safety versus parent recovery hindered it. The authors call for stronger organizational and policy support so families receive steadier, better linked care.
pmc-13536815:
Wencan Wang leads a 2026 multicenter study building a deep learning tool to predict neck lymph node spread in voice box cancer before surgery. Standard scans miss many small spread sites, so the tool reads contrast scans while mapping varied zones inside the main tumor. Records for 381 patients supplied training and outside testing. Performance was compared with standard image features and with a three-dimensional learning model, alone and combined.

The zone-aware model beat both comparison models in outside testing. A combined stack of all three models scored highest overall. Both the zone-aware and combined models also separated patients into survival groups with clearly different outcomes. The authors present the tool as support for personal surgical planning, pending wider validation.
pmc-13537515:
Jurásková and colleagues released SeqUIaSCOPE, an open-source software platform that assembles one cancer patient's test results into a single case, in a 2026 paper. Precision cancer care now yields genomic variants, gene fusions, and activity profiles for each patient, which geneticists stitch together by hand, slowly and inconsistently. The platform was built for testing rather than research alone.

Jurásková's system pairs two views. One is an embedded genome browser for checking alterations base by base. The other is a dynamic pathway map showing how a patient's changes converge across body networks. Reporting templates can be tailored to each institution, and it runs on local machines or clusters so sensitive patient data never leaves the site. The code is free under an open license with fake example data, a live demo, and container packages for all major systems. It aims to make multi-omics testing practical for labs.
pmc-13538515:
Kenshiro Shikano and colleagues found that deleting two brain proteins keeps mice lean through two routes. Published in 2026, the mouse study removed nerve-made proteins GL and GM, both made in the brain's hunger hub. Earlier gain-of-function work showed these proteins spur feeding, but their natural roles were unclear.

Mice lacking both proteins ate less and burned more energy, staying lean. Their brains raised a hunger-cutting signal, and their brown fat burned hotter through more heat-making protein 1. Blocking the two proteins' signals likewise cut feeding and shifted nerve firing. A human gene variant near the NPGM site also tracked obesity, hinting the findings may bear on human weight control. Readers get two new targets for obesity treatment.
pmc-13539715:
Afsaneh Ranaei, Elaheh lael-Monfared, and Nooshin Peyman test whether self-care carries the benefit of digital health literacy for teenagers with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 survey study. A total of 250 adolescents completed validated questionnaires on finding and using online health information, diabetes self-care habits, and diabetes-specific quality of life. Correlations, regression, and mediation models traced the pathways.

Most participants scored low on digital health literacy. Stronger literacy tracked with better self-care and better quality of life, while self-care itself tracked most strongly with quality of life. A mediation check confirmed that self-care carried a significant part of the literacy effect on quality of life. The authors argue that teaching teenagers to handle online health information should anchor technology-based diabetes education.
pmc-13539815:
Kamil Deveci and four colleagues compare, in a 2026 single-hospital study, two versions of a bedside score used to grade organ failure and predict death in sepsis. The long-used SOFA score recently gained an update that reflects modern organ support and new thresholds.

Records covered 222 adults treated for sepsis between December 2023 and August 2024, and both scores were worked out from admission data. Each added point raised the odds of dying in intensive care by a similar amount for both versions. Overall accuracy for predicting intensive care death was nearly identical, though the newer score was slightly more specific. The authors find little real-world gain from the update here.
pmc-13539915:
Dowon Lee, Eun Ji Park, Jae-young Kwon, Hyae Jin Kim, Siyun Moon and Boo-young Hwang published this 2026 randomised, double-blind trial of dexmedetomidine in lung surgery patients. The drug, a sedative that also relieves pain, might cut opioid needs after video-assisted thoracoscopic lobectomy, removal of a lung lobe through small incisions, but evidence was limited. Sixty-eight patients receiving epidural and general anaesthesia were assigned to dexmedetomidine or saline, with 61 analysed.

The dexmedetomidine group used less patient-controlled epidural pain relief over the 48 hours after surgery, and needed fewer rescue pain boluses in the recovery unit. Their muscle relaxant dose during surgery was lower. Pain scores matched the saline group, except at one hour after surgery, when the drug group reported less pain. Satisfaction scores ran higher in the dexmedetomidine group. The authors conclude dexmedetomidine around surgery eases early pain and trims pain relief use.
pmc-13540815:
Daan J van den Brink and colleagues build new laboratory tests in a 2026 study. The tests measure what malaria vaccine antibodies can do. Good antibodies coach immune cells to swallow the parasite's surface protein. Antibody levels alone do not prove protection. Function matters as well.

Bright beads carried a repeated stretch of that surface protein. The beads were fed to two cell models in dishes. One model acted like monocytes, the other like neutrophils. Malaria research had rarely used the second model. Both tests sorted antibody subclasses apart. They also showed which cell receptors each subclass used. The tests proved precise and sensitive on real trial serum.
pmc-13542215:
Hongwei Sun and six colleagues stress, in a 2026 laboratory study, the medicinal herb Panax notoginseng with simulated drought to see how water shortage changes its chemistry and prized active compounds. The plant is valued for saponins used against heart and brain vessel disease, and climate change is drying its growing regions.

Seedlings tolerated moderate doses of a drought-mimicking chemical for a week, yet growth, pigments, and protective enzyme activity all shifted markedly. Stress markers rose in leaves and roots, while five key saponins peaked at a middle dose rather than the harshest one. Chemical profiling found more than eleven thousand changed metabolites, concentrated in fat, amino acid, and pigment pathways. The results guide watering decisions for quality harvests.
pmc-13543415:
Anniesmitha K's team reviewed technology-enhanced learning in 2026 for teaching neuroanatomy, a subject health students famously find hard because its structures are tangled and three-dimensional. The team kept only randomised controlled trials from 2013 to 2023 and judged them with an adapted Kirkpatrick model, which grades learning from learner reaction up to lasting behaviour change. Nine trials made the cut.

Students liked virtual reality, 3D views, and stereoscopic modules, with better confidence and understanding. Augmented reality drew more mixed reactions that hinged on design quality. Test-score gains showed in several trials, above all for 3D and virtual reality tools, though not in all. The methods seemed to help most with spatial grasp and interest. Few trials looked beyond short-term results, so the authors call the technology a hopeful partner to classic teaching rather than a proven takeover.
pmc-13543615:
Carlos Bustamante-Recuenco and colleagues published a 2026 retrospective study of treating complex anal fistulas with the patient's own microfragmented fat. The fat was processed by the LIPOGEMS system and injected into the tract after closing its inner opening. Complex fistulas recur often, and conventional surgery risks continence. Twenty-eight patients treated at one centre between 2019 and 2025 were reviewed, most with high transsphincteric fistulas and three quarters already operated on before.

Only two complications occurred, and the typical hospital stay was a single day. After a median follow-up of about eleven months, overall healing reached 46.4 percent, running higher in first-time cases and in fistulas at the back. Closure typically took under three months. In a group where most treatments had already failed once, the authors judge the fat therapy safe and its healing rate encouraging for a sphincter-saving option.
pmc-13544315:
Vallabhaneni and colleagues present a 2026 case report of lipedematous scalp, a rare condition where the scalp's fatty layer thickens and feels boggy. A 52-year-old woman had seven years of patchy hair loss with tender, itchy, spongy swelling across the top and back of her scalp. The team set her case against the small published literature on this condition and its hair-loss form.

The report gathers imaging and tissue findings that support the diagnosis and reviews what treatments have been tried, since no standard therapy exists. Her history included lupus and other conditions, which the authors weigh as possible links. Rare scalp disorders are easy to misread as common hair loss. A case that pairs photos, scans, and tissue results gives other clinicians a firmer pattern to match when they meet the same boggy feel.
pmc-13544715:
Guojun Li and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a modified vertebroplasty for a patient who could not lie face down. Vertebroplasty is the cement injection that stabilises a fractured spine bone. A 70-year-old woman with one-sided paralysis after a brain haemorrhage had an acute osteoporotic fracture of the third lumbar vertebra. Spasticity and postural instability ruled out the standard prone position, and a one-sided needle approach usually spreads cement unevenly.

The team worked with her lying on her side, threading the needle through the facet joint to reach a more central, forward position. They then injected cement at the doughy stage so gravity helped it cross the midline. Imaging afterward showed satisfying two-sided fill with no leaks, and her pain eased immediately with clear functional gains. Position, trajectory, and gravity were deliberately coupled, a template for patients standard positioning excludes.
pmc-13545115:
Pauline Kang and colleagues published a 2026 study profiling Australian adults who say they are short-sighted, using the long-running 45 and Up cohort. Despite myopia's rise, Australian prevalence and its links to general health were thinly documented. Among 21,384 survey responses analysed, 54.3 percent reported myopia, a share the authors themselves judge likely too high because it rests on self-report rather than eye measurement.

Self-reported myopes were more often female, younger within the cohort, urban, and highly educated, with education the strongest predictor of all. They rated their health and quality of life worse and reported more visual and physical impairment, plus more diabetes and cancer, and more cardiovascular and chronic lung disease. Shared lifestyle and environmental roots may explain the clustering, the authors suggest, and the profile argues for treating eye health as part of whole-body health in this population.
pmc-13546715:
Momota Rani Debi and colleagues compared in 2026 three feed additives for broiler chickens against a plain diet and the standard antibiotic approach, as farms seek safer replacements for antibiotic growth promoters. Two hundred forty chicks were divided among plain feed, feed with moringa leaf powder, feed with yeast, and feed with a small antibiotic dose, for 35 days.

Antibiotic birds finished heaviest, though yeast birds matched them on feed efficiency. Moringa and yeast groups produced meat with more protein, better water holding, and better keeping quality, and moringa birds laid down more bone mineral. Dressing yield beat the plain diet in every supplemented group. The authors conclude that moringa or yeast can produce safer, better meat even if raw growth slightly trails antibiotics.
pmc-13547215:
Yousef Asiri and colleagues combined in 2026 a deep learning image model with classic machine learning classifiers to map farmland around Najran City in Saudi Arabia from satellite pictures. Water is scarce in such arid regions, so watching agricultural land closely matters for sustainable management. Their hybrid used a DenseNet121 network to extract features from 2020 Landsat 8 images, then handed those features to either a decision tree or an XGBoost classifier.

The XGBoost pairing won clearly, reaching overall accuracy near 99 percent and beating a stand-alone neural network while costing less computing effort. The authors propose the hybrid as a practical decision support tool for tracking land cover change in dry environments.
pmc-13547415:
Jiajun Liu and colleagues rated 228 short videos about chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on three Chinese platforms in 2026, using standard scales for transparency, quality, reliability, and how usable patient material is. Douyin, Kwai, and Bilibili draw huge audiences seeking health guidance, and the lung disease affects nearly a hundred million adults in China.

Douyin scored best on transparency, reliability, and overall quality, while Kwai drew the most visible engagement yet scored lower on quality and actionability. Bilibili's longer videos were easiest to understand. Accounts run by organizations outscored individual creators. Likes, comments, and shares showed no relationship with medical quality, leading the authors to warn that popularity is a poor guide for patients and to call for clearer sourcing.
pmc-13548615:
Dingyuan Tu and colleagues combine a metabolic index with a frailty count to flag advanced cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, in a 2026 analysis of United States survey data. The syndrome's late stages mean multi-organ trouble and high risk. Using national examination data from nearly seven thousand adults with the syndrome, the team weighted results to the population and compared their combined index against its parts and cousins.

Adults in the highest quarter of the combined index had more than ten times the odds of advanced disease seen in the lowest quarter. Risk climbed in a curved dose pattern as the index rose. The combined score also separated advanced from early disease better than the frailty index or any metabolic variant alone. The authors suggest that joining metabolic strain with physical decline captures the syndrome's danger better than either side alone.
pmc-13548715:
Marco Lizwan and Ming Li Cynthia Chia report a stubborn fluid leak through a keyhole surgery wound after lung removal, in a 2026 case report. A seventy-one-year-old man had a right lower lung lobe removed by video-assisted surgery and went home on day two after an uneventful start. Two weeks later, clear fluid from around the lung began seeping through the access incision.

Bandaging, pressure, and antibiotics failed to seal the leak. Reopening the wound showed clean fluid with no infection, no lung tissue poking through, and no air leak. The surgeons anchored a polypropylene mesh to the neighboring rib to reinforce the chest wall, after which the wound stabilized and the problem never returned. The authors offer mesh reinforcement as a considered option for such rare leaks once infection is excluded, not as routine practice.
pmc-13550315:
Jie Zhu and colleagues fuse three tools into one protein that hunts toxic amyloid clumps in the Alzheimer's brain and feeds them to the cleanup system, in a 2026 mouse study. Amyloid oligomers poison neurons, yet earlier binders could not get microglia, the brain's scavenger cells, to swallow and digest them, and the indigestible load strains the cells' waste system. The engineered protein combines an oligomer-specific antibody fragment, a peptide that summons microglia, and a tag that recruits the autophagy machinery.

In dishes, the fusion protein beat its parent antibody at driving microglial uptake and autophagy-based clearance. In Alzheimer's model mice, tiny doses every three days improved cognition and cut amyloid deposits, while the parent did nothing. Waste pathway markers shifted toward active cleanup with calmer inflammation. The authors call it a proof of concept for disposal-focused Alzheimer's therapy.
pmc-13550415:
Naif S Alshammari and colleagues assemble a federated learning system that lets organizations train an intrusion detector together without pooling their network data, in a 2026 paper. Their design, SecureTrust-FL, layers several guards onto the shared training: a blockchain ledger scoring each participant's trustworthiness, noise-based differential privacy, adversarial training against crafted inputs, and zero-trust checks throughout. Three public attack datasets stood in as separate clients with mismatched data.

Across the uneven collections, the system scored around ninety-three percent accuracy with similar balanced scores and a strong discrimination index. Stronger privacy noise cost detection quality, and adversarial perturbations knocked performance down noticeably, exposing where defenses must harden. The trust ledger kept an auditable record of participation and weighting. The authors present the framework as a workable union of privacy, trust, and security for collaborative defense.
pmc-13550615:
Xiaoping Wang, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 case study of a coal mine roadway in weak rock at the Liuzhuang mine in China. Digging nearby tunnels disturbed the track cross-cut, squeezing its cross-section. Field measurements, a scaled physical model, and computer simulation were combined to explain the failure and design a repair.

Deformation depended on rock strength, support resistance, and digging disturbance, with stress zones from neighboring tunnels overlapping. A combined repair using cables along the whole roadway, steel sets, and an inverted arch cut displacement growth sharply compared with shed support alone. Simulations confirmed lower stress peaks after repair, and the authors present the combined system as guidance for similar weak-rock roadways.
pmc-13551515:
Monique da Silva Bonjour, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 molecular study of a spittlebug that damages South American pasture grasses. Nymphs of Mahanarva spectabilis feed on plant sap and hide in foam they secrete, which shields them from stress. The team sequenced RNA from nymphs and profiled proteins from the foam-producing Batelli gland.

The assembly yielded over one hundred thousand gene transcripts, rich in detoxification enzymes, transporters, and cuticle proteins, with many genes showing alternative splicing. Protein profiling confirmed 500 gland proteins, led by heat shock chaperones and energy enzymes. Together the data point to candidates behind sap feeding and foam production, offering targets for understanding and perhaps controlling the pest.
pmc-13551715:
Hormuzd A. Katki and Li C. Cheung published a 2026 methods paper strengthening a design meant to make cancer screening trials smaller and faster. Their Intended Effect design tests stored blood or tissue from the control group later, restricting analysis to people who would test positive, where screening can act. Simulations tested cheaper sampling, signal decay in stored specimens, and missed collections.

Testing all specimens from people with the main outcome plus half of the rest kept nearly all the design's power while halving the testing load. Power usually stayed above a standard analysis even if screening falsely reassured some negative testers, the authors report. Missed control collections could bias results, yet corrections restored accuracy, supporting a planned pilot in a multicancer detection trial.
pmc-13551915:
Jing-qi Kong, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 protocol for a cluster-randomized trial of motivation support to prevent obesity in early adolescents. Most youth obesity programs fade quickly, and early adolescents crave autonomy, so the trial targets motivation itself. Grounded in self-determination theory joined with the theory of planned behavior, schools will be randomized to an autonomy-support program or control, with four follow-ups over two years.

Outcomes span autonomous motivation, health behaviors, and body fat measures, letting the team trace the full path from motivation to behavior to weight. The authors expect the design to show whether supporting choice sustains healthy habits longer than behavior-only programs. The trial was registered in August 2024 under the identifier given in the article.
pmc-13552215:
A Fella, C Christoforou, and T C Papadopoulos reported a study of brain waves in Greek-speaking children who struggle to read. Children in grades three and six took a word task. They judged whether letter strings were real words or made-up words that looked similar. Brain waves locked to each item were recorded during the task. Two waves were studied: an early one for visual processing and a later one for word access. The study appeared without a printed year.

Younger struggling readers showed larger early waves than peers. That pattern hints at less efficient early processing. Older groups did not differ on the early wave. Children with reading problems in both grades showed smaller late waves. That gap points to differences in how the brain reaches stored words. The team values brain measures in Greek, a language with regular spelling.
pmc-13552515:
Annabella D Lynch, leading four colleagues, published a 2026 study of tapentadol, a dual-action pain drug, as a candidate analgesic for horses. Six horses received three escalating single oral doses and one intravenous dose in a four-period design, with blood levels of the drug and its main breakdown product measured by mass spectrometry.

Oral doses peaked in blood within about an hour, faster at higher doses, and peak levels rose steeply and variably with dose in the reported means. The breakdown product reached far higher levels than the parent drug after oral dosing and peaked much later, reflecting gut and liver processing. Tapentadol was well tolerated at every dose tested, and the authors supply the numbers needed to design dosing studies for equine pain.
pmc-13553615:
Chao Guo and three colleagues build a 2026 gene-based model to guess who will respond to a class of drugs for bone marrow cancers. These drugs, called hypomethylating agents, are standard care for several such diseases, yet fewer than half of patients gain from them. The team hunted for gene groups whose activity tracked with response. They then shrank that group into a score built from twenty-nine genes.

The score split patients into likely responders and likely non-responders with near-perfect sorting in the test data. It held up across other groups, disease types, drugs, and timing of blood draws. Patients in each group also differed in how long they stayed free of disease and how long they lived. Pathways tied to cell growth rose with higher risk scores.
pmc-13554115:
Fahmida Khatoon leads a five-author team linking low vitamin D to inflammation in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 hospital study. The group covered 556 people, including 426 patients whose bodies resist insulin and 130 healthy peers. Blood tests measured vitamin D, two inflammation signals, sugar control, and insulin resistance. Fat tissue samples were checked for how strongly the inflammation genes were switched on.

Patients held far less vitamin D in blood than healthy peers. Their inflammation signals ran much higher in blood, and the fat tissue genes were switched on roughly three times as strongly. Lower vitamin D tracked with higher inflammation, worse sugar control, and stronger insulin resistance. The link held after other factors were weighed, hinting vitamin D shapes this inflammation.
pmc-13554215:
Kalyani B Karunakaran leads a six-author team comparing risk-gene activity in human and monkey brains in a 2026 study. About two thousand genes tied to depression, Alzheimer's disease, and schizophrenia were mapped across both species. Where and when those genes switch on may show how evolution shaped the human mind. Depression genes lit up widely across the human brain, but stayed in deep regions in macaques.

Schizophrenia genes spread across human cortex, deep brain, and cerebellum alike. Alzheimer's genes woke after birth in monkey cortex and memory areas, and more broadly in humans. The spatial patterns for depression genes actually ran opposite between species. The authors link these shifts to human feeling and thinking, and to our weakness for these disorders.
pmc-13555915:
Danny P Nielsen leads a fourteen-author team swapping diets between two woodrat species to see who copes with new plant toxins in a 2026 study. One species eats broadly, while the other specialises on a narrow, toxic menu. Wild-caught animals faced compounds from familiar and novel plants in lab feeding trials. Intake, movement, gut microbes, and gene activity were tracked across the gut.

The generalist barely reacted to the new diet. The specialist drank more water, moved less, and switched on detox genes across its digestive tract. Its gut microbes also shifted far more than the generalist's. Those strong responses still likely fall short in the wild, where toxin hits arrive without warning. Feeding strategy, the authors argue, governs range shifts.
pmc-13556015:
Ahmet Kurtoğlu and four colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether exercise can undo the heart changes that come with a sedentary life and obesity. Inactivity is linked to a pattern of heart shrinkage, stiffening, and poorer blood flow control. Following standard review guidelines, they searched three databases for randomised trials from 1990 to 2025 and pooled the results with a random-effects model.

Twelve trials with 477 participants qualified. Training lowered resting heart rate and systolic blood pressure, and it raised stroke volume, the amount of blood the heart pushes out with each beat. Measures of heart muscle contraction also improved, while overall pumping fraction changed less clearly. Checks for publication bias and one-study-at-a-time removal supported the pattern. The review supports exercise as a practical way to restore heart function in inactive adults.
pmc-13556215:
Feng and co-authors found a 2026 weakness in Klebsiella pneumoniae, a drug resistant bacterium that shrugs off many antibiotics. Its survival depends on surviving oxidative attack, run by a sensor protein called SoxR. That sensor carries an iron sulfur cluster it needs in order to work.

Zinc displaces that cluster, weakening the sensor and switching off its defence axis, Feng showed. Without the defence, the bacteria became far more sensitive to superoxide stress from vitamin K3 in lab tests. Pairing zinc with vitamin K3 killed the pathogen, including strains resistant to ciprofloxacin, with resistance rarely arising. In wax moth larvae, an infection model, the pairing improved survival and no host toxicity was detected at the doses used.
pmc-13558515:
Mark Lebwohl and colleagues report a registry study, published in 2026. It covers the psoriasis drug tildrakizumab. The patients had already tried a different class of biologic drug. The team used the North American CorEvitas registry. They followed 186 such patients starting the drug between 2018 and 2024. They tracked how long patients stayed on it. Skin changes and quality of life were tracked too.

Fifty-seven percent were still on the drug after at least a year. Most patients improved at one year. Clinician and patient measures both improved. Three quarters were on their third or later advanced therapy. The authors say switching to this drug is a reasonable option after the earlier class.
pmc-13558715:
Xiao Teng and nine colleagues built in 2026 a planning framework that estimates a new city district's carbon emissions before a single building rises. It couples three models that usually run apart. One model spreads investment money across the plan. A second estimates emissions from land use. A third counts traffic emissions. All exchange numbers through a shared data layer. Each round of building then reshapes the next round's travel and energy picture.

Three ideas drive the design. An elasticity rule links investment concentration to emission patterns. A symbolic coupling scheme updates parameters across models during iteration. Feedback control turns a display tool into a forecasting one. Trials on a representative district showed the framework could surface low-carbon strategies under different investment intensities. Planners gain a way to price carbon consequences while the plan is still pencil, not concrete.
pmc-13560115:
Wenqing Si and colleagues test a combined blood index against hypertension among Chinese adults in midlife and beyond. Their 2026 cross-sectional study uses the 2011 and 2015 biomarker waves of a national aging survey, keeping 11,797 participants from an initial pool of 25,873. The index divides glycated hemoglobin by HDL cholesterol, joining chronic sugar exposure with lipid metabolism in one number.

Higher values tracked with higher odds of hypertension after full adjustment for social, lifestyle, and metabolic factors. People in the high group carried 38 percent higher odds than those in the low group in the adjusted comparison. Spline analysis showed the relationship bending rather than running straight, a nonlinear pattern. The authors caution that a cross-sectional snapshot shows association only, never cause or prediction. They call for prospective studies to test whether the index adds anything to standard risk assessment.
pmc-13562515:
Hassan Heidari and two colleagues devise a greener way to pull the heart drug verapamil out of blood plasma before measuring it. Verapamil treats high blood pressure and chest pain, but plasma is a messy fluid that hides small drug amounts. Their 2026 method builds a solvent from nonanoic acid and a common salt-like compound. Adding acid or alkali flips the solvent between water-loving and water-shunning states, so it can grab the drug and then separate cleanly. Ultrasound speeds the mixing step.

After tuning the conditions with a structured design, the method measured verapamil across 200 to 2000 nanograms per millilitre of plasma. It could detect amounts down to about 62 nanograms per millilitre and recovered roughly 60 percent of the drug. A standard greenness scoring tool rated the procedure well. The authors present the switchable solvent as a flexible, low-waste option for drug testing in complex samples.
pmc-13562715:
Liangzheng Yu and colleagues mapped how pseudorabies virus, a pig virus that can inflame the brain, drives runaway inflammation. The virus was known to trigger strong inflammatory responses in mice, pigs, and rarely people, but the mechanism was unclear. Their 2026 study tested whether PANoptosis, a combined form of cell death that blends three death pathways, plays a role. Experiments spanned cell lines, mouse immune cells, and live mice.

Infection switched on the PANoptosis pathway and assembled its core scaffold, while the transcription factor IRF1 rose and activated sensor genes that feed the process. Blocking IRF1 or the death pathway cut the release of inflammatory messengers HMGB1 and interleukin-1 beta, and blocking it in mice protected brain tissue and improved survival after infection. The authors point to PANoptosis as a possible treatment target in severe viral inflammation.
pmc-13563415:
Rebecca H. Neiberg and ten colleagues ask whether older people who join research studies actually look like the older public. If they do not, findings may mislead the very patients medicine serves. The 2026 analysis pooled 3,671 participants, average age 69, from 19 studies run at Wake Forest University School of Medicine between 2002 and 2023. The team compared enrollees with people who were phone-screened but never joined, and with census figures for the local catchment area.

Only about one screened person in nine enrolled. The clearest skews were age and schooling: adults over 75 made up 18 percent of enrollees against 29 percent locally, while anyone with some college reached 80 percent against 24 percent locally. Black participants were slightly overrepresented, at 19 against 14 percent. Sex and white ethnicity matched well. The authors urge recruiters to chase the oldest old and the less schooled, whose absence bends results.
pmc-13563715:
Junyi Luo and nine colleagues build a camouflaged nanoparticle that starves a childhood kidney cancer into collapse. Wilms tumour, the commonest kidney cancer of childhood, turns deadly when it spreads to the lungs, and treatment limits how hard doctors can push. The 2026 design exploits disulfidptosis, a death route where disulfide stress snaps the cell's inner scaffolding. Their particle wears a cell-membrane coat marked for the tumour flag CD276, and it carries two cargoes: BAY-876, which blocks glucose entry, and L-cystine, which raises the disulfide load.

Inside tumour cells the pairing cut the energy supply while piling on stress, so scaffold proteins clumped and the actin frame fell apart. Redox readings confirmed the imbalance. In mouse models of the tumour, including lung spread, the platform shrank disease, lightened lung deposits, and extended survival without harm. The authors offer the squeeze-from-both-sides as a design principle.
pmc-13563815:
Elena Buzan and six colleagues read complete mitochondrial genomes to untangle the family history of Europe's roe deer, and catch genes that crossed species lines. Ice ages split the deer into refuges, and contact with the Siberian roe deer later muddied the map. Their 2026 team sequenced 52 mitogenomes from Slovenia, Poland, and France, then merged them with 24 sequences from both roe deer species, giving 76 genomes and 59 distinct maternal lines. Network maps and a time-calibrated family tree organised the diversity.

The three known European clades, Eastern, Central, and Western, stood firm, with Central lines turning up inside France. Two Polish deer carried mitochondrial lines that nested inside the Siberian species, evidence that hybridisation moved a mother's genome across the species border. Dating placed those lines inside established Siberian branches, and selection scans found only faint pressure on a few codons. Whole mitogenomes, the authors show, resolve what fragments blur.
pmc-13563915:
Yogesh Murugan, Vaibhavkumar N. Shrivastav, and Hari Krishna Akurathi pooled Asian studies, in a 2026 review, on how often muscle loss occurs in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Ten studies covering 2,371 patients in five Asian countries used the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia criteria, in either the 2014 or 2019 version.

About one third of patients met the criteria for sarcopenia, with no real difference between the two versions of the criteria. Older age, very low body weight, and advanced lung disease raised the odds. Readers gain a regional prevalence figure and a reminder to screen lung patients for muscle loss alongside breathing problems.
pmc-13569215:
Bruno Henrique Sardinha de Souza and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether soybean plants bitten by caterpillars become tougher for the next caterpillars, comparing one resistant and one susceptible variety. Leaf damage, caterpillar survival and weight, defense enzyme activity, protective compounds, and plant growth were measured after earlier feeding injury.

Earlier injury reduced feeding and survival in patterns that depended on variety. The resistant variety carried higher baseline levels of several defense enzymes, and injury raised one protective inhibitor only in that variety.
