Certain flavonoid compounds marked each variety, yet injury did not raise them, and growth carried no clear cost. Breeders get a nuanced picture of which defenses switch on after attack.
pmc-13571715:
Carretero-Gracia and colleagues wrote in 2026, in Spanish, about the microbes behind flare-ups in severe asthma and how knowing them shapes treatment choices. Antibiotics are often given in these flare-ups despite guidelines, with little gain unless bacterial infection is clear. At a Spanish hospital asthma unit, the team tracked 227 patients with severe asthma over two years. Close to half were on newer biologic therapies. The infectious nature of most flare-ups was studied in depth.

Carretero-Gracia recorded 135 flare-ups, and 103 of them in 80 patients had microbe testing. Viruses, above all rhinovirus, were the most common finds, while the bacterium Haemophilus influenzae was the leading bacterial one. Patients with widened airways, bronchiectasis, showed more bacterial detection and more antibiotic use. Later flare-ups in the same patient often had a different cause than earlier ones, which supports fast microbe testing to guide personal treatment.
pmc-13572315:
Ebadu Areb and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, phloretin, a natural compound found mostly in apples, as a functional feed ingredient for livestock. Biomedical research knows the compound well, yet farm animal evidence stayed thin, so the authors gathered studies on its actions, production routes, and practical uses.

Phloretin fights oxidation and inflammation by quieting one major inflammatory pathway, switching on antioxidant defenses, and tuning sugar and fat handling through an energy-sensing pathway. Those actions support gut barrier strength, resilience under stress, and possibly growth and reproduction. Dosing and proof in production animals remain scarce, and the review marks exactly where feed trials should go next.
pmc-13573415:
Antoine Perrin, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 field study of two mosquito forms in western Switzerland. The Culex pipiens complex carries West Nile and Usutu viruses in Europe. Its two forms differ in habitat taste, one leaning urban and one natural, and they can cross-breed. Past work rarely split them along a clear landscape gradient.

Traps ran at 57 sites from May to September 2025, and gene tests told the forms apart. Farm landscapes suited all forms and hybrids. City growth favoured the pipiens form but not molestus, which ran against the usual story. Forest cover cut the share of hybrids. Warmth raised the presence of all forms, while rain showed no effect. The split results warn that virus risk maps must treat each form on its own terms.
pmc-13574815:
Chuangli Jing, with seven colleagues, reports a 2026 radar method that tracks a creeping landslide group in fine time detail. The Xiongba slides on the Tibetan Plateau's edge move without pause and threaten towns below. Satellite radar watches them well but sees only along its beam and revisits too rarely.

The team first turned beam-wise motion into true downslope motion for four named slides. A smart filter then merged passes from two orbit paths, filling the gaps between visits. Sentinel-1 records from 2018 to mid 2024 show all four slides still active. The lead slide crept fastest, near ninety-five millimetres a year on one path. The new filter cut error by about a third versus the standard one and halved the wait between reads. Gravity and river wear drive the creep, with rain as the trigger.
pmc-13575115:
Euan Hall and three colleagues compare image models for spotting weeds that are partly hidden by crops, in a 2026 study for precision farming. Automated weed detection lets farmers spray only where needed, cutting chemical use. Hidden leaves remain a weak point for field systems.

The team tested two vision transformer models against two standard convolutional networks under set levels of hiding: none, 25 percent, and 50 percent. One transformer, ViT-B16, grew more accurate as hiding increased, reaching 86 percent at the highest level. The other models fell back, landing between 45 and 76 percent. Statistical checks put model design as the main driver of accuracy. The authors suggest hybrid designs that blend transformer reach with cheaper convolutional processing.
pmc-13576815:
Miha Pirc and five colleagues review whether the curve of an implant crown where it exits the gum affects gum stability at the front of the mouth. Their 2026 systematic review with meta-analysis pooled trials of concave versus convex shapes. Single implants in the smile zone can suffer gum recession that spoils appearance.

Four trials with 144 implants and a year of follow-up were found, with 128 implants feeding the pooled maths. Convex shapes showed a trend toward more recession, by 0.31 millimetres on average, though the gap missed clear statistical significance. Leaving out one trial made the concave advantage significant at 0.43 millimetres in the same units. Results pointed the same way across studies. The authors advise concave contours during temporary and final restoration to protect soft tissue.
pmc-13578315:
Xiaohan Sun and Hanhui Liu pair two methods to forecast the mental state of college students, in a 2026 study of smart teaching tools. Mood and stress data unfold over time and bend in complex ways, which trips up simple models. Their base model reads sequences well but is fussy about its settings, and poor settings trap it in weak answers early.

A whale inspired search method, tuned with a chaos based start and a niche rule that spreads the search, picks those settings instead. On a public data set of student behavior and survey scores, the paired model beat classic models and rival tuned versions by clear margins. The authors see the tool as a way for schools to spot strain early and step in sooner.
pmc-13579215:
Chengwu Xie and colleagues predict a new class of magnetic material that ties crystal handedness to electric charge order, in a 2026 theory study. Altermagnets are a fresh kind of magnet whose spins cancel overall yet split energy bands in a wavy pattern. The team focuses on crystals with a built in twist, shaped like a left or right hand, and names a metal organic framework as the prime candidate.

In that material the spin pattern locks to the crystal twist. Flipping the internal magnetic order creates a small electric polarization and reverses its sign. Swapping the crystal to its mirror twin flips the sign again, giving two switches for one property. Light and electron responses differ by state, offering ways to read the setting. The authors pitch the class for memory devices that hold data without power.
pmc-13587515:
Bo Wang and colleagues build a scoring chart to spot early memory and thinking loss in people with type 2 diabetes. The patients at issue also show white matter bright spots on brain scans, a sign of small vessel wear, and mild cognitive impairment in this group often goes missed until it deepens. Their 2026 study drew 1,175 such patients from one hospital in Cangzhou and split them into a building set and a checking set.

Eight measures fed the final chart. Among them were blood sugar level and swing, time spent in target range, a waist measure adjusted for weight, a kidney strain marker, and the scan grade of white matter change. The chart sorted patients with fair accuracy in both sets, and its risk calls matched real outcomes closely. The authors offer it as a desk tool for flagging patients who need early help.
pmc-13590515:
Meekang Sung and colleagues mapped trauma-linked distress in 22 lands with the Global Flourishing Study, with 202,898 people picked to mirror each land. Distress here means being upset by past trauma, a broad gauge, not a strict clinic diagnosis. Nine life traits and thirteen childhood traits were weighed with a meta-study by land.

Rates ran from 16 percent in Poland to 53 percent in Egypt. Young people, gender-diverse people, split couples, jobless people, less schooled people, migrants, and church-goers each week said they felt more distress. Child abuse, tight family funds, feeling odd one out, parents split, and poor health at age twelve each raised later risk, with abuse key in 21 lands.
pmc-13591715:
Juan Javier Bru-Ruiz and five colleagues review, in 2026, how clinicians decide when an athlete can safely return to play after a hamstring injury. These tears are the most common injury in active adults and often recur, with over half of repeats landing in the first month. No shared standard guides the return call. The team searched four databases and kept 22 studies, then weighed the quality of each.

Pain checks proved the most common yardstick across studies. The authors advise never using pain alone: strength tests, flexibility and range checks, imaging, and top speed sport specific drills should join the call. Clearer weighted criteria, they argue, could cut relapse rates and the costs of long layoffs.
pmc-13592415:
Pol Salles leads a 2026 team mapping strain inside flexible oxide membranes with fine X-ray beams while the films stretch and bend. Freed from stiff wafers, single crystal oxide sheets can be strained far past film limits, tuning their magnetic and electronic traits. Averages alone hide patchiness, so the team tracked strain both as bulk values and as point by point maps on polymer carriers.

Thinner membranes took strain from the carrier most faithfully, and stretch and bend left different strain patterns. Local unevenness grew past the average once stress rose, which would smear the temperature where magnetism fades across the sheet. Stacked and twisted sheets passed strain upward with loss. Salles and the team frame the method as a base for rational flexible device design.
pmc-13594115:
Manuel Gil-Lozano and a large team show that silencing a cluster of small regulatory RNAs in the liver can reset blood sugar and fat balance in mice. The cluster, called miR-379/miR-410, sits in a gene region known for shaping metabolic tissues early in life, and its members climb sharply in the livers of obese humans and mice.

The team expressed a decoy molecule only in liver cells of adult mice, soaking up the whole cluster at once. Treated animals showed lower triglycerides and LDL cholesterol, lower resting blood sugar, and better glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in both sexes. Liver cells gained more and healthier mitochondria alongside stronger insulin signaling. The approach also improved metabolism in male mice modeling type 1 diabetes and diet-driven pre-diabetes, suggesting a cluster-wide target for metabolic disease.
pmc-13597515:
Mohamed Mohssen and co-authors severed the spinal cord's link with the gut in mice and watched the gut microbes unravel over six months. Using genome-resolved reads on 333 samples, their 2026 study built more than six thousand draft microbial genomes into a new catalog of the lab mouse gut.

Broken signals shifted the gut community in ways that depended on how bad the injury was, on sex, and on time, with one friendly species, Lactobacillus johnsonii, steadily thinned. Feeding that microbe back to injured mice blocked the metabolic defects and body-wide inflammation the injury would otherwise cause. Community models suggested the microbes' sugar sharing networks had been rewired, starving the lost species. The authors present the work as proof that a healthy spinal cord governs the gut, and that genome-informed microbe therapy can repair the fallout.
pmc-13602115:
Aritra Mukherjee, Michael J Grayling, and James M S Wason examine what happens when a clinical trial adjusts its size midway while outcomes are still pending. Sample size re-estimation lets a trial correct early guesses about variability or event rates, preserving planned power. When the main outcome arrives slowly, recruitment keeps running, and extra 'pipeline' patients may overshoot the re-estimated size.

The authors derive how final sample size distributes under different delay lengths, for continuous and binary outcomes. They judge the damage with error measures plus two new ones: delay impact and cost. Longer delays inflated average sample size and power. Trials whose re-estimated size shrank below the original plan suffered most, often ending over-powered and expensive. When the re-estimated size stayed above the plan, delay hurt far less. The paper lets designers price the wait before choosing this design.
pmc-13609415:
Dragana Jordanov and five colleagues explore the crystal forms and electronic behavior of yttrium oxysulfide, a host material behind glowing display phosphors. Pure Y2O2S has drawn less attention than its doped versions, which light up screens and long-afterglow products. The team ran a crystal structure search over the compound's energy landscape, then three levels of quantum mechanical refinement. They examined the finds' electronic structure.

The search confirmed the known alpha phase, matching the observed trigonal structure, as the stable form. It also surfaced four unknown metastable polymorphs, labeled beta through epsilon. Electronic analysis showed a wide-bandgap semiconductor with an indirect energy gap. Comparing the phases hinted that some could flip from an indirect to a direct bandgap, a change prized for light-emitting applications. The authors present the polymorph map as a guide for engineering this material family.
pmc-13610015:
Constantine Zalagkitis leads a sixteen-author team pooling ninety trials of a sports trick: swishing a carbohydrate drink and spitting it out. Rinsing the mouth with sugar solution, without swallowing, seems to trigger brain reward and motor centers and lift performance. Their systematic review and meta-analysis, registered in advance, gathered ninety crossover controlled trials in adults of any fitness level and measured effects across many outcomes.

Small benefits appeared repeatedly. Distance covered, speed, and workload all improved slightly, with effect sizes between 0.17 and 0.25, and performance times shortened. Maximum voluntary contraction also improved modestly, on thinner support. Muscular endurance, maximum power output, and maximum oxygen uptake showed no effect. Most participants across the trials were male, which limits how far the findings stretch. The authors conclude the rinse gives a small, outcome-dependent edge whose practical worth depends on the sport and the stakes, rather than a universal performance booster.
pmc-13613815:
Rong Liu and colleagues report a 2026 gene study of Ardisia gigantifolia, a medicinal plant found only in China and now critically endangered, with a narrow range and small wild groups. Gardens that grow rare plants off-site can protect them, yet only if the garden stock still holds the wild gene mix. The team read DNA from 67 plants using a method that samples many spots across the genome.

Three wild groups came from towns in Yunnan Province, while a fourth group grew at the South China Botanical Garden from stock taken at a Yunnan farm. Genetic diversity in the wild groups was quite low, a warning sign for a rare plant. Comparing garden plants with wild ones shows a representation gap: some wild gene variety is missing from the saved collection, which tells keepers what to collect next.
pmc-13614815:
Clare Cheng, Ho Kok On, and Narasimhan Kannan Laksmi present a 2026 case report of a 15-year-old girl with struma ovarii, a rare ovarian tumour made mostly of thyroid tissue. She came to care with a painless lump in the left side of her belly that had been felt for three months. Scans showed a large growth on the ovary, and surgeons removed it through an incision down the middle of the lower belly.

Struma ovarii usually appears in women of child-bearing age, so reports in teenagers are scarce. Its signs are vague, which makes it easy to confuse with other ovarian growths. The authors walk through how they reached the diagnosis and chose their surgical plan. For doctors who meet a large, quiet belly mass in a teenager, the case widens the list of causes worth considering.
pmc-13616915:
Nazanin Tavakoli and Paul A. Dirmeyer present a 2026 global dataset that measures how strongly land and atmosphere influence each other. The link runs mainly through soil moisture, which splits surface energy between evaporation and heating and so shapes clouds, rain, drought, and heat waves. Climate models need such measures to check whether their simulated coupling matches the real world.

The dataset gives correlation and coupling indices between soil moisture and surface heat fluxes, plus a measure of how long soil moisture anomalies persist, at two fine grid resolutions. Several satellite and flux products are combined so that measurement errors and spread between products can be stated openly. Checks across product combinations showed consistent spatial patterns. The authors offer the data for forecast testing, model tuning, and work in ecology, hydrology, and soil science.
pmc-13617315:
Christopher R. D'Adamo and ten colleagues run a randomized, double-blind trial comparing four supplement strategies for raising coenzyme Q10, a compound central to cell energy production and antioxidant defense. One hundred fifty healthy adults took label doses for eight weeks of ubiquinone, ubiquinol, geranylgeraniol, a combination of ubiquinol with geranylgeraniol, or a placebo. Blood levels of coenzyme Q10 were the main outcome, with mood and health surveys as secondary checks.

Ubiquinone, ubiquinol, and the combination each raised blood levels clearly more than placebo, while geranylgeraniol alone showed no effect. The combination outperformed plain ubiquinone, though it matched ubiquinol alone. No group differed from placebo on the wellbeing surveys, and side effects were rare everywhere. The authors conclude the direct forms work, and they propose a factorial trial to test whether geranylgeraniol truly adds anything.
pmc-13618715:
Chaonan Ma and Misbah Ullah Khan systematically review long noncoding RNAs tied jointly to hypoxia, oxygen starvation inside tumors, and pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death. They assess the RNAs as prognostic markers in lung cancer. These RNA signatures might flag patients headed for worse outcomes, but the findings were scattered. Following standard review guidelines, they searched five databases to November 2025 for studies linking the signatures' expression to survival.

Twenty-seven studies qualified and fourteen supplied numbers for pooling. High signature expression came with about fifty percent higher adjusted hazard of death overall, with a stronger effect in lung adenocarcinoma and a clear signal persisting in advanced-stage disease. Mechanistic work tied some RNAs to oxygen sensing and others to death signaling, with two genes, HIF-1a and caspase-1, as network hubs. Because studies disagreed markedly, the authors demand standardization and outside validation before clinical use.
pmc-13618915:
Jae Hyun Kim and thirteen colleagues run a phase 2 trial of low-concentration nanoparticle cyclosporine eye drops for dry eye. They test whether a fifth or two fifths of the standard dose can match the conventional product. Patients were randomized, double-blind, to the drops at two strengths or to Restasis, the standard emulsion. Tear volume change after twelve weeks was the main endpoint, with surface staining, tear stability, and symptom questionnaires tracked throughout.

Tear volume rose in all three groups by twelve weeks with no differences. The low-dose drops improved tear volume earlier, by week four, though between-group gaps never reached significance, and one low dose beat the standard on conjunctival staining at weeks four and eight. Corneal scores, tear breakup time, and symptom scales improved everywhere without group differences. The authors conclude the low-concentration drops deliver efficacy and safety comparable to the established product.
pmc-13620115:
Harold Nathan Tan and ten colleagues reviewed outcomes for patients with rare thymic tumors treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors at a major cancer center, in a 2026 paper. The thymus trains immune cells, so tumors there often tangle with autoimmunity. Records from 2010 to 2024 covered forty-two patients with thymic carcinoma, thymoma, or thymic neuroendocrine tumors, treated with single drugs or combinations.

Immune side effects struck sixty percent of patients and every thymoma patient in the group, with severe cases in about a fifth and one death from lung inflammation. Muscle and nerve syndromes appeared, including a combined muscle weakness and heart muscle inflammation. Tumors shrank in about a fifth of those who could be measured, and most achieved at least disease control. Patients who developed immune side effects actually faced lower death risk. Certain gene changes predicted outcomes in opposite directions, which the authors say argues for careful patient selection.
pmc-13621715:
Jack Scanlan and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study of malignant ascites, the fluid that builds up in the belly of many patients with advanced ovarian cancer. The fluid carries cancer cells that clump into small balls called spheroids. The team asked what proteins fill the fluid and how living in it changes the cancer cells.

Using tools that identify many proteins at once, they compared fluid from patients with blood serum and grew cancer cell lines in the fluid. The ascites raised cell survival and helped spheroids form, yet drug killing stayed in line with results in normal culture fluid. The fluid switched on proteins tied to cell surfaces and the material around cells, including one called TGM2 that the team confirmed with staining. The authors call this a pilot study and urge testing in a larger group.
pmc-13621815:
Yixuan Xu leads a team studying whether coenzyme Q10, a nutrient found in food and sold as a supplement, can repair age-related problems in megakaryocytes. These large bone marrow cells make platelets, the small blood cells that form clots. In old age the cells work poorly and platelets can become too reactive, raising clotting risk.

Aged male mice received the nutrient for twelve weeks, and a human cell line was used for closer tests. Treated mice showed better growth and maturing of the marrow cells, plus signs of stronger autophagy, the cell's own recycling system. A protein called COPS3 rose after treatment, and blocking it weakened part of the benefit, so it seems to help drive the effect. Platelet counts stayed the same, but platelets clumped less readily, which the authors see as a useful lead.
pmc-13624315:
Emil E Jonescu and colleagues published a 2026 monitoring study of sound, light, and temperature inside a palliative care unit, where patients near the end of life are sensitive to surroundings. Guidelines describe sleep-supportive conditions, yet few units have been measured against them. The team placed loggers in single and shared rooms of a city hospital ward.

Sensors recorded every minute across two month-long periods. Noise ran hot around the clock: night averages reached the mid-fifties in decibels and daytime levels passed sixty, with little quieting after dark. Lighting failed in both directions, spiking above sleep-friendly levels at night while staying too dim by day to anchor body clocks. Temperature barely moved across the day, missing the dip that aids sleep. The authors argue ward design should be treated as part of care, not the container for it, and call for design fixes backed by measurement.
pmc-13624815:
Kwon Hui Seo, publishing in 2026, answers a comment on an earlier review of ketamine and esketamine given around surgery. The review had pooled studies to ask whether these drugs cut nausea and vomiting after general anesthesia. A commenter raised method and clinical concerns, and this reply explains the choices behind the pooled endpoint.

Seo clarifies that the combined measure counted nausea on its own rather than adding nausea and vomiting scores, which would count some patients twice when both struck. Vomiting was still tracked apart, since it is a reflex with its own weight, unlike the felt sense of nausea. Timing differed across the source studies, and the reply walks through how that spread was handled, keeping the original conclusions in place.
pmc-13627115:
Faisal and colleagues introduce in 2026 AudioHate-DB, a speech dataset for detecting hate in spoken English delivered with a Bengali accent. Written hate speech resources are plentiful, but accented speech from South Asia is barely covered. That gap holds back both detection systems and speech recognition.

The dataset holds 3,018 phone-recorded audio samples built from a controlled inventory of 1,006 sentences, split almost evenly between hateful and neutral content. Hateful sentences each carry at least one term from a list of 23 slurs and profanities sorted into six categories. Speakers of different genders from several regions recorded in ordinary indoor and outdoor settings, and both raw and noise-cleaned versions are supplied. Baseline tests with four standard models topped out with a recurrent network reaching accuracy just under eighty-four percent on this dataset.
pmc-13630315:
Liyun Wu and three colleagues built a scoring system for graduate education quality in mining engineering in China. The field ties to national energy security. It also ties to the industry's green, smart turn. Their framework stacks five dimensions, twelve sub-criteria, and twenty-six measures into one structure.

Structural modelling first mapped how the measures drive one another. An expert-fed probability network then scored the system's state. The overall chance of a positive rating landed near half, a middling verdict. Course quality was the strongest area. Setting the target to its best state highlighted key levers. Course renewal speed stood out. So did practical training oversight and supervisors' own technical updating. Research platform support lagged as the weak node. It needs investment.
pmc-13632315:
Agus Santosa and three colleagues published this 2026 qualitative study on designing digital support for tuberculosis care in Indonesia. Tuberculosis treatment lasts months, and patients need steady support and monitoring at local clinics. Digital reminder tools exist, yet many were built without asking the people who must use them. The team interviewed eighteen people in Banyumas District: six patients, six family members, and six program nurses.

Three themes came out of the interviews. Sticking with treatment is a long, shifting struggle rather than a one-time choice. Families want to help but often lack clear channels to coordinate with clinics. Nurses struggle to track everyone and follow up on time. The authors turned these needs into design requirements, including adjustable reminders, role-based messaging, clinician dashboards, and follow-up records. Their blueprint aims at coordinated care that fits real clinic workflows.
pmc-13634415:
Wallisson Bruno de Morais Pacheco and colleagues catalogued the proteins in ram sperm and semen fluid, hunting for signs of how well semen survives freezing. Breeders freeze ram semen for artificial insemination, yet some males' sperm thaw badly. The team collected samples from twelve tropically adapted rams and froze them. Rams were classed as high or low freezability by how much movement their sperm kept after thawing.

Mass spectrometry identified over fifteen hundred sperm proteins in each group. High-freezability sperm carried more protective proteins: immune-related factors, protein guards, and helpers keeping cell structure sound and resisting cell death. Low-freezability sperm leaned on energy-burning machinery instead. Semen fluid told a matching story: protective, stabilizing proteins in the high group, stress signals in the low. The authors call their semen fluid catalogue the deepest yet for rams, a base for picking better breeding males.
pmc-13634715:
Xin Yue and eight colleagues published this 2026 study of raw potato starch as a bone-protecting feed for meat ducks. Weak bones fracture easily in farmed ducks, hurting welfare and profits. The starch resists digestion and ferments in the gut, which may calm inflammation that eats bone. First the team described the starch: smooth round granules with a particular crystal form. Then they ran two feeding trials in young ducks.

In the first trial, ducks fed a fixed share of the starch built more bone mineral, and less leaky guts tracked with better bones. The second trial triggered gut inflammation with an irritant, which thinned and weakened the bones. Adding the starch reversed that bone loss. Blood phosphorus rose, inflammatory marrow signals fell, and bone-eating cell activity dropped. The authors propose the starch as a whole-body strategy against inflammation-driven bone loss.
pmc-13636615:
Frank Agbogbo and David Dismuke published this 2026 review of how gene therapy vectors are manufactured. Recombinant adeno-associated virus, a harmless carrier retooled to deliver genes, now anchors many approved therapies after sixty years of research. Demand is about to jump, since developers want the same carriers for common diseases such as arthritis, heart failure, diabetes, and Parkinson's disease, not only rare ones. Today's factories cannot supply that scale cheaply or safely enough.

The authors trace progress in molecular design, process development, and plant operations over three decades. Gains in yield and purity have steadily improved the economics. Their forecast leans on borrowing the antibody industry's playbook: intensified processes that pack more output into smaller footprints, plus automation that steadies quality. Continued engineering of the carrier itself also matters. The review closes with the challenges that still gate wider access to these therapies.
pmc-13637115:
John Tolladay and Christopher Yau published this 2026 study linking weather and environment to prescribing volumes across England. Climate is blamed for many health pressures, yet its mark on drug demand was unknown. The team merged fifteen years of monthly practice-level prescriptions with weather, air quality, flooding, and deprivation data, matched by place. They examined heart and breathing medicines and antibiotics with two methods that handle tangled, linked exposures.

Temperature stood out as the one steady driver. Hotter months brought more heart and breathing prescriptions and fewer antibiotics. Rain, floods, and most pollutants showed small or trivial effects once seasons were counted. Regional and social differences between practices dwarfed every weather-and-air signal. The authors read prescribing demand as steadier against weather swings than feared. Climate planning for health services, they argue, should focus on slow change rather than bracing for monthly shocks.
pmc-13639215:
David M Horton and four colleagues present a 2026 study of how often therapy sessions meet affects who finishes PTSD care. They compared three proven talk and exposure treatments for trauma.

Data came from sixty-six trials with eighty-four treatment arms. Next to one talk therapy, patients were a bit less likely to finish exposure therapy. They were about twice as likely to finish the eye movement therapy. Meeting more than once a week doubled the odds of finishing exposure work. The team also found wide gaps in how trials define finishing, and they ask for one shared rule.
pmc-13642115:
Sergejs Boroviks led a 2026 experimental study of a plasmonic metasurface that shows the resonant lattice Kerker effect in the near-infrared, where reflection is suppressed in a narrow band. Directional scattering arises when electric dipole and quadrupole modes are excited together in the tiny meta-atoms, promising strong near-field gain that in theory should greatly boost doubled light. The team tested whether that boost survives in real tests, backing measurements with simulations and multipole analysis.

The enhancement proved elusive in practice, very sensitive to lab conditions, so the expected sharp rise in doubled output did not reliably appear. That gap between theory and bench is the paper's central lesson. Builders of nonlinear devices get a candid guide to the pitfalls, with suggestions for sidestepping them, rather than another record claim that falls apart outside ideal settings.
pmc-13647415:
Yitong Niu and seven colleagues test whether machine learning can predict what remains inside kapok fiber after chemical pretreatment, using only a handful of experiments. Kapok is a light, hollow tropical fiber with renewable promise, but wax and lignin make it hard to process in water. Thirty-three pretreatment runs varied acid, hot water, or alkali conditions, time, and temperature. Models were judged by leaving one run out at a time, a strict test for tiny datasets.

Cellulose content proved the most predictable of the three fiber components. A gradient-boosted tree model did best alone, and a wrapper model that predicts all three components together improved every score. Temperature drove most change in the sugar-based components, while the chemical environment mattered more for lignin. The authors position small-data learning as a useful exploratory compass for fiber processing, while warning that thirty-three runs demand cautious validation.
pmc-13649215:
Xiaoling Chen and two colleagues identify a previously unreported variant in the RPL15 gene in a fetus with hydrops fetalis, a dangerous build-up of fluid, who died before birth. Variants in this gene cause a form of Diamond-Blackfan anaemia, and fewer than ten had been described, often with fetal fluid build-up and growth restriction.

Sequencing the fetus and both parents revealed a frameshift change that deletes a single letter of the gene's code. Laboratory tests showed the altered message decays faster and yields far less protein, explaining the severity. Reviewing earlier cases, the authors note heart defects and reduced fetal movement as recurring features, and they describe this as the first documented perinatal death tied to the gene.
pmc-13649515:
Huan Yang and two colleagues studied how older workers' views of their own aging shape how well they thrive at work. Firms face an aging staff and need staff aged 45 and up to stay keen to learn and grow. The team joined a scenario test with 178 people and a survey of 225 more.

Workers who viewed their own aging in a warm light tended to thrive more. Lower felt stress carried much of that link: a warm view eased stress, and ease fed thriving. The chain ran stronger for women than for men. The authors offer tips for firms that want to turn age from a feared burden into a resource.
pmc-13650915:
Wei Han Zhao and two colleagues test whether the ratio of two amino acids in feed, arginine to lysine, changes how growing pigs use their diet. Both amino acids feed protein building and nitrogen handling, so their balance, rather than either amount alone, might steer digestion and metabolism.

One hundred sixty-five pigs were assigned by weight to three diets with rising ratios and followed for fifteen weeks across eleven pens per diet. Growth, feed intake, and feed efficiency never differed between diets, and fecal scores stayed similar throughout. The middle ratio improved digestion of nitrogen and energy in the early weeks, though the advantage faded later and never converted into faster growth. Blood markers shifted only in isolated, curved patterns. The authors judge the practical value of the middle ratio unproven and call for work on why the early benefit disappears.
pmc-2574415:
Engler, Kandzia, and Marillonnet introduce a one-pot, one-step precision cloning method with high throughput. Cloning joins DNA pieces so cells will build a chosen protein. Popular earlier methods were efficient and flexible, but left extra sequence scars that added unwanted amino acids to the final protein.

Their simpler method assembles pieces cleanly, without leaving those extra residues behind. Several fragments can be joined in a single reaction, which suits large projects. Clean, fast assembly speeds synthetic biology, where teams routinely build and test many DNA designs in parallel.  Scar-free proteins behave more like their natural counterparts in later assays.
pmc-2592715:
Zhang, Liu, Meyer, and co-authors introduce MACS, a model-based method for analysing ChIP-Seq data. ChIP-Seq maps where proteins bind DNA across the genome, using machines that read huge numbers of short DNA pieces. Raw read counts alone cannot say which binding peaks are real.

MACS models how reads pile up along DNA, so true binding sites stand out from background noise. That statistical step turned a flood of short reads into reliable maps of protein binding. The tool became a standard part of genome analysis, used in studies of gene control in health and disease.
pmc-3163615:
Bromet, Andrade, Hwang, and co-authors report cross-national data on major depressive episodes under DSM-IV definitions. Major depression ranks among the leading causes of disability worldwide. Yet survey data were missing for many countries, especially low- and middle-income ones.

The authors present how common depression is, how much it impairs daily life, and which groups are most affected, across the countries surveyed. Comparable figures expose gaps in care and challenge the idea that depression is mainly a rich-country problem. Health planners use such data to argue for mental health services.  Treatment coverage lagged far behind need in many of the surveyed countries.
pmc-3292515:
Sørensen, Van den Broucke, Fullam, and co-authors review the concept of health literacy and its place in public health. Health literacy concerns the knowledge and skills people need to handle the hard demands that modern health care places on them. Its importance was increasingly recognised when they wrote.

Yet no consensus existed on its definition or on its core dimensions. The authors gather competing definitions and models and work toward an integrated view. A shared concept matters because health literacy programmes and surveys cannot be compared, or improved, without one.  European policy work on health information drew heavily on their integrated model.
pmc-3485615:
Yan, Zhong, Xu, and co-authors identify a liver protein as the functional receptor used by hepatitis B and D viruses to enter cells. Hepatitis B remains a major public health problem, and people also infected with its satellite virus, hepatitis D, suffer more severe disease. Both viruses enter through the same envelope proteins.

The team shows the entry doorway is a bile-salt transporter on liver cells, called sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide. Finding the receptor solved a decades-old puzzle. It opened routes to entry-blocking drugs and to better lab models of hepatitis infection.
pmc-3491415:
Akalin, Kormaksson, Li, and co-authors present methylKit, an R package for analysing genome-wide DNA methylation profiles. Methylation is a mark placed on cytosine bases of DNA. It is pivotal for gene control, for how cells take on distinct roles, and for cancer growth.

High-throughput methods now profile those marks across whole genomes, producing data that need fast, careful handling. methylKit rapidly analyses such profiles, comparing the marks between groups and flagging regions that differ. Open software helped this field spread beyond specialist computing centres.  Cancer studies of these marks adopted the package for comparing tumours against healthy tissue.
pmc-5418815:
Hasin, Seldin, and Lusis reviewed multi-omics approaches to disease in 2017. High-throughput technologies had revolutionized medical research in a short span of years. Gene chip arrays made genome-wide association studies possible at scale. Tools that read transcript levels across the genome then gave rise to integrative genetics.

Other omics technologies followed, covering proteins, metabolites, and more. Multi-omics combines these layers to see a disease process whole, rather than one molecule type at a time. A gene variant may matter only through the protein and pathway changes it causes. Layered data can reveal those chains and point to drug targets. The review maps how to join the layers without drowning in data.
pmc-5837715:
Fernando Hartwig, George Davey Smith, and Jack Bowden proposed a stronger Mendelian randomization method in 2017. The approach uses genes to test whether a risk factor truly causes a disease. It often relies on summary data from very large genetic studies.

A key threat is pleiotropy, where a gene affects the outcome through other paths. The authors base their method on the idea that the most common gene effect is the valid one. Simulations and examples show this modal approach holds up when other methods bend. It gives researchers one more check before claiming a cause.
pmc-7100515:
Xiuyuan Ou, Yan Liu, Xiaobo Lei, and coauthors characterized the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in 2020. Beta coronaviruses had caused three zoonotic outbreaks in under two decades. Almost nothing was known about the newest virus's entry machinery at the time.

Using harmless virus shells carrying the spike, the team tested which cells it can enter. The spike uses ACE2 and needs cutting by cell proteases to fuse. Antibodies raised against the earlier SARS spike showed limited cross-reaction. Those findings set early expectations for vaccines and antibody drugs aimed at the spike.
pmc-8728215:
Donovan Parks and colleagues reported in 2021 on the Genome Taxonomy Database, an ongoing effort to give bacteria and archaea one consistent family tree. The database builds its taxonomy from genomes themselves, keeping the ranks even and the branching in line with evolutionary history. Its source genomes come from a major public archive of assembled genomes.

The edition described here spans more than a quarter of a million bacterial genomes and several thousand archaeal ones. The authors explain how genomes are quality checked and placed, and how names are normalized across ranks. Microbiologists lean on this census because older naming schemes often grouped unrelated organisms together.
pound-cathay-1915:
Ezra Pound published Cathay in 1915, his crystalline versions of classical Chinese poems, drawn from Ernest Fenollosa's notes. The Imagist manifesto in practice, the slim book remade English poetry's sense of what an image can do in verse. Pound knew no Chinese then; he worked from Fenollosa's cribs and Japanese readings of Li Bai and others.

The River-Merchant's Wife, a letter of love and separation, has become the most loved poem in the book. Exile's Letter and The Jewel Stairs' Grievance show longing rendered in clear things, with no comment or excess of words. War poems from old Cathay landed in 1915 with bitter force for readers of the Western Front's first year in France. Pound's versions, whatever their liberties, taught English verse economy, clarity, and the charged single image. Cathay remains the doorway through which modern English poetry met China.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-159-19:
September 15, 1920, in volume 159 of Punch, opens with Charivaria, a run of brief jokes on the week's reports. Weddings, teeth, and trade unions all pass under the column's dry eye.

Prohibition meetings in Scotland are said to have drawn fifty thousand people, more aliens than the column thought Scotland held. At an Oldbury wedding a brick was thrown at the bridegroom, though confetti is cheap. Fourteen thousand false teeth stolen in east London remain missing, trade unionists protest the jobless insurance act, and one hundred fifty brass bands prepare to play at the Crystal Palace.
ricardo-essay-profits-1815:
Ricardo's Essay on the Influence of a Low Price of Corn on the Profits of Stock appeared in 1815. The short name is the Essay on Profits. Corn meant grain, and its price governed wages across the economy. Ricardo builds a spare model farm economy to trace the effects.

Cheap corn lowers wages, raises profits, and shifts income among classes, in his model. That corn model became the core of his later Principles of Political Economy. The text here comes from McCulloch's 1846 edition of Ricardo's Works. Landowners and manufacturers fought over corn laws with his ideas as weapons. The essay shows his method at its purest.
roth-an-inquiry-into-the-animism-and-fol:
Walter Edmund Roth, a government ethnologist in British Guiana, set out to study the spirit beliefs of its native peoples in full. His 1915 inquiry, published by the Bureau of American Ethnology, treats animism as a system worth taking seriously.

Roth examines beliefs about the soul, its journeys during sleep and after death, and the spirits of animals, plants, and places. He gives long attention to kanaima, the feared practice of ritual killing and revenge. Myths, charms, and shamans' rites fill out the account. The study's order and patience made it a standard work on South American belief.
savigny-geschichte-roem-rechts-ma-vol1-1:
Friedrich Carl von Savigny opened his History of Roman Law in the Middle Ages with a first volume in German in 1815. Savigny, a Berlin professor, asked what happened to Roman law in the centuries after Rome fell. The common story said it had vanished; his research showed it had lived on in cities, courts, and church practice.

Volume 1 traces the Corpus Juris through the early medieval centuries, following Roman law in Italy, France, and the German lands. Savigny works from charters, chronicles, and law books that few had read. The book founded the modern study of legal history and the historical school of law with it. Its motto, that law is a people's living spirit rather than a ruler's command, runs through the whole vast work that followed.
shahnama-warner-vol-7-1915:
Volume 7 of the Warner brothers' Shahnama of Firdausi appeared in 1915. Seven volumes into the nine-volume set, the English reader is deep in the later books of Persia's national epic. Firdausi wrote the Book of Kings to preserve his people's past as Arab rule reshaped Persia.

Late Sasanian kings, their wars, and their courts fill this volume, with the empire's strength slowly failing. Famous rulers appear in Persian tradition's own telling, not in Greek or Arab versions. The Warners' notes explain customs, names, and points where manuscripts differ. The volume carries the long story toward its sad close, when the old Persian empire falls and the epic's world ends.
sollas-ancient-hunters-1915:
W. J. Sollas, an Oxford geologist, published Ancient Hunters in 1915 in a revised second edition. He retold the Stone Age through its successive peoples and their tools. Neanderthals, Aurignacians, and Magdalenians each receive long treatment.

Sollas matched each ancient group to a living hunting people he saw as similar. That method, called the unilinear view, treated cultures as rungs on one ladder. Modern scholars reject the ladder but keep much of his fossil record. The book captures early anthropology at its most confident. His accounts of cave art and burial customs drew wide public interest as well.
sombart-quintessence-capitalism-epstein-:
Werner Sombart studied the modern businessman in The Quintessence of Capitalism, translated by M. Epstein in 1915. Dutton published the English edition in New York. Sombart asks what spirit drives the builders of modern business. He treats that capitalist spirit as a product of history, not of nature.

Bourgeois virtues and bold venture meet in his portrait of the type. Thrift, calculation, and daring combine in changing measure across the centuries. The book crowns the German historical school of economics in English. Sombart's answers differ sharply from Marx's, though both stress history. Readers meet a rich psychology of enterprise. Its portraits still provoke debate.
spr-proceedings-vol27-1914-1915:
Parts sixty eight through seventy form volume twenty seven, spanning 1914 and 1915. War breaks over Europe in the middle of this volume's years. The Society for Psychical Research keeps publishing through the first shock. Telepathy work and trance sittings continue on the record.

Soldiers' and families' strange experiences begin to color the case files. Apparitions of the fallen would soon fill the society's postbag. Mediumship reports hold their long, checked form amid the change. Volume twenty seven catches the archive as the old world ends. The debate of 1882 to 1930 gains a wartime chapter here. Its tone stays measured against the times.
spr-proceedings-vol28-1915:
Volume twenty eight, dated 1915, consists of part seventy one alone. War now shapes every society meeting behind the printed page. The Society for Psychical Research still prints its evidence in full. Trance sittings and telepathy reports take their usual careful shape.

Cases touched by the fighting reach the files with the old standards applied. Names, dates, and witnesses stand checked as in peacetime. The society's refusal to lower its bar is the volume's quiet point. It forms one wartime brick in the long archive wall. Later volumes would face the flood of bereaved sitters. Here the record stays spare and firm. Judgment is left, as always, open.
spurzheim-physiognomical-system-1815:
Johann Gaspar Spurzheim helped Franz Joseph Gall frame the science of the skull. His book of 1815 set out their joint scheme in English. It claims the brain holds set organs for set traits of mind. Bumps on the skull, they held, show the size of each organ.

Spurzheim gives charts of the head and lists of traits, from love of kin to a bent for math. He tells how to read a skull by touch and sight. The book launched the craze for head reading in Britain and the States. Crowds paid to hear him speak on the new science.
stendhal-on-love-woolf-1915:
Stendhal tried to explain how love grows in On Love, the treatise the Woolfs translated in 1915. His famous word for the process is crystallization. The mind decks the beloved in perfections, as a bare branch left in a salt mine comes out coated in diamonds. The image anchors his whole theory of love.

Drawing on tales from Italy and his own keen watching, Stendhal sorts love into kinds and traces its birth, doubts, and hopes. The essay made him a founder of the psychology of love in fiction as well as theory. Novel readers still open it to see how the author of great romances thought love works.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Volume 15 of The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine contains The Mandrake and The Rhemese. The Mandrake retells, in English verse, the plot Machiavelli made famous in his comedy of the same name, set in Florence.

The poet shows us a Florentine blockhead, the greatest ever seen below. He has wed a prudent, beautiful, good-humored wife. Every voice sings her praises. She deserved a better husband than Nicia Calfucci. Despairing of a child, Nicia falls for a scheme built on the mandrake root, which promises an heir at a price he is too foolish to reckon. The Rhemese, a tale of Reims, keeps the volume in France for its second piece of trickery.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-15:
Suspicion troubles Pisistratus in Part XV of The Caxtons, the family novel he narrates himself. The son of a bookish father, he watches a friend's character with a young man's heat. Home, as always in this tale, is the measure he returns to.

Nothing in what has happened, the narrator says, would justify the suspicions that torment him, apart from his view of Vivian's character. He recalls how youth in easy company can take a keen interest in a flawed, bright companion. Such interest, he argues, need not dull a young man's dislike of vice. It can sit beside a warm love of what is good and noble.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
Number 15 of volume 1 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated February 18, 1897. It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. William Beverley Harison, the publisher, opens with a letter to the subscribers of Current Events. He has bought that paper's subscription list and goodwill. He offers his own paper in its stead, at $1.25 until the end of 1897. His regular price is two dollars and a half a year.

The lead news concerns the treaty with Great Britain. There is new cause, the paper says, to think it will be defeated in the Senate, or delayed. The trouble concerns the building of the Nicaragua Canal. That canal will cross the narrow neck of Central America. It will join the Atlantic Ocean with the Pacific. Ships will no longer need the long, dangerous voyage around Cape Horn.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
The Ormsby Don Quixote, Cervantes' tale in English, opens Volume 1, Part 15 here. Chapter forty-two treats what further took place in the inn, and several other things worth knowing. The opening closes the captive's long tale.

With the captive's last words, Don Fernando speaks in praise. In truth, captain, he says, the manner of relating the remarkable adventure has been a source of delight to all who heard it. The inn company, gathered around stories within the main tale, now turns back toward its own affairs. Cervantes lets praise for good telling stand as the bridge between tales.
the-lives-of-alchemystical-philosophers-: Only a garbled title page is present here, so the lives themselves do not appear. What can be read names the book as the Lives of Alchemystical Philosophers. Its full title promises a critical catalogue of books in occult chemistry. It also promises a selection of the celebrated treatises on the theory and practice of the Hermetic Art. It was printed in London by Macdonald and Son for Lackington, Allen, and Company of Finsbury Square in 1815. The text around the title page is too scrambled to support any claims.
the-merchant-of-venice-pg1515: William Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice shows only its scene list and cast of characters here, so the play itself does not appear. The scenes alternate between Venice and Belmont, ending in a court of justice in Act Four. The cast names the Duke of Venice, the Princes of Morocco and Arragon as suitors to Portia, Antonio the merchant, and Bassanio his friend. Shylock heads the second household, with Tubal and the clown Launcelet Gobbo also listed.
the-moon-endureth-tales-and-fancies-pg71:
John Buchan's collection The Moon Endureth: Tales and Fancies pairs short tales with poems throughout. Its contents list ten sections. Stories such as The Company of the Marjolaine, A Lucid Interval, The Lemnian, and The Grove of Ashtaroth are each followed by a song or short verse piece. The list openly notes that Chapter 9 is missing from the electronic text.

An opening poem, From the Pentlands Looking North and South, starts the volume. Its speaker stands in a mossy, mist-clad solitude at dawn, clouds drawn around his feet and no breeze or guest troubling the quiet. Sudden movement down the steeps of sky breaks that stillness as the verses begin. A sibling record of the collection shows only a shorter contents list and no poem.
the-principal-navigations-voyages-traffi: Volume VIII of Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, edited by Edmund Goldsmid, covers Asia, Part I. Transcriber's notes record that Hakluyt's spelling is retained, abbreviations expanded, and sidenotes labelled as his own. The set's other records hold volumes on Tartary, the Muscovy Company, and America. What is present for this volume is the preliminary matter and title pages; the first Asian narratives are not included in the leaves at hand.
the-scientific-monthly-october-to-decemb: All that is present here is a Project Gutenberg header. It names The Scientific Monthly, Volume I, October to December 1915. The header also covers The Popular Science Monthly, Volume LXXXVI, July to September 1915. The e-text is numbered 987 and dated July 1997. The rest of the pages shown are the project's standard notices. They cover copyright warnings, donations, and release dates. No article, contents list, or editorial text from the 1915 monthly itself appears. Its contents therefore cannot be described from what is preserved.
tob-0015:
Archbishop William Wake's eighteenth-century translations gather writings the church left outside the New Testament in The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles. Volume one, Mary, contains the Protevangelion of James, an early account of Mary's birth and childhood and of Jesus's infancy. Wake's collection also reaches toward notes and letters associated with figures like Clement and Ignatius across its volumes.

Suppressed is Wake's provocative word; most of these texts were simply never canonized, though churches debated some for centuries. Their stories, including an aged Joseph, Mary's parents Joachim and Anna, and midwives at the nativity, shaped medieval art and devotion deeply. Readers meet the New Testament's cast-offs in stately English.
tob-0115:
Priests and thinkers of late Roman Egypt wrote dialogues in which Hermes Trismegistus, the thrice-great, teaches chosen pupils. Eight of those tractates form this selection of the Corpus Hermeticum. Hermes speaks of God, the making of the cosmos, and the soul's climb back toward light.

The teachings blend Greek philosophy with Egyptian religion, and Renaissance readers took them for wisdom older than Moses. Magicians, theologians, and artists all drank from this spring. Modern scholars place the texts in the first centuries of the common era. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10415:
James Legge's classic English version of the Analects presents twenty books of brief sayings and dialogues preserving Confucius's teaching. Disciples compiled the record after his death from remembered conversations. Short exchanges, sometimes only a sentence or two, carry nearly all of it, often opening with the Master said.

Honor your parents, keep your word, study constantly, and govern by virtue rather than force: these counsels recur in many settings. Rulers, students, and family members all receive instruction fitted to the moment. The Analects became the moral backbone of Chinese civilization for two thousand years, and Legge's translation remains a standard way in for English readers.
tob-10815:
Three Initiates compressed Hermetic wisdom into seven working principles in The Kybalion, first published in 1908. The plain Gutenberg text of that classic is what stands here. Principles include mentalism, summed up as the All is Mind, correspondence in as above, so below, and vibration: everything moves, nothing rests.

Unlike a scripture to be admired, the principles are presented as tools meant to be used on oneself and one's circumstances. Each receives a short chapter with axioms and explanation. Brief enough to read in an evening, the book has been quoted for a century wherever modern Hermetic and New Thought teaching circulates, and argued over just as long.
tob-4015:
Giorgio Vasari, painter, architect, and tireless gossip, effectively invented art history in his Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors and Architects. Volume one begins with Cimabue and Giotto, the pioneers who, in Vasari's story, pulled painting out of the Byzantine dark toward natural life. Anecdote, judgment, and hero-worship fill every life.

Vasari knew workshops, patrons, and surviving works at first hand, though he never let a missing fact spoil a good story. The Renaissance here tells its own story, arranging masters as a rising line toward perfection. Later research corrects him often, yet his framework, progress through great individuals, still shapes how art is taught.
tob-4115:
Reynold A. Nicholson, the great Cambridge scholar of Persian, translated Rumi's Mathnawi with a full commentary. Volume one opens the vast poem Jalal al-Din Rumi composed in thirteenth-century Konya. The song of the reed flute sounds first: cut from its bed, it cries for home, like the soul exiled from God.

Tales of kings, fools, lovers, and parrots carry the teaching from story to story. Nicholson's version, begun in 1925, became the definitive English Mathnawi, praised for accuracy and grace alike. Verified from the 1919 edition record, volume one starts Sufism's supreme poem on its long, winding road.
tob-4214-10715:
Counsels and Maxims gathers Schopenhauer's rules for daily life, in Saunders's crisp English translation. The thinker who called existence a mistake still wanted to help readers suffer less. His counsel is worldly and dry-eyed: guard your privacy, expect little from others, and enjoy solitude.

He advises readers to keep money matters quiet, to bear fools with patience, and to rest happiness only on what lies in their own power. Some maxims sting; many prove wise with age. The short pieces read well in sittings of a few pages. Few self-help books since have matched its candor or its style.
tob-4215:
Rudolf Steiner's Philosophy of Spiritual Activity, also known as The Philosophy of Freedom, appeared in Hoernlé's translation under its alternate English title. Written before Steiner's esoteric period, it argues that free will is real and that thinking itself is a spiritual activity the thinker can observe. Steiner considered this book the foundation of everything he later built.

Knowledge, freedom, and moral individualism are worked out philosophically, without appeal to revelation or clairvoyance. Action is free, he claims, when it flows from ideas the individual has made fully conscious. His most philosophical and most accessible book, it lets readers judge Steiner the thinker separately from Steiner the occult teacher.
un-ga-res-15: Two money panels of the United Nations owe their shape to Resolution 15, passed on 13 February 1946. Rule changes fix the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions at nine members, with at least two finance experts of known standing. A second panel, the Committee on Contributions, gets ten members. The same rules set out how the first panels would draw lots for one, two, and three year terms.
un-ga-res-a-69-15:
Small island states won a plan of their own at a world meet in Samoa, and Resolution A/69/15 adopts its text. The third world meeting on Small Island Developing States sat at Apia from 1 to 4 September 2014, at the highest level. The Assembly thanks the state and people of Samoa for hosting the meet and for all their support of it.

The outcome text bears a long name: the SIDS Accelerated Modalities of Action, or SAMOA Pathway. It is annexed to the vote in full. Heads of state and chiefs at Apia restated their pledge to the lasting growth of small island lands. Such lands face sharp risks, from rising seas to far markets, and the plan sets swift paths for aid and joint work.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 15, adopted on 13 February 1946, amended the Assembly's provisional rules of procedure to fix the makeup of two budget bodies. The Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions was set at nine members, at least two of them noted finance experts, and the Committee on Contributions at ten. Added rules set staggered first terms, so part of each body would be chosen for three years and part for two.

General Assembly resolution 69/15 was adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014. It endorses the outcome of the third International Conference on Small Island Developing States. The conference was held in Apia, Samoa, from 1 to 4 September 2014. The resolution itself is short; its substance is the long annexed document it adopts.

That annex, the SIDS Accelerated Modalities of Action (SAMOA) Pathway, sets out how small island states and their partners should pursue sustainable development. It takes account of the islands' special vulnerability to sea-level rise and climate change. It reaffirms the earlier Barbados Programme of Action and Mauritius Strategy. It calls for genuine, durable partnerships across economic growth, oceans, and food security. It also calls for them across water, energy, and disaster risk. Endorsement by the Assembly turned a conference outcome into the United Nations framework for island development for the following decade.
un-sc-res-1315:
Sierra Leone's war crimes were set on the road to a court on 14 August 2000. The Council voiced deep concern at the very serious crimes committed against Sierra Leone's people and at United Nations staff. Impunity reigned in the country. The Lomé amnesty, the Council recalled, could not cover genocide, crimes against humanity, or war crimes. Sierra Leone's president had written on 12 June asking for help.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to negotiate an agreement with Sierra Leone's government to create an independent special court. He was to recommend its reach. The court should cover crimes against humanity, war crimes, and other grave breaches of humanitarian law, plus set crimes under Sierra Leonean law. It should be able to try those who bear the greatest responsibility. The court's fairness and independence had to be secured, and a report on the plan was due to the Council.
un-sc-res-1415:
The Golan Heights observer force came up for renewal in May 2002. On 30 May 2002 the Security Council renewed UNDOF for seven months. The new term ran until 31 December 2002. The Secretary-General had reported on the force two weeks earlier. The Council also restated its rule on protecting peacekeepers from disease. Little else in the text changes the mission's shape.

As usual, the parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. That 1973 text demanded a ceasefire and a move toward peace. The Secretary-General owed a report at the end of the term. UNDOF's soldiers kept their posts between Israeli and Syrian lines. The routine renewal masked a border that stayed tense beneath the calm.
un-sc-res-15:
Claims of border raids in the north of Greece led the Security Council to send its own team to look, under Resolution 15, passed on 19 December 1946. Greece, Yugoslavia, Albania, and Bulgaria had each laid claims and charges before the Council. The charges dealt with a state of unrest along the Greek border with the three states to its north. In the Council's view, the facts must be found before any firm word can be given.

A Commission of Investigation is set up under Article 34 of the Charter. One member from each state on the Council, as it will stand in 1947, forms the team. It must reach the ground by 15 January 1947 and report back at the soonest date. The probe was the young Council's first field test of its peace powers.
un-sc-res-1515:
A step-by-step plan toward two states in the Middle East won the Council's backing on 19 November 2003. The plan was called the Road Map. It had been drawn up by the Quartet, a group of four: the United Nations, the United States, the European Union, and Russia. Tragic and violent events in the region were still going on. Resolution 1515 was adopted unanimously.

The Council endorsed the Quartet's performance-based Road Map to a permanent two-state solution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The parties were called on to meet their obligations under the plan. They had to work with the Quartet to reach its goal. The Council restated its vision of the region. Two states, Israel and Palestine, would live side by side within secure and recognized borders. It also repeated its demand for an immediate end to all acts of violence, including terrorism, provocation, incitement, and destruction.
un-sc-res-1615:
Georgia and Abkhazia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1615, adopted on 29 July 2005. The Abkhaz side still refused to discuss the paper on sharing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi. Talks on Abkhazia's status had not even begun. Whoever shot down a United Nations helicopter in 2001, killing nine, was still unknown.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 31 January 2006. It urges the Abkhaz side to take up the powers paper at last. Both sides must drop warlike talk and restart the peace work in earnest. A letter of intent on refugee returns should be signed fast. The remaining police officers for the Gali sector must be let in.
un-sc-res-1815: Security Council Resolution 1815 is held here as a transcription of the official record, sourced from English Wikisource. Its paragraphs demonstrate the Council's way of turning politics into text: agree on a description of events, then agree on what follows from it. The entry preserves that agreed text whole, exactly as the members left it.
un-sc-res-1915: Resolution 1915 is a Security Council act preserved here in its official-record wording, sourced from English Wikisource. The text's life in the record is permanent, unlike the meeting that produced it. Readers get the permanent part complete: the situation as the fifteen members stated it and the decision they collectively imposed on it.
un-sc-res-2015:
Piracy trials are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2015, adopted on 24 October 2011. Navies caught many Somali pirate suspects but few faced trial anywhere. A United Nations report had set out how special anti-piracy courts might work in Somalia and nearby states. Kenya and the Seychelles were already trying suspects with outside help.

The Council decides to keep studying the plan for specialized courts backed by international support. The Secretary-General must consult Somalia and regional states, with the United Nations drugs and development agencies. He should report what help the courts need, how suspects and proof would be transferred, and what the courts would cost. The text also stresses that Somalia itself bears the main duty to end piracy.
un-sc-res-215: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 215, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 1965. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-315: The decision entered as Resolution 315 forms part of the Council record catalogued for 1964. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-415: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 415 is catalogued here under 1977. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Morocco regained independence from France in March 1956. The kingdom moved fast to claim its place among states. Its UN application reached the Council that summer. Resolution 115 was adopted unanimously on 20 June 1956 at the 731st meeting.

Members recommended that the General Assembly admit Morocco. The Assembly did so that November, in a landmark admissions round. Many new states entered the UN the same season. For Morocco, the seat crowned its return to sovereignty. It also began the kingdom's long UN involvement with the Western Sahara question. That file would return to the Council again and again in later decades.

Crimes in Sierra Leone's war demand a court, and Resolution 1315, adopted on 14 August 2000, starts building one. The Council voiced deep alarm at grave crimes against Sierra Leoneans and UN staff, and at the impunity that prevailed. Sierra Leone's government and West African leaders were both working to end the war for good.

The Council asked the UN chief to work out a pact with Sierra Leone for a stand-alone special court. Its job would be to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for crimes against humanity, war crimes, and other grave breaches of the laws of war on Sierra Leonean territory since 1996. Negotiations produced the Special Court for Sierra Leone.

A seven-month term, not six, marks this Golan renewal of 2002. On 30 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1415 without dissent. The Secretary-General's May report on the observer force lay before it. That force, UNDOF, had watched the Israel-Syria split zone since 1974.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order pairs a truce with peace talks. The mandate then runs seven months, to 31 December 2002. The extra month lined the renewal cycle up with the calendar year. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. It must cover events and steps taken toward Resolution 338.

Greece and its northern neighbours had traded charges over disturbed conditions and border violations in northern Greece, and on 19 December 1946 the Council decided the facts had to come first. Albania, Bulgaria, and Yugoslavia were the neighbours named. Before drawing conclusions, the Council wanted evidence gathered on the ground.

Acting under Article 34 of the Charter, it set up a Commission of Investigation with one member from each Council state as constituted in 1947. The commission was to reach the area by 15 January 1947 and report its findings as soon as possible. It could work across northern Greece and other relevant places, call on officials and citizens for information, and send early reports if needed.

Resolution 1515 is a UN Security Council endorsement of the Middle East Roadmap, adopted unanimously on 19 November 2003, amid continuing Israeli-Palestinian violence. It recalls the Council's core texts, including Resolutions 242, 338, and 1397, and repeats the demand for an immediate end to violence, terror, and incitement.

The resolution endorses the Quartet's phased Roadmap, drawn up by the United States, Russia, the European Union, and the United Nations to end in two states living side by side. It calls on both parties to fulfill their Roadmap obligations in cooperation with the Quartet. By adopting the plan itself, the Council gave the Roadmap the standing of a UN-endorsed framework.

Georgia's observer mission is extended amid a stalled peace process in Resolution 1615, adopted on 29 July 2005. The Abkhaz side still refused to discuss the 'Basic Principles' paper on dividing competences between Tbilisi and Sukhumi. A security-guarantees meeting had been cancelled. The 2001 shooting down of a UNOMIG helicopter, which killed nine people, remained unsolved. Geneva meetings of the Group of Friends had kept momentum.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, to 31 January 2006. It insists Abkhazia's status must be settled within the Georgian state. It urges the Abkhaz side to accept the principles paper and negotiate. It demands progress on refugee and displaced-person returns, which it calls a special responsibility of the Abkhaz side. It presses for the UNOMIG civilian police to deploy fully in the Gali sector and for those behind the helicopter attack to be identified and brought to justice.

The race to lead the UN ended behind closed doors in 2006. Kofi Annan's two terms were nearly done. The Council met in private on 9 October 2006 to pick its choice. Resolution 1715 came out of that closed 5547th meeting. No vote count was made public in the text.

The members put one name to the General Assembly: Ban Ki-moon. He was South Korea's foreign minister. His term would run from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2011. The Assembly backed the choice days later. Ban became the eighth person to hold the post. He led the UN through the Haiti quake and the Arab Spring's first years. This one-line text set that decade in motion.

The Beirut bombing investigation commission is extended until 31 December 2008 on 2 June 2008. Its March report described steady progress in the inquiry into the February 2005 attack and other attacks in Lebanon since October 2004. Its head had asked for more time to keep the investigation stable and continuous.

The commission's outstanding professional work in hard conditions is praised, and the extension is granted. The commission is to keep helping the Lebanese authorities and report on progress as asked. The step also bridged toward the start of the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, which the Council had decided in 2007 to establish to try those accused in the case.

One large trial at the war crimes court for the former Yugoslavia ran into delays in early 2010. Resolution 1915, adopted on 18 March 2010, makes a narrow change to help that trial finish. An earlier decision had let two temporary judges stay past the end of their terms. They were finishing the Popović case, and judgment had been expected by the end of March.

Unforeseen problems pushed the judgment back. The Council therefore extended the same arrangement for a few more months. The court could keep up to thirteen temporary judges at once, one above its normal maximum. The arrangement would end on 30 June 2010, or when the Popović case ended, whichever came first. Nothing else about the court changed. One case simply needed more time to reach its judgment.

Prosecuting Somali pirates is the focus of Resolution 2015, adopted on 24 October 2011. Many captured suspects were still being released without trial. Hostage-taking continued in inhuman conditions. A Secretary-General's report had set out how specialized anti-piracy courts could work. It said courts in Somaliland and Puntland might reach international standards in about three years given enough help.

The Council demands a complete set of Somali counter-piracy laws, covering financiers and organizers as well as attackers, with a report from the Somali authorities by 31 December 2011. It urges all states to criminalize piracy at home and to report their measures by the same date. It decides to keep considering, urgently, specialized anti-piracy courts in Somalia and the region with substantial international support. Their reach must extend to the criminal networks' key figures. It asks for detailed implementation proposals within 90 days.

Two months after its first cease-fire demands in the India-Pakistan war, the Council spoke again on 5 November 1965. Resolution 215 regrets the delay in reaching a full cease-fire. Troops had still not pulled back to the lines held before 5 August 1965.

The Council reaffirmed Resolution 211 in all its parts. India and Pakistan were told to order their forces to cooperate with the United Nations and stop all military activity. The two governments had to work out an agreed plan with an envoy of the Secretary-General. Their representatives would meet the envoy to set a timetable for the withdrawals. A progress report was due within three weeks.

Half a year more for the Cyprus peacekeeping force was granted on 15 June 1972, as had happened many times before. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 6 May, found the force still needed to preserve peace. The government of Cyprus agreed it should continue beyond 15 June. Resolution 315 records that decision.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint. They were also told to speed up their joint efforts toward the Council's goals. The calmer climate on the island was to be used in a constructive way. The extension runs to 15 December 1972.
